units.tr: TO THE REVEREND, MOST NOBLE AND MOST DISTINGUISHED MAN, LORD FRANCISCUS MARESCALLUS, most honoured Dean of the Reverend Chapter of Bremen, and most worthy Provost at the Gate of Heaven, his Lord and much honoured Patron, wishes salvation from the Lord Jesus.

units.la: DVPLEX hominum de Philosophia male sentientium genus, Reuerende, nobilissime, ac spectatissime Domine Decane, Patrone plurimum honorande, Reipublicæ Christianæ insigniter pernitiosum esse opinor. Primum genus dico eorum, qui propter pauca, quæ in libris paganorum Philosophorum, a decretis & sanctitate nostræ religionis abludere, & aliena aquilinis cernunt oculis, non modo cetera quam plurima vere & utiliter ab illis tradita reiiciunt, sed omnem etiam cuiusuis Philosophiae Christianam cognitionem rodunt, calumniantur, ac tanquam certam animorum pestem, ex hominum, praesertim Christianorum, societate exterminandam iudicant, clamant. Videlicet isti Philosophiae rudes, omnisq; liberalis doctrinae experies, omnes sui similes esse cuperent, quominus in multitudine ipsorum appareret inscitia. Ac olim quidem Julianus, quo tectior & callidior, eo acrior & pernitiosior Christianorum hostis, vi nulla putauit magis se Christianis obesse, eorumq; religionem vehementius labefactare posse, quam si eis omnium bonarum artium studiis interdixisset. Huc quoque spectat quorundam Sectariorum nostri temporis artificiosa calliditas, ad rauim usq;, Philosophiam, reconditioresq; disciplinas, Christianis repudiandas & exsecrandas esse clamantium, quo nimirum facilius homines indocti ac simplices, argumentis quibusdam ipsorum, in speciem modo probabilibus, captiosisq; conclusiunculis circumuenti atq; irretiti in eorum pertrahantur errores, hi profecto suis vociferationib. id videntur postulare (ς κλαν μέγα αἴτημα est) ut homines sint animalia bruta, quib. ipsi, tanquam vulpes anseribus, impune quiduis concionari possint. In hoc etiam, meo iudicio, similiter facere cere isti Philosophiae hostes videntur, ut fecisse quo-dam Philistaeos, Sacrae prodiderūt literae, qui omnes fabros ferrarios, armorumq; artifices Hebraeis abstulerunt, ut inermes, nec bellū vltro illis auderent inferre nec illatum ab illis facile propulsarent.
units.tr: There are two kinds of men who think ill of philosophy, Reverend, most noble and distinguished Lord Dean, my most honoured Patron, and I judge both to be remarkably harmful to the Christian commonwealth. I mean first the sort who, because of a few things in the books of the pagan philosophers that they see with eagle eyes as differing from the decrees and holiness of our religion, and as foreign to it, not only reject the many other things those writers taught truly and usefully, but also disparage, slander and cry out that all Christian knowledge of any kind of philosophy must be cut off, and judge that it must be banished from human society, especially Christian society, as a certain plague on souls. Clearly these men, untrained in philosophy and without experience of any liberal learning, would wish everyone to be like themselves, so that their own ignorance would not be so conspicuous in a crowd. Indeed Julian of old, the more cunning and sly, and therefore the more bitter and dangerous enemy of the Christians, thought he could harm them by no force more than by forbidding them the study of all the good arts, and that in this way he could shake their religion more violently. To this also tends the artful cunning of certain sectarians of our own time, who shout till they are hoarse that philosophy and the more recondite disciplines must be rejected and cursed by Christians, obviously so that simple and unlearned people may more easily be led into their errors, caught and ensnared by certain arguments of theirs, plausible only in appearance, and by captious little syllogisms. Surely by their clamour these men seem to demand (as they say, a great request [ς κλαν μέγα αἴτημα]) that men be brute beasts, among whom they, like foxes among geese, may preach whatever they like with impunity. In this, in my judgement, these enemies of philosophy seem to act like the Philistines, of whom the sacred letters tell, who took away all the smiths and makers of arms from the Hebrews, so that they were unarmed and dared neither to make war on them nor easily to repel an attack from them. Certainly these enemies of philosophy seem to do the same thing in this respect.

units.la: Sed aiunt illi, errasse Philosophos Ethnicos: errarunt sane, sed sunt illi quidem errores Philosophorum, non Philosophiae: hominum, non artium: carpant, tollant illos: hanc & has nobis, quaeso, relinquant, sibi reseruent. Istos errores Philosophorum, qui norunt Orthodoxam Philosophiam, videre & refellere poterunt, qui non norunt, non poterunt. Non eget fides nostra Philosophiae fundamentis & praesidiis, non ea tamen reiicit. Domina famulae sape vtitur ministerio. Non desiderat religio nostra humanae sapientiae ornamenta: ea tamen prorsus non aspernatur: sua vituta & munita est, suaq; luce splendet, sed quae docere & hominibus persuadere studet, ea sit rationibus, exemplis, & similitudinibus e Philosophia vera petitis, quasi aspersa & condita sunt, iucundius audiuntur, facilius intelliguntur, promtius creduntur, constantius retinentur. Aduersus hoc hominū genus, qui quicquid bene arant vitula Philosophiae arant, & eam tamen, tanquam rem Deo inuisam, diuinis literis contrariam, & noxiam iis, qui Christianam doctrinam profitentur, conuitiis proscindere publicis non erubescunt, Commentarius hic meus potissimum disputat, ut veritas Philosophiae Orthodoxae asserta suam adversus hos harmostas ingratos tueatur innocentiam.
units.tr: But those men say that the pagan philosophers erred. They did err indeed, but those errors belong to the philosophers, not to philosophy; to men, not to the arts. Let them attack and remove those errors; but let them leave us philosophy and its branches, I beg, and keep them for themselves. Those who know Orthodox philosophy will be able to see and refute the errors of the philosophers; those who do not know it will not be able. Our faith does not need the foundations and props of philosophy, yet it does not reject them. The mistress often makes use of the service of her maidservant. Our religion does not require the ornaments of human wisdom, yet it by no means despises them: it is defended and fortified by its own power and shines with its own light; but when it seeks to teach and persuade men, it is heard more pleasantly, understood more easily, believed more readily and retained more firmly if its teaching is, as it were, sprinkled and seasoned with arguments, examples and comparisons drawn from true philosophy. Against this kind of men, who whatever they plough well they plough with philosophy's calf, and yet, as though it were a thing hateful to God, contrary to the divine letters and harmful to those who profess Christian doctrine, are not ashamed to tear it apart with public insults, this commentary of mine argues chiefly, so that the truth of orthodox philosophy, once asserted, may defend its innocence against these ungrateful sharp-tongued critics.

units.la: Alterum genus est eorum, qui divina, ut vocat, Platonis & Aristotelis ingenia, uberrimamq; cunctarum rerum scientiam cum excellenti eloquentia coniunctam, usque eo admirantur & amplexantur, ut eos velut numina & Deos a lapsibus immunes Philosophiae, tanquam Anthropolatrae & Prosopolatrae adorent, eorumque decreta Philosophica, tanta animi assensione complectantur, vix ut credant, quicquid esse posse probabile, quod improbetur ab illis, aut quod ab illis probetur, improbabile.
units.tr: The second kind is of those who admire and embrace so greatly the so-called divine minds of Plato and Aristotle, and their vast knowledge of all things joined with excellent eloquence, that they worship them as gods and divinities free from the lapses of philosophy, like Anthropolaters and Prosopolaters; and they receive their philosophical decrees with such assent of mind that they can hardly believe anything to be probable which those men disapprove, or improbable which they approve.

units.la: O miseras hominum mentes, o pectora caeca.
units.tr: O wretched minds of men, O blind hearts.

units.la: Quid enim vilius & abiectius, aut quae maior animi caecitas esse potest, quam nihil per se sapere, nihil iudicare, totum ex alieno sensu iudicio pendere? Nulla ducì ratione, sed quasi pecudes aliorum sententia nutuque tantum moveri ac regi?
units.tr: For what is more base and abject, or what greater blindness of mind can there be, than to know nothing by oneself, to judge nothing, and to hang all one's judgement on another's opinion? To be moved and ruled by the opinion and nod of others alone, like cattle, without any reason?

units.la: Ab hoc etiam servili hominum genere nos segregamus: verum eorum conatus infringere studemus hoc libello in primis, qui maledicentiae suae virus in veram, nunquam a se intellectam, Philosophiam hodie euomunt, ut contemtum optima Philosophiae in Christianorum orbem inducant, quo fefenestra aperiatur omnibus haereticis, & hi semina errorum suorum sine contradictione impune disseminare possint.
units.tr: We separate ourselves from this slavish kind of men too; but we strive above all in this little book to break the efforts of those who in our day vomit the poison of their slander against a true philosophy which they have never understood, in order to bring contempt for the best philosophy into the Christian world, so that a window may be opened for all heretics and they may be able to scatter the seeds of their errors unopposed and with impunity.

units.la: Tenuis autem haec mea commentatio gloriam innocentis Philosophiae spirans, Te reuerendum, nobilissimum & spectatissimum virum, adoptat patronum, qui magnis me Tibi devinctum habes beneficiis: elapsis quippe annis duobus bis singulare in me collocasti beneficium, quo rem meam familiarem liberaliter auctam, benefice inuisti. Anno igitur hoc tertio a me Tibi grati animi Symbolon debetur, quod cum non habeam in censu meo literario aliud, hoc quod publice pono, eaque qua par est, observantia, offero impense oro, ut boni facias.
units.tr: This slight commentary of mine, breathing the glory of an innocent philosophy, takes you, Reverend, most noble and distinguished man, as its patron, since you have bound me to yourself by great kindnesses. For in the two years that have passed you have twice conferred an unusual favour on me, by which you generously increased my estate and helped me greatly. In this third year, then, I owe you a token of grateful mind; and since I have nothing else in my literary stock, I offer you this which I publish, with the respect that is due, and I earnestly beg you to accept it kindly.

units.la: Indignum hoc diffiteor nominis tui inscriptione, indignum umbra virtutis, sapientiae, auctoritatis & honoris tui, si statum, stylum, ingenium, artem auctoris poderes, quae omnia sunt perexigua. Philosophum sane non decet multis perorare, aliter hic de genere, de familia, de fortuna, de loco in Capitulo, de gratia qua vales apud Principe, de amore populi, de singulari auctoritate multa dicerem, quae omnia suam merentur laurum, & laudem, nec non instar adamantis vim attrahendi me scriptore habent, ut te prae aliis Patronum fore huius commentationis ex animo peroptem. Sed vehementius mouet me insignes animi tui virtutes, rerum & scientia &
units.tr: I admit that this is unworthy of the inscription of your name, unworthy of the shadow of your virtue, wisdom, authority and honour, if you weigh the author's rank, style, talent and craft, all of which are very slight. Indeed it is not fitting for a philosopher to speak at length; otherwise I would say much here about your family, your birth, your fortune, your place in the Chapter, the favour you enjoy with the Prince, your love among the people, and your singular authority, all of which deserve their own laurel and praise, and which, like a magnet, have a power to draw me as author, so that I earnestly wish you above others to be patron of this commentary. But the outstanding virtues of your mind move me more strongly: your knowledge of things and learning, § 4 your devout prudence, in which especially your inner and outer honour lives; to which I add the burning love you have for letters and learned men, which my own experience also confirms.

units.la: § 4 prudētia pia, in quib. præcipue internus & extern honor viuit, quib. addo flagrātem amorem erga literas & literatos, mea etiā experientia comprobatum. Quod si igitur non respuas, animi grati mei, quod offero, qualecunq; ἀγαλμάτιον, sed ea manu capias, qua mente offertur, spero Te officiosi animi observantiam sensurum. Vale, Dominus Iesus Te Tuag omnia, quam diutissime & quam benignissime, salua & incolumia conseruet & tueatur, Stadæ dabam anno 1600. Mense Augusti.
units.tr: If therefore you do not reject what I offer, this little gift of my grateful mind, whatever it is [ἀγαλμάτιον], but take it with the hand in which it is offered with a mind of goodwill, I hope you will feel the observance of a dutiful spirit. Farewell. May the Lord Jesus preserve and protect you and all yours, as long and as graciously as possible, safe and sound. Given at Stade, in the year 1600, in the month of August.

units.la: De contrariis vitiis vanæ Philosophiæ Pseudo Aristotelicæ.
units.tr: On the contrary vices of vain Pseudo-Aristotelian Philosophy.

units.la: Primum.
units.tr: First.

units.la: Philosophia ne sit impia.
units.tr: Let philosophy not be impious.

units.la: Secundum.
units.tr: Second.

units.la: Philosophia ne sit iniusta & iniqua in proximū.
units.tr: Let philosophy not be unjust and unfair towards one's neighbour.

units.la: Tertium.
units.tr: Third.

units.la: Philosophia ne sit falsa, nec hominum nitatur traditionibus.
units.tr: Let philosophy not be false, nor rest on the traditions of men.

units.la: Quartum.
units.tr: Fourth.

units.la: Philosophia ne sit Sophistica & fuco tincta.
units.tr: Let philosophy not be sophistical and tinged with deceit.

units.la: Quintum.
units.tr: Fifth.

units.la: Philosophia ne sit serua.
units.tr: Let philosophy not be a slave.

units.la: Sextum.
units.tr: Sixth.

units.la: Philosophia ne sit inutilis & futilis.
units.tr: Let philosophy not be useless and trifling.

units.la: Septimum.
units.tr: Seventh.

units.la: Philosophia ne sit immodesta ac inflata.
units.tr: Let philosophy not be immodest and puffed up.

units.la: Octauum.
units.tr: Eighth.

units.la: Philosophia ne sit perturbata & promiscue confusa.
units.tr: Let philosophy not be disordered and indiscriminately confused.

units.la: Nonum.
units.tr: Ninth.

units.la: Philosophia ne sit obscura & difficilis.
units.tr: Let philosophy not be obscure and difficult.

units.la: Decimum.
units.tr: Tenth.

units.la: Philosophia ne sit vasta nimis & prolixa, validum, fallaciam & deformitatem pariens.
units.tr: Let philosophy not be excessively vast and prolix, strong-willed, producing fallacy and deformity.

units.la: Undecimum.
units.tr: Eleventh.

units.la: Philosophia ne sit indoctis ac ignaua, ne sit admomonitionis studiosæ impatiens.
units.tr: Let philosophy not be contemptuous of the untaught and idle, nor impatient of admonition offered in a spirit of earnest study.

units.la: Duodecimum,
units.tr: Twelfth.

units.tr: Finally, let philosophy not be hypocritical, pretending and dissembling, nor in the meantime be seditious, tumultuous, or a bloody persecutor.

units.la: III. Ex Epist. ad Rom. 1. vers. 21. & 22.
units.tr: III. From Romans 1:21 and 22.

units.la: IV. Ex dictis scriptura, hominis naturalis & animalis caecitatem ac impotentiam in spiritualibus asserentibus.
units.tr: IV. From the words of Scripture asserting the blindness and incapacity of the natural and animal man in spiritual matters.

units.la: V. Ex Eccles. c. 1. Sextum ab exemplo Patrum.
units.tr: V. From Ecclesiastes chapter 1. Sixth, from the example of the Fathers.

units.la: Humana repelluntur sophismata humanæ auctoritatis aduersus Philosophiam. Et quidem.
units.tr: Human authority refutes the sophisms drawn from human authority against philosophy. And indeed:

units.la: I. Ab exemplo Patrum, a Philosophia in errores abductorum.
units.tr: I. From the example of the Fathers, who were led into errors by philosophy.

units.la: II. Ab auctoritate Patrum Ecclesiasticorum, Philosophiam improbantium & damnantium. Ratione sophismata aduersus Christianam Philosophiam sequentibus modis repelluntur.
units.tr: II. From the authority of the ecclesiastical Fathers, who disapproved and condemned philosophy. Sophisms against Christian philosophy are refuted by the following methods, drawn from reason.

units.la: I. A qualitate causarum efficientium Philosophiam humanam ad qualitatem Philosophiæ concludendam.
units.tr: I. From the quality of the efficient causes, concluding the quality of human philosophy from them.

units.la: II. A variis dissensionum & opinionum monstrosarum sectis.
units.tr: II. From the various dissensions and the monstrous opinions of the sects.

units.la: III. Ab utilitate & fine.
units.tr: III. From its usefulness and end.

units.la: IV. Ab erroribus religionis Christianæ veritati contrariis.
units.tr: IV. From the errors of the Christian religion, which are contrary to the truth.

units.la: V. Ab exemplo Apostolorum, Philosophia non imbutorum.
units.tr: V. From the example of the Apostles, who were not steeped in philosophy.

units.la: VI. A Logica damnum religioni inferente.
units.tr: VI. From logic, which brings harm to religion.

units.la: Vbi Quæstio.
units.tr: Here the question is:

units.la: An Logica Theologo sit utilis & necessaria? Affirmatur.
units.tr: Is logic useful and necessary for the theologian? It is affirmed.

units.la: Vltimo.
units.tr: Lastly.

units.la: Ab incertitudine Philosophiæ.
units.tr: From the uncertainty of philosophy.

units.la: PHILOSOPHIAE CHRISTIANÆ OTHONIS CASMANNI Pars Prior,
units.tr: Othonis Casmanni Philosophiae Christianae, Pars Prior,

units.la: VERAM ET CHRISTIA-NAM PHILOSOPHIAM AS-serens & demonstrans. CAPVT I.
units.tr: Asserting and demonstrating the true and Christian philosophy. CHAPTER I.

units.la: De Christianæ Philosophiæ definitione, vbi de Sapientia.
units.tr: On the definition of Christian philosophy, where wisdom is discussed.

units.la: DE Philosophia Christiana, ad-uersus omnis Philosophiæ ini-quos censores & calumniato-res, disceptaturis, primum quid sit ea Philosophia, quæq; eius propria <bl>ἓσία</bl>, cognoscendum est.
units.tr: Before we debate with all the unfair critics and slanderers of philosophy, we must first understand what this philosophy is and what is its proper essence [οὐσία].

units.la: Melius autem hæc non poterit cog-nosci & dignosci, quam si eius defini-tio proponatur & excutiatur. Defini-tio tio enim est amplissimum principium scientiæ. Picol. lib. de Mundo, cap. 2. Et anchorarum omnium firmissima. Scal. Exerc. 301. Sect. 1. Imo τᾶσυ ἐπιστήμαι δὶ ἐσομένων γίνονται. Aristot. 2. post. cap. 14. Proinde recte M. Tullius: Omnis quæ à ratione suscipitur de aliqua re institutio, debet à definitione proficisci, ut intelligatur quid sit id, de quo disputetur.
units.tr: This can best be known and distinguished by setting out its definition and examining it. For a definition is the very first principle of a science, and the firmest of all anchors (Scaliger, Exercises 301, sect. 1). Indeed, the sciences of things arise through definitions (Aristotle, Posterior Analytics 2, ch. 14). So Marcus Tullius rightly says: "Every line of reasoning undertaken about any subject ought to begin from a definition, so that it is understood what the thing is that is being disputed."

units.la: Definitio autem nobis erit hoc loco duplex, ὀνοματώδης, & πραγματώδης seu χσιώδης.
units.tr: Here our definition will be twofold: nominal [ὀνοματώδης] and real [πραγματώδης], or essential [οὐσιώδης].

units.la: Ονομαλώδης est nominis explicatio, qua Philosophia definitur studium seu amor sapientiæ. Vnde Philosophus dicitur studiosus, seu amans sapientiæ.
units.tr: The nominal definition is an explanation of the name. In this sense philosophy is defined as the study or love of wisdom, and so the philosopher is called a student or lover of wisdom.

units.la: Hinc Philosophia Christiana est studium Christianæ sapientiæ: ut Ethnica, mundana, carnalis est studium, & amor Ethnicæ, mundanę, carnalis sapientiæ. Illa veræ, hæc aberrantis sæpenumero est sapientiæ. At aberrans sapientia, potius est stultitiæ non absimilis.
units.tr: Hence Christian philosophy is the study of Christian wisdom, just as pagan, worldly and carnal philosophy is the study and love of pagan, worldly and carnal wisdom. The former pursues true wisdom, the latter a wisdom that very often goes astray; and a wisdom that goes astray is hardly different from folly.

units.la: 1. Apodeixis ex nominis Notatione.
units.tr: 1. Proof from the notion of the name.

units.la: Qui debent esse studiosi sapientiæ, debent etiam esse studiosi Philosophiæ: valet ex vi nominis.
units.tr: Those who ought to be students of wisdom ought also to be students of philosophy. This follows from the force of the name.

units.la: Atqui veri Dei cultores debent esse studiosi sapientiæ. Omnibus enim commendatur sapientiæ. tia, qua sapiant. Salomon.Prouerb.cap.8. inquit Sapientia: Ad vos homines clamo, humanum genus appello: Discite imperiti sapientiam. Item, Ego amatores meos amo, meque qui diligenter quaerunt, inueniunt. Item, Audite disciplinam & sapiente, neve negligentes estis. Beatus homo, qui me audit, excubans ad meas fores quotidie, observando ostiorum meorum postes. Nam qui me inuenit, vitam inuenit, & obtinet a Iehoua fauorem.
units.tr: But those who worship the true God ought to be students of wisdom, for wisdom is commended to all, that they may become wise. Solomon, in Proverbs 8, has Wisdom say: "I call out to you, men; I address the human race: learn wisdom, you untrained ones." Likewise: "I love those who love me, and those who seek me diligently find me." Likewise: "Hear instruction and be wise, and do not be negligent. Blessed is the man who hears me, watching daily at my gates and waiting at the posts of my doors. For whoever finds me finds life, and obtains favour from the LORD."

units.la: At loquitur Sapiens de vera sapientia: Neq; ego de vana & falsa. Ergo non de Philosophia Ethnicorum. Ethnicorum si quae falsa sunt, philosophica non sunt. Non Philosophiae est, quod est Ethnici, vt Ethnici, vt nec Theologiae datur, quod hominis est male feriati, calumniatoris & impii. Ethnici quaesiuerūt sapientiam, at non inuenerunt in omnibus: Imo in ratiocinationibus suis, scilicet sophisticis, stulti facti sunt. Sed hac de re in parte secunda.
units.tr: But the Wise Man speaks of true wisdom, not of vain and false wisdom. Therefore he is not speaking of the philosophy of the pagans. Whatever is false among the pagans is not philosophical. What belongs to pagans as pagans is not philosophy, just as what belongs to a man who is idle, a slanderer and impious is not theology. The pagans sought wisdom, but did not find it in all things; indeed, in their own reasonings, namely the sophistical ones, they became fools. But I shall deal with this matter in the second part.

units.la: Veri igitur Dei cultores debent esse Philosophiae amatores & studiosi, eius, inquam, quae Christiana est & ab erroribus est repurgata.
units.tr: Therefore the true worshippers of God ought to be lovers and students of philosophy, namely of that philosophy which is Christian and has been purged of errors.

units.la: Definitio sequitur πραγματώδης, rei scilicet explicatio, quae à quibusdam exacte constitui posse negatur, vt à Picolom. de Introductione in scient. de natura. à variis autem si nō perfecte, saltem imperfecte definitur.
units.tr: The definition follows the real [πραγματώδης] mode, that is, an explanation of the thing itself. Some deny that this can be defined exactly, as Piccolomini does in his work on the introduction to the sciences of nature; but it is defined, if not perfectly, at least imperfectly, by various writers.

units.la: Plato alicubi vocat meditationem seu commentationē mortis: solutionem animi à corpore: conuersionem nem animi ad ea, quæ vera sunt & diuina. E Stoicis nonnulli, diuinarum & humanarum rerum scientiam (quidam addunt, qua hic fas) nonnulli, meditationem artis ad vitam accommodatæ. Aristoteles in Metaphysicis dicit, Esse scientiam contemplatricem veritatis. Plato item alicubi vocat multarum rerum scientiam, in dial. de Phil. Alibi acquisitionem scientiæ, in Euthyd. Plerunque autem eam ad Moralem restringit. Max. Tyr. Serm. 16. Philosophia est diuinarum & humanarum exacta scientia, quæ vel virtutes vel ratiocinationes pulcras conuenientissimæ vitæ ac studiorum commodorum dispenset. Speusi. de Plat. def. Philosophia est appetitus sapientiæ, contemplatio veritatis, ut veritas est. Ammon in Porph. Philosophia est rerum, qua res sunt, cognitio. Idem. Est rerum diuinarum, humanarumque, & causarum, quibus continentur, cognitio. Idem. Philosophia est similitudo Dei, quoad natura humana patitur.
units.tr: Plato somewhere calls philosophy "the meditation or practice of death, the release of the soul from the body, the turning of the soul to those things that are true and divine." Some of the Stoics call it "the knowledge of divine and human things" (some add "insofar as it is lawful here"), and others "the meditation on an art adapted to life." Aristotle in the Metaphysics says it is "the contemplative science of truth." Plato also somewhere calls it "the knowledge of many things" (in the dialogue on philosophy), and elsewhere "the acquisition of knowledge" (in the Euthydemus), though for the most part he restricts it to morals. Maximus of Tyre, Sermon 16: "Philosophy is the exact science of divine and human things, which dispenses either virtues or fine reasonings most suited to the life and the advantages of study." Speusippus, in his definitions from Plato: "Philosophy is the desire for wisdom, the contemplation of truth as truth is." Ammonius, on Porphyry: "Philosophy is the knowledge of things as they are." The same: "It is the knowledge of divine and human things and of the causes by which they are held together." The same: "Philosophy is the likeness of God, as far as human nature allows."

units.la: Ex nostratibus quidam definiunt, eam esse ordinatum artium liberalium systema. Nobis eam ita describere liceat:
units.tr: Among our own writers some define it as "an ordered system of the liberal arts." We may describe it thus:

units.la: Philosophia est ordinata literatæ sapientiæ comprehensio. Ordinata: Eius enim partes partes ordine inter se digestas requirimus.
units.tr: Philosophy is the ordered grasp of learned wisdom. "Ordered": for we require its parts to be arranged in order with respect to one another.

units.la: Literatam dicimus sapientiam, quia non quamuis describimus, sed eam, quae est literis erudita.
units.tr: We call the wisdom "learned" because we do not describe any wisdom whatsoever, but that which is instructed by letters.

units.la: Haec si aberrans immiscet errores ac Ethnicos paganismos, dici potest Ethnica: Si carnis & mundi phronema sequitur, carnalis & mundana; at imperfecta, deficies, vana vspiam & adulterata: Si Dei & rei veritatem sequitur, vera & germana fuerit.
units.tr: If this wisdom mixes in errors and pagan fancies, it may be called pagan; if it follows the carnal and worldly mind [φρόνημα], it is carnal and worldly; but if it is imperfect, defective, vain or adulterated anywhere, it is so in that part; if it follows God and the truth of the matter, it will be true and genuine.

units.la: Christiana igitur Philosophia nobis est ordinatum systema sapientiae Christianae ad salutarem tum cognitionem Veri, tum actionem Boni.
units.tr: Christian philosophy, therefore, is for us the ordered system of Christian wisdom, serving both the saving knowledge of the true and the practice of the good.

units.la: Huic opponitur vana, praedatrix, & deceptrix Philosophia, de qua Paulus ad Col. 2. Videte, ne quis vos depraedetur per Philosophiam, & inanem deceptionem, secundum traditionem humanam, secundum Elementa mundi, & non secundum Christum.
units.tr: Opposed to this is the vain, plundering and deceiving philosophy, of which Paul says in Colossians 2: "See to it that no one plunders you through philosophy and empty deceit, according to human tradition, according to the elements of the world, and not according to Christ."

units.la: Christiana sapientia est Christianis convenniens rerum diuinarum & humanarum intelligentia & scientia; quaq; Christiani recte sapiunt.
units.tr: Christian wisdom is the understanding and knowledge of divine and human things that suits Christians, and by which Christians rightly judge.

units.la: Huic opponitur vana, falsa & simulata sapientia, quae est rebus, tum diuinis, tum humanis non conueniens intelligentia ac scientia; adeoq; inanis sapientia, posletque generaliter dici Sophistica.
units.tr: Opposed to this is the vain, false and feigned wisdom, which is an understanding and knowledge that does not suit either divine or human things; and since it is an empty wisdom, it can generally be called sophistry.

units.la: Christiana sapientia triplici perficitur Lumine, Naturae, Artis seu Doctrinae, & Gratiae.
units.tr: Christian wisdom is perfected by a threefold light: that of nature, that of art or doctrine, and that of grace.

units.la: 2. Apodeixis generalis e definitione.
units.tr: 2. General demonstration from the definition.

units.la: Literatam sapientiam nemo nisi insanus & male literatus odio & conuiciis prosequitur.
units.tr: No one but a madman and a poorly educated person hates and reviles literate wisdom.

units.la: Atqui Philosophia nostra est literata sapientia, seu est systema doctrina de literata sapientia.
units.tr: But our Philosophy is literate wisdom, or is a system of teaching about literate wisdom.

units.la: Ergo Philosophiam nostram nemo nisi insanus, & male literatus, odio & conuiciis prosequitur.
units.tr: Therefore no one but a madman and a poorly educated person hates and reviles our Philosophy.

units.la: Propositionis robur est ex oppositione sapientiae & insaniae. Vt enim sapiens & sanus sapientiam amat, se enim ipse odisse non potest: est per sapientiam sapiens. Ita insanus non nisi amat insaniam, odit vero & conuiciatur sapientiam. Bene etiam literatus qui est, vere literatum literato amore complectitur: Ergo & male literatus, is est in literatorum familia hypocrita & nominalis (vt ita dicam) bene literatam non aeque fert sapientiam. Simile enim gaudet sibi simili.
units.tr: The force of the proposition lies in the opposition between wisdom and madness. For just as the wise and sane person loves wisdom, since he cannot hate himself, and is wise through wisdom, so the madman loves only madness and hates and reviles wisdom. Likewise the truly literate person embraces truly literate things with a literate love. Therefore the poorly literate person, who is in the family of the literate only as a hypocrite and in name only (as I may put it), does not bear well-educated wisdom with equal favour. For like delights in like.

units.la: Apodeixis ex definitione speciali.
units.tr: Demonstration from the special definition.

units.la: Christiana sapientia veritatis & bonitatis aemula Christiano praesertim literato est amanda, non amandanda.
units.tr: Christian wisdom, a rival of truth and goodness, is to be loved, and especially by the literate Christian; it is not to be unloved.

units.la: Atqui Philosophia Christiana, est Christiana sapientia doctrina veritatis & bonitatis studiosa.
units.tr: But Christian Philosophy is the teaching of Christian wisdom, which is zealous for truth and goodness.

units.la: Ergo Philosophia Christiana Christiano praesertim literato est amanda non amandanda.
units.tr: Therefore Christian Philosophy is to be loved, and especially by the literate Christian, not unloved.

units.la: Cautio. Ne dixeris hic vtrobique terminos quatuor. Propositio enim prioris syllogismi eandem vim veritatis retinet, quam haec: Literata sapientia systema seu doctrina, &c. Vt etiam posterioris propositio: Doctrina Christiana sapientia, qua est veritatis & virtutis aemula, est amanda Christiano: Hanc qui negat non est facto Christianus, sed aut ignarus & imperitus, aut malitiosus; vano tantum nomine gaudens. Item:
units.tr: Caution. Do not say here that there are four terms on either side. For the proposition of the first syllogism keeps the same force of truth as this one: literate wisdom is a system or teaching, etc. So too the proposition of the second: Christian teaching, which is a rival of truth and virtue, is to be loved by the Christian. Whoever denies this is not truly a Christian, but either ignorant and inexperienced, or malicious, rejoicing only in an empty name. Likewise:

units.la: Qui ordinatam Christianae sapientiae doctrinam odit & reiicit, is neque verum, neque bonum amat & persequitur.
units.tr: Whoever hates and rejects the ordered teaching of Christian wisdom does not love or pursue what is true and good.

units.la: Ratio. Christiana enim sapientia est veri magistra, & boni praeceptrix.
units.tr: The reason: For Christian wisdom is the teacher of truth and the instructress of goodness.

units.la: Atqui Christianam Philosophiam odit & reiicit, is ordinatam Christianae sapientiae doctrinam edit & respuit.
units.tr: But whoever hates and rejects Christian Philosophy rejects and spurns the ordered teaching of Christian wisdom.

units.la: Ergo qui Philosophiam Christianam odit & aversatur, neque verum neque bonum amat & prosequitur.
units.tr: Therefore whoever hates and shuns Christian Philosophy neither loves nor pursues what is true and good.

units.la: CAP. II. De veritate Philosophica.
units.tr: CHAP. II. On philosophical truth.

units.la: CHristiana igitur sapientia tum vera est, tum utiliter operosa seu eupractica.
units.tr: Christian wisdom, therefore, is both true and usefully operative, or practical.

units.la: Vera, quia veri cognitione Philosophos seu sui studiosos imbuit.
units.tr: It is true, because it imbues philosophers, or those who study it, with knowledge of the truth.

units.la: Vera sapientia est vera rerum, cum diuinarum, tum humanarum intelligentia, quae est vera cum rebus, quae intellectu percipiuntur, conuenientia, & Scientia, quae est vera cum rebus, quae sciuntur ὁμολογία & congruentia.
units.tr: True wisdom is a true understanding of things, both divine and human, which agrees truly with the things that are grasped by the intellect; and knowledge, which agrees truly with the things that are known, is homologia [ὁμολογία] and congruence.

units.la: Philosophia itaque nostra est sapientis veritatis studiosa ac æmula. Unde recte eam Aristoteles dixit; Scientiam veritatis contemplatricem:
units.tr: Our philosophy, therefore, is a zealous student of, and a rival to, wise truth. Hence Aristotle rightly called it the science contemplating truth:

units.la: Contemplatricis enim finis est veritas: actricis opus, in Metaphys. Sapientis est speculari alterutrum axiomati insit verum an falsum. lib. de sapientia. Philosophanti circa quamque methodum, ac non respicienti solum ad actionem, proprium est, non negligere, aut aliquid praetermittere, sed declarare veritatem in vnaquaque re. 3. polit. cap. 5.
units.tr: For the goal of the contemplative is truth, while the work belongs to the active. In the Metaphysics: It is the mark of the wise to consider whether the truth or falsehood inheres in each axiom. Book on Wisdom: It is proper to the philosopher, in each method, and not only regarding action, not to neglect or omit anything, but to declare the truth in each thing. Politics 3, ch. 5.

units.la: Veritas autem est vel ipsarum rerum, vel conuenientia & conformitas cum rebus.
units.tr: Truth, moreover, is either that of the things themselves, or the agreement and conformity with things.

units.la: Hoc ita Scholastici Dd. proposuerunt: Veritas triplex est; Prima est in rebus, & est esse Rei, secundum propriam rei Entitatem: Secunda est in intellectu, & est adæquatio intellectus ad rem, & conceptus rei, vt vera est: Tertia est formata à secunda, & primæ signum, & est in sermone, cum de re, vt est enunciatur, & de re, quæ non est, enunciatur vt non est.
units.tr: The Scholastic doctors put it thus: Truth is threefold. The first is in things, and is the being of a thing according to its own entity. The second is in the intellect, and is the adequation of the intellect to the thing, and the concept of the thing as it is true. The third is formed from the second, and is a sign of the first, and it is in speech, when something is stated about a thing as it is, and something that is not is stated as not being.

units.la: Rerum ipsarum veritas, est in ipsis rebus, ipsa rerum essentia, vt sunt, existentia, vt existunt, apparentia vt vere apparent.
units.tr: The truth of the things themselves lies in the things themselves: the very essence of things, as they are, as they exist, as they appear to truly appear.

units.la: Huic contraria est falsitas, quæ itidem in rebus ipsis est, quæ aut omnino non sunt, nec existunt, aut non esse apparent.
units.tr: Opposed to this is falsity, which likewise lies in the things themselves: those things which either altogether are not and do not exist, or appear not to be.

units.la: Huius veritatis Philosophia vera omnino, & in primis esse debet studiosissima: & philosophus verus philosophabitur ad rerum & entium veritatē, non ad hominum autoritatem, traditionem, opinionem.
units.tr: Philosophy ought to be wholly true, and above all most zealous for this truth; and the true philosopher will philosophise according to the truth of things and beings, not according to the authority, tradition or opinion of men.

units.la: Conuenientia & conformitas cum rebus est aut Metis aut Orationis: λόγῳ scilicet Interioris aut Exterioris. Cum rerum enim veritate conuenit hominis mens aut oratio.
units.tr: The agreement and conformity with things is either of the mind or of speech: that is, of inner or outer logos [λόγῳ]. For the mind or the speech of man agrees with the truth of things.

units.la: Mentis cum prima, quæ est rerum, veritate conformitas est primum in apprehensione seu perceptione, deinde in compositione & diuisione: Tertio in ratiocinatione seu discursu, quarto in scientia.
units.tr: The conformity of the mind with the first truth, that of things, comes first in apprehension or perception, then in composition and division, third in reasoning or discourse, and fourth in knowledge.

units.la: Apprehensionis seu perceptionis conuenientia est, qua mentis apprehensio est rerum, quæ apprehenduntur, veritati conformis; quaque à philosophi mente ita apprehenduntur & percipiuntur, vti sunt res, rerum veræ species.
units.tr: The agreement of apprehension or perception is that by which the mind's apprehension of the things apprehended conforms to the truth; and by which they are apprehended and perceived by the philosopher's mind just as they are, the true species of things.

units.la: De hac loquitur Eudemus lib. 7. cap. 1. Tria sunt in anima, quæ domina, (τὰ κύρια) sunt actionis & veritatis, sensus, mens, appetitus. Mens igitur rerum species per sensus veras recte debet ap-preprehendere, nec in apprehensione hallucinari & aberrare.
units.tr: Eudemus speaks of this in Book 7, ch. 1: There are three things in the soul which are masters (ta kyria [τὰ κύρια]) of action and truth: sense, mind, and appetite. The mind, therefore, must rightly apprehend the true species of things through the senses, and must not wander or err in apprehension.

units.la: Compositionis & diuisionis conuenientia est, qua mens percepta & apprehensa per sensus, adeoque alia simplicia noemata rerum, ita inter se componit, vti rerum veritas & consensus suadet, ita etiam à se diuidit, vt rerum natura sua dissensione imperat.
units.tr: The agreement of composition and division is that by which the mind, having perceived and apprehended things through the senses, and thus other simple notions of things, combines them with one another as the truth and agreement of things suggests, and likewise divides them from one another as the nature of things commands by their dissent.

units.la: Omnis itaque notionum in mente philosophantis compositio esto conformis naturali rerum, quarum sunt notiones, consensioni, & verae earum apprehensioni.
units.tr: Therefore let the composition of all notions in the mind of the philosopher conform to the natural agreement of the things of which they are notions, and to their true apprehension.

units.la: Omnis item diuisio rerum seu notionum in mente eiusdem esto conformis rerum, quarum sunt notiones, affectioni ac naturali dissensioni, qua à se diffident, & diuidi volunt; c-sto item conueniens rerum ipsarum verae perceptioni seu apprehensioni.
units.tr: Likewise let every division of things, or of notions, in the mind of the same man conform to the disposition and natural dissent of the things of which they are notions, by which they differ from one another and wish to be divided; and let it likewise agree with the true perception or apprehension of the things themselves.

units.la: Hinc Aristot. in fine 7. de Ente docet, Ens esse tanquam verum, & non ens tanquam falsum, seu, quod est, id verum esse, prima scilicet veritate, quod non est, falsum: idq; ex compositione quadam ac diuisione oriri. Namq; totum simul antiphasi comprehensum est, quae si diuidatur, in affirmationem & negationem diuidetur: affirmatio si applicetur compositis, id est, quae iam duos terminos habet, vti Animal album, est negatio, animal non album, tunc veritas etiam oritur: falsitas etiam in contradictione huius diuisionis,&c.
units.tr: Hence Aristotle, at the end of Book 7 of the Metaphysics, teaches that being is called true, and non-being false; that is, what is, is true, by the first truth, and what is not is false; and this arises from a certain composition and division. For the whole is comprehended at once in an opposition, which, if it is divided, is divided into affirmation and negation. If the affirmation is applied to compounds, that is, to what already has two terms, as white animal, the negation is not white animal; then truth arises, and falsity also arises in the contradiction of this division, etc.

units.la: De hac veritate verum est, quod ait Aristoteles lib.4.de Ente: Verum & falsum in rebus nō sunt, sed in dianœa scilicet compositionis & diuisionis magistra: alioquin falsum est.
units.tr: Concerning this truth, what Aristotle says in Book 4 of the Metaphysics is true: True and false are not in things, but in the dianoia [διάνοια], the mistress of composition and division; otherwise the thing is false.

units.la: Mens igitur philosophi veri conuenit sua intelligentia non tantum cum rebus simplicibus, quatenus entia: sed etiam cum rebus compositis, dum earum notiones conuenienter vel componit affirmando, vel diuidit negando.
units.tr: The mind of the true philosopher, therefore, agrees in its understanding not only with simple things, insofar as they are beings, but also with composite things, while it combines their notions by affirming or divides them by denying, in accordance with the truth.

units.la: Ratiocinationis & discursus conuenientia est, qua mens ex vere perceptis & conuenienter compositis, vel diuisis raciocinatur, & discurrendo alia deducit, pro affectione & natura rerum, ex quarum notionibus rite ac iuste aliquid deduci ac extrui debet.
units.tr: The agreement of reasoning and discourse is that by which the mind reasons from things truly perceived and rightly composed or divided, and by discoursing draws other conclusions, according to the disposition and nature of things, from whose notions something ought to be properly and justly deduced and constructed.

units.la: Mens proinde philosophi veri in discurrendo & vnum ex alio deducendo ita versatur, vt primum veritatem rerum, ex quibus deductio fieri debet, & quæ ex aliis deduci debent, exploret, exploratam componat aut diuidat, & ex composita aut diuisa rerum, notionum, & sententiarum inde factarum affectioni conuenienter aliud quid extruat: Vbi primum illud ex quo, deinde illud, quod ex alio deducendum, probe perpendit & veritati congruenter agitat.
units.tr: Accordingly, the mind of the true philosopher, in discoursing and deducing one thing from another, so conducts itself that it first examines the truth of the things from which the deduction must be made, and of those which must be deduced from others; having examined them, it composes or divides them, and from the composed or divided things, notions and judgments thus formed, it constructs something else in agreement with their disposition; where it first weighs well that from which, and then that which is to be deduced from another, and proceeds in accordance with the truth.

units.la: Scientiæ denique conformitas est, qua ita mens cum prima rerum veritate scite sciendo illas conuenit, vt ita sciat, sicut sunt, existunt, apparent; ita sciat, sicut apprehendit & primum vere cognouit; ita sciat, sicut composuit aut diuisit: ita sciat, sicut vere discursu ratiocinante eas agitauit, & alias ex aliis extruxit.
units.tr: Finally, the conformity of knowledge is that by which the mind, knowing skilfully, agrees with those things in accordance with the first truth of things, so that it knows them as they are, exist and appear; knows them as it apprehended and first truly recognised them; knows them as it composed or divided them; and knows them as it truly moved them about in reasoning discourse and constructed others from others.

units.la: Hæc ergo est ὁμολογία mentis apprehendentis, componentis ac diuidentis, discurrentis, & scientis cum rerum veritate, apprehensione, compositione, diuisione, discursu ac agitatione, & scientia. Hic nullum dissensum, discrepantiam nullam, qua fieri potest, admittet Christianus & verus philosophus.
units.tr: Thus this is the agreement [ὁμολογία] of the mind that apprehends, composes and divides, reasons discursively, and knows, with the truth of things in apprehension, composition, division, discursive reasoning, handling and knowledge. Here the Christian and true philosopher will admit no disagreement, no discrepancy whatsoever.

units.la: Orationis conuenientia cum rerum veritate est vel Pronunciatæ, vel Scriptæ: Linguæ vel Calami.
units.tr: The agreement of speech with the truth of things is either spoken or written: of the tongue or of the pen.

units.la: Pronunciatæ est orationis ore seu lingua pronunciatæ cõuenientia, cum rebus, quarum est pronunciatio.
units.tr: Spoken agreement is the agreement of speech uttered by mouth or tongue with the things about which it is uttered.

units.la: Vera itaque Philosophia docet pronunciare primum Rei, deinde Menti conuenienter. Rei, vt pronunciet, vti res est: Menti, vt pronunciet, vti mens res ipsas apprehendit, apprehensas expendit, & cognouit iudicauit q. Recte enim D. Goclenius: Perfectissima est Veritas illa, cum oratio conuenit menti & menti rei.
units.tr: True philosophy therefore teaches us to pronounce in accordance first with the thing, then with the mind. With the thing, so that it pronounces as the thing is: with the mind, so that it pronounces as the mind apprehends the things themselves, weighs what it has apprehended, and judges what it has come to know. For Goclenius rightly says: That truth is most perfect when speech agrees with the mind, and the mind with the thing.

units.la: Scriptæ est orationis scriptæ seu literis consignatæ conuenientia, cum rerum natura & affectione, & cum mentis perceptione, rerum dispositione, agitatione, iudicio & scientia.
units.tr: Written agreement is the agreement of written speech, or speech committed to letters, with the nature and condition of things, and with the mind's perception, the arrangement, handling, judgment and knowledge of things.

units.la: Orthodoxa itaque Philosophia est ita, vt dictum, veritatis rerum, & mentis, orationisq;, cum hac veritate conuenientis studiosa & æmula.
units.tr: Orthodox philosophy is therefore, as said, the zealous and emulous pursuit of the truth of things, of the mind and of speech agreeing with this truth.

units.la: Quapropter Philosophus nobis est Orthodoxus ille, qui ita studet, quantum sat est, de rebus sentire, vt sunt, existunt, apparent: ita satagit rerum notiones animo concipere, componere vel diuidere, agitare ratiocinando, vt fert rerum veritas; ita res nosse, deque notis ita loqui, dicere, scribere, vti natura, affectio & veritas rerum, siue diuinarum, siue humanarum permittit.
units.tr: Hence the orthodox philosopher for us is one who strives, as far as is enough, to think of things as they are, exist and appear; who labours to conceive in his mind the notions of things, to compose or divide them, and to handle them by reasoning as the truth of things requires; and to know things and to speak, say and write of what is known as the nature, condition and truth of things, whether divine or human, permits.

units.la: Apodeixis 3.
units.tr: Demonstration 3.

units.la: Quisquis Christianos ab amore & studio sapientiæ veritatis & veracis sapientiæ auocat & abducit, is eos vel clam, vel aperte ad amorem & studium Sophisticæ falsitatis, & mendacis, stoliditatis fuco carnalis sapientiæ seuocat & deducit.
units.tr: Whoever draws and leads Christians away from love and pursuit of wisdom of truth and true wisdom, that man summons and leads them, secretly or openly, to love and pursuit of sophistical falsehood and the lying stupidity, the paint of carnal wisdom.

units.la: Ab vno enim contrariorum qui aliquem auocat uocat & arcet, is ad alterum seuocat & viam sternit.
units.tr: For he who calls away and keeps someone from one of two contraries summons him to the other and lays the path.

units.la: Qui Christianos ab amore & studio sana & vera Philosophia abstrahit & absterret, eosdem etiam vel palam vel clam, ab amore & studio sapientis veritatis & veracis sapientia abstrahit & abssterret. Est enim illa, vt supra, &c.
units.tr: He who draws and frightens Christians away from love and pursuit of sound and true philosophy also draws and frightens them away, either openly or secretly, from love and pursuit of wise truth and true wisdom. For that philosophy is, as above, etc.

units.la: Ergo qui Christianos ab amore & studio sana & vera Philosophia deducit & abstrahit, eosdem, vel clam, vel aperte, ad insanum amorem & perniciosum studium sophisticae falsitatis & mendacis stoliditatis, fuco carnalis sua sapientia pellicit.
units.tr: Therefore whoever leads and draws Christians away from love and pursuit of sound and true philosophy secretly or openly entices those same people, by the paint of his carnal wisdom, to the insane love and pernicious pursuit of sophistical falsehood and lying stupidity.

units.la: Item:
units.tr: Likewise:

units.la: Qui erudita & sapientis veritatis flagrat amore, is eam rerum literatam deperit scientiam, qua mens res, vt sunt, existunt & sensibus apparent, apprehendere, componere & diuidere eas sua natura conuenienter, de iis recte ratiocinari & iudicare, denique earum solidam habere ac promptam scientiam studet. Et contra: qui flagrat impio literata & sapientis veritatis odio, is eam affectat, aliisque propinat ignorantiam pessimam, qua mens non studet res cognoscere & percipere, vti sunt, existunt & apparent, sed, vt non sunt nec apparent, estque osor rerum veritatis, sed res metitur ex vani sui cerebri vanis somniis: is res sua affectioni inconuenienter & contrarie componit aut diuidit, is sophistice de rebus male conceptis & dispositis struit absurdorum paralogismorum struem: is res non vt earum fert natura & veritas, nouit, sed vana rerum seu non entium figmenta vanis creat phantasmata, eaque turpi lucro lucro vendit, & tribunitiis clamoribus extollit: hæc est, fallax est & grauidus, tumidusque manibus stro-phis & sophismatis sophista.
units.tr: Whoever burns with love of learned and wise truth desires that literate knowledge of things by which the mind strives to apprehend the things as they are, exist and appear to the senses, to compose and divide them in accordance with their nature, to reason and judge rightly about them, and finally strives to have a solid and ready knowledge of them. And conversely: whoever burns with impious hatred of learned and wise truth aims at and offers to others the worst ignorance, by which the mind does not strive to know and perceive things as they are, exist and appear, but, as they are not and do not appear; and is a hater of the truth of things, measuring things by the empty dreams of its own vain brain. He composes or divides things inconsistently and contrary to their nature; he builds by sophistry a structure of absurd paralogisms from badly conceived and arranged things; he knows things not as their nature and truth bear them, but creates vain phantasms from vain fictions of things or non-things, and sells them for base gain and extols them with tribune-like clamours. This is a sophist: deceitful, heavy, and puffed up with sophisms and tricks of hands.

units.la: At vero, qui Philosophiæ orthodoxæ ardet religioso amore, is literatæ & sapientis amore est inflammatus: Qui vero sanæ Philosophiæ odio flagrat iniquo, is flagitioso etiam ac impio erudita ac sapientis adeoque sanctæ veritatis odio furiose est incensus. Ergo qui Philosophiæ, &c.
units.tr: But indeed, whoever burns with religious love of orthodox philosophy is inflamed with love of learning and wisdom; whoever on the other hand flames with wicked hatred of sound philosophy is furiously incensed with a shameful and impious hatred of learned and wise, and so holy, truth. Therefore whoever loves philosophy, etc.

units.la: CAP. III.
units.tr: CHAPTER III.

units.la: De vtili εὐπραξία Philosophiæ.
units.tr: On the useful eupraxia [εὐπραξία] of Philosophy.

units.la: SIc Philosophia est vera, id est, profitetur veritatē sapientem, paritq; veri cognitionem: Nihil igitur nisi verum, Philosophicum: Falsum omne ἀφιλόσοφον.
units.tr: Thus philosophy is true, that is, it professes wise truth and produces knowledge of the truth. Therefore nothing is philosophical except what is true; everything false is unphilosophical [ἀφιλόσοφον].

units.la: Εὐπρακτικὰ deinde & vtiliter operosa est Christiana ac orthodoxa Philosophia, vt sui studiosos cognitæ veritatis doceat salutarem in vita εὐπραξίαν.
units.tr: Next, Christian and orthodox philosophy is practical and usefully active, so that it teaches those who study it a saving eupraxia [εὐπραξία] in life, as the truth is known.

units.la: Non enim nuda scientia continetur, neque otiosæ est sapientiæ, neq; veritatis infructuosæ, quæ careat veris ac vtilibus in hominum vita operibus: Vti enim fides Christiana sine operibus est mortua; Ita etiam hæc sapientia, hæc scientia, hæc veritas literata nō edens vtiles sui in vita nostra fructus, est inanis, & mortuum sapientiæ exanimis, scientiæ otiosæ, & veritatis intus latētis, viresque nullas exerentis cadauer vel spectrum. Phi-
units.tr: For it does not consist of bare knowledge, nor is it an idle wisdom or a barren truth that lacks true and useful works in human life. Just as Christian faith without works is dead, so too this wisdom, this knowledge, this literate truth, if it does not yield useful fruit in our life, is empty: it is a dead body of wisdom without spirit, an idle knowledge, a truth lying hidden within and putting forth no strength, a corpse or a ghost. Phi-

units.la: Philosophiæ itaque literata sapien- tia, sapiensque veritas est salutaris, vti- lis & operosa (sipie & vtiliter adhibeā- tur) tum ad pietatem erga Deum, ad- eoque gloriam Dei, tum ad alios in vi- ta hac communi vsus vtiles.
units.tr: Therefore literate wisdom and wise truth of philosophy are saving, useful and active, (provided they are applied wisely and usefully), both to piety toward God, and so to the glory of God, and to others, being useful for them in this common life.

units.la: Est autem <bl>εὐπραξία</bl>Philosophię, qua per cognitionem, & scientiam sapien- tis veritatis homines Philosophi me- liores, & ad veram beatitatem conse- quendam magis appositi, eiusdemque magis capaces redduntur.
units.tr: Now the eupraxia [εὐπραξία] of philosophy is that by which, through the knowledge and science of wise truth, people become better philosophers and are made more fit to attain true blessedness and more capable of it.

units.la: ᾿Ευπραξία ergo spectat hominis Phi- losophi beatitatem seu felicitatem, quam literata sapientia & sapienti veri- tate iuuat & prouehit in hac hominis vita.
units.tr: So the eupraxia [εὐπραξία] looks to the blessedness or happiness of the philosophical man, which literate wisdom and wise truth help and advance in this human life.

units.la: Itaque scientia veritatis & consilio sapientiæ actionem boni, in homine gubernat.
units.tr: Thus knowledge of the truth, together with the counsel of wisdom, governs the doing of good in a human being.

units.la: Actiones autem hominis regit ita, vt sapientia & scientia, literataque ve- ritas inseruiant religiose Deo, aliis hu- maniter, sibi sapienti & verum scienti vtiliter.
units.tr: It governs human actions in such a way that wisdom, knowledge and literate truth serve God in piety, serve others humanely, and serve the wise person who knows the truth, for his own benefit.

units.la: Deo Philosophia omnem sapienti- am & veritatem cognitam ita conse- crat, vt totam ad eius gloriam in hac vita propapropagandam transferat, vel transferre studeat.
units.tr: Philosophy consecrates to God all wisdom and truth it has come to know, in such a way that it carries all of it over, or strives to carry it over, to propagate his glory in this life.

units.la: Proximo seu aliis hominibus cognitionem sapientem veritatis Philosophia vera ita dicat, vt sicut suis, hoc est, sapientis & scientis, ita & alius, praesertim vero Christiani veri commodis eam commodare velit.
units.tr: True philosophy so speaks to one's neighbour, that is, to other people, the wise knowledge of truth, that it wishes to make it serviceable to the advantage of others, especially of the true Christian, just as it does to its own followers, that is, the wise and learned.

units.la: Sibi, hoc est, sui studiosi, scienti & vere sapienti, suam sapientiam & veritatem vult ita prodesse, vt secundum Deum autori sapiat & sancte prosit.
units.tr: It wishes its wisdom and truth to benefit the one who studies it, the one who knows and truly is wise, so that it may be wise toward its author according to God and profit him in holiness.

units.la: Hinc adeo est, vt in sanctis literis ea celebretur sapientia, quae est in observatione mandatorum Dei, & cuius caput est reuerentia ac timor Dei.
units.tr: Hence it is that in the holy letters that wisdom is praised which lies in keeping the commandments of God, and whose beginning is reverence and the fear of God.

units.la: Plato etiam in Theæteto solum iustum vere sapientem appellat, cum per iustitiam sit similimus Deo.
units.tr: Plato too, in the Theaetetus, calls only the just man truly wise, since through justice he is most like God.

units.la: Atque in Appendice legum ait vere sapientem illum dici, qui cum diuina speculatus fuerit, recte de humanis sapit, eaque congruenter moderatur.
units.tr: And in the appendix to the Laws he says that he is rightly called truly wise who, having contemplated divine things, judges human things rightly and governs them accordingly.

units.la: Per hanc sapientiam, inquit Piccolomin. gradu 5. homo similis Deo redditur: per hanc non tantum sublimia cognoscit, verum insuper ad eorum imitationem moderatur humana, in hac intelligentia, scientia radii refulgent, per hanc altissima rerum causa cognoscuntur, & cuncta in congruentem finem dirigantur.
units.tr: Piccolomini, grade 5, says: through this wisdom a human being is made like God; through it he not only knows lofty things but, moreover, governs human affairs in imitation of them; in this understanding and knowledge the rays shine forth; through it the highest causes of things are known, and all things are directed to a fitting end.

units.la: Omne itaq; philosophicum debet esse ἐυπρεφκτικὸν, hominique salutarem & vtilem continere doctrinam: omnisque sapientia & cognitio philosophica esse debet efficax & actuosa (vt ita loquar) ad hominis vtilitatem & salutē iuuandam & ornandam: nihil noxium, nihil inutile & futile philosophicum.
units.tr: Therefore everything philosophical ought to be useful [εὐπρακτικόν], and to contain a doctrine saving and useful to a human being: all philosophical wisdom and knowledge ought to be effective and active (so to speak) for helping and adorning human usefulness and salvation; nothing philosophical should be harmful, useless or trifling.

units.la: Proindeq; Christianus philosophus sapiat,& sibi, & aliis.
units.tr: Accordingly, the Christian philosopher should be wise both for himself and for others.

units.la: Sibi sapiat primum cognitione Veri,vt veritatem sibi quærat, & cognoscat ad Dei gloriam,suamque salutem. Deinde actione Boni, vt veritatem cognitam exprimat vita actionibus, adeoque scientia & veritatis professioni respondeat vita actio, ad Dei gloriam & salutem suam.
units.tr: He should be wise for himself, first, by knowing the truth, so that he seeks out and knows the truth for the glory of God and his own salvation. Then, by doing good, so that he expresses the known truth in the actions of his life, and so that his life's actions correspond to his profession of knowledge and truth, for the glory of God and his own salvation.

units.la: Aliis item sapiat Philosophus Christianus primum scientiam Veri cum aliis communicando ad Dei gloriam & aliorum salutem.Deinde actionem Boni exerendo, suam bonitatem ad alios deriuando ad Dei gloriam & aliorum commodum.
units.tr: Likewise, the Christian philosopher should be wise for others: first by sharing the knowledge of truth with others, for the glory of God and the salvation of others; then by carrying out the doing of good, passing on his goodness to others, for the glory of God and the benefit of others.

units.la: 4. Apodeixis.
units.tr: 4. Apodeixis.

units.la: Quisquis auerso est animo à salutari literata sapientia & veritatis vtiliter operosa doctrina; is sua & alio& aliorum inuidet felicitati ac saluti. Ratio:
units.tr: Whoever is turned in mind away from the saving literate wisdom and the usefully active doctrine of truth, begrudges both his own and others' happiness and salvation. The reason:

units.la: Etenim, vt ostendimus, hæc ipsa literata sapientia & actuosa vtilisque veritatis sapientis scientia hominum beatitati & saluti magno est adiumento & ornamento.
units.tr: For, as we have shown, this very literate wisdom, and the active and useful wise knowledge of truth, is a great help and ornament to the blessedness and salvation of human beings.

units.la: Atqui quisquis superbe vel malitiose fastidit sanam philosophiam nostram, is est auerso animo a salutari literata sapientia & veritatis vtiliter operosa doctrina.
units.tr: But whoever proudly or maliciously despises our sound philosophy is turned in mind away from the saving literate wisdom and the usefully active doctrine of truth.

units.la: Etenim sana Philosophia Christianorum est non tantum magistra & ministra sapientis veritatis: sed etiam salutaris in vita vniuersa εὐτυξίας: vt iam dictum.
units.tr: For sound Christian philosophy is not only the teacher and minister of wise truth, but also the saving eupraxia [εὐπραξία] throughout the whole of life, as has already been said.

units.la: Ergo qui superbe vel malitiose fastidit & spernit sanam nostram Philosophiam, is sua & aliorum inuidet felicitati ac saluti. Summatim:
units.tr: Therefore whoever proudly or maliciously scorns and despises our sound philosophy begrudges both his own and others' happiness and salvation. In summary:

units.la: Nemo Christianorum, ne dum sanus Theologus (de insanis quid?) eam rodit vel odit doctrinam, quae parit cognitionem veri & actiones boni in vita humana.
units.tr: No Christian, much less a sound theologian (what of the unsound?), gnaws at or hates the doctrine that produces knowledge of truth and good actions in human life.

units.la: Atqui sana Philosophia (de insana quid?) parit eam veri cognitionem & boni in vita hominum actiones.
units.tr: But sound philosophy (what of the unsound?) produces that knowledge of truth and those good actions in human life.

units.la: Nemo igitur Christianorum, ne dum sanus Theologus sanam rodit vel odit Philosophiam, nisi simul velit haberi & esse omnis Veri & Boni insanus rosor & osor.
units.tr: Therefore no Christian, much less a sound theologian, gnaws at or hates sound philosophy, unless he at the same time wishes to be held and to be an insane gnawer and hater of all truth and goodness.

units.la: In specie autem Philosophia medetur hominis læso & corrupto animo: unde & medicina animi dici solet.
units.tr: In particular, philosophy heals the wounded and corrupted soul of a human being, and for this reason it is commonly called the medicine of the soul.

units.la: Animi enim facultates omnes per hominis lapsum & peccatum sunt corruptæ & deprauatæ, præcipue vero eæ, quibus sapientiæ & veritatis studiosus maxime eget, vt sunt intellectus, conscientia, voluntas, & memoria.
units.tr: For all the faculties of the soul were corrupted and depraved through the fall and sin of man, especially those which the student of wisdom and truth most needs, such as the understanding, the conscience, the will, and the memory.

units.la: His omnibus sana Philosophia facit medicinam, vt homo æger convalescat, & corruptus restituatur.
units.tr: Sound philosophy makes a remedy for all of these, so that the sick man may recover and the corrupted man be restored.

units.la: Intelligentiam præceptis ac regulis sapientiæ & veritatis literatæ imbuit ac informat, vt recte intelligat, eaque in omnibus bene & pie vtatur. Affert primum scientiam præceptorum sapientiæ, deinde etiam praxeos & vsus pii ac honesti scientiam.
units.tr: It imbues and forms the understanding with the precepts and rules of wisdom and literate truth, so that it understands rightly and uses them well and piously in all things. It brings first the knowledge of the precepts of wisdom, and then also the knowledge of the practice and use of what is pious and honourable.

units.la: Conscientiam docet à teneris curare, & sic sapientiæ ac veritatis lenioribus admonitionibus, recte gestorum collaudationibus, male factorum acrioribus castigationibus, excitat & assuefacit, vt prompta sit & vigilans ad sapientiam hauriendam, & sapientiæ veritatisque edendas actiones, non autem segnis vel somnolenta aut contumax.
units.tr: It teaches the conscience to be cared for from tender years, and thus stirs it up and accustoms it, by the milder admonitions of wisdom and truth, by commendation of right deeds, and by sharper rebukes for wrong ones, so that it is ready and watchful to draw in wisdom and to perform the actions of wisdom and truth, and is not sluggish, drowsy or stubborn.

units.la: Christianus inde Philosophus conscientiam suam non nisi inuitissimus offendit ac lædit.
units.tr: Hence the Christian philosopher would offend or injure his conscience only most unwillingly.

units.la: Voluntatem hominis corruptam & rebellem corrigit, frænat, ac rectius informat, vt quod bene nouit mens, id recte etiam velit voluntas, vt cognita sapientiæ ac veritatis documenta, ad salutarem humanæ vitæ vsum transferre satagat, bona & vera velit & persequatur, mala & falsa nolit & auersetur, fræna iniiciat cupiditatibus, ne iis transfuersum rapiatur. Christianum enim decet Philosophū, vt non tam doctus, quam bonus & pius sem-per & esse & haberi velit.
units.tr: It corrects, bridles and more rightly forms the corrupt and rebellious will, so that what the mind knows well, the will also rightly wishes; so that it strives to carry the learned precepts of wisdom and truth over into the saving use of human life, wills and pursues what is good and true, and refuses and turns away from what is evil and false, and puts bridles on the desires so that they are not dragged off course. For it befits the Christian philosopher to wish always to be and to be held not so much learned as good and pious.

units.la: Memoriam, quæ à nonnullis mater dicitur sapientiæ, ita præceptis suis excolit & firmat, vt vera & bona intellecta & approbata diu retinere queat, & cum iudicio aliquando promptèque expromere, & ad vsum traducere. Philosophus enim verus veritatis & sapientiæ præcepta in memoriæ thesaurum reponit, nec vult ex libro & charta videri eruditus, sine libro autem magis esse mutus, quam piscis.
units.tr: Memory, which by some is called the mother of wisdom, it so cultivates and strengthens with its precepts that it can retain for long the true and good things understood and approved, and at times bring them forth with judgement and readily, and put them to use. For the true philosopher stores the precepts of wisdom and truth in the treasury of memory, and does not wish to appear learned from a book and paper; without a book, however, he is more mute than a fish.

units.la: QVÆSTIO. An Philosophia hominis naturam & perfectionem procuret & instauret.
units.tr: QUESTION. Whether philosophy restores and renews the nature and perfection of man.

units.la: Aff.
units.tr: Affirmative

units.la: Ad euentilandam hanc quæstionem primum consideranda est integritatis humanæ perfectio: secundo corruptio & corruptæ naturæ humanæ indigentia. Tertio ipsa restauratio indigentiæ humanæ succurrens.
units.tr: To unravel this question, we must first consider the perfection of human integrity; second, the corruption of human nature and its need; and third, the restoration that meets human need.

units.la: Homo cum à Deo primum est creatus, & huic terrenæ vitæ ac cœlesti destinatus, fuit naturalibus viribus integer, & spiritualibus dotibus ornatus & auctus, adeo vt vtrique vitæ viuedæ, quam plenissime sufficeret. Et quidem, quantum ad scientiam ac sapientiam, de qua, hoc loco, præcipua iustituitur commentatio, fuit rerum omnium tam diuinarum, quam humanarum, scientia imbutus, quę tum ad hanc præsentem vitam bene beateque viuendam, tum ad cœlestem consequendam, & ad Deum recte colendum pertinuerunt. Quae ad neutrum horum fecerunt, necessarium esse negant scholastici. Dd. vt harum rerum scientia homini integro attribuatur. Ideoque excipiunt cognitionem futurorum contingentium, cogitationum cordis alius, numerorum quibus stellae & arenę maris singulę comprehenduntur.
units.tr: When man was first created by God and destined for this earthly life and the heavenly one, he was whole in his natural powers, and adorned and enriched with spiritual gifts, so fully sufficient for both kinds of life. And indeed, as regards knowledge and wisdom, which is the chief subject of this discussion, he was imbued with knowledge of all things, both divine and human, which pertained both to living well and blessedly in this present life and to attaining the heavenly one and worshipping God rightly. The scholastic doctors deny that knowledge of those things which served neither of these ends must be attributed to whole man. Hence they exclude knowledge of future contingent things, of the thoughts of another's heart, and of the numbers by which each star and each grain of sea sand is counted.

units.la: Sapientia itaque & scientia hominis integri fuit rerum tum diuinarum & spiritualium, tum humanarum & mundanarum.
units.tr: The wisdom and knowledge of whole man, therefore, concerned divine and spiritual things as well as human and worldly things.

units.la: Quo ad res diuinas & coelestes, praeditus fuit vera veri Dei cognitione, vera item omnium diuinarum rerum ad vitam spiritualem & coelestem sufficientium notitia: adeo vt deum ex integra mente, ex omnibus viribus, ex tota anima, & proximum vti seipsum sancte amaret, & creatorem cultu sanctissimo veneraretur. Quo ad res ceteras, erat ita conditus homo, vt rerum humanarum, naturalium, mathematicarum, ciuilium & oeconomicarum scientia excelleret. Erat ita factus, vt piscibus maris, volatilibus coeli, bestiis, reptilib. atq; vniuersae terrae dominio optimo, & ad Dei creatoris in creaturas imperium per imaginem conformato praeesset. Dominium autem hoc rerum omnium mundanarum seu terrenarum cognitionem intelligentiamque veritatis, nec non earundem vsum ipsis conuenientem ac prudentiam complectebatur.
units.tr: As to divine and heavenly things, he was endowed with true knowledge of the true God, and likewise with true knowledge of all divine things sufficient for spiritual and heavenly life, so that he loved God with his whole mind, with all his strength and with his whole soul, and loved his neighbour as himself, and worshipped the Creator with most holy worship. As to other things, man was so constituted that he excelled in knowledge of human, natural, mathematical, civil and domestic matters. He was made so that he had the best dominion over the fishes of the sea, the birds of the heavens, the beasts, the reptiles and the whole earth, presiding over them as God the Creator's rule over creatures is reflected in his image. This dominion over all worldly and earthly things embraced knowledge and understanding of their truth, as well as their fitting use and prudence.

units.la: Ita fuit a Deo factus, vt rationalem reliquarum rerum vsum sibi concessum haberet, vt rationis suæ munere, res quasuis intelligenter & prudenter tractare posset: ideoque in hoc statu, vt nouit omnium rerum naturas, proprietates, differentias, similitudines, disi-militudines, communionem & veritatem, ita eas mentis discursu agitauit, ita iis in diiudicando recte est visus. Ita erat affectus, vt propriis significantissimisque nominibus certa ratione formatis, singula, quæ offerebatur, appellaret, essentiam rerum, & istas, quæ intrinsecus latent, motusque & affectiones cient, proprietates perspiceret, vocibusque quasi signis expressis sapienter definiret, in omnibus & de omnibus constantissimo iudicio, ratiocinatione prudentissime adhibita concluderet, adeoque omnia & rationis & orationis officia proptissime exequeretur, & in suæ vitæ conuenientem vsum conuertere posset. Cœli etiam cœlestiumque siderum vires ac motus non ignoraret. Ita denique erat à Deo armatus necessaria cognitione, vt humanæ, ciuilis & œconomicæ vitæ rationes haberet perspectissimas, vt quomodo inter se homines politice viuere, quo humanitatis, amicitiæ & cognationis iure sociari, quibus modis legitime sociari, quid quisque licite sequi, & ad Ecclesiæ ac Reipub. salutem præstare debeat, perspectum haberet. Hæc alia homo integer, acumine à Deo dato, scientia à Deo infusa, perspicacitate intelligentiæ diuinitus concessa intueri, & viribus ad ea concessis præstare potuit.
units.tr: God made him so that he had the rational use of the other things granted to him, so that by the gift of his reason he could handle any things intelligently and prudently. In that state he knew the natures, properties, differences, similarities, dissimilarities, interconnections and truth of all things, and so he worked them over in the discourse of his mind, and so he judged them rightly. He was so disposed that, with proper and most expressive names formed by a sound rule, he named each thing presented to him; he perceived the essences of things and the properties that lie hidden within and stir up motions and affections; he wisely defined them by words expressed as signs; he drew conclusions about all things with most constant judgment, applying reasoning most prudently; and so he carried out all the duties of reason and speech most aptly and could turn them to the use suited to his life. Nor was he ignorant of the powers and motions of the heavens and the stars. Finally, he was so armed by God with necessary knowledge that he had a most thorough understanding of the principles of human, civil and domestic life: how men might live together politically, by what right of humanity, friendship and kinship they might be joined, by what lawful means they might associate, what each may lawfully pursue, and what he ought to contribute to the welfare of the Church and the commonwealth. Whole man could behold these things with the keen insight given by God, with knowledge infused by God and with the perceptiveness of understanding divinely granted, and could accomplish them with the powers given for that purpose.

units.la: Homo autem integer & liber, libertate vo-luntaluntatis aduersus Dei interdictionem abutes, vbi sponte defecit ad inobedientiam ex esu pomi prohibiti, omnes vires eius & facultates animi & corporis miserabiliter corruptæ sunt.In animo quidem, cuius perfectio est scientia & sapientia, de qua hic, penitus fuit obscurata, & in eius locum ignorantia & insipientia, iusto Dei iudicio, nostraque culpa successit.
units.tr: But whole and free man, abusing the freedom of his will against God's prohibition, when he willingly fell into disobedience by eating the forbidden fruit, had all his powers and faculties of mind and body miserably corrupted. In the mind, whose perfection is the knowledge and wisdom we are discussing here, these were utterly obscured, and in their place ignorance and foolishness followed, by God's just judgment and our own fault.

units.la: Sapientiæ diuinarum rerum, horribilis earundem surrogata est ignorantia, & defectus vacuitasque cognitionis in rebus Dei, quæ nimirum pertinent, vel ad purum eius cultum, vel ad vitam æternam; successit ἀδυναμία, qua mens non potest per se percipere res spirituales; vanitas qua iudicat verum esse falsum & contra; aptitudo ad concipiendum & cogitandum malum tantum. Remansere quidem notitiæ quædam de bono & malo; quales sunt Esse Deum, esse Deum vindicem scelerum, esse vitam aliquam æternam, &c. vti docet Paulus in Epistola ad Rom. cap. 1. Quoniam quod de Deo cognosci potest, manifestum est in ipsis: Deus enim iis manifestum fecit: ipsius enim inuisibilia dum ex rebus conditis cognoscuntur, ex creatione mundi perspiciuntur, &c. Verum hæ notitiæ & generales tantum & corruptæ sunt, & tantum excusationi tollendæ inseruiunt.
units.tr: In place of the wisdom of divine things came a dreadful ignorance of them, and a defect and emptiness of knowledge of God's things, which pertain either to his pure worship or to eternal life. In place of it came inability (ἀδυναμία), by which the mind cannot of itself perceive spiritual things; vanity, by which it judges the true to be false and the reverse; and a readiness to conceive and think only evil. Certainly some notions of good and evil remained, such as that God exists, that God avenges crimes, that there is some eternal life, and so on, as Paul teaches in the Epistle to the Romans, chapter 1: Because what may be known of God is manifest in them, for God has shown it to them; for his invisible things, since they are understood from created things, are seen from the creation of the world, and so on. But these notions are only general and corrupt, and serve only to remove excuse.

units.la: Sapientia & scientia rerum humanarum naturalis, qua homo luce primæue naturæ omnia perspiciebat, penitus obscurata & infirmata est.
