Subsecuta est lapsum & peccatum rerum rum naturalium & ciuilium ignoratio ingens, vnde dominium illud recte administrari non potest, cum cuiusque rei vsus ex natura eius perspecta, & ad alia recte comparata definien- dus non teneatur, erroresque ex ignorantia nascantur,& homini perniciosi, & naturæ con- trarii.Præterea malitia, prauitasque mentis,& sibi ipsa in abusu rerum priuato peruerse no- cet, & vitam communem ac politicam ex ig- norantia veri & boni vehementer afflictam, vehementius aliquando perturbat. Ratio de- nique ipsa& lumen intelligentiæ tum in per- spiciendo & excogitando, tum in disponendo, & iudicando infinitis difficultatibus implica- tur, vt suo muneri satisfacere, sine ope alius, recte non possit.
units.tr: The wisdom and knowledge of natural and human things, by which man in the light of first nature perceived all things, was utterly obscured and weakened. After the fall and sin there followed a vast ignorance of natural and civil things, so that the dominion described above cannot be rightly administered, since the use of each thing is not determined from a clear knowledge of its nature and from rightly relating it to others; and errors arise from ignorance, harmful to man and contrary to nature. Moreover, the malice and perversity of the mind harms itself in the misuse of things, and sometimes greatly disturbs common and political life, which is grievously afflicted by ignorance of the true and the good. Finally, reason itself and the light of understanding are entangled in endless difficulties, both in perceiving and devising, and in arranging and judging, so that without the help of another it cannot rightly fulfil its office.

units.la: Sic denique orationi multum decessit lapsu hominis, ipsa enim lingua, non ita expedite munera sua, & quæ vitæ necessitas requirit, præstare potest.En igitur hominem corruptū, infirmum, nudum, egenum, erroribus malitiaque oppressum, vbique fluctuantem, nusquam non periclitantem, nullibi firmiter consistentem, multis vitiis animi corporisq; coopertum:hinc facile hominis corrupti indigentia æstimari potest.
units.tr: Thus speech too was much diminished by the fall of man, for language itself cannot perform its functions as readily as the necessities of life require. Here, then, is man corrupted, weak, naked, needy, oppressed by errors and malice, wavering everywhere, in danger everywhere, settled nowhere firmly, and covered with many vices of mind and body. From this the need of corrupt man can easily be estimated.

units.la: Indigentia itaque, qua homo misere miser laborat, est defectus & vacuitas cognitionis, scientiæ & sapientiæ in rebus tum diuinis ac spiritualibus,tum humanis,naturalibus & po- liticis, qua neque ad vitam hanc terrenam sa- tis commode transigendam, neque ad cœlestem inueniendam & acquirendam est idone-us. Indigentia ergo est partim sapientiæ diui-næ, partim humanæ ad felicitatem hominis necessariæ.
units.tr: The need, then, under which man miserably labours in his wretchedness, is the defect and emptiness of knowledge, science and wisdom, both in divine and spiritual things and in human, natural and political things, by which he is not fit to get through this earthly life with reasonable comfort, nor to find and acquire the heavenly one. The need is therefore partly for divine wisdom and partly for human wisdom, both necessary for human happiness.

units.la: Vtraque sapientia est in homine inftauran-da & restituenda: restituitur autem gratia & beneficio Dei sapientis.
units.tr: Both kinds of wisdom are to be restored and re-established in man; but they are restored by the grace and benefit of God, who is wise.

units.la: Defectus diuinæ sapientiæ ac scientiæ, quæ ad felicitatem vitæ æternæ hominisque falu-tem confert, hæc, inquam, indigentia, qua ad omne bonum spirituale prorsus est ineptus, tollitur à Deo, eiusque spiritu sapientiæ & veritatis per verbum suum salutiferum, seu do-ctrinam sapientiæ diuinæ, quæ dicitur Theologia, qua paulatim in nobis deperdita diuina-rum rerum sapientia restauratur & restituitur.
units.tr: The defect of divine wisdom and knowledge, which contributes to the happiness of eternal life and to man's salvation, this need, I say, by which he is wholly unfit for any spiritual good, is removed by God, through his Spirit of wisdom and truth and through his saving Word, or the doctrine of divine wisdom called Theology; by it the divine wisdom, lost in us little by little, is restored and re-established.

units.la: Hæc docet hominem veri Dei cognitione ex reuelato eius verbo, quod Deus fit Vnus & Trinus, qualis fit attributis: quæ sint Dei opera scitu nobis ad salutem necessaria, quod & quomodo omnia ab æterno libere & fapien-ter decreuerit; quod & quomodo nos & omnia crearit, creataque gubernet ac administret in cœlo & in terra: quod & quomodo Deus meditatus fit, & moliatur nostri in Christo instaurationem, adeoq; nostram salutem: quod & quomodo Christus homo factus, officio sibi à Deo patre delegato functo nobis salutem acquisiuerit; quod & quomodo nos acquisitæ salutis participes fiamus; quod & quomodo nos vocet ad salutem participandam, offeratque gratiam; quod & quomodo eam Deus nobiscum gratiose communicet, &c. & quid vicissim nostri fit officii,&c.
units.tr: This doctrine teaches man the knowledge of the true God from his revealed Word: that God is one and three, and what his attributes are; what God's works are that we need to know for our salvation, and what and how he freely and wisely decreed all things from eternity; what and how he created us and all things, and what and how he governs and administers created things in heaven and on earth; what and how God has planned and undertakes our restoration in Christ, and so our salvation; what and how Christ, made man, by the office delegated to him by God the Father, has acquired salvation for us; what and how we become sharers in the salvation acquired; what and how he calls us to share in salvation and offers grace; what and how God graciously communicates it with us, and so on; and conversely, what our duty is, and so on.

units.la: Defectum sapientiæ humanæ explet idem Deus omnis sapientiæ per Philosophiam specialiter dictam,seu humanam, per doctrinam artium humanitatis earumque rectam ac prudentem institutionem. Defectus hic primo apparet in veritatis rerum ignorantia, & erroris facilitate. Deinde in difficultate vtedi tum ratione nostra ad intelligendum & iudicandu, tum oratione ad necesisitatem dignitatemque rerum cum aliis communicandarum. Tertio in lubrico vsu, & periculosa rerum cognoscedarum experientia. Quarto in affectuum animi iudiciique conturbatione. Huic defectui institutio philosophica multum medetur. Rerum naturalium ignorantiam tollit studium fanum & eupracticon Physicę, præcepta Christianæ Ethicæ, œconomicæ, politicę, iurisprudentiæ, &c. Rationem hominis expolit & instituit suis præceptis Logica. Orationem hominis puram formant Grammaticæ præceptiones, modificatam & exornatam reddit elocutio & pronunciatio rhetorica.
units.tr: God, the same God who is all wisdom, makes good the lack of human wisdom through philosophy, which is specifically called human, namely through the teaching of the liberal arts and their right and prudent instruction. This lack shows itself first in ignorance of the truth of things and in the ease with which we fall into error. Second, it shows in the difficulty of using our reason to understand and judge, and of using speech to communicate things with others as their necessity and dignity require. Third, it shows in the slippery practice and dangerous experience of getting to know things. Fourth, it shows in the disturbance of the emotions of the mind and of judgment. Philosophical instruction greatly remedies this lack. The study of natural things, sound and practical, removes ignorance of nature; the precepts of Christian ethics, economics, politics and jurisprudence do the same. Logic refines and trains the human reason with its rules. Grammatical precepts shape pure human speech, and rhetorical elocution and delivery make it refined and adorned.

units.la: Vsum rerum regit ipsa artium constantior ratio, iudiciumque firmius & crebrius artificium. Affectuum motus sedant moralis Philosophiæ, quæ percipue ex sapientiæ diuinæ oraculis huc solent transferri, documeta, vt nihil de ceteris dicam artibus,quantum illæ ad hominis felicitatem & perfectionem naturalem,suæ informationis opera conducant.
units.tr: The more settled method of the arts governs the use of things, and the skill of the arts makes judgment firmer and more frequent. The movements of the emotions are calmed by moral philosophy, whose teachings are usually drawn out chiefly from the oracles of divine wisdom. (I say nothing here of the other arts, how far they contribute, by their work of forming us, to human happiness and natural perfection.)

units.la: Ipse autem Deus propter lapsum, naturam nostram non plane substulit, nec naturalia penitus deleuit, sed semina quaedam reliquit & vires, quibus Deo rorem diuinae suae benedictionis affluudente, nostroque labore & studio accedete, ad perfectionem quandam perduci possumus. Hic itaque oportet Paulum (liceat mihi hoc nostris accommodare) plantare, Apollinem rigare, Dominum vero dare incrementum: In sudore & labore nobis est victitandum: Deus laboribus nobis sapientiam rerum humanarum nunc vendit. Etenim a Deo quidem donorum suorum iusto distributore est naturae quaedam relicta bonitas, seu habilitas ac aptitudo facultatum animae rationalis, ite sensuum; a Deo est ingenium & intellectus, voluntatis desiderium, Musarumque amor: Institutio tamen praeter Dei opem & benedictionem requirit diligentem ac fidum tum praeceptorem, tum discipulum, vtriusque operam ac indefessum studium. Cum primis vero, cum tantum quisque calleat, quantum exercet, & visus sit anima praeceptorum artis, sine crebro visu, & prudenti artium exercitatione sapientia nostra est quasi intermortua. Sed tandem ita argumentor: Per quod Deus sapientiam hominis instaurat, per id quoque hominis naturam & perfectionem quae in hac vita sperari potest, reparat. Scientia enim & sapientia est animi perfectio. Atqui Deus sapientiam hominis divinam & salutiferam per Philosophiam divinam doctrinamque verbi instaurat, eiusdem sapientiam am humanam regit quidem diuina, sed reparat ac restituit quomodocunque per Philosophiam humanas artes humaniores. Ergo per Philosophiam quoque perfectionem nostram hic inchoat Deus, in aeterna vita consummaturus.
units.tr: God himself, because of the fall, did not wholly take away our nature, nor utterly destroy natural things, but left certain seeds and powers, by which we can be brought to a certain perfection, when God's dew of his blessing flows down upon them and our labour and zeal come to them. Here, then, we must (let me adapt this to our purpose) say that Paul plants, Apollos waters, but the Lord gives the increase: we must live by sweat and labour; God now sells us the wisdom of human things for our labours. For from God, the just distributor of his gifts, there is left to nature a certain goodness, that is, the capacity and aptitude of the faculties of the rational soul, as also of the senses; from God come talent and understanding, the desire of the will, and love of the Muses. Yet instruction, besides God's help and blessing, requires both a diligent and faithful teacher and a diligent and faithful pupil, and the effort and tireless zeal of each. Above all, since each person knows only as much as he practises, and the soul of the precepts of an art seems to be lost without frequent looking at them and prudent practice of the arts, our wisdom is, as it were, half dead. But I argue at last thus: Whatever through which God restores human wisdom, by that same means he also repairs and perfects the nature of man as far as it can be hoped for in this life. For knowledge and wisdom are the perfection of the mind. But God restores human wisdom, which is divine and saving, through divine philosophy and the doctrine of the Word; he governs that same human wisdom indeed by divine means, yet he repairs and restores in whatever way it is done, through philosophy, the human arts and the more humane studies. Therefore God also begins our perfection here through philosophy, to be brought to completion in eternal life.

units.la: Perfectio autem hominis duplex est, Spiritualis & Naturalis: utraque tanta & ea, quanta & quae in hanc vitam & hominem cadere potest: Alioquin constat in hac vita numeris omnibus absolutum esse nihil. Utraque partes complectitur duas; prima est tollere ἀδυναμίαν, qua homo est ineptus: Altera est conferre homini facultatem & dexteritatem, vita huius partes sine errore & periculo recte administrandi, eaque cauendi, quae vitae felicitatem eam impediunt aut labefactant. Perfectio haec & aufert malum, quod est in hominis natura, & restituit bonum malo contrarium.
units.tr: The perfection of man is twofold, spiritual and natural; each is as great, and of such a kind, as can fall to this life and to man: otherwise it is certain that nothing in this life is perfect in every respect. Each has two parts: the first is to remove ἀδυναμία, by which man is unfit; the second is to give man the ability and skill to manage the parts of this life rightly, without error and danger, and to guard against whatever hinders or weakens the happiness of life. This perfection both takes away the evil that is in man's nature and restores the good contrary to the evil.

units.la: Spiritualis perfectio est, quâ spiritus Dei in nobis per Philosophiam ac sapientiâ ex verbo eius haustam ad vitæ æternæ beatitatem efficit.
units.tr: Spiritual perfection is that by which the Spirit of God in us, through philosophy and the wisdom drawn from his Word, brings us to the blessedness of eternal life.

units.la: Naturalis perfectio est, quâ idem in nobis per artes Philosophicas humanæque Philosophiæ & sapientiæ doctrinam à diuina correctam, natura, arte & vsu comparatam ad vitæ huius commoditatem feliciorem efficit.
units.tr: Natural perfection is that by which the same Spirit in us, through the arts of philosophy and the doctrine of human philosophy and wisdom, corrected by the divine, gained by nature, art and use, makes us happier in the comfort of this life.

units.la: Illam hanc in eodem subiecto tollere, & vicissim, negamus, hanc vero illi inseruire, ancillari, ac valde vtilem esse asseueramus. Neque est absurdum, sed admodum frequens ac vsitatum, Vnam disciplinam alteri in vsu commuani muni huius vitæ mutuas præstare operas: Divinamque, quod deest humanæ Philosophiæ, ut gubernatricem submini strare. Deus autor utriusque sapientiæ diuinæ & humanæ: Deus non ratum sui verbi est autor, sed & ipsius Naturæ (non quidem corruptæ, sed integræ, integrandæ, & integratæ.) Deus autor est omnis perfectionis & spiritualis in homine, & naturalis. Lux gratiæ & spiritus lumen naturæ, quatenus natura, non tollit, sed perficit, illa huius est instauratio & perfectio. Sed alibi hac de re.
units.tr: We deny that the one takes away the other in the same subject, and conversely; but we affirm that the latter serves and is subordinate to the former and is very useful. Nor is it absurd, but quite frequent and customary, for one discipline to render mutual services to another in the common use of this life, and for the divine to supply, as its guide, what human philosophy lacks. God is the author of both divine and human wisdom: God is the author not only of his Word but also of Nature itself (not corrupted, but whole, to be made whole, and made whole). God is the author of every perfection in man, both spiritual and natural. The light of grace and the light of nature's spirit, insofar as nature does not destroy but perfects, the former is the restoration and perfection of the latter. But on this matter elsewhere.

units.la: CAP. IV. De sapientia vera diuina.
units.tr: CAP. IV. On true divine wisdom.

units.la: HActenus de Christianæ Philosophiæ vera sapientia, literis interim tinctā: sequitur istius partitio è subiectis: Est enim vera sapientia diuina vel humana.
units.tr: So far concerning the true wisdom of Christian philosophy, meanwhile colored by letters. There follows its division according to its subjects: true wisdom is either divine or human.

units.la: Vera diuina sapientia est de rebus diuinis earumque diuinæ veritati conformis sapientia, diciturque Theosophia.
units.tr: True divine wisdom is the wisdom concerning divine things and conforming to divine truth, and it is called theosophy.

units.la: Hæc diuinitus inspirata hauritur ex verbo Dei, per viros Spiritu Dei actos, Prophetas & Apostolos, conscripto vel approbato.
units.tr: It is drawn from the Word of God, divinely inspired, written down or approved through the prophets and apostles, who were moved by the Spirit of God.

units.la: Hæc est canon seu regula homini Christiano ad salutem, tum credendorum, tum faciendorum.
units.tr: This is the canon or rule for the Christian man, for salvation, both of what is to be believed and of what is to be done.

units.la: Hæc est humanæ sapientiæ magi-stra, reformatrix, instauratrix & du-ctrix.
units.tr: This is the teacher, reformer, restorer and guide of human wisdom.

units.la: Hæc est sapientia spiritus, quæ vita est & pax : cui opponitur sapientia ac prudentia carnis, mundi, terrena, dæ-moniaca, quæ est mors & inimicitia aduersus Deum.
units.tr: This is the wisdom of the Spirit, which is life and peace. Opposed to it are the wisdom and prudence of the flesh, of the world, earthly and demonic, which is death and enmity against God.

units.la: Theosophia hæc doctrinam Chri-stianæ fidei, seu credendorum, & vitæ seu faciendorum continet.
units.tr: This theosophy contains the doctrine of the Christian faith, that is, what is to be believed, and the doctrine of life, that is, what is to be done.

units.la: Doctrina fidei explicat capita credendorum tum de Deo, tum de operibus Dei.
units.tr: The doctrine of faith sets out the articles to be believed, both concerning God and concerning the works of God.

units.la: De Deo primum essentia vno, deinde personis trino.
units.tr: Concerning God, first of the one essence, then of the three persons.

units.la: Essentia vno, per descriptionem, & attributa Dei.
units.tr: Of the one essence, through the description and attributes of God.

units.la: Personis trino, vt patre, filio & spiritu sancto.
units.tr: Of the three persons: Father, Son and Holy Spirit.

units.la: De operibus Dei credendum I. Decretum. II. Decreti executio.
units.tr: Concerning the works of God we believe: I. the decree; II. the execution of the decree.

units.la: Decretum de rebus vniuersis gubernandis, vel de certis creaturis eligendis, vel reprobandis.
units.tr: The decree concerns the governing of all things, or the choosing or rejecting of certain creatures.

units.la: Decreti executio est, tum Generalis, tum Specialis.
units.tr: The execution of the decree is both general and special.

units.la: Generalis est rerum tum creatio,
units.tr: The general execution is the creation of things,

units.la: tum creatarum rerum gubernatio in rebus vel Conseruandis, vel Deseren-dis, nempe permissione defectionis vel peccati, cuius tum autor, Diabolus & homo, tum multiplex est distributio: deinde immissione afflictionis & poe-næ, vbi pœnarum & afflictionum varia genera.
units.tr: and the governing of created things, either in preserving or in forsaking them, namely by permitting defection or sin, of which the author is both the devil and man, and of which there is a manifold distribution; then by the sending of affliction and punishment, where there are various kinds of punishments and afflictions.

units.la: Specialis executio est certarum, vt rationalium creaturarum, precipue vero hominum tum saluatio, tum damnatio.
units.tr: The special execution is the salvation or the damnation of certain rational creatures, and especially of men.

units.la: Saluatio fit ex misericordi gratia Dei salutis tum acquisitione, tum acquisitæ communicatione.
units.tr: Salvation comes from the merciful grace of God, both through the acquisition of salvation and through the communication of what has been acquired.

units.la: Acquisitio salutis fit àChristo incarnato per functionem officii mediatoris eidem incumbentis.
units.tr: The acquisition of salvation is made by Christ incarnate, through the performance of the office of mediator that rests upon him.

units.la: Christi itaque tum est incarnatio, tum officium.
units.tr: Thus there is in Christ both the incarnation and the office.

units.la: Incarnatio Christi ostendit, quis qualisque pepererit nobis salutem, vbi Christi persona vna in duabus naturis, assumente diuina, & assumpta humana, & vtriusque naturæ hypostatica vnione, eamq; consequente κοινωνία ἰδιωμάτων.
units.tr: The incarnation of Christ shows who and of what kind he was who brought us salvation: the one person of Christ in two natures, the divine nature assuming and the human nature assumed, with the hypostatic union of both natures, and the communication of properties [κοινωνία ἰδιωμάτων] that follows from it.

units.la: Officium Christi ostendit quomodo is dois nobis salutem acquisierit, estque triplex, Prophetico, sacerdotale & regium.
units.tr: The office of Christ shows how he acquired salvation for us, and it is threefold: prophetic, priestly and kingly.

units.la: Acquisitae salutis communicatio sequitur, quae fit partim in hac vita, partim in altera.
units.tr: The communication of the acquired salvation follows, and it takes place partly in this life, partly in the next.

units.la: In hac fit vita primum oblatione acquisitae salutis per vocationem, quae fit praedicatione verbi, scilicet legis & Euangelii.
units.tr: In this life it first happens through the offering of the acquired salvation by calling, which is effected by the preaching of the Word, namely of the law and of the Gospel.

units.la: Secundo collatione oblatae salutis per fidem a Deo donata in Christum, eaque fit iustificatione per remissionem peccatorum, & imputationem iustitiae Christi, deinde per sanctificationem spiritus sancti: adeoque simul per regenerationem in adoptionem filiorum Dei.
units.tr: Second, through the bestowing of the offered salvation by faith, which God gives in Christ. This takes place in justification, through the remission of sins and the imputation of the righteousness of Christ, and then through sanctification by the Holy Spirit; and so at the same time through regeneration into the adoption of the sons of God.

units.la: Tertio oblatae & collatae salutis obsignatione & speciali applicatione, quae fit per Sacramenta Testamenti, primum veteris, nempe per circumcisionem & pascha, deinde nunc novi, nempe per Baptismum & coenam Domini Iesu.
units.tr: Third, through the sealing and special application of the offered and bestowed salvation, which is effected through the sacraments of the testament: first of the old, namely circumcision and the Passover, and then of the new, namely baptism and the Lord's Supper of Jesus.

units.la: In altera vita communicabitur salus illa electis mortuis & resuscitatis per consummatam & plenariam glorificationem, ad vitam aeternam. Damnatio est iusta reproborum ad mortem æternam.
units.tr: In the other life that salvation will be imparted to the elect, who have died and been raised, through complete and full glorification, unto eternal life. Damnation is the just condemnation of the reprobate to eternal death.

units.la: Fitque iusta Dei hominũ in peccata lapsorum desertione, hominum illorũ impœnitentia, incredulitate, hypocrisi, induratione, &c. & postea iusta iudicis ad ignem æternum adiudicatione, cruciatuque nunquam finiendo.
units.tr: It comes about through God's just desertion of men who have fallen into sin, through the impenitence, unbelief, hypocrisy, hardening, etc., of those men, and afterwards through the just adjudication of the judge to eternal fire and to torment that shall never end.

units.la: Doctrina superest vitæ Christianæ, quæ debet fidei professioni respondere, vt cursu eius ad vitam & salutem contendentes, grati glorificemus Deum: damnationem vero & mortem euitantes, ingrati non offendamus Deũ. Ideoque tradit capita faciendorum & omittendorum.
units.tr: There remains the doctrine of Christian life, which ought to answer to the profession of faith, so that we, striving toward life and salvation in its course, may glorify God in gratitude, and, avoiding damnation and death, may not offend God by ingratitude. Therefore it hands down the articles of what is to be done and what is to be omitted.

units.la: Vitæ autem Christianæ tum norma est, tum opera bona.
units.tr: Of the Christian life there is both a norm and good works.

units.la: Norma est lex Dei.
units.tr: The norm is the law of God.

units.la: Lex Dei duabus constat tabulis, &c.
units.tr: The law of God consists of two tables, etc.

units.la: Opera bona sunt varia &c.
units.tr: Good works are various, etc.

units.la: Hæc qualiscunque est, & rudis profecto adumbratio sapientiæ diuinæ primis tantum informata lineis, in sacro codice passim descripta plenissime, de qua Theologi plenius.
units.tr: This, whatever its quality, is indeed a rude outline of divine wisdom, formed only in its first lines, described throughout in the sacred codex most fully; concerning it the theologians speak more fully.

units.la: §. Apodeixis.
units.tr: §. Apodeixis.

units.la: Qui in minimis ducit diuinam sapientiam, is et ... iam in postremis habet veram viam ac rationem consequenda salutis, & de Christiana repub. illam contemnendo ipse contemptus male meretur.
units.tr: He who esteems divine wisdom in the smallest matters ... already has in the last place the true way and method of attaining salvation, and by despising the Christian commonwealth he himself, being despised, deserves ill.

units.la: At qui Christianam philosophiam ex omni parte ducit in minimis, is etiam diuinam sapientiam salutiferam illam in Dei verbo reuelatam doctrinam habet in postremis. Quia philosophia est verae & literatae sapientiae doctrina. Illa autem sapientia primum est diuina, deinde est humana, & hæc quidem illius discipula, illique humili submissione subiecta.
units.tr: But he who esteems Christian philosophy in every respect in the smallest matters also has in the last place that saving divine wisdom, the doctrine revealed in the Word of God. For philosophy is the doctrine of true and learned wisdom. That wisdom is first divine, then human, and the latter is indeed the disciple of the former, subject to it in humble submission.

units.la: Ergo qui Christianam philosophiam ex omni parte despicatui habet & deridet, is veram viam ac rationem consequenda salutis & vita æterna procul dubio habet in postremis.
units.tr: Therefore, he who holds Christian philosophy in contempt and mocks it in every respect undoubtedly has, in the last place, the true way and method of attaining salvation and eternal life.

units.la: CAP. V.
units.tr: CHAPTER V.

units.la: De sapientia humana seu philosophia in specie dicta.
units.tr: On human wisdom, or what is specifically called philosophy.

units.la: HÆc de diuina seu rerum diuinarum & mysteriorum sapientia strictim: Humana vera sapientia nobis hic dicitur, non hominum carnalium carnalis & mundanorum mundana sapientia, quæ potius est insipientia & inimicitia aduersus Dei & rei veritatem: Sed rerum humanarum veritati conueniens intelligentia & scientia. Diciturque specialiter nomine Philosophiæ.
units.tr: So much for divine wisdom, or the wisdom of divine things and mysteries, in brief. Human wisdom, which is what we are dealing with here, is not the carnal wisdom of carnal men, or the worldly wisdom of worldly men, which is rather foolishness and enmity against God and the truth of things, but the understanding and knowledge that agrees with the truth of human things. It is called by the special name philosophy.

units.la: Res autem humanæ hoc loco sunt inge-
units.tr: The things of man, in this place, are

units.la: in genere omnes res, praeter res & mysteria diuina ac sacrosancta, quae in mundo sunt, queque sub hominum cadunt intelligentiam & cognitionem, siue sint entia realia, siue plasmata rationis, modo eorum intelligentia vera, faciat ad hominum fructuosam sapientiam.
units.tr: in general all things that exist in the world, apart from divine and most holy things and mysteries, and that fall under human understanding and knowledge, whether they are real beings or products of reason, provided that their true understanding contributes to a fruitful human wisdom.

units.la: Sapientia humana caste, sobrie ac religiose obseruat, sequitur, reueretur maiestatem sapientiae diuinae, quae humanae, vt alicubi deficientis, est complementum quoddam, perfectio & ἐπανόρθωμα.
units.tr: Human wisdom, when it is chaste, sober and religious, follows and reveres the majesty of divine wisdom. Human wisdom, which is somewhat deficient in places, is a kind of completion, perfection and correction by divine wisdom.

units.la: Haec lumen naturae ac rationis potissimum sanae, experientia non fallente obfirmatae, affectatur, quod ipsum gratiae lumen non perimit, sed perficit, quod sacrum flamen non abolet, sed adolet, quod caelestis aura purius & illustrius reddit, nō vero extinguit, sicut fere obscurior alicuius stellae lux perficitur ab illapsu radii solis.
units.tr: This wisdom is pursued chiefly by the light of nature and of reason, especially a sound reason confirmed by experience that does not deceive. The light of grace does not destroy this light but perfects it; the holy breath does not extinguish it but kindles it; the heavenly breeze makes it purer and brighter and does not put it out, just as the rather dim light of some star is perfected by the falling of a ray of the sun.

units.la: Praecipue vero, quoniam Deus est ipsissima veritas ac sapientia, verbum autem Dei ipsissimae veritatis ac sapientiae verbum, ac proinde quia vera sapientia ac prudentia, sapiensque, prudens. dens, ac certissima & infallibilis veritas, plurimarum etiam humanarum & politicarum rerum ac quaestionum in S. sancta Theologia continentur; ideo vera ac vere Christiana Philosophia, verusque ac vere Christianus philosophus, diuinam sapientiam verbi Dei vnice reueretur, & assiduè intuetur, neque quidquam, vllo modo contra Dei sapientiam & verbum aut confingit, aut asserit, aut defendit, sed perpetuo probe meminit, se in Deum, Deique verbum, in S. baptismo iurasse, adeoque in Christum, (qui ipsissima veritas est) baptizatum, & Christo per spiritum sanctum arctissime vnitum, firmissimeque incorporatum esse: ac proinde sibi nihil quicquam contra Deum & Christum suum, contra eius verbum ac sapientiam, vllo modo statuendum, credendum, disputandum aut docendum esse. Timor enim domini est omnis sapientiae caput & basis.
units.tr: Above all, since God is very truth and wisdom itself, and the Word of God is the word of very truth and wisdom, and since true wisdom and prudence, and the wise and prudent person, and the most certain and infallible truth, are contained in holy Theology, including a great many human and political matters and questions, therefore the true and truly Christian philosophy, and the true and truly Christian philosopher, reveres the divine wisdom of the Word of God alone and constantly contemplates it. He neither invents, nor asserts, nor defends anything in any way against the wisdom and Word of God. Rather, he always remembers well that in holy baptism he swore to God and the Word of God, and so was baptized into Christ (who is very truth itself), and is most closely united and firmly incorporated into Christ through the Holy Spirit. Accordingly, nothing whatever against God and his Christ, against his Word and wisdom, is to be established, believed, disputed or taught by him in any way. For the fear of the Lord is the beginning and foundation of all wisdom.

units.la: Ethnicos itaque paganos & atheos potius, quam veros & Christianos philosophos, vera illa & Christiana nostra Philosophia etiam in specie sic vulgo appellata, censet omnes eos, quicunque AristoAristotelem eiusque interpretes ac se-ctatores errantes, quicumque Plato-ne eiusq; asseclas exorbitantes à via ve-ritatis & sapientiæ veræ, quicumque quemuis alium philosophum, contra diuinam sapietiam verbum ve Dei sen-tientem aut statuetem,sectantur,tuen-tur & vanis distinctionibus coloribus-que, taliú philosophorú sententias sal-sas colorant,fucant,interpolant,& vel cum Dei sanćto verbo temere ac cōtra conscientiā conciliare annituntur:qui deliria ac paganismos ethnicorū phi-losophorum per suam duplicis verita-tis Chymæra & futilissimarum distin-ctiuncularum Pandoram cum sapien-tiæ diuinæ oraculis consentire clami-tant.
units.tr: Therefore that true and Christian philosophy of ours, which is commonly called by this specific name, considers pagans and atheists rather than true and Christian philosophers to be all those who follow, defend and embellish Aristotle and his interpreters and followers when they err; all those who stray from the way of truth and true wisdom by following Plato and his adherents; and all those who follow any other philosopher who thinks or asserts things against the divine wisdom and Word of God. Such people, with empty distinctions and colors, dress up, falsify and tamper with the opinions of such philosophers, and rashly strive to reconcile them with the holy Word of God, against their own conscience. They loudly claim that the delusions and paganism of the heathen philosophers agree with the oracles of divine wisdom, using their chimera of a twofold truth and their Pandora of the most trivial little distinctions.

units.la: Christianus philosophus Christia-norum sapientiā tam rerū humanarū, quam diuinarum,potius stabilit,quam paganismos & atheismos ethnicorum etiam maximi nominis : gloriam Dei & autoritatem verbi Dei potius, quam gloriam & autoritatem Aristotelis vel Platonis, &c.sartam tactam conseruat: nouit hanc vanam mundi sapientiam ac paganam philosophiam esse stultitiam tiam & abominationem coram Deo. 1.Cor.2.Colos.2.1.Timot.6.
units.tr: The Christian philosopher establishes the wisdom of Christians, both human and divine, rather than the paganism and atheism of the heathen, even of those of greatest name. He keeps intact and inviolate the glory of God and the authority of the Word of God rather than the glory and authority of Aristotle or Plato, etc. He knows that this vain worldly wisdom and pagan philosophy is foolishness and an abomination before God. 1 Cor. 2; Col. 2; 1 Tim. 6.

units.la: Schola Christianorum philosophica, merito male audit, & ab imperitis harmostis, vt & piis cordatisque Theologis reprehenditur, confertur cum pomis Sodomiticis,& nescio quibus aliis rebus nihili ac nauci, quod sit schola nugarum, superstitionum, paganismorum, impiorum atheismorum & mendaciorum. Meminerit philosophus in scholaChristiana Aristotelem, aut quemuis alium philosophum, non posse esse supra Christū, Dei & veritatis sapiētiā, cedat creatori creatura in veritate ac sapientia : Neque existimet philosophus nō in solo Theologico auditorio, dogmata Christianæ sapientiæ ac fidei, valere, credi atque defendi debere: sed legem Dei in sua schola æque, atque in aliis obseruari debere: Deum tam ius in philosophum habere, quam in quemuis alium, etiam vilissimum sutorem, cui non licet in sua schola seu officina mendacia & nugas tractare.
units.tr: The Christian philosophical school is rightly ill spoken of, and is reproached by unskilled critics, as well as by pious and judicious theologians. It is compared with Sodomite apples and I know not what other worthless and trifling things, because it is a school of trifles, superstitions, paganism, impious atheism and lies. Let the philosopher in the Christian school remember that Aristotle or any other philosopher cannot stand above Christ, the wisdom of God and of truth; the creature must yield to the Creator in truth and wisdom. Nor let the philosopher think that the doctrines of Christian wisdom and faith have force, and ought to be believed and defended, only in the theological lecture hall, while the law of God is not equally observed in his own school as in others. God has as much right over the philosopher as over any other person, even the humblest cobbler, who is not permitted to handle lies and trifles in his own school or workshop.

units.la: Philosophus Christianus in philosophiæ verae tractatione non ludet, sed serio aget: cum veritate & Deo iocari non licet. Philosophus perinde atque alius de omni verbo otioso, quodcunque ex ore ipsius egressum fuerit, reddet coram Deo rationem. Ideoque defensione paganismorum & errorum a philosophorum non ludificabit tenerā adolescentiam.
units.tr: The Christian philosopher will not play in the treatment of true philosophy but will act in earnest, since it is not permitted to jest with truth and with God. The philosopher, like everyone else, will give an account before God of every idle word that has come out of his mouth. Therefore he will not, by defending the paganism and errors of the philosophers, mock the tender youth.

units.la: Neque enim disputandi gratia (imo ingenium petulanter ostentandi gratia) licet coram Deo, nostris philosophis nugari & mentiri, non licet veritatem inuoluere, auditores reddere dubios, præbere scandalum, ethnicorum falsa commenta & proponere & petulanter tueri. Philosophia candidæ & apertę veritatis amatrix, sophisticam omnem auersatur.
units.tr: For it is not permitted before God for our philosophers to trifle and lie for the sake of disputation (or rather, for the sake of showing off their wit with impudence); it is not permitted to obscure the truth, to make hearers doubtful, to give offence, or to propose and impudently defend the false inventions of the heathen. Philosophy, the lover of plain and open truth, shuns all sophistry.

units.la: Duplex vero illa veritas vnius eiusdemque rei, vna Theologica sapientiæ diuinæ, altera Philosophica, sapientiæ humanæ, est diabolicum ad omnes errores atque atheismos excusandos & defendendos accomodatissimum figmentum. Verum vnum ac simplex, suique perpetuo simile: falsum autē multiplex, suique perpetuo dissimile.
units.tr: That twofold truth of one and the same thing, one theological, of divine wisdom, the other philosophical, of human wisdom, is a diabolical fabrication most suited to excusing and defending all errors and atheisms. The truth is one and simple, and always like itself; falsehood is manifold and always unlike itself.

units.la: Omne verum, testante etiam Aristotele, ipsum sibi ipsi per omnia consentit. Inter verum & falsum, medium nullum. Sermo etiam philosophi, sit etiam etiam, non non: si quid praeter haec adiungitur, a malo proficiscitur.
units.tr: Every truth, as Aristotle also testifies, agrees with itself in all things. Between truth and falsehood there is no middle. The speech of the philosopher too should be yes, yes; no, no; whatever is added beyond these comes from evil.

units.la: Verum vero consonat etiam in officina philosophica: & verū a falso quam primum ibidem discrepat.
units.tr: True things agree even in the philosophical workshop, and as soon as possible truth differs from falsehood there as well.

units.la: Veritas etiam unius eiusdem rei sincera secum nullo modo pugnat: Ideoque sana Philosophia seu humana sapientia, & Theosophia seu diuina sapientia sibi inuicem non contradicunt, aut se inuicem euertunt: Vera quippe utraque sapientia, si quando in quaestione aliqua coincidat, de una eademque re, uno eodemque modo accepta, unam eandemq; veritatem pronunciat; secus enim nequaquam erit vera, sed nugax & pagana.
units.tr: The sincere truth of one and the same thing in no way conflicts with itself. Therefore sound philosophy, or human wisdom, and theosophy, or divine wisdom, do not contradict or overthrow each other. For if both true wisdoms happen to coincide in some question, concerning one and the same thing, taken in one and the same way, they pronounce one and the same truth; otherwise one of them would by no means be true, but trifling and pagan.

units.la: Non est Philosopho nostro autoritas Aristotelis, vel alius cuiusuis cum veritate, non opinio, persuasio & praeiudicium cum vera ratione, non ratio verisimilis cum necessaria veritate imprudenter & imprudenter confundenda. Haec pauca praelibare volui in humanae sapientiae, quam Philosophiam speciali nomine dicimus, propterea quod multorum & deprauationi & conuiciis sit obnoxia, principio, vt intelligat lector, me quamuis non tueri philosophandi rationem.
units.tr: For our philosopher, the authority of Aristotle or of any other person is not to be confused rashly with truth; opinion, persuasion and prejudice are not to be confused with true reason; probable reasoning is not to be confused with necessary truth. I have wished to touch briefly on these few points concerning human wisdom, which we call philosophy by its special name, because it is liable to the depravation and abuse of many. This is at the beginning, so that the reader may understand that, although I do not defend the manner of philosophizing, I...

units.la: Apodeixis 6.
units.tr: Apodeixis 6.

units.la: Quisquis humanarum rerum sapientiam omnem ducit impudenter & imprudenter infra se, & scientiam rerum mundanarum philosophicam alto animo spernit ac pro stercore habet: is extra se raptus rerum furiosa ignorantia non magni facit & sui ipsius & rerum earum, quarum vsu communis vita haec destitui non potest commode, cognitionem. Permagna enim stultitia est, ea aut nescire velle, aut eorum scientiam asininis conuiciorum onerare plaustris, quorum indiget quotidianus vita vsus, & sine quibus ipse in hoc mundo & vita esse ac versari non potest.
units.tr: Whoever rashly and foolishly holds all the wisdom of human affairs beneath himself, and with lofty spirit despises the philosophical knowledge of worldly things and counts it as dung, such a man, carried out of himself by a frenzied ignorance, sets no great store by knowledge of himself and of those things whose use this common life cannot conveniently do without. For it is great foolishness either to wish not to know these things, or to load their knowledge with asinine insults as with wagon-loads, when the daily use of life requires them, and without which a man cannot exist or live his life in this world.

units.la: At vero quisquis philosophiam specialiter appellatam, hoc est, studium rerum humanarum, seu ad hominem hominisque scientiam pertinentium, parui ducit, is etiam omuem rerum humanarum & mundanarum verum ac vtilem sapientiam impudenter ac imprudenter pro stercore habet. Est enim Philosophia non modo diuinarum, sed etiam humanarum rerum scientia, vt Cic. in off. describit.
units.tr: But whoever makes little of philosophy, as it is specially called, that is, the study of human affairs, or of things pertaining to man and human knowledge, he also rashly and foolishly holds as dung all true and useful wisdom of human and worldly things. For philosophy is "the knowledge not only of divine but also of human things," as Cicero describes it in his De Officiis.

units.la: Ergo quisquis hanc philosophiam pro stercore habet, is extra se ignorantia furore raptus, nō magni facit, & sui & rerum earum cognitionem necessariā quarum vsu communis hac vita vtiliter & commode non potest carere.
units.tr: Therefore whoever holds this philosophy as dung, that man, carried out of himself by the frenzy of ignorance, sets no great store by the knowledge of himself and of those things, which this common life cannot usefully and conveniently go without.

units.la: CAP. VI.
units.tr: CAP. VI.

units.la: De Philosophiæ causis procreantibus.
units.tr: On the efficient causes of philosophy.

units.la: PHilosophia porro hæc specialiter dicta, seu sapientia humana est artium humanitatis seu humaniorū, vulgo liberalium ordinata comprehensio & doctrina.
units.tr: This philosophy, taken in the specific sense, or human wisdom, is the ordered comprehension and teaching of the arts of humanity, or the humane arts, commonly called the liberal arts.

units.la: Ergo quicquid est hac ratione Philosophicum, id est comprehensum omne artibus humanioribus & humanæ sapientiæ syntagmate: Et quicquid hisce artibus legitime traditis continetur, id pertinet ad hanc Philosophiam. Hinc adeo est quod Plato Philosophiam dicat Ἐμπειρίαν τεχνῶν πασῶν τῶν ἀξιολόγων. Hinc Cicero ait omnes artes, quæ ad humanitatem pertinent habere quoddam commune vinculum, & quasi cognatione quadam inter se contineri: Unde etiam Philosophia solet appellari ςυγκυκλοπαιδία.
units.tr: Therefore whatever is philosophical in this sense is wholly contained in the humane arts and in the system of human wisdom, and whatever is contained in these arts when they are properly taught belongs to this philosophy. Hence Plato calls philosophy [Ἐμπειρία τεχνῶν πασῶν τῶν ἀξιολόγων], experience of all the worthy arts. Hence Cicero says that all the arts that pertain to humanity have a certain common bond and are held together by a kind of kinship. Whence philosophy is also commonly called [ἐγκυκλοπαιδία], encyclopaedia.

units.la: Ars autem hæc humanior est methodica scientificorum præceptorum comprehensio. Vt Philosophia est tota artium humaniorum comprehensio: ita ars ipsa est præceptorum scientificorum methodica syllepsis seu systema.
units.tr: This humane art is a methodical comprehension of scientific precepts. As philosophy is the whole comprehension of the humane arts, so the art itself is a methodical grasp or system of scientific precepts.

units.la: Seu est methodica præceptorum verorum, homogeneorum & ad vtilem finem vitæ spectantium comprehensio.
units.tr: Or it is a methodical comprehension of true precepts that are homogeneous and bear on the useful end of life.

units.la: Ars hæc scientificis constat præce-ptis, quia ita debent esse conformata, vt sint accommodata ad pariendam scientiam, quæ scientia artium præce-ptis comparata, etiã dicitur ars & ha-bitus in mente artificis bene agendi, scilicet secundum artis præcepta.
units.tr: This art consists of scientific precepts, since they must be so framed that they are fitted to produce science; and the science acquired from the precepts of an art is itself also called an art, and is a habit in the mind of the craftsman of acting well, namely according to the precepts of the art.

units.la: Artes hæ ἐγκυκλοπαιδίᾳ Philoso-phica comprehensæ dicûtur Philoso-phicæ: quarum consideramus primum quædam argumenta prima, deinde distributionem & totã œconomiam.
units.tr: These arts, comprised in the philosophical encyclopaedia, are called philosophical arts. Of them we shall consider first certain primary arguments, and then their division and whole economy.

units.la: Ex argumentis primis Philosophicarum artium primo loco occurrunt discutiendæ causæ, quarum aliæ sunt Externæ, aliæ Internæ.
units.tr: Among the primary arguments concerning the philosophical arts, the causes must be examined first; of these some are external and some internal.

units.la: Externæ causæ manentes extra Philosophiam, Philosophicasque disciplinas sunt Efficiens & Finis.
units.tr: The external causes, which lie outside philosophy and the philosophical disciplines, are the efficient and the final cause.

units.la: Efficiens prima vniuersalis est Deus omnis boni fons, & omnis sapientiæ autor. Qui largitur sapientiam omnem, is etiam humanam hominibus dat sapientiam. At Deus ille omnisapiens affectu & effectu, essentia & efficientia largitur omnem sapientiam veram. Danielis 2. Respondit Daniel & dixit: Sit nomen Dei benedictum à seculo & vsque in seculum. Nam sapientia & potentia eius est: Et ipse mutat tempora & articulos temporum. rum, transfert reges & constituit reges. Dat sapien‐tiam sapientibus, & scientiam scientibus, & gnaris intelligentiam. Ipse revelat profunda & abscondi‐ta, novit quod in tenebris est, & lux cum eo habitat. Unde & Iacobus Apostolus cap. 1. hortatur nos: Quod si cui vestrum deest sapientia, postulet a Deo, qui dat omnibus simpliciter, nec exprobat: Et dabitur ei. Sapientissimus hominum id suo calculo & experimento testatum facit. cap. 7. Sap. Sapientia, inquit, est inexhaustus hominibus thesaurus: quo qui utuntur, ii cum Deo coeunt in amicitiam, ob doctrinae dotes commendati. Mihi quidem dedit Deus ut sententiose loquerer, & iis digna, quae mihi concessa sunt, cogitarem: quippe qui & sapientia sit auctor & sapientum moderator. Etenim in eius manu & nos sumus & sermones nostri, omnisque prudentia & artium peritia. Is enim mihi dedit rerum cognitionem verissimam, ut sciam mundi statum & elementorum effectionem. Principium & finem & medium temporum, solstitiorum vicissitudines, & tempestatum mutationes, annorum orbes & siderum situs, & naturas animantium, & bestiarum animos, & ventorum impetus, & ratiocinationes hominum, & stirpium differentias, & radicum vires: Denique quaecunque vel occulta sunt, vel aperta, novi, utpote cum me omnium opifex docuerit sapientia. Inest enim in ea spiritus sagax, sanctus, unigenus, multiplex, subtilis, agilis, expeditus, incontaminatus, clarus, innoxius, boni studiosus, acutus, ineluctabilis, beneficus, humanus, fixus, firmus, securus, omnipotens, omnia contemplans, & omnes mentis puros tenuesque spiritus obiens. Nam quoniam quouis motu mobilior sapientia omnia pra puritate penetrat, obitque. Est enim quidam vapor diuina potentia, & syncera gloria omnipotentis effluentia, quo fit vt nihil in eam cadat polluti. Est enim lucis æterna splendor, & intaminatum actionis Dei speculum, & imago bonitatis eius. Et cum sit vna, omnia potest: & in seipsa permanens, omnia renouat: & per secula in sanctas animas migrans, Dei amicos & vates efficit. Nihil enim amat Deus, nisi sapientia contubernalem. Idem prouerb.cap.2. prabe aurem sapientia, applica animum ad prudentiam. Nam si intelligentiam vocabis, si prudentiam voce tua interpellabis, si eam, vt argentum, atque pecuniam quaeres ac vestigabis, ita Iouae metum percipies, Deique cognitionem inuenies. Etenim Ioua dat sapientiam: ex eius ore licentia est atque prudentia, itque probis profectum reseruat, protegens gerentes se syncere, mores æquos, piorumque suorum institutum tuens atque conseruans.
units.tr: The first and universal efficient cause is God, the fountain of all good and the author of all wisdom. He who bestows all wisdom also gives human wisdom to men. But that God, all-wise in affection and effect, in essence and efficacy, bestows all true wisdom. Daniel 2. Daniel answered and said: Blessed be the name of God from age to age, for wisdom and power are his; and he changes the times and the seasons, transfers kings and sets up kings. He gives wisdom to the wise and knowledge to those who know, and understanding to the discerning. He reveals deep and hidden things; he knows what is in darkness, and light dwells with him. Hence also the Apostle James, in chapter 1, exhorts us: If any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask of God, who gives to all generously and without reproach, and it shall be given him. The wisest of men attests this by his own reckoning and experience, Wisdom chapter 7: Wisdom, he says, is an inexhaustible treasure to men; those who use it become friends of God, commended for the gifts of teaching. God has indeed given me to speak with judgement and to think things worthy of what has been granted me, since he is both the author of wisdom and the guide of the wise. For both we and our words are in his hand, and all prudence and skill in the arts. For he has given me a most true knowledge of things, so that I know the state of the world and the constitution of the elements: the beginning, end and middle of times, the changes of the solstices and the variations of the seasons, the cycles of years and the positions of the stars, the natures of living things and the dispositions of beasts, the violence of winds and the reasonings of men, the differences of plants and the powers of roots. In short, I know whatever is hidden or open, since wisdom, the artificer of all things, has taught me. For in her is a spirit that is keen, holy, unique, manifold, subtle, nimble, unhindered, undefiled, clear, harmless, eager for good, sharp, irresistible, beneficent, humane, steadfast, firm, secure, almighty, overseeing all things, and passing through all pure and subtle minds. For wisdom, more mobile than any motion, penetrates and pervades all things by reason of her purity. For she is a breath of the power of God and a pure emanation of the glory of the Almighty; therefore nothing defiled falls into her. For she is the eternal radiance of light, an unspotted mirror of the working of God, and an image of his goodness. And though she is one, she can do all things; remaining in herself she renews all things, and passing through the ages into holy souls she makes them friends of God and prophets. For God loves nothing but the one who dwells with wisdom. The same in Proverbs chapter 2: Incline your ear to wisdom, apply your heart to understanding. For if you call for insight and lift up your voice for prudence, if you seek her as silver and search for her as for money, then you will understand the fear of the Lord and find the knowledge of God. For the Lord gives wisdom; from his mouth come knowledge and prudence, and he stores up sound wisdom for the upright, protecting those who walk sincerely, guarding the paths of justice and preserving the way of his faithful.

units.la: Prima itaque causa Efficiens Philosophiæ est ipsa Sophia omniscia, ex cuius plenitudine deriuantur riuuli in omnes sapientes, seu a qua omnis proficiscitur sapientia: est ipsa patris æterna sapientia λόγος, in quo omnes thesauri sapientiæ & cognitionis sunt abscONDITI: Est ipse spiritus sapientiæ omnem in omnibus sapientibus sapientiam efficiens.
units.tr: The first efficient cause of philosophy, therefore, is Wisdom herself, who knows all things, from whose fullness streams flow into all the wise, or from whom all wisdom proceeds: she is the eternal wisdom of the Father, the Word, in whom all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden; she is the Spirit of wisdom himself, producing all wisdom in all the wise.

units.la: Ab hac prima sapientia & sapientiæ causa, descendunt causæ secundæ, quibus cum illa sapientiam communicat, quique sapientiam à Deo nacti sapientes appellantur.
units.tr: From this first wisdom and cause of wisdom descend the secondary causes, with whom she shares her wisdom, and who, having received wisdom from God, are called wise.

units.la: Sunt autem hi homines artifices sapientes longo vsu experientiaque edocti, & spiritu sapientiæ & prudentiæ scientiæque præditi, & à Deo ad artes illas conscribendas excitati.
units.tr: These men are skilled craftsmen, taught by long practice and experience, endowed with the Spirit of wisdom, prudence and knowledge, and roused by God to write down those arts.

units.la: Horum artificum alii veram diuinam sapientiam & scientiam cum hac humana, hoc est, rerum humanarum intelligentia coniunxere, vt veri Dei cultores: alii vero vera diuina sapientia destituti rerum humanarum præclara cognitione præcelluerunt, vt idololatræ ac gentiles seu pagani Philosophi, quibus quidem spiritus Dei dona quædam excellētis ingenii, iudicii, intelligentiæ ac sagacis indagationis concesserit, sed quia luce supernæ sapientiæ & gratiæ caruerunt, non nunquam quosdam errorum ac paganismorum næuos adspersérunt Philosophiæ.
units.tr: Of these craftsmen, some joined true divine wisdom and knowledge to this human wisdom, that is, to understanding of human affairs, as worshippers of the true God; but others, lacking true divine wisdom, excelled in an outstanding knowledge of human affairs, like the idolaters and gentiles, or pagan philosophers, to whom the Spirit of God indeed granted certain gifts of excellent talent, judgement, understanding and keen inquiry, but because they lacked the light of heavenly wisdom and grace, they sometimes sprinkled blemishes of error and paganism upon philosophy.

units.la: Quo vero artifex quiuis propius abfuit à sapientiæ cœlestis gratia & scientia, quoque rerum veritati (non hominum minum traditioni & autoritati) plus tribuit operæ,quo pluta expertus vero vlu obseruauit, quoque rationis luce fuit illustrior; Eo etiam certiora præcepta,meliores commentationes, dexteriores disceptationes nobis reliquit, eo vtiliores artes in Philosophiæ familiam intulit.
units.tr: Moreover, the closer any craftsman has been to the grace and knowledge of heavenly wisdom, and the more effort he has given to the truth of things (not to the tradition and authority of men), the more he has learned and observed by true practice, and the more he has been illumined by the light of reason, the more certain precepts, the better commentaries and the more skilful disputations he has left us; and the more useful the arts he has introduced into the family of philosophy.

units.la: Omnes autem hi autores, & artifices varia & multa pro vi & efficacitate diuersorum donorum illis à Deo concessorum, ad ædificium Philosophicum extruendum, vti ad fabricam Solomonici templi varii varia contulerunt.
units.tr: All these authors and craftsmen, however, have contributed various and many things, according to the power and efficacy of the different gifts granted them by God, to the building up of the philosophical edifice, just as for the construction of Solomon's temple various people contributed various things.

units.la: Donorum etiam in hac sapientiæ domo sunt diuersa genera, sunt non pares diuisiones, licet vnus sit sapientiæ spiritus. Vnicuique datur artifici, (sit fas, illud Apostolicum ad hæc etiam eruditæ sapientiæ studia, quæ sine singularibus Dei, omnis scientiæ scaturigine, non perficiuntur, pie, non petulanter applicare) donorum certa mesura, prout expedit. Nam huic quidem per spiritum datur sermo sapientiæ, alii sermo scientiæ secundum eundem spiritum, alii alia & discrepantia dona conceduntur. Sed hæc omnia efficit vnus ille spiritus, diuidens peculiariter vnicuique sicut vult.
units.tr: There are also different kinds of gifts in this house of wisdom, and the divisions are not equal, although there is one Spirit of wisdom. To each craftsman is given, a measure of gifts fitting to his need (let it be permitted to apply devoutly, not wantonly, that Apostolic saying to these studies of learned wisdom as well, which cannot be brought to completion without the particular gifts of God, the fountain of all knowledge). For to one is given through the Spirit the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge according to the same Spirit, and to others different and diverse gifts are granted. But all these things are produced by that one Spirit, who distributes to each one individually as he wills.

units.la: Quod si quis in hoc Philosophico ædificio extruendo super fundamentum Veritatis & sapientiæ vtilis, aurum, argentum, lapides preciosos, ligna, fœnum, stipulam superstruxerit, cuiusque opus examen sincerum manifestabit: Dies etiam & tempus, cuius filia est veritas, declarabit, & cuiusque opus, quale sit, ignis Veritatis & sapientiæ veræ probabit.
units.tr: But if anyone, in building this philosophical edifice upon the foundation of truth and wisdom, has added useful gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay or straw, the sincere examination will reveal each one's work. The day and time, of which truth is the daughter, will also declare it, and the fire of truth and true wisdom will test what sort of work each one has done.

units.la: 7. Apodeixis.
units.tr: 7. Apodeixis.

units.la: Donorum Dei contemptores & derisores sunt in ipsum Deum extreme ingrati, ac digni qui æternum istis Dei benevola & benefica liberalitate oblatis donis priuentur, si habeant, si non, quibus nunquam conferantur. Oblatam enim Dei gratiam & beneficentiam, qui cæca superbia & pertinacia respuit, Deus non potest non tanquam ingratam bestiam auersari.
units.tr: The despisers and mockers of God's gifts are in the highest degree ungrateful toward God himself, and they deserve to be deprived forever of these gifts, offered by God's kind and bountiful generosity, if they have them, and never to receive them if they do not. For God cannot help but turn away from the ungrateful beast who, through blind pride and obstinacy, spurns the grace and kindness that is offered.

units.la: Sana & Christiana Philosophia contemptores & derisores, sunt donorum Dei, non sane vulgarium & vilium, (quamuis nullum ex Dei muneribus sit vile) singularium & summe vtilium contemptores & derisores. Sunt enim primum Artes humanitatis omnium sanorum confessione, dona Dei non contemnenda. Sapientia etiam {s}am illa, qua in rerum humanarum tractatio- ne recte sapimus, scientia rerum scitu etiam hac in vita vtilium, est a Deo, tanquā & omnis boni, & omnis sapientiae, & bonorū donorū autore, & perpetim profluente fonte, vti est demonstratum. Ideoq; non Cicero ethnicus ille tam ingratus fuit vnquam Deo donatori suo, quam non nulli, aut imperiti Philosophiae ofores, aut malitiosi eiusdem canes ac rosores: Ille enim 1. Tuscula. ait: Philosophia mater omnium bonarum artium, nihil est aliud, nisi (vt Plato ait) bonum & inuentum Deorum. Hac nos primum ad Deorum cultum (arrigis aures calumniator? demitte, Philosophia, qua talis, non idolatriam, non deorum illorum, sed generatim esse Deum, Et esse Deum colendum suasit, distingue essentiam rei ab eius accidentibus) tum ad modestiam, magnitudinemque animi erudiuit, eademque ab animo, tanquam ab oculis caliginem dispulit, vt omnia supera, infera, prima, vltima, media videremus. (Conatum specta & lauda, successum infelicem obpaganismos secutum deplora.) Idem de vniuerf. Nullum bonum Philosophia optabilius, nullum praestantius neque datum est mortalium generi, deorum consensu, neque dabitur.
units.tr: The despisers and mockers of a sound and Christian philosophy are despisers of gifts of God that are indeed not common or cheap (although no gift of God is cheap), but singular and supremely useful. For first, by the universal confession of all sound people, the liberal arts of humanity are gifts of God not to be scorned. Likewise, that wisdom by which we rightly judge in the management of human affairs, and the knowledge of things worth knowing even in this life, come from God, as from the author of all good, all wisdom and all good gifts, and as a fountain flowing without end, as has been shown. Therefore the heathen Cicero was never so ungrateful to God his giver as some are, either unskilled enemies of philosophy or malicious dogs and gnawers of it. For he says in the first book of the Tusculan Disputations: Philosophy, the mother of all the good arts, is nothing other than (as Plato says) a good and discovered gift of the gods. It first taught us the worship of the gods (do you prick up your ears, slanderer? put it down, Philosophy, such as you are, did not persuade us to idolatry or to those gods of theirs, but generally that there is a God, and that God is to be worshipped; distinguish the essence of a thing from its accidents), then it trained us to modesty and greatness of soul, and the same philosophy dispelled the darkness from the soul as from the eyes, so that we could see all things, the high, the low, the first, the last, the middle. (Look at the attempt and praise it; lament the unhappy outcome that followed from paganism.) In the same work: No good is more desirable than philosophy, no excellence has been given to the human race, by the consent of the gods, nor will it be given.

units.la: Ergo Philosophiae sanae comtemptores & deriforesfunt praeclarorum Dei donorum ingrati contemptores, neque digni qui tantis fruantur donis.
units.tr: Therefore the despisers and mockers of sound philosophy are ungrateful despisers of the excellent gifts of God, and they are not worthy to enjoy such gifts.

units.la: Non est candidi pectoris, sed peruersi impostoris, rem ipsam propter abusum & malum successum criminari: & vitia hominum ipsis affricare artibus. At qui hodie ex alto despiciunt, & calumnia-rum, scurrilium que scommatu fulminibus in Phi-losophiam nostram detonant, rem ipsam per se bo-nam, & laudabilem Philosophiam propter abusum & successum alicubi minus optatum, qui est ex illo-rum hominum mala qualitate, qui eam coluerunt, aut auxerunt, criminantur, & hominum pagano-rum vitia & lapsus deplorandos affricare satagunt ipsis artibus philosophicis.
units.tr: It is not the mark of an honest heart but of a perverse impostor to accuse the thing itself on account of abuse and a bad outcome, and to fasten the vices of men upon the arts themselves. Yet those who today look down from on high and thunder against our philosophy with the lightning-bolts of calumny and buffoonish mockery, accuse philosophy, a thing good and praiseworthy in itself, of abuse and of an outcome somewhere less desired, which comes from the bad character of those men who cultivated or advanced it; and they labor to fasten upon the philosophical arts themselves the vices and lapses of pagan men, which ought to be lamented.

units.la: Quapropter qui hodie ex alto ita contemnen-do & fulminando in sanam nostram detonant Phi-losophiam, non sunt candidi pectoris homines, sed sophistae ac impostores.
units.tr: Wherefore those who today thunder from on high with such contempt and fury against our sound philosophy are not men of an honest heart, but sophists and impostors.

units.la: CAP. VII.
units.tr: CAP. VII.

units.la: De Philosophicarum artium principiis, quibus artifices usi eas genuerunt.
units.tr: On the principles of the philosophical arts, which the craftsmen used when they produced them.

units.la: ARtifices porro illi ingeniosi à Deo excitati in artium Philosophica-rum constitutione, usi sunt Sensu & Ratione, Christianus addit: illuminata spiritu veritatis. His inquam gnaui & periti artifices usi, omnes nobis artes pepererunt.
units.tr: Those ingenious craftsmen, roused by God to establish the philosophical arts, used the senses and reason; the Christian adds: enlightened by the Spirit of truth. Using these, I say, skilled and experienced craftsmen have brought forth all the arts for us.

units.la: Sensus artificum, bene affectus nec impeditus, nō quidem magister & doctor est praeceptorum & artium, sed eius beneficio artifices omnis generis exempla, id est, singularia seu res sin-gulagulares, sensibus quippe obuias notarunt & deprehenderunt, atq; ita mentiseu rationi suggesserunt.
units.tr: The senses of the craftsmen, being well disposed and unimpeded, are not indeed the teacher and instructor of the precepts and arts; but by their help the craftsmen noted and detected examples of every kind, that is, particular things or singular objects, which lie open to the senses, and so they passed them on to the mind or reason.

units.la: Ratio deinde, qua vsi artifices, tum inuentrix est, tum iudicatrix seu excultrix.
units.tr: Then reason, which the craftsmen use, is both inventive and judging, or refining.

units.la: Ratione inuentrice ita vtitur artifex, vt tum obseruet res singulares sensuum beneficio notatas & deprehensas, tum colligat seu inducat generalia ex singularibus sufficienter collectis.
units.tr: The craftsman uses inventive reason in such a way that he both observes the particular things noted and detected by the aid of the senses, and gathers or infers general truths from the singulars sufficiently collected.

units.la: Obseruat autem res a sensibus notatas, & animaduersas per Empeirian, vel per Historian.
units.tr: He observes the things noticed by the senses and taken note of through empeiria or through historia.

units.la: Per Empeirian seu experientiam ac vsum obseruat res singulares, quas ita se habere ipse experitur; quam Plato tanti fecit, vt vel soli huic artium inuentionem, asscripsisse videatur in Gorgia: O Chaerepho, ait, multa artes, hominum sunt experientia prudenter inuenta. Experientia siquidem efficit, vt artificiose, inexperientia vero vt temere vita nostra progrediatur; & scientia & ars hominibus per experientiam. Experientia siquidem artem genuit, inexperientia autem temeritatem. Quod dictum in tato habuit precio P. Ramus, vt optauerit in Metaphysicis, literis aureis in vestibulo philosophicarum scholarum omnium inscriptum esse, vt illuc accedentibus persuasum effet, nullum in artibus documentum recipiendum, quod ab usu & experientia verorum exemplorum observatum, & inductum non esset: Mille siquidem, inquit, somnia & deliramenta itaque in artes liberales nequaquam irrepsissent.
units.tr: Through empeiria, or experience and practice, he observes particular things which he himself experiences to be so. Plato valued this so highly that he seems in the Gorgias to have ascribed the invention of the arts to it alone: O Chaerephon, he says, many arts of men have been prudently discovered by experience. For experience makes our life proceed skilfully, but inexperience makes it proceed carelessly; and science and art come to men through experience. For experience produced art, but inexperience produced rashness. P. Ramus held this saying in such high regard that in his Metaphysics he wished it inscribed in golden letters in the vestibule of all philosophical schools, so that it would be impressed on those who approach: that no teaching in the arts should be received which has not been observed and inferred from the practice and experience of true examples. For, he says, a thousand dreams and follies would by no means have crept into the liberal arts.

units.la: Per Historian observat res, quas non ipse experitur, sed ab aliis proditas & animaduersas sedulo ac dextre ad mentem transmittit ac observat.
units.tr: Through historia he observes things which he does not experience himself, but which have been reported and noted by others, and he carefully and skilfully passes them on to the mind and observes them.

units.la: Colligit deinde & inducit ex specialibus exemplis recte observatis, ac sufficienter collectis generalem aliquam regulam, ac praecepti constitutionem. Est enim hic inductio nihil aliud, quam sensib. perceptarum & mente observatarum rerum, earumque singularium plena atque sufficiens collectio, accumulatio, ut inde statuatur generale aliquod theorema.
units.tr: Then he gathers and infers from specific examples rightly observed, and sufficiently collected, some general rule and the establishment of a precept. For induction here is nothing other than the full and sufficient collection and accumulation of things perceived by the senses and observed by the mind, and of those singulars, so that some general theorem may be set up from them.

units.la: Ratio insuper iudicatrix & excultrix artificis, praecepta seu theoremata ita inventa & collecta excolit, & diiudicando informat. Diiudicat autem praecepta, tum seorsum singula, eorum scilicet veritatem ac bonitatem regulis & legibus scientificis explorando; tum coniunctim omnia inter se coordinando, & methodice disponendo.
units.tr: Moreover, the judging and refining reason of the craftsman refines and shapes the precepts or theorems so found and collected, by judging them. He judges the precepts, first each one separately, namely by testing their truth and goodness by scientific rules and laws; and then all together, by arranging them among themselves and disposing them methodically.

units.la: His itaque artifex, nempe sensu & ratione: sensu non fallente, ratione non cœca & corrupta, vtitur in artium philosophicarum constituenda fabrica.
units.tr: Thus the craftsman uses these, namely sense and reason: sense that does not deceive, and reason that is neither blind nor corrupt, in building up the philosophical arts.

units.la: Apodeixis 8.
units.tr: Apodeixis 8.

units.la: Sensuum, sine hallucinatione, & quidem non semel apprehendentium experientia, qui contradicit, rationi ac menti recte obseruanti, & dextre iudicanti qui fidem omnem derogare nititur; is omnium rerum humanarum & sensilium & intelligibilium introducere satagit incertitudinem & vagam ac scepticam dubitationem.
units.tr: Whoever tries to strip all faith from the experience of the senses, which apprehend things without hallucination and not just once, and from reason rightly observing and judiciously weighing, he strives to introduce uncertainty and a vague and sceptical doubt into all human things, both sensible and intelligible.

units.la: At qui artibus philosophicis rite informatis temere contradicit, eisque fidem omnem, propter hominum erratum aut abusum, detrahere conatur; is humanorum sensuum sine hallucinatione, & quidem non semel apprehendentium experientia contradicit; & rationi hominis recte obseruati, & dextre iudicanti fidem derogare satagit. Nam, vti iam patet, artes philosophicas sensu & ratione bonus parit artifex; vel, vt Aristoteles recenset, artium instrumenta ac principia sunt sensus, obseruatio, experientia & inductio.
units.tr: But whoever rashly contradicts the philosophical arts rightly formed, and tries to take away all faith from them on account of men's error or misuse, he contradicts the experience of human senses, which apprehend without hallucination and not just once; and he strives to take away faith from the reason of a man who observes rightly and judges well. For, as is now plain, a good craftsman produces the philosophical arts by sense and reason; or, as Aristotle lists, the instruments and principles of the arts are sense, observation, experience and induction.

units.la: Ergo qui artibus recte formatis indicit calumniarum bellum, vt eas fide indignas persuadeat, is rerum humanarum omnium vagam incertitudinem & stolidam dubitationem ex orco reuocare satagit.
units.tr: Therefore whoever declares war by calumnies on the arts rightly formed, in order to persuade that they are unworthy of faith, he strives to recall from the underworld the vague uncertainty and foolish doubt of all human things.

units.la: CAP. VIII. De fundamento artium philosophicarum.
units.tr: CHAPTER VIII. On the foundation of the philosophical arts.

units.la: ARtifex vero, præcepta artium, & artes ipsas progignens, sensuum beneficio, & rationis obseruatione, ac iudicio bene vtens; fundamento & firmo & stabili debet inniti, id autem sic describimus:
units.tr: The craftsman, however, who produces the precepts of the arts and the arts themselves, and who makes good use of the senses, of observation of reason, and of judgment, ought to rest on a foundation that is solid, firm and stable. We describe this foundation as follows:

units.la: Vera ratio, vsu bono firmata, sapientia diuina & pietatis obseruans.
units.tr: True reason, confirmed by sound use, observing divine wisdom and piety.

units.la: Non
units.tr: Not

units.la: Autoritas humana rationis vacua, non præiudicata opinio, non impietatis studiosa ac inutilis futilitas.
units.tr: Mere human authority without reason, a prejudiced opinion, a useless triviality bent on impiety.

units.la: Vera dico Ratio, quia debet rerum veritati respondere. Vsum postulo bonum, bene, & veritati conuenienter, ac sapienter philosophantium; obseruantiam requiro Christianam diuinæ sapientiæ ac doctrinæ, contra quam nemo philosophatur Christianorum, sed eam in multis basin statuit veritatis.
units.tr: I say true reason, because it must correspond to the truth of things. I require sound use, that is, of philosophizing well, in keeping with truth and wisely; I require the Christian observance of divine wisdom and doctrine, against which no Christian philosopher philosophizes, but which in many respects he sets as the base of truth.

units.la: Christianus igitur Philosophus noster, non autoritatem & præiudicatas tantum Philosophorum, vel veterum, vel recentiorum opiniones statuet basin, vt inde artium theoremata, & Philosophiam exstruat. Ineptit ille, quisquis etiam sit, Philosophus, qui nihil in artibus ponendum aut admittendum censet, nisi id ipsum ab aliquo Philosopho, quem admirat, vt Aristotele, Platone, Zabarella, Ramo, mo, &c. arte dignum prius fit iudicatum. Si quid autem ab horum aliquo ita cogitatum & æstimatum, & deinceps dictum, scriptum aut factum esse acceperit, religionem aut grande nefas esse arbitratur, vel tantillum ab hoc ipso deflectere. Eius enim tanquam Dei cuiusdam, qui errare aut labi non possit, nullo modo possit, vestigiis vnice insistendum esse profitetur. Imo quidam non verecundius de diuinis mysteriis, quam de quibuscunq; adamati Philosophi, vt plerunque Aristotelis aut Rami, alioquin summorum Philosophorum scriptis cogitare solent. Hos mittimus.
units.tr: Our Christian philosopher, therefore, will not take as his base the mere authority and prejudiced opinions of philosophers, whether of the ancients or of the moderns, from which to build the theorems of the arts and philosophy. That man is foolish, whoever he may be as a philosopher, who thinks that nothing should be placed or admitted in the arts unless it has first been judged worthy of the arts by some philosopher he admires, such as Aristotle, Plato, Zabarella, Ramus, etc. If he has heard that something has been thought, valued, and afterwards said, written or done by one of these, he considers it a matter of religion, or a great crime, to depart in the slightest from it. For he professes that he must follow only in the footsteps of this man as of some god who cannot err or slip, and that in no way may he do otherwise. Indeed, some think about the divine mysteries no more reverently than about the writings of whatever philosophers they are infatuated with, as most often about Aristotle or Ramus, or otherwise the writings of the greatest philosophers. We pass over such men.

units.la: Vera Philosophia & orthodoxus Philosophus non nititur auctoritate, non opinione, nō persuasione, sed rerum veritate, natura, & firma ratione. Neque enim penes testantem veritas est aut falsitas, sed penes rem ipsam, verum aut falsum, id est, testans non est veritatis rei fundamentum, nec facit veritatem. Præclarissime igitur Christianus Cicero, Lactantius ille Firmianus, diuinarum Institit. lib.2. cap. 8.Cum sapere, (inquit) id est, veritatem quærere omnibus sit innatum, sapientiam ipsi sibi adimunt, qui sine vllo iudicio inuenta maiorum probant, & ab aliis pecudum more ducuntur. Sed hoc eos fallit, quod maiorum nomine positum, non putant fieri posse, vt aut ipsi plus sapiant, quia minores vocantur, aut illi desipuerint, quia maiores. Cum Christiano autem illo Cicerone belle & Ethnicus ille consentit: ita enim is in proœmio lib.1.de Natura pulcerrime: non tam authoritas, inquit, in dif in disputando, quam rationis momenta quaerenda sunt. Quinetiam obest plerunque iis, qui discere volunt, authoritas eorum, qui docere se profitentur. Desinunt enim suum iudicium adhibere, id habent ratum, quod ab eo, quem probant, iudicatum videt. Nec vero soleo probare, id quod de Pythagoricis accepimus, quos ferunt, si quid affirmarent in disputando, cum ex iis quaereretur, quare id ita esset, respondere solitos, Ipse dixit; Ipse autem erat Pythagoras. Tantum opinio praeiudicata poterat, ut etiam sine ratione valeret authoritas. Sed & verissime Plato, vel sub eius persona Socrates in Charmide (ut & Talaus in commentariis suis, in caput 32. citat) non considerandum est, quis dixerit, sed utrum vere dicatur, necne. Et in Gorgia Polo iuveni ardore quodam iuvenili de beata vita differenti, & veritate testium plurium nitenti, ita reponit Socrates: Ego unus tibi non assentior: non enim me rationibus cogis, sed falsis testibus contra me productis, ex ipsa veritatis substantia me deicere moliris. Ego vero nisi te unum testem adduxero mihi assentientem, nihil existimatione dignum in his, quae tractamus, perfecisse me arbitror, nihil etiam te perfecturum puto, nisi ego unus solusque tibi assentiar.
