Et ibidem paulo ante: O Pole, ait Socrates, redarguere me conaris oratorio more, velut hi qui in iudiciis convincere se putant: nam illic alii alios convincere sibi videntur, postquam sermonum, quos habuerunt, multos & claros testes produxerint: qui vero contraria dicit, unum aliquem aut nullum adducit. Verum hic redarguendi modum mo-
units.tr: True philosophy and the orthodox philosopher rest not on authority, not on opinion, not on persuasion, but on the truth of things, on nature and on firm reason. For truth or falsehood does not lie in the one who bears witness, but in the thing itself, which is true or false; the witness is not the foundation of the truth of a matter, nor does he make it true. Therefore that most excellent Christian Cicero, Lactantius Firmianus, in the second book, eighth chapter of the Divine Institutes, says admirably: Since wisdom, that is, the seeking of truth, is innate in all men, those take wisdom away from themselves who, without any judgment, approve the discoveries of their elders and are led by others like cattle. But this escapes them: because the things are put forward under the name of their elders, they do not think it possible either that they themselves might know more, because they are called younger, or that those others might have been foolish, because they are called elder. That heathen man agrees finely with this Christian Cicero, for he says in the preface to the first book of On the Nature of the Gods most beautifully: In disputing, not so much authority as the weight of reasons is to be sought. Indeed, the authority of those who profess to teach is usually a hindrance to those who want to learn. For they cease to use their own judgment; they hold as settled whatever they see has been judged by the one they approve. Nor do I usually approve of what we have heard about the Pythagoreans, who, they say, when they affirmed something in disputation and were asked why it was so, were accustomed to answer, He himself said it; and he was Pythagoras. So much could a prejudiced opinion do that authority was valid even without reason. But Plato also speaks most truly, or Socrates in his person in the Charmides (as Talaeus too cites in his commentaries, on chapter 32): one must consider not who has said a thing, but whether it is truly said or not. And in the Gorgias, when the young Polus, with a certain youthful ardour, disputes about the happy life and relies on the testimony of several witnesses rather than on truth, Socrates replies thus: I alone do not assent to you. For you do not compel me by reasons, but you strive to throw me down from the very substance of truth by false witnesses brought against me. But I think that unless I bring forward you alone as a witness assenting to me, I have accomplished nothing worthy of esteem in the matters we are treating, and I think you will accomplish nothing either, unless I alone and only I assent to you. And a little earlier in the same place: O Polus, says Socrates, you try to refute me in the manner of orators, as those who think they convince in the law courts. For there, each seems to convince the other once they have produced many and distinguished witnesses to the speeches they have made; but the one who says the contrary brings forward one or none. But this manner of refutation is

units.la: D i menti nullius est ad veritatem: aliquando enim etiam falsa testimonia contra aliquem afferri possunt à multis, & qui aliquid esse videntur. Et in Protagora: ad disputationes si viri conueniunt tales, quales nostrum se plurimi praedicant, haudquaquam aliena voce opus est, neque poetarum, quos percontari de his, qui scribunt, non datur, & qui eorum testimonia in medium afferunt, alii hoc, alii aliud, poetae dicunt sentire, neque tamen conuincere rem possunt, de qua differunt, aut expedire.
units.tr: of no one's mind toward the truth: for sometimes even false testimonies can be brought against someone by many, and by those who seem to be somebody. And in the Protagoras: When men such as many of us claim to be meet for disputations, there is by no means need of a voice from outside, nor of the poets, whom it is not possible to question about what they write, and who, when their testimonies are brought forward, one says they think this, another that, and yet they cannot convict or resolve the matter they dispute about.

units.la: Tales ergo confabulationes viri sapientes omittunt, ipsique inter se colloquuntur, vicissimque ingenii periculum faciunt. Disputationes autem huiusmodi, vt arbitror, ego & tu imitari debemus, & poetis posthabitis, nostris rationibus rem ipsam discutere, facereque tam ingenii, quam veritatis periculum. Et in Critone: Nam ego is sum (ait Socrates) non modo nunc, sed & semper, qui meorum nulli paream, praeterquam rationi, quae mihi ratiocinandi optima videtur. Atqui & Aristoteles ipse Rami illud fundamentum suo nobis testimonio egregie confirmat, cum 6. cap. Ethicorum li. 1. ait, oportere Philosophum veritatis seruanda causa sua etiam ipsius dogmata abiicere & tollere: item cum 2. Metaphysic. cap. 1. Philosophiam definit esse scientiam veritatis: item cum in libris de interpretatione ait, non ideo hoc vel illud verum aut falsum esse, quia ab hoc vel illo affirmatum aut negatum sit, &c. Neque omnino Philosophus vllus tam videtur id propositum habuisse (ait Talaeus) vt rationibus suis contra aliorum autoritates staret, quam Aristo-
units.tr: Therefore wise men omit such idle talk and converse among themselves, and in turn test their own ability. Disputations of this kind, as I think, you and I ought to imitate, and, setting the poets aside, to examine the matter itself with our own reasons, making a test of our talent as well as of the truth. And in the Crito: For I am such a man, Socrates says, not only now but always, that I obey none of my own faculties except reason, which seems to me the best for reasoning. Indeed Aristotle himself, by his own testimony, strongly confirms this foundation of Ramus, when in chapter 6 of the first book of the Ethics he says that a philosopher, for the sake of truth, must reject and abandon even his own dogmas; likewise in chapter 1 of the second book of the Metaphysics he defines philosophy as the science of truth; likewise in the books On Interpretation he says that this or that is not true or false because it has been affirmed or denied by this or that person, etc. Nor does any philosopher seem to have had this aim so much (says Talaeus) as to stand by his own reasons against the authorities of others, as Aristotle did,

units.la: Aristoteles, vt qui cōtra omnes omnium ho-minum fere aut horitates liberrime & senserit & scripserit, idque frequenter in ore habuit, Amicus Plato, amicus Socrates sed magis tamen amica veritas: ideoque & contra Platonis praeceptoris, cuius per viginti annos discipulus fuerat, ideas & alia eius dogmata multis in locis: itemque contra alios antiquiores Philosophos, vt in Acroasi cōtra Melissum, Parmenidem, Anaxagoram, & cæteros confidenter philosophatus fuerit.
units.tr: Aristotle, who, as one who thought and wrote most freely against almost all the authorities of almost all men, often had on his lips: Plato is a friend, Socrates is a friend, but truth is a friendlier friend. And so he philosophized boldly, in many places, against Plato, his teacher, whose disciple he had been for twenty years, and against his ideas and other dogmas; likewise against other more ancient philosophers, as in the Acroasis against Melissus, Parmenides, Anaxagoras and the rest.

units.la: Quidam non de plebe Philosophus (vt ad institutum nostrū reuertamur) Philosophicarum artium duplex statuit principium, Internum & Externum.
units.tr: A certain philosopher, not of the common sort (so that we may return to our purpose), laid down a twofold principle of the philosophical arts: an internal and an external one.

units.la: Internum est ipsa hominis natura, suis instructa viribus, luce naturali à Deo homini relicta, (addo, diuina etiam illustrata) lucens: cui tribuit dexteritatem exercendi & sagacitatem intellectus.
units.tr: The internal principle is human nature itself, equipped with its own powers, shining with the natural light left to man by God (I add, also illumined by divine light); to it he assigned the skill of exercising and the sagacity of the intellect.

units.la: Dexteritas exercendi illi est in viribus naturæ, quibus se & communem vitam tueri nititur, quibusque labore multiplici adhibito, perfectionis suæ opera perficit, atque imitatione quadam vtens, proprio motu & ductu, quę quasi imperfecta quodammodo expe-ritur. ritur, meliora edere conatur, donec tandem ad constantem rectitudinem integritatemque sua elaboravit.
units.tr: The skill of exercising lies in the powers of nature, by which man strives to protect himself and his common life; and by applying these powers with manifold labour, he brings his own perfection to completion, and, using a certain imitation, by his own motion and guidance, he tries, in a manner, to make better what has been tried in an imperfect way, until at last he has worked it out to a settled rectitude and integrity.

units.la: Sagacitas intellectus est mentis nostrę in differendo vis & dexteritas, qua inueniuntur minus nota, & iudicantur quæ inuenta fuerunt, ad rerum aliquam obtinendam notitiam.
units.tr: The sagacity of the intellect is the power and skill of our mind in discerning, by which things less known are discovered, and what has been discovered is judged, so as to obtain some knowledge of things.

units.la: Sagacitas hæc in sensibus exterioribus, interioribus, & ipsis intelligendi facultatib. cernitur: sensus exteriores singularia atque indiuidua comprehedunt, eaque ad interiora certo modo deferunt, vbi sub speciebus formata, ab intellectus luce videntur, æstimantur & concipiuntur, perceptarumque rerum notiones & ideæ formantur, idque ad notitiam animo concipiedam & iudicandam.
units.tr: This sagacity is seen in the external senses, in the internal senses, and in the faculties of understanding themselves: the external senses apprehend singular and individual things and convey them in a certain way to the internal faculties, where, formed under species, they are seen, valued and conceived by the light of the intellect, and notions and ideas of the things perceived are formed, for the purpose of conceiving and judging knowledge in the mind.

units.la: Externum principium licet primū naturæ viribus vniuersis, industriaque sit editum: tamen extra sagacitatis illius & virtutis insitæ complexum deprehenditur in politissimis & optimis, in expeditis & constantissimis naturæ operibus, in vsu vitæ ad sufficientiam vndiquaque perfecto.
units.tr: Although the external principle was first put forth by nature's full powers and industry, it is nonetheless found within the compass of that acuteness and inborn virtue, in the most polished and excellent, the most efficient and steadfast works of nature, and in the use of life, perfected on every side to sufficiency.

units.la: Vsus hic labore, industria & diuino adspaadflatu ad defectus naturalis imple-tione plene elaboratus sagacitati subii-citur, vt ex eo institutionis doctrina ar-tificiose colligatur, cuius ductu & be-neficio perfectionem quandam ex ar-tibus desideratam, & vitae necessariam adipiscatur. &c.
units.tr: This use, elaborated by labour, industry and divine inspiration to complete what nature lacks, is subjected to acuteness, so that from it the teaching of instruction is skilfully gathered, and by its guidance and benefit one attains a certain perfection of the arts that is desired and necessary for life. &c.

units.la: 9. Apodexis.
units.tr: 9. Apodexis.

units.la: Nemo sana mentis eam doctrinam maledico car-pit dente, & Christiana fidei plura detrimenta, quam adiumenta importare proclamat, quam vera ratio rerum veritati impense studens, quam vsus bonus recte philosophantium, quam diuina sapien-tia norma fulcit, regit ac perficit: veram enim ra-tionem in rebus humanis qui ferre nequit, is patronus videtur falsitatis, ad hominum pla-cita & opiniones autoritatesque sophistican-tis, is brutae ac irrationali stupiditati ac igno-rantiae velificari videtur: Vsum qui negligit laudatum, & sapienti veritati non reclaman-tem, negligit hominum sapientum perpetuo consensu stabilitam consuetudinem: Regu-lam diuinę sapientiae, ἀθέος est, qui non admit-tit etiam in rerum mundanarum pia & pru-denti administratione.
units.tr: No one of sound mind bites at that teaching with a malicious tooth, or proclaims that it brings more harm than help to the Christian faith, who is not a champion of the truth; a teaching which true reason, zealous for the truth of things, supports, governs and perfects, which the good use of those who philosophise rightly, and divine wisdom, uphold. For whoever cannot bear true reason in human affairs seems to be a patron of falsehood, and one who yields to the opinions, beliefs and pretended authorities of men; he seems to sail over to brutish and irrational stupidity and ignorance. Whoever neglects the praised use, which does not oppose sound wisdom, neglects the custom established by the constant agreement of wise men. Whoever does not admit the rule of divine wisdom, even in the pious and prudent government of worldly things, is an atheist [ἄθεος].

units.la: Atqui qui Christianam Philosophiam probris, scommatis, & maledictis vexat, eamque Christiana Reipub. ac fidei pestem afferre exitialem clamat, eam doctrinam vituperat exterminandamque suadet, quae fulcitur veritatis rerum studiosa ratione, bo hoc est, quæ res vt sunt, existunt & vere apparent, apprehendit, concipit, disponit, disputando discutit, arguit, illustrat, quæ calculo vsus optimi & ab omnibus sapientibus approbati comprobatur, quamque sapientia verbi diuini corrigit, perficit.
units.tr: But whoever harasses Christian philosophy with reproaches, jeers and abuse, and cries that it brings a deadly plague to the Christian commonwealth and faith, condemns that teaching and urges that it be banished, although it is supported by a reason devoted to the truth of things, that is, which grasps, conceives and arranges things as they are, which exist and truly appear, which discusses, argues and illustrates them by disputation; which is confirmed by the touchstone of the best use, approved by all wise men; and which the wisdom of the divine Word corrects and perfects.

units.la: Ergo qui Christianam rodit Philosophiam eaque explosione omnium dignam proclamat, patrocinatur falsitati, velificatur brutæ & asininæ stupiditati ac anserinæ credulitati, sapientum consensum negligit, & sapientiæ diuinæ parum aut nihil in artibus humanitatis tribuit. Assumptio vera est: quia fundamentum huius Philosophiæ est vera ratio vero vsu firmata, & diuinæ sapientiæ regulis emendata.
units.tr: Therefore whoever gnaws at Christian philosophy and proclaims that it deserves to be cast out with contempt, takes the side of falsehood, sails over to brutish and asinine stupidity and goose-like credulity, neglects the agreement of the wise, and assigns little or nothing of divine wisdom to the arts of humanity. The assumption is true, because the foundation of this philosophy is true reason, confirmed by true use and corrected by the rules of divine wisdom.

units.la: CAP. IX. De Philosophiæ & artium fine & fructu.
units.tr: CHAP. IX. On the end and fruit of philosophy and the arts.

units.la: ADhuc causas efficientes artium Philosophicarum dispeximus: Finis Philosophiæ Christianæ & artium eius, est vtilis in vita humana vsus, teste artis definitione.
units.tr: So far we have considered the efficient causes of the philosophical arts. The end of Christian philosophy and of its arts is useful use in human life, as the definition of the art attests.

units.la: Etenim Philosophia præcipue nostra est donum Dei, testibus & ethnicis Platone & Cicerone aliisque, & Christianis Theologis Eusebio, Iustino, Clemente & aliis, qui ab Hebræis docent Philosophiam ad Græcos tandem demanasse. Et Apostolus ad Rom. 1. cap. Deum, Deum, ait, gentibus hoc manifestasse.
units.tr: For philosophy is above all a gift of God, as attested by the pagans Plato and Cicero and others, and by the Christian theologians Eusebius, Justin, Clement and others, who teach from the Hebrews that philosophy at last flowed down to the Greeks. And the Apostle in Romans chapter 1: God, God, he says, has made this manifest to the nations.

units.la: Dei autem dona hominibus conferuntur non frustra, sed propter insignem aliquam vtilitatem, præsertim vero ea dona, quæ communia multis ad vniuersam hominum societatë referuntur.
units.tr: Now the gifts of God are bestowed on men not in vain, but for some remarkable usefulness, especially those gifts which are common to many and relate to the whole society of men.

units.la: Deinde cum Philosophia sit studiû sapientiæ & veritatis,& Christiana Christianæ: quis nõ agnosceret eius sapientiæ scilicet & veritatis oblatæ, collatæ & vsurpatę fines eximios & vere augustos? Si quis dubitat aut nescit admiranda sapientiæ non tantum rerum diuinarum, sed etiam humanarum, quâ hic speciatim Philosophiam dicimus, opera, audiat sapientissimum de vtraque sapientia differentem Sap.8. Sapientiam non vincit improbitas, quin ea ab extremo ad extremum valentior pertingat, & cuncta probe administret. Hanc ego, inquit Salomon, a teneris adamans quaesiui, & mihi sponsam ducere studui, eius pulcritudinis amore captus. Ea generositatis est gloriosa, Dei conuictu vtens, & omnium adamata Domino. Est enim Dei scientia antistes, & eiusdem operum praeses. Quod si diuitiæ res est in vita expetenda, quid sapientia
units.tr: Next, since philosophy is the study of wisdom and truth, and Christian philosophy that of Christian wisdom, who would not recognise the outstanding and truly august ends of that wisdom and truth, offered, brought together and put to use? If anyone doubts or does not know the admirable works of wisdom, not only of divine things but also of human things, which we here call philosophy in particular, let him listen to the wisest man, speaking of both kinds of wisdom, in Wisdom chapter 8: Wickedness does not overcome wisdom; she reaches powerfully from one end to the other and orders all things well. I loved her from my youth and sought her as my bride, enamoured of her beauty. She is glorious in her noble birth, sharing God's company, and loved by the Lord of all. For she is the teacher of God's knowledge and the director of his works. If riches are a thing to be desired in life, what is

units.la: pientiæ pietia locupletius? quæ efficit omnia. Quod si operatur prudentia, quis ea in rerum natura magis est artifex? Quod si quis iustitiam amat, iustitiæ labores sunt virtutes. Temperantiam enim edocet & prudentiam, iustitiam & fortitudinem, quibus nihil est hominibus in vita utilius. Sin quis multarum rerum peritiam expetit, hæc & antiqua nouit, & futura coniicit: Sermonum fallacias & obscurarum quæstionum solutiones callet: monstra prodigiaque prænoscit, & temporum ac tempestatum euentus. Hanc ergo mihi ad vitæ societatem adsciscere decreui, sciens mihi bona daturam consilia, & curarum ac doloris lenimēto futuram. Per quam & gloriam apud vulgus, & honorem apud seniores consequitur iuuenis. Acutus inueniar in iudicio, & in conspectu potentum admirandus: Principibus me coram stupentibus, qui me & tacentem manebunt, & loquentem attendent, pluribusque differente me manum ori admouebunt: per hanc consequar immortalitatem, & æternam posteris memoriam relinquam. Administrabo populos, mihique gentes subiicientur, me vel auditum horrendi metuent tyranni, & vulgo bonus & bello fortis exstabo, & in ea domum meam ingressus, acquiescam. Nihil enim nim acerbitatis & doloris habet eius commercium atque comuictus ; sed delectationem ac lætitiam. Hæc apud me cogitans, & animo perpendens, esse in sapientiæ cognatione immortalitatem, inque eius & amicitia iucundam delectationem, & manuum laboribus inexhaustas diuitias, & colloquutionis exercitatione prudentiam, & sermonum communicatione claritatem, conabar circumiens eam mihi cooptare, &c.
units.tr: richer than wisdom? She produces all things. If prudence works, who is a greater craftsman in the nature of things? If anyone loves justice, the labours of justice are virtues. For she teaches temperance and prudence, justice and fortitude, and nothing is more useful to men in life. But if anyone desires skill in many things, she knows both things of old and conjectures the future. She understands the fallacies of words and the solutions of obscure questions; she foreknows portents and prodigies, and the outcomes of times and weather. I have therefore resolved to take her into the partnership of my life, knowing she will give me good counsels and be a comfort in cares and grief. Through her the young man obtains glory among the common people and honour among the elders. I shall be found keen in judgment and admirable in the sight of the powerful, princes standing amazed at me: they will keep silent when I am silent and attend when I speak, and when I speak at length they will lift their hands to their mouths. Through her I shall attain immortality and leave an eternal memory to posterity. I shall govern peoples, and nations will be subject to me; tyrants will fear me even when they only hear of me; among the common people I shall stand out as good, and in war as brave; and entering my house, I shall rest in her. For her company and fellowship have nothing bitter or painful in them, but delight and joy. Thinking these things over in my mind and weighing them: that in kinship with wisdom there is immortality, and in her friendship a pleasant delight, and from the labours of the hands inexhaustible riches, and from the practice of conversation prudence, and from the sharing of speech renown, I set out to make her my own, &c.

units.la: Vtilis autem ille in vita humana vsus tam late se extendit, quam late patet rerum, quæ Philosophiæ subiiciuntur, & de quibus vtiliter philosophamur, vsus.
units.tr: Now that useful use in human life extends as widely as the range of things that are subject to philosophy, and about which we philosophise to good purpose.

units.la: Estque cum primis hominis ipsius quædam instauratio & perfectio ad gloriam Dei sapientissimi & potentissimi comparata per eloquetem sapientiam.
units.tr: And it is above all a certain restoration and perfection of man himself, prepared for the glory of the most wise and most powerful God, through eloquent wisdom.

units.la: Instauratio & perfectio intelligitur hic non quæuis, vt ea quæ fit spiritu regenerationis in Theosophia, sed qua hominis natura ignara & depravata doctrinæ ac artium institutione ad vtilem scientiam, sapientiamq;, vsu item ac doctrinarum exercitatione ad vitæ actionumq; quandam felicitatem informata, & emendata instauratur, & quodammodo ita perficitur, de qua supra & infra. Eaque praecipue spectatur in hominis mente ac oratione.
units.tr: Here restoration and perfection are understood not in every sense, as that which takes place by the Spirit of regeneration in theosophy, but in the sense that human nature, ignorant and depraved, is restored and corrected by instruction in doctrines and arts, and formed to useful knowledge and wisdom, and likewise by use and the exercise of the disciplines to a certain felicity of life and actions; and it is in some measure made perfect in this way, as discussed above and below. And this is chiefly seen in the mind and speech of man.

units.la: Mens hominis instauratur intellectus collustratione, & voluntatis flexione.
units.tr: The mind of man is restored by the illumination of the understanding and the bending of the will.

units.la: Intellectus illustratur veritatis cognitione, adeoque sapientiae luce. Hinc ratio multo illustrior rerum scientia & intelligentia praedita. Hinc Picus Mirand. ait: Philosophia humana adiuuat contemplationem cum intellectum illuminat, & indirecte errores remouet, quibus plerunque ob ignorantiam inuoluuntur, & animum videtur inflammare, & ad aeternorum memoriam ex fluxis & temporariis traducere, & sacra eloquia facilius atque enucleatius apprehenduntur. Demosthenem dixisse accepimus, Omnem naturam praclariorem & illustriorem fieri, si ratio quaedam conformatioque doctrinae accesserit: longe vero maxime iis, quibuscunque initio meliorem paulo, quam aliis sortiri contigit: Illis enim sese tantum vincere, his vero aliis etiam praestare accidit.
units.tr: The understanding is illuminated by the knowledge of truth, and so by the light of wisdom. Hence reason, endowed with a much brighter knowledge and understanding of things. Hence Pico della Mirandola says: Human philosophy helps contemplation when it illuminates the intellect, and indirectly removes the errors in which men are usually entangled through ignorance; it seems to inflame the mind and to lead it from fleeting and temporal things to the memory of eternal ones; and sacred utterances are grasped more easily and more clearly. We have heard that Demosthenes said: Every nature becomes more famous and more illustrious if some reason and formation of learning is added to it; far most of all for those to whom it has fallen by lot to be a little better at the start than others. For it happens that these men surpass only themselves, while the others surpass even other men.

units.la: Intellectus quo melius intelligit, eo magis intellectus, nominis officio respondens. Mens quò illustriori sapien- tia est tincta, eo ipsa illustrior; Ratio quo magis rerum intelligentia infor- mata, eo melius ratiocinatur, quo me- lius ratiocinatur, eo magis ratio.
units.tr: The more clearly the understanding understands, the more truly it is understanding, answering to the office of its name. The more the mind is tinged with clearer wisdom, the more illustrious it is itself. The more reason is formed by knowledge of things, the better it reasons; and the better it reasons, the more it is reason.

units.la: Rationis facultates inueniendi & iudicandi, ingenium dico & iudicium ars Philosophica instituit, instaurat, perficit: Vsum rationis in omnib. pru- denter gubernat. Ratio quo perfecti- or, homo eo, qui est formatus ratione, hoc est, cuius forma est ratio, perfecti- or. Inueniendi & iudicandi vis in ani- ma quo præstantior, eo certe ipsa ratio animæ præstabilior.
units.tr: The art of philosophy instructs, restores and perfects the faculties of reason, I mean the ingenuity and judgement for finding and judging; it prudently governs the use of reason in all things. The more perfect reason is, the more perfect is the man who is formed by reason, that is, whose form is reason. The more excellent the power of finding and judging in the soul, the more certainly is reason itself more excellent in the soul.

units.la: Voluntas deinde animæ seu mentis humanæ præceptis Philosophiæ flecti- tur ad fugam vitiorum, & virtutum ap- petitionem. Philosophia enim (præser- tim Christiana & sana) cultura est ani- mi, vt Cicero loquitur, quæ extrahit vi- tia radicitus, & præparat animos ad satus accipiendos. Est animi medicina, est vi- tiosorum peccatorumque nostrorum ab illa petenda omnis medicina. Sine hac fieri nō potest, vt sanus sit animus, ait idem.
units.tr: The will of the human soul or mind is then bent by the precepts of philosophy to flee vices and to seek virtues. For philosophy (especially Christian and sound philosophy) is, as Cicero says, a cultivation of the mind, which pulls up vices by the roots and prepares the mind to receive the seed. It is the medicine of the mind, and all remedy for our vices and sins must be sought from it. Without it, as the same author says, the mind cannot be sound.

units.la: Philosophia itaque voluntas ho nis corrigitur & rectius informatur, vtpote quæ valde sit corrupta, & magis ab omnis generis affectibus, appetitionibus, libidinib. exagitetur, vt velit bonum, nolit malum. Bona enim & vtilia, quæ intellectus cognouit, approbat voluntas, mala, quæ itidem intellectus talia iudicat & deprehendit, auersatur. Philosophia, inquam, sana in vero vsu, quem monstrat, voluntatem philosophi ad pium præceptorum & artium cognitarum vsum, ad virtutes autorum, quos legit, imitandas, vitiaque fugienda adsuefacit; vt nimirum studia Philosophiæ honesta abeant in hominum mores. Proinde Cicero ait in Pilonem: Philosophia virtutes continet & officii & bene viuendi disciplinam, quam qui profitetur, grauissimam personam mihi sustinere videtur.
units.tr: Therefore the will of man is corrected by philosophy and more rightly shaped, since it is greatly corrupted and is driven about by affections, appetites and lusts of every kind, so that it may will the good and refuse the evil. For the will approves the good and useful things that the intellect has known, and shuns the evil things, which the intellect likewise judges and recognises as such. Sound philosophy, I say, by the true use it displays, accustoms the will of the philosopher to the pious practice of the precepts and the arts he has learned, to imitating the virtues of the authors he reads, and to avoiding vices, so that the honourable studies of philosophy may pass over into the conduct of men. Accordingly Cicero says against Piso: Philosophy contains the virtues and the discipline of duty and of living well, and the man who professes it seems to me to sustain the most serious character.

units.la: Ita in perficiendo homine, animum & rationem eius expolit, informat, perficere laborat: Orationem humanam excolit ita Philosophia suis præceptis, vt eam primum puram & emendatam reddat, deinde puritatem sermonis modificatione eleganti, figuraratione, vocis modulatione & gestuum omni decore exornet. Ani-
units.tr: Thus, in perfecting the man, philosophy polishes and shapes his mind and reason and labours to bring them to perfection. It adorns human speech by its precepts, first making it pure and correct, and then decking the purity of speech with elegant arrangement, figures of speech, modulation of the voice and every grace of gesture. The mind...

units.la: Animum ita Philosophia hæc variarum & utilium rerum imbuit necessaria scientia, vt animo homo sit sapiens: os & linguam format pura & ornata elocutione, vnde homo sapiens etiam eloquens dicitur. Immane quantum præstat homo sapienti eloquentia, & eloquenti sapientia præstans! Ratione autem & oratione distat homo & discriminatur à bestiis: hæc igitur, quo fuerint excellentiora, eo homo totus & excellétior & perfectior. Data enim hominis differentia excellentiore & perfectiore, homo ipse dabitur excellentior & perfectior.
units.tr: Philosophy imbues the mind with the necessary knowledge of many useful things, so that the man is wise in mind; and it shapes the mouth and tongue with pure and ornate expression, whence a wise man is also called eloquent. How greatly does a man excel who has wisdom together with eloquence, and who excels in wisdom together with eloquence! Man is distinguished and set apart from the beasts by reason and speech; therefore the more excellent these are, the more excellent and perfect the whole man becomes. For if the distinguishing mark of man is more excellent and perfect, man himself will be given as more excellent and perfect.

units.la: Eloquentem hanc sapientiam hominis si condit sal pietatis & honestæ vitæ, hoc est, si sapientiæ & scientiæ respondet vitæ ratio, si ab eloquentia non abludit animus & vita, mores & actiones: multo perfectior est homo.
units.tr: If this eloquent wisdom is seasoned with the salt of piety and an honourable life, that is, if the course of life corresponds to wisdom and knowledge, and if the mind and life, morals and actions do not differ from the eloquence, then man is far more perfect.

units.la: Docet autem Philosophia nostra & in primis vrget coniunctionem sinceram scientiæ & vsus, sapientiæ & morum, eruditionis & vitæ: odit & prohibet diuortium inter mentis scientiam, & vitæ vsum. Vnde merito Tullius exclamat 5. Tusculan. O vitæ, Philosophia, dux, virtutis indagatrix, expultrixq; vitiorum: quid non modo nos, sed omnino vita hominum sine te esse potuisset? Tu urbes peperisti, tu dissipatos homines in societatem vitae conuocasti. Tu eos inter se primo domicilio, deinde coniugiis, tum literarum & vocum communione iunxisti. Tu inuentrix legum, tu magistra morum, & disciplina fuisti. Tu vita tranquillitatem largita nobis es, & terrorem mortis sustulisti.
units.tr: Our philosophy teaches, and above all insists upon, the sincere union of knowledge and practice, of wisdom and morals, of learning and life; it hates and forbids a divorce between the knowledge of the mind and the practice of life. Hence Tully rightly exclaims in the fifth book of the Tusculan Disputations: O Philosophy, guide of life, seeker out of virtue and expeller of vices, what could not only we, but the whole life of men, have been without you? You founded cities; you called scattered men together into fellowship of life. You joined them first by a common dwelling, then by marriage, then by the sharing of letters and speech. You were the inventor of laws, the teacher of morals and of discipline. You bestowed on us the calm of life and removed the terror of death.

units.la: Apodeixis 10.
units.tr: Apodeixis 10.

units.la: Cuius finis bonus est, id ipsum, si per legitima tendit media, quoque bonum censetur communi hominum sanorum iudicio.
units.tr: Whose end is good, that very thing, if it proceeds by lawful means, is also judged good by the common judgement of sound men.

units.la: Iam humana Philosophia, & praesertim quidem vera, finis est bonus: Quoniam illi proposita est vitae humanae utilitas, quam spectat quidem non vulgarem. Ad eum autem consequendum finem, utitur legitimis mediis, doctrinae institutione, & perceptae doctrinae necessaria exercitatione. Non profecto abs re dixit Plato in Euthy. Philosophiae studium, ut assequamur, curandum est, ut diuinum. Et in Symp. Philosophiae sermones & utiles sunt & delectabiles. De Rep. Philosophia vera veritas necessaria est, nec temerarius eius particeps esse potest.
units.tr: Now human philosophy, and especially true philosophy, has a good end, since the usefulness of human life is set before it, a usefulness which it regards, and not a common one. To attain this end it uses lawful means: the instruction of teaching and the necessary practice of the doctrine received. Plato said, not without reason, in the Euthydemus: "The study of philosophy must be pursued, so that we may attain it, as something divine." And in the Symposium: "The discourses of philosophy are both useful and delightful." In the Republic: "True philosophy is a necessary truth, and no rash person can be its partaker."

units.la: Alibi: Philosophia nullum unquam bonum mortalium generi deorum munere contingit nec continget. Sed missis testimoniis: Magna sane vt vis, ita vtilitas est in hominum vita veritatis & sapientiae pientiæ ac scientiæ rerum, quarum in vsu quotidiano fere versamur.
units.tr: Elsewhere he says: "Philosophy has never yet come to the human race as a good of mortals by the gift of the gods, nor will it ever come." But setting aside testimonies: truly great is both the power and the usefulness of truth and wisdom in human life, and of the knowledge of things, with which we are engaged in daily use.

units.la: At Philosophia profitetur doctrinam veritatis, sapientiæ & scientiæ rerum, quas apud se versat vsus in vita communi. Proinde ipsa Philosophia est necessaria etiam homini, qua homo.
units.tr: But philosophy professes the doctrine of truth, of wisdom and of the knowledge of things, which use in common life employs. Accordingly, philosophy itself is necessary even for man, as man.

units.la: Quamobrem humana etiam Philosophia est per se bona. Iam, quod bonum per se, id nemo bonus calumniatur, vt malum. Finem hunc quod quidam ex Philosophiæ cultoribus non sint nacti, id adscribendum aut abusui, aut virium imbecillitati eorum, qui non recte eam didicerunt, aut male eadem vsi sunt, etiam rei optimæ abusus potest esse pessimus. Imo res quo excellentior & nobilior, eo eius abusus est pestilentior.
units.tr: Wherefore human philosophy too is good in itself. Now, no good person slanders what is good in itself as evil. That some of the cultivators of philosophy have not attained this end is to be ascribed either to abuse, or to the weakness of those who have not learned it rightly or have used it badly; even the best thing can be most harmful when abused. Indeed, the more excellent and noble a thing is, the more pestilent its abuse.

units.la: Rursum.
units.tr: Again.

units.la: Aduersarius & obtrectator boni publici & communis Christianorum vtilitatis, Reipub. Christianæ non emolumentum, sed detrimentum spirat.
units.tr: An adversary and detractor of the public good and of the common advantage of Christians breathes not the benefit but the harm of the Christian commonwealth.

units.la: Atqui quem cepit iniquum sanæ Philosophiæ humanæ odium, is est aduersarius & obtrectator boni publici & communis Christianorum vtilitatis. Osor quippe & rosor Philosophiæ, odit & rodit eius finem, qui est vtilis in vita humana vsus, si in vita humana, etiam in Christiana. Imo Christianæ Reipub. magis interest saluam tueri sanæ Philosophiæ salutem, cum ea sit custos sanæ veritatis & verae sapientiæ; imo in Repub. Christiana aduersus hostes veritatis & sapientiæ, armis vtriusque acrius est depugnandum. Ergo quem cepit iniquum sanæ Philosophiæ odium, is Reipub. Christianæ non emolu-mentum, sed detrimentum sperat.
units.tr: But whoever has been seized by an unjust hatred of sound human philosophy is an adversary and detractor of the public good and of the common advantage of Christians. For one who hates and gnaws at philosophy hates and nibbles at its purpose, which is the useful exercise of human life, and in human life, Christian life included. Indeed, it is more in the interest of the Christian commonwealth to preserve the safety of sound philosophy, since it is the guardian of sound truth and true wisdom; indeed, in the Christian commonwealth, one must fight more fiercely with the weapons of both against the enemies of truth and wisdom. Therefore, whoever has been seized by an unjust hatred of sound philosophy hopes for harm, not benefit, for the Christian commonwealth.

units.la: Rursum.
units.tr: Again.

units.la: Homini, qui aut ignorantia aut malitia induc-ctus insigne perfectionis naturæ ipsius in hac vita adiumentum inuidet, eidem felicitatem inuidet. Perfectio enim hominis qualiscunque, est felicitas etiam hominis qualiscunque.
units.tr: Whoever, moved either by ignorance or by malice, begrudges a man the outstanding aid of nature's own perfection in this life, begrudges him happiness as well. For a man's perfection, of whatever kind, is also a man's happiness, of whatever kind.

units.la: At Philosophiæ artes, aurea illa Dei dona qui fastidit & sublatas cupit, is etiam homini, quocunque tandem idfiat modo, eo modo homini inuidet magnum perfectionis & instaurationis in hac vita adiumentum. Ergo &c.
units.tr: But whoever scorns the arts of philosophy, those golden gifts of God, and desires them taken away, begrudges man, in whatever way it may come about, the great aid of perfection and restoration in this life. Therefore, etc.

units.la: CAP. X.
units.tr: CAP. X.

units.la: De materia artium philosophicarum.
units.tr: On the matter of the philosophical arts.

units.la: DE causis efficientibus & fine ac fructu artium Philosophicarum hactenus dictum: Internæ causæ materia & forma earum sunt.
units.tr: So far I have spoken of the efficient causes, the end and the fruit of the philosophical arts. Their internal causes are matter and form.

units.la: Materia artium Christianæ Philosophiæ sunt scientifica præcepta, quæ nimirum apta nata sunt scientiam parere, quæque legibus scientificis sunt informata.
units.tr: The matter of the arts of Christian philosophy consists of scientific precepts, namely those which are by nature fitted to produce knowledge and which are shaped by scientific laws.

units.la: Leges scientificæ informantes præcepta scientifica sunt lex veritatis, lex iustitiæ, & lex sapientiæ.
units.tr: The scientific laws that shape scientific precepts are the law of truth, the law of justice, and the law of wisdom.

units.la: Lex veritatis sancit & requirit in ar-tium præceptis veritatem.
units.tr: The law of truth sanctions and requires truth in the precepts of the arts.

units.la: Christianæ igitur Philosophiæ præcepta debent esse vera. Nullum præceptum falsum. Reiicit itaque Philosophia nostra ex suis præceptis omnem falsitatem, quippe sanctæ & solius veritatis studiosissima.
units.tr: Therefore the precepts of Christian philosophy ought to be true. No precept should be false. Our philosophy therefore rejects every falsehood from its precepts, being most devoted to what is holy and to truth alone.

units.la: Veritas autem præceptorum prædita est conditionibus tribus.
units.tr: The truth of the precepts, moreover, has three conditions.

units.la: Prima est ut sit necessaria, absoluta & constans, fallere nescia, ut inquam, veritas illa sit immutabilis & perpetua.
units.tr: The first is that it be necessary, absolute and constant, unable to deceive; that is to say, I mean that this truth be unchangeable and perpetual.

units.la: Omne itaque præceptum Christianæ, hoc est, verae Philosophiae est perpetuae, constantis, immutabilis & non fallentis veritatis, ut nunquam non sit verum.
units.tr: Every precept of Christian, that is, true, philosophy is therefore of perpetual, constant, unchangeable and non-deceiving truth, so that it is never not true.

units.la: Nullu itaq; præceptum Christianæ Philosophiæ debet esse contingenter, mutabiliter & fallibiliter verū. Quod enim contingenter est verum, fallere potest, mutatur. Philosophia adeo hæc semper veritati, nūquam falsitati, qua nihil est hominum naturæ magis inimicum, itemque fortunæ, id est, incōstantiæ & mutabilitati, locum in artibus dat. Secunda est, ut veritas (qua fieri po-test) sit vniuersalis, de omni. Est autem de omni verum axioma artis, & tum ei vniuersalis veritatis conditio inest, cum vniuersum consequens verum est de vniuerso & omni antecedente.
units.tr: No precept of Christian philosophy ought therefore to be true contingently, changeably and fallibly. For what is true contingently can deceive and is subject to change. Philosophy thus always gives place in the arts to truth, never to falsity, which is most hostile to human nature, and likewise to fortune, that is, to inconstancy and mutability. The second is that the truth (as far as it can be) be universal, of every case. A axiom of an art is true of every case, and the condition of universal truth is present when the universal consequent is true of every universal and every antecedent.

units.la: Præceptum igitur artis Christianæ optamus esse vniuersalis veritatis, vt nihil possit esse sub communi & vniuersali antecedente, de quo nō semper dici possit commune & vniuersale consequens. Sunt autem quædam singularia: hic distinguimus inter rei existentiam, & notionem artificiosam, inter præceptum de re, & rem singularem, cuius præceptum.
units.tr: We wish therefore the precept of the Christian art to be of universal truth, so that nothing can lie under a common and universal antecedent of which a common and universal consequent cannot always be stated. There are, however, some singulars: here we distinguish between the existence of a thing and its artificial notion, between a precept about a thing and the individual thing of which it is the precept.

units.la: Particularem itaque veritatem, id est fallentem & variabilem non amat Philosophia nec tolerat in præceptis scientificis, quia iam vera essent, iam falsa, & ita incertitudo veritatis dubitationem animis docētium & discen-tium iniiceret.
units.tr: Philosophy therefore does not love a particular truth, that is, one that deceives and varies, nor does it tolerate one in scientific precepts, because it would now be true and now false, and so uncertainty of truth would instil doubt into the minds of teachers and learners.

units.la: Tertia conditio veritatis, quam Philosophica & nostra scientifica præcepta postulant, est affirmatio, seu affirmatio asseuerationis, vt nimirum discentem aliquid certi doceant.
units.tr: The third condition of truth, which our philosophical and scientific precepts demand, is affirmation, or affirmation of assertion, so that they teach the learner something certain.

units.la: Præceptum ergo nostrarum artium Philosophus iubet esse affirmatum aut affirmato theoremati æquipollens, vt doceat, hoc est, sit scientificum.
units.tr: The philosopher therefore commands that the precept of our arts be affirmative, or equivalent to an affirmed theorem, so that it teaches, that is, is scientific.

units.la: Nullum nostræ Philosophię præceptum optamus negatum, quia dedocet potius, indicat quid res non sit, adeoque non parit scientiam. Non enim facit scire, qui dicit, quid res non sit.
units.tr: We wish no precept of our philosophy to be negative, because it unteaches rather than teaches; it indicates what a thing is not, and so does not produce knowledge. For whoever says what a thing is not does not make anyone know it.

units.la: Lex iustitiæ requirit præcepta iusta, præcipit enim iustitiam, vt vnicuique arti & præcepto artis iusta ac debita tribuantur.
units.tr: The law of justice requires just precepts, for it enjoins justice, so that what is just and due is assigned to each art and to each precept of an art.

units.la: Hæc iustitiæ lex vnicuique arti, & præcepto tribuit suum, amãdat omne iniustitiam. Nullum itaq; præceptum iniustum admittit vera Philosophia.
units.tr: This law of justice gives each art and precept its own, and abhors all injustice. Therefore true philosophy admits no unjust precept.

units.la: Huius legis sanctione optamus, artium quasi finibus & terminis accurate distinctis vnicuique arti sua propria & essentialia tribui præcepta.
units.tr: By the sanction of this law we wish each art, with its limits and boundaries carefully distinguished as it were, to be assigned its own and essential precepts.

units.la: Ægre ferimus, vllo modo aliena admisceri, ne confundantur artium diuersarum præcepta, quantumuis vsum earum coniunctum exoscVlemur: æquabilis enim iustitiæ nostra ars est studiosissima.
units.tr: We cannot bear for anything foreign to be mixed in in any way, lest the precepts of different arts be confused, however much we may welcome their combined use; for our art is most devoted to even-handed justice.

units.la: Huius legis imperio optamus talē ipsorum præceptorum cōstitutionem, vt quæuis artium præcepta è partibus inter se essentialibus, hoc est, iis, quarum sit essentialis nexus cōstituantur. Tum autem iudicamus partes inter se essentiales & axioma iustum ac essentiale, cum altera est de alterius essentia, ita quidem vt eam vel constituat, vel constitutam immediate sequatur, seu potius indiuulso nexu & semper ei inhæreat, nec ab ea diuelli vnquam possit.
units.tr: By the authority of this law we wish the precepts themselves to be so constituted that each precept of the arts is made up of parts essentially connected with one another, that is, parts between which there is an essential bond. We judge parts to be essentially connected, and a proposition to be just and essential, when one part belongs to the essence of the other, so that it either constitutes it or immediately follows it once constituted; or rather, when it is joined by an unbroken bond and always cleaves to it, never able to be torn away from it.

units.la: Non itaque fert ars nostræ Philosophiæ præceptum constans ex accidentalibus, seu accidentali nexu cohærentibus partibus, siquidem inde violatur constans præcepti veritas.
units.tr: Therefore the art of our philosophy does not admit a precept consisting of accidental parts, or of parts cohering by an accidental bond, since the constant truth of the precept is thereby violated.

units.la: Lex sapientiæ seu prudentiæ, præter necessariam ac absolutam seu perpetuam, præter item iustā & coessentialem consanguineamque veritatē, qua fieri potest, sancit suprem am veritatis conditionem ac necessitatem.
units.tr: The law of wisdom or prudence, besides the necessary, absolute or perpetual truth, and besides the just, co-essential and kindred truth, as far as it can be, enjoins the highest condition and necessity of truth.

units.la: Etenim primo præcipit sapientem generalium de generalibus, specialium de specialibus documentorū Philosophicorum informationem. Vult-que que vt quæ generalia sunt, generatim tradantur, quæ vero speciala speciatim & per species specialibus documentis doceantur.
units.tr: For first it prescribes that the wise instruction of philosophical teachings be of generals concerning generals and of specials concerning specials. It also wills that what is general be delivered generally, but what is special be taught specially and by the special teachings of each species.

units.la: Auersatur itaque Philosophia vera artium talia præcepta, quibus inæqualia prorsus proponuntur, & specialia cum generalibus, & hæc vicissim cum illis insipienter commiscentur; quibus quod vniuerso generi cōuenit per species docetur, aut quod vni alicui speciei proprium est, vniuerso attributur generi. Sapientis itaque æqualitatis est studiosissima.
units.tr: Therefore true philosophy of the arts avoids such precepts, in which things quite unequal are proposed, special things together with general, and these again are foolishly mingled with those; or in which what belongs to the whole genus is taught by species, or what is proper to some one species is attributed to the whole genus. It is therefore most devoted to wise equality.

units.la: Deinde imperat, vt artium præcepta sint catholica & cōstent è partibus reciprocis, & æque late patentibus. Fastidit itaque Philosophia, si aliter haberi potest, præceptum imprudenter compositum ex partibus inæqualibus, non catholicis, non reciprocis; adeoque exterminat ex suis finibus omnē tautologiam, ac ociosam & odiosam earundem rerum iterationem, vtpote, quæ est prudentis & doctæ breuitatis amantissima.
units.tr: Next it commands that the precepts of the arts be catholic and consist of reciprocal parts, extending equally widely. Philosophy, if it can be otherwise, therefore disdains a precept imprudently composed of unequal, non-catholic, non-reciprocal parts; and so it banishes from its borders all tautology and the idle and tedious repetition of the same things, as being most fond of the brevity of the prudent and learned.

units.la: Apodeixis. 2.
units.tr: Apodeixis (Demonstration). 2.

units.la: Natura sequitur semina quisque suæ; & cuique suum suum pulcrum. Verax, iustus, prudens magni semper facit artium documenta vera, iusta & prudentia, veram, iustam & sapientem docetia & parientia scientiam: Mendax, iniustus & imprudens delectatur mendacibus, iniustis ac confusis, deinde imprudentibus ac stolidis praeceptionibus, fallacia mendacia, confusionem iniustam, & insipientem imprudetiam, sub praetextu contrariarum virtutum tradentibus.
units.tr: Each follows the seeds of his own nature, and to each his own is beautiful. The truthful, just and prudent man always values the true, just and prudent precepts of the arts, which teach and produce true, just and wise knowledge. The liar, the unjust and the imprudent delight in false, unjust and confused precepts, and then in foolish and stupid rules, which under the pretext of contrary virtues hand down deceitful lies, unjust confusion and senseless imprudence.

units.la: Quicunque autem sana Philosophia veras artes plurimi facit, is etiam maximi facit semper documenta artium vera, iusta & prudentia documenta, veram, iustam & sapientem parientia scientiam: Quicunque vero odit & calumniatur veras sanae Philosophiae artes, is parui certe facit veritatem, iustitiam & prudentiam in documentis, in iis vero amplectitur, si non malitiose, saltem ignoranter, & stolide, mendacia, iniustitiam, ac insipientem imprudentiam: amat aut falsa, aut mutabiliter & incerto vera, aut nihil docentia praecepta: amat aut promiscue confusa, aut instabili nexu coherentia documenta, si modo documenta: amat inaequalia & coccysmis tautologicis referta deliria.
units.tr: Whoever values the true arts of sound philosophy highly always values most the true, just and prudent teachings of the arts, which produce true, just and wise knowledge. Whoever hates and slanders the true arts of sound philosophy certainly values truth, justice and prudence in teachings but little, and in their place embraces, if not maliciously then at least ignorantly and stupidly, lies, injustice and senseless imprudence. He loves either falsehoods, or truths that are changeable and uncertain, or precepts that teach nothing. He loves either things jumbled together in confusion, or teachings held together by an unstable connection, if they can be called teachings at all. He loves unequal, nonsensical deliria crammed with cuckoo-like tautological repetitions.

units.la: Ergo qui odit & calumniatur scientifica hac artium sanae Philosophiae praecepta, de quibus hactenus, is mendax, veritatis perpetuae ofor, is inconstans, constantis & vniuersalis veritatis rosor: is est iniustus, non faciens magni documenta iuste informata, susque deque ferens sint ne promiscue, an vero distincte omnia in disciplinis proposita, is est stolide lide imprudens, inaqualitatis & inanis tautologia idem garrientis sine iudicio admirator.
units.tr: Therefore whoever hates and slanders these scientific precepts of the arts of sound philosophy, which we have discussed so far, is a liar and a hater of perpetual truth. He is inconstant and a gnawer away at constant and universal truth. He is unjust, not valuing rightly formed teachings, and he treats it as all one whether everything set out in the disciplines is jumbled together or distinctly ordered. He is foolishly imprudent, an admirer without judgment of inequality and of empty tautology, which babbles the same thing over and over.

units.la: Verae itaque, quam excolimus & vnice amamus, Philosophiae Christianarumque artium materia, bona est ac preciosa, quia vera, quia constans, quia certa, quia vtilis ad doctrinam, quia iusta, hoc est, propria & cognata, essentialis, non aduentitia, ex ipsa rei essentia promanans, vel ei firmissimo affectionis nexu conglutinata; quia sapiens & prudens: Nihil in ea (si modo non impediat ingenii humani imbecillitas, & rerum intricata obscuritas, quae tamen si impediunt, noli iniquè calumniari, noli deridere conatus tendentes ad istam virtutem: Vt desint vires, tamen est laudanda voluntas; conatui etiam sua laus) falsi, nihil contingentis incertitudinis & mutabilitatis: nihil in ea iniustitiae, alieni, peregrini, superuacui, parergi, adeoque inutilitatis ociosae: nihil in ea imprudentiae, inaequalitatis, odiosae & fastidiosae repetitionis. Quid hic te, amice, offendit, bonus non es, hanc bonam si non amas sapientiae materiam: Quid hic, quod reprehendas habes? ἀδυναμίαν. Affer & confer vires tuas, requisita artificis ne sepone, & conatus ille si non semper & vbique perfruetur optato & proposito, non plane sua destituetur tamen & laude & vtilitate. Labor, Constantia, Iudicium.
units.tr: The matter of true philosophy, which we cultivate and alone love, and of the Christian arts, is therefore good and precious: because it is true, constant, certain and useful for teaching; because it is just, that is, proper and kindred, essential and not adventitious, springing from the very essence of the thing or bound to it by the firmest bond of affinity; and because it is wise and prudent. There is nothing in it of falsehood, nothing of accidental uncertainty and mutability (if the weakness of human genius and the intricate obscurity of things does not stand in the way; and where they do stand in the way, do not unjustly slander or mock the attempts that aim at this virtue: Though strength be lacking, the will is still to be praised; the effort too has its own praise). There is nothing in it of injustice, nothing alien, foreign, superfluous or merely incidental, and so nothing of idle uselessness. There is nothing in it of imprudence, inequality, or hateful and tedious repetition. What offends you here, friend? You are not good if you do not love this good matter of wisdom. What here do you find to reprehend? Inability [ἀδυναμίαν]. Bring and contribute your strengths, do not set aside what the craftsman requires, and that effort, if it does not always and everywhere enjoy the desired aim and purpose, will nonetheless not be wholly deprived of its praise and usefulness. Labour, constancy, judgment.

units.la: CAP. XI. De forma artium Christianae Philosophiae.
units.tr: CAP. XI. On the form of the arts of Christian philosophy.

units.la: FOrma Christianæ Philosophiæ, seu potius artium philosophicarum est ordo & methodus scientifica, qua præcepta vera, iusta & prudentia ita inter se disponuntur, vt ipsa natura, cuius æmula est ars, exigit; & possint esse accommodata ad scientiam optime generandam, vt felicius à docente possint explicari, & facilius à discente intelligi & memoriæ mandari.
units.tr: The form of Christian philosophy, or rather of the philosophical arts, is a scientific order and method in which true, just and prudent precepts are arranged among themselves as nature itself requires (art being nature's imitator). It is so arranged that it can be best adapted to generating knowledge, so that the teacher can explain it more successfully and the learner can grasp it more easily and commit it to memory.

units.la: Hoc autem ordine generalissimum quodque præceptum primo loco ponitur, secundum secundo, tertium tertio, & ita deinceps distinctis gradibus sequuntur & subiiciuntur, quæ minus generalia sunt, tandemque ad finem reseruantur & substituuntur, quæ sunt specialissima, progrediendo nimirum à generalissimo, per subalterna siue interiecta & intermedia, vsque ad specialissima & infima, vel ab vnitate, per media genera, ad indiuiduam multitudinem descendëdo, vt loquitur Plato.
units.tr: In this order the most general precept of each kind is placed first, the second precept second, the third third, and so on by distinct degrees. Those that are less general follow and are placed under them, and at last those that are most specific are reserved and set down at the end. The order proceeds, that is, from the most general through subordinate, or intervening and intermediate, precepts down to the most specific and lowest, or, as Plato says, descends from unity through the middle kinds to the individual multitude.

units.la: Generalissimum autem præceptum est, quod natura est notissimum, hoc est, quod claritate & notitia sua est primum, nec aliunde lucem & notitiam suam sumit, sed aliis, nempe sequetibus tibus specialioribus claritatem ac lu-cem quasi præfert ac largitur.
units.tr: The most general precept is the one that is best known by nature, that is, the one that is first in clarity and knowledge. It does not take its light and knowledge from elsewhere but, as it were, bears and bestows clarity and light on the more specific precepts that follow.

units.la: Subalterna præcepta sunt interiecta & intermedia inter generalissimum & specialissimum præceptum, ideoque ea à superioribus semper lucem assu-munt,& inferioribus communicant.
units.tr: Subordinate precepts are those that lie between the most general and the most specific precept. Therefore they always receive light from the higher ones and communicate it to the lower.

units.la: Specialissima vero sunt illa, quæ à proximis superioribus illuminantur quidem & claritatem accipiunt,sed inferiorib. se vicissim largiri non possunt.
units.tr: The most specific precepts are those that are indeed illuminated by their nearest superiors and receive clarity from them, but cannot in turn bestow anything on what is below them.

units.la: Sic itaque in nostris artibus absolu-te notius & prius, hoc est, natura clari-us præcedit, vt, quemadmodum in ca-tena perpetuo inferiores annuli à su-perioribus,& superiores tandem ex su-premo aliquo seu extremo omnes de-pendent, & inter se connexi sunt, vt semper alter trahat alterum, & medius extremos mutuo nexu sibi colliget & adstringat: ita semper consequés theo-rema ex antecedente dependeat & nectatur, mediumque à superiori in-telligentiæ lumen accipiat,quod vicis-sim cum inferiori communicet, & ita antecedens consequenti, prius poste-riori,cognitionis & explicationis quasi facem præferat.
units.tr: So in our arts, that which is absolutely better known and prior, that is, which by nature is clearer, comes first. As in a chain the lower links always depend on the higher, and the higher finally all depend on some supreme or last link, and are joined together so that each draws the next, and the middle links bind the extremes to themselves with a mutual bond, so too each consequent theorem should depend on and be linked to its antecedent. The middle term receives the light of understanding from the higher and passes it on to the lower, so that the antecedent, prior to the consequent, holds forth, as it were, the torch of knowledge and explanation.

units.la: Hoc ordine nihil excogitari potest, ad iuuandam rerum intelligentiam, & inter se veram conuenientiam, ad confirmādam memoriam vel diuinius vel vtilius : Memoria enim dogmata tali dispositione cognita & perspecta tenacissime comprehendit & fideliter retinet, quæ alioqui sine tali ordine difficilime hærere potuerant. Hic ordo didascalicus veræ Philosophiæ maximum est Dei donum, hic præstat conuenientem, perspicuam ac iustam artium dispositionē: hic largitur distinctiorem scientiarum & artium cognitionem. Vnde veteres non male dixerunt: Methodus est certa rerū tradendarum ratio, qua celerrime ad peritiam deuenitur.
units.tr: Nothing can be devised that helps the understanding of things and their true agreement with one another, or that strengthens the memory more divinely or more usefully, than this order. For memory grasps and firmly retains doctrines known and clearly seen in such an arrangement, which without such order could hardly have stuck at all. This didactic order is the greatest gift of God to true philosophy. It supplies a fitting, clear and just arrangement of the arts, and it bestows a more distinct knowledge of the sciences and arts. Hence the ancients did not wrongly say: "Method is a sure way of handing down things, by which skill is reached most quickly."

units.la: Hæc ordinis dispositio sola singularis ac mira (testamur experientiam, rumpantur vt Ilia Momis, quorum quidam hunc successum non arti, sed Satanæ, ô Satanæ squamas, tribuunt) est intelligentiæ, distinctæ cognitionis ac memoriæ & constituendæ & confirmandæ magistra. Ordinate enim discendo, facilius discimus. Hoc enim Christianus & methodicus Philosophus phus spectat vnicum, vt discetes disciplīæ, quam tradit, distinctiorem & faciliōrem cognitionem hauriant, quod semper fit procedendo ab absolute & natura notioribus. Hic est de coelo lapsus ordo scientificus, quo recte & rite docemus, quo facile edìscimus, quo facile percipimus, & omnia bene.
units.tr: This arrangement of order alone is singular and wonderful (we bear witness from experience; let them burst like the bowels of Momus, those who ascribe this success not to art but to Satan, O the scales of Satan!). It is the mistress who establishes and confirms understanding, distinct knowledge and memory. For when we learn in order, we learn more easily. The Christian and methodical philosopher aims at this one thing: that his learners should draw from the discipline he teaches a more distinct and easier knowledge, which always happens when one proceeds from what is better known in itself and by nature. This is the scientific order fallen from heaven, by which we teach rightly and properly, by which we learn by heart easily, by which we grasp easily, and by which everything goes well.

units.la: Apodeixis. 12.
units.tr: Apodeixis. 12.

units.la: Quacunque doctrina veritatis, iustitiæ & prudentiæ stipata virtutibus bono ac iusto dispositæ est ordine hominum intelligentiæ & memoriæ insigniter inseruiente, ea plurimas & maximas commoditates continet, & Christianæ Reipub. affert.
units.tr: Whatever doctrine of truth, justice and prudence, furnished with virtues, is set out in good and right order, serving the understanding and memory of men remarkably well, that doctrine contains very many and very great advantages, and brings them to the Christian commonwealth.

units.la: Ordo enim bonus est ingens Dei donum. Deus ipse est Deus ordinis, non confusionis, non Deus ἀτάξίας: Deus vult ordinem & εὐκοσμίαν (vt bene scribit quidam Theologus) coli. Plato hoc sciuit qui in Tim. ait: Deum ordinem rebus confusis induxisse: in Gorg. Ordinem & ornatum in omnibus rebus requiri. De legibus scribit: Ordinis ac legis cum ciuitas particeps est, omnia bene facta sunt, vt pleraque, quæ ordine carent, aut male ordinata sunt, ex bene ordinatis alia quædam soluunt. In leg. app. Ordinem quod habet, magnum sapientiæ indicium habet. Speusippus ita definit ordinem: Ordo est concentus operationum ad se inuicem, communionis proportio, vicissitudinis in omnibus causa, obtemperatio ad percipiendum idonea. Mercurius in Pim. and. Ordo fieri à deformitate tate nequit; Eget autem deformitas domino, qui ordinem afferat. Chalcidius in Plat. Tymæum ait: Ordo non potest esse sine harmonia, harmonia est analogia comes, analogia est cum ratione, ratio est comes indiuidua prouidentia, prouidentia non est sine intellectu: intellectus non est sine mente: mens Dei modulata est, ordinauit, excoluit omnem corporis continentiam. Ergo ordo est diuina opificis Dei origo.
units.tr: For good order is a great gift of God. God himself is the God of order, not of confusion, not the God of disorder [ἀταξία]. God wills that order and decorum [εὐκοσμία] be cultivated, as a certain theologian writes well. Plato knew this, who says in the Timaeus: God introduced order into confused things; in the Gorgias: Order and adornment are required in all things. He writes in the Laws: When the state shares in order and law, all things go well; whereas most things that lack order, or are badly ordered, dissolve some of the well-ordered things. In the Epinomis: The great sign of wisdom is the order it has. Speusippus defines order thus: Order is the harmony of operations with one another, a proportion of fellowship, the cause of interchange in all things, a fitness for being perceived. Mercurius in the Pimander: Order cannot come from deformity. Deformity needs a lord who brings order. Chalcidius, on Plato's Timaeus, says: Order cannot exist without harmony; harmony is the companion of analogy; analogy is with reason; reason is the inseparable companion of providence; providence is not without intellect; intellect is not without mind; the mind of God has shaped, ordered and adorned every continuity of the body. Therefore order is the divine origin of the Creator God.

units.la: Rebus, ait Phil in Rhet. si desit ordo, oratio dat sine mente sonum. Et Scaliger Exer. 303. Sect. 9. maxima subtilitatis pars in libris sapientum est oeconomia. Sed amans nimium ordinis extra ordinem.
units.tr: "Where order is lacking," says Philo in the Rhetoric, "speech gives only a sound without mind." And Scaliger, Exercitations 303, section 9: "The greatest part of subtlety in the books of the wise is economy [arrangement]." But one who loves order too much goes outside order.

units.la: Iam vero doctrina verae Philosophiae est veritatis, iustitiae & prudentiae stipata virtutibus in praeceptis, vt supra cap. praeced. est etiam vel debet esse optimo & maxime scientifico ordine disposita. Id hoc cap. vnice expetimus. Videamus autem quid iuris, & voti nostri sit, non vero quid facti, vel alicuius delinquentis deliquii.
units.tr: Now the doctrine of true philosophy, furnished in its precepts with the virtues of truth, justice and prudence (as was said in the preceding chapter), is also, or ought to be, set out in the best and most scientific order. This is what we seek in this chapter alone. But let us see what is right and what is our wish, not what is the fact, or the fault of some offender.

units.la: Ergo doctrina verae Philosophiae plurimas & maximas continet commoditates, easque bene adhibita affert Christianae Reipub.
units.tr: Therefore the doctrine of true philosophy contains very many and very great advantages, and, when used well, brings them to the Christian commonwealth.

units.la: Rursus
units.tr: Again

units.la: Qui inquinat criminoso nomine, naturali & maxime scientifico ordine dispositam, veris item iustis ac sapientibus documentis constantem doctrinam: is merito omnibus bonis nomine non tantum falsitatis, iniustitiae, & insipientiae, sed etiam affectatae ἀταξίας & confusionis imperitae suspectus est, summamque Reipub. Christianae inuidet vtilitatem.
units.tr: Whoever defiles with a criminal name a doctrine arranged in a natural and, above all, scientific order, and consisting of true, just and wise teachings, is rightly suspected by all good people not only of falsehood, injustice and folly, but also of deliberate disorder [ἀταξίας] and untutored confusion, and he grudges the Christian commonwealth its greatest usefulness.

units.la: At qui veras vera Philosophiæ artes criminoso inquinat nomine, is eodem cōspurcat impietatis vo- mitu doctrinam ex præceptis veris, iustis & sapien- tibus, optimo & maxime scientifico ordine confla- tam & ordinatam, maximeq; suo ordine hominibus Christianis fructiferam.
units.tr: But whoever defiles the true arts of true philosophy with a criminal name, by that same vomit of impiety befouls a doctrine compiled and ordered from true, just and wise precepts, arranged in the best and most scientific order, and by its very order most fruitful for Christian people.

units.la: Vt enim iam nihil de præceptis ita (vt optauimus) constitutis addamus, Ordinis & Methodi, de qua iam vim & fructum admirari satis non possum. Eius enim vis se effundit in docentium gloriam, & in discentiū magnam vtilitatē. Quo ad docētes: Vt n. in hoc mundo θεογνωσίας παιδευτηρίῳ admiranda Dei sapientia apparet, adeo vt qui plane nō sit asino Cumano stolidior nō possit non cōfiteri, omnia hæc σοφῶς ὑπὸς δημιουργὸς καὶ φιλοζώῳ τεχνήματα εἶναι: Ita si rectum ordinem adhibeat in disciplinarum systematibus, quin magna docentium sapientia arguatur: Si vero omnia confundant, quin stultitiæ & cerebri male affecti τέκμηριον sit manifestissimum, non est dubium. Nihil enim est vel in animo, vel opere sapientis admirabilius ordine. Scalig. exerc. 2. Arrigant hic aures, & capiant sibi hoc illi, qui data opera, illud τὸ σκότιον Heracliti, si non ore, certe animo circumferunt, & semper ἀείζωον cupiunt, atque ita docere, vt discipuli maneant discipuli, Doctores vero doctores, suisque minutulis distinctionibus iuuentutem discendi cupidam remorantur, adeo, vt quid discas & quomodo discas plane nesciās, vt exclamare possis; Quo teneam vultus mutantem Prothea nodo? vel potius ab excellenti doctrina prohibent, non secus ac Lycii apud Ouidium, qui Latonam sitientem, quo minus ex fonte hauriret aquam, prohibebant. Sunt ergo & illi cum Latona alloquendi:
units.tr: For, to add nothing further about the precepts so constituted (as we have wished), concerning Order and Method, whose force and fruit I cannot sufficiently admire. Its force pours forth both into the glory of teachers and into the great usefulness of learners. As for teachers: just as in this world, the school of the knowledge of God [θεογνωσίας παιδευτηρίῳ], the admirable wisdom of God appears, so that whoever is not plainly more stupid than the Cumaean ass cannot but confess that all these things are skilfully made by the craftsman who loves living things [σοφῶς ὑπὸ δημιουργοῦ καὶ φιλοζώου τεχνήματα εἶναι]. So if teachers use right order in the systems of their disciplines, the great wisdom of the teachers is surely proved; but if they confuse everything, it is beyond doubt a most manifest sign of folly and of a badly disordered brain. For there is nothing more admirable, either in the mind or in the work of a wise man, than order. Scaliger, Exercitations 2: "Let those prick up their ears, and let those take this to themselves, who on purpose carry about, if not in their mouth then at least in their mind, that 'dark' saying of Heraclitus [τὸ σκότιον], and always desire the 'ever-living' [ἀείζωον], and so teach that pupils remain pupils and teachers remain teachers, and with their tiny distinctions hold back the youth eager to learn, so that you utterly do not know what you should learn or how, and could cry out: 'With what knot shall I hold Proteus as he changes his shape?' Or rather, they keep them from excellent learning, no differently than the Lycians in Ovid, who forbade thirsty Latona to drink from the spring. So to them too Latona must be addressed:"

units.la: Quid prohibetis aquas? vsus communis aquarũ est,Non solem proprium natura, nec aera fecit,Nec tenues vndas, ad publica munera veni.
units.tr: "Why do you forbid the waters? The use of water is common; Nature made neither the sun, nor the air, nor the thin waves, as private property; I have come to the public gifts."

units.la: Et digni sunt illi, vt non secus ac Lycii, in ranas conuertantur, hoc est, vt ad rastra, ad asinorum & boum greges, ad porcorum haras amandentur, vbi nihil est, quod authoritati suæ metuant. Facilime enim ibi, vt poma illa Æsopica natare poterunt, & imperium inter beluas obtinere.
units.tr: And they deserve, like the Lycians, to be turned into frogs; that is, to be driven off to the rakes, to the herds of asses and oxen, to the pig-sties, where there is nothing they need fear for their authority. For there, like those Aesopic apples, they will be able to float very easily, and hold rule among the beasts.

units.la: Discentes vero vtilitatem. Quia hæc progressio confert & rerum intelligentiæ & memoriæ. Intelligentiæ. Τεὶνικώτατα enim primo loco constituta sequentium omnium discuti-unt & disiiciunt obscuritatem. Cognitio enim particularium ex vniuersalium notitia pedet.
units.tr: As for the usefulness to learners: this progression contributes both to the understanding of things and to the memory. To understanding: for principles that are most skilfully placed first dispel and scatter the obscurity of everything that follows, since knowledge of particulars depends on knowledge of universals.

units.la: Zab. lib. 1. de Method. c. 14. Memoriæ. Si enim a specialibus ad generalia progrediaris, fieri non poterit, quin repetitionibus & κοκκυσμοῖς inutilibus omnia personent. Hoc iam si fiat, rerum discendarum multitudo citra necessitatem accumulabitur. Hæc demum discentibus plus quam molesta est ac tædiosa. Vt enim vascula oris angusti superfusam humoris copiam respuunt, sensim vero influentibus, vel etiam instillantibus, complentur: Ita paucula facile memoriæ infiguntur, plurima simul edisцere si coneris longe citius effluent, quam aquæ ex dolio, quod Danaides implere voluerunt. Ergo qui veras vera Philosophia artes criminoso inquinat nomine, is merito omnibus bonis nomine non tantum falsitatis, iniustitia & insipientia, quatenus proba illa in ipsa praecepta vera, iusta & prudentia redundant: sed etiam affectata ἀ τἀξίας & confusionis (qui enim odit ordinem amat ametho-diam) suspectus est, adeoque insigne affert Christiana Reipub. damnum, inuidens eidem tantarum virtutum felicitatem.
units.tr: Zabarella, On Method, bk. 1, ch. 14. To memory: if you proceed from particulars to generals, it will be impossible for everything not to resound with repetitions and useless cuckoo-cries [κοκκυσμοῖς]. If this is done, the multitude of things to be learned will be piled up without any necessity, and in the end this is more than troublesome and tedious for learners. For just as little vessels with narrow mouths reject a copious supply of liquid poured over them, but are filled gradually as it flows in, or even drips in, so a few things are easily fixed in the memory; if you try to learn very many at once, they will run out much more quickly than water from the cask the Danaids tried to fill. Therefore whoever defiles the true arts of true philosophy with a criminal name is rightly suspected by all good people not only of falsehood, injustice and folly, inasmuch as those upright precepts overflow with true, just and prudent teaching, but also of deliberate disorder and confusion (for he who hates order loves disorder [ἀμεθοδίαν]), and so inflicts a notable loss on the Christian commonwealth, grudging it the happiness of such great virtues.

units.la: CAP. XII.
units.tr: CAP. XII.

units.la: De Philosophia vera subiecto.
units.tr: On the subject of true Philosophy.

units.la: HActenus de vera Philosophiæ causis: Subiectum Philosophiæ, est Recipiens vel Occupans.
units.tr: Thus far on the causes of true Philosophy. The subject of Philosophy is either the receiving subject or the occupying subject.

units.la: Recipiens subiectum Philosophiæ, quatenus possidetur & scitur, est hominis mens.
units.tr: The receiving subject of Philosophy, insofar as it is possessed and known, is the mind of man.

units.la: Sapientiæ enim & scientiæ rerum non est aliud subiectum, quam mens & anima hominis.
units.tr: For the subject of wisdom and of knowledge of things is nothing other than the mind and soul of man.

units.la: Philosophia est rerum vera sapiëtia & scientia.
units.tr: Philosophy is the true wisdom and knowledge of things.

units.la: Hæc est naturalis, vel infusa, vel acquisita studio.
units.tr: This is either natural, or infused, or acquired by study.

units.la: Deus homini primum indidit scientiam & sapientiam insignem, quæ fuit pars non infima imaginis suæ, vti cognoscimus ex testimonio Moßs, ex cap.17. Ecclesiastici, & ex 7. Ecclesiastæ.
units.tr: God at the first implanted in man knowledge and wisdom of an outstanding kind, which was no small part of his image, as we know from the testimony of Moses, from Ecclesiasticus chapter 17 and from Ecclesiastes chapter 7.

units.la: Mentem itaque Deus scientiæ & sapientiæ veræ adeoq; Philosophiæ subiectum in prima rerum creatione fecit & statuit.
units.tr: Therefore God made and established the mind as the subject of knowledge and true wisdom, and so of true Philosophy, in the first creation of things.

units.la: Deus enim in exordio mundi animalia omnia creauit in suo quęque genere perfecta, tam secūdum perfectiones specificas, quam singulares.
units.tr: For God at the beginning of the world created all animals perfect in their own kind, both in their specific and in their individual perfections.

units.la: Ergo & hominem perfectum iisdem perfectionis modis condidit.
units.tr: Therefore he also created man perfect in the same modes of perfection.

units.la: Quemadmodum igitur homo creatus est perfecto corpore, ita credendum est, eum factum esse, animo mentequae perfectum.
units.tr: Just as man was created with a perfect body, so we must believe he was made perfect in soul and mind.

units.la: Sed naturalis perfectio mentis est sapientia & scientia.
units.tr: But the natural perfection of the mind is wisdom and knowledge.

units.la: Deinde homo primus à Deo conditus integer, debebat primus hominum Doctor & animalium rector esse: quare perfecta facultate docendi & regendi eum præditum fuisse constat.
units.tr: Further, man, created first and whole, ought to have been the first teacher of men and ruler of the animals; it is therefore evident that he was endowed with a perfect ability to teach and to rule.

units.la: At hæc non possunt præstari sine sapientia & scientia.
units.tr: But these cannot be accomplished without wisdom and knowledge.
