units.la: Signum enim scientis est, ait Aristoteles, posse alios docere.
units.tr: For, as Aristotle says, the sign of one who knows is being able to teach others.

units.la: Acquiritur etiamnum & comparatur scientia & sapientia, tum natura, tum doctrina ita vt recipiatur mente.
units.tr: Knowledge and wisdom are still acquired and obtained, both by nature and by teaching, in such a way that they are received by the mind.

units.la: Naturam dico dispositionem & habitudinem naturalem ad disciplinas capessendas in anima tum sentiente, tum ratiocinante.
units.tr: By nature I mean the natural disposition and aptitude for taking up disciplines, in the soul both sensitive and reasoning.

units.la: In sentiente, nam sensuum beneficio omnes artes inueniuntur & percipiuntur.
units.tr: In the sensitive soul, for all the arts are discovered and perceived by the benefit of the senses.

units.la: In ratiocinante scilicet νοητικῇ vel θεωρητικῇ. Νοητικὴ habet εὐφυίαν & μνήμην.
units.tr: In the reasoning soul, namely the intellectual [noētikē] or theoretical [theōrētikē] faculty. The intellectual faculty has good parts [euphuia] and memory [mnēmē].

units.la: Εὐφυία seu ingenium hic est cum iudicio coniunctum, scilicet homini innata facultas inveniendi & iudicandi.
units.tr: Good parts, or talent, here is joined with judgement; namely, the faculty of invention and judgement innate in man.

units.la: Μνήμη seu memoria est facultas metis, ea quae percepimus, fideliter retinendi & prompte reddendi.
units.tr: Memory is the faculty of the mind to retain faithfully what we have perceived and to reproduce it readily.

units.la: Προαίρεσις est animi eiusmodi facultas, qua à natura trahimur ad cognitionis alicuius & scientiae cupiditatem & studium.
units.tr: Choice [prohairesis] is that faculty of the soul by which we are drawn by nature to a desire and zeal for some knowledge and science.

units.la: Ex hac naturali facultate & affectione nascitur tandem habitus.
units.tr: From this natural faculty and affection there finally arises a habit.

units.la: Et sic mens suis facultatibus laborat ad scientiam doctrinarum sibi comparandam, vt eam comparatā in se reponat, ipsaque illa perficiatur atq; exornetur.
units.tr: And so the mind labours with its faculties to acquire for itself the knowledge of the disciplines, so that, once acquired, it may store it within itself, and be itself perfected and adorned by it.

units.la: Est itaque omnis scientiæ Philosophicæ subiectum recipiens Mens: hæc in homine sedes eius est. Hæc quo maior in mente, eo mens nobilior, & quo mens suis instructa facultatibus est diuinior, eo scientia & sapientia & promptius accipitur, & nobilius possidetur, & vtilius exercetur.
units.tr: Therefore the mind is the receiving subject of all philosophical knowledge; this is its seat in man. The greater the mind's capacity, the nobler the mind; and the more divine the mind is, furnished with its faculties, the more readily knowledge and wisdom are received, the more nobly they are possessed, and the more usefully they are exercised.

units.la: Subiectum occupans, in qua Philosophia exercetur, est quæuis res literatæ scientiæ & piæ eruditioni, adeoque humanioribus literis & artibus subiecta, siue ea sit significata, siue significans, siue sit vniuersalis, siue generalis. Quarumcunque igitur rerum est literata sapientia & liberalis scientia, in iis tradendis & explicandis rite Philosophia versatur.
units.tr: The occupying subject in which Philosophy is practised is whatever matter belongs to learned knowledge and godly erudition, and so is subject to the humane letters and arts, whether it is signified or signifying, whether universal or general. Philosophy therefore properly concerns itself with the teaching and explaining of whatever matters contain learned wisdom and liberal knowledge.

units.la: Humana igitur Philosophia exercetur earum rerum omnium humanarum, hoc est, ad hominem literatum eiusque vtilem scientiam pertinentium, quæ inquam in literati hominis, hoc est, Philosophi cadunt cognitionem in vita humana salutarem, doctrina.
units.tr: Human Philosophy is therefore exercised on all human matters, that is, on those things pertaining to the learned man and his useful knowledge, which, I say, fall under the knowledge of the learned man, that is, of the philosopher, as teaching salutary for human life.

units.la: 13. Apodeixis.
units.tr: 13. Apodeixis (Demonstration).

units.la: Quicquid Deus hominis menti indidit, quocunque que idem Deus mentem humanam perfici & exornari primum voluit & ad huc vult, id quia bonum, nemo bonus male vituperare & non vtile ac necessarium homini proclamare ausit. Deus enim sapientissimus non nisi bona mentibus humanis insculpsit, non nisi vtilibus & necessariis dotibus ac donis eas perfecit & ornauit.
units.tr: Whatever God has implanted in the mind of man, and whatever God wished, and still wishes, the human mind to be perfected and adorned with, since it is good, no good man would dare to disparage as bad or to proclaim not useful and necessary for man. For God, most wise, has engraved on human minds nothing but good things, and has perfected and adorned them only with useful and necessary endowments and gifts.

units.la: Atqui sanam & veram Philosophiam Deus meti hominis in principio mundi indidit, sana & vera Philosophia eius mentem voluit perfici & exornari, tanquam insigni dono, quo & suam referret imaginem. Nam indidit Deus creator hominis animo non modo sapientiam & scientiam rerum diuinarum, verum etiam naturalium, mundanarum & humanarum praecellentem. Hac tanquam egregia virtute mente hominis perfici & condecorari voluit, quippe perfecit & condecorauit deliberato voluntatis sapientissimae consilio. Adhuc vult mentes nostras hoc sapientiae & scientiae rerum dono perfici & ornari, quia vult vt ad imaginem suam quotidie reformemur.
units.tr: But God the Creator implanted in the mind of man, at the beginning of the world, sound and true Philosophy; he wished the mind to be perfected and adorned by sound and true Philosophy as by a distinguished gift, by which it might also reflect his own image. For God the Creator implanted in the soul of man not only wisdom and knowledge of divine things, but also of natural, worldly and human things, surpassing all. He wished the mind of man to be perfected and adorned by this as by an excellent virtue, and indeed he perfected and adorned it by the deliberate counsel of his most wise will. He still wishes our minds to be perfected and adorned with this gift of wisdom and knowledge of things, because he wills that we be daily reformed into his image.

units.la: Sapientia autem & scientia veritatis rerum, est magna pars istius imaginis. Atque Philosophia vera hanc literatam sapientiam & veritatis rerum humanarum & aliarum scientiam eruditam profitetur & continet.
units.tr: Wisdom and knowledge of the truth of things is indeed a great part of that image. And true Philosophy professes and contains this learned wisdom and this knowledge of the truth of human and other things.

units.la: Ergo veram hanc Philosophiam nemo bonus vituperare, & homini non vtilem nec necessariam proclamare ausit.
units.tr: Therefore no good man would dare to disparage this true Philosophy, or to proclaim it not useful and not necessary for man.

units.la: Item:
units.tr: Likewise:

units.la: Ea res, quae literata sapientiae & vtili scientiae subiiciuntur, scitu non sunt inutiles, sed potius vtiles. Atqui doctrina vera Philosophia in iis rebus, quae literatae sapientiae & vtili scientiae subiiciuntur, docendis versatur & occupatur. Proinde doctrina vera Philosophiae scitu homini non inutilis sed vtilis censenda est.
units.tr: Those things which are subject to learned wisdom and useful knowledge are worth knowing; they are not useless, but rather useful. But true Philosophy is occupied and engaged in teaching those things which are subject to learned wisdom and useful knowledge. Therefore the teaching of true Philosophy is to be judged worth knowing for man, not useless but useful.

units.la: CAP. XIII.
units.tr: CAP. XIII.

units.la: De Christiana Philosophia adiunctis 12. virtutibus.
units.tr: On the twelve virtues that accompany Christian Philosophy.

units.la: VERAE nostrae Philosophiae, quae simul est Christiana & orthodoxa, si Aristotelica, siue Ramea nominari velit, haec studia, has virtutes, has proprietates exoptamus.
units.tr: These are the studies, virtues and properties we desire for our true Philosophy, which is at once Christian and orthodox, whether it wishes to be called Aristotelian or Ramist.

units.la: Studium & virtutem Philosophiae nostrae optamus in omnibus literatis, Christianae pietatis, charitatis, veritatis, modestiae, ordinis, libertatis, utilitatis, perspicuitatis, doctae breuitatis, sedulae docilitatis, candoris, concordiae.
units.tr: We desire for our Philosophy, in all who study it, the following virtues: Christian piety, charity, truthfulness, modesty, order, freedom, usefulness, clarity, learned brevity, diligent teachability, candour and harmony.

units.la: Has virtutes Philosophiam nostram comitari, his Philosophum Christianum stipatum incedere, immane quantum discupimus.
units.tr: We greatly long for these virtues to accompany our Philosophy, and for the Christian philosopher to walk attended by them.

units.la: Primum itaq; Philosophiae tam humanae quam diuinae studium, prima virtus est; Christianae pietati dare piam operam.
units.tr: The first, then, of the study of Philosophy, both human and divine, is this virtue: to devote careful effort to Christian piety.

units.la: Vera itaque Philosophia est Christiana stianæ pietatis ministra, & quidem studiosissima veræ in contemplando sapientiæ, & in agendo prudentiæ. Christianus ergo Philosophus Deum ac sanctum Dei verbum, doctrinam & pietatem Christianā unice veneratur, nec quicquam, quod ei vllo modo refragatur, aut confingit, aut asserit, aut credit, aut defendit.
units.tr: True Philosophy is therefore the handmaid of Christian piety, and especially eager for true wisdom in contemplation and for prudence in action. The Christian philosopher, accordingly, reveres God, his holy Word, and Christian doctrine and piety alone, and neither invents, asserts, believes nor defends anything that in any way runs counter to them.

units.la: Secundū est, studere charitati Christianæ.
units.tr: The second is to pursue Christian charity.

units.la: Vera itaque Philosophia est Christianæ charitatis fidelis promotrix, nemini noxia, mansueti amoris & beneficentiæ excultrix, non maleuola, non maledica, non calumniosa. Christiani ergo Philosophi est, non odisse & persequi, sed diligere, & ferre proximum etiam in quibusdam Philosophicis modeste dissentientem, bene etiam dicta non sophistice calumniari, & malitiose ex insectatione aliorum sibi laudem quærere.
units.tr: True Philosophy is therefore a faithful promoter of Christian charity, harmful to no one, a cultivator of gentle love and beneficence, not ill-willed, not slanderous, not calumnious. It is therefore the Christian philosopher's part not to hate and persecute, but to love, and to bear with a neighbour who dissents modestly even on some philosophical points; not to slander with sophistry even well-said things, nor to seek praise for himself maliciously by attacking others.

units.la: Tertium est veritatem impense adamare, & perpetuo studio prosequi.
units.tr: The third is to love truth earnestly and to pursue it with constant zeal.

units.la: Vera itaque Philosophia est studiosissima non tam opinionum & authoritatis, quam sapientis & prudentis veritatis: vnde & scientia veritatis dicitur. Hinc etiam Christiani Philosophi est nugas & paganismos detestari, veritatem philosophicam pluris pluris facere, quam authoritatem & opinionem omnium Philosophorum, illam sectari, profiteri, tueri.
units.tr: True Philosophy is therefore most eager not so much for opinions and authority as for wise and prudent truth; whence it is also called the knowledge of truth. Hence it is also the part of the Christian philosopher to detest trifles and pagan follies, to value philosophical truth far above the authority and opinion of all philosophers, and to follow, profess and defend it.

units.la: Quartum est, toto animo in modestiam & humilitatem incumbere.
units.tr: The fourth is to apply oneself with all one's mind to modesty and humility.

units.la: Vera itaque Philosophia est observantissima modestiae & humilitatis, auersatur superciliosum fastum, gloriosam philautiam & Thrasonicam gloriationē. Christianus itaque Philosophus superbia omnis osor des-e, suo ingenio, suis item inuentis vel dogmatis humiliter & modeste sentit ac iudicat.
units.tr: True Philosophy is therefore most observant of modesty and humility; it shuns haughty pride, vainglorious self-love and boastful bragging. The Christian philosopher, therefore, hating all pride, judges and thinks humbly and modestly of his own talent and of his own discoveries or doctrines.

units.la: Quintum est, ponere animum & curam in methodo & ordine accurato.
units.tr: The fifth is to give one's mind and care to method and exact order.

units.la: Vera itaque Philosophia est sedula eximii ordinis & methodicae claritatis mater & nutrix. Vnde etiam Christianus Philosophus ordine sua disponit optimo, fugit & auersatur monstrosam & perturbatam rerum, sine vlla methodo, perplexitatem.
units.tr: True Philosophy is the diligent mother and nurse of excellent order and methodical clarity. Whence also the Christian philosopher arranges his material in the best order, and flees from and avoids the monstrous and confused entanglement of things without any method.

units.la: Sextum est, touere & retinere modestam ac prudentem iudicandi libertatem.
units.tr: The sixth is to hold to and keep a measured and prudent freedom of judgement.

units.la: Vera itaque Philosophia mentis & iudicii libertatem permittit, non tyrannicam seruitutem imponit. Vnde & Christia-nus nus Philosophus libertatis Philosophitæ amans, non instar serui pecoris iurat in verba magistri, cui mentem & linguam vendit suam, sed suum quoque & ingenium & iudicium libere & modeste adhibet.
units.tr: True Philosophy grants freedom of mind and judgement; it imposes no tyrannical servitude. Whence the Christian philosopher, a lover of philosophical freedom, does not, like a slavish sheep, swear to the words of a master to whom he sells his mind and tongue, but uses his own talent and judgement freely and modestly.

units.la: Septimum est, studere vtilitati & vero vsui, non otiosæ futilitati.
units.tr: The seventh is to pursue usefulness and genuine practice, not idle futility.

units.la: Vera itaque Philosophia studiosa est veræ & vtilis, non autem fucatæ, ac spinosis tricis & subtilitatibus inutilibus, futilibusque distinctionibus fatuæ eruditionis. Hinc quoque Christianus Philosophus omnia sua studia ad vtiles & salutares in vita humana vsus confert, omnisque generis perplexas tricas ac quisquilias, plus futilitatis quam vtilitatis habentes, auersatur.
units.tr: True Philosophy is devoted to what is true and useful, not to what is painted over, nor to thorny tangles and useless subtleties, nor to the trivial distinctions of foolish learning. Hence the Christian philosopher also directs all his studies to useful and salutary uses in human life, and shuns all intricate tangles and trifles that have more futility than usefulness.

units.la: Octauum est, perspicuitate lucem doctrinis inferre.
units.tr: The eighth is to bring light to doctrines by clarity.

units.la: Vera itaque Philosophia præceptorum & exemplorum, phrasium & terminorum claram amat lucem, obscuras odit tenebras. Proinde Christianus Philosophus formulas loquendi cultiores, politiores, & ad docendum accommodatiores, adeoque expedita claritate perspicuas, tam in exemplis quam præceptis aliisque operibus aucupatur.
units.tr: True Philosophy loves the clear light of precepts and examples, of phrases and terms, and hates dark shadows. Therefore the Christian philosopher seeks out forms of speech that are more refined and polished, better suited to teaching, and thus transparently clear with unhindered lucidity, in examples as in precepts and in his other works.

units.la: Nonum est, sectari dilucidã ac moderatam breuitatem.
units.tr: The ninth is to pursue clear and measured brevity.

units.la: Philosophia igitur vera est amantissima facilis & perspicuæ breuitatis, garrulæ multitudinis, difficilisque vastitatis inimica. Vnde & Christianus Philosophus obleëtat se moderata & docta breuitate, vastissimas spinas ac difficultates in tot & tantis libris, præceptis, obseruationibus, exceptionibus repetitis fastidit.
units.tr: True Philosophy is therefore most fond of easy and clear brevity, and the enemy of garrulous abundance and difficult vastness. Hence the Christian philosopher restrains himself with moderate and learned brevity, and disdains the vast thorns and difficulties of so many great books, precepts, observations and repeated exceptions.

units.la: Decimum est, piæ docilitati & operosæ sedulitati studere.
units.tr: The tenth is to strive for pious teachability and diligent application.

units.la: Vera itaque Philosophia præcipit patientem docilitatem, & assiduum in inquirendo & inueniendo, in examinando & iudicando, non alienum, sed proprium etiam studium. Ergo Christiani Philosophi est, percupidum esse discendi, patieter correctionem admittere, veriora & meliora monstranti cedere, assiduo studio inquirendi & inueniendi, examinandi & iudicandi ardere & proficere.
units.tr: True Philosophy enjoins patient teachability and constant effort in inquiring and discovering, in examining and judging, as a study that is not foreign but its own. Therefore it is the part of the Christian philosopher to be most eager to learn, to admit correction patiently, to yield to those who show truer and better things, and to burn with constant zeal for inquiring, discovering, examining and judging, and to make progress.

units.la: Vndecimum est, nauare operam candori & synceritati.
units.tr: The eleventh is to take pains for candour and sincerity.

units.la: Vera ergo Philosophia fuci, sophisticæ, & fallacium argutiarum ignara, aperti candoris amatrix, candidam amplectitur synceritatem. Ea de re Christianus etiam Philosophus syncerum exosculas candorem, scapham dicit scapham, nihil impie simulat aut aut dissimulat ad alicuius gratiam, veritatem non inflectit & inuoluit, cognita vitia non colorat aut excusat.
units.tr: True Philosophy is ignorant of pretence, sophistry and deceitful cleverness, a lover of open candour, and embraces honest sincerity. For this reason the Christian philosopher also embraces sincere candour, calls a spade a spade, feigns or dissembles nothing impiously to win anyone's favour, does not bend or wrap up the truth, and does not colour or excuse known faults.

units.la: Vltimum est, paci & concordiæ studium suum dare.
units.tr: The last is to devote one's zeal to peace and harmony.

units.la: Vera igitur Philosophia literata Reip. pacem tuetur, concordiam animorum consentientium spirat. Quapropter Christianus Philosophus studio sanctissimæ pacis pacate & amice philosophatur, studet discentium ædificationi, non calumniosis clamoribus, sed rationibus, non turbulentis sophismatis, sed argumentis, non bannis & proscriptionibus, sed documentis & fraternis admonitionibus, non armis & flammis, sed legitimis disputationibus agit.
units.tr: True Philosophy therefore guards the peace of the learned republic and breathes the harmony of agreeing minds. Accordingly the Christian philosopher, out of zeal for the most holy peace, philosophizes calmly and amicably, aims at the edification of his students, acts not with calumnious clamours but with reasons, not with turbulent sophisms but with arguments, not with banishments and proscriptions but with teaching and brotherly admonitions, not with weapons and flames but with lawful disputations.

units.la: Hæc igitur sanctæ syncerææque Philosophiæ fundamenta, has Christianorum Philosophorum virtutes & fructus, si non habemus, votis exoptamus.
units.tr: If we do not have these foundations of holy and sincere Philosophy, these virtues and fruits of Christian philosophers, we desire them with our prayers.

units.la: Apodeixis 14.
units.tr: Apodeixis 14.

units.la: Qui male habet & iniquo fert animo præcipuas Christianas virtutes, eum necesse est malitioso & diabolico flagrare odio Dei & omnium bonorum. Christianæ enim virtutes vt sunt à Deo, ita etiam à Deo omnibus præcipiuntur. Præcepta Dei qui fert acerbe, is Dei voluntatem non potest potest non odisse: qui vero Dei odit volunta-tem, eum & Dei inimicum esse necesse est. Omnis homo bonus est & censetur virtutum beneficio: qui igitur auersatur ipsas virtutes, is & ipsos bonos æquo animo perferre non potest.
units.tr: He who is ill at ease with, and bears with ill temper, the chief Christian virtues must of necessity burn with a malicious and diabolical hatred of God and of all good things. For Christian virtues, as they are from God, so are they also enjoined by God on all men. Whoever bears God's precepts bitterly cannot but hate God's will; and whoever hates God's will must necessarily be an enemy of God too. Every good man is judged to be such by the benefit of the virtues; he who turns away from the virtues themselves cannot also bear the good men themselves with an even mind.

units.la: At vero quisquis male habet & iniquo fert animo Christianam Philosophiam, eiusque fundamenta, ac virtutes, eam eiusque vsum Christiane & prudenter gubernantes, is præcipuas Christiana vita virtutes grauiter & iniquo patitur animo, quicquid etiam ore & vita hypocrisi simulet.
units.tr: But indeed, whoever is ill at ease with and bears with ill temper Christian Philosophy, and its foundations and virtues, and who governs it and its use in a Christian and prudent way, bears grievously and with an ill mind the chief virtues of the Christian life, however much he may pretend otherwise with his mouth and by a hypocritical life.

units.la: Etenim Christianæ pietati, cuius gratia eliminandam illam ex orbe Christiano clamat, non sincere studet, quam nos principaliter in constitutione & vsu Philosophiæ spectandam iubemus. Non studet charitati Christianæ, quam regulâ Philosophiæ theoreticæ ac practicæ optamus. Nō studet humilitati ac modestiæ, superbe quippe ignoratam impetit doctrinam, nec se suamque curtam agnoscit supellectilem. Non veritati sanctæ ipsarum rerum studet; autoritati quippe & hominum opinionibus traditionibusq; plus tribuit, quibus minus Philosophia. Non Methodo & ordini accurato, quem cum primis vera affectat Philosophia, fauet. Non libertati iudicandi, quam amplectitur sana Philosophia, sed forte abiectæ & pigræ seruituti se subiicit. Non vtilitati seu vero vsui, cuius studiosam se sancta profitetur Philosophia, sed forte ociosæ futilitati operam nauat. Non lucem & perspicuitatem tatem amat, cuius cultrix est nostra Philosophia. Non claras & moderatas breuitati, quae nostris est in deliciis, sed perplexae prolixitati forte se aggregat. Non docilitati & in studiis sedulitati dat operam. Non candorem & sinceritatem, non denique pacem & concordiam amplectitur Christianam, quas omnes sibi comites & amicas officiosas virtutes adiungit sana & orthodoxa Philosophia.
units.tr: For he does not sincerely pursue Christian piety, for the sake of which he cries out that this philosophy must be removed from the Christian world; yet we bid that piety be regarded chiefly in the constitution and use of Philosophy. He does not pursue Christian charity, which we desire to be the rule of theoretical and practical Philosophy. He does not pursue humility and modesty: proudly he assails a doctrine he does not know, and he does not recognise that his own stock of equipment is slender. He does not pursue the holy truth of things themselves; for he gives more weight to authority, to the opinions of men and to traditions, to which Philosophy gives less. He does not favour method and careful order, which true Philosophy above all strives for. He does not submit to the freedom of judgement which sound Philosophy embraces, but perhaps subjects himself to a lazy and abject servitude. He does not labour for usefulness or true practice, to which holy Philosophy professes itself devoted, but perhaps spends his effort on idle triviality. He does not love light and clarity, of which our Philosophy is the cultivator. He does not join himself to clear and moderate brevity, which is our delight, but perhaps to perplexing prolixity. He does not devote himself to teachableness or diligence in study. He does not embrace Christian candour and sincerity, and finally not peace and concord, all of which sound and orthodox Philosophy joins to itself as companions and dutiful friends.

units.la: Ergo qui hanc molesto & iniquo fert animo, licet contrarium verbis & factis praeseferat, reipsa tamen Dei & omnium bonorum flagrat impio & diabolico odio.
units.tr: Therefore, whoever bears this with displeasure and ill temper, although he displays the contrary in words and deeds, in reality burns with an impious and diabolical hatred of God and of all good things.

units.la: CAP. XIV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIV.

units.la: De contrariis vitiis vanae Philosophiae Pseudaristotelicae.
units.tr: On the contrary vices of vain Pseudo-Aristotelian philosophy.

units.la: VAnam deinde & no Christianam Philosophiam amandamus, quae contrariis est deformata vitiis. Est vero ea vel Pseudaristotelica vel Pseudoramea.
units.tr: Next, we exclude from the Christian philosophy we love the vain and non-Christian philosophy, which is deformed by vices contrary to the others. It is either Pseudo-Aristotelian or Pseudo-Ramist.

units.la: Pseudaristotelicae haec vitia superioribus virtutibus opposita reiicimus.
units.tr: We reject these vices of Pseudo-Aristotelian philosophy, which are opposed to the virtues above.

units.la: 1. Philosophia ne sit impia. Impietas itaque Idololatria, seu Prosopolatria, & Apotheosis Aristotelica exulet a Philosophia nostra, quae ex Aristotele, eiusque placitis, vel ex alio aliquo magni nominis Philosopho nugacissimum fabricatur numen. Qua de Deo, Christo, Prophetis & Apostolis eorum verbo potius, quam de suo Aristotele, vel alio pagano Philosopho, eiusque placitis & opinionibus dubitat: Qua Philosophos in suo lyceo legi Dei perinde ut alios homines subiectos esse non statuit: sed creatorem fortassis hoc in loco scilicet philosophico, creaturae cedere debere somniat: Philosophis quippe in auditorio philosophico, Christianae religionis ac fidei dogmata non esse posita, sed in templo & auditorio Theologico tantum valere, credi & defendi debere automat. Qua impios quoque Aristotelis, aliorumque paganismos & atheismos sacrae scripturae aduersos per suam duplicis veritatis Chimaeram, ac ex inanissimis infinitarum ac futilissimarum distinctiunculam sacculis colorat, excusat, propugnat, vel inepte cum Dei verbo conciliat, atque ita existimationem Aristotelicam vel Platonicam cum magna ignominia veritatis, pietatis, nominis & existimationis Christianae, immodicis onerat laudibus, adeoque, inquam, tenebras appellat lucem. Hanc impietatem a nostra Philosophia nostra Philosophus amandari vult, quae tyrannicam Monarchiam mono more in Scholas introducit.
units.tr: 1. Let philosophy not be impious. Let impiety, that is idolatry or worship of persons, and the Aristotelian apotheosis, be banished from our philosophy, which fashions from Aristotle and his tenets, or from some other philosopher of great name, a most trifling divinity. It doubts concerning God, Christ, the Prophets and the Apostles, taking their word rather than that of its own Aristotle or some other pagan philosopher and his tenets and opinions. It does not hold that philosophers in their lyceum are subject to the law of God just as other men are, but dreams that the Creator must yield, perhaps in this philosophical place, to the creature. It maintains that the dogmas of the Christian religion and faith have no place in the philosophical lecture room, and that they are valid only in the temple and the theological lecture room, and must be believed and defended only there. It also colours, excuses and defends the impious doctrines of Aristotle and of other pagans and atheists opposed to Holy Scripture, through its own chimera of a double truth and through a multitude of most empty and trivial distinctions, or it foolishly reconciles them with the Word of God. In this way it burdens the Aristotelian or Platonic reputation with immoderate praise, to the great disgrace of truth, piety, the name and reputation of Christianity; and so, I say, it calls darkness light. Our philosopher wants this impiety banished from our philosophy, which introduces a tyrannical monarchy in the schools in the manner of a single ruler.

units.la: 2. Philosophia ne sit iniusta & iniqua in proximum,
units.tr: 2. Let philosophy not be unjust and unfair toward its neighbour.

units.la: Iniustitia igitur omnis, hoc est, obtrectatio, maleuolentia, maledicentia ac virorum optimorum, ac verè Christianæ religioni ac pietati addictissimorum, propter Aristotelem vel alium veterem Philosophum, eiusve edicta contra charitatem Christianam iniqua, proscriptio in metallum, ad incendium, ad excidium vel ad carceres condemnatio à Christiana Philosophia charitatis obseruatissima exulet: quia hæc non ita maleuola, non ita maledica est, non ita calumniosa, nec propter philosophicas quasdam de rebus humanis vel aliis dissensiones, quenquam ita temere diris direque devouet, & proscribit.
units.tr: Therefore let all injustice be banished from Christian philosophy, the most faithful observer of charity: that is, all detraction, ill will, slander, and the condemnation of the best men, who are most devoted to true Christian religion and piety, on account of Aristotle or some other ancient philosopher, or of his edicts, which are unfair toward Christian charity; the proscription to the mines, to the fire, to destruction, or to prison. For this philosophy is not so ill-natured, not so slanderous, not so calumnious, and does not so rashly curse and proscribe anyone with dire imprecations on account of certain philosophical or other disagreements about human affairs.

units.la: 3. Philosophia ne sit falsa, nec hominum nitatur traditionibus.
units.tr: 3. Let philosophy not be false, nor rest on the traditions of men.

units.la: Falsitas itaque omnis & mendacia absint à Philosophia nostra, cuius fundamentum sit sola veritas sapiens & eloquens. Non sit eidem loco veritatis Aristoteles, non sit ei loco sanæ rationis Aristotelis & interpretum opinio & persuasio, non sit ei loco solidorum argumentorum, Aristotelicorum aberrantium somnia & testimonia: non crepet, duplicet & triplicet Aristotelem, sed veritatem.
units.tr: Therefore let all falsity and lies be absent from our philosophy, whose foundation is only wise and eloquent truth. Let Aristotle not stand in the place of truth for it, nor the opinion and persuasion of Aristotle's interpreters in the place of sound reason; let it not have the dreams and testimonies of erring Aristotelians in the place of solid arguments. Let it not shout up, double and triple Aristotle, but truth.

units.la: 4. Philosophia ne sit sophistica & su- co tincta.
units.tr: 4. Let philosophy not be sophistical and steeped in sophistry.

units.la: Fucus itaque omnis & dolus sophisticus: omnes nugæ, sophismata, cavilli, calumniæ, à Christiana Philosophia exterminantor.
units.tr: Therefore let all paint and sophistical trickery be banished from Christian philosophy: all trifles, sophisms, quibbles and calumnies.

units.la: 5. Philosophia ne sit serua, adulatrix, credula & vile mancipium.
units.tr: 5. Let philosophy not be a slave, a flatterer, credulous, and a base servant.

units.la: A nostra itaque Philosophia secedit servitus atque captivitas Aristotelica, parasitica adulatio, quam comitatur nugax credulitas, ac vesana socordia. Unde & Philosophus Christianus non iurat in Aristotelis vel alius alicuius veteris verba, nulli Philosopho s, linguam & mentem, rationemque, imo ingenium ac iudicium vendit ac mancipat, non ullius autoritati etiam antiquissimi Philosophi parasitice & seruiliter adulatur. Vana Philosophia habet hodie multos suorum Philosophorum parasitos, qui aduersus veram Philosophiam satis strenue debacchantur. Vti & hodierna Mataeologia nonnullos non Theologos, sed Theologorum seruos & parasitos, aduersus autem Orthodoxos impudenter calumniando, & thrasonice debacchando plus satis proteruos habet. Credula nimirum non est sana Philosophia, sed proprium vult adhiberi iudicium, ut Sophistarum fucum & tricas ineptas suo beneficio olfaciamus.
units.tr: Therefore servitude and Aristotelian captivity, parasitical flattery, which is accompanied by silly credulity and frenzied stupidity, withdraw from our philosophy. Hence the Christian philosopher does not swear by the words of Aristotle or of any other ancient, nor does he sell or hand over his tongue, mind, reason, indeed his talent and judgment, to any philosopher, nor does he flatter the authority of even the most ancient philosopher in a parasitical and servile way. Vain philosophy today has many parasites of its own philosophers, who rage quite vigorously against true philosophy. Likewise today's Matheology has some who are not theologians but servants and parasites of theologians, and who are altogether too insolent in impudently slandering and boastfully raging against the Orthodox. Certainly sound philosophy is not credulous; rather, it wants its own judgment applied, so that by its help we may smell out the paint and silly tricks of the sophists.

units.la: 6. Philosophia ne sit inutilis & futilis.
units.tr: 6. Let philosophy not be useless and trifling.

units.la: Omne ergo nugacis ac fucatæ spinosis tricis & subtilitatibus subtilibusque futilitatibus fatuæ sapientiæ studium arceatur à Philosophia nostra. Hæc etenim omnis generis ociosas & spinosas Aristotelicorum & aliorum opiniones, disputationes, quæstiones, plus subtilitatis, difficultatis, ac fatuitatis, quam veræ sapientiæ, facilitatis & utilitatis complexas execratur, vana autem Philosophia istas nugas & quisquilias, ut divina mysteria & divina oracula admiratur ac sectatur.
units.tr: Therefore let all study of foolish wisdom, dressed up with thorny tricks, subtleties and trifling niceties, which is mere trifling, be kept away from our philosophy. For it abhors the idle and thorny opinions, disputations and questions of Aristotelians and others of every kind, which contain more subtlety, difficulty and foolishness than true wisdom, ease and usefulness. Vain philosophy, on the other hand, admires and pursues these trifles and rubbish as if they were divine mysteries and divine oracles.

units.la: 7. Philosophia ne sit immodesta ac inflata.
units.tr: 7. Let philosophy not be arrogant and puffed up.

units.la: Omnis itaque superciliosus fastus & superba Φιλαυτία, quæ alto quodam spiritu de se suisque Aristotelicis placitis de suo Aristotele, de interpretum illius sapientia & Philosophia thrasonice gloriatur, à Christiana Philosophia exterminetur, & prorsus exulat.
units.tr: Therefore let all haughty pride and arrogant self-love be utterly banished from Christian philosophy: the self-love that boasts boastfully, with a lofty spirit, of itself and its Aristotelian tenets, of its Aristotle, and of the wisdom and philosophy of his interpreters.

units.la: 8. Philosophia ne sit perturbata & promiscue confusa.
units.tr: 8. That philosophy should not be disordered or confusedly jumbled.

units.la: Pessimum itaque ordinem ac perturbatam sine vlla vera methodo perplexitatem, scopasq; dissolutas respuit sana Philosophia.
units.tr: Sound philosophy therefore rejects the worst order, a disordered tangle without any true method, and scattered brooms swept in every direction.

units.la: Nobis itaque non est Philosopus bene sanus, qui perplexam, dissipatam, & disturbatam in conscribendis & explicandis sua Philosophiae disciplinis observat, ita nil nisi dissolutissimas scopas in illis liceat deprehendere.
units.tr: For our philosopher, if he is really sound, is not one who in writing up and setting out the disciplines of his philosophy keeps them tangled, scattered and disturbed, so that nothing can be found in them but the most loosely bound brooms.

units.la: 9. Philosophia ne sit obscura & difficilis.
units.tr: 9. That philosophy should not be obscure or difficult.

units.la: Philosophicorum itaque documentorum vitetur obscuritas: facessat itaque hinc tam exemplorum quam praeceptorum, tam terminorum, quam phrasium horrida (si alia haberi possunt) barbaries, deformis inelegantia, aenigmatica difficultas. Noster itaque Christianus Philosophus non delectatur stylo intricato & terminis obscuris, quos saepius ne quidem ipse Oedipus divinando assequi potest, fugit item confecta, difficilima, ridicula, puerilia, abecedaria, chaerilea, & ad communem vitae ac studiorum usum ineptissima exempla.
units.tr: Obscurity in philosophical teaching is therefore to be avoided. Away then with the harsh barbarism (if other words can be found), the ugly inelegance and the riddling difficulty, in examples and precepts, in terms and in phrases alike. Our Christian philosopher takes no delight in an intricate style and obscure terms, which often not even Oedipus himself could work out by guessing. He likewise shuns examples that are far-fetched, very difficult, ridiculous, childish, elementary, a Chaerilean sort, and wholly unsuited to the common use of life and of study.

units.la: 10. Philosophia ne sit vasta nimis & prolixa, taedium, fastidium & deformitatem pariens.
units.tr: 10. That philosophy should not be excessively vast and long-winded, producing weariness, distaste and deformity.

units.la: Ab hac itaque Philosophia segregatur omnis futilis ac odiosa prolixaque garrulitas, librorum ac praeceptionum, observationum & exceptionum ingens multitudo ac vastitas. Taediosum quippe, fastidiosum & ingratum tum est in Aristotelicis interpretum spinis ac difficultatibus vastissimis, imo in vnius alicuius libri explicatione & commentatione per maximam partem iuuentutis, sæpe vitæ detineri & hærere.
units.tr: So all trifling, tedious and wordy verbosity is kept apart from this philosophy, as is the huge multitude and vastness of books, precepts, observations and exceptions. For it is wearisome, distasteful and unrewarding to be held and stuck for most of a young person's life among the thorns and very vast difficulties of the Aristotelian commentators, indeed in the explanation and commentary of a single book.

units.la: 11. Philosophia ne sit indocilis ac ignaua, ne sit admonitionis studiosæ impatiens.
units.tr: 11. That philosophy should not be unteachable and lazy, nor impatient of admonition offered in a studious spirit.

units.la: Pertinaciam itaque in erroribus obstinatam, indocilemque ac occæcatam mentem odit nostra Philosophia: Hæc se moneri, corrigi, emendari, obiurgari, melioraque ac veriora doceri modeste non moleste patitur. Hæc non mauult cum homine, quem suspicit, errare, quam cum veritate recte sentire. Ignauia omnis secura & socors excutiatur à Philosopho nostro, inquirat sedulo in rerum veritatem, aliorum scripta & dogmata examinet. Suum & ingenium & iudicium adhiberi, quæ prohibet, interphilosophandum, est minus sincera Philosophia.
units.tr: Our philosophy therefore hates a mind that is obstinate in its errors, unteachable and blinded. It does not allow itself to be warned, corrected, amended, rebuked, and taught better and truer things, except modestly and without resentment. It would rather err with a man it respects than think rightly against the truth. Let our philosopher shake off all careless and slothful idleness; let him search diligently into the truth of things and examine the writings and doctrines of others. It is less than sincere philosophy to forbid the use of one's own wit and judgement, which is what philosophizing among others amounts to.

units.la: 12. Denique Philosophia ne esto hypocritica, simulans & dissimulans, nec interim esto seditiosa, tumultuosa, persecutrix, sanguinaria.
units.tr: 12. Finally, philosophy should not be hypocritical, pretending and dissembling, and yet at the same time be seditious, turbulent, persecuting and bloodthirsty.

units.la: A vera proinde Philosophia exulet omnis hypocrisis & minime sincerus affectus, ne Philosophus in Aristotelis vel alius, ne in sua suæ secta gratiam modo simulet, modo dissi-mulet, modo aiat, modo neget, adeoque mira-biliter omnia inflectat & inuoluat, argutu-lisque rationib. ac præcipue distinctiunculis coloret & excusat, idque contra conscienti-am. Interim autem non sit Ate & turbatrix omnium ἔρις, non sit tuba seditionum, ratio-nibus, non conuiciis & calumniis, argumen-tis non sophismatis, documentis & fraternis admonitionibus, non bannis & proscriptio-nibus, probationibus & legitimis disputa-tionibus, non armis, ferro, flammis, incen-diis, excidiis agat: Ne, ut quorundam Ma-taeologia hodie tollit conscientiarum liber-tatem, ac miserrimam tyrannidem & ser-vitutem hominum introducit, sic Philoso-phia nostra libertatem animi, mentis & iu-dicii vi & minis tollat, & miserrima faciat hominum philosophantium mancipia.
units.tr: Therefore all hypocrisy and insincere feeling must be banished from true philosophy. The philosopher must not, to gain the favour of Aristotle or of any other, or of his own sect, now pretend and now dissemble, now affirm and now deny, and so wonderfully twist and entangle everything, colouring and excusing it with subtle arguments and above all with petty distinctions, and that against his conscience. Nor, on the other hand, should he be a Ate and a stirrer-up of all strife, a trumpet of sedition. Let him act by reasons, not by abuse and slander; by arguments, not sophisms; by teaching and brotherly admonitions, not by bans and proscriptions; by proofs and lawful disputations, not by arms, iron, flames, fires and destruction. For just as the Matæology of some today takes away freedom of conscience and introduces the most wretched tyranny and slavery of men, so our philosophy must not take away freedom of spirit, mind and judgement by force and threats, and make the philosophizing men into most wretched slaves.

units.la: Apodeixis 15.
units.tr: Demonstration [Apodeixis] 15.

units.la: Expultrix vitiorum eorum, à quibus abhorrere & abstinere vere Christianus debet, neutiquā Chri-stiano est negligenda.
units.tr: That which expels those vices from which a true Christian ought to shrink and abstain is by no means to be neglected by a Christian.

units.la: Atqui Philosophia vera est talium vitiorum ex-pultrix, à quibus iussu Dei omnis Christianus & abhorrere & abstinere debet. Est etenim, vt iam à sana Philosophia exterminata & expulsa vi-tia optauim, expultrix idololatrias & apothe-oseos Aristotelis hominis Ethnici, docti quidem dem ad miraculum, at profani, paganismorum & aliorum errorum. Est expultrix falsitatis, iodii ac inuidiae iniustae, subtilis futilitatis, falsarum opinionum & inanis persuasionis, ac praecipitis praeiudicii, fuci & doli sophistici, impudentis proteruiae ac immodestae audaciae, seruitii humani & nimiu abiecti, superciliosi fastus ac philautias, pertinacis ac ignauae indocilitatis, obscuritatis, prolixitatis, amethodias, hypocrisios & discordiae ac inhumanae crudelitatis & calumniae, &c.
units.tr: Yet true philosophy is an expeller of such vices, from which every Christian ought by God's command both to shrink and to abstain. For, as we have already said, sound philosophy drives out and expels vices: it expels idolatry and the deification of Aristotle, a heathen man, learned indeed to a marvel but profane, and paganisms and other errors. It expels falsehood, envy and unjust hatred, idle subtlety, false opinions and empty persuasion, and rash prejudgement; the smoke and trickery of sophistry; shameless insolence and immodest audacity; human servitude and excessive abjection; haughty pride and self-love; obstinate and lazy unteachability; obscurity, prolixity, lack of method; hypocrisy, discord, inhuman cruelty and calumny, and so on.

units.la: Ergo vera Philosophia Christiano neutiquam est negligenda, ne dum calumniis oneranda.
units.tr: Therefore true philosophy is by no means to be neglected by a Christian, much less to be burdened with calumnies.

units.la: CAP. XV.
units.tr: CHAP. XV.

units.la: De vitiis vanae Philosophiae Pseudorameorum.
units.tr: On the vices of the vain philosophy of the Pseudo-Ramists.

units.la: SI Aristotelica Philosophia est vera illa, de qua tantopere gloriatur, (disputare hoc iam non est animus) Pseudoaristotelicos eos dico, qui Aristotelicae Philosophiae ducem ac doctorem verum non assectatur. Sic si Ramea Philosophia est vera illa, (de qua nos) Pseudorameos dico, qui Rameae Philosophiae (non ex autore eiusque adiunctis aestimandae, sed ex praeceptis, & legibus) vestigiis non insistunt. Veritas hic valeat, non autoritas, Res, non persona. sona. Pseudorameorum hæc notata inuenio à quodam sincere candido Philosopho vitia, quæ etiam à se Philosophia Christiana alienissima esse iubet.
units.tr: If Aristotelian philosophy is that true philosophy about which its followers boast so much (I have no wish to dispute that point now), then I call Pseudo-Aristotelians those who do not follow the true leader and teacher of Aristotelian philosophy. Likewise, if Ramist philosophy is the true one (and I say this as one of us), I call Pseudo-Ramists those who do not walk in the footsteps of Ramist philosophy, to be judged not by its author and his associates but by its precepts and laws. Let truth prevail here, not authority; the thing, not the person. I find these faults of the Pseudo-Ramists noted by a certain sincere and candid philosopher, faults which he also insists that Christian philosophy must keep entirely far from itself.

units.la: 1. Pythagoricum illud & plusquam Pötificium, αὐτὸς ἔφα Ramus dixit, à cadidæ veritatis studiosa Philosophia absit. Vt enim Ramei non hoc Aristotelicis concedunt, neque sibi licitum existiment. Absit & Anthropolatria & Profopolatria Rami. Apotheosis hæc utring par est in pariter nimiü honorantibus & adorantibus idola secta sua.
units.tr: 1. That Pythagorean saying, more than papal, "he himself said it" [αὐτὸς ἔφα], "Ramus said it," must be kept away from a philosophy devoted to the pure search for truth. For the Ramists do not grant this to the Aristotelians, nor do they think it permissible for themselves. Let the worship of Ramus as a man, and the worship of his persona, be far away too. This deification is equally fitting for both sides, who honour too much and adore the idols of their own sect.

units.la: 2. Nimia libertas & præceps iudicium temere nimis castigans & flagellans præcepta Rameæ, vel veræ Philosophiæ, à nasutulis nudiusteritus natis, Christianam Philosophiam sibi nō bene propitiam habet. Ne abeat illa obiurgandi libertas in temerariam calumniandi petulantiam, qua præcepta & præceptorum Philosophicorum ordinem sine iusta causa immutat & transformat.
units.tr: 2. Excessive liberty and rash judgement, which rashly censure and lash the precepts of Ramist or of true philosophy, come from upstarts, half-naked and only just born, and they do not keep Christian philosophy well disposed toward them. Let that freedom of rebuke not turn into a rash petulance of slander, by which without just cause they alter and transform the precepts and the order of philosophical precepts.

units.la: 3. Impiam contra Christianæ charitatis canonem contendedi libidinem aspernatur orthodoxa Philosophia in iis, quibus pietas & charitas Christiana nō est cordi, quibus volupe est per sef-quipequipedalia Ciceronianis verbis elata maledicta & conuicia aduersus sanos Aristoteleos, quibus, vt multis nunc & antea, veritas est cordi, & pios Rameos agere, mordaci contentionis œstro agitati.
units.tr: 3. Orthodox philosophy rejects the impious lust for contention, which goes against the rule of Christian charity. It is found in those to whom piety and Christian charity are not dear, who take pleasure in curses and insults, which they hurl in ten-foot-long Ciceronian words against sound Aristotelians, to whom, as to many both now and before, truth is dear, and who harass pious Ramists, goaded on by the biting gadfly of contention.

units.la: 4. Philautiam intolerabilem & immodestum fastum quorundum detestatur sana & humilis veritatis cultrix Philosophia, in iis, qui ingeniolo suo præfidenter confidunt, humilitatis ac modestiæ Philosophicæ immemores malunt esse & videri garruli ( sine rerum solida sapientia) superciliosi (quia plus habent in mente, quam in ente) ac proterui ( omnis scilicet rerum inops eruditio est audax, modo verborum sit copiosa supellex, vti videre est in indoctis illis Hierophantis, quibus in cathedra solis licet esse disertis.)
units.tr: 4. Sound and humble philosophy, the lover of truth, detests the intolerable self-love and immodest arrogance of certain men. These men, confident in their own little wit, forget the humility and modesty proper to philosophy. They prefer to be, and to be seen as, chatterers without solid wisdom in things, haughty ("for they have more in their mind than in their being") and brazen. ("Every erudition lacking substance in things is bold, provided there is a rich stock of words, as one may see in those uneducated hierophants, who may be eloquent only from their lecture chair.")

units.la: 5. Rerum ignorantiam & abiectam curam vera non laudat Philosophia, in iis Rameolis, & minorum getium Ramearum diis, qui de instrumentis & modis rerum & artium tractandarum ita sunt soliciti, vt rebus cognoscendis parum aut nihil curæ ac temporis tribuant. Vacuum vas, tinniens æs. Quis sine rebus sapit? Ignorantia rerum excludit rectā rationem tractandi. Oportet enim rerum affectioni respondere omnem rerum tractationem. Verba sunt rerum tantum symbola. Modus tractationis ex visceribus rerum promitur. Res bene q noscit, bene res tractare videtur, si modi& τρόπῳ παιδείας scientia accesserit Ramea.
units.tr: 5. True philosophy does not praise ignorance of things or abject carelessness. This is found in those little Ramists, minor gods of the Ramist tribe, who are so concerned with the instruments and methods of handling things and arts that they devote little or no care or time to knowing the things themselves. An empty vessel gives a tinkling sound. Who is wise without things? Ignorance of things excludes the right way of handling them, for every treatment of things must answer to their nature. Words are only tokens of things. The manner of treatment must be drawn from the inner parts of things. He who knows things well seems to handle them well, if Ramist knowledge of method and the mode of teaching [τρόπῳ παιδείας] is added.

units.la: 6. Nimium omne in legibus cōformandorum praeceptorum & methodi non amat vbiuis Philosophia vera imbecillitatis & multæ ignorantiæ sibi conscia, nec in hac vita ad summum perfectionis gradum conscensura. Nouit se suo metiri pede: non vbique & vsque quaque, (vbi formarum cognitio obscura, difficilis, confusa ah quam in multis! vbi igitur (formis scilicet ignoratis) perfectæ illæ nostræ definitiones?) vrget nimis exquisitum suū κατὰ πάντᾱς, καθ' αὑτὸ, & καθόλου πρῶτον. Libra saepe est aspicienda, in quam se inclinet partem, libra inquam humanæ sapientiæ & probabilitatis. Methodū amat Philosophia, vti veritatem, vt Theologia pietatis studiosum & ordinis: At curiositatem nimium quorundam sciolorum rum in minutulis sapientulorum non adamat.
units.tr: 6. True philosophy, aware of its own weakness and much ignorance, and not going to climb in this life to the highest degree of perfection, does not everywhere love excessive concern for the laws of formulating precepts and method. It knows to measure itself by its own foot. It does not press its exquisite rules of "in every case, in itself, and universal first" [κατὰ πάντᾱς, καθ' αὑτὸ, καθόλου πρῶτον] everywhere and in every way. Where knowledge of forms is obscure, difficult and confused, and how often that is! Where then, with the forms unknown, are those perfect definitions of ours? The balance must often be consulted, to see toward which side it inclines: the balance, I say, of human wisdom and probability. Philosophy loves method, as it loves truth, as theology loves piety and order. But it does not love the excessive curiosity of certain shallow men in the minute trifles of their little wisdom.

units.la: 7. Nimiæ breuitatis obscuritatem odiosam parientis amica nostra non est Philosophia: æquabilem amat ipsis rebus, æquabilem captui discentiū. Non vult artes suas esse nudum sine carne, & sine corpore sceleton, non vult eas esse ideas vmbratiles & vmbras sine soliditate corporea, non vult ideales & tabulares (liceat ita loqui) tantum artes, sed reales etiam.
units.tr: 7. Our philosophy is no friend to the obscurity that comes from excessive brevity, which is odious. It loves a measure that suits both the things themselves and the grasp of learners. It does not want its arts to be a naked skeleton without flesh or body, nor shadowy ideas and shadows without bodily solidity. It does not want arts that are only ideal and tabular (if I may so speak), but real as well.

units.la: 8. Iniuriam & immodestiam hanc quorundam Rameorum vera & candida non probat Philosophia, qua mutato propositio Aristotelis & aliorum, aliud fingentes, calamum stringunt in fictas à le vmbras, hoc est, Aristoteli affingunt hoc animi propositum, quasi voluerit accurata & didascalica methodo omnes nobis describere & adumbrare artes, cum commentatorem & disceptatorem in plerisque egerit. Philosophia itaque candoris non ignara, sed obseruans, vult distinguere nos inter artificem accuratione methodi molientem artium conformationem, & inter commentatorem disputando sæpe elicientem veritatis splenspledorem, & in vtramque partem disceptantem.
units.tr: 8. True and candid philosophy does not approve this injustice and immodesty of certain Ramists. They change the proposition of Aristotle and others, feigning something else, and draw the pen against shadows of their own making. That is, they ascribe to Aristotle an intention of mind, as if he had wished to describe and sketch all the arts for us with an accurate and didactic method, when in most places he acted as commentator and disputant. Philosophy, therefore, not ignorant of candour but mindful of it, wants us to distinguish between the artificer who builds the structure of the arts with methodical precision, and the commentator who, while disputing, often brings out the splendour of truth and argues on both sides.

units.la: 9. Amiciri optat nostra Philosophia, non nudari, quare eorum Rameorum non arridet ei nuditas & sterilitas in commentando & explicando, qui artium precepta non satis explicant, qui res ipsas, earumque naturam, proprietates, differentias & conuenientias sicco pede transeunt, nec explanant, in generalibus tantum apicibus hærentes, in ipsam rerum raro penetrantes medullam.
units.tr: 9. Our philosophy wishes to be clothed, not stripped. Therefore it does not delight in the nakedness and barrenness of those Ramists who, in commenting and explaining, do not sufficiently unfold the precepts of the arts. They pass dry-shod over the things themselves, their nature, properties, differences and agreements, without explaining them, clinging only to general points and rarely penetrating to the very marrow of things.

units.la: 10. Nimium etiam illud, odio est sanç & eruditæ Philosophiæ, quo se tanquam catenis alligatos nonnulli ex Ramea familia somniant; ad solas definitiones ac distributiones, & quidem ad meras & nimis multas, sæpe etiam nimis obscuras dichotomias, diuisiones, subdiuisiones, minutas sectiones; interim plane omittetes intermediarum illustrationum, proprietatum, cō- uenientiarum, differentiarum, aliarumque rerum & circumstantiarum expositionis sanam doctrinam: Etiam illi ipsi, qui dum commentari debent & illustrare, velificantur, methodi odiosis sectionibus. Distinctiones dichotomias regat prudentia. Doctor nō semper artificiosus artis formator, sed aliquando est commentator. Negligi tamen non vult in commentatione, methodi rationem, prudetem mediocritatem amat: Excessum & Nimium odit.
units.tr: 10. That, too, is hateful to sound and learned philosophy, and some of the Ramist family dream of being bound as if by chains: to definitions and distributions alone, and indeed to mere and far too many, often too obscure dichotomies, divisions, subdivisions and minute sections. Meanwhile they completely omit the sound teaching of intermediate illustrations, properties, agreements, differences and the exposition of other things and circumstances. Even those who, when they ought to comment and illustrate, sail on with the odious sections of method. Let prudence govern dichotomies and distinctions. The teacher is not always the artificer who forms an art; sometimes he is a commentator. Yet philosophy does not want the rule of method to be neglected in commentary. It loves prudent moderation and hates excess and "too much."

units.la: II. Contemptum temerarium & impium veterum Philosophorum, qui pro sua mensura, ad Philosophiæ tabernaculum extruendum sua contulere dona, inique fert Christiana Philosophia. Rameos itaque illos non magnifacit, qui Aristotelem, Ciceronem, Quintilianum, & aliorum vtilium volumina spernunt, eaq; nec ipsi legunt, nec ferre possunt, nec aliis legere libenter concedunt, aut si legunt, non perpendunt tamen, nec quæ vera & vtilia sunt, inde transfumunt, sed carpunt & calumniantur: Vt quidam hoc seculo Mataeologi legunt Orthodoxorum quidem scripta, sed vt inueniant, quod calumnientur, aliis vero lectione interdicunt. Ramei hi non sunt veri, qui quod in aliis improbant, sibi licere autumant.
units.tr: II. Christian philosophy bears unjustly the rash and impious contempt of the ancient philosophers, who, each according to his measure, contributed their gifts to building the tabernacle of philosophy. So it does not hold in high esteem those Ramists who scorn the volumes of Aristotle, Cicero, Quintilian and other useful writers. They neither read them themselves, nor can bear them, nor willingly allow others to read them. Or if they do read them, they do not weigh them, nor carry over from them what is true and useful, but pluck at them and slander them. So too certain Mataeologi of this age read the writings of the Orthodox, but only in order to find something to slander, while forbidding others to read them. These are not true Ramists, who think it allowed to themselves to do what they condemn in others.

units.la: 12. Denique sana & suæ imperfectionis memor optima Philosophia censuram nimis acrem, & nimis altum sapientem acerbe fert eorum, qui sibi imaginantur, se esse à Pontifice vel Imperatore creatos Aristarchos & censores omnium, imo inquisitores haereticae prauitatis: ideoque ne quidem optimis & probatissimis tam veteribus, quam recentibus auctoribus labeculam, nescio quam, aspergere studet, vt scilicet ipsi doctissimis, etiam in rebus per se veris carpendis, doctiores videantur.
units.tr: 12. Finally, sound philosophy, mindful of its own imperfection, bitterly bears the overly sharp censure and the overly lofty wisdom of those who imagine themselves to have been made Aristarchuses and censors of all by the Pope or the Emperor, indeed inquisitors of heretical depravity. Therefore it does not even try to cast the least little stain on the most excellent and most approved authors, both ancient and recent, so that they themselves may seem more learned than the most learned, by carping at things which are true in themselves.

units.la: Apodeixis 16.
units.tr: Apodeixis 16.

units.la: Sincera ea est Philosophia, quae etiam suorum cultorum vitiis ac naevis non parcit, eaq; à se vult esse remotissima, atque refert in male feriatorum male affectam mentem & voluntatem.
units.tr: That philosophy is sincere which does not spare even the vices and blemishes of its own practitioners, and which wishes to be most remote from them, and attributes them to a badly disposed mind and will among those who are idle in the wrong way.

units.la: At vero Christiana quam colere est animus, etiam suorum cultorum naevis ac lapsibus non parcit, sed aperit eos ac indicat: eosq; tribuit non sibi, quippe quae per se pura est, sed male affecte menti & voluntati eorum, in quibus sui qualiscunque habitat cognitio, sed male vsurpata.
units.tr: But Christian philosophy, which we desire to cultivate, likewise does not spare the blemishes and lapses of its own practitioners, but brings them to light and points them out; and it assigns these not to itself, since it is pure in its own nature, but to the badly disposed mind and will of those in whom whatever knowledge of it dwells, yet misused.

units.la: Christiana itaque Philosophia, quam votis expetimus, est sincera; si sincera, non nisi a malo, & insincero animo, laceranda conuiciis.
units.tr: Christian philosophy, therefore, which we desire with our prayers, is sincere; and if it is sincere, it should be assailed with insults only by a malicious and insincere spirit.

units.la: CAP. XVI. De Philosophiae distributione generatim.
units.tr: CHAP. XVI. On the division of philosophy in general.

units.la: HActenus de Christianæ Philosophiæ causis, effectis, subiectis, adiunctis, & contrariis vitiis: Superest eiusdem distributio, cuius primum generalem adumbrationem in variis Philosophis, deinde singulas partes dispiciemus.
units.tr: Thus far I have treated the causes, effects, subjects, adjuncts and contrary vices of Christian philosophy. There remains its division. I shall first examine its general outline as given by various philosophers, and then consider its individual parts.

units.la: Philosophia varie à variis Philosophis varios respectus & affectiones ipsarum partium & artium inter se intuentibus & considerantibus, indeque distributionem aliam atque aliam extruentibus, distribuitur.
units.tr: Philosophy is divided in different ways by different philosophers, who look at and consider the various aspects and relations of its parts and arts among themselves, and so construct one division or another.

units.la: Vetus est distinctio Philosophiæ, cuius meminit Ioan. Franc. Pic. Mir. in examine van. doct. gent. Philosophiam, inquit, bimembrem plerique fecere. Nam Xenophanes Colophonius vniuersum illud supremum Philosophiæ genus in physicum & logicum diuisit morali prætermisso. Archelaus Athenien sis in moralem & physicam diuisit Logica prætermissa. Aliqui aiunt Cyrenaicos Philosophiam in duas diuisse partes, Ethicam & Logicam, natural praetermissa. Idem postea: Philosophiam in tres partes diuidendam Plato autor fuit, in logicam, physicam & moralem, quem secuti sunt Xenocrates, Aristoteles & Stoici: quamquam alii partes, alii locos, alii species, alii genera: sed Stoicorum alii infex partes diuiserunt, Dialecticam, oratoriam, ciuilem, naturalem, Theologiam, moralem. Porphyrius in actiuam & contemplatiuam diuidendam censuit.
units.tr: There is an old division of philosophy, which Giovanni Francesco Pico della Mirandola mentions in his Examination of the Vanity of the Gentile Doctrines: Most people, he says, have made philosophy twofold. For Xenophanes of Colophon divided the whole of philosophy into physics and logic, leaving out ethics. Archelaus of Athens divided it into ethics and physics, leaving out logic. Some say the Cyrenaics divided philosophy into two parts, ethics and logic, leaving out natural philosophy. Again, later: Plato was the author of dividing philosophy into three parts, logic, physics and ethics, which Xenocrates, Aristotle and the Stoics followed; although others have used parts, others places, others species, others genera; but some of the Stoics divided it into further parts: dialectic, rhetoric, civil, natural, theology, moral. Porphyry thought it should be divided into active and contemplative.

units.la: Recens est, ex antiquo tamen delibata Platone, Philosophiae partitio in Propaedium & Paedium, vt quibusdam placet.
units.tr: A more recent division, though drawn from the ancient Plato, is the partition of philosophy into Propaedia and Paedia, as some prefer.

units.la: Propaedia illis est prima pars litera-tae Philosophiae, quae compelectitur propaedeumata & mathemata prima, id est, artes generales reliquarum omnium facultatum, & artium tractandarum instrumenta.
units.tr: For them, Propaedia is the first part of literate philosophy. It comprises the propaedeumata and the first mathemata, that is, the general arts that prepare all the other faculties, and the instruments of the arts to be pursued.

units.la: Haec prima pars Philosophiae a quibusdam solet appellari nomine Logices, voce generaliter accepta, & artium dicendi. Estque duplex pro duplici facultate & munere, qua Deus homine prae ceteris ornauit animantibus, Logica rationis, & Logica orationis seu sermonis.
units.tr: This first part of philosophy is commonly called by some by the name of Logic, the word being taken in a general sense, along with the arts of speaking. It is twofold, corresponding to the twofold faculty and function by which God adorned man above the other animals: the logic of reason and the logic of speech.

units.la: Logica rationis, Dialectica est, quæ docet rationis munere & beneficio res omnes rite tractare, omniaque negocia, certa ratione & prudenter expedire. Hæc omnium artium liberalium est generalissima & communissimum instrumentum, caput, dux, magistra & ministra omnium reliquarum artium, atque adeo suæ ipsius informatrix & moderatrix, imo omnes omnino hominum actiones, cogitationes & consilia complectitur ac moderatur.
units.tr: The logic of reason is Dialectic, which teaches how to handle all things rightly by the office and benefit of reason, and how to carry out all affairs with sound judgement and prudence. It is the most general and most common instrument of all the liberal arts, the head, guide, teacher and servant of all the other arts, and indeed the informer and regulator of itself. Nay, it embraces and governs all the actions, thoughts and counsels of men without exception.

units.la: Logica orationis est, quæ docet rationem res omnes munere & usu sermonis rite tractandi. Estque duplex, aut enim agit de sermonis puritate, aut vero de eius ornatu & modificatione.
units.tr: The logic of speech teaches how to handle all things rightly by the office and use of speech. It is twofold, for it deals either with the purity of speech or with its ornament and modification.

units.la: Ars de sermonis puritate duplicem videtur continere doctrinam. Prima est, quæ vocum singularum docet significationes, dicique solet Lexicon & Dictionarium. Altera est, quæ vocum adsignificationes ad bene loquendum tradit, diciturque Grammatica.
units.tr: The art concerning the purity of speech seems to contain a twofold teaching. The first teaches the meanings of single words, and is usually called lexicon or dictionary. The second teaches the adsignifications of words for speaking well, and is called grammar.

units.la: Ars de sermonis ornatu agit de orationis iam puræ per certas affectiones & modificationes exornatione.
units.tr: The art concerning the ornament of speech deals with adorning speech that is already pure, through certain affections and modifications.

units.la: Oratio autem ita affecta & modificata cata (voce latius sumpta) vel Soluta est & pedestris, vel Ligata. Illa prosa dicitur, nec certis adstringitur numeris: haec numeris adstringitur perpetuis, diciturq; poetica.
units.tr: Speech so affected and modified (taking the word more broadly) is either loose and prose-like, or bound. The former is called prose and is not bound by fixed measures; the latter is bound by continuous measures and is called poetic.

units.la: Paedia sequitur, quae paedeumata ipsa, & sapientem rerum homini vtilium doctrinam complectitur, & quidem in humana Philosophia, artes & facultates speciales rerum doctrinam docentes: quae versantur aut circa naturam, aut circa vitam & mores hominum.
units.tr: Paedia follows. It comprises the paedeumata themselves and the wise teaching of things useful to man; and indeed, in human philosophy, the special arts and faculties that teach the knowledge of things, which are concerned either with nature or with the life and morals of men.

units.la: Circa naturam versatur Mathematica & Physica.
units.tr: Mathematics and physics are concerned with nature.

units.la: Mathematica est Physicae quaedam administra, vt quae attingit certam conditionem rerum Physicae subiectarum, scilicet quantitatem. Mathematica igitur est ars quantitatis, quae est vel numeri vel mensurae.
units.tr: Mathematics is a certain handmaid of physics, since it attends to one condition of the things that physics studies, namely quantity. Mathematics is therefore the art of quantity, which is either of number or of measure.

units.la: Mathematica tractans numeros dicitur Arithmetica: hanc subiecto generaliorem arbitrarer, quam vt ad res solas physicas adstringatur.
units.tr: Mathematics dealing with numbers is called arithmetic. I would consider this to have a wider subject than to be confined to physical things alone.

units.la: Mathematica tractans mensuras & spacia seu magnitudines dicitur Geometria, seu potius Metrica. Hinc aliae artes, vt Geodæsia, Mechanica, &c. ef-florescunt.
units.tr: Mathematics dealing with measures and spaces, or magnitudes, is called geometry, or rather metrics. From this spring other arts, such as geodesy, mechanics, and so on.

units.la: Physica mundū totum sibi subiicit, agitque de rebus quibusuis naturalibus creatis, estque Pneumatologia & Somatologia; hæc de corporibus, illa de spiritibus creatis disserit. Ex Physica plurimæ artes suum ortum ducunt, & inde cum primis dependet medicina. Circa mores & vitam hominis versatur Ethica, quæ est quasi praxis quædā omnium artium Philosophicarum ad hominum salutem seu felicitatem ciuilem, seu mundanam comparata; diciturque Ethica seu Philosophia moralis, quæ est generalis vel specialis, illa Ethica speciatim, hæc politica dicitur: hinc Iurisprudentia efflorescit.
units.tr: Physics takes the whole world as its subject and treats of all created natural things. It is pneumatology and somatology: the latter discourses of bodies, the former of created spirits. Most arts derive their origin from physics, and medicine depends above all on it. Ethics is concerned with the morals and life of man. It is, as it were, a kind of practice of all the philosophical arts, directed to the salvation or civil and worldly felicity of men. Ethics, or moral philosophy, is either general or special; the special is called ethics properly, and the other is called politics. From this jurisprudence flourishes.

units.la: Alia diuisio.
units.tr: Another division.

units.la: Ars liberalis aut rationem informat, aut ratione informatur. Rationem informans ars dicitur Logica. Ars quæ ratione informatur, est Generalior, aut Specialior.
units.tr: A liberal art either informs reason or is informed by reason. The art that informs reason is called Logic. The art that is informed by reason is either more general or more special.

units.la: Generalior est ars Orationis vel Quantitatis.
units.tr: The more general is the art of speech or of quantity.

units.la: Orationis ars est puræ vel ornatæ.
units.tr: The art of speech is either of pure or of ornate speech.

units.la: Puræ orationis ars docet aut vocum cum significationes, vt ordinatum Lexicon, aut vocū adsignificationes, & structuras vt Grammatica. Oratio ornata est Soluta vel Ligata: illius Rhetorica, huius Poetica dicitur: quam Rhetorica ornet vtramque.
units.tr: The art of pure speech teaches either the meanings of words, as in an ordered lexicon, or the adsignifications and constructions of words, as grammar does. Ornate speech is either loose or bound: the former is called rhetoric, the latter poetic; and rhetoric adorns both.

units.la: Ars quantitatis Mathematica est, eaque discretæ, vt Arithmetica, numerorum; vel continuæ, vt Geometria, magnitudinis. Ars specialior aut naturam tractat, vt Physica, vnde plures aliæ prodeunt disciplinæ, aut vitam hominis, vt Ethica, & Politica.
units.tr: The art of quantity is mathematics, and it is either discrete, as arithmetic, of numbers, or continuous, as geometry, of magnitude. The more special art either deals with nature, as physics, from which several other disciplines arise, or with the life of man, as ethics and politics.

units.la: Alia diuisio Philosophiæ.
units.tr: Another division of philosophy.

units.la: Philosophicæ doctrinæ seu disciplinæ liberales, continent doctrinam rerum, vel doctrinam modi, quo res sunt tractandæ.
units.tr: The liberal philosophical doctrines or disciplines contain either the doctrine of things or the doctrine of the manner in which things are to be treated.

units.la: Doctrina rerum tradit obiecta intellectionis nostræ, estque vel Vniuersalis vel Particularis.
units.tr: The doctrine of things sets out the objects of our understanding, and it is either universal or particular.

units.la: Vniuersalis dicitur prima Philosophia quæ tractat de ente vniuerse.
units.tr: The universal doctrine is called first philosophy, which treats of being in general.

units.la: Particularis tractat de ente definite, seu de particulari ente, estque magis Theoretica vel Practica.
units.tr: The particular doctrine treats of being in a definite sense, or of particular being, and is either theoretical or practical.

units.la: Theoretica magis est doctrina Essentiæ vel Quantitatis. Essentiæ, & quidem dem vel Transnaturalis vel Naturalis.
units.tr: Theoretical doctrine is either the doctrine of essence or of quantity. Of essence, and this is either transnatural or natural.

units.la: Transnaturalis, est essentiae spiritualis seu incorporeae, vt Pneumatologia, & quidem in specie Angelographia.
units.tr: Transnatural doctrine is of spiritual or incorporeal essence, as pneumatology, and in particular angelography.

units.la: Naturalis, est essentiae corporatae, diciturque in specie Physica, quae est corporum vel coelestium, vbi Astronomia, vel sublunarium, quae multarum est partium, quo pertinet Geographia, Optica, & Musica. Astronomiae & Geographiae coniunctio est Cosmographia. Physicae praxis est, Ars Medica.
units.tr: Natural doctrine is of corporeal essence and is called, in particular, physics. It concerns either heavenly bodies, where there is astronomy, or sublunary bodies, which have many parts; to these belong geography, optics and music. The combination of astronomy and geography is cosmography. The practical side of physics is the medical art.

units.la: Quantitatis Theoretica magis ars est Mathesis seu Mathematica, quae est vel Arithmetica, nempe Numerorum, vel Geometria, nempe Magnitudinum, eius pars vel praxis est Geodesia.
units.tr: The theoretical art of quantity is mathesis or mathematics, which is either arithmetic, namely of numbers, or geometry, namely of magnitudes. Its part or practical side is geodesy.

units.la: Practica particularis ars est Moralis, nempe Ethica & Politica, in qua continetur Oeconomica, hinc efflorescit Iurisprudentia Romana, specialis Politica.
units.tr: The practical particular art is moral philosophy, namely ethics and politics, in which economics is contained. From this springs Roman jurisprudence, a special kind of politics.

units.la: Doctrina modi quo res tractantur, complectitur artes dirigentes intellectionē nostram, seu ministras & quasi instrumenta, quae sunt artes Logicae, tum Sermonis tum Rationis.
units.tr: The doctrine of the manner in which things are treated embraces the arts that direct our understanding, serving as its instruments and, as it were, tools. These are the logical arts, both of speech and of reason.

units.la: Sermonis puri Grammatica: ornati Rhetorica. Rationis, Logica seu Dialectica.
units.tr: The grammar of pure speech; rhetoric of ornate speech. Of reason, logic or dialectic.

units.la: Alia diuisio artium Philosoph.
units.tr: Another division of the philosophical arts.

units.la: Ars philosophica est vel Generalis vel Specialis.
units.tr: The philosophical art is either general or special.

units.la: Generalis est instrumentorum, & consideRat λόγον, vel πρῶτον, vel δεύτερον.
units.tr: The general art concerns the instruments and considers the word [λόγον], either first [πρῶτον] or second [δεύτερον].

units.la: Πρῶτον λόγον considerat Logica, ars Rationis.
units.tr: Logic, the art of reason, considers the first word [πρῶτον λόγον].

units.la: Δεύτερον λόγον considerat ars, vel Purum, vel Modificatum. Purum Grammatica, Modificatum seu ornatum Rhetorica.
units.tr: The art that considers the second word [δεύτερον λόγον] is either pure or modified. The pure is grammar; the modified or ornate is rhetoric.

units.la: Specialis est ars rerum, quæ considerantur vel ad se, vel ad aliud. Ad & in se considerantur res, vt sunt, diciturq; Philosophia prima Aristotelicis.
units.tr: The special art concerns things, which are considered either in themselves or in relation to something else. Things are considered in and of themselves as they are, and this is called first philosophy by the Aristotelians.

units.la: Ad aliud, nempe qua referuntur ad vsus humanos, idque vel in Natura vel in Actione.
units.tr: Things are considered in relation to something else, namely insofar as they relate to human uses, and this either in nature or in action.

units.la: In Natura, & quidem Abstracte vel Concrete.
units.tr: In nature, and this either abstractly or concretely.

units.la: Abstracte in Numero, hinc Arithmetica: vel in Magnitudine, hinc Geometria.
units.tr: Abstractly, in number, whence arithmetic; or in magnitude, whence geometry.

units.la: Concrete, quo Physica pertinet, scilicet ars scrutandi Naturam, quæ est sensuum, vt Optica & Musica, vel ipsorum corcorporum, & quidem cœlestium, vt Astrologia, vel sublunarium, &c.
units.tr: Concretely, to which physics belongs, namely the art of investigating nature. This is either of the senses, as optics and music, or of the bodies themselves, both heavenly, as astrology, and sublunary, and so on.

units.la: In actione, quæ est hominis bene agere, hinc Ethica.
units.tr: In action, which is man doing good, whence ethics.

units.la: Ars bene viuendi vel singularis, vel in societate.
units.tr: The art of living well is either individual or social.

units.la: Singularis, si homo seorsim viuat, hinc Ethica de Moribus.
units.tr: Individual, if a man lives apart, whence the ethics of morals.

units.la: In societate, eaque vel domestica, hinc Oeconomica, vel ciuili, hinc Politica.
units.tr: Social, and this either domestic, whence economics, or civil, whence politics.

units.la: Alias diuisiones plures apud alios inueneris, meliores tibi reserua, nos hic non tam connexiones concatenatas artium, quam ipsarum artium veritatem & bonitatē spectamus. Vnde iam surgit
units.tr: You will find many other divisions among other writers; reserve the better ones for yourself. Here we look not so much at the linked chains of the arts as at the truth and goodness of the arts themselves. From this now arises

units.la: Apodexis 17.
units.tr: Apodixis 17.

units.la: Quacunque artes homini post fidem in Christum & voluntatis sanctificationem, in hac vita magna afferunt perfectionem & voluptatem: ha non sunt contemnenda homini Christiano, magni sunt cum primis facienda literato Theologo.
