units.tr: Whatever arts bring great perfection and pleasure to man in this life, after faith in Christ and sanctification of the will, are not to be despised by the Christian man and are above all to be highly esteemed by the learned theologian.

units.la: Atqui artes & doctrinæ Philosophicæ, quibus de agimus, homini post fidem in Christum & voluntatis sanctificationem magnam afferunt in hac vita seu huius vitæ curriculo perfectionem & voluptatem.
units.tr: But the arts and philosophical doctrines with which we are concerned bring great perfection and pleasure to man in this life, or in the course of this life, after faith in Christ and sanctification of the will.

units.la: Etenim hæ efficiunt, vt secundum sanum intellectum viuat homo, id est, rerum naturas distindistinđte intelligat, cognoscat & iudicet, vnde summa & inæstimabilis in mente voluptas oritur. Ad hoc autem requiruntur tria. 1. Res cognoscenda, quæ iam in natura est, 2. facultas naturalis illas res intelligendi, fluens ab anima hominis rationali. 3. Dispositio certa, per quam illa naturalis potentia in actum, ordinaţ& sine errore, deducitur, quæ dispositio iam ordinarie per disciplinas iam recitatas & artes Philosophicas acquiritur. Harum enim aliæ res ipsas in natura positas, tanquam obiecta intellectionis nostræ monstrant & tradunt, vt mens nostra variarum & vtilium rerū cognitione imbuatur: aliæ vero certis normis & regulis hominis operationes, nempe cogitationem & intellectum de rebus, deinde cogitationum significationem per voces, quæ fit sermone & scriptione, dirigunt & ordinant.
units.tr: For these bring it about that man lives according to sound understanding, that is, he understands, knows and judges the natures of things distinctly, and from this arises supreme and inestimable pleasure in the mind. For this three things are required. (1) The thing to be known, which already exists in nature; (2) the natural faculty of understanding those things, flowing from the rational soul of man; (3) a certain disposition by which that natural power is brought into act, ordered and without error. This disposition is ordinarily acquired through the disciplines already recited and the philosophical arts. For some of these show and deliver the things themselves, placed in nature, as objects of our understanding, so that our mind is imbued with knowledge of various and useful things. Others direct and order, by certain norms and rules, human operations: namely thought and understanding of things, and then the expression of thoughts through words, which is done by speech and writing.

units.la: Ergo artes & doctrinæ Philosophicæ homini Christiano non sunt contemnendæ, sed in primis literato Theologo maximi faciendæ.
units.tr: Therefore philosophical arts and doctrines are not to be despised by the Christian man, but are to be esteemed most highly, especially by the learned theologian.

units.la: Sed ad singulas descendamus artium speciēs: Si singularum artium Philosophicarum scientia & honestus vsus hominibus præsertim literatis, & Christiane eruditis summum ornamentum & ingens afferunt emolumentum: neutiquam ipsæ artes, quas suo ambitu complectitur Philosophica peripheria, è scholis & templis Christianorum sunt explodenda, & ad inferorum barathrum amandanda. At quod antecedit, verum esse, in sequentibus capitibus demonstrabitur.
units.tr: But let us descend to the individual kinds of arts. If knowledge and honest use of each of the philosophical arts bring great ornament and considerable advantage to men, especially to those who are learned and Christianly educated, then by no means are the arts themselves, which the philosophical circle embraces in its scope, to be driven out of the schools and churches of Christians and consigned to the pit of hell. That the preceding is true will be demonstrated in the following chapters.

units.la: GAP. XVII.
units.tr: Chapter XVII.

units.la: De Christiana Philosophia GRAMMATICA.
units.tr: On Christian Philosophy: Grammar.

units.la: ORdiamur artium singularum commolumentum, ornamētum; maiestatem, ab artibus, quas dicunt, Logicis, quarum aliæ hominis Orationē aliæ Rationem suis informant documentis. Artes, vt vidimus, quæ orationem hominis expoliunt, aut Puritatem eidem afferunt, aut Ornamentum.
units.tr: Let us begin with the benefit, adornment and dignity that the arts called Logical bring to each art. Some of them shape a person's speech, others his reason, by their teachings. As we have seen, the arts that polish human speech either give it purity or give it ornament.

units.la: Puritatem sermoni humano conciliat Grammatica, cuius proprium opus est pura locutio, quæ conficitur ex vocibus per Syntaxin.
units.tr: Grammar gives human speech purity. Its proper task is pure speech, which is made up of words by means of syntax.

units.la: Eius igitur partes duæ sunt Etymologia & Syntaxis.
units.tr: Its parts are therefore two: etymology and syntax.

units.la: Etymologia singularum vocū proprietates interpretatur. Huius doctrinæ de vocum proprietate duo sunt summa capita. Primum agit de sonis vocalibus, id est, in voce sonantibus, eamque constituentibus & formantibus, quales sunt litera & syllaba.
units.tr: Etymology explains the properties of individual words. There are two main heads of this doctrine of the properties of words. The first deals with vocal sounds, that is, sounds that are sounded in the voice and that constitute and form words, such as letter and syllable.

units.la: Secūdum caput agit de vocum differentiis, quæ exponuntur communibus affectionib. & speciebus. Affectiones illæ sunt Accentus & Notatio. Species sunt, Vox numeri seu numero variabilis, quæ fine flexili numerum adsignificat, vt Nomen & Verbum: Et Vox sine numero, quæ fine inflexili nullum numerum adsignificat, vt Adverbium & Coniunctio.
units.tr: The second head deals with the differences of words, which are explained by their common affections and kinds. The affections are accent and notation. The kinds are: a word that is variable in number, which by an inflected ending signifies number, such as noun and verb; and a word without number, which by an uninflected ending signifies no number, such as adverb and conjunction.

units.la: Syntaxis vocum structuram interpretatur. Eius species sunt Conuenientia, cui opponitur ex ellipsi fere nata Anomalia dissensionis: Et Rectio, cui opponitur Anomalia Antiptoseos.
units.tr: Syntax explains the structure of words. Its kinds are agreement, to which is opposed the anomaly of disagreement arising almost from ellipsis, and government, to which is opposed the anomaly of antiptosis.

units.la: Apodeixis 18.
units.tr: Demonstration 18.

units.la: Quidquid sermonis puri facultatem immensam omnium nationum & gentium hominibus liberalissime communicat, quicquid puri sermonis gloriam, mirificamque laudem Theologis, Iureconsultis, Medicis promptissime humanissimeque impertit, cuiusque beneficio illi ipsi recondita facultatum suarum mysteria in publicam lucem, publicumque conspectum, summa cum nominis gloria, & infinita mortalium felicitate proferunt & depromunt: id profecto homines, præcipue vero Theologi nostri, Iureconsulti, & Medici non despicatui habebunt, & vbi eius lacte sunt enutriti & exsatiati, non calcitrabunt pedibus, nec desidebunt, sed in amore hoc illis atque delitiis merito suo erit.
units.tr: Whatever most generously gives men of all nations and peoples the immense faculty of pure speech, whatever most readily and kindly bestows on theologians, jurists and physicians the glory and wonderful praise of pure speech, and by whose benefit they bring forth and display the hidden mysteries of their own faculties into public light and public view, with great renown and infinite happiness for mortals: such things men, and especially our theologians, jurists and physicians, will certainly not despise. Once they have been nourished and satisfied with its milk, they will not kick out with their feet or sit idle, but will rightly hold it in love and delight.

units.la: Atqui Grammatica Philosophia nostra sermonis puri facultatem immensam omnium nationum & gentiu hominibus se debita cum diligentia colentibus affert, & tantis, vt iam dictum, donis cultores suos, suos, Theologos, Iureconsultos & Medicos beat & ornat. Testetur hic ipsa & loquatur experientia: adducetur contrariorum oppositio firmata experientia testimonio.
units.tr: But our philosophical Grammar brings the immense faculty of pure speech of all nations and peoples to those who cultivate it with due diligence, and with such gifts, as already said, it blesses and adorns its devotees: theologians, jurists and physicians. Let experience itself bear witness and speak here: the opposing of contraries will be brought forward, confirmed by the testimony of experience.

units.la: Ergo Grammaticam homines praesertim literati, vt Theologi nostri, Iureconsulti, &c. non despicatui, sed in amore & delitiis habebunt.
units.tr: Therefore men, especially the learned such as our theologians, jurists, etc., will not despise Grammar, but will hold it in love and delight.

units.la: CAP. XVIII.
units.tr: CAP. XVIII.

units.la: De Christianae Philosophiae Rhetorica.
units.tr: On the Rhetoric of Christian Philosophy.

units.la: PVritati orationis ornamenta addit pars Rhetorica.
units.tr: The rhetorical part adds ornaments to the purity of speech.

units.la: Docet haec bene dicere, hoc est, docet orationem troporum luminibus variare, figurarum insignibus exornare, modulatione vocis permulcere, ac denique dignitate gestus excitare. Mirabiles huius artis effectus pertentamus elocutione & pronunciatione.
units.tr: It teaches to speak well, that is, it teaches that speech should be varied with the lights of tropes, adorned with the distinctions of figures, softened by the modulation of the voice, and finally roused by the dignity of gesture. We test the wonderful effects of this art through elocution and delivery.

units.la: Elocutio docet genera ornamentorum, quibus ipsum orationis corpus in se condecoratur, adhibet orationi codimenta & tempestiuum candorem, prudentiae interim non neglecta lege. Haec ornamenta indit iam tropo, hoc est, modificatione orationis, per mutationem vocis à propria significatione in aliam: iam figura, hoc est, mutatione tione habitus orationi à simplici & vulgari consuetudine in eam, quæ non ita obseruat syntaxeos ordinem, & quæ orationi adiungit animi motum. Iam enim figurare docet orationem dictionibus apte & iucunde inter sese resonantibus, & ita quasi mollem ac delicatam affert ei venustatem: Iam vero totam sententiam aliquo animi motu afficit, eique virilem quasi dignitate nervos & thoros affert.
units.tr: Elocution teaches the kinds of ornament by which the very body of speech is adorned in itself; it gives speech its seasonings and a seasonable brightness, while not neglecting the rule of prudence. It puts these ornaments on in the following way: now by the trope, that is, by a modification of speech, through the change of a word from its proper meaning to another; now by the figure, that is, by a change in the form of speech from the simple and common usage to one that does not observe the order of syntax so strictly, and that adds an emotion of the mind to the speech. For it teaches that speech should be shaped with words that resonate with one another aptly and pleasantly, and so it gives it a kind of soft and delicate charm. Again, it moves the whole sentence with some emotion of the mind, and gives it, as it were, sinews and muscles of manly dignity.

units.la: Ornatum deinde & modificatione vocum, figurationeque in se coloratum ac pictum orationis corpus, deinde quasi viuifico spiritu oratoris Rhetorica nostra animat & viuificat: docet enim tropis figurisque exornatum sermonem recte & decore pronunciare, quod fit si iono vocis accommodato, gestuque corporis bene conformato inter dicendum vtatur orator.
units.tr: Then our Rhetoric animates and quickens the body of speech, adorned and coloured and painted with the modification of words and the shaping of figures, as if with a living spirit from the orator. For it teaches that speech adorned with tropes and figures should be delivered correctly and gracefully, which is done if the orator, while speaking, uses a tone of voice suited to the matter and a well-ordered bodily gesture.

units.la: Apodeixis 19.
units.tr: Apodeixis 19.

units.la: Quibus ex officio vocationis est bene dicendum, illi ad artem bene dicendi Rhetoricam animum & oculos amicos non inuidos & luridos adiicient.
units.tr: Those who by the duty of their calling must speak well will add to the art of rhetoric a mind and eyes that are friendly, not envious and malicious.

units.la: At literatis Theologis, Iureconsultis &c. ex officio vocationis est bene dicendum. Adiiciant itaque illi animum candidum, non maleuolum, linguam commendatricem, non maledicam, oculos amicos, non liuidos luidos insigni Dei muneri Rhetorica. Nam Quic-quid est praestabile, admirabile, efficax, iucundum in oratione, hoc oratori, Theologo, Iureconsulto, &c. est optabile.
units.tr: But for learned theologians, jurists and others, speaking well is a duty of their calling. Let them therefore add to the distinguished gift of God, rhetoric, a candid mind, not an ill-disposed one; a commending tongue, not a slanderous one; friendly eyes, not spiteful ones. For: whatever in speech is excellent, admirable, effective, and pleasing, is desirable for the orator, the theologian, the jurist, and so on.

units.la: Atqui vero quid praestabilius est, quam posse hominum coetus dicendo tenere, mentes allicere, voluntatem impellere quo velis, & unde velis deducere? Quid tam admirabile, quam rem propositam ornate pronunciare, troporum luminibus variare, insignibus figurarum exornare? Quid tam efficax in dicendo, quam virtus Rhetorica, quae si recte adhibeatur, mirabiles ostentat effectus in oratore & in auditoribus, hi illum exhorrescunt, stupefacti dicentem intuentur, in eo exclamant, hunc Deum inter homines putant. Reginam hominum & flexanimā non male eam Philosophi dixerunt. Auditores vis capere & permouere? Elocutione & pronunciatione id pertentes. Vis vincere? Rhetorica machinamenta adhibeas.
units.tr: And indeed: what is more excellent than to be able to hold a gathering of men by speaking, to attract minds, to drive the will wherever you wish and lead it from wherever you wish? What is so admirable as to deliver a proposed matter ornately, to vary it with the lights of tropes and adorn it with the distinctions of figures? What is so effective in speaking as the power of rhetoric, which, if rightly employed, shows wonderful effects in the orator and in the hearers: they shudder, stand amazed as they look on the speaker, cry out about him, and think him a god among men. The Philosophers rightly called it the queen of men and the mover of souls. Do you wish to win over and stir your hearers? Strive for it through elocution and delivery. Do you wish to conquer? Employ the machinery of rhetoric.

units.la: Quid tam iucundum cogitatu atque auditu, quam modulatione vocis permulcere, dignitate gestus excitare? Haec omnia Rhetorica in rebus veris & licitis prudenter vsurpata praestat.
units.tr: What is so pleasing to think upon and to hear as to soothe with the modulation of the voice and rouse with the dignity of gesture? Rhetoric, when prudently applied to true and lawful matters, provides all of these things.

units.la: Rhetorica igitur est Theologo & aliis literatis, imo quibuscunque bene dicendum ex officio, insigniter optabilis.
units.tr: Rhetoric is therefore remarkably desirable for the theologian and other learned men, indeed for anyone who must speak well by duty.

units.la: CAP. XIX.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIX.

units.la: De Christiana Logica.
units.tr: On Christian Logic.

units.la: RATionis ars dicitur Dialectica & Logica. Diuina huius artis maiestas, vtilitas inaestimabilis.
units.tr: The art of reason is called Dialectic and Logic. The divine majesty of this art and its inestimable usefulness are great.

units.la: I. Docet bene differere, docet ratione hu-mana in rebus omnibus, ipsis rebus convenienter, sapienter & prudenter uti: Est ars humani intellectus, qua hominis & intellectus humani operationes & cogitationes ordinantur & diriguntur, in rerum cognitione. Proinde non immerito Cicero. I. de Leg. artem definit intelligendi. Quemadmodum sensus non recte sentiunt sola vi & determinatione naturæ sine vllis normis: ita etiam ratio siue intellectus & cogitationes hominis, sine normis artis huius directricis, post lapsum & per lapsum depravatæ recte operari non possunt. Veram itaque Logicam non abs re dicunt sapientiæ, tum humanæ, tum diuinæ χεῖρα καὶ ὄργανον, quo si unquam alias, hoc maxime tempore opus est, quo nihil fere aliud, quam sacra & profana subtilissime, atq; etiam nonnunquam sophistice & veteratorie disputantur, sicut hoc ostendunt disceptationes Theologorum, Iureconsultorum, Medicorum & Philosophorum, quæ sunt in medio.
units.tr: I. It teaches us to reason well. It teaches us to use human reason in all things, fittingly, wisely and prudently, in accordance with the things themselves. It is the art of the human intellect, by which the operations and thoughts of a human being and of the intellect are ordered and directed in the knowledge of things. Hence Cicero, in the first book of his De Legibus, not without reason defines it as the art of understanding. Just as the senses do not perceive correctly by the power and determination of nature alone without any rules, so too reason or the intellect and the thoughts of a human being, without the rules of this directing art, cannot function rightly, since they have been corrupted by the Fall and through the Fall. So they rightly call true Logic a hand and an instrument [χεῖρα καὶ ὄργανον] of wisdom, both human and divine. If ever it was needed, it is needed especially now, when almost nothing else is disputed so subtly, and sometimes even sophistically and craftily, both sacred and profane matters, as the controversies of theologians, jurists, physicians and philosophers, which are current everywhere, show.

units.la: Logica autem hæc hominis rationem, ingenium & iudicium, & cogitationes in rebus cognoscendis formans & gubernans, primum suis consiliis ac præceptis instituit intellectum simplicem, dirigitque hominis cogitationes in rebus & notionibus simplicibus apprehendendis ac intelligendis: Eaque pars dicitur Inuentio, quia inueniendi argumenta præcepta tradit, & iis inuentionem augmentorum informat & efficit. Ita autē docet inuenire argumenta, vt intellectus ac ratio nostra probe consideret rerum affectiones, quarum sunt notiones & argumenta inuestiganda, ita vt Logica argumētorum inuentio respondeat rerum ipsarum affectioni, ex earum enim mutua habitudine & schesi, non nostra opinione, metiri docet argumenta, & constituere. Vnde qui intelligentiæ (uæ vi & directione penitius & accuratius res earumque affectiones perspexerit, acutius pariter & accuratius argumenta notionesque rerum scientificas intellexerit & inuenerit.
units.tr: This Logic, moreover, which shapes and governs a person's reason, wit and judgment, and the thoughts by which we know things, first trains the simple intellect by its counsels and precepts, and directs a person's thoughts in grasping and understanding simple things and notions. This part is called Invention, because it gives precepts for finding arguments, and by these it shapes and brings about the discovery of new material. It teaches us to find arguments in such a way that our intellect and reason carefully consider the properties of things, whose notions and arguments are to be investigated, so that the invention of arguments in Logic corresponds to the very properties of the things. For it teaches us to measure and establish arguments by the mutual relation and proportion of the things themselves, not by our own opinion. Hence whoever has looked more deeply and accurately into things and their properties by the power and direction of understanding will equally understand and discover arguments and scientific notions of things more keenly and accurately.

units.la: Deinde Logica nostra instituit intellectum compositum, vt felicius & melius in notionibus coniunctis seu complexis(vt vocant)operandis & dignoscendis versetur: diciturque Dispositio, tio, quia tradit praecepta rectè argumen-ta disponendi, & suis praeceptis efficit bonum disponendi in mente habitum: dicitur Iudicium, quia tradit regulas de dispositis argumentis bene iudicandi, efficitque Logicum de dispositis argu-mentis Iudicium per dispositionis re-gulas.
units.tr: Next, our Logic trains the intellect in composition, so that it may more happily and better deal with and distinguish notions that are joined or, as they are called, complex. It is called Disposition, because it teaches the precepts for arranging arguments rightly, and by its precepts it produces in the mind a good habit of arranging. It is called Judgment, because it gives rules for judging well about arranged arguments, and by the rules of arrangement it produces logical judgment about arranged arguments.

units.la: Regit itaque, dirigit, ac informat hæc logicæ pars mentis compositam in intelligendo facultatem, dirigendo nempe cogitationes de duorum argu-mentorum, terminorum ac notionum ad se inuicem legitima coordinatione & habitudine: Adeoque ἐννοίᾳ mentis formatur, & efformatur Iudiciu Noc-ticum. Vel dirigendo cogitationes dia-noeticas, vt dianoias officio rectè vta-tur ratio, adeoque legitimo discursu v-num ex alio deducat & exstruat, & re-cte veritatique rerum conuenienter ab vno ad aliud cogitationem suam moueat. Hinc effloresçit dexteritas Iudicii Dianoetici. Docet autem hæc dianoias humanæ Logica doctrina formare duplicem discursum, Syllogi-sticum & Methodicum.
units.tr: This part of Logic therefore governs, directs and shapes the mind's faculty of composition in understanding, namely by directing the thoughts toward the lawful co-ordination and relation of two arguments, terms and notions to one another. Thus the noetic judgment is formed and fashioned [ἐννοίᾳ] in the mind. Or it directs the dianoetic thoughts, so that reason uses its discursive function rightly, and by lawful discourse deduces and builds up one thing from another, and moves its thought from one point to another correctly and in agreement with the truth of things. Hence the skill of dianoetic judgment flourishes. This doctrine of human Logic teaches us to form a twofold discourse: syllogistic and methodical.

units.la: Syllogisticum quidem, dum docu-menmentis suis docet cogitationes mentis ita agitare & mouere, vt ex notionis, termini seu argumenti tertii cum duobus apte repetita collocatione iudicemus duorum argumentorum illorum, quæ constituunt quæstionem, ad se invicem dispositionem & ordinationem veram vel falsam esse, seu potius ludicium informat consequentiæ & inconsequentiæ. Methodicum vero discursum dirigit, dum cogitationes nostræ mentis ita mouet ab vna doctrinæ siue tractationis alicuius sententia & parte, ad alteram progrediendo, vt quælibet sententia & pars pro naturæ suæ claritate præponatur, vel obscuritate postponatur, adeoque iudicetur rerum & sententiarum inter se cohærentia & conuenientia ad faciliorem doctrinæ tum traditionem, tum traditæ perceptionem, tum etiam perceptæ memoriam. Hinc ludicium ordinis & confusionis. Atque sic Logica omnes intelligentiæ humanæ gradus dirigit ac instituit, primo simplicium veram apprehensionem, deinde compositionem ac diuisionem seu duarum notionum conceptum,& inter se ordinationem.
units.tr: The syllogistic discourse, in so far as it teaches by its rules to set the thoughts of the mind moving in such a way that, by the fitting and repeated placing of a third notion, term or argument with the two others, we judge whether the two arguments that make up the question stand in a true or false relation and order to one another; or rather, it shapes the judgment of consequence and inconsequence. The methodical discourse it directs in so far as it moves our mind's thoughts from one opinion or part of a doctrine or treatment to another, advancing in such a way that each opinion and part is placed first according to the clarity of its nature, or put later according to its obscurity, and so we judge how the things and opinions cohere and agree with one another, for an easier teaching of the doctrine, an easier perception of what is taught, and also an easier memory of what has been perceived. Hence the judgment of order and confusion. And so Logic directs and orders all the grades of human understanding: first the true grasp of simple things, then the composition and division, that is, the conception of two notions and their ordering among themselves.

units.la: Tertio ipsum discursum dianoeticum.
units.tr: Third, the discursive reasoning itself.

units.la: Apodeixis 20.
units.tr: Demonstration 20.

units.la: Quaecunque ars rationis mentisque humanae munera promptissime expedit, quae particulam illam divinae mentis hominibus insitam viuifico quodam calore recreat, quae denique lumine suo omnium rerum magnarum campos vehementer collustrat, quae nemo ratione sua recte vsurus carere potest, quae ex artium orbe sublata tollitur sol ex mundo, quae est regina, magistra, directrix, ministra, imo ars omnium artium; illam summo iure tanquam de caelo lapsam suspicient & obseruabunt homines, qui sunt Logica animalia: quo enim Logica quis magis fuerit excultus, eo magis fuerit Logicum animal, si Logicum magis animal, eo etiam perfectior homo: Perfectior quippe si fuerit hominis forma Ratio, perfectior quoque fuerit homo ipse. Eandem, inquam, artium magistram & ministram literati cum primis Theologi, Iureconsulti, Medici, Philosophi in summo loco & precio habebunt.
units.tr: Whatever art most readily dispatches the functions of reason and the human mind, which revives that particle of the divine mind implanted in men with a certain life-giving warmth, which finally illumines with its light the fields of all great things, which no one who is going to use reason rightly can lack, which, taken away from the orbit of the arts, removes the sun from the world, which is queen, teacher, director, servant, indeed the art of all arts: men who are Logical animals will receive and observe it with the highest right, as if it had fallen from heaven; for the more someone has been cultivated in Logic, the more he is a Logical animal, and the more he is a Logical animal, the more perfect is the man too: for if reason is the form of man, the man himself will be the more perfect. The literate, especially theologians, jurists, physicians and philosophers, I say, will hold this same mistress and servant of the arts in the highest place and esteem.

units.la: Atqui Logica Christiana est eiusmodi diuina & augusta ars. Etenim, vt ex multis pauca delibem philosophica, nulla est disciplina, quae magis excitet, iuuet, acuat ingenium hominis, quam Logica. Nulla est ars, quae iudicium hominis, hoc est, dispositionem mentis ad solide cogitandum & percipiendum, quid verum, quid falsum, quid consequens, quid vero inconsequens: quid ordinatum, quid vero confusum sit, dexterius informet ac firmet.
units.tr: But Christian logic is such a divine and august art. For, to pick a few points from many philosophical ones, there is no discipline that more stirs up, aids and sharpens the human intellect than logic. There is no art that more aptly forms and strengthens human judgment, that is, the disposition of the mind to think solidly and to perceive what is true or false, what follows and what does not follow, what is ordered and what is confused.

units.la: Haec dirigit cogitationes hominis, vt recte cogitent, inueniant, disponant, iudicent. Hæc facit, vt ordine doceas & scribas, quæ recte cogitasti. Hæc facit, vt bene discas, quod altei bene te docet. Oportet enim intellectum discentis conformari intellectui docentis, per normas Logicas. Per Logicam non solum scimus, sed etiam nos scire scimus. Hinc illa inæstimabilis in intellectu lætitia & voluptas, quam generat Logica dubitationum optima Medica. Hinc sublata dubitatione per Logicæ medicinam, constantia in veritate, ne facile ab ea seducaris. Logica facit, vt ab aliis tractata dextre retexas, & penitius introspiciendo tractationis intimam essentiam, rectius intelligas. Hæc tibi ad omnis generis erudita colloquia & collationes.
units.tr: Logic directs a person's thoughts so that they think, discover, arrange and judge correctly. It makes you able to teach and write in an orderly way what you have thought correctly. It makes you able to learn well what another teaches you well. For the learner's understanding must be conformed to the teacher's understanding, by logical rules. Through logic we not only know, but also know that we know. Hence comes that inestimable joy and pleasure in the intellect, which logic, the best medicine for doubts, produces. Hence, once doubt is removed by the medicine of logic, there comes constancy in the truth, so that you are not easily led away from it. Logic enables you, when others have treated a subject, to unravel it correctly, and by looking more deeply into the inner essence of the treatment, to understand it more accurately. It makes you ready for learned conversations and discussions of every kind.

units.la: Hæc sola facit, vt possis intimam scientiam ac habitum reliquarum disciplinarum tibi acquirere; quia Logica est magistra disponendarum omnium artium, & hac ratione suæ ipsius genitrix & formatrix. Logica te sola regit, vt comparato scientiæ alicuius vero habitu, secundum eum recte opereris, hoc est, præcepta cognita ad usum in vita utilem traducas.
units.tr: This alone enables you to acquire for yourself the inner knowledge and mastery of the other disciplines, because logic is the mistress who arranges all the arts, and for this reason is their own mother and former. Logic alone governs you, so that, once you have acquired a true mastery of some science, you may work correctly according to it, that is, apply the precepts you have learned to useful practice in life.

units.la: Ergo homines summo iure Logicam tanquam cœlitus nobis Dei munere concessum donum suspicient, amplexabuntur, osculabuntur, & cum primis nostri Theologi & alii literati eam in amoribus & deliciis, in animis, & oculis habebunt, non criminabuntur.
units.tr: Therefore men will receive with the highest right logic as a gift of God granted to us from heaven, will embrace it, kiss it, and especially our theologians and other literate men will hold it in their loves and delights, in their minds and eyes, and will not accuse it.

units.la: CAP. XX.
units.tr: CHAPTER XX.

units.la: De Arithmetica.
units.tr: On Arithmetic.

units.la: Postquam tres artes Logicas & omnium generalissimas & primas expediuimus, recto itinere in Mathematicorum campos expatiabimur.
units.tr: Having dispatched the three logical arts, which are the most general and primary of all, we shall now proceed by a straight path into the fields of the mathematicians.

units.la: Mathesis est doctrina quantitatis.
units.tr: Mathematics is the doctrine of quantity.

units.la: Estque Arithmetica & Geometria: Vtriusque erudita iucunditas, & ampla vtilitas. Illa quātitatem discretam, scilicet numerum, hæc quantitatem continuam, scilicet magnitudinem exponit.
units.tr: It comprises arithmetic and geometry, each of which offers learned delight and wide usefulness. The former sets forth discrete quantity, namely number; the latter continuous quantity, namely magnitude.

units.la: Arithmetica est Simplex, incomparatos (liceat ita loqui) seu simplices numeros tractans, vel Comparata.
units.tr: Arithmetic is simple, dealing with unrelated numbers (if I may so speak), that is, simple numbers, or it is comparative.

units.la: Illa perficitur Notatione, id est, modo scribendi numeros, eorumque naturam explicandi, & Numeratione, quæ e duobus datis inuenit tertium.
units.tr: The former is carried out by notation, that is, the manner of writing numbers and explaining their nature, and by numeration, which from two given numbers finds a third.

units.la: Hæc rursus simplex & homogeneorum numerorum tum integrorum, prima in Additione & Subductione, & secunda in Multiplicatione & Diuisione: tum partium, in qua dati numerandi sunt partes.
units.tr: This in turn is simple, dealing with homogeneous numbers, both whole, first in addition and subtraction, and second in multiplication and division; and also of parts, in which the given numbers are to be numbered as parts.

units.la: Eaque rursus est Accidentalis, dicitur reductio.
units.tr: This in turn is accidental, and is called reduction.

units.la: Estque partium ad Partes, vel partium ad Integra: vel Essentialis, quæ partes augendo minuendove numerat.
units.tr: It is either of parts to parts or of parts to wholes; or it is essential, which counts by increasing or diminishing the parts.

units.la: Mista numeratio opponitur simplici, estque heterogeneorum, in qua dati numerandi sunt integra cum partibus.
units.tr: Mixed numeration is opposed to simple, and is of heterogeneous numbers, in which the given numbers are wholes together with parts.

units.la: Comparata Arithmetica comparatorum terminorum naturam explicat.
units.tr: Comparative arithmetic explains the nature of compared terms.

units.la: Comparatio autem est vel Terminorum, & dicitur Ratio, quarum vna est æqualitatis, altera inæqualitatis, & ita deinceps in subdistributionibus inæqualitatis: vel est Rationum comparatio & proportio. Eaque est Arithmetica vel Geometrica. Qua de arte videris Ramum, Schonerum, Salignacum, Vrstisium, Frisium & alios.
units.tr: Comparison, however, is either of terms, and is called ratio, of which one is of equality and another of inequality, and so on through the subdivisions of inequality; or it is the comparison and proportion of ratios. This is arithmetical or geometrical. On this art you may consult Ramus, Schoner, Salignac, Ursitius, Frisius and others.

units.la: Apodaxis 21. Generalis.
units.tr: Demonstration 21, General.

units.la: Qua disciplina reliquis artibus maximam affert vtilitatem hominibusque cuiuscunque conditionis opes largitur insignes, non est nauci facienda, sed tanti æstimanda, quantos affert artibus & hominibus fructus.
units.tr: This discipline brings the greatest usefulness to the other arts and bestows remarkable riches upon men of every condition. It is not to be held in contempt, but to be valued as highly as the fruits it brings to the arts and to men.

units.la: At Mathematica disciplina artib. & hominibus vsui sane est maximo. Vnde Socrates apud Platonem ait, quod Mathematica diligentius sit asseruanda, quam decem oculorum millia, quod, vt opinor, sine Mathesi Philosolosophus in Philosophorum Schola, & homo in mundi schola, non plus videat, quam Polyphemus ab Vlysse occœcatus in suo antro.
units.tr: But mathematical discipline is certainly of the greatest use to the arts and to men. Hence Socrates in Plato says that mathematics is to be guarded more carefully than ten thousand eyes, because, as I think, without mathematics the philosopher in the school of philosophers, and the man in the school of the world, sees no more than Polyphemus, blinded by Ulysses, in his cave.

units.la: Quid autè & quantum oculorum & lumi-nis Mathesis afferat philosophantibus patet, primùin Musica, quæ fere nihil aliud est, quæ Arithmetica in auditu, in sonis, in concentibus, in eorum intervallis, &c. 2. In optica, est enim fere quædam Geometria in luce, umbra, colore, visus ipsius natura, & facultate, hallucinatione, è situ, motu, numero, veritate, quantitate, figura, seu visus ipse rectus sit, seu indirectus, è speculorum, seu diversorum mediorum densitate & raritate. 3. In Physica hoc patet, quæ beneficio quantitatis optime & cognoscuntur, & sæpe describuntur. Imo omne corpus Physicum dicitur mathematico corpore præditum. Omne corpus quâtum. Omnia corpora numerantur. Deus ipse in creatione mundi & corporum mundanorum fuit Geometra. Nam cum immensitatis æternæ spacia definire statueret, Geometria in primis usus est, quæ longitudinum, latitudinum spacia terminaret, omniumque symmetriam, rationem, proportionem, similitudinem discerneret. 4. In Astrologia patet, quæ fere est Arithmetica numeratio motuum cœlestium, quæ fere est Geometrica globorum cœlestium, & stellarum, secundum longitudinis, latitudinis, altitudinis spacia figuratio, & dimensio, adeo ut nil sit aliud Astrologia, quam Arithmetica & Geometria quædam in usu coniunctio.
units.tr: What and how much light and sight mathematics brings to philosophers is clear. First, in music, which is almost nothing other than arithmetic in hearing, in sounds, in harmonies, in their intervals, etc. Second, in optics, for it is almost a certain geometry in light, shadow, colour, the nature and faculty of sight itself, illusion, from the position, motion, number, truth, quantity and figure of things seen, whether vision is direct or indirect, and from the density and rarity of mirrors or of various media. Third, in physics this is clear, since by the benefit of quantity bodies are best known and often described. Indeed every physical body is said to be endowed with a mathematical body. Every body is quantified; all bodies are numbered. God himself, in the creation of the world and of the worldly bodies, was a geometer. For when he determined to define the spaces of eternal immensity, he especially used geometry, which bounds the spaces of lengths and breadths and discerns the symmetry, ratio, proportion and similarity of all things. Fourth, it is clear in astrology, which is almost an arithmetical reckoning of celestial motions, which is almost a geometrical figuring and measuring of the celestial spheres and stars according to the spaces of length, latitude and height, so that astrology is nothing other than a certain conjunction of arithmetic and geometry in use.

units.la: §. In Medicina patet idem: Teste enim ipso Hippocrate principe medicorum, oportet medicum Arithmeticam & Geometriam non solum ad splendorem vitæ, sed ad Medicinæ vsum studiosè perdiscere. Arithmeticam quidem, vt morborum intensiones, remissiones, periodos, mutationes & iudicia; Geometriam vero ad ossium situm, ordinem, luxationem, repositionem, contritionem, refectionem, compositionem, exemptionem, afflictionem, denique; ad omnē curationem. In politicis & ethicis, quantæ sit vtilitatis Mathesis, satis declarant ipsæ virtutes, quæ definiuntur bonarum actionum & administrationum ratione, proportione, & symmetria.In Theologia idem non est obscurum. Nam Mathescos ignarus in multis locis erit cæcus, vt in 38. cap. vbi Geometrice à Deo mundum factum esse, eiusque dimensiones, longitudinem, latitudinem & altitudinem mensuratas, & terram ipsam Geometrico pondere in vniuersitatis medio suspensam disputat. Sic in cap. 11. Sap. non intelliget quid sit illud: Deum omnia creasse in numero, mensura, & pondere. Non capiet diuina oracula de fabrica mundi, terræque basibus & situ; oracula mechanica, de vectibus & templo Solomonico: oracula optica de loco lucis & tenebrarum; oracula Astronomica de Pleiadibus, Orione, Arcturo, Boote, de cæli imperio in terras: oracula Geographica de terræ mensura & c.8. In Iuresonsultorum codice idem liquet, audiatur enim l. 13. ff. de liberis & posthumis, cuius hæc sunt clarissima verba: si ita scriptum sit, si filius mihi natus fuerit, ex besse heres esto, ex reliqua parte uxor mea heres esto: si vero filia mihi nata fuerit, ex triente heres esto, ex reliqua parte uxor heres esto: & filius & filia nati essent, dicendum, assem distribuendum esse in septem partes: ut ex his filius quatuor, uxor duas, filia unam partem habeat, ita enim secundum voluntatem testantis, filius altero tanto amplius habebit, quam uxor. Sed satis in genere.
units.tr: §. In medicine the same is evident, for, as Hippocrates himself, the prince of physicians, testifies, the physician must diligently learn arithmetic and geometry not only for the splendour of life but for the practice of medicine. Arithmetic indeed serves for the intensities, remissions, periods, changes and crises of diseases; geometry for the position, order, dislocation, reduction, crushing, restoration, composition, removal and affliction of bones, and in short for every cure. In politics and ethics, the usefulness of mathematics is sufficiently shown by the virtues themselves, which are defined by the ratio, proportion and symmetry of good actions and administrations. In theology the same is not obscure. For one ignorant of mathematics will be blind in many places, as in chapter 38, where he discusses that the world was made geometrically by God, and its dimensions, length, breadth and height measured, and that the earth itself is suspended in the middle of the universe by a geometric weight. So in Wisdom chapter 11 he will not understand what that means: that God created all things in number, measure and weight. He will not grasp the divine oracles on the fabric of the world and the foundations and position of the earth; the mechanical oracles on levers and the temple of Solomon; the optical oracles on the place of light and darkness; the astronomical oracles on the Pleiades, Orion, Arcturus, Bootes, and the dominion of heaven over the earth; the geographical oracles on the measure of the earth, and so on. In the code of the jurists the same is clear, for let us hear law 13 of the Digest, de liberis et posthumis, whose most clear words are these: if it be written thus: if a son is born to me, let him be heir to two-thirds, and let my wife be heir to the rest; but if a daughter is born to me, let her be heir to one-third, and let my wife be heir to the rest; and if a son and a daughter should both be born, it must be said that the as is to be divided into seven parts, so that the son has four parts, the wife two, and the daughter one; for in this way, according to the will of the testator, the son will have twice as much as the wife, and more by that amount. But enough in general.

units.la: Specialis Apodeixis de Arithmetica.
units.tr: A Particular Demonstration concerning Arithmetic.

units.la: Cuius artis magna sunt dignitates, magnaque in vita communi utilitates, easi non esset in artium & disciplinarum exoptabilium numero, adsciscenda & accersenda etiamnum esset. Atqui Arithemetica magna sunt dignitates, magna in vita communi utilitates. Cernitur enim eius usus amplissimus & pernecessarius in mercatura, in miftione rerum & temperatura, in Reipub. rationibus, in constituendis vectigalibus, in iudicando, in dirimendis controuersiis diuidui, in re militari, & in quo non?
units.tr: The arts and disciplines that have great worth and great usefulness in common life would, if this were not so, not be counted among the desirable arts and sciences, and would still have to be admitted and invited in. But arithmetic has great worth and great usefulness in common life. For its use is seen to be very wide and very necessary in trade, in the measuring and mixing of goods, in the affairs of the commonwealth, in fixing taxes, in judging, in settling disputes over inheritances, in warfare, and in what else not?

units.la: Ergo ut ars utilissima hominum negociis Arithmetica colenda & expetenda est. Neque potest ex parte huius male audire Philosophia.
units.tr: Therefore, as the most useful art for the business of men, arithmetic is to be cultivated and sought after. Nor can philosophy, on this account, be ill spoken of.

units.la: CAP. XXI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXI.

units.la: De Geometria.
units.tr: On Geometry.

units.la: GEometria multum à Ramo nostro elaborata, luci & vsui exoptato est restituta, ars inquam, bene metiendi, cui subiicitur magnitudo, cuius extremum dicitur Terminus: quęque est Linea, vel Lineatum.
units.tr: Geometry, greatly worked over by our Ramus, has been restored to the light and the use it deserved. It is the art, I mean, of measuring well, whose subject is magnitude, whose extremity is called the terminus, and which is either a line or a lined figure.

units.la: Linea recta est vel obliqua, habetque affectiones, perpendiculum & parallelismum. Lineati sunt tum affectiones, tum species.
units.tr: A line is either straight or oblique, and it has two affections, the perpendicular and parallelism. Both the affections and the species belong to the lined figure.

units.la: Affectiones sunt angelus & figura.
units.tr: The affections are angle and figure.

units.la: Species vero superficies & corpus.
units.tr: The species are surface and body.

units.la: Superficies est plana vel gibba. Plana est rectilinea in triangulo & triangulato, vel obliquilinea in circulo. Gibba est sphærica vel varia. Corpus denique est planum vel gibbum. Planum pyramis, & pyramidatum &c. Gibbum sphæra, Conus, Cylindrus. Vide Ramum, Schonerum, Snellium, &c.
units.tr: A surface is either plane or curved. A plane surface is rectilinear in a triangle and in what is triangulated, or curvilinear in a circle. A curved surface is spherical or irregular. Finally, a body is either plane or curved. A plane body is a pyramid, and pyramidal things, etc. A curved body is a sphere, a cone, a cylinder. See Ramus, Schoner, Snellius, etc.

units.la: Apodeixis 22.
units.tr: Demonstration 22 [ἀπόδειξις]

units.la: Si Geometria dignitates per vniuersam hominis vitam sunt diffusæ, si ad reliquas disciplinas physicas, politicas, Theologicas percipiendum, ad infinita belli pacisque opera conficiendum valde sunt accommodatæ: vtique nemo nisi rerum ignarus, & hominum vitaque vsui inuidus eam parui & nihili faciet.
units.tr: If the dignities of geometry are spread through the whole of human life; if it is very well suited to be grasped alongside the other physical, political and theological disciplines, and to carry out the countless works of war and peace: surely no one, unless ignorant of things and begrudging to human life and its use, will think it of little or no worth.

units.la: At verum prius. Etenim vis scire quam facultatem mundi ille Architectus summus in fabricando machinandoque vniuersitatis opifi-cio cio adhibuerit? Adi numen Geometricū. Vis scire quo numine terra in medio mūdi posita conquieuerit? Adi numen Geometricum. Vis scire, quæ vis effecerit, vt plantæ, vt arbores, vt animantes suum statum tueantur? Adi numen Geometricum. Geometriæ theorema est: Magnitudo infinite secatur. At nos Geometricis armis sectionem illam verissime & affirmari & negari posse conuincemus. Legitur apud Polybium omni laude cumulatum historicum de duab. Græciæ vrbibus: quarum altera Megalopolis fuerit in ambitu 50. stadiorum: altera Lacedæmon, quæ alias Sparta dicitur, 48. stadiorum: & tamen idem Polybius Lacedæmoné duplo fuisse Megalopoli maiorem contestatur. O rem, inquies, incredibilem, & artium legibus contrariam: imo vero Geometricæ artis legibus valde consentaneam. Sed infinitus foret Geometriæ splendor, si singula eius lumina commemorare vellem. Hoc igitur breuissime dicam: quod sedemus, quod surgimus, quod stamus, quod ambulamus, quod progredimur, illud nos Geometriç debemus. Ergo & posterius.
units.tr: But first, the truth. For do you wish to know what skill the supreme Architect of the world employed in fashioning and contriving the workmanship of the universe? Approach the geometrical deity. Do you wish to know by what power the earth, placed in the middle of the world, rests? Approach the geometrical deity. Do you wish to know what force makes plants, trees and living creatures preserve their state? Approach the geometrical deity. The theorem of geometry is: magnitude is infinitely divisible. But with geometrical weapons we shall prove most truly that this division can both be affirmed and be denied. In Polybius, a historian heaped with every praise, we read of two cities of Greece: one of them, Megalopolis, had a circuit of fifty stadia; the other, Lacedaemon, which is also called Sparta, forty-eight stadia. Yet the same Polybius attests that Lacedaemon was twice as large as Megalopolis. O incredible thing, you will say, and contrary to the laws of the arts! Indeed, it is very much in agreement with the laws of the geometrical art. But the splendour of geometry would be endless if I wished to recount each of its lights. So I will say this very briefly: that we sit, that we rise, that we stand, that we walk, that we advance, we owe all this to geometry. Thus the latter as well.

units.la: CAP. XXII.
units.tr: CAP. XXII.

units.la: De Optica.
units.tr: On Optics

units.la: ARithmetica & Geometria relicta, ad illas, quæ his multum vtuntur veniamus, & quidem primum videamus Opticam, iam diu satis à Scholis nostris exulante. Ea autem est ars radiaturæ, seu bene videndi. Hic explicatur tum visibile, tum visio.
units.tr: Leaving arithmetic and geometry behind, let us come to those arts that make much use of them. First let us look at Optics, which has for some time been driven out of our schools. This is the art of radiation, or of seeing well. Here both the visible and the act of seeing are explained.

units.la: Visibile radiat per medium. Radiare est per radios speciem suam diffundere.
units.tr: The visible radiates through a medium. To radiate is to spread its image abroad by means of rays.

units.la: Radius est rectus vel obliquus, ratione casus, qui fit per medium pellucidum, hoc est, impune radiis peruiū: quod est radians & aspectabile, vt aqua, crystallus, vitrum, vel non radians & nō aspectabile, vt aer, cælum, &c. Medio huic opponitur opacum. Hic doctrina de radiatione visibilis per medium varia.
units.tr: A ray is straight or oblique, depending on the angle, and passes through a transparent medium, that is, one through which rays pass unimpeded. Such a medium is either radiant and visible, like water, crystal, glass, or non-radiant and invisible, like air, the sky, etc. Opposed to this medium is the opaque. Here the teaching on the radiation of the visible through a medium is set out in its various forms.

units.la: Visibile porro est primarium vel secundarium. Illud per se, hoc per accidens dici solet.
units.tr: The visible is further either primary or secondary. The former is usually called visible in itself, the latter visible by accident.

units.la: Visibile primarium per se radiat, est lux & color. Vnde visibile ipsum luminosum & coloratum. Vtrique accidit splendor.
units.tr: The primary visible, which radiates in itself, is light and colour. Hence the visible itself is luminous and coloured. Brightness belongs to both.

units.la: Lux est primaria vel secundaria.
units.tr: Light is either primary or secondary.

units.la: Hic de luce & luminoso corpore, eiusque varia radiatione: Item de oppositis vmbra, & tenebris. Vmbræ projectio varia: forma item diuersa, nempe Recta vel Versa. Color lucis ope radiat. diat, tractatur hic, quatenus optica permittit consideratio.
units.tr: Here we treat of light and the luminous body, and of its various radiation; likewise of the opposites, shadow and darkness. The projection of shadow varies, and its shape also differs, namely straight or inverted. The colour of light radiates by means of ..., and is treated here so far as optical consideration allows.

units.la: Visibile per accidens seu secundarium & aliis sensibus & dianoia percipitur, vt, interuallum, situs, figura, magnitudo, numerus, motus, quies, similitudo, diuersitas, &c.
units.tr: The visible by accident, or secondary, is perceived both by the other senses and by the reasoning mind, as interval, position, figure, size, number, motion, rest, likeness, difference, etc.

units.la: Visio fit 1.organo tum vniuersò tum particulari, 2. fit intra oculum, &c. & quomodo, &c.
units.tr: Vision occurs (1) through an organ, both in general and in particular; (2) it occurs within the eye, etc., and how, etc.

units.la: Est vero Simplex vel Composita. Simplex fit solo incidentiæ radio.
units.tr: Vision is either simple or compound. Simple vision comes about by the single ray of incidence alone.

units.la: Estque Confusa vel Distincta. Illa, qua totum visibile simul confuse videtur. Quomodo fiat, &c. Hæc, qua visibile per radium, qui est axis opticæ figuræ, hinc inde oberrantem distincte videtur. Hac visione quomodo visibile per se & per accidens videatur, explicatur speciatim.
units.tr: And it is either confused or distinct. The first is when the whole visible object is seen confusedly at once; how this happens, etc. The second is when the visible object is seen distinctly through the ray which is the axis of the optical figure, wandering to and fro. By this kind of vision it is explained, in particular, how the visible is seen both in itself and by accident.

units.la: Composita visio est geminata, & fit radiis incidentiæ & obliquationis. Estque reflexa, vbi doctrina Catoptrica traditur, vel refracta, vbi doctrina Mesoptrica, iucunda valde, explicatur.
units.tr: Compound vision is doubled, and comes about through rays of incidence and of deflection. It is either reflected, where the doctrine of catoptrics is taught, or refracted, where the doctrine of mesoptics, which is very pleasant, is explained.

units.la: Apodeixis 23.
units.tr: Apodeixis 23.

units.la: Quicquid humano generi admirabiles suas diuinitas & pene diuinas grata quasi mente exhibet, id neutineutiquam desiderari in bene constituta Repub. pa- tiamur. At Optica nobis admirabiles suas diuitias & pene diuinas largitur, vt ostendunt Euclidis, Al- hazeni, Vitellonis, P. Rami, Friderici Risneri, alio- runque summorum Opticorum egregia monumen- ta. Hac egent in suis operibus conficiendis nō modo Mechanici, sed etiam reliquarum ar- tium cultores. Hac destitutus Physicus semi- caecus est. Magnum lumen ab hac accipit As- tronomia. Sine hac pleraque meteora, quae sunt ἐμφάσεις, Physiologus perfecte intelligere non potest. Sine hac multa pulcra Proble- mata idem soluere erudite non potest, de qui- bus eruditissime monet & disserit Philoso- phus Germaniae nostrae magnus Rod. Gocle- nius. Eam igitur artem scilicet Opticam desiderari in Repub.literaria ne patiamur.
units.tr: We would not allow whatever gives the human race its admirable riches and near-divine gifts, offered with a grateful mind, to be wanting in a well-ordered commonwealth. Yet Optics offers us its admirable riches and near-divine gifts, as the outstanding monuments of the greatest opticians show: Euclid, Alhazen, Vitellio, Peter Ramus, Friedrich Risner, and others. Not only mechanics but also the practitioners of the other arts need this art in carrying out their works. Without it the natural philosopher is half-blind. Astronomy receives great light from it. Without it the physiologist cannot fully understand many meteors, which are [ἐμφάσεις] appearances. Without it he cannot learnedly solve many fine problems, on which our great German philosopher Rudolph Goclenius advises and discourses most learnedly. Therefore let us not allow that art, namely Optics, to be wanting in the literary commonwealth.

units.la: CAP. XXIII.
units.tr: CAP. XXIII.

units.la: De Musica.
units.tr: On Music.

units.la: AB Optica ad Musicam flexanimā semper ad excitandos & permul- cendos animos adhibitam, ad relaxa- tionem & remissionem animi, à gra- uioribus curis, comparatam transcea- mus. Nostra autem Musica explicat primum Sonos, deinde Modos.
units.tr: Having dealt with optics, we pass on to music, which is soul-bending and always used to stir and soothe the mind, and which is designed for relaxing and easing the mind from heavier cares.

units.la: In Sono consyderantur species & af- sectio.
units.tr: In sound, we consider its kinds and its affections.

units.la: Specie Sonus est Vnisonus & Dispar, qui rursum est Continuus vel Interruptus, qui rursus est Diaphonus, vt Ditonus & Semiditonus, vel Paraphonus, vt Diatessaron & Diapente, vel Antiphonus, vt Diapason, cuius diuisio est Harmonica & Arithmetica, vbi de intervallis & ordine dextro & sinistro, &c. Affectio Soni est in mensura, quæ considerat notas earumque differentias, & dimensiones, vt binariam, ternariam, seu triplam, &c.
units.tr: By kind, sound is either unison or dispar. The dispar sound is in turn continuous or interrupted, and again it is diaphonous, as ditone and semiditone, or paraphonous, as diatessaron and diapente, or antiphonous, as diapason. Its division is harmonic and arithmetic, where one treats of intervals and of order, right and left, etc. The affection of sound lies in measure, which considers the notes, their differences and dimensions, such as binary, ternary or triple, etc.

units.la: Modus Musicus est octaua, nempe quinta cum quarta connexa; huius considerantur tum species tum affectiones. Specie modus est Perfectus, vel Imperfectus.
units.tr: A musical mode is the octave, namely the fifth joined with the fourth. Both its kinds and its affections are considered. By kind, the mode is either perfect or imperfect.

units.la: Imperfectus est quarta aut quinta.
units.tr: The imperfect mode is the fourth or the fifth.

units.la: Quarta dicitur Tetrachordum, idque ordinarium vel extraordinarium, &c.
units.tr: The fourth is called the tetrachord, and this is either ordinary or extraordinary, etc.

units.la: Perfectus modus est ipsissima octaua, vbi de modis omnibus quatuordecim, &c.
units.tr: The perfect mode is the octave itself, where one treats of all fourteen modes, etc.

units.la: Apodeixis 24.
units.tr: Apodeixis 24.

units.la: Ars, quæ in hac molesta vita conducit ad recreationem, quæ est fessorum à laboribus iucunda cessatio; ad institutionem vitæ, quæ est morum disciplina, & affectuum moderatio: ad animi puriorem contemplationem templationem, nimirum ad veritatis inquisitionem, & ad affectuum scelerumque expiationem; denique ad laudes Dei concinendas: illa equidem hominum generi non est negligenda, sed singulari amore & studio discenda.
units.tr: Music is an art that in this troublesome life serves for recreation, which is the pleasant rest of those worn out by labours; for the ordering of life, which is the discipline of morals and the moderation of the passions; for purer contemplation of the mind, namely for the inquiry into truth, and for the expiation of the passions and of sins; and finally for singing the praises of God. Certainly it is not to be neglected by the human race, but is to be learned with singular love and zeal.

units.la: Atqui Musica ad illa quatuor summopere conducit, vti multis ostendit Ioannes Casus, qui in musicis laudibus est multus & pene effusus. Musica de seipsa loquens audiatur: Vinco, flecto, rego, cantu, dulcedine, plectro Dira, cruenta, feros, tartara, monstra, viros. Languentes releuo, morituros excito, mæstos Erigo, pallentes munio, vinco Deos.
units.tr: Now music contributes greatly to those four ends, as John Cassius shows at length, who is full, almost lavish, in praise of music. Let music be heard speaking for itself: "I conquer, I bend, I rule, by song, by sweetness, by the plectrum; I subdue the dire, the bloody, the wild, the infernal regions, monsters, and men. I relieve the languishing, I rouse the dying, I raise the sorrowful, I fortify the pale; I conquer gods."

units.la: Musica proinde hominum generi non negligenda, quod sæpe recreandum, instituendum, & affectuum moderatione regendum, cui sæpe res multæ operose sunt perquisitandæ, quod sæpe laudat Deum in sono tubæ, in Psalterio & Cithara, in tympano & chordis, in cymbalis bene sonantibus, & cymbalis iubilationis.
units.tr: Music, therefore, is not to be neglected by the human race, since it is often needed for recreation, instruction, and the regulation of the passions; for it often calls for many laborious inquiries; and it often praises God with the sound of the trumpet, with the psaltery and harp, with the timbrel and strings, with well-sounding cymbals, and with cymbals of jubilation.

units.la: CAP. XXIV.
units.tr: CHAPTER 24.

units.la: De Christiana Physica.
units.tr: On Christian Physics.

units.la: PHysicæ Christianæ fundamēta tria postulamus, Verbum sapientissimi Naturæ Architecti Dei, Veram Rationem, & non fallentem Experientiam. Expurgatas cupimus futiles & inutiles subtilitates, sublatos paganismos Dei verbo contradicentes.
units.tr: We lay down three foundations for Christian physics: the Word of God, the most wise Architect of nature; true reason; and experience that does not deceive. We wish to purge away futile and useless subtleties, and to remove the pagan notions that contradict the Word of God.

units.la: Physica autem hæc latissime patens, vniuersum mundum conditum sibi subiiciens,agit de rebus naturalibus,id est,natura, hoc est, vi & facultate à Deo rebus creatis indita, praeditis. Hæc autem, qua generalis, habet partes duas Pneumatologiam de spiritibus creatis, adeoque Angelographiam & (qua specialis) Somatologiā quæ explicat corporum naturam. Natura autem corporum explicatur generaliter & specialiter.
units.tr: This physics, which extends very widely and subjects the whole created world to itself, deals with natural things, that is, with nature, which is the power and faculty implanted in created things by God. In its general part it has two divisions: pneumatology, concerning created spirits, and with it angelography; and, in its special part, somatology, which explains the nature of bodies. The nature of bodies is explained both in general and in particular.

units.la: Generaliter corporum affectiones & qualitates Physicæ:
units.tr: In general: the affections and qualities of bodies, of physics:

units.la: Specialiter singula corporum naturalium genera & species exponuntur.
units.tr: In particular: the individual kinds and species of natural bodies are set out.

units.la: Vnde Somatologia agit aut de corporibus magis constantibus nimirum cœlestibus, vbi explicatur Ouranographia, doctrina de cœlo, & Astrologia, doctrina de astris eorumqj motu.
units.tr: Hence somatology deals either with the more permanent bodies, namely the heavenly ones, where ouranography, the doctrine of heaven, and astrology, the doctrine of the stars and their motions, are explained.

units.la: Huc refertur à nonnullis doctrina Sphærica Astrologiæ inseruiens, Gnomonica, Meteoroscopia, Theoriæ Planetarum, &c. Sed de his alibi. Aut agit de corporibus minus constantibus, & his quidem aut Primis, vulgo Simplicibus, aut inde ortis, vulgo Concretis.
units.tr: To this some refer the spherical doctrine that serves astrology, gnomonics, meteoroscopy, the theories of the planets, and so on. But of these elsewhere. Or it deals with less permanent bodies, and these either with the primary ones, commonly called simple, or with those arising from them, commonly called compound.

units.la: Corpora Simplicia Elementa sunt, quoquorum doctrina dicitur Stœcheolo- gia, cui subiicitur Geographia, &c. Hydrographia, &c. Ex Astronomiæ & Geographiæ coniunctione nascitur Cosmographia.
units.tr: Simple bodies are the elements, whose doctrine is called stoicheology, under which come geography, etc., and hydrography, etc. From the union of astronomy and geography arises cosmography.

units.la: Corpora orta seu concreta & elementata sunt aut inanimata, aut animata seu viuentia (licet metalla & mineralia quasi intermedium quid esse videantur, unde ars Metallica.)
units.tr: Bodies that arise, or are compound and elemental, are either inanimate or animate, that is, living. (Metals and minerals seem to be a kind of intermediate between these, whence the art of metallurgy.)

units.la: Inanima corpora sunt Meteora, & illorum doctrina dicitur Meteorologia.
units.tr: Inanimate bodies are meteors, and their doctrine is called meteorology.

units.la: Animata corpora viuentia sunt, eorumque doctrina dicitur Psychologia.
units.tr: Animate bodies are living, and their doctrine is called psychology.

units.la: Animata corpora sunt plantæ & animalia.
units.tr: Animate bodies are plants and animals.

units.la: Plantæ sunt corpora tantum vigentia & viuentia, seu vegetabilia, vt stirpes, doctrina hæc in genere Bitologia, sed in specie, Botanica vel Botanologia appellatur, vulgo Herbarium.
units.tr: Plants are bodies that merely grow and live, or vegetable things, such as stalks. This doctrine in general is called bitology, but in particular botany or botanology, commonly herbal lore.

units.la: Animalia sunt corpora vita & sensu prædita, eorumque doctrina dicitur Zoographia, vulgo Historia animalium.
units.tr: Animals are bodies endowed with life and sense, and their doctrine is called zoography, commonly the natural history of animals.

units.la: Animalia aut sunt Irrationalia, vt bruta, aut Rationalia, vt homines. Hic igiigitur tractatur Anthropologia, cuius partes sunt duæ, Humana Psychologia, de anima hominis, & Somatotomia ac Anatomica corporis humani.
units.tr: Animals are either irrational, such as the brutes, or rational, such as men. Here therefore anthropology is treated, which has two parts: human psychology, concerning the soul of man, and somatotomy and anatomy of the human body.

units.la: Huic Physicæ subordinatur Medicina, ars medendi, seu de valetudine, tum quæ est, conseruanda, tum quæ læsa vel amissa est, recuperanda.
units.tr: Subordinate to this physics is medicine, the art of healing, concerned with health: both with preserving it where it exists, and with recovering it where it has been impaired or lost.

units.la: Apodixis 25.
units.tr: Demonstration 25.

units.la: Nefarium ac scelestum est ei disciplinæ aspergere labem aut ociosæ inutilitatis, aut Dei gloriæ detrahentis impietatis; cuius scientia homini illiterato & literato affert pietatis augmentum, cognitionem scilicet Dei naturalem, summam & vtilitatem, & discendi necessitatem & veram iucunditatem.
units.tr: It is wicked and criminal to stain that discipline either with the blemish of idle uselessness or with the impiety of detracting from the glory of God. Its knowledge brings to the unlettered and the lettered alike an increase of piety: namely the natural knowledge of God, its chief use, the necessity of learning it, and its true delight.

units.la: Atqui Physicæ disciplina cognitio hominem deducit ad pietatis cultum, dum Deum conditorem naturarum contemplatio nobis intelligendum exhibet, & ex creaturis inuisibilia Dei, æterna scilicet eius maiestas, sapientia & potentia cognoscuntur: hæc adeo necessaria & vtilis est, vt liberalium artium, & manuariorum opificiorum studiosi ea care-re vtiliter nequeant. Nam vt primo eruditæ literaturæ officinam ingrediamur, ϑεραπαινα famulam nempe & ministram superiori & germanæ Philosophiæ inseruientem aspicite. An non Grammatici artifices artem docent sermonis & bene loquendi in vocibus cum simplicibus, tum coniunctis? At Physica sermonis naturam & vocis per sua instrumenta, lingua, palapalatum, fauces, pulmones, asperam arteriam, dentes & labia formationem erudite demonstrat. An non oratoria dicendi vis sententiarum figuris suis, animos auditorum commouet & perturbat, perfundit gaudio & moerore, inflammat ira & misericordia? At Physica quomodo hae animorum affectiones & concitationes fiant, sola aperit. An non item Rhetor, corporis in agendo motu & virili laterum inflexione, decentique (vt Quint. nominat) chironomia se moderari debet? Sed horum motuum instrumenta, musculos, neruos & tendones esse docet Physica: Hinc Cicero oratorem suum Physicorum experte esse no vult. An no rationis humanae ars est Logica? Sed qd Physica? Mentis & rationis vim explicat, quomodoq; suas in ratiocinando & iudicando functiones obeat, definit. Propaidias igitur philosophicae studiosus, naturae contemplatione vix poterit carere. Sed superior illa Philosophia, quam ϑαυμαν Plato appellat, prorsus suo decore & ornamentis denudata, nullam apud eruditos merebitur gratiam. Ethicam enim, cu in virtutum explicatione tota occupetur, eae vero pro duplici animae facultate bipartitae, aliae intelligetiae, aliae voluntatis exsistant; nunquam perfecte mete complecteris, nisi e fontibus Physicorum ipsius mentis, eiusque facultatis geminae intelligentiam hauseris. Optica etiam videndi rationem tradens intelligentiae tuae vim & notionem fugiet, si non Physiologica schola te erudierit, quid sit ipsa visio, quomodo fiat, an vifiuos radios extra oculum emittendo, an vero rerum fimulachra intus recipiendo. Quod fi porro ad supremas illas Academicarum disciplinarum conscenderis facultates, en primum Ars Medica ceu fobo- les matrem suam salutabit, osculabitur, vene- rabitur Physicam nostram: riuulus vnde fcatu- riit, limpidum agnoscet fontem suum, ex cu- ius dulcedine nisi Medicus riuuli illius (im- mensi dixissem pelagi) salsedinem temperare didicerit, id est, omnia ratione & arte adhibi- ta administrare nouerit (dum ex Physica mor- borum, rerumq; caeterarum naturalium cau- fas prospexerit) empiricus & agyrta, id est, prę- ftigiator & circulator circumforaneus saluta- bitur. Postea Iureconsultorum chorus multa- rum legum intelligentiam scholis refert phy- ficis acceptam: vt rationem, cur anno duode- cimo foemina, 14. vero masculus pubes de iure pronuntietur (foeminis enim plerunque eo anno menses fluere incipiunt, qui fluxus indicat, ipsas esse conceptioni aptas: dum enim menses fluunt, femen maturum & prolificum indicatur. In masculis etiam vis generandi tum maturuit, ac mouetur, siquidem sperma iusto calore excoctum & perfectum in suis vasis genitalibus contentum habent.) Item praesumptio illa de non edito foetu in lucem, mense nono, cur inconstans, & pro constitutione, vel foetus, vel naturae praegnantis, contingens sit. In sacrosancta demum Theosophia (quam loco primo nominare debuissem) salutis nostrae paedagoga & ministra, vix atque ne vix quispiam plurimorum spiritus sancti oraculorum suauem degustabit nucleum, sed rudis rudem mordere corticem cogetur, qui ad ea Physicæ cognitionem non attulerit. Moses enim in rerum Genesi totus admirandam spiritat naturæ explicationem, adeo vt Christianæ Physicæ autor Danæus Physicam generalem ex S. Literarum adytis plene peti posse affirmet. Deinde in Physico prato tot fragrantes similitudinum pulcerrimarum flores decerpti in sacrum Theologiæ Paradisum propagati sunt: vt sacrorum similium ex iis conscriptum librum Leuinus Lemnius promulgarit. Hinc est, quod nos Christus ad volatilia cœli, lilia agri, & fœnum, Salomon ad formicas, remittat. Quod Iobi dialogus multa de cœli reuolutionibus, astris, terra, mari, luce, ventis, pluuiis, tonitruis, fulminibus, niue, glacie: Item de animantibus, vt leonibus, capreis, ceruis, equo & Behemot, quem Elephantū multi putant, ac denique de Leuiathan maris vastissima bellua disceptet. Quid? quod admirandā hanc totius mundi fabricam Paulus Rom. 1. testetur mentem, obscuris & terrenis inuolutam latebris & tenebris ad cœlestia sublimiaque rapere, & quasi manu nos in Dei cognitionem ducere. Maximum ergo incrementum eruditionis, & ornamentum decoris ex Physicorum familia capere Literariam officinam manifesto constat. Hinc Manuariam illiberalium artium opificinam ingressi, si quam vim habeat in ea Physiologia, quamq; amplus eius sit vbi-que que vsus, explicare vellemus, dies nos defice-ret. Nihil nunc de Architectonica: nihil de Aurificina, & aliorum metallorû, item phar-macorum, officinis, quæ rerum sibi subiecta-rum exactam postulant cognitionem, dicam: sola autem vilatur Agricultura, in qua opifex cum fundi naturam, tum seminum bonitatem examinat, in arborû ac vitium putatione, ar-borû ipsarumq; fructuum vim exploratam ha-bet, herbarû vires & pecoris proprietate dig-noscit, ac in his omnib. administrandis, ex cer-tis cœli & elementorû signis temporû opportunitate colligit: vt meridiana luce clarius videre licet in Georgicis Virgilianis, quæ vere Physicam Agriculturæ vnicam arguunt administram. Hæc de vsu fructuque Physicæ: quam vero insatiabilis insit in explicatione naturæ ex cognoscendis rebus voluptas, non nisi speculatores venatoresq; naturæ norunt. Delitiæ enim artis huius tantæ sunt, vt non nisi ex extimo cœlo & à domiciliis nostris altissimo includi possint, vt quocunque te vertis, in Physicas delitias vestigia ponas & incurras, siue animo recum perlustres ætheriam illam & cœlestem mundi partem, vbi omnia sunt æterna, siue elementarem regionem, in aere meteora & volantes aues, in aqua natâtes pisces, in terra herbas & gradientes animantes, in intimis terræ visceribus metalla & lapides: ita satiabis te cognitis rerum naturis, vt omnibus rebus lôgissime Physicam cognitionem anteponas. Quantum etiam iucunditatis & delectationis fructum mens nostra inde capiat, vel hoc saltem docet, quod illud naturæ nostræ amicum & familiare sit, quod nos in rerum abstrusarum & scitu necessariarum cognitionem deducit: quandoquidem omnes scientiæ cupiditate rapimur. Scire autem quid aliud est, quam rerum causas, hoc est, ea quæ in hoc mundo sunt, & arti Physicæ subiecta penitus perspecta habere. In his quodammodo mens nostra, si interim pietatis Christianæ sale conspersa fuerit, acquiescit, & veluti in summo beatitatis gradu sistitur, ut recte cecinit Poeta: Felix, qui potuit rerum cognoscere causas. Tanto igitur cum vtilitatis amplissimæ, tum iucunditatis suauissimæ fructu, qui non ad studium Physiologicum amplectendum rapitur, qui colendum negat, is lumen rationis tollendum, hominibusque non amplius in mundo viuendum, seque cum ratione insanire, fateatur necesse est.
units.tr: Atqui the discipline of physics brings a man by its knowledge to the practice of piety, since the contemplation of God as the maker of natures is set before us to be understood, and from creatures the invisible things of God, namely his eternal majesty, wisdom and power, are known. This is so necessary and useful that students of the liberal arts and of the manual crafts cannot profitably do without it. For, to enter first the workshop of learned literature, look at the handmaid [θεραπαινα], namely the servant and minister serving the higher and true philosophy. Do not grammarians, as craftsmen, teach the art of speech and of speaking well, in simple and in compound words? Yet physics teaches learnedly the nature of speech and the formation of the voice through its instruments: tongue, palate, throat, lungs, windpipe, teeth and lips. Does not the power of oratory, with its figures of speech, move and disturb the minds of hearers, fill them with joy and sorrow, and inflame them with anger and pity? Yet physics alone reveals how these affections and agitations of the mind come about. Likewise must not the rhetorician moderate himself, in delivery, by the movement of the body, the manly bending of the sides, and a becoming gesture (as Quintilian calls it)? But physics teaches that the instruments of these motions are the muscles, nerves and tendons; hence Cicero does not want his orator to be ignorant of physics. Is logic not the art of human reason? But what of physics? It explains the power of mind and reason, and defines how it performs its functions in reasoning and judging. Therefore a student of propaedeutic philosophy will hardly be able to do without the contemplation of nature. But that higher philosophy, which Plato calls wonder [θαυμάζειν], stripped entirely of its grace and ornaments, will earn no favour among the learned. For ethics, which is wholly occupied in explaining the virtues, and these are divided into two according to the twofold faculty of the soul, some of the understanding and some of the will, you will never grasp perfectly unless you have drawn an understanding of the mind itself and its twofold faculty from the sources of physics. Optics too, in teaching the manner of seeing, will escape your grasp of its force and concept, unless the physiological school has taught you what vision itself is, how it happens, whether by emitting visual rays outside the eye or by receiving images of things within. If further you climb to those highest faculties of the academic disciplines, see: first the medical art, like a daughter, will greet her mother, kiss and venerate our physics. The rivulet whence it flows will recognise its clear spring. Unless the physician has learned to temper the saltiness of that rivulet (of the immense sea, I should have said) by its sweetness, that is, has known how to administer everything with reason and art, while he has looked into the causes of diseases and other natural things from physics, he will be greeted as an empiric and quack, that is, a charlatan and itinerant mountebank. Afterwards the choir of jurists brings to the schools its understanding of many laws, received from the teaching of physics: such as the reason why a woman is declared marriageable at twelve and a man at fourteen (for in women the menses generally begin to flow in that year, and this flow shows that they are then fit for conception: for while the menses flow, the seed is shown to be ripe and fertile. In males too the power of begetting then matures and is stirred, since they hold sperm cooked and perfected by due heat, contained in their genital vessels.). Likewise that presumption about a foetus not brought to light in the ninth month, why it is uncertain and may happen according to the constitution either of the foetus or of the pregnant nature. Finally, in sacrosanct theosophy (which I should have named first), the tutor and minister of our salvation, scarcely anyone, or hardly anyone, will taste the sweet kernel of the many oracles of the Holy Spirit; rather, whoever has not brought a knowledge of physics to them will be forced, as an untrained person, to bite the rind. For Moses, in the Genesis of things, breathes a wondrous explanation of nature throughout, so that Danaeus, the author of Christian physics, affirms that general physics can be fully sought from the sanctuaries of the Holy Scriptures. Then in the physical meadow so many fragrant flowers of most beautiful similitudes have been plucked and carried into the sacred paradise of theology, that Levinus Lemnius published a book of sacred similitudes drawn from them. Hence it is that Christ sends us to the birds of heaven, the lilies of the field and the grass, and Solomon to the ants. The dialogue of Job discusses at length the revolutions of the heavens, the stars, the earth, the sea, light, winds, rains, thunders, lightnings, snow and ice; likewise animals such as lions, roe-deer, stags, the horse, and Behemoth, whom many think to be the elephant; and finally Leviathan, the most vast beast of the sea. And what of it? Paul in Romans 1 bears witness that this admirable fabric of the whole world carries the mind, wrapped in obscure and earthly hiding-places and shadows, up to heavenly and lofty things, and as if by the hand leads us into the knowledge of God. Therefore it is manifest that the literary workshop draws the greatest increase of learning and ornament of beauty from the family of the physicists. Hence, if we wished to explain, on entering the manual workshop of the illiberal arts, what power physiology has in them and how wide its use is everywhere, the days would fail us. Now I will say nothing of architecture, nothing of the workshops of goldsmiths and of other metals, or of pharmacy, which demand an exact knowledge of the things subjected to them. But agriculture alone is taken up, in which the workman examines both the nature of the soil and the goodness of the seeds; in the pruning of trees and vines he has explored the power of the trees and of their fruits; he recognises the powers of herbs and the properties of livestock; and in managing all these things he gathers from the certain signs of the sky and the elements the right timing of the seasons. As may be seen clearer than midday light in the Georgics of Virgil, which truly prove physics to be the sole handmaid of agriculture. So much for the use and fruit of physics. But how insatiable is the pleasure in explaining nature and in knowing things, only observers and hunters of nature know.
