For the delights of this art are so great that they can be bounded only by the outermost heaven and the highest point from our dwellings. Wherever you turn, you may set your steps and run into physical delights, whether in mind you traverse that ethereal and heavenly part of the world, where all things are eternal, or the elemental region: in the air, meteors and flying birds; in water, swimming fish; on earth, herbs and walking animals; in the inner bowels of the earth, metals and stones. You will so satisfy yourself with the known natures of things that you will place physical knowledge far above all other things. How much fruit of enjoyment and delight our mind takes from it, this at least teaches: that it is a friend and familiar of our nature, leading us to the knowledge of hidden things that must be known, since all sciences seize us with desire. To know, however, is nothing other than to have the causes of things, that is, of those things that are in this world and subject to the art of physics, thoroughly perceived. In these our mind somehow rests, if meanwhile it has been seasoned with the salt of Christian piety, and is held as if on the highest step of blessedness, as the poet rightly sang: Happy is he who has been able to know the causes of things. Therefore whoever is not drawn to embrace the study of physiology, with so great a fruit of most ample usefulness and most sweet pleasure, and who denies that it must be cultivated, he must necessarily confess that he would have to extinguish the light of reason, that he should no longer live among men in the world, and that he is insane along with reason.

units.la: CAP. XXV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXV.

units.la: De Metaphysica Christiana.
units.tr: On Christian Metaphysics.

units.la: METAPHYSICAM Christianã emendatam, non atheismis & paganismis ignorantiæ & stoliditatis Ethnicæ conspurcatam expetimus, & à magno nostro expectamus Philosopho, ita cã delineante.
units.tr: We desire a Christian metaphysics, cleansed of the atheisms and paganisms of heathen ignorance and folly, and we look to our great Philosopher to sketch it thus.

units.la: Metaphysica est eorum communis doctrina, quæ sunt per altissimas causas & primas ma principia, seu est scientia entis, eaq; Vniuersalis, vel Particularis.
units.tr: Metaphysics is the common doctrine of those things which are known through the highest causes and highest principles, or it is the science of being, and this is either universal or particular.

units.la: Vniuersalis explicat de vniuersalissimis, seu sparsis per vniuersas disciplinas: diciturque Prima Philosophia, quę est scientia entis, qua ens.
units.tr: The universal part deals with the most universal things, that is, those spread through all the disciplines. It is called First Philosophy, which is the science of being insofar as it is being.

units.la: Huius affectiones communes, dicuntur Transcendentia, Verum, Bonum, Actus, Potentia, &c.
units.tr: Its common attributes are called the Transcendentals: True, Good, Act, Potency, etc.

units.la: Gradus & quasi species Entis sunt Substantia & Accidens.
units.tr: The degrees, as it were the kinds, of being are substance and accident.

units.la: Substantia est Independens vel Dependens. Accidens est, &c. Vide praedicamenta.
units.tr: Substance is either independent or dependent. Accident is, etc. See the predicaments.

units.la: Particularis scientia Entis Metaphysica seu transnaturalis est, quae explicat de parte aliqua Entis, nempe transnaturali. Et quidem primum de Deo, deinde de Mentibus.
units.tr: The particular science of being, metaphysics or the transnatural science, explains a certain part of being, namely the transnatural. And first it treats of God, then of minds.

units.la: Hic Deum explicari volunt, quatenus naturali lumine rationis cognosci potest, quae quidem licet sit manca & insufficiens ad salutem: tamen (si removeatur aberrantium gentium lapsus) vera esse potest, si Dei & ipsius rei veritati respondeat: adeoque hic nihil impietatis esse potest.
units.tr: Here they want God to be explained as far as He can be known by the natural light of reason. This light, though it is weak and insufficient for salvation, can nonetheless be true (if the error of the straying Gentiles is removed) provided it corresponds to God and to the truth of the thing itself. Therefore there can be nothing impious here.

units.la: Mentes quas Metaphysica explicat, sunt Angeli seu intelligētiȩ: Hic Pneumatologia spirituum creatorū, qui sunt à materia sensili & corporea abiunćti, locum habere potest. Sed spirit*uum veritati, quatenus hic fas scire, conueniens: vel animę hominum per se tantum consideratæ.
units.tr: The minds that metaphysics explains are angels or intelligences. Here a pneumatology of created spirits, who are separated from sensible and corporeal matter, can have its place, but only insofar as it is lawful and fitting to know them here. Or it may concern the souls of men considered in themselves alone.

units.la: Hæc Methaphysica, si fuerit recte informata, nō debebat à nonnullis, qui à sacris sunt Deo, flagellari & diris devoueri, diabolicæque ac Turcicæ impietatis accusari: lapsibus Ethnicorum condonent.
units.tr: If this metaphysics were rightly ordered, it should not have been scourged and cursed by some who are dedicated to God and accused of diabolical and Turkish impiety; let them pardon it for the lapses of the Gentiles.

units.la: Antiqui nostri eam prædicarūt esse instar aquilæ; Solis fœtum dixerunt; Nubilorum perruptricem: Scientiarū apicem & culmen: Solam esse liberam, nulli subiectam, ceteras scientias huic subiectas.
units.tr: Our forebears proclaimed it to be like an eagle; they called it the offspring of the Sun, the piercer of clouds, the summit and crown of the sciences, the only one that is free, subject to none, while the other sciences are subject to it.

units.la: CAP. XXVI.
units.tr: CAP. XXVI.

units.la: De Christiana Ethica & Politica.
units.tr: On Christian Ethics and Politics.

units.la: BAsin Ethicæ nostræ collocamus, Dei verbum & legem moralem, legem naturæ, sanam & rectam rationem, piam honestatis & morum experientiam.
units.tr: We lay the foundation of our Ethics in the Word of God and the moral law, the law of nature, sound and right reason, and the pious experience of honesty and good morals.

units.la: Ethica est doctrina bene viuendi. Eique propositȧ est vitæ honestas, integri-tegritegritas, sanctitas, ad eius felicitatem & beatitudinem.
units.tr: Ethics is the doctrine of living well. Its aim is an honest life, integrity and holiness, for the sake of its happiness and blessedness.

units.la: Partes eius duę sunt, Aretologia specialiter dicta Ethica & Politica. Illa docet interiorem animi rectitudinem & informationem per virtutes.
units.tr: Its two parts are Aretology, specifically so called, which is Ethics, and Politics. The former teaches the inner rectitude of the mind and its formation through the virtues.

units.la: Virtus est recta animi affectio bonarum & honestarum actionum effectrix. Est que tota in dilectione interiore & exteriore.
units.tr: Virtue is a right disposition of the mind, producing good and honourable actions. It consists wholly in inner and outer love.

units.la: Virtus est erga Deum, vel erga hominem.
units.tr: Virtue is directed either towards God or towards man.

units.la: Erga Deum virtus dicitur Dilectio Dei Theologis in genere, & Pietas, quæ est interna tantum, vt Dei agnitio & Timor, &c. vel externa simul vt invocatio, petitio, gratiarum actio, iuramentum, confessio, &c.
units.tr: Towards God, virtue is called by theologians in general the love of God, and piety. Piety is purely internal, such as the knowledge and fear of God, etc., or it is also external, such as invocation, petition, thanksgiving, oath, confession, etc.

units.la: Erga hominem est dilectio sui ipsius vel proximi.
units.tr: Towards man, virtue is love of oneself or of one's neighbour.

units.la: Erga se ipsum virtus, est prima vel coniuncta.
units.tr: Towards oneself, virtue is either primary or joined.

units.la: Prima vires hominis sanctitate & integritate particulariter informat: & quidē intellect<bl>9</bl> est vel voluntatis virtus.
units.tr: The primary virtue forms the powers of man in particular by holiness and integrity; and it is a virtue either of the intellect or of the will.

units.la: Intellectus dicitur Dianoetica vt sapientia & prudentia.
units.tr: The virtue of the intellect is called dianoetic, such as wisdom and prudence.

units.la: Voluntatis virtus dicitur Moralis instruit struit nos interna & externa rectitudi-ne.
units.tr: The virtue of the will is called moral; it instructs us in inward and outward rectitude.

units.la: Interna moderatur affectus, vel animum ad magna animat.
units.tr: The inward part moderates the affections, or spurs the mind on to great things.

units.la: Moderatrix affectuum est Temperantia & Modestia. Temperantia frænat voluptates & cupiditates.
units.tr: The moderators of the affections are temperance and modesty. Temperance bridles pleasures and desires.

units.la: Estque continentia & parsimonia.
units.tr: It is both self-restraint and frugality.

units.la: Continentia est in sobrietate & in castitate.
units.tr: Self-restraint lies in sobriety and chastity.

units.la: Modestia est in mansuetudine & humilitate.
units.tr: Modesty lies in gentleness and humility.

units.la: Virtus animum ad magna animans est animositas, seu fortitudo, cuius species sunt magnanimitas & patientia.
units.tr: The virtue that spurs the mind on to great things is high spirit, or fortitude, whose species are magnanimity and patience.

units.la: Internarum virium sic fuit per virtutes informatio: Externa est in morum moderatione, & dicitur ciuilitas, estque in sermone & gestu.
units.tr: Thus the formation of the inner powers through the virtues. The outer part lies in the moderation of conduct, and is called civility; it concerns speech and gesture.

units.la: In sermone faciendo vel continendo.
units.tr: Concerning speech, whether in speaking or in refraining from it.

units.la: Faciendo, ut comitas & urbanitas. Continendo, ut taciturnitas.
units.tr: In speaking, such as courtesy and urbanity; in refraining, such as taciturnity.

units.la: In gestu iuniorum dicitur verecundia, adultiorum dicitur decens gravitas.
units.tr: In gesture, in the young it is called modesty, and in adults it is called becoming gravity.

units.la: Coniuncta virtus hominis erga se est sui notitia & sui amor.
units.tr: The virtue of man joined to himself is self-knowledge and self-love.

units.la: Hæc de virtute hominis erga seipsum: virtus erga alios homines seu proximum, est Humanitas vel Iustitia.
units.tr: So much for the virtue of man towards himself. Virtue towards other men or one's neighbour is Humanity or Justice.

units.la: Humanitas est virtus officiola Benevolentiæ, vel Beneficentiæ.
units.tr: Humanity is the dutiful virtue of goodwill or beneficence.

units.la: Benevolentia est Generalis vel Specialis, quæ dicitur amicitia, eaque est Socialis vel Naturalis, aliis politica. Beneficentia est item varia, &c.
units.tr: Goodwill is general or special; the special kind is called friendship, and it is either social or natural, and for others political. Beneficence is likewise of various kinds, etc.

units.la: Iustitia est virtus cuiq; suum ex debito tribuens, estque Distributiua vel Commutatiua.
units.tr: Justice is the virtue that gives each person what is due to him, and it is either distributive or commutative.

units.la: Hæc de Ethica: Politica docet vitā politicam seu ciuilem in societate. Cuius partes sunt, Particularis & Vniuersalis.
units.tr: So much for Ethics. Politics teaches political or civil life in society. Its parts are particular and universal.

units.la: Particularis docet partes, id est, societates, ex quibus politicum cōstituitur corpus.
units.tr: The particular part teaches the parts, that is, the societies, of which the political body is made up.

units.la: Estque Familia aut Collegium.
units.tr: These are the family or the college.

units.la: Familiæ societas dicitur Oeconomia. Cuius tum est cōstitutio, tum administratio.
units.tr: The society of the family is called economics (household management). It has both a constitution and an administration.

units.la: Constitutio fit ex triplici iugo, coniugali, patrio & herili.
units.tr: The constitution arises from a threefold yoke: conjugal, paternal, and that of master and servant.

units.la: Administratio cōtinet 1. officia œconomica, 2. rei familiaris dispensationē.
units.tr: The administration contains (1) the economic duties and (2) the management of household property.

units.la: Collegium deinde est sacrū vel profanum, &c.
units.tr: Next, the college is either sacred or profane, etc.

units.la: Vniuersalis pars politicæ est de Repub.& Ciuitate, cuius item partes sunt duæ Constitutio & Administratio Reip. Constitutio fit ex magistratibus & subditis. Vbi de magistratus constitutione ordinaria vel extraordinaria. Administratio constitutæ Reip. Vbi primum de virtutibus & conditionibus boni magistratus ad officiorū executionē. 2. de consilio & administris ac consiliariis adiunctis. 3. de subditis eorumque conditionibus. 4. Species administrationis duæ, togata & bellica.
units.tr: The universal part of politics concerns the commonwealth and the state, and its parts are likewise two: the constitution and the administration of the commonwealth. The constitution arises from magistrates and subjects; here we treat of the ordinary or extraordinary constitution of magistracy. Administration of the established commonwealth: here, first, of the virtues and qualities of a good magistrate for the performance of his duties; second, of counsel, and of the attendants and counsellors who are joined to him; third, of subjects and their conditions; fourth, the two species of administration, civil and military.

units.la: Togata est Religiola vel Ciuilis.
units.tr: Civil administration is either religious or civil.

units.la: Bellica dicitur polemica, cuius item partes sunt iusta belli susceptio, & prudens belli administratio.
units.tr: Military administration is called polemic, and its parts are likewise the just undertaking of war, and the prudent conduct of war.

units.la: Species vniuersæ politiæ restant, scilicet Monarchia, & Polyarchia: & hæc quidem est Aristocratia vel Democratia.
units.tr: The remaining species of polity are monarchy and polyarchy; and polyarchy is either aristocracy or democracy.

units.la: Apodeixis 26.
units.tr: Apodeixis 26.

units.la: Ars quæ profitetur ex lege Dei & natura secundum rectam rationem, vitæ sanctitatem, morum honestatem, & virtutum decus ac officia, quæ omni ætati, omnibus hominibus, sua officia, quæ quid eis conueniat, legitime præscribit: quæ est optima & verissima animi cultura, actiones hominis vniuersas moderans, quæ denique iustitiæ est moderatrix, adeo adeoque Iurisprudentiæ ceu legum cunctarum scien-tiæfons & origo, illa equidem omni Christiano per-utilis & perquam necessaria.
units.tr: An art which, from the law of God and nature according to right reason, professes the sanctity of life, the honesty of morals, and the beauty and duties of the virtues; which legitimately prescribes to every age and to every person their duties and what is fitting for them; which is the best and truest cultivation of the mind, governing all the actions of man; which, in short, is the regulator of justice, and therefore the fountain and origin of jurisprudence, the science of all laws. Such an art is indeed most useful and altogether necessary to every Christian.

units.la: Atqui Ethica Christiana est eiusmodi ars, quæ profitetur doctrinam bene viuendi secundum legem Dei & naturæ, secundum morum & virtutum ho-nestatem, secundum rectam & regenitam rationem. Hæc excolit cum primis istam legem, de qua Paul. ad Rom. 1. nempe quam homines scriptam habent in cordibus suis. Hæc ars fundamentum & basis est Iurisprudentiæ, qua vitæ humanæ societas regitur & conseruatur. Hæc qui infi-ciatur, Christianam Ethicam legat, & intelli-gat & postea iudicet. Ergo, &c.
units.tr: But Christian Ethics is an art of this kind, which professes the doctrine of living well according to the law of God and nature, according to the honesty of morals and virtues, and according to right and regenerate reason. It especially cultivates that law of which Paul speaks in Romans 1, namely, which men have written in their hearts. This art is the foundation and basis of jurisprudence, by which human society is governed and preserved. Let whoever denies this read Christian Ethics, understand it, and then pass judgment. Therefore, etc.

units.la: Conclusio.
units.tr: Conclusion.

units.la: Cuius omnes partes sunt bonæ & vtiles, quarum-que partium bona est constitutio, ex ordine certo-rum documentorum exercitatione cognitorum ad vtilem vitæ finem: id ipsum totum bonum sit ne-cesse est. Atqui omnes & singulæ Philosophiæ hu-manæ partes & artes bonæ & vtiles, earumque con-stitutio & coniunctio est bona & vtilis. Vt hacte-nus est demonstratum. Tota igitur Philosophia humana ex artium liberalium comprehensione con-flata est bona & vtilis. Si bona, Væ illi, qui bo-num dicit malum.
units.tr: Each of its parts is good and useful, and the good constitution of those parts, arising from the orderly exercise of known precepts toward a useful end of life, must itself be a whole that is good. But all and each of the parts and arts of human philosophy are good and useful, and their constitution and combination is good and useful. As has been demonstrated so far. Therefore the whole of human philosophy, made up of the comprehension of the liberal arts, is good and useful. If it is good, woe to him who calls good evil.

units.la: Si bona, cur lacerat conuiciis Philosopho-mastix? Si bona, abusus quid nocebit rei bonæ? Malus ille, qui optima re & dono Dei pessi-me abutitur. Malus & ille, qui bonæ per se rei maledicit.
units.tr: If it is good, why does the scourge of philosophers tear it with insults? If it is good, what harm can abuse do to a good thing? He is wicked who most wickedly abuses the best thing, a gift of God; he too is wicked who curses what is good in itself.

units.la: Hactenus veræ Philosophiæ assertio & demonstratio.
units.tr: So far the assertion and demonstration of true philosophy.

units.la: OTHONIS CAS-MANNI PHILOSOPHIÆ Christianæ Pars posterior à vera Philosophia calumnias depellens.
units.tr: The Second Part of the Philosophy of Otto Casmann, Refuting the Calumnies Against Philosophy from True Philosophy.

units.la: QVi Philosophiæ bellum indicunt, vt vndique conflant seditiones & certamina serunt, ita aduersus Philosophiam, quam malitioso ignorantiæ odio premunt, ex rusticis & aliis male armatis, copias in fraudem dispositas, contrahunt; leuis etiam armaturæ militem, modo nomen suum queat profiteri, cogunt; vt ita numerosa manu coacta, in S. Philosophiæ perniciem coniurante, eam adoriantur, & terribilibus sepeq; monstrosis cum eius cultoribus contendant armis, eosque ex viuentium consortio tollant.
units.tr: Those who declare war on philosophy, just as they stir up seditions and sow strife on every side, so against philosophy, which they oppress with malicious hatred born of ignorance, they gather forces deceitfully arranged, drawn from rustics and others poorly armed. They also compel soldiers of light armour, provided only they can declare their name, so that with a numerous band assembled, conspiring to destroy holy philosophy, they may attack it and contend with its devotees with terrible and often monstrous weapons, and remove them from the company of the living.

units.la: Bellum autem, quod armis suscè ptis infertur Philosophiæ est vniuersale, aut particulare.
units.tr: The war waged against philosophy with arms taken up is either universal or particular.

units.la: Vniuersale bellum arma insana mouet in vniuersum Philosophiæ corpus: huius belli duces & velites, vt sunt audaciores, ita impudentiores.
units.tr: A universal war sets insane weapons in motion against the whole body of philosophy. The leaders and skirmishers of this war are as bold as they are shameless.

units.la: Vniuersalis belli arma depromun-tur ex armamentario partim autorita-tis, partim rationis. Agnosce igitur vi-tulam tuam Philosophiam, ô inique Philosophomastix; arare non posses, nisi hac vitula arares, & sulcos agro Philosophico induceres. Tanta Philo-sophiæ virtus est, vt impugnari neque-at, nisi ipsa etiam (ô quam æqua & be-nigna) ipsis hostibus impugnandi vires concedat: Hæc sine se impugnatur à nullo: Erubescitque, qui sine Philoso-phia, Philosophiæ resistere conatur.
units.tr: The weapons of a universal war are drawn from the armoury partly of authority, partly of reason. Recognise, then, your calf, O unjust scourge of philosophy: you could not plough unless you ploughed with this heifer and drew furrows in the philosophical field. Philosophy has such virtue that it cannot be attacked unless, in her goodness and fairness, she herself grants to her very enemies the strength to attack her. She is attacked by no one without her; and he is put to shame who tries to resist philosophy without philosophy.

units.la: Autoritas partim est sacra & diuina, partim humana & profana. Ex sacræ & diuinæ autoritatis armamentario ex-torquentur sequentia male fabrefacta arma.
units.tr: Authority is partly sacred and divine, partly human and profane. From the armoury of sacred and divine authority the following badly made weapons are wrested.

units.la: I. Classis arma diuinæ autoritatis capientium contra Philoso-phiam.
units.tr: I. The first class: weapons of divine authority taken up against philosophy.

units.la: Elenchus Sophismatis 1. ex Epistola ad Coloss. 2. vers. 8. con-torti.
units.tr: Objection (sophism) 1, twisted from the Epistle to the Colossians 2:8.

units.la: Videte, ne quis vos depræ-detur per Philosophiam, & inanè deceptio-nem, iuxta traditionem hominum, iux-ta ta elementa mundi, & nō iuxta Chri-stum.
units.tr: "See to it that no one spoils you through philosophy and empty deceit, according to the tradition of men, according to the elements of the world, and not according to Christ."

units.la: Responsio.
units.tr: Answer.

units.la: Hic Philosophia simpliciter neutiquam damnatur, de qua nos loquimur. Proinde ad Syllogismi prouocamus tribunal.
units.tr: Here philosophy, of which we are speaking, is not condemned simply and in any way. Therefore let us summon them to the tribunal of the syllogism.

units.la: Quidam captant vocem, Cauete; quidam vocem, Depraedetur, alii Inanem deceptionem arripiunt. Videamus primos: Sed heus constitua-tur quaestio suis limitata terminis. Quaeritur, an Christiano fas sit & vtile Philosophia nauare suam operam, praecipue vero ei, qui est a sacris? Affirmamus. Negant Aphilosophi. Fiat dianoia.
units.tr: Some seize on the word "Beware"; some on the word "spoil"; others snatch at "empty deceit." Let us look at the first. But come, let the question be set out, limited by its own terms. The question is: "Is it lawful and profitable for a Christian to devote his labour to philosophy, and especially for one who is set apart for sacred things?" We affirm. The unphilosophical deny. Let the argument be set out.

units.la: Quod cauendum est Christiano, id discere eidem fas & vtile non est. At Cauenda est Christiano Philosophia iussu & auctoritate D. Pauli. Ergo Philosophiam discere Christiano neque fas neque vtile est.
units.tr: "What a Christian must beware of, it is neither lawful nor profitable for him to learn. But a Christian must beware of philosophy by the command and authority of St Paul. Therefore it is neither lawful nor profitable for a Christian to learn philosophy."

units.la: Nego Subsumptum. Paulus enim non dicit, Cauete vobis a Philosophia; sed cauete ne quis vos depraedetur per Philosophiā: Cauēda est itaque depraedatio, quae fit per Philosophiam. At inquis: Per quod fit depraedatio, illud ipsum est fugiendum. At depraedatio fit per Philosophiam. Ergo Philosophia est fugienda.
units.tr: I deny the minor premise. For Paul does not say, "Beware of philosophy," but "Beware lest anyone spoil you through philosophy." Therefore what must be avoided is the spoiling that is done through philosophy. But you object: "That through which the spoiling is done must itself be fled from. But the spoiling is done through philosophy. Therefore philosophy must be fled from."

units.la: Propositionem distinguimus, per quod fit depraedatio, scilicet ita, vt id ipsum in se vel ex se habeat depraedandi vim: alioquin si aliunde scabies illa ipsi affricetur, non tam idipsum, quam eius scabies est fugienda. Effectus enim, qui causae est peregrinus, & alienae facultatis, ipsam causam vt non laudat, sic neque vituperat.
units.tr: We distinguish the major premise, "that through which the spoiling is done": namely, in such a way that the thing itself has the power of spoiling in itself or from itself. Otherwise, if that filth is rubbed on it from elsewhere, it is not so much the thing itself as its filth that must be avoided. For an effect which belongs to a cause but comes from a foreign power does not praise the cause, and so neither does it blame it.

units.la: Sic igitur repono par: Per verbum sacris literis scriptum (non ausim dicere Dei, quia verbum Dei ἐνοπτᾶς νοούμενον non est Dei verbum) multi Sophi-staeetiamnum hodie in tanta Euangelii luce multos deprædantur. Ergo verbum illud fugiendum. Male dicis intellectum & vsurpatum verbum Dei? Et ego dico, Philosophiam & male intellecta, & male vsurpatam.
units.tr: So I answer the parallel thus: "Through the word written in the sacred letters (I would not dare to say 'of God', because the word of God understood [ἐνοπτᾶς νοούμενον] is not the word of God), many sophists even today, in so great a light of the Gospel, spoil many people. Therefore that word must be avoided." Do you say that the word of God is misunderstood and misused? And I say the same of philosophy, both misunderstood and misused.

units.la: Tribuatur itaque effectus quilibet suæ causæ, quæ proprie per se agit, & quod est productum vi aliena, non tribuatur ei, cuius vi facti nihil est. Philosophia proprie in se non habet vim deprædandi; deprædatio itaque non fit vi Philosophiæ, sed eius, qui Philosophia abutitur ad deprædandum alios, pro eo ingenio, quo ipse ex depravata natura sua pollet. Verbum Dei etiam deprædatur etiamnum quosdam, & in nassam errantium præcipitat, at non qua verbum Dei, sed qua verbum eius, qui eidem affingit deprædantem vim & malum sensum. Caveamus itaque depraedationem Sectariorum & male feriatorum hominum, qui Philosophia abusi deprædantur homines, amemus sanctum sanæ Philosophiæ vsum. Caveamus verbi diuini malas contorsiones, animarum humanarum pessimas depraedatrices, caveamus abusum optimi verbi, optimæ rei; amemus vt vsum ita rem ipsam & verbum optimum.
units.tr: Let every effect be attributed to its own cause, which acts properly through itself; and what is produced by a foreign power is not to be attributed to that thing by whose power nothing has been done. Philosophy properly has in itself no power of spoiling; the spoiling is therefore not done by the power of philosophy but by that of the one who abuses philosophy to spoil others, according to the talent which he himself possesses from his depraved nature. The word of God too still spoils some people and throws them into the net of the erring; yet it does so not as the word of God but as the word of the one who attaches to it a spoiling power and a bad sense. Let us therefore beware of the spoiling done by sectaries and idle men, who spoil people by abusing philosophy; let us love the holy use of sound philosophy. Let us beware of the wicked distortions of the divine word, the worst spoilers of human souls; let us beware of the abuse of the best word and the best thing; let us love the thing itself and the word, as we love its use.

units.la: Verbum deprædari, qui captant sic argutantur: tur: Quod nos depraedatur est Christiano fugien-dum. Philosophia nos depraedatur. Ergo fugienda.
units.tr: Those who seize on the word "spoil" argue thus: "What spoils us is to be avoided by a Christian. Philosophy spoils us. Therefore it is to be avoided."

units.la: Respon. Propositio loquitur de eo, quod sua facultate depraedatur. Assumptio vero de eo, quod aliena vi depraedatur. Apostolus enim dicit: Per Philosophiam depraedari, non vero ipsam Philosophiam nos depraedari.
units.tr: Answer: The major premise speaks of that which spoils by its own power; the minor, of that which spoils by a foreign power. For the apostle says "to be spoiled through philosophy," not "philosophy itself spoils us."

units.la: Sed heus, tibi si dicerem: Caue ne quis te per vinum seducat ad illicitos amores. Hinc nunquid argutabere; Per quod quis seduci potest, hoc fugiendum. Per vinum autem seduci potest homo. Ergo vinum fugiendum? Aliud vinum per se bonum, aliud vini abusus, qui inebriat, cuius inebrietationis vi saepe homo accensus libidinis flamma seducitur. Vt itaque seductio non optimo Dei dono vino per se debetur, ita nec depraedatio optimo Dei dono Philosophiae, tanquam causa per se agenti tribui debet. Profecto si verum fateri licet, nullum Dei donum est vel excellentissimum, cuius abusus non possit pessima ex se (abusus dico) progignere mala. Imo, quo donum caelitus concessum est praestantius, eo eius abusus est perniciosior.
units.tr: But come, if I were to say to you, "Beware lest anyone lead you astray through wine into unlawful loves," would you not then argue: "That through which someone can be led astray must be avoided. But a man can be led astray through wine. Therefore wine must be avoided"? Wine in itself is good; the abuse of wine, which intoxicates, is another matter, and by the power of that intoxication a man, kindled by the flame of lust, is often led astray. Just as, therefore, the leading astray is not owed to wine, the best gift of God, in itself, so neither should the spoiling be attributed to philosophy, the best gift of God, as to a cause acting through itself. Indeed, if it is lawful to speak the truth, no gift of God is so excellent that its abuse cannot itself produce the worst evils. Nay, the more excellent the gift granted from heaven, the more harmful its abuse.

units.la: Deinde distinguas quaeso Philosophiam Ethnicam ab ea, quam hodie Christiana pietas Scholis delegauit. Quid Philosophiam dico, imo Philosophiae (per se bonae) intrusa peccata non a se sibi, sed ab ignaris sanae & sanctae fidei ac religionis, adeoque a veritatis via propter animi miserandas tenebras exorbitantibus importata. Agnoscat Theologus suae Theologiae iam etiam, pro pudor, immiscerí monstrosa & impia impii cerebri figmenta; hæc dubio procul non suæ dabit Philosophiæ, hoc est, Theosophiæ; quo iure igitur in pari causa tenebitur Philosophus?
units.tr: Next, please, distinguish the pagan philosophy from that which Christian piety today has assigned to the schools. I say philosophy; nay, errors thrust into philosophy (which is good in itself) not by itself but by the ignorant of sound and holy faith and religion, and so carried away from the way of truth by the pitiable darkness of their minds. Let the theologian acknowledge that, for shame, monstrous and impious fancies of an impious brain are now mixed into his own theology. Without doubt these will not be given to his philosophy, that is, his theosophy; by what right, then, will the philosopher be held liable in a like case?

units.la: Qui vrgent inanem deceptionem, ita argutantur:
units.tr: Those who press "empty deceit" argue thus:

units.la: Quod est inanis deceptio, id fugiendum est. Philosophia est inanis deceptio. Ergo fugienda.
units.tr: "What is empty deceit must be avoided. Philosophy is empty deceit. Therefore it must be avoided."

units.la: Respon. Inuertimus argumentum. Inanis deceptio est hominum depraedatrix. Sophistica est propriæ inanis deceptio. Sophistica igitur est hominum depraedatrix, de qua Paulus loquitur. Iam vero ipsis confitentibus & Aristotele & Platone Sophistica non est Philosophia, vt nec Sophista Philosophus. Videris Sophisticam meam. Ergo vera Philosophia non est vt inanis deceptio, sic nec hominum depraedatrix. Aliud interim fatemur esse insanam & deceptricem Philosophiam, quam non dignamur eius sancto nomine; aliud vero esse sanam & Christianam Philosophiam veritatis, sapientiæ & pietatis sedulo studiosam. Sed & ita argumentamur: Cui idem est in eodem loco Philosophia & inanis deceptio, is ibidem de vera Philosophia, eiusque vero vsu non loquitur, aut enim agit de vana Philosophia, aut de vera Philosophia abusu, aut de vtroque simul. At, vt plerique exponunt, Paulo in hoc loco idem est Philosophia & inanis deceptio. Ergo non loquitur de vera Philosophia bene vsurpata: sed aut de vana & insana Philosophia, aut de vera abusu, aut de vtroque. Idem Apostolus etiam verf. 4. dixerat pari sensu πΗ vitandam, non quidem simsimpliciter: Est enim S.quoque literis sua πα- Φανολογία, sed notanter, ne quis sermone vos circumueniat: quasi dicat, παραλογίζεσθαι πιθανολογία tantum damnanda & cauēda est. Hinc & sic colligere liceat: Per quod, seu quo, quis potest circumueniri, id damnandum est per se. At per sermonem & πιθανολογίαν, seu sermone, potest quis circumueniri. Ergo sermo per se damnandus, & πιθανολογία est cauenda omnis. At conclusio haec falsa est. Ergo aut propositio aut assumptio habet vitium: Estque neganda aut distinguenda. Assumptio est Pauli, at non simplici intellectu. Sermone persuadente, potest quis circumueniri, at non omni, sed aliquo, scilicet falsum suadente, non ipsa per se persuasione sermonis, sed abusu. Vnde & propositio est accipienda cum distinctione, per se & per accidens. Quid? quod quosdam ita interpretari videam: Ne quis vos deprædetur per Philosophiam deceptione inani. Et sane non est obscurum Apostolum loqui de eorum Philosophia, quæ oppressa tristi in multis caligine in summis rebus hallucinatur & Deo aduersatur, quæque nisi sanata diuinitus, & captiuata in obedientiam fidei fuerit, cœca fiducia sui deprædatur seipsam salutari instauratione oblata in Euangelio. Ita deprædabantur se & alios, eius ætatis Ethnici Philosophi, qui quod explosis sectis cæteris Platonis atque Aristotelis Philosophiam interpretantes vtramque coniungerent, Platonicos se nominabant; quique odio Christiani nominis, idolatricos cultus gētilium deorum, & illa portenta opinionum Philosophicarum mordicus retinere malebant, quam absurdæ & stultæ concioni Apostolorum accedere: quibus omnis doctrina Ecclesiæ, de lapsu & reparatione generis humani, de mediatore & promissione Euangelii, &c. stultitia visa est & dementiæ plena. Eadem ratione etiam nostræ ætatis ingeniosi Philosophi Aristultelici in scholis exteris, qui inter certamina Ecclesiæ, in extremam coniecti impietatem, ita tractant profanam & paganam Philosophiam, ut religio eis sit, à Philosophiæ paganismis & erroribus, ad diuinam Scripturæ veritatem discedere, ne parum Aristotelici videantur. Ab huius Philosophiæ inani & pagana deceptione omnibus cauendum apertis tibiis clamamus. Cauendum etiam veræ Philosophiæ Sophisticum abusum docemus. Et Apostolum de Pseudophilosophia ac sanæ Philosophiæ perniciosò abusu locutum omnes fere interpretes testantur, tum veteres tum recentiores.
units.tr: Answer. We turn the argument round. "Empty deceit is a spoiler of men. Sophistry is, properly speaking, empty deceit. Therefore sophistry is the spoiler of men, of whom Paul speaks." Now, since both Aristotle and Plato themselves confess that sophistry is not philosophy, so a sophist is not a philosopher either. You see my sophistry. Therefore true philosophy is not, like empty deceit, a spoiler of men. Meanwhile we admit that one thing is a mad and deceiving philosophy, which we do not honour with its holy name; but another thing is sound and Christian philosophy, diligently devoted to truth, wisdom and piety. But we also argue thus: "Whoever in the same passage treats philosophy and empty deceit as the same does not speak in that place of true philosophy or of its true use; for he either speaks of vain philosophy, or of the abuse of true philosophy, or of both at once. But, as most interpreters explain, for Paul in this place philosophy and empty deceit are the same. Therefore he does not speak of true philosophy rightly used, but either of vain and mad philosophy, or of its abuse, or of both." The same apostle, in verse 4, had said in the same sense that persuasive speech [πιθανολογία] is to be avoided, not simply indeed (for there is also a persuasive eloquence in the sacred letters), but with a warning, lest anyone deceive you with speech. As if he were saying that false reasoning [παραλογίζεσθαι] by persuasive speech [πιθανολογία] alone is to be condemned and avoided. Hence it may also be inferred in this way: "That through which, or by which, someone can be deceived must be condemned in itself. But someone can be deceived through speech and persuasive speech. Therefore speech is in itself to be condemned, and all persuasive speech is to be avoided." But this conclusion is false. Therefore either the major premise or the minor has a fault, and it must either be denied or distinguished. The minor premise is Paul's, but not in a simple sense. Someone can be deceived by persuasive speech, but not by every speech, only by some, namely that which persuades to falsehood; the fault lies not in the persuasion of speech in itself but in its abuse. Whence the major premise also is to be taken with a distinction, between what is in itself and what is by accident. What more? I see some interpreting it thus: "Lest anyone spoil you through philosophy by empty deceit." And certainly it is not obscure that the apostle is speaking of the philosophy of those who, oppressed by sad darkness in many matters, go astray in the highest things and oppose God, and who, unless healed by God and brought into obedience to faith, spoil themselves by blind confidence, refusing the saving restoration offered in the Gospel. Thus the pagan philosophers of that age spoiled themselves and others, who, having cast off the other sects and interpreting Plato and Aristotle, joined the two together and called themselves Platonists; and who, out of hatred of the Christian name, preferred to cling stubbornly to the idolatrous worship of the gentile gods and those monstrous philosophical opinions, rather than come to the absurd and foolish preaching of the apostles, to whom the whole doctrine of the Church about the fall and restoration of mankind, about the mediator and the promise of the Gospel, and so on, seemed foolishness and full of madness. By the same reasoning also the clever Aristotelian philosophers of our own age in the foreign schools, who, amid the conflicts of the Church, have been driven into the extremes of impiety, handle profane and pagan philosophy in such a way that they think it a matter of conscience to depart from the pagan errors of philosophy to the divine truth of Scripture, lest they should seem not Aristotelian enough. Against the empty and pagan deceit of this philosophy we cry out to all, with arms and legs wide open, that they must beware. We also teach that one must beware of the sophistical abuse of true philosophy. And nearly all interpreters, both ancient and recent, testify that the apostle spoke of pseudo-philosophy and of the pernicious abuse of sound philosophy.

units.la: Ex veteribus Augustinus lib. de moribus Ecclesiæ cap. 21. hunc locum citans ita interpretatur, ut dicat Apostolum caute loqui, ne ab amore sapientiæ deterrere videatur; ideo addi, per Elementa mundi. Theophilactus ob id addi inanem fallaciam putat. Idem colligi potest ex commentariis Hieronymi in hunc locum.
units.tr: Among the ancient writers, Augustine, citing this passage in his book On the Morals of the Church, ch. 21, interprets it to mean that the Apostle speaks cautiously, so as not to seem to deter people from the love of wisdom; for this reason, he says, the words through the elements of the world were added. Theophylact thinks that for this reason the words empty deceit were added. The same can be gathered from Jerome's commentaries on this passage.

units.la: Ex recentioribus iam occurrit 1. Flac. Illyricus in tractatu de ratione cognoscendi 5. lit. ubi ait Paulum non tantum de Pseudophilosophia (quam & nos vt sophisticam abominamur) sed & de vera Philosophia abusu & impostura loqui (quæ scilicet impostura est male abutentium vera Philosophia.) Deinde sic attexit:
units.tr: Among the more recent writers, the first to appear is 1. Flacius Illyricus, in his treatise on the method of knowing, at the fifth passage, where he says that Paul speaks not only of pseudo-philosophy (which we too abominate as sophistry) but also of the abuse and deception of true philosophy (this deception, clearly, being the work of those who misuse true philosophy). He then adds the following:

units.la: Nec tamen fanaticos homines sequi, quasi humanæ scientiæ sint prorsus inutiles aut etiam noxiæ ad cognitionem S. literarum & doctrinæ cœlestis: oportet enim discere linguas & eruditas Grammaticas. Vtilis ac plane etiam necessaria est Dialectica & Rhetorica, & reliquæ Philosophiæ cognitio, &c.
units.tr: Yet we should not follow fanatical men, as if human learning were altogether useless, or even harmful, for the knowledge of the holy letters and of heavenly doctrine. For one must learn languages and the learned grammars. Dialectic and rhetoric are useful and indeed quite necessary, and so is knowledge of the rest of philosophy, etc.

units.la: Moses Pflacherus in præfat. Anal. Typ. ait Paulum improbare vanum fallendi artificium & laqueos sophisticos & ἀπατηλὰς, quos nectere solebant hæretici, vt iis pios & orthodoxos decipérent, quod ita (ait) esse, non solum ipsa contextus Apostolici series, sed etiam vocabulum ἀπάτης a Paulo vsurpatum manifeste declarat.
units.tr: Moses Pflacherus, in the preface to his Analysis Typica, says that Paul condemns the empty art of deceiving, and the sophistical snares and deceptive [ἀπατηλὰς, apatēlas] devices, which heretics were accustomed to weave in order to deceive the pious and orthodox with them; that this is so (he says) is clearly shown not only by the sequence of the Apostle's argument, but also by the word deceit [ἀπάτης, apatēs], which Paul uses.

units.la: Nicolai Hemmingii in hunc Pauli locum commentationem eruditæ veritatis plenam adscribere placet.
units.tr: I am pleased to add the commentary of Nicolaus Hemmingius on this passage of Paul, a commentary full of learned truth.

units.la: Quemadmodum, inquit, perperam faciunt, qui hoc loco abutuntur ad damnandam vniuersam Philosophiam, quæ revera excellens donum Dei est: ita damnatur hoc dicto Pauli, qui ex corrupta Philosophia ecclesiæ Christi vllum dogma obtrudere tentant tanquam in negotio salutis necessarium. Vna est doctrina salutaris de cœlo allata, quæ continet omnes thesauros sapientiæ & cognitionis salutaris.
units.tr: Just as, he says, those act wrongly who in this passage misuse it to condemn all philosophy, which is in truth an excellent gift of God, so this saying of Paul condemns those who try to force on the Church of Christ any dogma from corrupted philosophy as if it were necessary to salvation. There is one saving doctrine, brought down from heaven, which contains all the treasures of wisdom and of saving knowledge.

units.la: Verum quemadmodum olim populus Israeliticus ad exstructionem tabernaculi vsus est opibus AEgyptiis: ita nos quoque sciamus vsurpandas esse Philosophiam. sophia vera partes, non ad destruendam Ecclesiam, sed ad ei destruendum. Etsi igitur solum verbum Dei salutare est hominibus, interea tamen non sunt contemnenda alia Dei dona, quae non parum suo quodam modo ad aedificationem Ecclesiae faciunt. Quis quaeso phrases scriptura intelligat sine Grammatica? quis partes longioris orationis? quis disputationum seriem? quis argumentorum virtutes percipiat, artis dialecticae rudis? An non Paulus in Episcopo requirit, ut sit aptus ad docendum, ut possit recte secare verbum Dei? quod fieri non posse sine Dialectica nemo non videt? An no pulcerrima ex Rhetorica lumina passim in scriptis Prophetarum & Apostolorum conspiciuntur, quae sine Rhetorica & schematum cognitione minime explicari possunt? Quam multa dicta sunt in Prophetis, Psalmis & scriptis Apostolicis, quae sine rerum naturalium usu intelligi nequeunt? An non vera Ethica pars legis divinae est? Unde oeconomica, & politicae leges, quas Deus non vult contemni, extructa sunt? In mathematis excelluisse veteres patriarchas non est dubium, in quibus Paulum quoque fuisse liberaliter institutum, vel ex eo apparet, quod contra Graecos ipsos Arati Astrologi testimonio sit usus. Qui Mosen legit, Arithmeticam & Geographiam agnoscet summe necessarias esse ad multorum locorum explicationem. David, Iob, Ieremias, ac multi alii sancti viri Musica delectati sunt. Cum igitur omnes partes Philosophiae sint utiles & eximia Dei dona, sacrilegii genus est, Philosophiam in universum damnare, qua ut utiliter uti possimus, seruemus sequentes regulas.
units.tr: But just as the people of Israel once used the wealth of the Egyptians for the building of the tabernacle, so we too should know that philosophy is to be used. True philosophy has the part of building up the Church, not of destroying it. Although, therefore, the word of God alone is saving for human beings, nevertheless the other gifts of God are not to be despised, for in their own way they contribute no little to the building up of the Church. Who, I ask, can understand the phrases of Scripture without grammar? Who can grasp the parts of a longer discourse? Who can perceive the sequence of disputations, or the force of arguments, if he is untrained in the art of dialectic? Does not Paul require in a bishop that he be apt to teach, so that he can rightly divide the word of God? That this cannot be done without dialectic, no one fails to see. Do not the most beautiful lights of rhetoric appear everywhere in the writings of the prophets and apostles, which can by no means be explained without rhetoric and knowledge of the figures of speech? How many things are said in the Prophets, the Psalms and the apostolic writings which cannot be understood without the use of natural things? Is not true ethics a part of the divine law? And from where were the laws of household management and of politics drawn up, which God does not wish to be despised? There is no doubt that the ancient patriarchs excelled in mathematics, and that Paul too was liberally educated in them is evident even from the fact that he used the testimony of Aratus, an astrologer, against the Greeks themselves. Whoever reads Moses will recognise that arithmetic and geography are highly necessary for the explanation of many places. David, Job, Jeremiah and many other holy men delighted in music. Since, therefore, all parts of philosophy are useful and outstanding gifts of God, it is a kind of sacrilege to condemn philosophy in general. In order to use it profitably, let us observe the following rules.

units.la: Prima, sit verbum Dei lidius lapis, ad quem exami-minenminentur, probentur, improbentur Philosophorum dicta. Aristoteles docet, Mundum ab æterno fuisse, sed hoc dictum ad scripturam examinatum, falsum esse conuincitur. Quare, non vera Philosophia axioma, sed philosophantis error iudicetur. Idem, vnam rerum omnium primam causam, nempe Deū ipsum rationibus Physicis demonstrauit, quæ demonstratio, quia congruit cum verbo Dei, amplectenda est & approbanda. Iuxta hanc regulam, sanctus Iustinus Philosophus & martyr multas sententias examinat, probat, improbat, potissimum in libro, cui titulus est ἀνατροπή, id est, euersio quorundam Aristotelicorum dogmatum. Item in libro ad Triphonem Iudæum. Item in libro contra Græcos Philosophos.
units.tr: First, let the word of God be the touchstone by which the sayings of the philosophers are examined, approved or rejected. Aristotle teaches that the world has existed from eternity, but when this saying is examined by Scripture, it is shown to be false. Therefore it is to be judged not a axiom of true philosophy but an error of the philosopher. Likewise, he demonstrated by physical arguments that there is one first cause of all things, namely God himself; this demonstration, because it agrees with the word of God, is to be embraced and approved. In accordance with this rule, the holy philosopher and martyr Justin examines, approves and rejects many opinions, chiefly in his book whose title is Anatropē [ἀνατροπή], that is, the overthrow of certain Aristotelian doctrines. Likewise in his book to Trypho the Jew, and likewise in his book against the Greek philosophers.

units.la: Secunda, adhibeatur Philosophia rerum sacrarum explicationi, non vt domina, sed vt ministra, quæ authoritati verbi Dei cedat. Sic Grammatica, Dialectica, Rhetorica, cæteraque Philosophiæ partes suo fungantur ministerio.
units.tr: Second, philosophy should be employed in the explanation of sacred things, not as mistress but as servant, yielding to the authority of the word of God. Thus grammar, dialectic, rhetoric and the other parts of philosophy should perform their ministry.

units.la: Tertia; quoties verbum Dei aliquid, quod absurdum in Philosophia videtur, commemorat, Philosophia se humiliet, agnoscat suam cæcitatem, corrigatur cœlestis Philosophiæ admonitione, & non quasi obtorto collo in suam sententiam verbum cœleste trahat. Recte enim Orpheus, vt citat Iustinus martyr, omnibus mortalibus mortales palpebræ in oculis imbecilles, ad videnda ea, quæ ad omnium rerum curatorem pertinent.
units.tr: Third: whenever the word of God mentions something which seems absurd in philosophy, philosophy should humble itself, acknowledge its own blindness, be corrected by the admonition of heavenly philosophy, and not drag the heavenly word into its own opinion as if by force. For Orpheus, as Justin Martyr cites him, rightly said that the eyelids of mortals are weak in the eyes of all mortals for seeing those things which pertain to the governor of all things.

units.la: Quarta: Omnia philosophorum dicta, quæ cum verbo Dei pugnāt, vt vt plausibilia rationi videtur, reiiciantur ac damnentur, tanquam cœlestis Philosophiæ sophia præsentissimum venenum. Rectissime enim monuit Hilarius, sensum scripturis non esse inferendum, sed e scripturis petendum.
units.tr: Fourth: all sayings of the philosophers which fight against the word of God, however plausible they may seem to reason, are to be rejected and condemned, as the most dangerous poison of the wisdom of heavenly philosophy. For Hilary rightly warned that a meaning is not to be brought into the Scriptures, but to be sought from the Scriptures.

units.la: Quinta: Decreta Philosophorum, quæ non pugnant cum verbo, si demonstrationes aut probabiles rationes habent, recipiatur ac amentur, idq; maxime, si ad rerum conservationem, aut ad mores formandos faciunt.
units.tr: Fifth: The decrees of the philosophers which do not fight against the word, if they have demonstrations or probable reasons, are to be received and loved, especially if they serve the preservation of things or the forming of morals.

units.la: Sexta: Exemplis & dictis Philosophicis utatur Theologus prudenter, hoc enim interdum fieri potest valde utiliter, quia exempla & dicta congruentia cum verbo sæpe vehementiores stimulos habent. Sic Salomon pigrum ad formicam mittit, ut ab ea discat sapientiam. Dominus nos ad serpentes & columbas mittit, ut ab illis prudentiam, ab his simplicitatem discamus. Thiresias parochus Thebanus, tametsi Ethnicus, tyranno minanti sibi exitium, eo quod vera quidem sed non placentia diceret, respondit: Veritatem te o Tyranne fortiorem alo. Hoc exemplum non incommode adduci posset ad animandos Christi ministros, ut constantes sint in docenda & defendenda veritate. Simili modo Physica exempla ciconiarum, halcyonum &c. sumi possunt in commendationem pietatis erga parentes & benemeritos.
units.tr: Sixth: The theologian should use philosophical examples and sayings prudently, for this can sometimes be done very usefully, because examples and sayings agreeing with the word often have more powerful spurs. Thus Solomon sends the sluggard to the ant, that he may learn wisdom from her. The Lord sends us to serpents and doves, that we may learn prudence from the one and simplicity from the other. Tiresias, the Theban seer, although a heathen, when a tyrant threatened him with death because he said things that were true but unwelcome, replied: "I nourish a truth stronger than you, O tyrant." This example could fittingly be adduced to encourage the ministers of Christ, that they may be steadfast in teaching and defending the truth. In a similar way, physical examples, such as those of storks, halcyons and so on, can be drawn upon in commendation of piety towards parents and benefactors.

units.la: In reprehensionem exemplum viperarum Ioannes & Christus obiecerunt Iudaeis. Ad eundem modum axiomata Philosophorum utiliter adhiberi possunt: quale est illud Platonis: Deus omnium bonorum αἴτιος & malorum omnium ἀναίτιος est. Sicut Paulus interdum Philosophorum dicta aspergit, ut ad Tit. 1. Epimenidis. 1. Cor. 15. Menandri. Act. 17. Arati testimonia adducit. Licet enim undique mutuari, quod àDeo profectum est.Has regulas sequutus Theo-logus, sentiet non inutilem sibi fore Philosophiam veram. Quare Philosophiæ studium ab omnibus bo-nis amandum censeo, ac necessarium iudico inprimis iis, qui in maioribus facultatib. in Medicina, Iurisprudentia & Theologia cum fructu versari cupiunt. Verum id sobrie fieri velim. Nam, qui vitam omnē in Ethnicis scriptis consumunt, gentiles ad postremum euadunt, nec ferunt se postea verbo Dei corrigi: imo contemnunt verbum, ac se cateris sapientiores impudenter prædicant, adeo vt à conuitiis, quoties occasio datur, abstinere non possint. Non igitur patrocinatur hic Pauli locus Philosophiæ contemptoribus, sed iis tantum, qui eam intra suos terminos, & quasi intra suum circulum manere non sinunt. Non enim proprie hic accipitur Philosophiæ nomen, sed pro acumine hominum, qui fallaciter illa ad decipiendum abutebantur, id quod satis conuincit praesentis loci peristasis. Quod enim supra per πιϑανολογίαν, idem hic per Philosophiam & inanem fraudem iuxta traditionem hominum, quæ abducit à Christo, intelligit. Retineatur igitur Philosophia & ametur. Hactenus Hemmingius. Alius quidam male propitius Philosophus ita sophisticatur:
units.tr: As a rebuke, John and Christ used the example of vipers against the Jews. In the same way, the axioms of the philosophers can be usefully employed; such is that saying of Plato: God is the cause [αἴτιος, aitios] of all good things and free from blame [ἀναίτιος, anaitios] for all evils. Just as Paul sometimes sprinkles in the sayings of philosophers, as in Titus 1 (Epimenides), 1 Cor. 15 (Menander), and Acts 17 (he adduces the testimony of Aratus). For since anything true, from whomever it comes, is from God, it is lawful to borrow from every quarter. A theologian who follows these rules will find that true philosophy will not be useless to him. Therefore I think the study of philosophy should be loved by all good men, and I judge it necessary above all for those who wish to engage profitably in the higher faculties of medicine, jurisprudence and theology. Yet I would have this done soberly. For those who spend their whole life on heathen writings end up as heathens, and afterwards cannot bear to be corrected by the word of God; indeed they despise the word, and shamelessly proclaim themselves wiser than others, to such an extent that they cannot refrain from insults whenever an occasion is given. This passage of Paul therefore does not lend support to the despisers of philosophy, but only to those who do not allow it to remain within its own bounds, as if within its own circle. For the name of philosophy is not taken here in its proper sense, but for the keenness of men who misused it fallaciously for deceiving; the context of the present passage sufficiently proves this. For what above he understood by persuasive speech [πιθανολογίαν, pithanologian], here he understands by philosophy and empty deceit according to the tradition of men, which leads away from Christ. Let philosophy therefore be retained and loved. Thus far Hemmingius. Some other rather ill-disposed philosopher reasons sophistically as follows:

units.la: Depraedatores hominum per inanem fallaciam, sunt cauendi & è scholis eliminandi.
units.tr: Plunderers of men through empty deceit must be guarded against and removed from the schools.

units.la: Philosophi sunt depraedatores hominum & praecipue iuuentutis per inanem fallaciam.
units.tr: Philosophers are plunderers of men, and especially of young people, through empty deceit.

units.la: Philosophi igitur sunt cauendi & ex scholis eiciendi.
units.tr: Philosophers, therefore, must be guarded against and cast out of the schools.

units.la: Subsumptum negamus: Philosophi enim, qua Philosophi, non sunt depraedatores hominum: Sunt enim e sui natura & iure officii veritatis & sapientiae studiosi, ut supra vidimus.
units.tr: We deny the minor premise. Philosophers, as philosophers, are not plunderers of men. By their nature and the proper duty of their office they are lovers of truth and wisdom, as we have seen above.

units.la: Qui autem depraedatur, per inanes fallacias depraedatur. At hic est Sophista, qui fallacias proprie nectit & decipulas struit.
units.tr: But whoever plunders does so through empty deceits. Now this man is a sophist, who properly weaves deceptions and sets snares.

units.la: Philosophus autem non est Sophista, neque Sophista Philosophus, nisi apparens & simulator. Huic igitur Sophistae reponamus parem conclusiunculam:
units.tr: A philosopher, however, is not a sophist, and a sophist is not a philosopher, except in appearance and pretence. So let us answer this sophist with a similar little syllogism:

units.la: Depraedatores hominum per inanes fallacias sunt cauendi. At Theologi nonnulli sunt hominum depraedatores per inanes fallacias. Ergo Theologi nonnulli sunt cauendi.
units.tr: Plunderers of men through empty deceits must be guarded against. Some theologians are plunderers of men through empty deceits. Therefore some theologians must be guarded against.

units.la: At, inquis, concedo assumptum, de Theologis iis, qui sunt falsi Doctores & sophistomanias morbo diuexantur, non autem de sinceris.
units.tr: But you will say: I concede the minor premise, but only of those theologians who are false teachers and are troubled by the disease of sophistic madness, not of the sincere ones.

units.la: Recte sane, & nos tuum assumptum amplectimur, si de nonnullis accipis Nomine, non Re Philosophis, qui sunt Sophistae & titulo Philosophiae superbiunt. Sicut hi Theologi tibi sunt Mataeologi: ita & isti Philosophi nobis sunt Sophistae. Sicut abutitur Mataeologus verbo Dei ad seductionem: ita Sophista Philosophiae decretis, sed falsatis, abutitur ad decipiendum. At probas assumptum.
units.tr: Quite right, and we accept your minor premise, provided you take it of some who are philosophers in name only, not in fact, who are sophists and pride themselves on the title of philosophy. Just as these theologians are, to you, mata-theologians, so those philosophers are, to us, sophists. As the mata-theologian abuses the Word of God for seduction, so the sophist abuses the doctrines of philosophy, though falsified, to deceive. But you prove the minor premise.

units.la: Per Philosophiam agentes sunt Philosophi.
units.tr: Those who act through philosophy are philosophers.

units.la: At depraedantes per inanem fallaciam agunt hoc per Philosophiam. Ergo depredatores per inanem fallaciam sunt Philosophi.
units.tr: But those who plunder men through empty deceit act through philosophy. Therefore plunderers of men through empty deceit are philosophers.

units.la: Propositio vera est, quatenus per Philosophiam & ex eius recte formato decreto & consilio agunt: quatenus vero per eius abusum, à veritate rei & Dei discedentem, vel per paganismos Ethnicorum Philosophorum, qui non sunt sanæ Philosophiæ decreta, vel per propria cerebri phantasiam & inique iudicantem affectum agunt, non sunt Philosophi, quia non agunt per Philosophiam, qua Philosophia est. De his igitur assumptum Pauli intelligimus. Et hoc reponimus: Per Theologiam agentes sunt Theologi, scilicet sanam non corruptam. At depredates gregè per inanes fallacias agunt per Theologiam scilicet corruptam, depravatam, seu per praetextum verbi Dei aut non recte intellecti, aut adulterati. Ergone depredantes abusu Theologiæ gregem tibi sunt Theologi, an vero Mathologi?
units.tr: The major premise is true insofar as they act through philosophy, and in accordance with its rightly formed doctrine and counsel. Insofar as they act through its abuse, a departure from the truth of the matter and from God, or through the paganisms of the heathen philosophers, which are not the doctrines of sound philosophy, or through the fancy of their own brains and a passion that judges unjustly, they are not philosophers, because they do not act through philosophy as philosophy is. It is of these men, then, that we understand Paul's minor premise. And we answer thus: Those who act through theology, namely sound and uncorrupted theology, are theologians. But plunderers of the flock who act through empty deceits act through theology that is corrupt and depraved, or under the pretext of the Word of God either misunderstood or adulterated. Therefore, do plunderers of the flock who abuse theology count as theologians for you, or rather as mata-theologians?

units.la: Elenchus Sophismatis 2. ex Epistola 1. ad Cor. cap. 1. & 2.
units.tr: Refutation of the Second Sophism, from the First Epistle to the Corinthians, chapters 1 and 2

units.la: Scriptum est enim: Abolebo sapientiam sapientum, & intelligentiam intelligentium tollam è medio. Vbi sapiens? Vbi scriba? Vbi disquisitor seculi istius? Nonne infatuauit Deus sapientiam mundi huius? &c.
units.tr: For it is written: I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and I will bring to nothing the understanding of the prudent. Where is the wise? Where is the scribe? Where is the disputer of this world? Hath not God made foolish the wisdom of this world? etc.

units.la: Responsio.
units.tr: Answer.

units.la: Nihil quicquam hic audimus Philosophiam à Paulo damnari.
units.tr: We hear nothing here at all about Paul condemning philosophy.

units.la: M
units.tr: M

units.la: At extrui fulmen damnatorium ex verbis Pauli contendunt.
units.tr: But they contend that a thunderbolt of condemnation has been built from the words of Paul.

units.la: Sed videamus fabricam inde extructam, & iudicemus.
units.tr: But let us look at the structure built from it, and judge.

units.la: Sapientia quae a Deo perditur, aboletur & infatuatur, ut Theologia ita & scholis Christianis est perniciosa.
units.tr: The wisdom that is destroyed and made foolish by God is pernicious to theology, and likewise to Christian schools.

units.la: At Philosophia est illa sapientia, quae a Deo tollitur, aboletur & infatuatur.
units.tr: But philosophy is that wisdom which is taken away, destroyed and made foolish by God.

units.la: Ergo Philosophia est ut Theologia perniciosa, ita & Scholis Christianorum exitiosa.
units.tr: Therefore philosophy is pernicious to theology, and likewise destructive to the schools of Christians.

units.la: Haec est illa extructa fabrica in Philosophiae perniciem. Sed assumptio syllogismi conflictatur cum falsitate insigni. Philosophia quidem est amor & studium sapientiae. Sed non eius, quam Deus proprie dicitur aboliturus in Iesaia & sublaturus e medio, & infatuasse: neque eius, quae depraedatur & inanis est deceptio: sed sapientiae verae, scientiae & intelligentiae rerum divinarum & humanarum verae. Et hanc dissipiendam nouimus a falsa & simulata sapientia, de qua hic agit Paulus, quae rebus tum divinis, tum humanis non est conveniens, sed aberrat ratiocinatione inani & sophistica. Sapientiae illius studiosa est Philosophia nostra, quae rectae rationis regulam sectatur, non eam, quae pravae & corruptae dictamen audit.
units.tr: This is the structure built for the ruin of philosophy. But the minor premise of the syllogism clashes with a notable falsehood. Philosophy is indeed the love and pursuit of wisdom. But it is not that wisdom which God is said properly to destroy in Isaiah, and to take away and make foolish; nor is it that empty and plundering deception; it is true wisdom, the true knowledge and understanding of divine and human things. We know that this wisdom is different from the false and feigned wisdom of which Paul speaks here, which is not fitting either to divine or to human things, but goes astray through empty and sophistical reasoning. Our philosophy is a pursuer of that wisdom; it follows the rule of right reason, not the reasoning that hears the dictates of a corrupt and depraved mind.

units.la: Non autem Apostolum loqui de vera Philosophia, seu sapientia Philosophica, quam ipse efficit, ostendo ex analysi disputationis Paulinae. Quaestio est de schismatibus Corinthiorum.
units.tr: That the Apostle is not speaking of true philosophy, or of philosophical wisdom which he himself produces, I show from an analysis of Paul's argument. The question concerns the divisions among the Corinthians.

units.la: Horum exponit oblique procreantem cau- sam, nempe vanitatem tum ambitiosorum do- ctorum, qui affectabant sapientiae & eloquen- tiae laudem: tum stultorum auditorum, qui ista in doctoribus admirabantur, & propter iu- diciorum de istis rebus diuersitatem in partes & factiones scindebantur, iis nempe Doc to- ribus singuli adhaerentes, quos ceteris sapien- tia atque eloquentia praestare iudicabant. Ho- rum igitur omnium & Doctorum & audito- rum, vanitatem perstringit Apostolus, negat- que se euangelizasse cum sapientia sermonis (non tamen quauis) id est, negat se more mundanorum oratorum solicitum fuisse de verbis atque sententiis, quibus orationem su- am redderet exornatam & probabilem. Affert autem rationem huius sui facti: ne scilicet inanis redderetur crux Christi, hoc est, ne doctrina de cru- ce Christi euanesceret & sine fructu audiretur. Dū enim animus intentus est ornamentis orato- riis, vt vel delectet dicendo, vel delectetur au- diendo, negligitur interim nucleus doctrinae, in quem solum animus est intendendus & Do- ctori & auditori: vel sic intelligi potest: ne Euan- gelio crucis Christi adimatur proprius effectus sci- licet fides, eaque adscribatur docentium eloquen- tia.
units.tr: He indirectly sets out the cause that produced them, namely the vanity both of the ambitious teachers, who sought the reputation of wisdom and eloquence, and of the foolish hearers, who admired such things in their teachers and were split into parties and factions because of their differing judgments about these matters, each adhering to those teachers whom they judged to surpass the rest in wisdom and eloquence. Paul, then, censures the vanity of all of them, both teachers and hearers. He denies that he preached the gospel with excellence of speech (though not with any kind of speech), that is, he denies that, like worldly orators, he was anxious about words and sentences by which he might make his discourse ornate and persuasive. He gives, however, the reason for this his conduct: lest the cross of Christ should be made void, that is, lest the doctrine of the cross of Christ should fade away and be heard to no effect. For while the mind is intent on oratorical ornaments, so that it either delights in speaking or delights in hearing, the kernel of doctrine is meanwhile neglected, and this is the one thing to which the mind of both teacher and hearer ought to be directed. Or it may be understood thus: lest the proper effect of the gospel of the cross of Christ, namely faith, be taken from it, and ascribed to the eloquence of the teachers.

units.la: Hinc sequuntur duae prolepses. Prior est: At sermo crucis est stultitia. Respondet Paulus. Non est per se stultus, sed iis videtur stultus, qui non credunt ei & pereunt: Quia nobis credentibus est potentia Dei. Posterior: At homines sapientes, erudiri, & periti stultitiam æstimant. Respondet Paulus. Esto sint sapientes secundum mundum, sed quia Dei sapientiam, quæ in Euangelio patefit, contemnunt, propter veram sapientiam contemptū à Deo infatuabuntur: idque probat testimonio Iesaiæ, &c. Hinc sic argumentamur:
units.tr: From this follow two prolepses. The first is: But the word of the cross is foolishness. Paul replies: It is not foolish in itself, but it seems foolish to those who do not believe it and perish. For to us who believe it is the power of God. The second is: But wise men, the learned and the skilled, reckon it foolishness. Paul replies: Granted they are wise according to the world, yet because they despise the wisdom of God revealed in the gospel, they will be made foolish by God on account of the true wisdom they have despised. And he proves this by the testimony of Isaiah, etc. From this we argue thus:

units.la: Ea sapientia à Deo aboletur & infatuatur, quæ est mundi, & quæ sapientiam Dei in Euangelio patefactam contemnit.
units.tr: That wisdom is destroyed and made foolish by God which belongs to the world and despises the wisdom of God revealed in the gospel.

units.la: At vera Philosophia non est eiusmodi sapientia. Primum non est mundi, quia mundus sapit ex carne & iudicio corruptæ & depravatæ rationis, de diuinis & spiritualib. carnaliter iudicat. Sapientia Philosophiæ nō est carnis seu carnalis, iudicans de spiritualibus carnaliter, neque sequitur rationem corruptam sed rectam. Licet Philosophi multi carnales & mundani sint, & habeant corruptam rationem: Non tamen sequitur, ipsam Philosophiam propterea esse carnalē, mundanā & corruptæ rationis sapientiam.
units.tr: But true philosophy is not such a wisdom. First, it is not of the world, because the world judges by the flesh and by the judgment of a corrupt and depraved reason, and judges fleshly things about spiritual matters. The wisdom of philosophy is not of the flesh or fleshly, judging spiritual things carnally, nor does it follow a corrupt reason but a right one. Although many philosophers are carnal and worldly and have a corrupt reason, it does not follow that philosophy itself is for that reason carnal, worldly, and a wisdom of corrupt reason.

units.la: Instat aliquis: Quales sunt Philosophi, talis est Philosophia.
units.tr: Someone objects: Such as the philosophers are, such is philosophy.

units.la: At Philosophi sunt mundani, carnales, & depravatæ mentis.
units.tr: But the philosophers are worldly, carnal, and of a depraved mind.

units.la: Ergo & ipsa Philosophia talis est.
units.tr: Therefore philosophy itself is such too.

units.la: Respon. Propositio nō est vera per se. Nam à qualitate concreti ad qualitatem abstracti, ideo non valet consequentia, quia plus est in cōcreto, nempe subiectum cum forma, quam in abstracto. Iam qualitas ex parte subiecti, vt hominis, non continuo est qualitas ex parte formæ, vt Philosophi qua talis. Neque etiam ex artificis qualitate est æstimandum ipsum artificium seu ars. Deinde si ex assumpto fiat reflexio iudicii de propositione; propositio erit particularis sic: Quales sunt multi Philosophi, talis est Philosophia. At multi sunt mundani & carnales: Assumptio alioqui non erit generaliter vera. Non enim omnes Philosophi sunt mundani & carnaliter affecti seu non renati: Et in orbe Christiano sunt Philosophi, iique veri. Sed heus: Quales sunt Theologi, talis Theologia. At sunt Sophistæ avari & contentiosi. Ergone talis tua Theologia? Dices recte qualitatem Theologi, ut hominis maleferiati, non efficere qualitatem Theologia. Dicam & ego recte; qualitatem Philosophi, tanquam hominis profani, non inferre qualitatem ipsi Philosophiæ. Tu si distinguis inter Theologum & mataeologum, distinguam & ego inter Philosophum Ethnicum & Christianum. Hæc de membro primo.
units.tr: I answer: the major premise is not true in itself. For the inference from the quality of a concrete thing to the quality of an abstract thing is invalid, because there is more in the concrete, namely the subject together with its form, than in the abstract. Now the quality on the part of the subject, as of a man, is not always the quality on the part of the form, as of a philosopher as such. Nor is the artifice itself or the art to be judged by the quality of the craftsman. Next, if the judgment is reflected back from the minor premise upon the major, the proposition will be particular, thus: Such as many philosophers are, such is philosophy. But many are worldly and carnal. The minor premise, otherwise, will not be generally true. For not all philosophers are worldly and carnally disposed, or unregenerate; and in the Christian world there are philosophers, and true ones. But look: Such as theologians are, such is theology. But some are greedy and contentious sophists. Is your theology therefore such? You will rightly say that the quality of a theologian, as a wicked man, does not produce the quality of theology. I too shall rightly say that the quality of a philosopher, as a profane man, does not bring the quality into philosophy itself. If you distinguish between a theologian and a mata-theologian, I too shall distinguish between a heathen philosopher and a Christian one. So much on the first member.

units.la: Deinde non spernit, neque reiicit vera Philosophia sapientiam in Euangelio patefactam, sed eam honorat & amplexatur, imo se veræ sapientiæ diuinæ etiam amatricem & obsequentem profitetur famulam. Licet multi ex Philosophis profanis sapientiam hanc ferre non potuerint.
units.tr: Further, true philosophy does not scorn or reject the wisdom revealed in the Gospel. It honours and embraces that wisdom, and even professes itself the lover and obedient handmaid of true divine wisdom. Yet many of the profane philosophers could not bear this wisdom.

units.la: Vrget igitur aliquis sic: Quod agit Philosophus & sapiens, id agit vi Philosophiæ & sapientiæ, seu ut Philosophus & sapiens.
units.tr: Someone therefore presses the point: What a philosopher and a wise man does, he does by the power of philosophy and wisdom, or as a philosopher and wise man.

units.la: At Philosophi multi, & quidem hi sapientes, de quibus loquitur Apostolus, sapientiam Dei contemnunt. Ergo hoc faciunt vi Philosophia & sapientia.
units.tr: But many philosophers, and indeed these wise men of whom the Apostle speaks, despise the wisdom of God. Therefore they do this by the power of philosophy and wisdom.

units.la: Respon. Propositio tum vera erit, cum Philosophus erit ipsa Philosophia. Philosophus habet scientiam Philosophiae, secundum quam scientiam potest agere: sed quia est & voluntarium agens, & nonnunquam carni & affectibus indulget, ideo saepe dissimiliter agit. Sed in aurem: Quod agit Theologus, id agit vi Theologia ut Theologus. At ille saepe sophisticatur & calumniatur audacter, & quidem impune. Ergo vi Theologia & ut Theologus calumniatur & sophisticatur. At consequens aegre admittes: aperi igitur oculos, & in altera antecedentium videbis vitium.
units.tr: Reply: The proposition would be true only if the philosopher were philosophy itself. The philosopher has the knowledge of philosophy, and by that knowledge he is able to act; but because he is also a voluntary agent, and sometimes indulges the flesh and the passions, he often acts unlike it. But let me put this quietly to you: What a theologian does, he does by the power of theology, as a theologian. Yet he often plays sophist and slanders boldly, and indeed with impunity. Therefore by the power of theology and as a theologian he slanders and plays sophist. You will hardly admit the conclusion, so open your eyes, and you will see the fault in one of the premises.

units.la: Deinde sicut stultitia, quatenus dicitur de Evangelio eiusque praedicatione, non est vera stultitia, sed quae videtur esse hominibus infidelibus, qui pereunt: ita sapientia sapientum hic non est vera sapientia, sed quae videtur illis sapientia, qui cruce Christi derident: adeoque est apparens imo falsa. Ergo eadem ratione Philosophia carnalis, mundana, Dei sapientiam stultam aestimans, non est vera & sana, sed falsa & insana hominum male iudicantium opinio, quae sub praetextu Philosophiae mundanis proponitur.
units.tr: Further, just as foolishness, as it is said of the Gospel and its preaching, is not true foolishness but what seems foolishness to unbelieving men who perish, so the wisdom of the wise here is not true wisdom but what seems wisdom to those who mock the cross of Christ; and so it is apparent, indeed false. Therefore, by the same reasoning, carnal and worldly philosophy, which judges the wisdom of God to be foolish, is not true and sound but the false and mad opinion of men who judge badly, which is put forward to the worldly under the pretext of philosophy.

units.la: 3. Inquiunt alii: Σοφία λόγυ damnatur a Paulo, qui illam a se removet, & opponit potentia divina.
units.tr: 3. Others object: The wisdom of words [σοφία λόγου] is condemned by Paul, who removes it from himself and sets against it the power of God.

units.la: At Σοφία λόγυ sapientia dicendi est pars Philosophia.
units.tr: But the wisdom of words is a part of philosophy.

units.la: Ergo saltem illam partem damnat.
units.tr: Therefore he condemns at least that part.

units.la: Respon. Propositionem negamus, quia est fallacia a dicto secundum quid. Deinde etiam captio est accidentis. Etenim eum simpliciter non damnare λόγω σοφίας, & dicendi peritiam indicat verf.5. praecedens, vbi Deo gratias agit, quod Corinthii sint ditati omni loquendi facultate, omniq; cognitione, & vocat gratiam Dei illis datam in Christo. Loquitur igitur de abusu sermonis & dicendi. Carpit enim vanitatem ambitiosorum Doctorum qui affectabant sapientiae & eloquentiae laudem in praedicando Euangelio. Ab hac se excludit, & huic opponit Dei potentiam. Nota itaque vani esse Theologi loquendi peritia applausum vulgi, laudemque alicuius eruditionis & eloquentiae aucupari.
units.tr: Reply: We deny the proposition, because it is a fallacy of the statement made in a qualified sense, and besides it is a fallacy of accident. For the preceding verse 5 shows that he does not condemn the wisdom of words [λόγω σοφίας] absolutely, nor skill in speaking, since there he gives thanks to God that the Corinthians have been enriched with every faculty of speech and all knowledge, and he calls the grace of God given to them in Christ. He therefore speaks of the abuse of speech and of eloquence. For he attacks the vanity of ambitious teachers who aimed at the praise of wisdom and eloquence in preaching the Gospel. He excludes himself from this and opposes to it the power of God. Note, then, that skill in speaking is empty in a theologian when it seeks the applause of the crowd and the praise of some learning and eloquence.

units.la: 4. obiiciunt: Sapientia Graecorum damnatur. At Philosophia est sapientia Graecorum. Ergo ipsa Philosophia damnatur.
units.tr: 4. They object: The wisdom of the Greeks is condemned. But philosophy is the wisdom of the Greeks. Therefore philosophy itself is condemned.

units.la: Propositio probatur ex 22. verf. cap. 1. prioris ad Corinth. Assumptio probatur, quod Graeci propterea sint dicti sapientes, quia fuerint Philosophi.
units.tr: The proposition is proved from verse 22 of the first chapter of the first Epistle to the Corinthians. The assumption is proved because the Greeks were called wise for no other reason than that they were philosophers.
