units.la: Respon. Quomodo sapientia Graecorum damnetur patebit ex Pauli scopo, qui est, praedicationem Euangelii opinione hominum animalium esse stultam. Probat hoc ex effectis per distinctionem. 1. Quia Iudaei petunt signum, id est, nolunt credere in Christum, nisi ad eorum placitum edatur miracula. 2. Graeci quaerunt sapientiam, id est, argumenta quae naturalis rationis vi possint comprehendere. At nos ita signa ad placitum Iudaeis non edimus, neque ad sapientiam seu placitum humanae manæ rationis docemus. Ergo videtur nostra prædicatio stulta. Ergo sapientia Græcorum repudiatur, quatenus lumine naturalis rationis ac sapientiæ metiri volunt Euangelium, & hoc cum nequeant, stultum esse putant Euangelium. Primum igitur loquitur Apostolus de sapientia naturalis & cœcæ rationis, quam nos in Philosophia dominari non permittimus, sed sapientiam rectæ rationis postulamus. Deinde' loquitur de sapientia rationis se non subiicientis mysteriis & sapientiæ diuinæ, sed stultam reputantis. At nos in Philosophia hominis sapientiam requirimus diuinæ sapientiæ & mysteriorum Dei obseruantissimam: diuinam sapientiam regulam & normam nostræ facimus. Tertio non simpliciter damnat Apostolus argumenta vi naturalis rationis deprompta, sed eorum intempestiuum vsum in mysterio doctrinæ Euangelicæ ac salutis, ex proprio hominis cerebro salutis modum concludentium. Philosophia denique (vt est in subsumpto) ipsa non fuit sapientia Græcorum, nedum specialis illa aberrans in modo salutis, quem mens non potest comprehendere, sapientia. Proinde cum hæc sapientia fuerit falsa sapientia, non fuit Philosophia Græca vera, sed quædam sophistica aberrans, quam resecat Christianus Philosophus. Imo ipse error non fuit ipsius Philosophiæ, sed hominum, qui se sapientes arbitrabantur salutis in Euangelio patefactum modum impugnantium & deridentium.
units.tr: Reply: How the wisdom of the Greeks is condemned will be clear from the Apostle's aim, which is to show that the preaching of the Gospel is foolish in the opinion of natural men. He proves this from its effects, by a distinction. (1) The Jews ask for a sign, that is, they are unwilling to believe in Christ unless miracles are performed to their liking. (2) The Greeks seek wisdom, that is, arguments which can be grasped by the power of natural reason. But we do not perform signs at the pleasure of the Jews, nor do we teach according to the wisdom or pleasure of feeble human reason. Therefore our preaching seems foolish. Therefore the wisdom of the Greeks is rejected, insofar as they want to measure the Gospel by the light of natural reason and wisdom, and since they cannot do this, they think the Gospel foolish. First, then, the Apostle speaks of the wisdom of blind natural reason, which we do not allow to rule in philosophy, but whose demand is the wisdom of right reason. Second, he speaks of the wisdom of a reason that does not submit itself to the mysteries and the divine wisdom, but regards them as foolish. We, however, in philosophy require the wisdom of man to be most obedient to divine wisdom and to the mysteries of God; we make divine wisdom our rule and norm. Third, the Apostle does not condemn absolutely the arguments drawn from the power of natural reason, but their untimely use in the mystery of Gospel doctrine and of salvation, when men conclude from their own brain the manner of salvation. Finally, philosophy (as the minor premise says) was itself not the wisdom of the Greeks, much less that special wisdom which goes astray about the way of salvation, which the mind cannot grasp. Therefore, since that wisdom was false wisdom, Greek philosophy was not true philosophy but a certain sophistical error, which the Christian philosopher cuts away. Indeed the error itself was not of philosophy but of men who thought themselves wise and who attacked and mocked the way of salvation revealed in the Gospel.

units.la: 5. obiicitur ex ca.2. Quod Christo, spiritui san-cto, & fidei opponitur, id vtique in Christiana Theologia & Repub.tolerari non debet.
units.tr: 5. It is objected from chapter 2: What is opposed to Christ, to the Holy Spirit, and to faith ought certainly not to be tolerated in Christian theology or the commonwealth.

units.la: At Philosophia opponitur Christo, spiritui san-cto, & fidei.
units.tr: But philosophy is opposed to Christ, to the Holy Spirit, and to faith.

units.la: Ergo Philosophia in Christiana Theologia at Repub.tolerari non debet.
units.tr: Therefore philosophy ought not to be tolerated in Christian theology or the commonwealth.

units.la: Assumptio probatur.
units.tr: The minor premise is proved.

units.la: Eminentia sermonis & eloquentia Christo Iesu verf.1. & 2. persuasoria humana sapientia verba spiritui & potentia Christi verf. 4. & hominum sapientia fidei opponitur verf.5.
units.tr: The excellence of speech and eloquence is opposed to Christ Jesus (vv. 1 and 2), and persuasive words of human wisdom are opposed to the Spirit and the power of Christ (v. 4), and the wisdom of men is opposed to faith (v. 5).

units.la: At Philosophia docet eminentiam sermonis & sapientia, persuasoria humana sapientia verba, & ipsam hominum sapientiam.
units.tr: But Philosophy teaches the excellence of speech and wisdom, persuasive words of human wisdom, and the wisdom of men itself.

units.la: Ergo Philosophia opponitur Christo, spiritui & fidei.
units.tr: Therefore Philosophy is opposed to Christ, to the Spirit and to faith.

units.la: Respon. Propositio Syllogismi nisi certo oppositionis modo intelligi debeat, vix subsistet: Non enim omnis & quaeuis oppositio inter Christum, eius spiritum, & nostram fidem, inferre potest exclusionem eius, quod illis opponitur, a foro Theologorum & Reipublicae Christianae. Nam in ipsa doctrina Theologica & Repub.Christiana, multa possunt opponi his tribus, quorum tamen vtrobique & vsus & dignitas est permagna.
units.tr: Reply: Unless the major premise of the syllogism is understood in a definite sense of opposition, it will hardly stand. For not every and any opposition between Christ, his Spirit and our faith can justify the exclusion of what is opposed to them from the forum of the theologians and the Christian commonwealth. Indeed, in theology itself and in the Christian commonwealth, many things can be opposed to these three, and yet the use and the dignity of such things are very great on both sides.

units.la: Sed discutiamus assumptum eiusque Prosyllogismum. Philosophiam primum Christo oppoopponi posse, vt disparatum, non negamus. At Paulus, inquis, opponit illa in scientia Christiani. Nego. Non veni, inquit Paulus, in eminentia sermonis aut sapientiæ. Tu assumis: Philosophia docet istorum eminentiam. Respondeo 1. aliud est esse, aliud docere. Quaternarius terminorum numerus Logico est suspectus. 2. Vera Philosophia non docet quamuis eminentiam sermonis & sapientiæ, sed eam, quæ primo est salutaris & rebus æqualis: imo etiam si vis comparationem instituere ad rudiores. Paulus autem loquitur de grandiloquentia ampullas proiiciente, & plausibilibus humanæ, id est, carnalis sapientiæ argumentis elata. Nam respicit ad vanitatem ambitiosorum sesquipedalia verba proiicientium & captantium eloquentiæ & intempestiuæ eruditionis humanæ gloriam.
units.tr: But let us examine the minor premise and its prosyllogism. That Philosophy can be opposed to Christ, as something disparate, we do not deny. But you say that Paul opposes these things in the knowledge of the Christian. I deny it. Paul says: "I did not come in excellence of speech or of wisdom." You assume: Philosophy teaches their excellence. I reply: (1) To be is one thing, to teach is another. The number of four terms is suspect to a logician. (2) True Philosophy does not teach any excellence of speech and wisdom of the kind you mean, but only that which is first saving and equal to things; indeed, even if you want to set up a comparison with the cruder sort. Paul, however, speaks of grandiloquence that casts away bombast and is elated by the plausible arguments of human, that is, carnal, wisdom. For he has in view the vanity of ambitious men who fling about long-winded words and seek the glory of eloquence and of untimely human learning.

units.la: Philosophiam deinde opponi spiritui & potentiæ Dei ais. Non nego, illam his opponi posse, vt disparatum. At Paulus, inquis, opponit illam spiritui & potentiæ Dei. Nego. Sermo meus, ait Paulus, non fuit in persuasoriis humanæ sapientiæ verbis, sed in demonstratione spiritus, &c.
units.tr: You say next that Philosophy is opposed to the Spirit and the power of God. I do not deny that it can be opposed to these, as something disparate. But you say: Paul opposes it to the Spirit and the power of God. I deny it. My speech, says Paul, was not in persuasive words of human wisdom, but in demonstration of the Spirit, etc.

units.la: Respon. 1. Aliud est esse, aliud docere persuasoria humanæ sapietiæ verba. Numera terminos in Prosyllogismo.
units.tr: Reply: (1) To be is one thing, to teach persuasive words of human wisdom is another. Count the terms in the prosyllogism.

units.la: Docet quidem Philosophiæ ars Rhetorica artem dicendi ad bene persuadendum, at non tantum ex capsula sapientiæ humanæ, sed etiam ex elegantissimo rosario diuinæ sapientiæ. Non ad ostentationem, sed ad veritatis legitigitimam persuasionem & sanctam ædificatio- nem.
units.tr: The art of Rhetoric, which is part of Philosophy, does indeed teach the art of speaking so as to persuade well, but not only from the casket of human wisdom; it also draws on the most elegant rosary of divine wisdom. It does so not for display, but for the legitimate persuasion of the truth and for holy edification.

units.la: Paulus autem hic agens de ministro verbi, vult, vt valere iubeat ambitiosam Rhetoricam profanorum oratorum, & eloquentiæ mundanæ affectatione. Legitimum interim Rhetoricæ vsum non improbat, quem & S. Spiritus obseruat, quatenus nimirum adhiberur modeste ad Ecclesiæ ædificationem.
units.tr: Paul, however, speaking here of the minister of the Word, wishes him to bid farewell to the ambitious Rhetoric of the profane orators and to the affected eloquence of the world. Meanwhile he does not disapprove of the lawful use of Rhetoric, which the Holy Spirit also observes, insofar as it is used modestly for the edification of the Church.

units.la: Secundo spectat hic Paulus ad res sacras & earum tractandarū modum, vt videre est verf. 13. Quæ loquimur, non sermonibus, quos docet humana sapientia, sed quos docet Spiritus sanctus, spiritualibus spiritualia aptantes. Homogenea vult hic adhiberi, ne permisceantur profana sacris, iuxta illud : Qui loquitur, loquatur vt eloquia Dei.
units.tr: Secondly, Paul here looks to sacred things and the manner of handling them, as is seen at verse 13: What we speak, we speak not in words taught by human wisdom, but in words taught by the Holy Spirit, fitting spiritual things to spiritual. Here he wishes that what is of the same kind be used, lest profane things be mixed with sacred, in accordance with that saying: Whoever speaks, let him speak as the oracles of God.

units.la: Tertio Philosophiam opponi fidei, damus vt disparatum.
units.tr: Thirdly, we grant that Philosophy is opposed to faith, as something disparate.

units.la: At Paulus, inquis, opponit illam hic fidei. Nego. Ait, ais tu; Fides vestra non consistit in sapientia hominum. At Philosophia non est sapientia hominum, neque tantum, neque quæ- uis.
units.tr: But you say that Paul opposes it here to faith. I deny it. He says, as you say: Your faith does not rest in the wisdom of men. But Philosophy is not the wisdom of men, neither only that, nor any kind of it.

units.la: At doceat hominum sapientiam, vt dicis, quid tum? Non enim sequitur: Fides nostra, non consistit in sapientia hominum. Ergo sapientia hominum, (dico vera, non opinione tantum) est explodenda ex foro Theologorum. Nam aliud est fidem stabiliri sapientia hominum, ita, vt ad eā requiratur grandiloquentia & acumen rationum humanarum : aliud vero Philosophiam aduer-
units.tr: But, you say, if it teaches the wisdom of men, what then? For it does not follow: Our faith does not rest in the wisdom of men. Therefore the wisdom of men (I mean true wisdom, not mere opinion) must be banished from the forum of the theologians. For it is one thing for faith to be established by the wisdom of men, so that grandiloquence and the keenness of human arguments are required for it; but it is another thing for Philosophy to be opposed

units.la: adueríari fidei, & hinc illam plane explodi.
units.tr: to faith, and for this reason to be utterly banished.

units.la: Nullius hominis pii fides nititur humana sapientia, nec nititur hominum verbis & scriptis, nec etiam ipsis operibus bonis.
units.tr: The faith of no godly man rests on human wisdom, nor does it rest on the words and writings of men, nor even on their good works themselves.

units.la: Ergone è Theologia & foro Reip. Christianæ explodi debent sapientia rerum humanarum, verba & scripta hominum, & ipsæ virtutum actiones? Nectatur propositio & infirmitas patebit.
units.tr: Therefore should the wisdom of human things, the words and writings of men, and the very actions of virtue be banished from theology and from the forum of the Christian commonwealth? Let the proposition be examined, and its weakness will be plain.

units.la: 6. obiicitur: Sapientia, quæ opponitur Dei sapientia, & non est prædicanda, est sapientia principum seculi huius qui abolentur, versf.6,7.
units.tr: 6. It is objected: The wisdom that is opposed to the wisdom of God and is not to be preached is the wisdom of the rulers of this age, who are brought to nothing (vv. 6, 7).

units.la: At Philosophia est talis sapientia seculi huius.
units.tr: But Philosophy is such a wisdom of this age.

units.la: Ergo opponitur Dei sapientia, neque est prædicanda.
units.tr: Therefore it is opposed to the wisdom of God, and is not to be preached.

units.la: Respon. Assumptio simpliciter dicta & accepta non est vera.
units.tr: Reply: The minor premise, taken simply as stated, is not true.

units.la: Nam Philosophia vera, non est sapientia principum huius seculi, vel seculi huius, qui & abolentur, & errant, & saepe inflectunt suas opiniones. Sed est studium sapientiæ, quæ est scientia rerum (non principum placitis, neque secularium & mundanorum opinionibus) & Dei veritati conformis. Aliud est philosophari ad placita & opiniones hominum, a qua Philosophorum secta nostram Philosophiam dispescimus, aliud ad rerum veritatem philosophari. Secundo nemo nostrum dicit sapientiam Philosophicam seu Philosophorum decreta esse instar oraculorum diuinorum in suggestu praedicanda & populo proponenda. Paulus loquitur de se & sui similibus, quos opponit ponit Doctoribus Corinthiorum ambitiosis, nec vult ministrum Dei placita Philosophica & humana, sed Dei eloquia gregi Christiano propinare.
units.tr: For true Philosophy is not the wisdom of the rulers of this age, or of the age, which both come to nothing and err, and often change their opinions. Rather, it is the pursuit of wisdom, which is the knowledge of things (not the decrees of rulers, nor the opinions of worldly and secular men), and conformable to the truth of God. There is a difference between philosophizing according to the decrees and opinions of men, from which sect of philosophers we separate our Philosophy, and philosophizing according to the truth of things. Secondly, none of us says that philosophical wisdom, or the decrees of philosophers, are to be proclaimed from the pulpit and set before the people as the oracles of God. Paul speaks of himself and his like, whom he sets against the ambitious teachers of the Corinthians, and he does not want the minister of God to serve up philosophical and human decrees, but the words of God to the Christian flock.

units.la: 7.ex cap. 3. sic opponunt quidam hunc Achilleum:
units.tr: 7. From chapter 3, some oppose this argument thus:

units.la: Stultitia est exterminanda è scholis & templis.
units.tr: Foolishness is to be banished from schools and temples.

units.la: At Philosophia humana est stultitia coram Deo.
units.tr: But human Philosophy is foolishness before God.

units.la: Ergo est exterminanda è scholis & templis.
units.tr: Therefore it is to be banished from schools and temples.

units.la: Assumptum probant verf. 18. & 19. cap. 3.
units.tr: The minor premise is proved at verses 18 and 19 of chapter 3.

units.la: Nullus seipsum seducat, si quis sibi videtur esse sapiens inter vos in hoc seculo, stultus fiat ut fiat sapiens. Sapientia enim mundi huius est stultitia apud Deum, &c. Atqui Philosophia est mundi huius sapientia.
units.tr: Let no one deceive himself. If anyone among you seems to be wise in this age, let him become foolish that he may become wise. For the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God, etc. Yet Philosophy is the wisdom of this world.

units.la: Respon. Assumptionem prosyllogismi negamus. Philosophia enim, ut saepius iam est demonstratum, non est mundi huius sapientia.
units.tr: Reply: We deny the minor premise of the prosyllogism. For Philosophy, as has often been demonstrated already, is not the wisdom of this world.

units.la: Et ut, quod res est, dicam, si Philosophia esset seculi & mundi huius sapientia, de qua hoc loco Paulus loquitur, eam neque in templis neque in scholis vllum debere locum invenire cum omnibus orthodoxis prolixe fateor.
units.tr: And, to say what is the case: if Philosophy were the wisdom of the age and of this world, of which Paul speaks in this place, I freely confess with all the orthodox that it ought to find no place either in the temples or in the schools.

units.la: Loquitur enim Paulus de peruersa opinione Corinthiorum, quam de suorum doctorum ambitiosorum & in speciem admirabilium, sapientia conceperant. Er horum quidem sapientiam dicit seculi & mundi huius sapientiam mirifice ampullantem, sed apud Deum seu iudicio Dei stultitiam.
units.tr: For Paul speaks of the perverse opinion of the Corinthians, which they had formed from the wisdom of their ambitious teachers, who were admired in appearance. Indeed he calls the wisdom of these men the wisdom of the age and of this world, marvellously puffed up, but foolishness before God, or in the judgment of God.

units.la: Atqui Philosophia non est eiusmodi sapientia mundi, quia non est rei & Dei veritati conformis, sed repugnans scientia. Philosophia veritatis est studiosa. Mundani si aberrant & sapientes se venditant, quid hoc ad Philosophiam? Neque enim sapientia est pelagus promiscuum, in quod omnes cuiuslibet sapientiae riuuli, confluunt. Non est quiduis vere sapiens, quod titulo fertur sapientiae. Et quia hic stultitiam vocat mundanam sapientiam, ideo opinione tantum hominum rudium & veritatem ignorantium dicitur sapientia. Atque si ipsi sapientes se proclamassent eo tempore philosophos, qui tanta cum grandiloquentia hominum occuparant animos, nunquid statim ipsi fuissent veri philosophi? In Logicis distinctio succurrit. Aliud est aliquid secundum Dici, aliud secundum Esse. Et noueris mi homo, multa dici de subiecto, quae tamen non insunt. Multi etiam, & sapientes & orthodoxi Theologi gestiunt salutari. At quia tales videri volunt & vocitari, continuo reuera sunt sapientes & orthodoxi? Non crediderim. Videri velle, & dici velle, non efficit ipsum quod videri & dici volumus, in nobis esse.
units.tr: Yet Philosophy is not that kind of worldly wisdom, because it is not a science conformable to the truth of things and of God, but opposed to it. Philosophy is zealous for truth. If worldly men go astray and boast themselves wise, what has this to do with Philosophy? For wisdom is not a common sea into which all the streams of any kind of wisdom flow. Whatever is carried under the title of wisdom is not therefore truly wise. And because here he calls worldly wisdom foolishness, therefore wisdom is spoken of only by the opinion of rude men who are ignorant of the truth. And if the wise men themselves, who with such grandiloquence occupied men's minds, had at that time proclaimed themselves philosophers, would they at once have been true philosophers? Logic supplies a distinction here: one thing is something according to what is said, another according to what is. And you should know, my friend, that many things are said of a subject which yet do not belong to it. Many, even wise and orthodox theologians, strive to be considered so; but because they want to be seen and called such, are they therefore in very truth wise and orthodox? I should not think so. To wish to be seen and to wish to be called does not make the very thing we wish to be seen and called to be in us.

units.la: Elenchus Sophismatis tertii ex Epistola ad Rom. 1. verf. 21. & 22.
units.tr: Refutation of the third sophism, from Romans 1:21–22

units.la: Vani facti sunt in ratiocinationibus suis, & obtenebratum est desipiens cor eorum. Quum se profiterētur esse sapientes, stulti facti sunt.
units.tr: They became vain in their imaginations, and their foolish heart was darkened. Professing themselves to be wise, they became fools.

units.la: Responsio.
units.tr: Answer.

units.la: Hic nulla prorsus fit mentio Philosophiæ. Est igitur inde necessitate consequentiæ deducenda. Fiat itaque periculum. Qui vani fiunt seu evanescunt in suis ratiocinationibus, & qui cum profiteantur se sapientes, stulti fiunt: eorum sapientia est fugienda.
units.tr: Here there is no mention at all of philosophy. It must therefore be deduced by a necessary consequence. Let us test it. Those who become vain, or vanish away, in their reasonings, and who, professing themselves wise, become fools, their wisdom is to be shunned.

units.la: Atqui Philosophi Ethnici vani facti sunt in ratiocinationibus suis, quique cum profiterentur se sapientes, sunt stulti facti.
units.tr: But the heathen philosophers became vain in their reasonings, and, professing themselves wise, became fools.

units.la: Ergo Ethnicorum sapientia est fugienda. Iam vero Ethnicorum sapientia est Philosophia. Ergo & Philosophia est fugienda.
units.tr: Therefore the wisdom of the heathen is to be shunned. Now the wisdom of the heathen is philosophy. Therefore philosophy too is to be shunned.

units.la: Respon. Propositio catenus est vera, quatenus sapientia ista, quæ dicitur, facit evanescere & infatuari ratiocinantes: at hæc sapientia non vera sed apparens sapientia, stoliditas est nomine sapientiæ, inanique fuco tincta & colorata. Philosophia autem est veræ sapientiæ & sapientis veritatis æmula & obseruans.
units.tr: Answer: The major premise is true only so far as that so-called wisdom makes reasoners vanish away and grow foolish. But this is not true wisdom; it is an apparent wisdom, which is folly bearing the name of wisdom, tinted and coloured with an empty dye. Philosophy, however, is the rival and the follower of true wisdom and of the truth of the wise.

units.la: Alias rerum potest esse scientia ac sapientia, in se quidem bona at abusu evanescens, & stolidos faciens se male abutētes. Posita enim hac propositione, & inde assumpto abusu verbi diuini male intellecti, & eius corruptela, ita potest quis argutari: Qui vani fiunt ratiocinando, & qui cum se sapientes profitentur, sunt stulti, eorū sapientia & doctrina fugienda. At multi Theologi vani fiunt in mysteriorum diuinorum discusdifcussionibus & de iis ratiocinationibus, & dum se sapientes & orthodoxos profitentur, fiunt stulti & hæretici. Ergo multorum Theologorum sapiētia & doctrina est fugienda.
units.tr: Otherwise, there can be a knowledge and wisdom of things which is good in itself but vanishes away through abuse, making fools of those who misuse it. For if this proposition is laid down, and from it there is assumed the abuse of the divine Word, misunderstood and corrupted, one may argue thus: Those who become vain by reasoning, and who, professing themselves wise, are fools, their wisdom and doctrine are to be shunned. But many theologians become vain in their discussions of the divine mysteries and in such reasonings, and while they profess themselves wise and orthodox, they become foolish and heretical. Therefore the wisdom and doctrine of many theologians is to be shunned.

units.la: Ita etiam venit intelligenda argumentatio de Philosophia: quia in assumpto non omnes Philosophi, sed quidam & quidem Ethnici illi, qui ideo euanuerūt & stulti facti sunt, quod male ratiocinati, ex principiis naturæ, mutarunt gloriam incorruptibilis Dei in efformatam imaginem mortalis hominis. Eorum itaque & eatenus sapientia est fugienda: hoc est, vt Theologorum sophistica ratiocinatio ex verbo Dei corrupto & perverso, ita Philosophorum inanis sapientia: Et ratiocinatio ex principiis naturę male intellectis & perperam adhibitis extructa est vitanda.
units.tr: In the same way the argument about philosophy must be understood. For in the assumption it is not all philosophers who are meant, but certain heathen ones, who vanished away and became foolish because, reasoning badly from the principles of nature, they exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for an image in the likeness of mortal man. Therefore the wisdom of these men, and to that extent, is to be shunned. That is to say, just as the sophistical reasoning of theologians from a corrupt and perverted Word of God is to be avoided, so too the empty wisdom of philosophers, and the reasoning built from the principles of nature misunderstood and wrongly applied, is to be avoided.

units.la: Ad ass.ergo dicimus, eā primo loqui de Philosophis non omnibus sed paganis aberrantibus, secundo de Philosophis non vt Philosophis sed vt sophistis, (sicut de Theologo sophisticante ex Dei verbo loquens, non loquitur de eodem vt Theologo, sed vt sophista:) tertio nō loquitur de vero ratiocinationis vsu, & vera natura, sed abusu, & erroribus non ratiocinationis syllogisticæ, sed male affectæ sophisticæ. Neque sane ob abusum rei, est trahenda in ius veritas rei. Loqui autem Apostolum non de Philosophicarum ratiocinationum vero & legitimo vsu, Philosophicaque sapientia, vti est vera, & donum dei, etiam in Ethnicis, ipse probat eodē hoc in cap. siquidem dem tribuit ei maximum beneficium, quod scilicet pagani Dei potétiam cognouerint per inuisibilia creaturarum, & maiestatem diuinitatis nonnihil perceperint ex mundi fabrica: Sed hoc vituperat, quod Deum ita cognitum, non honorarint vt Deum, deinde quod eidem non fuerint grati, tertio quod gloriam Dei transtulerint ad efformatam imaginem mortalis hominis. Sic hodie etiam vspiam non solum Philosophi, sed etiam Theologi quidam, Deum, vt cognoscunt, non colunt, Deo non sunt grati, & gloriam incorruptibilis Dei mutant in mortalis hominis efformatam imaginem. Hos si dixeris Theologos, dicam & illos Philosophos, si non veros dixeris, dicam & illos non veros Philosophos. Neque profecto inde concludes propterea esse ipsam Theologiam, propter hos ingratos & stolidos idolopoietas & idololatras, repudiandam.
units.tr: So to the assumption we reply: first, the Apostle is speaking not of all philosophers but of erring pagans; second, he is speaking of philosophers not as philosophers but as sophists (just as, when speaking of a theologian who sophisticates from the Word of God, one does not speak of him as a theologian but as a sophist); third, he is not speaking of the true use and true nature of reasoning but of its abuse and of errors, not of syllogistic reasoning but of a badly disposed sophistry. Nor indeed should the truth of a thing be dragged into court on account of its abuse. That the Apostle is not speaking of the true and lawful use of philosophical reasoning, or of philosophical wisdom as it is true and a gift of God, even among the heathen, he proves in this very chapter. For he grants them the greatest benefit, namely that the pagans knew the power of God through the invisible things of creation, and perceived somewhat of the majesty of the Godhead from the fabric of the world. But what he finds fault with is this: that, though they knew God in this way, they did not honour him as God; then that they were not thankful to him; and third, that they transferred the glory of God to an image in the likeness of mortal man. So today too, in various places, not only philosophers but also some theologians know God, but do not worship him as God, are not thankful to him, and exchange the glory of the incorruptible God for an image in the likeness of mortal man. If you call these theologians, I shall call those philosophers too; if you deny they are true, I shall say those philosophers are not true philosophers either. Nor will you indeed conclude from this that theology itself is to be rejected because of these ungrateful and foolish image-makers and idolaters.

units.la: Sed mentem Pauli in ipsius verbis latentem ex dispositione videamus. Explicat peccatum gentilium Deum cognoscentium quidem, sed in veritatem iniuriarum, ex partibus suis diuersis: prima est; non glorificant verum Deum: Secunda: colunt idola. In his consistit iniusta illa veritatis detentio. Posterior pars habet gradus duos, internam & externam idololatriam. Interna est haec: Euanescunt, excæcantur, stulti ac insipientes fiunt. Modus quo euanescunt, &c. additur, scilicet, per ratiocinationes suas, quibus se ipsi excæcant ac sibi ipsi imponunt, progressi nimirum a veris principiis de Deo, quod vnus sit, quod coeldus sit, ad falsas conclusiones: deficientibus nimirum ipsos naturalibus principiis in ipso statim limine. Ex ipsis enim statim, quod falsum est, assumunt, ex quo rursus falsum concludunt, & ita fiunt stulti. Ergo 1. loquitur de iis gentibus, qui notitiam Dei habuere naturalem.
units.tr: But let us look at the mind of Paul, hidden in his words, by way of their arrangement. He explains the sin of the Gentiles, who knew God but held the truth in unrighteousness, by its different parts. The first is: they did not glorify the true God. The second: they worshipped idols. In these two things that unrighteous holding back of the truth consists. The latter part has two degrees, internal and external idolatry. The internal is this: they vanished away, were blinded, and became foolish and senseless. The manner in which they vanished away, etc., is added: namely, through their own reasonings, by which they blinded themselves and deceived themselves, proceeding, of course, from true principles about God, that he is one and that he is good, to false conclusions, since the natural principles failed them right at the threshold. For straight away they assume what is false, and from this they in turn conclude what is false, and so they become foolish. Therefore, first, he is speaking of those peoples who had a natural knowledge of God.

units.la: Paulus autem naturalem illam cognitione non reiicit, nec vituperat, sed magni facit. Ergo & lumen naturæ ac rationis, ex mundi fabrica colligens Deum, & cognoscens quadantenus naturâ eius, non aspernatur nec criminatur. Ait enim: Deus eis manifestum fecit. Ergo & lumen naturæ recte vsurpatum, est ex Dei munere & manifestatione.
units.tr: But Paul does not reject or find fault with that natural knowledge; he holds it in high regard. Therefore he does not despise or accuse the light of nature and reason either, which gathers God from the fabric of the world and knows his nature to some extent. For he says: God has made it manifest to them. Therefore the light of nature, rightly used, is also a gift and a manifestation of God.

units.la: 1. loquitur de iis, qui veritatem luce rationis & naturæ visam in iniustitia detinet, sed sponte prolabuntur ad cæcitatem & turpitudinem. Ergo veritas ista suam obtineat laudem, sed eius iniusta detentio vituperetur exemplo Pauli. Notent hoc, qui veritatem non modo naturæ, sed etiam gratiæ lumine cognitam habent, & tamen malunt se oblectare nugis paganorum, & in eorum cæcitate cæcutire, imo illorum erroribus patrocinari, quam Deum secundum agnitam veritatem glorificare. Scilicet illis maior autoritas Ethnici magistri, quam veritas & naturalis & cœlestis.
units.tr: First, he is speaking of those who hold down in unrighteousness a truth seen by the light of reason and nature, but who of their own accord slip into blindness and baseness. Therefore that truth should receive its praise, but its unrighteous suppression should be censured, as Paul's example shows. Let those note this who have the truth known not only by the light of nature but also by the light of grace, and yet prefer to delight themselves in the trifles of the pagans and to grow blind in their blindness, or rather to defend their errors, rather than to glorify God according to the truth they have recognised. Clearly, for them the authority of a heathen master outweighs both natural and heavenly truth.

units.la: 3. loquitur de gentibus excæcatis & colentibus idola: At hi non amplius visam, nisi accusante conscientia, veritatem vident, proinde veritatem non intelligunt. Hi quomodo Philosophiæ nomine possint honorari nō video. Sicut improprie illis decus Theologiæ competit, qui excæcati idololatræ sunt.
units.tr: Third, he is speaking of the Gentiles who were blinded and worshipped idols. But these men see the truth no longer, except as their conscience accuses them, and therefore they do not understand the truth. How such men can be honoured with the name of philosophy, I do not see. Just as the glory of theology belongs improperly to those who are blinded idolaters.

units.la: 4.loquitur de gentibus propter cæcitatem, ex naturæ principiis non recte concludentibus,& de iis, qui destituti illis, nec verum assumunt, nec verum concludunt, & ita euanescunt.
units.tr: Fourth, he is speaking of the Gentiles, who because of their blindness did not draw correct conclusions from the principles of nature, and of those who, lacking those principles, neither assume what is true nor conclude what is true, and so vanish away.

units.la: Ergo loquitur non de veris & logicis ratiocinationibus, sed de vanis & ἀλόγοις sophisticationibus, quarum causa est ipsa hominis iniusta veritatis detentio, & iusta Dei excæcatio & derelictio. Nequaquam igitur loquitur de Philosophis quatenus Philosophi sunt.
units.tr: Therefore he is speaking not of true and logical reasonings but of vain and irrational [ἀλόγοις] sophistications, whose cause is man's own unrighteous holding down of the truth, and God's just blinding and abandonment. By no means, then, is he speaking of philosophers insofar as they are philosophers.

units.la: Ex consequente denique elicitur hæc assumptio: Ethnicorum sapientia fuit Philosophia. Strenue nego, si de ea intelligis, quā hic euanescere & stultescere ait Apostolus. Patet negationis ratio ex iam dictis. Deducta itaque consequens conclusio euanescit & euadit stolida per ratiocinationem non veram, sed vanam ac stultam.
units.tr: Finally, the assumption is drawn from the consequent: the wisdom of the heathen was philosophy. I firmly deny it, if you mean that wisdom which the Apostle says vanishes away and grows foolish here. The reason for the denial is clear from what has already been said. The conclusion deduced as a consequence therefore vanishes away and becomes foolish through a reasoning that is not true but vain and foolish.

units.la: Elenchus Sophismatis 4. ex dictis Scripturæ hominis animalis & naturalis cæcitatem ac impotentiam in spiritualibus afferentibus deducti.
units.tr: Refutation of the fourth sophism, drawn from the statements of Scripture that the natural and animal man is blind and powerless in spiritual matters.

units.la: Cuius causa est peruersa & mala, cuius fundamentum est vanum & stolidum, cuius quoque norma ac regula est fallax, id ipsum malum, vanum, & fallax est.
units.tr: Its cause is perverse and bad, its foundation is vain and foolish, and its norm and rule is fallacious. The thing itself is therefore bad, vain and fallacious.

units.la: At humana Philosophia causa mala & peruersa est, nempe homines corrupti ac peruersi, fundamentum est vanum, nempe ratio humana & mens cæca hominis. Regula eiusdem est fallax, nempe hominis corrupti iudicium de veritate rerum ac experientia iudicans.
units.tr: But human philosophy has a bad and perverse cause, namely corrupt and perverse men. Its foundation is vain, namely human reason and the blind mind of man. Its rule is fallacious, namely the corrupt man's judgment about the truth of things, judging by experience.

units.la: Probatur: Quia Philosophiæ autores sunt homines corrupti non renati, quorum ratio cæca, mens vana, cor malum, voluntas peruersa, iudicium depravatum, sensus sæpe hallucinans. Gen. 6. Omne figmentum cogitationum cordis humani tantum malum est omni die. Genes. 8. Figmentum cordis humani malum est a pueritia. Ierem. 16. Peruersum est cor hominis atque præfractum. 1. Corin. 2. Animalis homo non percipit ea quæ sunt Spiritus Dei. Sunt enim ei stultitia, nec potest ea cognoscere, quia spiritualiter diiudicantur. Rom. 8. Sapientia carnis est inimicitia adversus Deum; Legi enim Dei non subiicitur, nam nec potest quidem. Ephes. 4. Gentibus tribuitur vanitas mentis, tenebræ cogitationum, & obstinatio cordis, &c.
units.tr: It is proved as follows. The authors of philosophy are corrupt, unregenerate men, whose reason is blind, mind vain, heart evil, will perverse, judgment depraved, and senses often hallucinating. Gen. 6: Every imagination of the thoughts of the human heart is only evil every day. Gen. 8: The imagination of the human heart is evil from youth. Jer. 16: The heart of man is perverse and stubborn. 1 Cor. 2: The natural man does not receive the things of the Spirit of God; they are foolishness to him, nor can he know them, because they are spiritually discerned. Rom. 8: The wisdom of the flesh is enmity against God; for it is not subject to the law of God, neither indeed can it be. Eph. 4: The Gentiles are given over to the vanity of their minds, the darkness of their thoughts, and the obstinacy of their hearts, etc.

units.la: Ergo ipsa humana Philosophia est mala, vana & fallax.
units.tr: Therefore human philosophy itself is evil, vain and fallacious.

units.la: Responsio.
units.tr: Answer.

units.la: I. Membra primum propositionis & assumptionis dispiciamus. Sunt autem tria. Quo ad primum: Malæ causæ sæpe potest esse bonus effectus, si scilicet malitia & bonitas sunt diversi generis, ita ut alia ratione sit malus artifex, alia ratione bonus eius effectus. Malus enim vitiis animi, effectum bonum arte externa elaboratum aliquando producit. Sic malus lus Christianus potest esse bonus artifex, vt apud Ariftotelem malus vir, potest esse bonus ciuis. Sed hac de re infra. Existat igitur ex familia Christianorum regeneratorum Philosophus, qui Philosophiam gignat & expoliat, vti hoc seculum eiusmodi non caret. Causa bona producet bonam Philosophiam: sed hic vereor contingentiam, vereor etiam Ariftarchum in regenerato inuenientem cum spiritu carnem, ne istam Philosophiam dicat partim spiritualem, partim carnalem, qui causa eius de vtroque participet.
units.tr: I. Let us first examine the members of the major premise and the minor premise. There are three. As to the first: a bad cause can often produce a good effect, if malice and goodness are of different kinds, so that the craftsman is bad in one respect and his product good in another. For a man evil in the vices of his mind may sometimes produce a good work, elaborated by external skill. Thus a bad Christian can be a good craftsman, just as, according to Aristotle, a bad man can be a good citizen. But more on this below. So let there arise, from the family of regenerate Christians, a philosopher who begets and refines philosophy, as this age does not lack such men. A good cause will produce good philosophy. But here I fear contingency, and I fear that Aristarchus, finding flesh together with spirit in the regenerate man, may say that this philosophy is partly spiritual and partly carnal, since its cause partakes of both.

units.la: Secundum membrum est de fundamento. Dicimus rationem & proprie & metonymice artium philosophicarum instrumentum & fundamentum, & rationem bene ratiocinantem & vniuersalia ex singularibus recte colligentem, & rationem ex ratiocinatione recto iudicio deductam. At no quamuis, sed rectam rationem recte ratiocinantem, veram item rationem recta dianoia deductam, qua possit fundari & niti. Non modo corruptam & lapsu lapsusque poena depravatam, sed cum primis praeter naturae relictum lumen, gratiae & spiritus lumine illustratam.
units.tr: The second member concerns the foundation. We say that reason, both properly and metonymically, is the instrument and foundation of the philosophical arts: reason reasoning well and rightly gathering universals from particulars, and reason deduced from ratiocination by right judgment. But not just any reason, rather right reason reasoning rightly, true reason also deduced by right thinking, on which philosophy can be founded and rest. Not reason merely corrupted and depraved by the fall and the punishment of the fall, but above all the light of nature that remains, illumined by the light of grace and the Spirit.

units.la: Tertium membrum sic declaramus: Iudicium cognitionis, sensuum & rationis non quoduis ad artium censuram admittimus, sed dextre iudicans ex infallibili sensuum cognitione, & fana reique veritati conueniente rationis perceptione, cogitatione, dianoea & dispositione. Sensuum postulamus experientiam non quomodolibet affectorum, sed sano-rum & non hallucinantium.
units.tr: We set out the third member thus. We do not admit just any judgment of knowledge, senses and reason to the censure of the arts, but that which judges rightly from the infallible knowledge of the senses, and from a sound perception of reason, agreeing with the truth of the thing, through thought, reasoning and disposition. From the senses we require experience not of any affected kind, but of sound senses that do not hallucinate.

units.la: Iam ad euentilationem assumpti acceda-mus. Fatemur per peccatum & lapsum vni-uersam hominis naturam esse misere depra-uatam, omnes animae vires vehementer labe-factatas, mentem esse obscuratam, voluntatem peruersam. Hanc generalitatem corru-ptionis humanae cocedimus in assumpto hoc, Omnes homines natura sunt praui, omnium homi-num ratio & mens natura est caeca & obscurata ignorantia tenebris, &c. At homo in hac vita non manet semper nec omnis in eodem statu. Iam qui est nondum illuminatus, cras vel alio tempore conuertitur & illuminatur. Neco-mnes homines Philosophiae ciuitatem con-dunt in statu deprauato, quidam saltem in Christianorum regione eam in statu restaura-tionis suae extruunt. Sed inquis: Ethnici fue-runt Philosophi architecti, at hi omnes corrupti & caeci.
units.tr: Now let us come to the refutation of the minor premise. We confess that through sin and the fall the whole nature of man is wretchedly depraved, all the powers of the soul greatly weakened, the mind obscured, the will perverse. We concede this general corruption of humanity in this premise: All men are by nature evil; the reason and mind of all men is by nature blind and obscured by the darkness of ignorance, etc. But man does not remain always in this life, nor is every man in the same state. Whoever is not yet enlightened will be converted and enlightened tomorrow or at some other time. Nor do all men build the city of philosophy in a depraved state; some, at least in the region of the Christians, build it in the state of their restoration. But you say: The Ethnic philosophers were the architects, but all of these were corrupt and blind.

units.la: Respondeo: Hi si lumen naturae sunt recte secuti, aliquid & quidem saepe admirandum nobis exhibuerunt: si ab eo aberrarunt, cor-rigatur error, & iam in nobis, qui videri volu-mus regenerati Christiani, lumen gratiae & spiritus coniungatur cum lumine naturae, & utrumque coniunctum naeuos tollat Ethnicorum, & defectus eorum ignorantiae expleat. Neque enim vno anno aut etiam saeculo philosophica scientia est suis absoluta numeris.
units.tr: I answer: if they followed the light of nature rightly, they often displayed to us something admirable; if they strayed from it, let the error be corrected. And now in us, who wish to be seen as regenerate Christians, let the light of grace and the Spirit be joined with the light of nature. Let the two joined together remove the blemishes of the Ethnics and supply what their ignorance lacked. For philosophical science is not brought to completion in one year, or even in one century.

units.la: Deinde assumptio loquitur de humana philosophia, rerumque humanarum scientia.
units.tr: Next, the minor premise speaks of human philosophy and the knowledge of human affairs.

units.la: Hic igitur nobis & Philosophiæ fert opem insignis Theologorum distinctio inter res terrenas seu corporales, & res cœlestes seu spirituales, & hinc inter scientiam ac doctrinam rerum illarum, & harum. Corrupta est natura hominis miserabiliter: at manset tamen intellectus & ratio intelligens & ratiocinans: manset etiam voluntas volens & appetens.
units.tr: Here the notable distinction of the theologians helps philosophy as well: between earthly or bodily things and heavenly or spiritual things, and hence between the science and teaching of the former and of the latter. The nature of man is miserably corrupted, but nevertheless the intellect remains, reason understanding and reasoning, and the will remains willing and desiring.

units.la: Mens non intelligit nec vult spiritualia voluntas, id est, quæ legis & Euangelii spirituali intellectu & visu constant, saluti hominis diuinitus destinata: at mens interim Dei beneficio intelligit terrena & humana, voluntas suopte nutu vult. Sic Enoch filius Cain politicam congregationem ordinasse, Iubal Musicam organicam inuenisse, Iubal Cain operarum fabrilium in ære auctor dicitur, & alii aliarum artium & liberalium & mechanicarum auctores perhibentur. Hic non tantum considerat pius generalem Dei actionem in non renatis, quos Deus excitat ad humani generis, & præcipue electorum commodum, vt has vel iistas artes inueniant, & excolant: sed etiam quandam specialem Dei ex certo eius consilio prodeuntem actionem, qua etiam in domis communibus & ad salutem non pertinentibus, suam vnicuique donorum mensuram admetitur, vt testatur ipsa quotidiana experientia.
units.tr: The mind does not understand, nor does the will desire, spiritual things, that is, those which consist in the spiritual understanding and perception of the Law and the Gospel, divinely destined for the salvation of man. But meanwhile, by God's benefit, the mind understands earthly and human things, and the will wills them by its own nod. Thus Enoch, son of Cain, is said to have set up a political community; Jubal is said to have invented organ music; Tubal-cain is named the author of working in bronze and iron; and others are reported as authors of other arts, liberal and mechanical. Here the pious man considers not only God's general action in the unregenerate, whom God stirs up for the benefit of the human race and especially of the elect, so that they may discover and cultivate these or those arts; but also a certain special action of God, proceeding from his certain counsel, by which, even in common matters not pertaining to salvation, a measure of his gifts is allotted to each person, as daily experience itself attests.

units.la: Diuinitus igitur intellectus hominis non renati etiam in mundanis rebus expolitur, licet accedat, vt medium, studium & exercitium. Sic Deo tribuitur intelligentia artificiose multa ad tabernaculum artificiose fabricandi, Exod. 31. quam ipse communicarat cum artificibus ad id destinatis. Adeoque est ex Dei donorum diuersa collatione, ingeniorum magnum discrimen: imo virtutum externarum & politicarum in variis Rerumpub. administratoribus ingens discrimen videtur.
units.tr: Thus the intellect of the unregenerate man is divinely refined even in worldly matters, although study and practice are added as the means. So skill in artfully making many things for the tabernacle is attributed to God, Exod. 31, which he himself had imparted to the craftsmen destined for that work. And so, from the diverse distribution of God's gifts, there is a great difference of talents; indeed, a great difference of external and civil virtues is evident among the various administrators of commonwealths.

units.la: Iam itaque Prosyllogismi vitium apparet, quia est impertinens. Assumptio agit de humana Philosophia, & rerum humanarum, externarum ac terrenarum scientia ac tractatione. At testimonia Prosyllogistica testantur de rebus diuinis ac coelestibus spirituali intellectu & actu constantibus ad salutem hominum.
units.tr: Now the fault of the prosyllogism is clear, because it is irrelevant. The minor premise deals with human philosophy and the knowledge and treatment of human, external and earthly things. But the prosyllogistic testimonies speak of divine and heavenly things, which consist in spiritual understanding and action for the salvation of men.

units.la: Instantia I.
units.tr: Instance I.

units.la: Omne figmentum cogitationis cordis humani tantum malum est omni die.
units.tr: Every imagination of the thoughts of the human heart is only evil all the day.

units.la: Philosophia humana est figmentum cogitationis cordis humani.
units.tr: Human philosophy is an imagination of the thoughts of the human heart.

units.la: Ergo Philosophia tantum mala est omni die.
units.tr: Therefore philosophy is only evil all the day.

units.la: Respon. Propositio est Dei ipsius verbum: Sed figmentum cogitationis cordis humani malum est & intelligitur, quatenus est cordis humani depravati, gratia Spiritus sancti destituti, & sibi suaeque prauitati derelicti. Iam autem Philosophia vera & artes humaniores non sunt merum figmentum cogitationum cordis humani, & quidem qua depravatum est, sed ex singusingulari & peculiari Dei actione in impiis etiam agente, dona Dei (vt supra vidimus.) Neque enim prauitas cordis & cogitationis corruptio eas genuit, sed rationis reliquae, Dei beneficio, & iudicii, singularia obseruantis & inducentis dexteriore operatione, quam Deus etiam ad humani generis salutem nobis immerito regit & iuuat. Deinde Moses hic caulam diluuii ostendit, adeo fuisse eam scilicet grauem vt extremo totius orbis exitio demerendo abunde sufficeret: antea quidem eam monstrauit in externis sceleribus, nunc hic altius conscendit, fuisse scilicet homines illos non habitu modo, & male viuendi consuetudine peruersos, sed interiorem malitiam altius infixam fuisse eorum cordibus, quam vt spes vlla resipiscentiae esset. Sensus itaque est, mundum tunc obduruisse in sua malitia, & adeo non redire ad bonam frugem, vel aliquem poenitentiae affectum concipere, vt continuo temporis progressu deterior fiat. Et quidem non esse paucorum dierum illam insaniam, sed obstinatam prauitatem, quam filii quasi hereditario iure acceptam a parentibus ad nepotes transmitterent.
units.tr: Reply: The proposition is God's own word. But the imagination of the thoughts of the human heart is evil, and is understood to be so insofar as the heart is depraved, destitute of the grace of the Holy Spirit, and abandoned to itself and its own wickedness. True philosophy and the humaner arts, however, are not mere imaginations of the thoughts of the human heart, at least not insofar as it is depraved. They are gifts of God, arising from God's particular and peculiar action, which also works in the impious (as we saw above). For neither the wickedness of the heart nor the corruption of thought produced them. They came from the remnant of reason, by God's kindness and judgment, which observes and induces particular things by a more favourable operation, and by which God also governs and aids the human race for its salvation, though we do not deserve it. Next, Moses here shows the cause of the flood: it was so grave that it was enough to bring about the destruction of the whole world at its extreme. Earlier he had shown this wickedness in outward crimes; now he goes deeper, showing that those men were perverted not merely in their habits and the custom of living badly, but that an inner malice was fixed more deeply in their hearts, so that there was no hope of repentance. The sense, therefore, is that the world had then grown hardened in its wickedness, and so far from returning to good conduct or conceiving any feeling of repentance, it became worse as time went on. And that madness was not of a few days' duration, but a stubborn perversity, which the sons received from their parents as if by hereditary right and passed on to their grandchildren.

units.la: Loquitur igitur proprie textus de iis, de quibus dicit vidisse Iehouam, quod multa esset malitia in terra. Bene tamen & congruenter elicitur generalis doctrina, de corde omnium hominum nascentium prauo. Sic Dauid cum dicit omnes defeciuisse, inutiles esse factos, neminem esse qui bonum agat, seculi quidem sui impietatem deplorat: Paulus tamen haec trahit ad omnes omnium ætatum mortales, & quidem merito, Roman. 3. An vero omnibus hominibus tanta peruersitas cordis, tanta prauitas & pertinacia in externis & internis flagitiis ac vitiis sit tribuenda, quanta istius temporis hominib. diluuio perdendis, norint Theologi: Assumptum nos simpliciter Syllogismi non damus.
units.tr: The text, then, properly speaks of those of whom it says that the LORD saw that the wickedness of man was great in the earth. Yet a general doctrine concerning the wicked heart of all men at birth is drawn from it, and rightly and fittingly so. Thus David, when he says that all have gone aside, have become unprofitable, and that there is none who does good, is bewailing the impiety of his own age; yet Paul draws these words to all mortals of all ages, and rightly so (Rom. 3). Whether such great perversity of heart, such depravity and obstinacy in outward and inward crimes and vices, is to be attributed to all men, as was the case with those men of that time who were to be destroyed by the flood, let the theologians determine. We do not simply grant the assumption of the syllogism.

units.la: Elenchus Sophismatis 5, ex Ecclesiaste cap. 1.
units.tr: Refutation of Sophism 5, from Ecclesiastes chapter 1.

units.la: RES omnes difficiles sunt, nec potest quisquam eas oratione explicare. Non satiatur oculus videndo, nec auris expletur audiendo. Item: Animum applicui ad quaerendum & ad sapienter inuestigandum, quicquid sub cælo fit. Hanc enim molestam occupationem exhibuit Deus humano generi, ut se in ea occupet. Vidi ergo omnia quae vidi sub sole vana esse & molestiae plena. Itē: Cogitaui, &c. Magnam mihi sapientiae & scientiae vim comparabo. Adieci ergo ad cognitionem tum sapientiae tum stultitiae: Sed intellexi id quoque esse animi molestiam. Quia in multa sapientia, multa molestia est. Et qui cumulat sapientiam cumulat dolorem.
units.tr: ALL things are difficult, and no one can explain them in speech. The eye is not satisfied with seeing, nor the ear filled with hearing. Likewise: I applied my mind to seek and to investigate wisely whatever is done under heaven. For God has given this troublesome business to the human race, that they should be occupied with it. I saw therefore that all the things I saw under the sun are vanity and full of vexation. Likewise: I thought, etc. I shall acquire for myself great power of wisdom and knowledge. I added therefore to the knowledge both of wisdom and of folly. But I understood that this too is a vexation of spirit. For in much wisdom is much grief, and he who increases knowledge increases sorrow.

units.la: Hinc ita colligitur.
units.tr: From this it is concluded as follows.

units.la: Quicquid vanū est, id in scholis & templis Christianorum nec locum nec vsum inuenit. Philosophia humana est vana: quia est sapientia humanarum rerum studium. Hoc autem vanum est attestante sapientissimo Solomone.
units.tr: Whatever is vain finds neither place nor use in the schools and churches of Christians. Human philosophy is vain, because it is the pursuit of wisdom about human things. Now this is vain, as the most wise Solomon attests.

units.la: Nam quod est difficile, insatiabile, molestiae plenum, doloris cumulatio, id homini vanum: praesertim cū nomine vanitatis insigniat illud Solomon.
units.tr: For what is difficult, insatiable, full of vexation, and an accumulation of sorrow, is vain to man, especially since Solomon marks it with the name of vanity.

units.la: Atqui studium Philosophiae seu humanae sapientiae est difficile, insatiabile, plenum molestiae, dolorem cumulans: vti ex testimoniis Solomonis patet. Vanum igitur.
units.tr: But the pursuit of philosophy, or of human wisdom, is difficult, insatiable, full of vexation, and heaps up sorrow, as is clear from the testimonies of Solomon. Therefore it is vain.

units.la: Exulet itaque Philosophia à Christianorum scholis, & templis.
units.tr: Let philosophy therefore be banished from the schools and churches of Christians.

units.la: Responsio.
units.tr: Reply.

units.la: Syllogismi & prosyllogismi assumptio fallit deceptione Dicti non simpliciter tanquam simpliciter. Sapientia enim rerum humanarum non simpliciter vana hic dici potest.
units.tr: The assumption of the syllogism and of the prosyllogism falls into the fallacy of the dictum, treating what is said in a qualified sense as if it were said simply. For the wisdom of human things cannot here be called vain simply.

units.la: Sapientia enim Solomonis Dei dono & munere acquisita miris laudibus extollitur in libro sapientiae. Deinde fuit ista sapientia & scientia Dei singulare donum. 1. Reg. 3. ait Deus: Ecce faciam iuxta verba tua, & dabo tibi cor sapiens & intelligens. 2. Paral. 9. At ita rex Solomon omnes terrae opibus & sapientia superavit. 1. Reg. 4. Dedit autem Deus sapientiam & intelligentiam admodum magnam Solomoni, & latitudinem cordis, secundum arenam, quae est iuxta littus maris. Et maior fuit sapientia eius sapientia mundi orientalium & Aegyptiorum, &c. Dei autem donum per se non est vanum.
units.tr: For the wisdom of Solomon, acquired as the gift and favour of God, is extolled with wonderful praises in the Book of Wisdom. Moreover, that wisdom and knowledge was a singular gift of God. In 1 Kings 3 God says: Behold, I will do according to your words, and I will give you a wise and understanding heart. In 2 Chronicles 9: and thus King Solomon surpassed all the kings of the earth in riches and wisdom. In 1 Kings 4: And God gave Solomon wisdom and understanding exceedingly great, and breadth of heart, like the sand that is on the seashore. And his wisdom surpassed the wisdom of all the people of the east and of Egypt, etc. But a gift of God is not vain in itself.

units.la: Quaestio proposita est Solomoni de vanitate tate & miseria hominum, in iis præcipue rebus ac studiis in quibus homines suam esse felicitatem positam existimant, cuiusmodi numerantur & disputantur 1. humana sapientia. 2. opes. 3. honores, potentia, & voluptates, atque horum omnium parandorum studium. Hic igitur primum agit de cognitionis & sapientiæ humanæ studio: idque vanum & miserum ostendit, tum comparate ratione summi ac veri boni, tū quatenus in eo homines summæ sibi felicitatis arcem collocant.
units.tr: The question put to Solomon concerned the vanity and misery of men, especially in those things and pursuits in which men think their happiness lies. Among these are, and are discussed: (1) human wisdom; (2) riches; (3) honours, power, and pleasures; and the pursuit of obtaining all of these. Here, then, he first treats of the pursuit of human knowledge and wisdom, and shows it to be vain and wretched, both when compared with the highest and true good, and insofar as men place in it the citadel of their supreme happiness.

units.la: Ergo non simpliciter, sed secundū quid reprehendit sapientiā humanā, nec damnat per se artes & scientias, quas sciuit esse dona Dei & vitæ humanæ ornamenta atque præsidia, in quibus grata de Deo fama sparsa est, vt ait Plato. Sciuit ipse pro tanta sapientia Solomon hominem conditum esse à Deo & in hoc mundo collocatum, vt esset operum Dei spectator, vt ex operum contemplatione in opificis eiusque sapientiæ, potentię, & bonitatis cognitionem & admirationem perduceretur. Ideoque sobria obseruatio & animaduersio ordinis & artis in mundi opificio, quam continent artes, & vtilis & necessaria est. Non igitur artes bonas earumve studium hic reprehendit Salomon, sed ostendere conatur, sapientiam humanam, quantacunque sit, non tamen vanitatis expertem esse: & eam quam in hoc mundo consequitur homo, si ad vitæ alterius sapientiam conferatur, stultitiam & miseriam esse. Vnde & Paulus 1. Corinth. 13. vers. 9. & 12. af12.affirmat nos nunc ex parte tantum cognoscere, & quasi per speculum & per aenigma cernere. Et Isocrates in Apologia: Videtur mihi, inquit, o Athenienses, revera solus Deus sapiens: humanam autem sapientiam parui, imo nihili faciendam esse. Et Arist. lib. 2. Metaph. cap. 1. vt, inquit, noctuarum oculi ad lumen diurnum affecti sunt: sic animi nostri se habent ad ea, quae in natura sunt clarissima: & Sapient. 9. versi. 13. Quis hominum consilia Dei intelligit? Nam cogitationes mortalium sunt infirmae: & opiniones nostrae sunt fallaces. Corpus enim corruptioni obnoxium, aggravat animam, & terrenum domicilium plenam cogitationis mentem deprimit. Lactantius lib. 1. in praefatione: Philosophi, inquit, non sunt adepti id quod volebant, & operam simul & industriam perdiderunt. Quia veritas, id est, arcanum illud summi Dei, qui fecit omnia, ingenio & sensibus propriis comprehendi non potest. Alioqui nihil inter Deu hominemq; distaret: si consilia & dispositiones illius Maiestatis aeterna cogitatio assequeretur humana. Et lib. 7. cap. 21. Si potest homo intelligere divina: potest & facere. Nam intelligere est quasi e vestigio subsequi. Non potest autem facere, quae Deus facit. Quia mortali corpore indutus est. Ergo nec intelligere quidem potest, quae fecit Deus. Et paulo post: Homo quia subiectus est passioni: subiecta est & sapientia eius errori. Et sicut hominis vitam res multa impediunt, quo minus possit esse perpetua: ita sapientiam quoque eius multis rebus impediri necesse est: quo minus in perspicienda penitus veritate perfecta sit. Est ergo cognitio & sapientia humana quae in hac vita comparatur paratur tenuis & exigua admodum : si ad Academia coelestis sapientiam conferatur. Hic enim exteriorem tantum rerum faciem aspicimus. Causas & naturas proprias rerum singularum non intelligimus. Estque cognitio nostra similis inspectioni, qua in cortice tantum rerum haret, nec in ipsam rerum naturam ingreditur. Ac proinde naturale hominis discendi cognoscendique studium & desiderium, mundo minime expletur.
units.tr: Therefore he does not condemn human wisdom simply, but in a certain respect; nor does he condemn the arts and sciences in themselves, which he knew to be gifts of God and ornaments and safeguards of human life, in which, as Plato says, a good report of God has been spread abroad. Solomon, for all his great wisdom, knew that man was created by God and placed in this world so that he might be a spectator of God's works, and that from the contemplation of the works he might be led to the knowledge and admiration of the Maker and of his wisdom, power, and goodness. Therefore a sober observation and attention to the order and art in the workmanship of the world, which the arts contain, is both useful and necessary. Solomon, then, does not here reprehend good arts or the study of them; he tries to show that human wisdom, however great it may be, is nevertheless not free from vanity, and that the wisdom which man attains in this world, if compared with the wisdom of another life, is folly and misery. Hence Paul also affirms (1 Cor. 13:9, 12) that we now know only in part, and see through a mirror and in an enigma. And Isocrates in the Apology: It seems to me, O Athenians, he says, that God alone is truly wise; and that human wisdom is of little worth, or rather must be counted as nothing. And Aristotle, Metaphysics book 2, chapter 1: as the eyes of owls are affected toward the light of day, so are our minds toward the things that are most clear in nature. And Wisdom 9:13: Who among men understands the counsel of God? For the thoughts of mortals are weak, and our opinions are uncertain. For the body, which is subject to corruption, weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind full of thought. Lactantius, book 1, in the preface: The philosophers, he says, have not attained what they wished, and have lost both their labour and their effort. For truth, that is, the secret of the highest God who made all things, cannot be grasped by human ingenuity and one's own senses. Otherwise there would be no difference between God and man, if human thought could reach the counsels and dispositions of that eternal Majesty. And book 7, chapter 21: If man can understand divine things, he can also do them. For to understand is almost to follow immediately after. But he cannot do what God does, because he is clothed in a mortal body. Therefore he cannot even understand what God has made. And a little later: Because man is subject to passion, his wisdom is also subject to error. And just as many things hinder the life of man so that it cannot be everlasting, so his wisdom must necessarily be hindered by many things, so that it is not perfect in perceiving the truth completely. Therefore the knowledge and wisdom that is acquired by human effort in this life is very thin and small, if it is compared with the wisdom of the heavenly academy. For here we look only at the outward appearance of things. We do not understand the causes and the proper natures of individual things. Our knowledge is like that of one who looks only at the bark of things and does not enter into the nature of the things themselves. And so the natural desire and longing of man to learn and to know is by no means satisfied by the world.

units.la: Atque haec prima est humanae scientiae vanitas, quod imperfecta fit. Non igitur Salomon hoc loco vel res ipsas, vel artes rerum quasi imagines damnat, neque ἀκαταληψίαν Anaxagoream vel Academicam probat aut tradit: sed sapientiae tantum humanae quae in hac vita comparatur, ad coelestem collatae vanitatem ostendit & supercilium Philosophicum deprimere conatur: vt oculos, & animos nostros ad Deum ipsum attollat, vbi coram cernemus, vt ait Paulus 1.Cor.10. id est, plenam & perfectam Dei ipsius & rerum ab ipso conditarum cognitionem consequemur, & consilium Dei de rerum creatione penitus perspiciemus.
units.tr: And this is the first vanity of human learning: it is imperfect. So Solomon here condemns neither things themselves nor the arts as images of things, and he neither approves nor teaches the Anaxagorean or Academic akatalepsia [ἀκαταληψίαν]. He points out only the vanity of the human wisdom that is acquired in this life, set beside heavenly wisdom, and he tries to humble philosophical pride, so that he may lift our eyes and minds up to God himself, where, as Paul says in 1 Cor. 10, we shall see face to face. That is, we shall attain a full and perfect knowledge of God himself and of the things created by him, and we shall thoroughly perceive God's purpose in creating things.

units.la: Misera igitur vanitas sapientiae humanae arguitur non simpliciter, sed 1. quatenus imperfecta. verf. 8. 2. quod eius opera nihil noui fiat aut geratur, quod nō ante in mūdo factum fit & gestum. 3. quod eius opera vetustate atque obliuione tandem deleantur. 4. quod mutilum & prauum eius opera non possit expleri & corrigi. 5. quod molestiam & dolorem pariat. Hinc vero, amice, concludit non esse in ea summum bonum ponendum. Et quis hoc? forte vanus.
units.tr: The vanity of human wisdom is therefore censured not absolutely, but (1) insofar as it is imperfect (v. 8); (2) because its works bring nothing new, and nothing is done or achieved that has not already been done and achieved in the world; (3) because its works are at last destroyed by age and oblivion; (4) because its maimed and crooked works cannot be completed and corrected; and (5) because it brings trouble and grief. From this, my friend, he concludes that the highest good is not to be placed in it. And who would say this? Perhaps some vain person.

units.la: Elenchus 6. Sophismatis ab exemplo Patrum à Philosophia in errores abductorum.
units.tr: Elenchus 6: the sophism from the example of the Fathers, who were led into errors by philosophy.

units.la: Estque hic Classis secunda capientium arma humanæ auctoritatis aduersus Philosophiā.
units.tr: This is the second class, which takes up the weapons of human authority against philosophy.

units.la: HActenus classem primam Philosophiæ arma diuinæ autoritatis, sed male contortæ, disiecimus. Diuinæ quidem autoritatis vis magna in probando, fides immota in credendo, si non adulteretur & detorqueatur, sed si in ea non hominis male affecti cerebrum & vana opinio, sed ipse Spiritus sanctus nobis loquatur.
units.tr: So far I have scattered the first class of weapons, the authority of divine writ, though it was twisted badly. The force of divine authority in proving and the unshaken faith in believing are great, provided it is not corrupted and distorted, and provided that it is not the brain of an ill-disposed man and his vain opinion that speaks in it, but the Holy Spirit himself speaking to us.

units.la: Sequitur Classis altera, quæ humanæ autoritatis tela iaculatur in Philosophiæ corpus.
units.tr: There follows the second class, which hurls the darts of human authority against the body of philosophy.

units.la: Humana est autoritate inferior multa: Et nisi diuina fuerit munita, & rationum bonarum firmamentis suffulta, parum autoritatis & fidei meretur apud eos, qui non ad hominum opiniones, sed ad rerum veritatem philosophantur.
units.tr: Much human authority is inferior. Unless it is fortified by divine authority and supported by the firm props of good reasons, it deserves little authority or belief among those who philosophize not according to human opinions but according to the truth of things.

units.la: Autoritas autem humana præcipue est Patrum sanctorum qui in primitiua & eam secuta Ecclesia floruerunt.
units.tr: Human authority, however, is chiefly that of the holy Fathers, who flourished in the primitive Church and in the Church that followed it.

units.la: Hi autipsi Philosophiæ placitis, quibus nimium tribuerunt, sunt in perniciosos præcipitati errores; aut aperte Philosophiam damnandam censuerunt. Ex primo membro hic consuitur Syllogismus:
units.tr: Yet these very men, through the tenets of philosophy to which they gave too much weight, have fallen into pernicious errors, or have openly judged that philosophy ought to be condemned. From the first member the following syllogism is put together:

units.la: Cuius ductu & studio magis in errorum perniciosorum Syrtes & scopulos abducimur & impellimur, id vtique homini Christiano parui faciendum, imo abiiciendum est.
units.tr: That by whose guidance and zeal we are led and driven more into the quicksands and rocks of pernicious errors is surely to be held of little account by a Christian man, indeed to be cast away.

units.la: Atqui ductu & studio Philosophiæ in errorum perniciosorum Syrtes & scopulos abducimur & impellimur, Imo, inquiunt, quanto magis excolitur ratio humana philosophicis studiis, tanto armatior aduersus Ecclesiam, eiusque doctrinam prodit.
units.tr: But by the guidance and zeal of philosophy we are led and driven into the quicksands and rocks of pernicious errors. Indeed, they say, the more human reason is cultivated by philosophical studies, the better armed it comes forth against the Church and its doctrine.

units.la: Non itaque est tanti faciendum studium Philosophiæ, sed potius Christiano fugiendum.
units.tr: Therefore the study of philosophy is not to be valued so highly; rather, it is to be shunned by a Christian.

units.la: Assumptum probant exemplis Iustini Philosophi, Clemetis & Origenis, qui ideo, quod Philosophiæ studiis fuerint antea consecrati, in maximos & plurimos prolapsi sint errores.
units.tr: They prove the assumption by the examples of Justin the philosopher, Clement and Origen, who, because they had been devoted to the study of philosophy beforehand, fell into the greatest and most numerous errors.

units.la: Iustinus enim educatus dicitur in studiis Philosophiæ Platonicæ. Proinde cum in Platonis schola viguit magnifica illa de ἀυτεξουσίῳ, siue libertate voluntatis humanæ opinio, ideo libertatem ad ipsa pietatis adeoque Deo placentia centia opera transfert. Socratem μετὰ τῆ λόγῳ vixisse, & ἐπὶ μέρος agnouisse Christum asseuerare non dubitat. Corporale regnum electorum post resurrectionē statuit: angelos ite mulierū amore victos procreasse dæmones, &c.
units.tr: Justin, it is said, was educated in the studies of Platonic philosophy. Accordingly, since that splendid opinion about free will (autexousion [αὐτεξουσίῳ]), or the liberty of the human will, flourished in Plato's school, he transfers liberty to the very works of piety and therefore of those pleasing to God. He does not hesitate to assert that Socrates lived with the Word [μετὰ τῆ λόγῳ] and knew Christ in part [ἐπὶ μέρος]. He holds that after the resurrection there will be a bodily kingdom of the elect; that angels, overcome by love of women, begot demons, and so on.

units.la: Responsio.
units.tr: Reply.

units.la: Propositio vera est, si quid per se abducit in errores, si quid vero ex accidenti, & per aliud, id neutiquam per se est abiiciendum. Assumptio de Philosophia loquens, falsa est si loquitur de studio abducente in errores per se: vera accipiatur seductio per aliud, & per accidens facta. Philosophiæ enim veræ studium non seducit nec errare facit, sed in veritatis & amorem & viam deducit, & errore liberat, si rectè & sobrie tractetur. Assumptionis Paralogismus est, non Prosyllogismus. Videamus pudendum eius errorem: Iustinus, Clemens, & Origenes fuerunt Philosophi. At iidem errores errarunt magnos. Quid ritè hinc concluditur? Ergo quidam Philosophi errarunt. Non autem hæc prodit conclusio: Philosophi, qua Philosophi errarunt, vel: Philosophia fecit eos errare. Sicut nec hoc: At illi fuerunt Christiani, & quidem Doctores Ecclesiæ. Ergo qua Christiani, & qua Doctores errarunt. Deinde non modo errarunt ex Doctoribus Ecclesiæ, qui Philosophi fuerunt: sed etiam qui Philosophiam non salutarunt, videantur doctrinæ inclinationes in omnibus Centuriis Magdeburgensium Centuriatorū. Denique non est consequens: Isti patres errarunt. runt. Ergo Philosophia fecit eos errare. Philosophia enim vera errorum non est genitrix, sed expultrix. Cur non ita argutaris: At fuerunt homines: Ergo qua homines errarunt. Mirifice oculati sumus in aliorum cognoscendis naevis, & insignes Arithmetici in aliorum numerandis lapsibus. Cogitemus nullum fuisse vnquam repertū ingenium omnibus numeris absolutum, quin suos habuerit errores & naevos.
units.tr: The proposition is true if something leads into error of its own nature; but if it does so accidentally and through something else, it is by no means to be rejected on its own account. The assumption, speaking of philosophy, is false if it means a study that leads into error of its own nature; it is true if the seduction is understood as happening through something else and by accident. For the study of true philosophy does not seduce or make men err, but leads them into love and the way of truth, and frees them from error, if it is handled rightly and soberly. The assumption is a paralogism, not a prosyllogism. Let us look at its shameful error. Justin, Clement and Origen were philosophers. But these same men fell into great errors. What is rightly concluded from this? That some philosophers erred. But this conclusion does not follow: that they erred as philosophers, or that philosophy made them err. Nor does this follow: they were Christians, and indeed teachers of the Church; therefore they erred as Christians and as teachers. Moreover, it is not only teachers of the Church who were philosophers that have erred; the tendencies of doctrine in all the Centuries of the Magdeburg Centuriators also show that some who did not hail philosophy have erred. Finally, it does not follow: those Fathers erred; therefore philosophy made them err. For true philosophy is not the mother of errors but their expeller. Why do you not reason this way: they were men; therefore they erred as men? We are wonderfully sharp-sighted in noticing the blemishes of others, and remarkable calculators in counting the slips of others. Let us reflect that no talent has ever been found that was perfect in every respect, but that each has had its own errors and blemishes.

units.la: Sed primum Iustinum Christi Philosophum & martyrem videamus. Is dicitur alicubi errasse. Esto. At ex Platonis schola secum asportauit eos errores. Esto. At vero, non vt Philosophi, sed vt hominis Ethnici. Erravit Plato, eiusque sectatores, non sane, vt Philosophi, sed vt homines veritatem non vbique assequentes, quique alicubi euanescunt in suis ratiocinationibus. In libero arbitrio erravit. Sed heus, censor, vspiam non vbique. In paraenesi enim ad Graecos ait: Neque enim natura vel ingenio humano res tam sublimes & diuinas hominibus assequi est possibile: Sed eo, quod coelitus in viros sanctos descendit, opus est gratuito dono. Caro prorsus summus, inquit in Epistola ad Zenam, nec quicquam in nobis habitat boni. In defensad Anton. Vt creatio, ita regeneratio est diuinae gratiae. Vspiam aberrauit à sinceritate huius doctrinae: sed vide quaesō quibus argumentis: i.est, prophetę docent pro operum meritis vnicuiq; retribui.2. Alioqui homo nō fuerit in causa qualiūcunq; factorum. 3. Homo idem ad contraria subin- de transit. 4. Homo à Deo est creatus, vt arbo- res & quadrupedes. 5. quia Deus dicit: Lauami- ni, mundi estote.
units.tr: But first let us look at Justin, the Christian philosopher and martyr. He is said to have erred somewhere. Granted. But he carried those errors with him from Plato's school. Granted. Yet not as a philosopher, but as an Gentile man. Plato erred, and his followers too, not indeed as philosophers, but as men who did not everywhere attain the truth, and who somewhere vanish in their own reasonings. He erred on free will. But look here, critic, not everywhere. For in his Exhortation to the Greeks he says: "Neither by nature nor by human ingenuity is it possible for men to attain things so sublime and divine; there is need of a gratuitous gift that has descended from heaven upon holy men." In the letter to Zena he says: "We are altogether flesh, and nothing good dwells in us." In the Defence to Antoninus: "As creation, so regeneration is of divine grace." Somewhere he strayed from the purity of this doctrine; but please see with what arguments. These are: (1) the prophets teach that each is repaid according to the merits of his works; (2) otherwise man would not be the cause of any works whatsoever; (3) man passes back and forth to contraries; (4) man was created by God, like trees and quadrupeds; (5) because God says: "Wash yourselves, be clean."

units.la: Hic agnoscimus paralogismos, at non omnes, ex Philosophia. Imo ideo non philoso- phice disputauit quia non logice. Neque sane hominis, & quidé præceptoris Ethnici, error, est ipsius Philosophiæ error. Deinde Iustinus fauit nimium Socrati, & quis nõ iure communis humanitatis? Christum, ait, agnouisse, & μετὰ τῆς λόγω vixisse. Esto: Minus vera si est Iustini sententia: Laudetur humanior asse- ctus, qui in multis harmostis non est hodie vel erga fratres. Sed num ideo vt Philoso- phus, aut ipsa Philosophia peccauit?
