An non & hodie inuenias, qui cum Melchisedecum, Abimelecum, Ruth Moabitidem, Rachab Chanaanitidem, Reginam Sabæ, Hyram, Ty- rium, Naaman Syrum, Niniuen Assyriorum ciuitatem in catalogo Christianorum esse docuerunt, eodem & iure Socratem esse volunt in eum referendum. Hiccine sola Philoso- phia, & quidem vera in culpa est? Denique corporale regnum & Angelorum concubi- tum non ex Philosophia, sed potius ex somno Iudeorum hausit.
units.tr: Here we recognise paralogisms, but not all of them come from philosophy. Indeed, he did not argue philosophically because he did not argue logically. Nor, truly, is the error of a man, and of a Gentile teacher at that, the error of philosophy itself. Next, Justin was too fond of Socrates, and who is not, by the right of common humanity? He says Socrates knew Christ and lived with the Word. Granted: if Justin's opinion is less true, let his more humane disposition be praised, which in many harsh men today is not even shown toward brethren. But did he sin as a philosopher, or did philosophy itself sin? Do you not find even today people who teach that Melchizedek, Abimelech, Ruth the Moabitess, Rahab the Canaanitess, the Queen of Sheba, Hiram the Tyrian, Naaman the Syrian, and Nineveh, the city of the Assyrians, belong in the catalogue of Christians, and who by the same right want Socrates to be counted among them? Is philosophy alone, and true philosophy at that, to blame for this? Finally, the bodily kingdom and the intercourse of angels were drawn not from philosophy but rather from the dreams of the Jews.

units.la: In huius viri scriptis inuenio plus candoris & pietatis, q forte omnes eius reprehensores habent. Quomodo fuerit vir iste sanctus, p Christi gloria egregie philosophans erga Græco-rum rum Ethnicam sapientiam (quam dicis Philosophiam ipse ignorans quid sit Philosophia) affectus ostendunt primo ipsius ad Graecos Paraenesis, cuius haec est generalis dissertatio: Quae religio praestantiores habet autores, & vetustior est, ea & verior est. Christiana religio habet praestantiores autores, & est vetustior Ethnica. Ergo est verior.
units.tr: I find more candour and piety in this man's writings than perhaps all his critics have. That this holy man philosophised outstandingly for the glory of Christ, and what his attitude was toward the Greeks' Gentile wisdom (which you call philosophy, though you do not know what philosophy is), is shown first by his Exhortation to the Greeks, whose general argument is this: The religion that has the more excellent authors and is older is also the truer. The Christian religion has the more excellent authors and is older than the Gentile religion. Therefore it is the truer.

units.la: Secundo defensio Christianorum ad Senatum Romanum, vbi tria agit. 1. Conqueritur Christianos iniquissime ad supplicia rapi ob solum nomen causa incognita. 2. Refutat ea, quae ipsis a gentilibus obiiciebantur. 3. Petit vt promulgare velit Senatus hanc Apologiam.
units.tr: Second, the Defence of the Christians to the Roman Senate, in which he does three things. 1. He complains that Christians are most unjustly dragged off to punishment for the name alone, the cause unknown. 2. He refutes the charges that the Gentiles brought against them. 3. He asks the Senate to be willing to publish this Apology.

units.la: Tertio idem offendit defensio Christianorum ad Antonium Pium Imperat. quae etiam orat ne gentiles puniant Christianos incognita causa.
units.tr: Third, the same Defence to the Emperor Antoninus Pius also makes the same point. It likewise begs that the Gentiles not punish Christians when the cause is unknown.

units.la: Quarto patet hoc ex initio Tryphonis, vbi ipse primo ait, Magnam esse Philosophiae dignitatem: Sed tamen nihil Philosophos Ethnicos certi de Deo nosse: patere id ex Platonis dogmatibus, qui tum de Deo, tum de animae natura, nihil certi, falsa multa docuerit.
units.tr: Fourth, this is evident from the beginning of Trypho, where he first says that philosophy has great dignity, but that the Gentile philosophers know nothing certain about God. This appears from the doctrines of Plato, who taught much that was false, and nothing certain, both about God and about the nature of the soul.

units.la: Itaque (attende amator & censor Iustini & eius Philosophiae) solam Christianam Philosophiam eiusmodi esse dicit, ex qua vera rerum diuinarum & humanarum cognitio sit haurienda. Primum igitur quantum profanae Ethnicorum Philosophiae tribuerit, hinc constat. Non itaque tanti eam fecit, vt pro eius erroribus depugnarit aduersus sanam doctrinam. nam. Deinde opponit eam Christianæ Philosophiæ & Theologiæ, ipse interim sanam & veram Philosophiam & amans & vsurpans: quia & Philosophus mansit & martyr Christi pro Christo & philosophando & moriendo factus est. A Græcorum vana Philosophia desciuit ad Christianorum sanam Philosophiam, vti se excusat in oratione ad Græcos exponens multas causas, cur ab ipsis desciuerit. Audiamus eas. Quia nihil sanctum in eorum ritibus. Quia Poetarum scripta plena sint rabie, & vinolenta quadam petulantia. Abusus hic est bonæ per se poeseos, & malignorum vitia sunt, non artis. Nam tota, inquit, Rhapsodia Homeri, ἀρχὴ καὶ τέλος γυνή. Theogonia Hesiodi nugax est. Dii Græcorum libidinosi, homicidæ, adulteri, &c. Ipse interim, inquam, Christianus Philosophus factus mansit. Hæc de Iustino philosophante martyre Christi.
units.tr: Therefore (note this, lover and critic of Justin and of his philosophy) he says that only Christian philosophy is of such a kind that from it the true knowledge of divine and human things is to be drawn. Hence it is clear how much he attributed to the profane philosophy of the Gentiles. He did not esteem it so highly that he fought for its errors against sound doctrine. Then he sets it against Christian philosophy and theology, while himself loving and using sound and true philosophy. For he remained a philosopher, and became a martyr of Christ, both by philosophizing and by dying for Christ. He turned from the vain philosophy of the Greeks to the sound philosophy of the Christians, as he excuses himself in his address to the Greeks, setting out many reasons why he left them. Let us hear them. Because there is nothing holy in their rites. Because the writings of the poets are full of rage and a certain drunken wantonness. This is an abuse of good poetry in itself; the vices belong to the wicked, not to the art. For, he says, the whole Rhapsody of Homer is "woman [γυνή] the beginning and end [ἀρχὴ καὶ τέλος]". The Theogony of Hesiod is trifling. The gods of the Greeks are lustful, murderers, adulterers, and so on. Meanwhile he himself, I say, remained a Christian philosopher. These things concern Justin, the philosophizing martyr of Christ.

units.la: Clementi quidam sunt iniquiores, eo quod pluris fecerit Philosophiam, siquidem frequens in adolescentia auditor optimi viri Pantæni excoluit animum omnis politioris literaturæ disciplina. Fuit itaque & Philosophus & Theologus: quia vero errauit, misera illis errauit tantum Philosophia. Clementis errores satis crassos agnoscimus, vt quod secundas nuptias vocat scortationem. At ex qua Philosophia huius erroris succum exsuxit? Deinde sufficientes hominibus esse vires, vt possint obedire mandatis, docet Christi in carnem aduentu. At Aristoteles istam & libertatem facultatem docet in Ethicis. At non qua Philosophus, sed qua homo Spiritu Dei destitutus. Neque vero ex Christi aduentu hoc docet. Tertio Christum hominem putauit fuisse impatibilem. Errauit ne hic Philosophia Clementis: Phantasia sane. At inquis est philosophicis visus argumentis. Non profecto logicis, sed alogis & sophisticis, ideo nec philosophicis, non argumentis, sed vanitatis incantamentis. Quarto docet quosdam ante Christū iuste viuentes seruatos esse per legem vel Philosophiam, sed defuisse eis fidem in Christum, quare in inferno expectasse Christi aduetum. Error hic, at non ex Philosophia proprie ortus est. Tribuit ei homo nimis Clemens Philosophis honestis, licet Ethnicis effectum non competens. Sophista non Philosophus erravit Clemens, &c.
units.tr: Some are more unfair to Clement, because he valued philosophy more highly. For, being a frequent hearer of the excellent man Pantaenus in his youth, he cultivated his mind in every discipline of the finer literature. He was therefore both philosopher and theologian. But because he erred, it was only philosophy that erred, to its misfortune. We recognize Clement's errors as rather gross, such as calling second marriages fornication. But from which philosophy did he suck the juice of this error? Next, that men have sufficient strength to obey the commandments, he teaches from the coming of Christ in the flesh. But Aristotle teaches this freedom and ability in his Ethics, though not as a philosopher, but as a man deprived of the Spirit of God. Nor indeed does he teach it from the coming of Christ. Third, he thought that Christ as man was impassible. Did Clement's philosophy err here? Phantasy, certainly. But you say it seemed so from philosophical arguments. Surely not logical ones, but illogical and sophistical ones; so not philosophical, not arguments at all, but the charms of vanity. Fourth, he teaches that some who lived righteously before Christ were saved through the law or through philosophy, but lacked faith in Christ, and so waited in hell for the coming of Christ. This error, however, did not arise properly from philosophy. Clement, a man too generous, attributed this to honest philosophers, though it does not fit the Gentiles' achievement. Clement erred as a sophist, not as a philosopher, and so on.

units.la: Hisce Philosophiae oseribus & Clementem obiicientib. non probabitur liber 1. Stromatū, fortasse & in eo errauit Philosophia. In hoc enim disserit 1. de vtilitate publicorum scriptorum. 2. de Philosophiae visu. Tertio de antiquitate doctrinae sacrę, in qua etiam docetur Graecos multa à Mose esse mutuatos. Breuiter excerpam hic argumenta, quibus demonstrat Philosophiam etiam Ethnicam esse vtilem.
units.tr: The first book of the Stromata does not prove the case against those who object to Clement with these charges against philosophy; perhaps philosophy erred in that book too. In it he discourses first on the usefulness of public writings, second on the sight of philosophy, and third on the antiquity of sacred doctrine, where it is also taught that the Greeks borrowed much from Moses. I shall briefly excerpt here the arguments by which he shows that even Gentile philosophy is useful.

units.la: 1. Si, inutilem esse Philosophiam demonstrare, est vtile, ipsa Philosophia est vtilis, sine qua hoc fieri nequit.
units.tr: 1. If to show that philosophy is useless is itself useful, then philosophy itself is useful, since without it this cannot be done.

units.la: 2. Experientia quoque & cognitione ipsa Graecorum Philosophia inutilitas est demonstranda, non verbis tantum.
units.tr: 2. The uselessness of Greek philosophy must be demonstrated also by experience and by knowledge itself, not by words alone.

units.la: 3. Prodest Philosophia ad varie probandum id, quod adducitur, & catechumenis affert admirationem, & precipua dogmata ad auditoris persuasionem deducit.
units.tr: 3. Philosophy serves to prove variously what is adduced, brings admiration to catechumens, and leads the principal doctrines to the persuasion of the hearer.

units.la: 4. Ipsa collatio dogmatum veritatem conciliat.
units.tr: 4. The very comparison of doctrines establishes the truth.

units.la: 5. Philosophia viam munit ad veritatem.
units.tr: 5. Philosophy paves the way to the truth.

units.la: 6. Conducit ad sapientiam, vbi mira sunt allegoria.
units.tr: 6. It leads to wisdom, where there are wonderful allegories.

units.la: 7. Discenda est necessario doctrina arguendi & refellendi, vt Sophistarum fallaces opiniones refutentur. Vnde apparet Philosophiam esse donu Dei. Philosophiam autem dico non Stoicam, nec Platonicam, nec Epicuream, nec Aristotelicam, sed quacunque ab his sectis recte dicta sunt, quae docent iustitiam cum pia scientia, hoc totum selectum voco Philosophiam.
units.tr: 7. The art of arguing and refuting must necessarily be learned, so that the fallacious opinions of the Sophists may be refuted. Hence it appears that philosophy is a gift of God. By philosophy I mean not the Stoic, nor the Platonic, nor the Epicurean, nor the Aristotelian, but whatever has been rightly said by these sects, which teaches justice together with godly knowledge. This whole selection I call philosophy.

units.la: 8. Graeca Philosophia particulam veritatis aeternae ex Theologia discerpsit. Haec ita Clemens non insulse disceptat.
units.tr: 8. Greek philosophy tore off a particle of eternal truth from theology. Clement argues this not unwittily.

units.la: Origenis denique errores, quorum multi sunt, Philosophiae imputantur. Celebre est vetustatis iudicium hoc de Origene. Vbi bene nemo melius. Vbi male nemo peius. Legimus quidem Origenem iuuenem annorum 18. cum in disciplinis, Dialectica, Rhetorica, Musica, Poesi, Arithmetica & reliquis liberaliter institutum, Alexandriae Grammaticam professum, obiterque in schola Pantaeni pietatis & doctrinae Christianae rudimenta docuisse. Legimus eundem in schola inter sacra etiam philosophicas & mathematicas disciplinas discentibus propositisse, & ad artium liberalium cognitionem discipulos adhortatum: Affirmavit uit enim adminiculo earum in explicatione literarum & disputationum opus esse. Triuit perpetuo Platonem, & multos doctos Pythagoricorum Philosophorum commentarios legit. Fuit itaque Philosophus.
units.tr: Finally, the errors of Origen, of which there are many, are charged to philosophy. Famous is the judgment of antiquity about Origen: where good, no one better; where bad, no one worse. We read indeed that Origen, at eighteen years of age, was trained in the disciplines (dialectic, rhetoric, music, poetry, arithmetic and the rest of the liberal arts), that he taught grammar at Alexandria, and that in passing he taught the rudiments of piety and Christian doctrine in the school of Pantaenus. We read that in his school he set before his learners, among sacred subjects, the philosophical and mathematical disciplines, and urged his pupils to a knowledge of the liberal arts, for he affirmed that they were needed for the explanation of letters and disputations. He constantly read Plato and many learned commentaries of the Pythagorean philosophers. He was therefore a philosopher.

units.la: At, inquis, & multos & magnos errauit errores. Fatemur. Pamphilus tamen presbyter in Apologia pro Origene refert imputatos esse ei a maleuolis aliquot errores. Conatur & Rufinus eum defendere. Defendit eum & Socrates ecclesiae historiae lib. 6. At Hieronymus ipsius scripta no fuisse depravata scribit & multos, eosque crassos errores impingit. Esto, fuerit pater monstrosorum errorum. At nunquid eius propterea scientia & eruditio culpanda? nunquid Philosophia in ius vocanda, eique omnia istius hominis vitia irroganda? Abusus est philosophica scientia Origenes, nec ad rerum veritatem, sed ad proprii cerebri figmenta multum videtur in istiusmodi naevis philosophatus. Quid enim, quaeso te, potest non contingere ei, qui propria tropice, & tropica proprie accipit. Maximus hic Rhetoricae & Philosophici instrumenti est abusus. Visus seruetur, tollatur artium abusus. Quis error no potest irrepere eius scriptis, qui stando libros dictat, qui limam non adhibet, cui inuito libri quodammodo extorquetur, cuius libri in Harpias quodammodo incidunt: qui interpretem nancisci tur arbitratu suo, quaedam adimentem, alia adiicientem, nonnulla mutantem. Cuiusmodi candore min translatione librolibrorum quorundam Origenis Ruffinus ipse se fatetur adhibuisse. Sed satis de eiusmodi Philosophis in Theologia naevos suos habentibus. Repetamus paralogismum:
units.tr: But, you say, he erred in many and great errors. We grant it. Yet Pamphilus the presbyter, in his Apology for Origen, reports that some errors were imputed to him by ill-wishers. Rufinus too tries to defend him, and Socrates defends him in Book 6 of the Ecclesiastical History. But Jerome writes that his writings were not corrupted, and charges him with many gross errors. Granted, he may have been the father of monstrous errors. But is his learning and erudition therefore to be blamed? Is philosophy to be summoned to court, and all the vices of that man to be charged to it? Origen abused philosophical learning, and he seems to have philosophized in such blemishes not for the truth of things but for the figments of his own brain. For what, I ask you, can fail to happen to a man who takes literal things tropically and tropical things literally? This is the greatest abuse of the rhetorical and philosophical instrument. Keep the use; remove the abuse of the arts. What error cannot creep into the writings of one who dictates books standing up, who does not apply the file, from whose unwilling hands his books are somehow extorted, whose books somehow fall into the hands of the Harpies, who takes an interpreter at his own discretion, omitting some things, adding others, changing some? Rufinus himself confesses that he applied this kind of candour in translating certain books of Origen. But enough of such philosophers who have blemishes in their theology. Let us repeat the paralogism:

units.la: Qui est Philosophus, & in doctrina fidei errat, eius erroris causa in homine est Philosophia:
units.tr: He who is a philosopher and errs in the doctrine of faith: the cause of that error lies in the man's philosophy.

units.la: At multi sunt Philosophi, & errant in doctrina fidei, ut Origenes, &c. Ergo in multis errorum causa est Philosophia.
units.tr: But many are philosophers and err in the doctrine of faith, as Origen does, etc. Therefore in many cases the cause of error is philosophy.

units.la: Propositionis veritas suspecta admodum est. Erroris enim causa efficiens non est in homine Philosophia vera, sed ignoratio verae Philosophiae, exorbitatio ab eius regulis, qua non philosophamur Rei & Dei veritati convenienter, non recta applicatio & vsurpatio decretorum Philosophiae ad propositas res, adeoque abusus. Huc accedit caro nostra, mēs caeca, cor & affectus peruersi, nimia & stulta ingenii cōfidentia & superbia, Sophisticae argutiae ad ostentationem adhibitae, inuidia, impatientia, autoritas eorū, quos amamus & sequimur, si in animis nostris lateat ignorantia, fluctuatio, curiositas, desideriorum seruitus, instabilitas, negligentia, admiratio personarum, onus peccatorum, facile in errores abducimur. Si propositio vera & constans esset, etiam sic possem concludere. Theologus qui est, & in doctrina aliqua errat, eius erroris causa est Theologia. At multi Theologi errant in aliqua doctrina. Ais & excipis: Disparratio est. Theologia nunquam facit errare, quia est ipsum Dei verbum. Respon. Philosophia etiam sana non potest errare, quatenus veritatis studiū & sapienti- am sequitur, vt sequi debet. Deinde Theologia, qua est Theologia, non errat, qua Orthodoxa, recte docet. At homo Theologia abutens, & verbum Dei non recte intelligens aut detorquens, potest errare. Nec tamen Theologia &verbum Dei est erroris causa, sed homo ignorans & mentem adulterinam verbo Dei affricans. Nec hoc valet : Qui est Theologus, & in actione vitæ errat, eius erroris & lapsus causa est Theologia. Nec valet hoc: Qui est Iureconsultus, & in doctrina fidei errat, eius erroris causa est Iurisprudentia. Vt nec hoc: Qui est Medicus, & errat in doctrina fidei, eius erroris causa est Medicina. Quod replicant, Philosophiam magis veritati Theologiæ resistere, id de vera Philosophia est falsum. Tollantur paganismi, & quicquid cum Dei verbo pugnat, ex corpore doctrinæ Philosophicæ, & par erit vbique ratio. Neque hoc in seculo Christiano sumus Ethnici, sed Christiani: Christiana itaque Philosophia, & Christianæ artes à nobis defenduntur.
units.tr: The truth of the proposition is highly suspect. For the efficient cause of error is not true philosophy in a man, but ignorance of true philosophy, a straying from its rules, by which we do not philosophize in agreement with the truth of the thing and of God; it is incorrect application and use of the principles of philosophy to the matters at hand, and so it is abuse. To this add our flesh, the blind mind, a perverse heart and affections, an excessive and foolish confidence in one's wit, pride, sophistical subtleties used for show, envy, impatience, and the authority of those whom we love and follow. If ignorance, wavering, curiosity, servitude to desires, instability, negligence, admiration of persons, and the burden of sins lie hidden in our minds, we are easily led into error. If the proposition were true and constant, I could conclude in the same way: He who is a theologian and errs in some doctrine: the cause of that error is theology. But many theologians err in some doctrine. You say in reply: the comparison is unequal, since theology never causes error, because it is the very Word of God. I answer: sound philosophy too cannot err, insofar as it pursues the study of truth and wisdom, as it ought to. Again, theology, as theology, does not err; as orthodox, it teaches rightly. But a man who abuses theology, not rightly understanding or twisting the Word of God, can err. Yet theology and the Word of God are not the cause of the error; the cause is the ignorant man who fits an adulterated mind to the Word of God. Nor does this hold: He who is a theologian and errs in the conduct of life: the cause of his error and fall is theology. Nor does this hold: He who is a jurist and errs in the doctrine of faith: the cause of his error is jurisprudence. Nor this: He who is a physician and errs in the doctrine of faith: the cause of his error is medicine. As for their reply, that philosophy resists the truth of theology more, this is false of true philosophy. Let paganism be removed, and whatever fights against the Word of God, from the body of philosophical doctrine, and the reasoning will be equal everywhere. Nor are we Gentiles in this Christian age, but Christians. Christian philosophy and Christian arts are therefore defended by us.

units.la: Elenchus 7. Sophism. ab autoritate Patrum Ecclesiasticorum Philosophiam improbantium & damnantium.
units.tr: Elenchus 7: a sophism from the authority of the ecclesiastical Fathers, who reject and condemn philosophy.

units.la: Quicquid Orthodoxa antiquitas, sancti patres, & Ecclesiæ Doctores tanquam pestilens improbant, & damnant, id vtique nos tanquam Christianæ Reipub. utile & salutare commendare ac tueri non debemus.
units.tr: Whatever orthodox antiquity, the holy Fathers and the teachers of the Church denounce and condemn as pestilential, we certainly ought not to commend or defend as useful and salutary to the Christian commonwealth.

units.la: Atqui Philosophiam Orthodoxa antiquitas & sancti patres unanimi fere consensu tanquam pestilens improbant, increpant & damnant.
units.tr: But orthodox antiquity and the holy Fathers, with almost unanimous consent, denounce, rebuke and condemn philosophy as pestilential.

units.la: ᾿Εξεργασία Assumpti patrum colligit testimonia contra Philos.
units.tr: Exergasia [ἐξεργασία]: the assumption; he gathers the testimonies of the Fathers against philosophy.

units.la: 1. Tertullianus hoc nomine damnat Philosophiam, quod ex ea hæreses producatur & animentur: sicut in libro contra Hermogenem inquit: Philosophorum ingeniis omnes hæreses animari. Ac libro primo aduersus Marcionem Philosophos hæreticorum Patriarchas vocat. Quo nomine & Dialecticam vituperat, in libro de præscriptione hæreticorum, vbi & hoc addit Paulũ Athenis ipso didicisse vsu, quod ad Colossenses scripserat, videte, ne quis vos circumueniat per Philosophiam. Ibidem & paulo ante: Hæ sunt doctrinæ hominum & damoniorum, prurientibus omnibus natæ de ingenio sapientiæ secularis, quam dominus stultitiam vocans, stulta mundi confusione etiam Philosophiæ ipsius elegit. Ea est enim materia sapientiæ secularis, temeraria interpres diuinæ naturæ dispositionis. Ipsæ denique hæreses à Philosophia subornantur. Et in Apologetico sæpe dicit: Nihil posse esse conuenientiæ inter Philosophos & Christianos. Ibidem: Quid simile Philosophis & Christianis? gratiæ discipulus & cœli fama negotiator & tor &
units.tr: 1. Tertullian condemns philosophy on this ground: that heresies are produced and kindled by it. In the book against Hermogenes he says: "All heresies are kindled by the wits of the philosophers." In the first book against Marcion he calls the philosophers "the patriarchs of heretics." On the same ground he also disparages dialectic, in the book On the Prescription of Heretics, where he adds that Paul learned at Athens, by experience, what he wrote to the Colossians: "See that no one deceive you through philosophy." In the same place, and a little before, he says: "These are the doctrines of men and demons, born of the itching ears of all, from the cleverness of worldly wisdom, which the Lord, calling it folly, chose even in philosophy itself through the foolish confusion of the world. For this is the material of worldly wisdom, a rash interpreter of the disposition of the divine nature. Finally, the heresies themselves are suborned by philosophy." And in the Apology he often says: "There can be no agreement between philosophers and Christians." Likewise: "What has a disciple of grace in common with a philosopher? What has a merchant of heavenly fame in common with one…tor &"

units.la: Hyphenated line-end words as printed; "tor &" at line end. tor & vita, verborum & factorum operator, & rerum ædificator & destructor: amicus & inimicus erroris, veritatis interpolator & integrator, & expressor & furator eius & custos.
units.tr: …tor & life, a doer of words and deeds, a builder and destroyer of things, a friend and enemy of error, a corrupter and restorer of truth, its expounder, thief and guardian.

units.la: 2.Cyprianus lib. 4. epist. 2. Inter Christianos, inquit,& Philosophos plurimum distat. Et cum Apostolus dicat, videte, ne quis vos depraedetur per Philosophiam & inanem fallaciam, vitanda sunt, quae non de Dei clementia veniunt, sed de Philosophia duriori praesumptione descendunt.
units.tr: 2. Cyprian, book 4, letter 2: "There is a very great distance between Christians and philosophers. And since the Apostle says, 'See that no one plunder you through philosophy and empty deceit,' those things are to be avoided which do not come from God's mercy but descend from the harsher presumption of philosophy."

units.la: 3.Lactantius libro 3.cap.13.inquit: Quoniam Philosophos errasse docui, qui summum bonum, cuius capiendi gratia generati sunt, non comprehenderunt, apparet falsam & inanem esse Philosophiam: quia nec instruit ad iustitiae munera, nec officium hominis rationemque confirmat. Sciant igitur errare se, qui Philosophiam putant esse sapientiam. Et lib. 7. cap. 2. Omnes Philosophiae sectas alienas esse a veritate necesse est, quia homines erant, qui eas constituerunt, nec ullum fundamentum, aut firmitatem possunt habere, quae nullis divinarum vocum fulciuntur oraculis. Et lib. 3. de falsa sapientia, cap. 2. Ego ne studiosos quidem sapientia Philosophos esse concesserim, quia illo studio ad sapientiam non perveniturl. Nam si facultas inveniendae veritatis huic studio subiaceret, & si esset id studium tanquam iter ad sapientiam, aliquando esset inventa. Cum vero tot temporibus, tot ingeniis in eius inquisitione contritis, non sit comprehensa, adparet nullam esse ibi sapientiam.
units.tr: 3. Lactantius, book 3, chapter 13: "Since I have shown that the philosophers have erred, who did not grasp the highest good, for the sake of which they were born, it is clear that philosophy is false and empty, because it neither trains men for the duties of justice nor confirms the office and reason of man. Let those who think philosophy is wisdom know that they are in error." And book 7, chapter 2: "All the schools of philosophy must be alien to the truth, because men founded them, and they can have no foundation or firmness, since they are supported by no oracles of divine voices." And book 3 On False Wisdom, chapter 2: "I would not even grant that the philosophers are zealous students of wisdom, since by that zeal they do not attain wisdom. For if the faculty of finding the truth lay in that pursuit, and if that pursuit were a way to wisdom, it would at some time have been found. But since, through so many ages and with so many minds worn out in its investigation, it has not been grasped, it is evident that there is no wisdom there."

units.la: 4. Ambrosius sermone vigesimosecundo in Psalmo centesimo decimooctauo: Postremo circa circa elementa mundi, phalerata magis, quam vera sapientia: vt est Philosophia omnis, quæ aliena quærit, cum sua nesciat: scrutatur cœli plagas, mundi spatia rimatur, quæ sibi prodesse non possunt: Deum ignorat, quem solum debeat inquirere. Ideo verus sapiens dicit: Si quis videtur sapiens esse inter vos in hoc sæculo, stultus fiat vt sit sapiens. Sapientia enim huius mundi stultitia est apud Deum. Elaborandum est igitur, vt stulti simus in hoc sæculo, nihil nobis cum Philosophia, ne fidem nostram per elementa mundi huius traducat à vero, ne quis assertionem nostram per Philosophiam depraedetur, sic enim Arianos in perfidiam ruisse cognouimus, dum Christi generationem putant vsu huius sæculi colligendam. Reliquerunt Apostolum, sequuntur Aristotelem. Reliquerunt sapientiam, quæ apud Deum est, relegerunt disputationis tendiculas, & aucupia verborum secundum Dialecticæ disciplinam: cum clamet Apostolus: Ne quis vos depraedetur per Philosophiam & inanem seductionem.
units.tr: 4. Ambrose, sermon 22 on Psalm 118: "Finally, concerning the elements of the world, philosophy is more showy than true wisdom. Such is all philosophy, which seeks what is foreign while not knowing its own: it scrutinizes the regions of heaven and searches the spaces of the world, which cannot profit it; it does not know God, whom alone it ought to seek. Therefore the true wise man says: 'If anyone among you seems wise in this age, let him become a fool, that he may be wise. For the wisdom of this world is foolishness before God.' We must therefore labour to be fools in this age, having nothing to do with philosophy, lest it turn our faith from the truth by the elements of this world, lest anyone plunder our assertion through philosophy. For we know that the Arians fell into unbelief in this way, while they think the generation of Christ is to be gathered by the practice of this age. They left the Apostle and follow Aristotle. They left the wisdom that is with God and gathered up the snares of disputation and the fowling-nets of words according to the discipline of dialectic, when the Apostle cries: 'Let no one plunder you through philosophy and empty deceit.'"

units.la: 5. Chrysostomus de Philosophis scribit in 2. cap.1. ad Corinth. hom.7. Cum omissa via, quam eis præcipit Deus, vt scilicet per eorum quæ videntur pulchritudinem conditorem suum cognoscerent, mentis cogitationisque habenas laxantes infirmi in impietatis pelagus se immerserunt: & quam primum malorum superaddiderunt profunditatem, cum dicerent nihil ex nihilo fieri, sed ex materia increata. Vnde innumeræ hæreses pullularunt, & in rebus quidem absurdissimis delati sunt. In quibus autem sanum aliquid imaginati sunt, quamuis tanquam in vmbra & somniis id intuerentur, inuicem dissendissenserunt, vt vtrinque irriderentur. Idem hom. 1. in Euangelium Ioannis. Quemadmodum sepulchra extrinsecus ornata, si exteriorem illam faciem amoueris, cadauerum sanie, & exesorum ossium plena reperiuntur: itidem in Philosophorum opinionibus detecta verborum superficie & ornatu, multa inania absurdaque deprehenderis, maxime vbi de anima philosophantur, nunc honore, nunc contumelia, nullo modo modestiaue adhibita eam afficientes. Hoc diabolicum certe est, nulla ex parte mediocritatem seruare, sed in alterutrum extremorum allectos animos ad errorem trahere, cum nunc ad diuinam substantiam, neque modo neque pietate seruata eam efferat: nunc in sues & in asinos, & abiectiora quoque animantia turpiter inducat. Item, Gentilium sapientia verba sunt duntaxat & fabulae, neque vllam habent sapientiam, gloria namque causa omnia faciunt, hom. 62. in 11. cap. Ioan. Item, Semper per Philosophos hoc egit Diabolus, vt oblitenderet nostrum genus nihil a brutis differre. Ibi multa dicit de Platone & eius legibus, hom. 4. in Acta Apost.
units.tr: 5. Chrysostom writes about the philosophers in homily 7 on 1 Corinthians 2: "When they neglected the way which God had prescribed for them, namely to know their Creator through the beauty of visible things, the weak, loosening the reins of mind and thought, plunged themselves into the sea of impiety. And they added to their evils the depth of the first, when they said that nothing comes from nothing, but from uncreated matter. Whence innumerable heresies sprouted up, and they were carried away into most absurd things. In those matters, however, in which they imagined something sound, though they saw it as if in shadow and dreams, they disagreed among themselves, so that they were mocked on every side." The same, homily 1 on John: "Just as tombs adorned on the outside, if you strip away that outward face, are found full of putrid corpses and gnawed bones, so in the opinions of the philosophers, once the surface and ornament of words is removed, you will find many empty and absurd things, especially where they philosophize about the soul, now honouring it, now insulting it, in no way keeping moderation or modesty. This is certainly diabolical: to keep no mean in any respect, but to draw minds lured to one or other extreme into error, since now they raise the soul to the divine substance, neither with measure nor with piety preserved, and now shamefully lead it down into swine and asses and even lower animals." Likewise: "The wisdom of the Gentiles is only words and fables and has no wisdom, for they do everything for the sake of glory," homily 62 on John 11. Likewise: "The devil has always worked through the philosophers to make our race blind to the fact that it differs in nothing from the brutes." There he says much about Plato and his laws, homily 4 on Acts.

units.la: 6. Paulinus in Epist. 1. ad Amandum. Quia videlicet in hoc omnis Philosophorum ars laborat, vt adsertione fictorum lucem veritatis obscuret, & inanium contentionum laqueis solicitatas a vero mentes implicet, & ingenii fraude decipiat, & fuco sermonis inducat.
units.tr: 6. Paulinus, letter 1 to Amandus: "For in this indeed all the art of the philosophers labours: to obscure the light of truth by the assertion of fictions, to entangle minds drawn away from the truth in the snares of empty contentions, and to deceive by the cunning of wit and induce them with the paint of speech."

units.la: 7. Isidorus lib. 1. c. 18. de summo bono. Philosophi gentilium, non sicut oportet dominum quaerentes, in angelos inciderunt praevaricatores, factusque est illis mediator ad mortem diabolus, sicut nobis ad vitam tam Christus. 8. Beda in. 7. c. Exod. Allegorice flu-mina AEgypti, erratica & lubrica Philosophorum sunt dogmata, quæ cum paruulos sensu ac intelligē-tia deceperunt, vbi crux Christi mundo huic lumen veritatis infudit, necis illorū pœna & reatus sangui-nis exigitur.
units.tr: 7. Isidore, book 1, chapter 18, on the highest good: "The philosophers of the Gentiles, not seeking the Lord as they ought, fell into the transgressing angels, and the devil became a mediator to them unto death, just as Christ is to us unto life." 8. Bede on Exodus, chapter 7: "Allegorically, the rivers of Egypt are the wandering and slippery doctrines of the philosophers, which, when they had deceived the little ones in sense and understanding, the cross of Christ poured the light of truth upon this world, and the punishment of their death and the guilt of their blood are exacted."

units.la: Idem in Lucam libro 4. cap. 6. Sapientia se-cularis quasi coluber per humum serpit, diuina autē de cœlestibus intonat. Et in Lucam c.15.lib.4. Siliquæ quibus porcos pascebat, sunt doctrinæ seculares, sterili suauitate resonantes, de quibus laudes idolorū fabularumq. ad Deos gentium vario sermone atque carminibus percrepant, quibus dæmonia delectatur. Vnde cum iste saturari cupiebat, aliquid solidum & rectum, quod ad beatam vitam pertineret inuenire volebat in talibus, & nō inueniebat. Et paulo post. Fame percunt, qui sine fine viuentes, vitam beatam vanis Philosophiæ studiis inquirunt. Sicut enim panis qui cor hominis confirmat, verbo Dei, quo mentem reficiat, assimilatur: ita siliqua, quæ & ipsa intus inanis, foris mollis est, & corpus non reficit, sed implet, vt sit magis oneri quam vsui, seculari sapientia non immerito comparatur: cuius sermo facundia plausu sonorus, sed virtute vtilitatis est vacuus.
units.tr: Bede again, on Luke, book 4, chapter 6: "Secular wisdom creeps along the ground like a serpent, but divine wisdom thunders from the heavens." And on Luke 15, book 4: "The husks with which he fed the pigs are secular teachings, resounding with a barren sweetness, through which the praises of idols and fables echo to the gods of the nations in varied speech and songs, with which demons are delighted. Hence, when that man wished to be satisfied, he wanted to find in such things something solid and right that pertained to a blessed life, and he did not find it." And a little later: "They perish with hunger who, living without end, seek a blessed life through the vain studies of philosophy. For just as bread, which strengthens the heart of man, is likened to the word of God, by which he refreshes his mind, so the husk, which is empty within and soft without, does not nourish the body but fills it, so that it is more a burden than a use. It is not unjustly compared to worldly wisdom, whose eloquence is loud with applause but empty of the power of usefulness."

units.la: Sed satis est: plura recensere possem ex aliis patribus vt Basilio magno & Augustino, item ex recentiorum scriptis, quæ Philosophiam videntur vituperare: verum quia aut eiusdem sunt argumenti, aut leuiora, aut ab ignaris Philosophiæ recentiorib. osoribus prolata, prudens ista prætereo.
units.tr: But that is enough. I could list more from other Fathers, such as Basil the Great and Augustine, and from more recent writers who seem to disparage philosophy. But since these either deal with the same argument, or are lighter, or were put forward by ignorant recent enemies of philosophy, I prudently pass them over. ## Response.

units.la: Responsio.

1. Patrum autoritas nobis est fanƈta, vt in dogmatibus Christianæ fidei, si autoritate Dei loquentis in sacra Scriptura nititur: alias placet nobis illud Hieronymi: Quod de Scripturis non habet autoritatem, eadem facilitate reiicitur, qua approbatur: Sic etiam ceteris in dogmatibus ad humanitatis studia pertinentibus; si armata est certis ac non fallentibus rationibus & argumentis, quæ patrum assertionibus fidem faciant. Alias placet nobis illud Augustini: Patres non sic leguntur tanquam ita ex eius testimonium proferatur, vt contra sentire non liceat, si cubi forte aliter senserint, quam veritas postulat. Non enim satis fidei habet autoritas ex paternitate aut ex antiquitate, quia vtraque potest errare. Habuerunt & patres & antiqui suos næuos & errores: circumtulerunt & ipsi sanguinem & carnem humanam; falli & ipsi sunt humanæ se infirmitati esse obnoxios. Quare in Patrum scriptis requirimus iudicium tum veritatis tum prudentiæ.
units.tr: 1. We hold the authority of the Fathers to be sacred, so that in the doctrines of the Christian faith it is valid when it rests on the authority of God speaking in holy Scripture. Otherwise we agree with Jerome: What does not have authority from the Scriptures is rejected with the same ease with which it is approved. The same holds for other doctrines pertaining to the humane studies: if a view is supported by sure and non-deceptive reasons and arguments, which make the Fathers' assertions credible. Otherwise we agree with Augustine: The Fathers are not read in such a way that their testimony is put forward as if it were not lawful to disagree with them wherever they perhaps thought otherwise than truth demands. For authority derived from paternity or antiquity is not enough to command belief, since both can err. Both the Fathers and the ancients had their blemishes and errors; they too carried about blood and human flesh, and they too, being subject to human weakness, could be deceived. Therefore in the writings of the Fathers we look for judgement, both of truth and of prudence.

units.la: 2. Propositio vera est non simpliciter, sed primo cum hac cautione, quatenus aliquid Patres improbarunt ac damnarūt certa & vera ratione. Alioqui improbantur quædam sine iusta ratione, quæ improbatio temeraria dicitur Damnatio, quæ sine veritatis ac iustitiæ fit iudicio, ipsa damnanda est. Secundo; quatenus tota antiquitas vnanimi consensu aliquid repudiat & reiici iudicat: Alioqui Patres inter se quia sæpe iudiciis ac sententiis dissentiunt, quiquidam possunt aliquid improbare, quod alii certis rationibus amplexantur, atque tum auctoritas antiquitatis diuisa sibi non satis constat. Tertio, quatenus isti Patres & Doctores idem vbique constanter improbant: Ceteroquin, si idem Doctor aliquid hoc loco non probat, alio vero loco commendat, testimonia illorum merito sunt suspectae fidei propter aut diuersitatem respectus, aut inconsideratam incogitantiam & inconstantiam. Proinde quarto acceptamus propositionem hoc sensu: Quicquid Patres & Ecclesiae Doctores improbant & iuste damnant, id eatenus & eo respectu & sensu, quo illi hoc improbant, nobis quoque vere est improbandum, vbi scilicet par est ius & ratio, militatque eadem improbationis causa.
units.tr: 2. The proposition is true not simply, but first with this caution: insofar as the Fathers disapproved and condemned something on a certain and true ground. Otherwise some things are disapproved without just cause, and such rash disapproval is called condemnation; a condemnation made without the judgement of truth and justice is itself to be condemned. Second: insofar as the whole of antiquity with one accord rejects something and judges it to be cast out. Otherwise, since the Fathers often differ among themselves in their judgements and opinions, some may disapprove what others embrace on sound grounds, and then the authority of antiquity, divided against itself, does not stand firm. Third: insofar as these Fathers and teachers consistently disapprove the same thing everywhere. Otherwise, if the same teacher does not approve something in one place but commends it in another, their testimonies are rightly of doubtful trust, either because of a difference in point of view or because of thoughtless carelessness and inconstancy. Therefore fourth, we accept the proposition in this sense: whatever the Fathers and teachers of the Church disapprove and justly condemn, that we too must truly disapprove, in so far as, and in the respect and sense in which they disapprove it, namely where the right and reason are equal and the same cause of disapproval applies.

units.la: 3. Assumptio, si accipitur de vera Philosophia simpliciter, nequaquam est vera. Abest enim, si omnium Patrum in Philosophos & Philosophiam intonantium excutiantur tonitrua & fulmina, Prima cautio, qua cum propositio est intelligenda. Quia aut sine omni ratione & iusta causa conluruntur in Philosophiae damnatoriam sententiam, aut infirmis & elumbibus innituntur rationibus: si inquam vera & sana Philosophia simpliciter accipitur.
units.tr: 3. The assumption, if it is taken of true philosophy simply, is by no means true. For it fails, if the thunderbolts and lightning of all the Fathers thundering against philosophers and philosophy are examined. First is the caution with which the proposition must be understood. For they either rage against philosophy in a condemnatory judgement without any reason or just cause, or they rest on weak and feeble arguments, if, I say, true and sound philosophy is meant simply.

units.la: Si accipitur de Philosophia, quaedam in parte manca & deformata, vt profanorum & Ethnicorum sua somnia pro philosophicis decretis venditantibus, assumptio simpliciter vera non est. Quod verum esse est probabile. Tum enim improbatio & damnatio spectat non partem sanam sed depravatam: aut sanæ partis abusum petulanter in veritatem Euangelicam insurgentem.
units.tr: If it is taken of philosophy in part maimed and deformed, such as the pagans and Gentiles who peddle their own dreams as philosophical doctrines, the assumption is not simply true. That this is true is probable. For then the disapproval and condemnation applies not to the sound part but to the corrupted one, or to the abuse of the sound part, wantonly turned against the Gospel truth as it rose up.

units.la: Quoad secundam cautionem, inuenimus non omnes orthodoxæ antiquitatis patres damnasse, & aspernatos Philosophiam. Quoad tertiam, ostendi posset, eosdem patres qui hic reiiciunt & criminantur, alibi magnifice extollere eandem Philosophiam.
units.tr: As to the second caution, we find that not all the Fathers of orthodox antiquity condemned and rejected philosophy. As to the third, it could be shown that the same Fathers who here reject and accuse it elsewhere extol the same philosophy magnificently.

units.la: Quapropter limitanda est assumptio sic: Atqui Orthodoxa Patrum sanctorum antiquitas eatenus Philosophiam odio habuit & damnauit, quatenus erroribus & paganismis profanorum Ethnicorum instructa & conferta, Euangelicæ de Christo veritati impedimentum & vim attulit; Eatenus in Philosophos acrius est inuecta, quatenus illi Sophistomaniæ gentilis æstro perciti, Sophisticis argutiis & nugamentis, in ipsos Christi ac veritatis professores Christianos stolide insurrexerunt.
units.tr: Wherefore the assumption must be limited thus: Yet the orthodox antiquity of the holy Fathers hated and condemned philosophy only insofar as, stuffed and crammed with the errors and paganisms of profane Gentiles, it brought hindrance and force against the Gospel truth concerning Christ; it attacked philosophers more fiercely only insofar as, stirred by the gadfly of Gentile sophistry-mania, they foolishly rose up with sophistical subtleties and trifles against Christ and the professors of the truth, who are Christians.

units.la: Videndum enim est diligentissima accuratione, ne ipsis patribus alienam affingamus calumniando, & ipsorum testimonia adulterando mentem, sed ut mentem aduertamus, quomodo ista protulerint, in qua quæstione disceptanda & tractanda versentur, quando & quibus cum disseruerint. Iam autem extra controuersiam est, hos Patres versatos esse in quæstione & argumento de veritate religionis Christianæ, ita hanc disputasse ut eam propugnarent, & paganam impugnarent; Disputasse eo tempore, quo ipsa Euangelii veritas erat in ipsas gentes disseminanda, & ad profanos Ethnicos proplantanda: rem illis fuisse non tam cum Christianis, quam cum paganis Christianam veritatem auersantibus, eludentibus & illudentibus, iisque non illiteratis & rudibus, sed literis & artibus Græcorum Philosophorum, adeoque Philosophiæ paganæ scientia tinctis & turgentibus. Ergo facile feremus hic iudicium in his Patrum disputationibus, quibus cum Philosophis paganis congressi sunt, non culpari & damnari Philosophiam sanam & veram, cuius nos defensionem suscepimus, sed paganam multis paganismis & impiis erroribus contaminatam, sed eius potius abusum Sophisticum Deo & veritati insultantem.
units.tr: For we must take the greatest care not to foist alien views on the Fathers themselves by slander, nor to corrupt their testimonies by distorting their meaning, but to attend to how they put these things forward, in what question they were engaged and treating, and when and with whom they disputed. Now it is beyond controversy that these Fathers were occupied with the question and subject of the truth of the Christian religion, and that they argued so as to defend it and attack paganism; that they disputed at the time when the very truth of the Gospel was being spread abroad among the nations and planted among the profane Gentiles; that their business was not so much with Christians as with pagans who opposed, mocked and derided Christian truth, and who were not unlettered and rude, but steeped and swollen with the letters and arts of the Greek philosophers, and so with the learning of pagan philosophy. Therefore we will readily bear the judgement that in these disputations of the Fathers, in which they contended with pagan philosophers, it is not sound and true philosophy, which we have taken up to defend, that is blamed and condemned, but pagan philosophy, contaminated with many paganisms and impious errors, or rather its sophistical abuse, which insults God and truth.

units.la: Culpant igitur merito patres in Philosophia quæ deprehenderunt culpanda, interim iidem infinitis locis eadem & vrūtur, & ipsam commendant. Sed cursim nonnulla in Profyllogismo testimoniorum videamus.
units.tr: Therefore the Fathers rightly blame in philosophy what they found blameworthy; meanwhile, in countless places, the same men use it and commend it. But let us briefly look at some items in the preliminary list of testimonies.

units.la: 1. Carpit Philosophos Tertullianus, quos tamen alibi a Prophetis multa accepisse, & quosdam lectitasse Mosen contendit, primū in libro aduersus Hermogenem. Non mirum ipsum Philosophis offensum fuisse. Hermogenes enim defendebat hanc quæstionem paganam: Materia prima est æterna, innata, infecta: adeoque Deus omnia condidit ex præiacente æterna materia. Hic error Hermogenis Philosophi. At non qua Philosophi, sed qua Ethnici Platonici vel Aristotelici. Succensuit itaque Philosophis κατὰ τι, propter hūc paganum errorem. rorem, idque non immerito. At cur esset culpanda Philosophia hoc errore purgata? Secundo inuehitur in Philosophos libro primo contra Marcionem actitantem ibi huius quaestionis causam, Duos esse Deos, unum bonorum, alterum malorum creatorem. Item Mundum Deo indignum opus, &c. quam sophisticis nugis tueri voluit. Hic iusto zelo in Marcionem intonat, & quidem simul Philosophos istius sectae notat, quod sint sectarum & haereseon patres. Quales isti fuerunt Philosophi Marcionitae, talis eorum Philosophia quam merito conuiciatur. Imo Hermogenes & Marcion videri volebant Theologi: nec tamen sequitur eos fuisse vetos. In horum Theologiam qui inuehitur haeresture, an is etiam veram deformaret Theosophiam? Non dicerem.
units.tr: 1. Tertullian attacks the philosophers, though elsewhere he contends that they received much from the prophets and that some of them read Moses; first in his book against Hermogenes. It is no wonder that he was offended with the philosophers. For Hermogenes defended this pagan question: Prime matter is eternal, unbegotten and uncreated, and so God made all things out of pre-existing eternal matter. This is the error of Hermogenes the philosopher. But it is an error not as a philosopher, but as a Platonic or Aristotelian pagan. So he was angered at the philosophers in a certain respect [κατὰ τι] on account of this pagan error, and not without reason. But why should philosophy be blamed when it has been purged of this error? Second, he inveighs against the philosophers in the first book against Marcion, who there pursues the cause of this question: There are two gods, one the creator of good things and the other of evil things. Likewise the world is a work unworthy of God, etc., which he wanted to defend with sophistical trifles. Here he thunders with just zeal against Marcion, and at the same time he marks the philosophers of that sect, because they are the fathers of sects and heresies. Such were the philosophers Marcionites, and such is the philosophy of which they are rightly reproached. Indeed Hermogenes and Marcion wished to appear as theologians, yet it does not follow that they were true ones. Is he who attacks the theology of these heretics to be understood as also distorting true theosophy? I would not say so.

units.la: 2. Cyprianus in hac epistola ad Antonianum agit contra Novatianum, itidem sophistice disputantem. Ait vero inter Philosophu & Christianum esse discrimen. Sane: Philosophus enim hic est paganus. Loquitur de Philosophia, quam Paulus vocauit depraedatricem & deceptricem. Ideo de sana non loquitur Philosophia: Opponit recte clementiam Dei erga peccatores, quam ignorat Philosophia illa, praesumptioni duriori Philosophiae qua vrgebat Novatius.
units.tr: 2. Cyprian, in this letter to Antonianus, argues against Novatian, who likewise disputes sophistically. He says indeed that there is a difference between a philosopher and a Christian. Certainly: for the philosopher here is a pagan. He speaks of the philosophy which Paul called spoiling and deceiving. So he is not speaking of sound philosophy. He rightly sets against it the mercy of God toward sinners, which that philosophy does not know, and against the harsher presumption of philosophy with which Novatius pressed.

units.la: 3. Lactantii inuectiuam dispiciamus paulo liberius, quam habet lib. 3. non agens de vera, sed pagana Philosophia.
units.tr: 3. Let us examine Lactantius' invective a little more freely, as it appears in book 3, which deals not with true but with pagan philosophy.

units.la: Retexamus librum in partes tres. Prima agit git de Philosophia vanitate, altera de Philosophorum. Tertia Philosophiam non esse sapientiam demonstrat.
units.tr: We unfold the book into three parts. The first deals with the vanity of philosophy, the second with the philosophers. The third demonstrates that philosophy is not wisdom.

units.la: 1. Philosophiam inanem & falsam esse demonstrat his rationibus. 1. Philosophia non est sapientia: quia est studium sapientiae. Nos non contradicimus. 2. Illo studio ad sapientiam non pervenitur. Ergo ne quidem sapientiae studiosi sunt Philosophi cap. 2. Antecedens de vana Philosophia, & diuina sapientia est verum. 3. In Philosophia neque scientia est, neque opinatio. Ergo non est sapientia. Non illa, quia Socrates & Academici eam sustulerunt. Non haec, quia Zenon & Stoici eam repudiarunt cap. 4. Sapientiam ipsam esse non dicimus. Philosophiam Socratis, Academicorum, Zenonis & Stoicorum diuexat, at haec hominum Philosophia diuersis opinionibus dissidentium. Neque haec est tota & ubique sana. Alius par Lactantio referens inuerteret dilemma, & in Philosophia veritatem scientiae & opinationis eodem more inferret. 4. Philosophia se ipsum conficit. Nam singula secta multarum sectarum iudicio stultitia coniunguntur. Omnes igitur vana, cap. 4. Antecedens de Philosophia ipsa non est verum; ut ostendit eius probatio ex sectis quae sunt hominum dissidentium. Hac ratione ipsa quoque Theologia hodie se conficeret & vanitatis arguerectur. 5. Aut est Natura scientia, aut non est. Non illud, quia nulla potest esse in homine interna & propria scientia ob fragilitatem conditionis humanae. mana.Non hoc, quia multa sunt quae natura ipsa nos scire, & vsus frequens, & vitae necessitas cogit. Ergo utrumque Philosophiae genus corruit. Vetus quod sibi scientiam vendicat, & nouum quod eam distrahit. cap. 5. Disserit igitur Lactantius de duabus contrariis Philosophorum sectis. Sed concluderet hic aliquis hoc: Ergo quorundam est scientia, quorundam non est scientia, sed probabilis opinatio. Et nos in sana Philosophia scientiam rerum quarundam profitemur, & agnoscentes nostram imbecillitatem in multis Naturae arcanis probabilitate maiori acquiescimus. Certe sinceriori hic aliquid sophisticae subolet. Agit autem contra Arcesilam corrigens Philosophos in physicis. Academici, inquit, ex rebus paucis obscuris argumentati sunt, nullam esse scientiam: Physici ex quibusdam apertis & claris omnia sciri posse. Recte quidem coarguit arrogantiam Philosophorum Arcesilas: Sed addere exceptionem debuit & dicere: Causas rationesque duntaxat rerum naturalium, quia sunt abditae, nesciri posse, quia nullus doceat, nec quaeri oportere, quia inueniri non possunt. cap. 6. Equidem nullam rerum naturalium scientiam qui plane haberi posse ait, ipse ignarus rerum quibus quotidie vtitur reuera est.6. In Ethicis de summo bono dissentiunt Philosophi. Hic recitat sententias varias Philosophorum cap.7. quas refutat cap. 8. & 9. Ipse summum bonum in sola religione ponit cap. 10. ostendens potuisse Philosophos summum bonum deductione reperire, quod non sit voluptas, luptas, diuitiæ, regnum, sed immortalitas. Unde concludit Philosophiam Ethicam esse vanam.
units.tr: 1. He shows that philosophy is empty and false by these arguments. (1) Philosophy is not wisdom, because it is the pursuit of wisdom. We do not contradict this. (2) By that pursuit one does not attain to wisdom. Therefore philosophers are not even lovers of wisdom (ch. 2). The antecedent, about vain philosophy and divine wisdom, is true. (3) In philosophy there is neither knowledge nor opinion. Therefore it is not wisdom. Not the former, because Socrates and the Academics abolished it; not the latter, because Zeno and the Stoics rejected it (ch. 4). We do not say that wisdom itself is this. He tears apart the philosophy of Socrates, of the Academics, of Zeno and of the Stoics, but this is the philosophy of men who disagree in diverse opinions. Nor is this whole and everywhere sound. Another, following Lactantius, would turn the dilemma around and infer in philosophy the truth of knowledge and of opinion in the same manner. (4) Philosophy destroys itself. For each sect, by the judgement of many sects, is joined to folly. Therefore all are vain (ch. 4). The antecedent, about philosophy itself, is not true, as its proof from sects, which are of disagreeing men, shows. By this reasoning theology too would today destroy itself and be convicted of vanity. (5) Either there is a natural knowledge or there is not. Not the former, because no inward and proper knowledge can be in man on account of the frailty of the human condition; not the latter, because there are many things which nature itself compels us to know, and frequent use and the necessity of life compel us. Therefore both kinds of philosophy collapse: the old, which claims knowledge for itself, and the new, which tears it apart (ch. 5). Lactantius therefore discourses on the two contrary sects of philosophers. But someone might conclude from this: therefore there is knowledge of some things, and of others there is no knowledge but only probable opinion. And we in sound philosophy profess knowledge of certain things, and, acknowledging our weakness, we rest in greater probability concerning many secrets of nature. Certainly here something of sophistry is smelled, though sincerer. He argues against Arcesilaus, correcting the philosophers in physics. The Academics, he says, argued from a few obscure things that there is no knowledge at all; the physicists from certain manifest and clear things that all things can be known. Arcesilaus indeed rightly refuted the arrogance of the philosophers; but he ought to have added the qualification and said: only the causes and reasons of natural things, because they are hidden, cannot be known, since no one teaches them, nor ought they to be sought, since they cannot be found (ch. 6). Indeed he who says that no knowledge of natural things can plainly be had is himself really ignorant of the things he uses every day. (6) The philosophers disagree about the chief good in ethics. Here he recites the various opinions of the philosophers (ch. 7), which he refutes (chs. 8 and 9). He himself places the chief good in religion alone (ch. 10), showing that the philosophers could have discovered the chief good by deduction, which is not pleasure, nor riches, nor kingdom, but immortality. Whence he concludes that ethical philosophy is vain.

units.la: Ergo de Ethica pagana loquitur (quamuis Plato multum viderit & innuerit, modo habeat non iniquum interpretem.) Hic igitur defectus corrigatur, vt corrigitur, à Philosopho Christiano, nec veræ Philosophię oborietur metuendum periculum.
units.tr: So he is speaking of pagan ethics (although Plato saw and hinted at much, provided he has a not unfair interpreter). This defect, then, is to be corrected, as it is corrected by a Christian philosopher, and there is no dangerous threat to true philosophy to be feared from it.

units.la: 7. Logicam & Physicam non pertinere ad recte viuendum: Ergo sic totam Philosophiam esse inanem. Lactantii hic ingens est Sophisma (pace bona dixerim, ignoscito) si ita intelligitur: Logica & Physica non sunt artes bene viuendi. Ergo sunt inanes. Putidum est sophisma. Ergo tota Philosophia est inanis: certe multo putidius. Si ita Logica & Physica nihil omnino faciunt ad rectam vitam. Falsum & ridiculum erit ei, qui penitius utriusque artis natura & finem Christiane perspexerit. Hic autem Lactantius ista occasione refellit commendationem Philosophiæ Ciceronis, cap. 13. & 14. Et definitionem Philosophiæ Senecæ, Philosophiam esse rationem recte viuendi. cap. 15. Distinguatur sana Philosophia, à morbida & scabiosa. Et alium qui culpat, ne culpetur ipse videat.
units.tr: 7. Logic and physics do not pertain to living rightly. Therefore all philosophy is empty. Lactantius's argument here is a huge sophism (with respect, and pardon me for saying so) if it is understood thus: Logic and physics are not arts of living well. Therefore they are empty. That is a rotten sophism. So all philosophy is empty is certainly far more rotten. If it means logic and physics contribute nothing at all to the right life, it will be false and ridiculous to anyone who has examined the nature and purpose of both arts more deeply and in the Christian manner. Lactantius, on this occasion, also refutes the commendation of philosophy given by Cicero (chs. 13 and 14) and Seneca's definition of philosophy, philosophy is the reason for living rightly (ch. 15). Let sound philosophy be distinguished from diseased and scabby philosophy, and let him who finds fault with another first see that he himself is not found at fault.

units.la: 8. E Philosophia nō vtilitas quæritur, sed oblectatio. Ergo abiicienda. Falsum est (si de vera loquimur Philosophia) antecedens: & vix tolerabile in Aristotelica pagana schola.
units.tr: 8. Philosophy is sought not for its usefulness but for its delight. Therefore it is to be cast aside. The antecedent is false (if we are speaking of true philosophy), and it is scarcely tolerable in the pagan Aristotelian school.

units.la: 9. Philosophia principium & origo apparet. Ergo non est sapientia. Hoc de argumento proxime dicturi.
units.tr: 9. Philosophy appears to have a beginning and an origin. Therefore it is not wisdom. We shall speak of this argument shortly.

units.la: In parte fecunda probat Philosophos ipsos (scilicet paganos : ipse enim Rhetor & Philosophus Christianus fuit) in magna vanitate versari. 1. A placitis Epicuri, quod nulla fit providentia, quod anima sint mortales, &c. At Epicurus Philosophus non ponit legem omnibus Philosophis: laborauerit morbo suo: nunquid igitur eodem omnes? 2. A placitis Stoicorum & Pythagoræ, de migratione animarum de corpore in alia corpora, de mortis bono, de vitæ malo: vbi mirifice exagitat Lactantius gratiarum actionem Platonis, qui fe gratias naturæ dixerit agere. Et quod homo natus eflet potius, quam brutum animal, & quod masculus potius quam fœmina, quod Græcus, quam barbarus, quod Atheniensis, & quod temporibus Socratis, cap. 19. 20. 21. Orator est hic Lactantius. Oratio secum sæpe rapit lapides, stercora, & puram aquam in rapido flumine. Horum næui quid obsunt Philosophiæ per fe consideratæ. Tollantur hominum figmenta, & Philosophia ex fui natura constituatur: modo possit: sed quantum potest: conatus etiam laudatur sæpe. Platonis mitiorem opto cefforem. 3. A minorum Philosophorum factis & dictis variis vt quod Democritus agros suos pascua publica fieri passus fit, quod Zenon peccata paria faciat: misericordiam inter vitia ponat: quod Xenophanes credidit dicentibus orbem lunæ 22. partibus maiorem esse quam terram cap. 22. At minorum, non maiorum gentium dus præscribunt nec officiunt. Ah quam lyn-
units.tr: In the second part he proves that the philosophers themselves (namely the pagans, for he himself was a rhetorician and a Christian philosopher) are caught up in great vanity. (1) From the tenets of Epicurus, that there is no providence, that souls are mortal, etc. But Epicurus, a philosopher, does not lay down the law for all philosophers; he suffered from his own disease. Are all, then, to be equated with him? (2) From the tenets of the Stoics and of Pythagoras, on the transmigration of souls from one body into other bodies, on the good of death and the evil of life. Here Lactantius marvellously harangues Plato's thanksgiving, in which he said he gave thanks to nature, that he was born a human being rather than a brute animal, that he was a man rather than a woman, a Greek rather than a barbarian, an Athenian, and born in the times of Socrates (chs. 19, 20, 21). Lactantius is an orator here. Oratory often sweeps away with it stones, dung, and clear water in a rushing river. What blemishes of this sort harm philosophy considered in itself? Let the fictions of men be taken away and philosophy be set up according to its own nature, provided it can be; but its effort, so far as it can go, is often praised too. I would wish for a gentler opponent than Plato. (3) From the various deeds and sayings of minor philosophers, such as that Democritus allowed his fields to become public pasture, that Zeno makes sins equal, that he counts pity among the vices, and that Xenophanes believed those who said the orb of the moon is twenty-two times larger than the earth (ch. 22). But these are the faults of minor peoples, not of the greater, and they neither prescribe for nor hinder them. Ah, how lynx-eyed we are at others' blemishes,

units.la: cei ceì sumus in alienis næuis, & quidem eorum, qui veram Dei veri cognitionem non habuerunt, ipsi misericordia digni, in nostris autem & multo grauioribus talpæ. 4. Ab iis qui Antipodes inducunt cap. 23. Hodie si rediuiuus doceret: Lactantius noster à nautis nostris ipse irrideretur.
units.tr: and indeed at the blemishes of those who did not have the true knowledge of the true God, men themselves worthy of pity; while at our own, which are much graver, we are moles. (4) From those who posit Antipodes (ch. 23). If he returned to life today and taught this, our Lactantius would be laughed at by our own sailors.

units.la: Parte tertia rursum probat Philosophiam non esse sapientiam, vbi confert Philosophiam &S. Theologiam seu religionem Christianam, & Philosophiæ Ethnicæ variam tribuit ἀδυναμίαν, quæ omnino concedatur necesse est Philosophię. Deinde alia affert ab ipsa confessione Philosophorum, qua se fassi sunt insipientes, item causam effectæ naturæ & fortunæ. Agnoscatur hic etiam Philosophiæ gentilis miseria: & laudetur Lactantii conclusio, Sapientiam hominis esse in hoc uno, ut Deum cognoscat & colat. Interim hoc velim cordatos considerare, præter sapientiam diuinarum rerum ad salutem, esse quoque sapientiam & intelligentiam rerum humanarum ad huius vitæ commoda promouenda non inutilem, sed necessariam. Prolixior hic fui: ideoque reliquos patres Philosophiam carpentes relinquo.
units.tr: In the third part he again proves that philosophy is not wisdom, where he compares philosophy with theology, or the Christian religion, and attributes to pagan philosophy various kinds of impotence, which must necessarily be conceded to philosophy in every respect. Then he brings forward other points from the very confession of the philosophers, by which they admitted themselves fools, and likewise the cause of nature and of fortune when they were produced. Let the misery of pagan philosophy be acknowledged here too, and let Lactantius's conclusion be praised: the wisdom of man consists in this one thing, that he know and worship God. Meanwhile I would have sensible readers consider this: besides the wisdom of divine things, which leads to salvation, there is also a wisdom and understanding of human things, which is not useless but necessary for promoting the conveniences of this life. I have been rather lengthy here, and so I leave aside the remaining Fathers who carp at philosophy.

units.la: Elenchus 8. Sophismatis.
units.tr: Elenchus of the 8th Sophism.

units.la: HActenus classis fuit secunda sophismatum, ex autoritate patrum ecclesiasticorum, concinnatorum: sequitur Tertia Classis sophismatum ex vana & deceptrice Ratione & fallacibus conclusiunculis cótortorum: quarum primum est à qualitate causarum efficientium Philosophiam humanam ad qualitatem Philosophiæ concludē-dam.
units.tr: So far was the second class of sophisms, put together from the authority of the ecclesiastical Fathers. There follows the third class of sophisms, drawn from empty and deceptive reasoning and from the fallacious little conclusions of the twisters. The first of these concludes from the quality of the efficient causes to the quality of human philosophy.

units.la: Mala arbor profert fructus malos, inquit Christus. Unde causa mala effectus est malus.
units.tr: A bad tree bears bad fruit, says Christ (Matth. 7.). Therefore a bad cause produces a bad effect.

units.la: Atqui humanæ Philosophiæ arbor & causa fuit mala: nempe, homines Ethnici, de quibus Paulus ad Ephes. 4. scribit, quod ambularint in vanitate mentis suæ, dum mentem habuerint obtenebratam, abalienati à vita Dei, propter ignorantiam, quæ est in illis & excæcationem cordis eorum, &c.
units.tr: But the tree and cause of human philosophy was bad: namely, the pagan men of whom Paul writes to the Ephesians (Ephes. 4.) that they walked in the vanity of their mind, having their understanding darkened, alienated from the life of God through the ignorance that is in them and the blindness of their heart, etc.

units.la: Ergo ipsa Philosophia, fructus Ethnico-rum, est mala.
units.tr: Therefore philosophy itself, the fruit of the pagans, is bad.

units.la: Responsio.
units.tr: Answer.

units.la: Fundamentum huius sophismatis supra etiam nonnihil labefactatū vidimus. Propositio verbis vtitur Christi, quæ ita habent: Omnis arbor putris non fert fructus bonos. Item: Arbor putris non potest ferre fructus bonos. Horum verborum sensus Physicus ac proprius est vtique generalis: Nulla enim arbor putris, qua putris, potest ferre fructus, nedum bonos. Putredo enim arboris vim generandi fructum suffocat aut plane enecat. Ethicus & Theologicus sensus; q improprius est, ex Christi mente haustus, itidem est vniuersalis, Arbor putris non potest ferre fructus bonos, fructus inquâ bonos ea bonitate, quæ isti putredini opponitur. Sic etiam Ethnicus, qua Ethnicus, non potest ferre fructus bonos, ea scilicet bonitate, quæ è diametro pugnat cum Ethnica malitia: hoc est, non potest Christianas ac spirituales virtutes proferre. Causa enim potest esse mala certo malignitatis respectu, quæ non aduersatur bonitati, cuius ratione bonus effectus eius dici potest. Malitia potest esse vitiorum animi, ac interim bonitas artificii, qua vitiis animi malus homo, potest nihilominus vt bonus artifex, artis & cognitionis bonitate, experientia item ac vsu instructus, boni artificii bonum opus producere.
units.tr: We have already seen that the foundation of this sophism was somewhat shaken above. The proposition uses the words of Christ: Every rotten tree does not bear good fruit. Likewise: A rotten tree cannot bear good fruit. The physical and proper sense of these words is certainly general: no rotten tree, insofar as it is rotten, can bear fruit, let alone good fruit. For rot suffocates or altogether kills the tree's power of producing fruit. The ethical and theological sense, which is figurative and drawn from Christ's meaning, is likewise universal: A rotten tree cannot bear good fruit, that is, fruit of that goodness which is opposed to that rot. So too the pagan, insofar as he is a pagan, cannot bear good fruit, namely of that goodness which stands in direct opposition to pagan wickedness; that is, he cannot produce Christian and spiritual virtues. For a cause may be bad in a certain respect of its wickedness, and yet not be opposed to goodness, by reason of which a good effect can be said to come from it. Wickedness of the mind may coexist with goodness of skill: a man who is evil in the vices of his mind may nevertheless, as a skilled craftsman, instructed in the good of art and knowledge and likewise in experience and practice, produce a good work of his craft.

units.la: Distinguantur itaque actiones hominum spirituales à corporalibus externis ac politicis. Homo renatus secundum spiritum bona & spiritualia edit opera, ac interim, vt malus artifex, vel etiam malus politicus, aberrare in opere certi artificii, cuius rationem non probe nouit. Sic homo non renatus mala & Deo non placentia edit opera, quia persona non placet, quæ non est per Christum reconciliata, quia fidem non habet in Christum viuificam: Opera, inquam, mala nec Deo grata, quatenus spiritualia debent esse & ad salutem destinata: Interim insignia opera externa & politica, vt artifex certi artificii bene gnarus, fabricare potest. Sic aliquis potest spiritu esse præditus prudentiæ politicæ & gubernationis, qui tamen destituitur Spiritu sanctificationis ac regenerationis, vti de Saule ait D. Brentius. Propositio proinde est intelligenda de negatione eius bonitatis, quæ antecedentis malitiæ proprie opponitur. Alioquin certa bonitas & quædam malitia subordinata esse possunt, nec statim se tollunt.
units.tr: Therefore let the spiritual actions of men be distinguished from their outward, bodily and political actions. A man reborn, according to the spirit, performs good and spiritual works, and yet, as a bad craftsman or even a bad statesman, may go wrong in the work of a certain craft whose principles he does not properly know. So too a man not reborn performs evil works, displeasing to God, because the person is not pleasing, since he has not been reconciled through Christ and does not have a living faith in Christ. I say he performs evil works, not pleasing to God, insofar as they ought to be spiritual and directed to salvation. Yet he can make remarkable outward and political works, as a craftsman well versed in a particular craft. Thus someone may be endowed with the spirit of political prudence and government, and yet lack the Spirit of sanctification and regeneration, as Brentius says of Saul. The proposition, therefore, must be understood as a denial of that goodness which is properly opposed to the preceding wickedness. Otherwise a certain goodness and a certain subordinate wickedness can exist together and do not at once cancel each other.

units.la: Deinde, Malæ causæ malus effectus est, prærequirit huius regulæ constantem veritatem: Qualis causa talis effectus. At sæpe hanc fallere notum est omnibus recte iudicantibus. Nam multa efficientia sunt, quæ non sunt vniuoca (ita enim loquuntur Logici Peripatetici) necessario cum effectu. Deus æternus, infinitus, immensus, & omnipotens est: at mundus & homo minime. Nec qualis effectus, talis semper est causa. An enim Deum dices corruptibilem, eo quod corruptibilium sit causa?
units.tr: Next, the rule that a bad cause produces a bad effect requires the constant truth of this rule: such a cause, such an effect. But it is well known to all who judge rightly that this rule is often broken. For there are many efficient causes which are not univocal (as the Peripatetic logicians put it) with their effect. God is eternal, infinite, immense and omnipotent; but the world and man are by no means so. Nor is the effect always of the same kind as its cause. For would you call God corruptible because he is the cause of corruptible things?

units.la: Ad assumptum respondemus; Philosophia causam esse malam, nō esse simpliciter verum. Causa enim Philosophiæ prima & princeps est bona, nempe Deus, vt supra demonstrauimus. Deus autem excitauit solertes artifices, quibus ipse est vsus in opere philosophico perficiendo. Excitauit, inquam, donorum suorum collatione, & singulari motu. Dimensus vero vnicuique, vt placuit, artifici dona sua. Artifices vero, per quos Deus egit, fuerunt homines, & quidem corrupti, imo etiam Ethnici, in rebus spiritualibus cæci. Instrumenta itaque Dei homines scilicet cœlestis veritatis ignari, si quid erroris asperserunt Philosophiae, id est ex parte hominum sua etiam excoeca ignoratione, vel Ethnicis opinionibus adiicientium, non vero ex causa principe, neque ex donis Dei, Ethnicis ad huius operis exedificationem concessis.
units.tr: To the minor premise we reply: That philosophy has a bad cause is not simply true. For the first and chief cause of philosophy is good, namely God, as we have demonstrated above. God roused skilful craftsmen, whom he himself used in bringing philosophy to completion. He roused them, I say, by bestowing his gifts and by a singular impulse. Moreover, he measured out his gifts to each craftsman as he pleased. The craftsmen through whom God worked were men, and indeed corrupt men, even pagans, blind in spiritual matters. Therefore, if these men, God's instruments, ignorant of heavenly truth, introduced any error into philosophy, this came from the men's side, that is, from their own blindness and ignorance, or from pagan opinions they added; it did not come from the chief cause, nor from God's gifts, which were granted to the pagans for the building up of this work.

units.la: In Ethnicis itaque illis, ut Platone & Aristotele, sunt consideranda duo, ipsa corruptae naturae caecitas, quae malos fert in Philosophia fructus, & Dei collata dona naturae lumen excitantia & polientia, quae per se bona sunt. Deinde artifices isti in philosophica fabrica construenda vsi sunt non malis quidem, sed bonis instrumentis, scilicet, obseruatione, experientia, singularium inductione & ratione, quae certe per se non sunt mala. Non ergo Philosophiae radix, arbor seu causa est mala, nisi ex vnius tantum causae interueniente vitiositate.
units.tr: In those pagans, then, such as Plato and Aristotle, two things must be considered: the blindness of corrupt nature itself, which bears bad fruit in philosophy, and the gifts bestowed by God, which awaken and polish the light of nature and are good in themselves. Moreover, in building the philosophical structure these craftsmen used not bad but good instruments, namely observation, experience, induction of particulars and reason, which are certainly not bad in themselves. Therefore the root, tree or cause of philosophy is not bad, unless the only vitiating factor is one intervening cause.

units.la: 1. Philosophiae causam omnem esse malam, & gentilem secundo inficiamur, distinguentes inter causam incoantem, & continuantem ac perficientem. Etsi enim fuerit causa Philosophiam ofdiens Ethnica, adeoque ob gentilium errores non probetur; non tamen continuans & perficiens Philosophiae causa, Dei item agens instinctu & motu, est gentilis & propterea, vt mala, abiicienda. Siquidem multi Christiani fide & spiritu Christi praediti, & Philosophiam excoluere, & paganismos auersantes eam emendauere. Neque enim opus aliquod prorsus, vt inutile, explodendum, in quod, vitio hominum, vitia quaedam irrepserunt. pferunt. Reiiciantur vitia, virtutes retineantur.
units.tr: First, we deny that every cause of philosophy is bad, and secondly that it is pagan. We distinguish between the cause that initiates and the cause that continues and perfects.
