For although a pagan cause may have initiated philosophy, and so philosophy is not to be approved because of the errors of the pagans, the cause that continued and perfected it, namely God acting by instinct and impulse, is not pagan and therefore should not be cast aside as bad. For indeed many Christians, endowed with faith and the Spirit of Christ, both cultivated philosophy and, rejecting paganism, corrected it. For no work is to be rejected entirely as useless merely because certain vices have crept into it through the fault of men. Let the vices be rejected, and the virtues retained.

units.la: 1. Ad complexionem dicimus, eam ex antecedente, nulla necessitate deduci: ratio dicta est. Totam Philosophiam malâ esse omnibus suis partibus, nemo adhuc ausus est effutire. Adeo enim osor & rosor Philosophiæ nondum frontem vngue impudentiæ perfricuit, vt nihil in ea boni agnoscerent.
units.tr: To the conclusion we say that it cannot be deduced from the premise by any necessity: the argument has been stated. No one has yet dared to babble that the whole of philosophy is bad in all its parts. For such a hater and carper of philosophy has not yet rubbed his brow with the fingernail of impudence so far as to fail to recognise anything good in it.

units.la: 2. Deinde si mala est quapiam sui parte tantum, vi istius consequentiæ deductæ mala censebitur, quatenus Ethnica, hoc est, quatenus scabiem paganismorum ipsi affricuere nonnulli eius cultores. Tollantur igitur paganismi, & ex veritatis cœlestis officina ei afferatur epanorthoma.
units.tr: Second, if philosophy is bad in some part of it only, then by the force of this deduced consequence it will be judged bad only insofar as it is pagan, that is, insofar as some of its devotees have rubbed the itch of paganism onto it. Let paganism therefore be removed, and let a correction be brought to it from the workshop of heavenly truth.

units.la: 3. Distinguatur etiam opus consideratum tum per se & ratione sui, tum ratione personæ opus producentis. Actio vitiata personæ vitio, totum opus per se in sua essentia & in genere suo consideratum non reddit abominabile. Precatio per se est opus non vituperandū, vitio personæ vitiatum, ipsum tamen in suo genere non exploditur.
units.tr: Third, the work under consideration must be distinguished both in itself and by reason of its own nature, and by reason of the person who produces it. An action vitiated by the fault of the person does not make the whole work, considered in itself, in its essence and in its kind, abominable. Prayer is in itself a work not to be condemned, though vitiated by the fault of the person; yet in its own kind it is not rejected.

units.la: 4. Eadem concludendi ratione efficeretur, & Medicinam, & maximam partem Iurisprudentiæ esse malam: quia Medicina agnoscit primos suos parentes paganos Hippocratem & Galenum: Iurisprudentia etiam continet multorum gentilium & imperatorum Christiani nominis hostium infensissimorum leges, quæ tamen nō propterea tam temeratemerario ausu exterminantur ex legum tabu-lis.
units.tr: By the same method of reasoning it would be shown that medicine, and the greater part of jurisprudence, are bad: because medicine acknowledges its first parents to be the pagans Hippocrates and Galen; and jurisprudence also contains the laws of many pagans and emperors, the most bitter enemies of the Christian name. Yet these are not therefore cast out of the law books with such rash boldness.

units.la: Eadem denique dianoias deductione multorum Theologorum & conciones & scripta adeoque opera, vt mala, ex Ecclesia Dei extruderentur. Mala causa est malus effectus. At multarum concionum & librorum per se quidem optimorum causae sunt malae, scilicet Theologi, non Christo, sed sibi & ventri suo seruientes, qui saepe sunt ipsis paganis philosophis deteriores. Ergo conciones & libri Theologici sunt mali. Item: Malae arboris malus est fructus. At insignia artificia & opificia saepe fiunt a malis arboribus, id est, ab atheis, paganis, & fide Christi destitutis. Ergo ista insignia artificia seu artificiosa opera sunt mala. Distinguamus igitur hominum impietatem, ab externorum operum non sine Dei singulari dono etiam ab impiis fabrefactorum, admirabili saepe bonitate.
units.tr: Finally, by the same deduction of argument, the sermons and writings, and thus the works, of many theologians would be thrust out of the Church of God as bad. A bad cause is a bad effect. But the causes of many sermons and books, excellent in themselves, are bad, namely theologians who serve not Christ but themselves and their bellies, and who are often worse than the pagan philosophers themselves. Therefore sermons and theological books are bad. Likewise: The fruit of a bad tree is bad. But remarkable arts and manufactures are often made by bad trees, that is, by atheists, pagans, and men destitute of faith in Christ. Therefore these remarkable arts or artful works are bad. Let us therefore distinguish the impiety of men from the outward works made even by impious men, which often have a wonderful goodness given by a singular gift of God.

units.la: Instant:
units.tr: They press further:

units.la: Quorum mens est vana & ignorantia tenebris obtenebrata, quorumque cor est excaecatum: ii in veritatis doctrina, cuius nomen sibi arrogat Philosophia, parum aut nihil efficiunt. Atqui expresse affirmat Paulus gentium mentes fuisse vanas, obtenebratas, ignaras, &c. Ergo gentes ista nihil potuerunt in veritatis doctrina efficere, nisi fortasse vanitatis labem veritati rerum adspergere.
units.tr: Those whose mind is vain and darkened in the shadows of ignorance, and whose heart is blinded: such men accomplish little or nothing in the doctrine of truth, whose name philosophy claims for itself. But Paul expressly affirms that the minds of the Gentiles were vain, darkened, ignorant, etc. Therefore the Gentiles could accomplish nothing in the doctrine of truth, except perhaps to smear the vanity's stain upon the truth of things.

units.la: Respondeo. Propositio tantum vera est de earum rerum veritate, quarum ignorantia, quarumque respectu vanitas & obtenebratio bratio intelligitur. Iam autem Apostolus loquitur à quo vim subsumpti mutuantur, de rebus, non quibusuis sed tantum spiritualibus, ad spiritualem vitam atque perfectionem nos deducentibus. Ait enim ipse in Epistola ad Corinth. Animalis homo non intelligit ea, quae sunt Spiritus Dei, nec potest intelligere, quia spiritualiter diiudicantur. Gentibus itaque hic detrahitur ista vanitate & ignorantia rerum coelestium spiritualis & intelligentia, & executio seu salutaris administratio: Et profecto mens & cor hominis non regenerati nihil cernit, nihil valet in iis, quae ad regnum Dei & ad spiritualem tum intelligentiam tum obedientiam pertinent. Philosophiae autem decreta, de quibus hoc loco disseritur, non sunt spiritualia rerum coelestium, & ad Dei regnum spirituale pertinentium.
units.tr: I reply. The proposition holds only for those things whose ignorance, and with respect to which vanity and darkening, are meant. But the Apostle, from whom the minor premise borrows its force, speaks not of just any things but only of spiritual things, which lead us to spiritual life and perfection. For he himself says in the Epistle to the Corinthians: "The natural man does not receive the things of the Spirit of God, nor can he understand them, because they are spiritually discerned." So by this vanity and ignorance the spiritual understanding of heavenly things is taken from the Gentiles, along with its practice and saving administration. Indeed the mind and heart of an unregenerate man perceive nothing and are worth nothing in those things which pertain to the kingdom of God, to spiritual understanding and to obedience alike. But the teachings of philosophy, of which we are speaking here, are not spiritual matters of heavenly things belonging to the spiritual kingdom of God.

units.la: Interim autem sunt res etiam aliae, quibus occupantur hominum mentes & actiones, nempe tum naturales, tum civiles, de quibus assumptio non loquitur, Philosophia autem eas profitetur. Quia autem quaedam femina ex priore natura Dei misericors sapientia, in nobis reliquit, res naturales & civiles seu externas quodammodo intelligimus, & tractamus etiam sine gratia regenerationis.
units.tr: Meanwhile there are also other things with which men's minds and actions are occupied, namely both natural and civil, and the minor premise does not speak of these, whereas philosophy professes them. Because a certain spark of the former nature, the merciful wisdom of God, has been left in us, we understand natural and civil or external things to some degree, and we handle them even without the grace of regeneration.

units.la: 9. Sophismatis Elenchus.
units.tr: 9. Elenchus of the Sophism.

units.la: QVod variis dissensionum & opinionum monstrosarum sectis est distractum, sibique bique neutiquam constans : id ipsum nullam habet nec tradit certam ac salutarem do- ctrinam.
units.tr: That which is torn apart by various dissensions and monstrous opinions, and is by no means consistent with itself, this very thing holds and delivers no certain and saving doctrine.

units.la: At Philosophia est variis dissensionum ac monstrosarum opinionum sectis distracta, dissidentium infinitis controuersiis agitata, nec sibi constat.
units.tr: But philosophy is torn apart by various dissensions and sects of monstrous opinions, agitated by the endless controversies of those who disagree, and it is not consistent with itself.

units.la: Ergo nullam nec habet nec tradit Phi- losophia certam ac salutarem doctrinam.
units.tr: Therefore philosophy neither holds nor delivers any certain and saving doctrine.

units.la: Assumptum probant tum veterum Philo- sophorum variis sectis ac dissentientibus opi- nionibus, quas in Aristotelis disceptationibus ac confutationibus videmus innumeras. Fue- runt enim Stoici, Peripatetici, Academici & Platonici, Epicurei, &c. tum recentium, quo- rum alii sunt à Secta Peripatetica, alii à Plato- nica & Socratica, alii à Ramea: & hi vicissim inter se sunt diuisi. De antiquis Ethnicis Phi- losophorum sectis disputant erudite Iustinus, Clemens, Tacianus, Theophilus, probantes Philosophos ipsos inter se dissentire & con- traria docere. Et Basilius ait Hom.1. Non opus est, vt nos contra illos pugnemus, cum illi mu- tuis dissensionibus sufficiant ad suam ipsorum do- ctrinam euertendam. Quæ & quot sint hodie philosophantium dissidentes sectæ loquitur præsens dies.
units.tr: They prove the minor premise both by the various sects and dissenting opinions of the ancient philosophers, which we see in countless numbers in the disputations and refutations of Aristotle. For there were the Stoics, Peripatetics, Academics, Platonists, Epicureans, and so on; and of the more recent philosophers, some belong to the Peripatetic school, some to the Platonic and Socratic, and some to Ramus, and these in turn are divided among themselves. Justin, Clement, Tatian and Theophilus learnedly discuss the ancient pagan sects of philosophers, proving that the philosophers disagree among themselves and teach contrary things. And Basil says in Homily 1: "There is no need for us to fight against them, since their mutual dissensions are enough to overthrow their own doctrine." What and how many dissenting sects of philosophers there are today, the present day itself tells.

units.la: Responsio.
units.tr: Answer.

units.la: Propositio est accipienda cum limitatione.
units.tr: The proposition must be taken with a limitation.

units.la: Si ipsum quod distractum est sectarum varietate rietate, suo vitio, suaque incostantia in partes abiit varias, adeoque si per se sibi non constat. Alioqui si ab externa quapiam causa ipsum diuellitur in partes diuersas, & si non ipsius, de quo quæritur, est varietas & inconstantia, sed aliunde ei à variis ingeniis illata, non est vera.
units.tr: If that which is torn apart by a variety of sects falls into various parts through its own fault and its own inconstancy, and so is not consistent with itself. Otherwise, if it is torn in different directions by some external cause, and if the variety and inconstancy at issue are not in the thing itself but are brought to it from elsewhere by various wits, then the proposition is not true.

units.la: 2. Si distractum per se nullam omnino doctrinæ certitudinem aut contineat, aut continere possit, si, scilicet, ab eo semotis hominum opinionibus, in integrum restituatur. Alioqui si per se veritatem & certitudinē doctrinę contineat in se, & obrutum variarum opinionum mŏstris lucem sanæ doctrinæ de se diffundere nequeat, culpa distractionis & inconstantis doctrinæ non est in ipso quod distrahitur, sed in distrahentibus & obruentibus sua mole opinionibus hominum. 3. Stante hac & concelsa propositione, Christianæ religionis etiam posset concludi inconstantia & incertitudo:
units.tr: 2. If what is torn apart contains in itself, or can contain, no certainty of doctrine at all, that is, if when men's opinions are removed from it, it is restored to its whole state. Otherwise, if it contains in itself the truth and certainty of doctrine, and yet, buried under the monstrous mass of various opinions, cannot diffuse the light of sound doctrine from itself, then the fault of the distraction and the inconstant doctrine lies not in what is torn apart but in those who tear it apart and bury it under the weight of human opinions. 3. If this proposition stands and is conceded, inconstancy and uncertainty could also be concluded of the Christian religion:

units.la: Quod distrahitur multitudine opinionum, & in varias facessit sectas monstrosis hominum disputationibus & dissidiis, id nec sibi constat, nec quippiam habet certa doctrina. Atqui Religio Christiana semper est in varias hominum opiniones & sectas dissecta, turbata & afflicta, & adhuc in eam omnis generis monstrosæ sectæ & hæreses distractis hominum dissidentium animis exundant. In testes aduocamus Annales Ecclesiasticos, grauissimum autorem Augustinum, & nostrorum etiam siue Theologorum siue Matæologorum Catalogos hæreticorum, sectarum & schismatum tum classes recensentes, vel etiam impugnantes.
units.tr: "What is torn apart by a multitude of opinions, and falls into various sects through the monstrous disputations and dissensions of men, neither is consistent with itself nor holds any certain doctrine. But the Christian religion has always been cut into various human opinions and sects, disturbed and afflicted, and still every kind of monstrous sect and heresy overflows into it from the minds of disagreeing men." We call as witnesses the Ecclesiastical Annals, the most weighty author Augustine, and also the catalogues of heretics, sects and schisms compiled by our own writers, whether Theologians or Matæologians, who list or even refute the classes.

units.la: Quid hinc? Ergone constabit sibi neutiquam ipsa Christianorum religio & doctrina sacra? Minime credo.
units.tr: What follows from this? Will the Christian religion and sacred doctrine therefore be by no means consistent with itself? By no means, I believe.

units.la: Assumptionem quidem concedimus, quo ad membrum prius, de inconstantia posterius inficiamur. Nam 1. Philosophia oneratur & agitatur misere varie dissidentium hominum sectis atque opinionibus. At ista Philosophiae in varias sectas diuulsio aliunde est, non ipsius culpa allata vel facta. Homines, qui philosophantur, quique varie sunt affecti, nec idem sentiunt, secedunt a se opinionibus in diuersa sectarum castra. Huius autem secessionis & distractionis causa in male affectis feriatisve hominibus est malitia satanae. Ille enim dissidiorum semina spargere satagit, nonnunquam etiam inter pios Christianae Religionis professores. Deinde Philautia hominum vitiosa, praesumptio, contendendi libido & alia: quae etiam in Theologis nonnunquam suam figunt sedem, & licet quidam sint pii, manent tamen in piis reliquiae carnis. Denique rerum de quarum veritate agitur saepe multiplex ignorantia. Satanae itaque malitia quid mirum, si hoc contentioso seculo, etiam piis Philosophis insidietur, si tot summis imponit Theologis? Multo minus mirum si agitarit dissentientium opinionum œstro gentiles Philosophos in regno tenebrarum captiuos. Philautia, contentio, curiositas, sitas, superiorum autoritas quid mirum si Philosophos in sectas opinionum diuidat; si iisdem vitiis abreptos hodie S. Sanctæ Theologiæ Doctores, tanquam fratres Cadmæos in mutua ruere vulnera videamus? & infinita concitare schismata? Ignorantia lapsos esse paganos illos ne miremur, cum in sanctis oraculis & sancti adhuc multa non videant; & in rebus naturalibus ac politicis sæpe ipsorum adhærescat scientia.
units.tr: We concede the minor premise as to its first part, and we deny the latter part, about inconstancy. For, first, philosophy is miserably burdened and agitated by the sects and opinions of men who variously disagree. But this splitting of philosophy into various sects comes from elsewhere and is not brought about by its own fault or doing. Men who philosophize, being variously disposed and not thinking alike, secede by their opinions into different camps of sects. The cause of this secession and division lies in men who are ill-disposed or idle, and in the malice of Satan. For he strives to scatter the seeds of dissension, sometimes even among the pious professors of the Christian religion. Next comes the vicious self-love of men, presumption, the lust for contention and other things, which sometimes fix their seat even in theologians; and although some are pious, remnants of the flesh remain in the pious. Finally, there is often a manifold ignorance of the matters whose truth is in question. What wonder, then, if in this contentious age Satan lays snares even for pious philosophers, if he has deceived so many chief theologians? Much less wonder if, with the goad of dissenting opinions, he has stirred up the Gentile philosophers, who were captives in the kingdom of darkness. What wonder if self-love, contention, curiosity, thirst and the authority of superiors divide philosophers into sects of opinion; if, carried off by these same vices, we see the holy doctors of sacred theology today rushing into mutual wounds like the Cadmean brothers, and stirring up endless schisms? Let us not be surprised that those pagans fell through ignorance, since even the saints do not yet see many things in the holy oracles, and in natural and political matters their knowledge often still clings to them.

units.la: Dissensio itaque est animorum, adeoque hominum philosophantium, non ipsius Philosophiæ. Attamen in ipsis Philosophiæ scholis sunt istæ sectæ. Ergo inde prodeunt. Et in scholis Theologorum sunt natæ sectæ. Ergo ex ipsa prodierunt Theologia. Impium dictu. Ex ipsis Apostolis egressi sunt Pseudoapostoli: Ex vobis ipsis exurgent viri loquentes perversa, ut seducant discipulos, ait Paulus: Exierunt ex nobis, ait Ioannes, sed non erant ex nobis.
units.tr: So dissension belongs to the minds, and so to the men who philosophize, not to philosophy itself. Yet these sects exist within the very schools of philosophy. Therefore they arise from it. And sects have arisen in the schools of the theologians. Therefore they have come forth from theology itself. This is impious to say. False apostles went out from the apostles themselves: "Out of your own selves will arise men speaking perverse things, to draw away the disciples," says Paul. "They went out from us," says John, "but they were not of us."

units.la: 1. Agnoscimus dissidia etiam hodierna Philosophorum, at tot neutiquam, quot miserum Ecclesiæ Christi corpus laceratur. Oportet esse hæreses, ait Apostolus, ut qui probati sunt, manifesti fiant.
units.tr: 1. We acknowledge the present dissensions of philosophers as well, but by no means so many as those by which the wretched body of the Church of Christ is torn. "There must be heresies," says the Apostle, "so that those who are approved may be made manifest."

units.la: Oportet esse Philosophorum dissentientium opiniones & sectas, ut disputationis philosophicæ malleo veritas rerum exprimatur. Nec sunt nostra dissidia tanta, quæ non possint consopiri & placide componi. Spes non deficit nos omnis. Philosophemur non ad MagiMagistrorum nostrorū & vetustatis veneran-dæ autoritatem, sed ad rerum ipsarum veritatem, ipsaque rerum veritas, Ratio, & Experientia iudices constituantur: Et nostra Philosophia multis in partibus multo erit sanior multorum Mataeologorum Theologia. Sed, vt vno verbo dicamus, qui vult ex enneade vel decade nostrarum sectarum Philosophię conficere inanitatem, illum prius amandamus, si Theologiæ Doctor salutari vult, ad myriadas suarum sectarum, eas si numerauit, & nobis poterit affricare scabiem male & varie dissentientium Philosophorum, quippe hæc est (si sano iudicio rem æstimamus) non abstracti, sed concreti (& quidē non concreti, qua Philosophus, sed potius, qua vel male institutus, vel non bene gnarus, vel aliorum vitiorum veritatis lucem non perferentium labe infectus: Nam in concreto & forma est a qua fit denominatio, & subiectum varie tum compositum, tum dispositum) Philosophiam insimulet inanis incertitudinis: at, scio, suas si viderit, nobis Ethnicorum vel etiam adhuc spirantium dissensiones non exprobrabit.
units.tr: There must be dissenting opinions and sects of philosophers, so that the truth of things may be beaten out by the hammer of philosophical disputation. Nor are our dissensions so great that they cannot be lulled to sleep and calmly settled. Every hope is not lost for us. Let us philosophize not by the authority of our teachers and venerable antiquity, but by the truth of things themselves; let the truth of things, reason and experience be the judges. Our philosophy will in many respects be much sounder than the theology of many Matæologians. But, to say it in a word: whoever wishes to make philosophy seem empty from our nine or ten sects, let him first be sent back, if he is a doctor of theology who wishes to be sound, to the myriads of his own sects, if he has counted them, and then he may rub into us the scab of badly and variously disagreeing philosophers. For this (if we judge the matter with sound judgment) is not an abstract but a concrete thing, and indeed concrete not as a philosopher is, but rather as one who is badly trained, or not well acquainted, or infected with the stain of other vices that do not bear the light of truth. For in the concrete there is both the form from which the denomination arises and a subject variously both composed and disposed. Yet, I know, if he looks at his own sects, he will not reproach us with the dissensions of the Gentiles or even of those still living.

units.la: 10. Sophismatis Elenchus.
units.tr: 10. Refutation of the Sophism.

units.la: Quod suis cultoribus nullam affert utilitatem, id in Christianorum scholis non debet tolerari.
units.tr: What brings no benefit to its devotees ought not to be tolerated in the schools of Christians.

units.la: At Philosophia suis cultoribus nullam omnino unquam attulit utilitatem, qua pra ceteris frui potuissent. Ergo Philosophia in scholis Christianorum non debet tolerari.
units.tr: But Philosophy has never at any time brought its devotees any benefit by which they could enjoy an advantage over others. Therefore Philosophy ought not to be tolerated in the schools of Christians.

units.la: Assumptum probant:
units.tr: They prove the assumption:

units.la: Siquidem Philosophia imbuti Ethnici, nihil inde reportarunt vtilitatis, à Deo nil nisi inexcusabilem damnationem, ab hominibus, nihil nisi ipsam vanitatem. Etenim (inquit ille) quid Homero profuit bellum Iliacum describisse, & multis eo opere fucum fecisse, dum falsa commemorat? Quos fructus percepit Hesiodus ex catalogo Genealogia Deorum, quos ipse fingendo cogesfit? Qua vtilitas manauit ad Orpheū ex eo, quod trecentos & sexaginta Deos confessus est? quos tandem reiecit in testamento suo, cum obiret morte, asserens vnum tantum esse Deum! Quem fructum consequutus est Aratus ex sua sphærographia mundani cycli? Aut quem fructum sensere alii qui iisdem incubuere studiis? Certe nullus alius laborū fructus ad eos peruenit, quam vana gloria hominum, quam ne quidem ipsi condigne consequi potuerunt. Sed quid veri ex eorum scriptis aut verbis elici potest? Quid vtilitatis Euripides, Sophocles & reliqui tragici scriptores ex suis cepere tragœdiis? At quem fructum Menander, Aristophanes, aliique comici tulere ex suis comœdiis? Herodotum & Thucydidem historia non iuuerunt, nec Pythagoram occulta & arcana, nec etiam Herculis columnæ. Diogeni quid Cynica Philosophia? Epicuro quid, asserere non esse prouidentiam? Empedocli quid, docere non esse Deos, citulit? Socrati quid comodi attulere dæmonia, qua inuocabat? Quid praeterea, quod iuraret perquam sanctè, sancte, canem, anserem, platanum, & AEsculapi-um fulmine tactum? nunquid ista viro conduxe-runt? praterea, quod voluntario animo nihil trepidans mortuus est, quam sperat post obitum mercedem nancisci? Quid Platoni profuit sua disciplina & Philosophia? Quid vtilitatis pepererunt reliquis sua dogmata Philosophi, qui plurimi fuere? Nolo enim omnes nunc, quia plurimi sunt, recensere. Haec quidem enarramus, vt demonstremus, & quasi obvoculos homini ponamus, impias & inutiles esse eorum sententias: nec ipsi veritatem assequuti sunt, nec alios ad veritatem cohortati sunt. Nam ex suis ipsorum, dum contraria sibi proferunt, scriptis, mendacii arguuntur. Quidam etiam sua destruxerunt dogmata. Nec solum se ipsos subuerterunt, verum nonnulli Philosophi etiam propria dogmata, infirma & irrita fecere. Itaque gloria eorum cessit in infamiam & stultitiam, vt inde habiti sint stulti & inglorii. Nam intellectu praediti facile eorum scripta intelligunt, eorumq; veritate perspiciunt. Aut enim loquuti sunt de diis, & deinceps docuere non esse Deos. Aut si de mundi generatione disseruerunt, postremo omnia fortuito & casu quodam sua sponte facta esse confessi sunt. Aut de providentia sermocinates, tandem statuere, mundum fortuito, nec providentia gubernari. Quid praeterea de moribus instituendis dicam: An non dum conantur de morum gravitate scribere, docuere adulteria, scortationem, atque omnem immunditiem perpetrare? Ad haec exosam & detestandam masculam venerem introduxerunt. Et vt haec magis grata & accepta sit mortamortalibus, canunt & Deos vsos concubitu non di-cendo, &c.
units.tr: For the Gentiles who were steeped in Philosophy gained nothing from it in the way of benefit: from God nothing but inexcusable damnation, and from men nothing but vanity itself. For (he says) what did it profit Homer to describe the Trojan War and to deceive many by that work, when he recounts falsehoods? What fruits did Hesiod gain from his catalogue and genealogy of the gods, which he himself invented? What profit flowed to Orpheus from his confessing that there are three hundred and sixty gods? Which he finally renounced in his will when he was dying, declaring that there is only one God! What fruit did Aratus obtain from his sphere-writing of the cosmic cycle? Or what fruit did others feel who devoted themselves to the same studies? Certainly no other fruit of their labours reached them except the empty glory of men, which they themselves could not even obtain as they deserved. But what truth can be drawn from their writings or words? What benefit did Euripides, Sophocles and the other tragic writers derive from their tragedies? And what fruit did Menander, Aristophanes and the other comic writers bear from their comedies? History did not help Herodotus and Thucydides, nor did the secret and hidden teachings help Pythagoras, nor the pillars of Hercules. What did Cynic philosophy do for Diogenes? What did it do for Epicurus to assert that there is no providence? What did it do for Empedocles to teach that there are no gods? What advantage did the spirit that Socrates invoked bring him? What more, that he swore so solemnly by the dog, the goose, the plane tree, and the thunderstruck Aesculapius? Did these things profit the man? Moreover, that he died with a willing mind, not trembling at all, because he hoped to obtain a reward after death? What did his teaching and philosophy profit Plato? What benefit did the doctrines of the other philosophers, who were very many, bring them? For I do not wish now to recount them all, since they are so numerous. We recount these things in order to show, and to set before a man's eyes as it were, that their opinions are impious and useless: neither did they attain the truth themselves, nor did they urge others to the truth. For they are convicted of falsehood by their own writings, while they put forward contrary things. Some even overthrew their own doctrines. Not only did they subvert themselves, but some philosophers also made their own doctrines weak and void. Thus their glory turned to infamy and folly, so that they are regarded as foolish and inglorious. For those endowed with understanding easily grasp their writings and perceive their truth through them. For either they spoke about the gods and then taught that there are no gods; or if they discoursed about the generation of the world, in the end they confessed that all things were made by chance and by some accident of their own accord; or, speaking about providence, they finally determined that the world is not governed by providence but by chance. What more shall I say about instituting morals? Did they not, while they were trying to write about the seriousness of morals, teach adultery, fornication, and every filthiness to be practised? Besides, they introduced the hateful and detestable male love. And that these things may be more pleasing and acceptable to mortals, they sing also that the gods used intercourse, not to mention it, etc.

units.la: Responsio.
units.tr: Response.

units.la: Par pari reponendum: quæstioni prolixæ, responsio debetur prolixa, præsertim si Solomonis isti prouerbio satisfacere volumus: Re-{1}sponde stulto secundum stultitiam eius. Propositionem veram agnoscimus, modo distinguamus vtilitatem: Est enim alia ad hanc vitam in rebus externis & politicis, seu ad perfectionem naturalem: Est item alia, ad æternam vitam consequendam in rebus spiritualibus, seu ad perfectionem spiritualem. Neutra vbi vtilitas, ibi locus nullus dandus scholis, vt scilicet inutilibus nugis discrucientur.
units.tr: Like must be answered with like: a lengthy question is owed a lengthy answer, especially if we wish to satisfy that proverb of Solomon: Answer a fool according to his folly (Prov. 26). We acknowledge the proposition as true, provided we distinguish the benefit. For there is one benefit for this life in external and civil matters, or for natural perfection; and there is another benefit for attaining eternal life in spiritual matters, or for spiritual perfection. Where neither benefit is found, no place is to be given to such things in the schools, so that men are not tormented with useless trifles.

units.la: Assumptionem de vera Philosophia intellectam rotunde negamus. Veram enim Philosophiâ, qui fructu suo destitui existimat, is ne limen quidem eius salutauit. Verum Prosyllogismus eius loquitur de pagana Philosophia, quam supra prorsus à vera & Christiana repurgata discreuimus. Verum in paganorum Philosophia agnoscimus quædam vtilia, & virtutes non spernendas, quædam etiam inutilia & vitia nulli Christiano imitanda. Miscet Prosyllogismus genus vtrumque. Si de vtilibus, quæ dicimus, loquitur disputator, distinguimus eam, vti factum in propositione. Si de inutilibus & lapsibus paganis non infimis, (vt certe tota probatio innuit) sciat nos non de vitiis Ethnicorum, sed de vera Philosophia, eiusq; effectis disceptare. Interim omnem vtilitate etiam Ethnicæ Philosophiæ detrahere non possumus.
units.tr: We flatly deny the assumption as it is understood of true Philosophy. For the one who thinks that true Philosophy is destitute of its fruit has not even greeted its threshold. But the prosyllogism speaks of pagan Philosophy, which we have above entirely distinguished from the true and Christian philosophy that has been purged. In pagan Philosophy we acknowledge certain things that are useful, and virtues not to be scorned; and also certain things that are useless and vices that no Christian should imitate. The prosyllogism mixes up both kinds. If the disputant speaks of the useful things, we distinguish as we did in the proposition. If he speaks of the useless things and the not-lowly lapses of the pagans (as the whole proof certainly implies), let him know that we are not disputing about the vices of the Gentiles, but about true Philosophy and its effects. Meanwhile, we cannot take away every benefit even of Gentile Philosophy.

units.la: Istis igitur gentilium, nō qua Philosophorum, sed qua hominum à Deo alienorum, & in multis cœcorum, noxiis erroribus & paganismis opponam, non meis, verum Doctissimi Theologi verbis, candide interim agnitis lapsibus; Philosophiæ etiam paganorum fructus non prorsus cōtemnendos. Rogo autem eum, qui hæc legit, vt distinguat non vituperandum conatum à perfecto euentu: Et sui memor potius miserorum miseretur, quibus defuit lux, qua nos gaudemus, quam illis petulanter insultet. Paulo altius repetere principia liceat.
units.tr: Therefore I will oppose those errors of the Gentiles, not as philosophers but as men alienated from God, and in many respects blind, harmful errors and paganisms, not in my own words but in the words of a most learned theologian, frankly acknowledging their lapses in the meantime; and I acknowledge that the fruits of pagan Philosophy are not to be despised altogether. I ask, however, the one who reads these things to distinguish a worthy endeavour from the perfect outcome; and, mindful of himself, let him rather pity the wretched, who lacked the light in which we rejoice, than insult them wantonly. Allow me to go back a little further to the first principles.

units.la: 1. Definiuerunt Philosophiam rerum diuinarum & humanarum, qua, scilicet, fas, quandam cognitionem. Tu si mauis, dicas conatū & cognoscendi desiderium. Non sane illud inane & inutile etiam in manifeste reprobo. At quamuis nonnulli hanc definitionem morose flagellent, nihil tamen habet, quod iure reprehendi possit, nisi forte id, quod, quæ Philosophia promittit, præstare non possit. Verum præstat forte plus, quam illi credant. In rebus humanis quid præstiterit? nemini obscurum est: artes inuenit, expoliit, & in ordinem ac methodum reposuit. De moribus erudite præscripsit, vitæ honestæ regula, Respublicas legibus ornauit, vt vere dictum sit, Philosophia est legum propugnaculum. In diuinis forte minus præstitit: sed hic libenter fatefatemur illius cœcitatem, quæ tamen nō tam ipsius facultatis, quam hominum vitio euenit. Fuit enim Philosophia organum Dei, quo sui cognitionem eis erat daturus Deus, imo dedit, modo recte vterentur: quod cum non fecerint, sufficiens fuit causa, vt essent coram Deo inexcusabiles, vt est ad Rom.1.
units.tr: 1. They defined Philosophy as a certain knowledge of divine and human things, which is, namely, lawful. If you prefer, say that it is the effort and desire of knowing. Certainly that is not empty or useless, even in the view of a manifest reprobate. But although some carp at this definition peevishly, it nonetheless contains nothing that can rightly be blamed, except perhaps that it cannot accomplish what Philosophy promises. Yet perhaps it accomplishes more than they believe. What has it accomplished in human affairs? No one is unaware: it invented the arts, refined them, and put them into order and method. It prescribed morals in a learned way, furnished the rule of an honourable life, and adorned commonwealths with laws, so that it has truly been said: Philosophy is the bulwark of the laws. In divine matters perhaps it accomplished less; but here we gladly confess its blindness, which, however, arose not so much from the faculty itself as from the fault of men. For Philosophy was an instrument of God, by which God was going to give them knowledge of himself, indeed did give it, if only they had used it rightly. Since they did not do so, there was a sufficient cause for them to be inexcusable before God, as it is in Rom. 1.

units.la: Cæterum, esto, tota cœca sit, vt est, interim laudabilis est conatus. Nulli Philosophi ad iustam Dei cognitionem peruenerunt, ergone Philosophia mala erit? non credo. Sed hoc dabitur, non sufficere ad vitam æternam. Quærenda alia media, in Christo scilicet. Interim conatus cognoscendi Deum & res diuinas, honestus imo necessarius est. Hunc cū profiteatur Philosophia, philosophemur sobrie, & Christum Dei filium, & in eo Deum patrem cognoscamus.
units.tr: Moreover, granting that it is wholly blind, as it is, nevertheless the effort is praiseworthy. No philosophers attained to a right knowledge of God: is Philosophy therefore bad? I do not think so. But this will be granted: it is not sufficient for eternal life. Other means must be sought, namely in Christ. Meanwhile the effort to know God and divine things is honourable, indeed necessary. Since Philosophy professes this, let us philosophize soberly, and let us know Christ the Son of God, and in him God the Father.

units.la: At in hac causa ne fallamur, ipsa Philosophia nos monet: quod scilicet in rebus diuinis hominis mens cœcutiat, adeoque etiam magis quam noctuæ oculi ad lucem Solis. Qua in re ingenuitas eius laudanda est, noluit enim in hac re tam ardua sibi nimium tribui, & agnouit se diuina maiestate obrui, vt se explicare commode nequeat.
units.tr: But that we may not be deceived in this matter, Philosophy itself warns us: namely, that in divine things the mind of man is blinded, and indeed more than the eyes of owls are to the light of the sun. In this respect its candour is to be praised, for it was unwilling to claim too much for itself in so arduous a matter, and acknowledged that it is overwhelmed by the divine majesty, so that it cannot explain it suitably.

units.la: Itaque cœcitatem hanc agnoscamus, vt quæramus in Christo hanc Philosophiæ partem quæ Dei cognitionem probe tradit. Præterea finis eius ad nos omnino pertinet. Is quisnam est? ὑπηρέτης τῆς ἀληθείας, vt ipsi testantur Philosophi. Et Iustinus ait, ὑπηρέτης τῆς ἀλη-θούς, θεὸς, unde probat indignos hoc nomine, qui veritatem, hoc est, ipsum non recte assequuti fuerint: ut revera indigni sunt hoc titulo omnes Ethnici Philosophi. Hinc erudite argumentatur idem Iustinus ad Antoniu Imperatore scribens: Decet, inquit, Philosophos τὸ ἀλη-θὲς μόνον τιμᾶν, vos estis Philosophi, & quidem pii diuti: ergo decet vos veritatem solam honorare, ut quae Philosophiae est finis. Nos in causa non admodum dissimili argumentamur, Philosophi est solum veritatem omnib. rebus anteferre: est enim finis suae professionis: at soli veri Christiani veritatem recte colunt, eamq; reb. omnib. praeferunt. Ergo soli Christiani dicendi erunt Philosophi. Huic quod respondere fuerint, non video, nisi quod Gentilium Philosophia longe alia sit, & ad finem hunc nunquam peruenerit. Ego vero repono, Philosophia, quamdiu Gentilis est, non suo respondet nomini: interim honestissimus est finis, ex quo efficitur honestissimā esse professionē. Quod vero addunt, finem hunc illam nō attigisse, quid tum? Ideone damnari debet conatus? non puto. Iuuetur misera & caeca Philosophia, ut ad illum finem perueniat, & salua res erit. Lex Dei honesta & bona est, quis negat? attamen illa nondum finem suum in hominibus obtinuit, ut scilicet tota seruetur ex totis viribus. Quid ergo isti respondebunt sic colligenti? Lex optatum finem non assequitur. Ergo seruanda non erat. Nonne illi responderent: imo ob illud magis vrgenda est lex, quia pauci boni sunt, & nulli toti satisfaciunt,
units.tr: Therefore let us acknowledge this blindness, so that we may seek in Christ that part of Philosophy which rightly teaches the knowledge of God. Moreover its end pertains entirely to us. What is it? servant of the truth [ὑπηρέτης τῆς ἀληθείας], as the philosophers themselves attest. And Justin says servant of the true God [ὑπηρέτης τῆς ἀληθοῦς θεοῦ], whence he proves that those who have not rightly attained the truth, that is, God himself, are unworthy of this name; as indeed all the Gentile philosophers are unworthy of this title. Hence the same Justin argues learnedly in writing to the Emperor Antoninus: It is fitting, he says, for philosophers to honour only what is true [τὸ ἀληθὲς μόνον τιμᾶν]; you are philosophers, and indeed pious ones: therefore it is fitting for you to honour the truth alone, since this is the end of Philosophy. We argue in a not very dissimilar case: It is the part of a philosopher to set the truth above all things: for this is the end of his profession. But only true Christians rightly cultivate the truth and prefer it to all things. Therefore only Christians will be called philosophers. I do not see what the opponents could answer to this, except that Gentile Philosophy is quite different and has never attained this end. But I reply: Philosophy, as long as it is Gentile, does not correspond to its name; meanwhile the end is most honourable, from which it follows that the profession is most honourable. But as to what they add, that Philosophy did not reach this end, what then? Ought the effort on that account to be condemned? I do not think so. Let wretched and blind Philosophy be helped, so that it may come to that end, and the thing will be safe. The law of God is honourable and good, who denies it? Yet that law has not yet attained its end among men, namely that it be kept wholly with all our strength. What then will they answer to one who reasons thus: The law does not attain its desired end. Therefore it was not to be kept. Would they not answer: rather, the law is to be pressed all the more for that very reason, because few are good and none satisfy it wholly,

units.la: recte fortasse. Sed nos etiam illud addimus, conatus vtrinque laudandos esse, & non fieri vel legis vel Philosophiæ culpa, quo minus homines per illam non iustificentur, vel per hanc ad solidam Dei cognitionem non veniant, sed potius hominum vitio. Si enim lex incideret in homines, qui illam plene seruarent, vtique illos iustos pronuntiaret, & Philosophia si idoneos nancisceretur cultores, vtique Dei cognitionem solidam traderet. Sed tam lex quam Philosophia nullos vnquam inuenerunt, nec inuenient extra Christum idoneos: ideo frustra est quod de fine non assequuto obiiciunt. Assequetur illum in Christo si commode applicetur. Accedit, quod sit Dei donum, quod vtique nemo calumniari debet temere.
units.tr: Perhaps rightly. But we add this as well: the effort on both sides deserves praise, and it is not the fault of the law or of philosophy that people are not justified by the one or do not come through the other to a firm knowledge of God; the fault lies rather with human beings. For if the law fell upon people who kept it fully, it would surely pronounce them righteous, and if philosophy found suitable devotees, it would surely impart a sound knowledge of God. But neither the law nor philosophy has ever found, or will ever find, anyone suitable outside Christ. So their objection about the unattained goal is groundless. The goal will be attained in Christ, if the law is rightly applied. Moreover, philosophy is a gift of God, and no one ought to slander it rashly.

units.la: Quod autem donum Dei sit, præter ipsos Philosophos qui hoc affirment, Platonem, Ciceronem, &c. ipsi Christiani Theologi fatentur, Eusebius, Iustinus, Clemens, aliique qui ab Hebræis docent Philosophiam ad Græcos tamen demanasse. Et Ap. ad Rom. 1. ait Deum illis manifestasse. A Deo igitur habuerunt, si quid boni habuerūt. Itaque Dei donum est. Quod vero illi afferunt de abusu, hoc libenter fatemur: sed pridem diximus abusum non esse Philosophiam, sed verum illius vsum, huncipsum Philosophiam esse censendam. Et sane abusus in multis est maior, quam vt facile dici possit. Ideo etiam libenter agnoscimus, eos in eo ipso malos esse interpretes, malos doctores pietatis, vt habet Iustinus, nus, imo furēs & patriarchas hæreticorum, vt Tertullianus.
units.tr: That philosophy is a gift of God is confessed not only by the philosophers who affirm it, such as Plato and Cicero, but also by Christian theologians themselves: Eusebius, Justin, Clement, and others who teach that philosophy came from the Hebrews to the Greeks. The Apostle also says in Romans 1 that God revealed it to them. Therefore, if they had anything good, they had it from God, and so it is God's gift. As for what they say about abuse, we gladly admit it; but we said some time ago that abuse is not philosophy, but its true use is what should be counted as philosophy. Indeed, the abuse is in many cases too great to be easily described. So we also readily acknowledge that in this very matter they are bad interpreters and bad teachers of piety, as Justin says, indeed thieves and patriarchs of heretics, as Tertullian says.

units.la: Interim aliquid boni habere concedendum est, quod illis Deus manifestauit, & in quo consentiant cum primis patriarchis. Id quale sit, suo explicabitur loco. Præterea Philosophia, omnia sua iubet tradere sine affectibus, nuda veritatis ratione. Secus certe oratores faciunt, qui indulgent omnibus modis affectibus, persuadere conantur quocunque tandem modo. Id non capit Philosophia, sed rationes sequi iubet: ac sine causa bona, saltem probabili nihil admittit. Cur igitur admittuntur oratores Ethnici ab his qui Philosophiam damnant? nō video cur illi huic sint præferendi.
units.tr: Meanwhile, it must be conceded that they have something good, which God revealed to them, and in which they agree with the first patriarchs. What kind of thing this is will be explained in its own place. Furthermore, philosophy bids that all its matters be taught without emotions, by the bare reasoning of truth. Orators certainly do otherwise: they indulge the emotions in every way and try to persuade by whatever means. Philosophy does not accept this, but bids us follow reasons, and it admits nothing without a good cause, or at least a probable one. Why, then, are pagan orators admitted by those who condemn philosophy? I do not see why they should be preferred to philosophers.

units.la: Item in rebus humanis, necessaria est εὐταξία. Philosophia autem nihil tradit nisi εὐταξίαν. Itaque necessaria est in rebus humanis. Et leges ciuiles inde ortæ sunt. Primi enim legumlatores omnes Philosophi fuerunt apud gentes, vt Solon, Lycurgus, Draco, Numa, Plato: Et de Republica nemo vnquam melius scripsit ipsis Philosophis. Hinc Alcidamas recte dixit, Philosophiam esse propugnaculum legum. Ratio est, quia fontes monstrat, & Iustinus ex Platone illud approbat: Nisi principes & subditi philosophentur, non posse beatas esse Respublicas. Interim libenter quoque hic fatemur, magnam esse illius infirmitatem, vt in Republica constituenda non obtineat id quod vult.
units.tr: Likewise, in human affairs good order (εὐταξία) is necessary, and philosophy teaches nothing but good order. Therefore it is necessary in human affairs, and civil laws have arisen from it. For among the nations the first lawgivers were all philosophers, such as Solon, Lycurgus, Draco, Numa and Plato; and no one has ever written better about the commonwealth than the philosophers themselves. Hence Alcidamas rightly said that philosophy is the bulwark of the laws. The reason is that it shows the sources, and Justin approves this from Plato: unless rulers and subjects philosophize, commonwealths cannot be happy. Meanwhile we gladly admit here too that philosophy is greatly weak, in that when a commonwealth is to be established it does not achieve what it wills.

units.la: Id Plato reipsa expertus est, toties frustra in Siciliam nauigado, & toties frustra Dionysium admonenmonendo. Ethnica Philosophia ipsa lex naturæ est, aut saltem illius pars, quæ diuinitus cordibus hominum impressa est. Studio vero & ingeniis Philosophorum mirifice exculta, vt potius inde commendanda sit Philosophia, quam explodenda.
units.tr: Plato himself experienced this in fact, sailing so often in vain to Sicily and so often in vain admonishing Dionysius. Pagan philosophy is itself the law of nature, or at least that part of it which has been divinely impressed upon the hearts of human beings. But it has been wonderfully refined by the study and talents of the philosophers, so that philosophy is to be commended for this rather than rejected.

units.la: Interea etiam hic fatemur illius imbecillitatem, imo si ita placeat, cæcitatem, quod male statuat de iustitia & viro iusto, quem non nisi ex actionibus pronunciat iustum dici posse, cum religio Christi doceat coram Deo iustos effici Christi merito, sine omni operum nostrorum respectu. Gratis, inquit Apostolus, iustificati estis, ipsius gratia, idque non ex nobis.
units.tr: Here too we admit its weakness, indeed its blindness, if you like, in that it wrongly lays down what justice is and who a just man is, saying that a man can be called just only from his actions, whereas the religion of Christ teaches that people are made righteous before God by the merit of Christ, without any regard to our works. "Freely," says the Apostle, "you are justified, by his grace, and that not of yourselves."

units.la: Hoc igitur discat Philosophia à Paulo Apostolo, & se intra suas metas contineat, de iustitia politica differat, & in ciuium conuentibus dicat, Iustus est, qui iusta fecerit, hoc est, à posterioribus sumi debet iudicium de virtutibus, vt nemo de virtute aliqua glorietur, nisi cuius vita ac mores, fructibus eius virtutis ornentur: quo sensu rectissime & piissime Philosophia statuit, neminem iustum esse, nisi qui iusta egerit. Coram Domino alia est ratio iustitiæ, quam nobis de suis thesauris, vt vestem induit.
units.tr: Let philosophy therefore learn this from the Apostle Paul, and keep itself within its own bounds: let it discuss civic justice, and in the assemblies of citizens let it say, "He is just who has done just things." That is, judgment about virtues must be drawn from their effects, so that no one boasts of any virtue unless his life and conduct are adorned by its fruits. In this sense philosophy rightly and piously lays down that no one is just except one who has done just things. Before the Lord, however, justice is reckoned on another basis, which he clothes us with from his own treasures, as a garment.

units.la: De Physica idem dici poterit. Illustris est illa adhuc, & fuit cognoscendi Deum via. De hac præcipue loquitur Apostolus Rom. primo, Quod ex visibilibus Deum inuisibilem cognouerint. Cœlum & terra testantur sapientissimū fui conditorem, & quantum ad Dei cognitionem in Philosophia contulerit, ex ipsis Philosophis cognosci potest. Aristoteles ex ordine causarum natur.eo peruenit, vt concluderet, vnum esse & æternum primum motorem rerum omnium. Locus est libro octauo Phys. vbi sic scribit: Φανερὸν ἐκ τούτων, ὅτ' ἀνάγκη, εἶναι τι ἓν, καὶ ἀΐδιον τὸ πρῶτον κινοῦν. Et in Metaph. vnum primum motorem, hoc est, Deum fatetur & statuit, citans versum Homeri: Non est bonum multos esse principes, vnus Deus esto. Cicero de natura Deorum, erudite colligit ex natura mentis humanæ esse Deum, qui rebus humanis consulat: quia mens humana prouidet multum. Oportet igitur mentem esse architectum, quæ illa hominis animo reuelet. Sic de meliore quadam sorte piorum colligit erudite: Fieri non potest vt optimi viri ad perpetuas miserias nati sint. At in hac terra, quanto quis melior, tanto iniquiore vtitur fortuna. Ergo superest, vt sit aliqua conditio melior, vbi boni bene & mali male habeant. Talia infinita produci ex Platone possunt: sed nolo in his esse longior. Artes quas Philosophiæ debemus in se reconditam habent certitudinem, vt Arithmetica, Geometria, tota Mathesis, quæ nihil aliud sunt, quam testimonia æterni Dei. Sic Dialectica methodum docendi nobis monstrat, qua certe in docenda etiam pietate carere non possumus. Monstrat quid res sit definiendo: partes apponit diuisionibus: ordinem causarum monstrat: quib. cognitis, mens facilius & libentius acquieacquiescit praeceptis, duci enim vult. Ad pietatem quoque facit non solum quia subministrat methodum docendi, sed etiam quia ad Dei cognitionem introducit. Placuit enim Deo hoc uti organo. Rom. 1. quę sit illius aeterna potentia & maiestas patefecit eis. Id nisi Apostolus diceret, vix piorum aures ferrent: sed dicendum est; & faciendum, quia verum est.
units.tr: The same may be said of physics. That science is still illustrious, and it was a way of knowing God. The Apostle speaks chiefly of this in Romans 1: "That from visible things they knew the invisible God." Heaven and earth bear witness to their most wise Creator, and how much philosophy has contributed to the knowledge of God can be learned from the philosophers themselves. Aristotle, from the order of natural causes, arrived at the conclusion that there is one eternal first mover of all things. The passage is in book 8 of the Physics, where he writes thus: "It is clear from these things that it is necessary that there be something one and eternal, the first mover" (φανερὸν ἐκ τούτων, ὅτι ἀνάγκη εἶναι τι ἕν, καὶ ἀΐδιον τὸ πρῶτον κινοῦν). And in the Metaphysics he acknowledges and affirms one first mover, that is, God, citing the verse of Homer: "It is not good for many to be rulers; let there be one God." Cicero, in On the Nature of the Gods, learnedly infers from the nature of the human mind that there is a God who cares for human affairs, because the human mind foresees much. "It is necessary, therefore, that there be a mind as architect, which reveals these things to the soul of man." Likewise he learnedly infers from the better lot of the pious: "It cannot be that the best men are born for perpetual miseries. But in this earth, the better a man is, the more unjust is the fortune he enjoys. Therefore it remains that there is some better condition, where the good fare well and the bad fare badly." Countless such things can be drawn from Plato, but I do not wish to be longer on these points. The arts which we owe to philosophy have certainty hidden within them, such as arithmetic, geometry and all mathematics, which are nothing other than witnesses to the eternal God. So too dialectic shows us a method of teaching, which we certainly cannot do without even in teaching piety. It shows what a thing is by defining it; it adds parts by divisions; it shows the order of causes, by which, once they are known, the mind more easily and willingly acquiesces in precepts, for it wishes to be led. It also serves piety, not only because it supplies a method of teaching, but also because it leads to the knowledge of God. For it has pleased God to use this instrument. Romans 1: "His eternal power and majesty he has made manifest to them." Unless the Apostle said this, the ears of the pious would hardly bear it; but it must be said and done, because it is true.

units.la: Interim non temere dixerim fuisse Graecis paedagogiam ad Christum, quemadmodum lex Iudaeis, quod tamen Clemens Alexan. serm. lib. 1. non dubitat affirmare:
units.tr: Meanwhile I would not rashly say that philosophy was a schoolmaster to the Greeks leading them to Christ, as the law was to the Jews, although Clement of Alexandria, in the first book of his Stromata, does not hesitate to affirm this.

units.la: Hoc quidem admiserim, quod ante adventum Christi ad politicam iustitiam necessaria illis fuerit. Post eius adventum, iam ad pietatem utilis & ad cultum Dei, tamen paedagogiam ad Christum, qualis lex fuit, non agnosco. Quare saltem hoc certo statuamus; piis adolescentibus philosophandum esse; nec solum per otium quod habet Clemens, ut qui bellaria ad cœnam inferant. Sed serio quoque quod habet Iustinus: illudque revera agnoscamus τῷ ὄντι μέγιστον κτῆμα καὶ πιμώτατον θεῷ. Praeterea cum iudicio philosophandum esse, ne erroribus nos committamus potius, quam sacris sententiis, quod Iustinus habet his verbis: ἄνευ Φιλοσοφίας, καὶ ὀρθῶ λόγῳ ἐκ ἂν παρείη φρόνησις. Διὸ χρὴ πάντα ἄνθρωπον φιλοσοφεῖν, καὶ τοῦτο μέγιστον καὶ πιμιώτατον ἔργον ἡγεῖσθαι. Solos etiam veros Philosophos honorandos, qui non sunt alii, quam qui Christum agnouerunt, & moribus magis, quam verbis philosophantur, vt viam etiam ad tribunalia litigantium nesciant, quod habet ex Plat. Euseb. libro 12. præp. cap. 20.
units.tr: I would indeed admit this much: that before the coming of Christ it was necessary for them in order to attain civic justice. After his coming, it is now useful for piety and for the worship of God; yet I do not acknowledge it as a schoolmaster to Christ in the way the law was. Therefore let us at least establish this as certain: pious young people ought to philosophize, and not merely at leisure, as Clement has it, as those who bring dainties to dinner. But also in earnest, as Justin has it; and let us truly acknowledge it as "the greatest and most precious possession, and most pleasing to God" (τῷ ὄντι μέγιστον κτῆμα καὶ πιμώτατον θεῷ). Furthermore, one must philosophize with judgment, lest we commit ourselves to errors rather than to holy sentences, as Justin puts it in these words: "Without philosophy and right reason, prudence cannot be present. Therefore every man must philosophize, and regard this as the greatest and most precious work" (ἄνευ Φιλοσοφίας, καὶ ὀρθῶ λόγῳ ἐκ ἂν παρείη φρόνησις. Διὸ χρὴ πάντα ἄνθρωπον φιλοσοφεῖν, καὶ τοῦτο μέγιστον καὶ πιμιώτατον ἔργον ἡγεῖσθαι). Only true philosophers are to be honoured, who are none other than those who have known Christ, and who philosophize more by their morals than by their words, so that they do not even know the way to the tribunals of litigants; this he has from Plato, Eusebius, Praeparatio Evangelica, book 12, chapter 20.

units.la: II. Sophismatis Elenchus.
units.tr: II. Refutation of the Sophism.

units.la: QVod scatet infinitis erroribus, & quidem religionis Christianæ veritati contrariis, id Christianus debet abominari.
units.tr: Whatever teems with countless errors, and indeed errors contrary to the truth of the Christian religion, a Christian ought to abominate.

units.la: Atqui Philosophia scatet infinitis erroribus, & quidem iis qui religionis Christianæ veritati aduersantur.
units.tr: But philosophy teems with countless errors, and indeed those that oppose the truth of the Christian religion.

units.la: Ergo Philosophiam Christianus debet abominari.
units.tr: Therefore a Christian ought to abominate philosophy.

units.la: Assumptio demonstratur longa inductione errorum, quos admiserunt partim Ethnici, partim Christiani Philosophi.
units.tr: The minor premise is demonstrated by a long list of errors admitted partly by pagan and partly by Christian philosophers.

units.la: Ex Ethnicorum gentilitate recensent primum errores immanes Ethnicorum in genere, quos enumerant Centuriarum scriptores. Deinde vero in specie Platonis & Aristotelis.
units.tr: First they list the monstrous errors of the Gentiles in general, as the writers of the Centuries enumerate them, drawn from the paganism of the nations. Then they list those of Plato and Aristotle in particular.

units.la: Platonis errores recenset And. Libauius in Schediasm. numero nonaginta duos, quos hodie nonnulli in vituperium vniuersæ trahunt Philosophiæ, vt 1. de communione vxorum & liberorum promiscua. 2. de malorum sobole extra patriam releganda. 3. de fabulosa vetustate historiarum mundi. 4. de Deo conditore mundi ad sempiternam ideâ ab ipso inspectam. 5. de mundo omnium genitorum pulcerrimo. 6. de omnium creatorum maxima simi-litudine cum Deo creatore. 7. de modo inani creationis diuinæ. diuina. 8. quod dixerit mundum esse animal intel-ligens aeternum. 9. quod hoc animal ad aliud ani-mal scilicet ideale in Deo sit conditum. 10. de dupli-ci ab illo ficto mundo, nempe intelligibili & exem-plari, & deinde sensibili. 11. de terra antiquissimo Deorum in coelo contentorum. 12. quod mundum faciat animal, eique nihilominus sensuum instru-menta adimat. 13. quod mundum dicat ali senio & consumptione sui. 14. quod mundum appellet De-um beatum. 15. quod animam mundi ponat in e-ius media parte. 16. quod animam mundi antiquio-rem mundo & prius factam asseueret, &c. Plura er-rata curiosius conquisita videris in Sched. A. Lib.
units.tr: Andreas Libavius, in his Schediasma, lists ninety-two errors of Plato, which some today drag out to disparage philosophy as a whole: 1. on the shared community of wives and children; 2. that the offspring of evil men should be banished from the homeland; 3. on the fabulous antiquity of the histories of the world; 4. that God made the world according to an eternal idea viewed by Him; 5. that the world is the most beautiful of all things that have been begotten; 6. that of all created things it bears the greatest likeness to God its Creator; 7. on the empty mode of divine creation; 8. that he called the world an eternal intelligent animal; 9. that this animal was made in God after another animal, namely the ideal one; 10. on the twofold world, which he feigned, namely the intelligible and exemplar world, and then the sensible world; 11. on the earth as the most ancient dwelling of the gods, contained in heaven; 12. that he makes the world an animal and yet takes from it the instruments of the senses; 13. that he says the world is nourished by old age and by its own consumption; 14. that he calls the world a blessed God; 15. that he places the soul of the world in its middle part; 16. that he asserts the soul of the world to be older than the world and made before it, etc. More errors, sought out more diligently, you may see in Libavius's Sched. A.

units.la: Aristotelis multa & magna errata videris in Patrum eorum, qui aduersus gentes scripsere scri-ptis: in disputationibus Peripateticis Francisci Patri-cii: in Disceptationibus Francisci Muti Consentini, & in dissertatione Henningi Rennemanni.
units.tr: Many and great errors of Aristotle you may see in the writings of those Fathers who wrote against the Gentiles; in the Peripatetic Disputations of Francesco Patrizi; in the Disceptationes of Francesco Mutio of Cosenza; and in the dissertation of Henning Rennemann.

units.la: Christianorum Philosophorum errores cumulant aut ex iis, qui Aristotelis Platonisve placitis erroribusque pertinacius insistunt, eosque aut palliant, aut tuentur: praesertim vero ex Doctoribus scholasticis fasciculum colligunt errorum: aut ex iis, qui Rameae Philosophiae suam nouant operam. Ramo autem obiectant haec crimina. 1. quod defecerit a venerada antiquitate. 2. quod nimio φιλοκωμίας & ἀπορίας studio distentus fuerit. 3. quod tres illas leges de conformandis artium praeceptis, contra Aristotelis mente furiosa (vt ipsi loquuntur) mēte traduxerit[?]. 4. quod Ramea breuitas afferat crassas tenebras bras & obscuritate ipsis praeceptis. 5. quod multoties praeter modum Aristotelem sit insectatus. 6. quod Philosophia Ramea viam quibusuis haeresibus sternat in negotio religionis, praecipue autem, quod secta, quam vocant, Calviniana multos quotidie surculos inde expullulare videamus, & nescio qua alia convicia iaculetur homines multi in optimam philosophandi rationem.
units.tr: They pile up the errors of Christian philosophers either from those who cling more stubbornly to the opinions and errors of Aristotle or Plato and either excuse or defend them; or especially from the scholastic teachers, whom they gather into a bundle of errors; or from those who labour to renew Ramist philosophy. And they bring these charges against Ramus: 1. that he departed from venerable antiquity; 2. that he was consumed by an excessive zeal for contention [φιλονικίας] and for puzzles [ἀπορίας]; 3. that he perverted those three laws on shaping the precepts of the arts against the mind of Aristotle, with a furious mind (as they themselves put it); 4. that Ramist brevity brings thick darkness and obscurity to the precepts themselves; 5. that he has attacked Aristotle beyond measure on many occasions; 6. that Ramist philosophy paves the way for all manner of heresies in matters of religion, especially since we see many shoots sprouting daily from the sect they call Calvinist; and whatever other insults many men hurl at the best method of philosophizing.

units.la: Responsio.
units.tr: Response.

units.la: Hoc sophisma est confutatum partim ex confusione erratorum, hominum Philosophiam profitentium, & ipsius verae Philosophiae: partim ex confusione paganae & Christianae Philosophiae: partim ex nimis curiosa inquisitione in scripta veterum, quae eo animo eorum accedit Lectionem, ut ex iis, araneorum instar, venena & errata rigidiore iudicio confiemus: partim ex vanis calumniis.
units.tr: This sophism has been refuted partly by confusing the errors of men who profess philosophy with true philosophy itself; partly by confusing pagan and Christian philosophy; partly by an overly curious inquiry into the writings of the ancients, which approaches their reading in order to extract from them, like spiders, poisons and errors, by a rather harsh judgment; and partly by empty calumnies.

units.la: Primo enim errores sunt errantium hominum non artium. At importantur in artes & earum systema: Respon. Haec non est artium constitutio, sed corruptio. Nos Philosophiam ex suae ipsius natura ac definitione metimur, non ex hominum variis modis nomine Philosophiae delirantium. Aliud est Theologus Erraticus, aliud Theologia. Theologorum naevi & lapsus non vitiant Theologiae sanctitatem. Neque (ut iam aliquoties est repetitum) hominum artificum seu artem aliquam tractantium aut docentium errores sunt imputandi ipsis artibus. Te seductum a veritatis religiosae, & sanctae fidei via, non TheoTheosophia, sed Theologus suis aberrantibus opinionibus decepit. Aliud itaque Plato & Aristoteles: aliud Philosophia.
units.tr: First, errors belong to erring men, not to the arts. But they are imputed to the arts and their system. Answer: this is not the constitution of the arts but their corruption. We measure philosophy by its own nature and definition, not by the various ways in which men rave under the name of philosophy. One thing is an erring theologian, another is theology. The blemishes and slips of theologians do not taint the holiness of theology. Nor (as has been said more than once) are the errors of craftsmen, or of men who practise or teach some art, to be imputed to the arts themselves. It was not theology but the theologian, with his erring opinions, who deceived you and led you from the way of religious truth and holy faith. So Plato and Aristotle are one thing; philosophy is another.

units.la: 2. Deinde aliud est vera & Christiana Philosophia, quæ veritate Dei & rei hominem ad sui perfectionem instituit: aliud vero Philosophia pagana, quæ Aristotelicis, Platonicis, aliorumque est conspurcata paganissimis & pudendis ignorantiæ gentilis opinionibus ac vanitatibus. Illam tuemur, hanc purgatam exoptamus. Corpus Philosophiæ vlceribus erratorum forte scatet: sanentur vlcera, tollantur vitia, & corporis sanitas retineatur ac defendatur. Aliud Philosophia nostra re-repurgata: aliud Platonica & Aristotelica ex paganissimorum concursu conflata (quæ dicitur) Philosophia.
units.tr: Second, true and Christian philosophy, which instructs man in the truth about God and things for his own perfection, is one thing; pagan philosophy, which has been defiled by the most pagan and shameful opinions and vanities of Gentile ignorance, found in the Aristotelians, the Platonists and others, is another. We defend the former and wish the latter purged. The body of philosophy perhaps teems with the ulcers of errors: let the ulcers be healed, the vices removed, and the health of the body kept and defended. Our philosophy is one, re-purged; the so-called Platonic and Aristotelian philosophy, compounded from the concourse of the most pagan men, is another.

units.la: 3. Nimis curiosa inquisitio & animaduersio in aliorum scripta ac labores, sepiuscule transilire solet legem charitatis; Erratum nonnunquam est, non probe intellectum. Candor hic postulatur, & modesta humilitas nostræ etiam imbecillitatis sibi conscia, præsertim in Ethnicorum scriptis versans, conatus bonos admirans, lapsus vero miserans. In aliorum næuis lyncei sumus & insigniter oculati, in nostris vero talpæ. Verum quia nonnulli ex ordine Theologorum in peccatis Philosophorum gentilium & aliorum, coaceruandis & exagitandis ita sunt solertes & iniquiores censores, vt inde Philosophiæ ipsius crimina à se conflata ebucciebuccinent, & vitia hominum affricent ipsi doctrinæ: age insaniamus cum illis, & inuiti etiam pudenda nonnullorum sanctissimorum Theologorum ipsis ante oculos ponamus detecta, non animo malo, sed eo qui cupiat vt & ipsi videant vanitatem consequentiæ stolidæ, & discant sibi etiam, suaeque Theologiæ cautius mercari & fabricari conclusiunculas. Ita arguitur:
units.tr: Third, too curious an inquiry and censure into the writings and labours of others often overleaps the law of charity; an error is sometimes merely a failure to understand properly. This candour is required, and a modest humility, conscious of our own weakness, especially when dealing with the writings of the Gentiles: admiring their good efforts and pitying their slips. We are lynx-eyed and remarkably sharp-sighted about others' blemishes, but moles about our own. Yet since some theologians are so skilful, and so unfair as censors, in heaping up and hunting down the sins of the pagan philosophers and others, that from them they trumpet forth the crimes of philosophy itself, which they have fabricated, and rub men's vices onto the doctrine itself, come, let us go mad with them, and, though unwillingly, set before their very eyes the shameful things disclosed about some most holy theologians. Not with an evil mind, but so that they too may see the emptiness of a foolish inference, and learn to be more cautious in trading and fabricating little conclusions for their own theology. The argument runs thus:

units.la: Quod scatet multis erroribus, id Christianus ab-ominari debet. Scripta Ethnicorum & aliorum Philosophorum scatent multis erroribus. Ergo scripta Philosophorū Christianus debet abominari. Responderi potest ad propos. Errores esse abominabiles, non id ipsum, in quo sunt errores, vel abominabile quid esse, non per se sed propter abominabiles errores. Ad assumptum.
units.tr: What teems with many errors, a Christian must abominate. The writings of the Gentiles and of other philosophers teem with many errors. Therefore a Christian must abominate the writings of philosophers. It may be answered to the major premise that errors are abominable, not that very thing in which the errors are; or that something is abominable not in itself but on account of the abominable errors. To the minor premise:

units.la: 1. Non omnia Philosophorum scripta scatent erroribus.
units.tr: 1. Not all the writings of philosophers teem with errors.

units.la: 2. Neque tota: Ergo probate omnia, & quod bonum est retinete. Ergo quod malum & erroneum, id ipsum abiiciamus.
units.tr: 2. Nor do they teem throughout. Prove all things, and hold fast what is good. Therefore let us cast away what is bad and erroneous.

units.la: 3. Aliud scripta Philosophorum, aliud Philosophia ipsa. Sicut aliud scripta Theologorum, aliud ipsa Theologia.
units.tr: 3. The writings of philosophers are one thing, and philosophy itself is another; as the writings of theologians are one thing, and theology itself is another.

units.la: Iam scripta Theologorum erratia assumamus.
units.tr: Now let us take up the erroneous writings of theologians.

units.la: Quod erroribus scatet multis, id Christiano est auersandum.
units.tr: What teems with many errors, a Christian must shun.

units.la: Atqui multa scripta veterum & recentium Theologorum scatent fœdis & multis erroribus. Ergo ne ipsa plane sunt abominanda, in quibus errores isti res isti latent? At quid tum, abominetur quis ista scripta in vniuersum. Nunquid ipsa Theologia propterea est abominabilis. Tollantur Theologorum errores, & sana nobis relinquatur Theologia.
units.tr: But many writings of ancient and recent theologians teem with foul and numerous errors. Therefore are those writings wholly to be abominated, in which those errors lie hidden? But what follows? Should anyone abominate those writings in general? Is theology itself therefore abominable? Let the errors of theologians be removed, and sound theology be left to us.

units.la: Assumptum est bimembre. 1. requirit de antiquis eorumque lapsibus ac erratis. Praetereo vetustiores illos, & praecipue erroribus grauidum Origenem, vide quaeso mecum paulo etiam intentiorib. oculis optimorum aliorumque Theologorum antiquorum, Tertulliani, Cypriani, Lactantii & aliorum scripta, quae & suis vspiam non destituuntur (vti censent Euangelici nostri) naevis & erroribus.
units.tr: The minor premise has two parts. 1. It concerns the ancients and their lapses and errors. I pass over the more remote ones, and especially Origen, who is full of errors. Look with me, with rather more attentive eyes, at the writings of the other excellent ancient theologians, Tertullian, Cyprian, Lactantius and others, which are nowhere free from blemishes and errors (as our Evangelicals think).

units.la: Tertullianus in suis monumentis 1. amplexus est Montani prodigiosum errorem de secundis nuptiis, quas prorsus damnat, in vita Origenis.
units.tr: 1. Tertullian in his works embraced Montanus's monstrous error concerning second marriages, which he utterly condemns, in the Life of Origen.

units.la: 2. Factus Montani blasphemi satelles appellat cum omnis veritatis deductorem, plusque Montano, quam Spiritui S. attribuit. ibid.
units.tr: 2. Having become a satellite of the blasphemous Montanus, he calls him the guide of all truth, and attributes more to Montanus than to the Holy Spirit. ibid.

units.la: 3. Militiam Christiano non convenire, de coron. milit.
units.tr: 3. That military service does not befit a Christian, De corona militis.

units.la: 4. Poenitentiam vnam tantum post Baptismum admittit. lib. 2. aduersus Marcionem.
units.tr: 4. He admits only one repentance after baptism. Book 2 against Marcion.

units.la: 5. Liberum arbitrium post lapsum ita euehit, vt Pelagius ipse vix ausus fuerit pari libertate de eo pronunciare. Non, poneretur, inquit, lex ei qui non haberet obsequium debitum legi in sua potestate. Eadem arbitrii potestas & libertas, qua fuit in Adam, etiam nunc efficit victorem de eodem Diabolo.
units.tr: 5. He so exalts free will after the fall that Pelagius himself scarcely dared to pronounce about it with such freedom. "The law would not be laid," he says, "upon one who did not have the due obedience to the law within his power." The same power and freedom of will that was in Adam still makes man the conqueror over the Devil himself.

units.la: 6.Hinc de prædestinatione errorsecutus est, quem prodit aduersus Marcionem. lib.8.
units.tr: 6. From this he fell into an error about predestination, which he sets out in book 8 against Marcion.

units.la: 7.Chiliastarum errore implicatus fuit. libro tertio.
units.tr: 7. He was entangled in the error of the Chiliasts. Book 3.

units.la: 8.Angelos rem habuisse cum filiis hominum. De velandis virginibus.
units.tr: 8. That the angels had intercourse with the daughters of men. On the veiling of virgins.

units.la: 9. Miras opiniones de generatione Diabolorum, & operationibus eorundem habet, quasi ipsi metalla & herbarum naturas monstrarint hominibus, quod ait Enochum retulisse. De habitu virginum.
units.tr: 9. He holds strange opinions about the generation of the devils and their operations, as if they had revealed to men the nature of metals and herbs, which he says Enoch reported. On the dress of virgins.

units.la: 10. Hominem ad imaginem Christi, eam nimirum, quam Christus repræsentauit homo factus, docet esse conditum: lib.de resur.carnis.
units.tr: 10. He teaches that man was created in the image of Christ, namely that image which Christ represented when he became man. Book on the resurrection of the flesh.

units.la: 11.Immodicus fuit in Martyrii laude, quasi eo veniam homines mereantur.
units.tr: 11. He was immoderate in praising martyrdom, as if men earned pardon by it.

units.la: 12. Defendit superstitiosa ieiunia, ridiculasque ceremonias Montanistarum: De ieiunio.
units.tr: 12. He defends superstitious fasts and the ridiculous ceremonies of the Montanists. On fasting.

units.la: 13.Operum merita nimis extollit castitatis inprimis & iustitiæ.
units.tr: 13. He extols the merits of works too highly, especially of chastity and righteousness.

units.la: 14. Nimis durus est, dum coronas à Christianis nullo loco, nullo tempore vult gestari. De corona militis.
units.tr: 14. He is too harsh in wanting Christians never, in no place and at no time, to wear crowns. On the soldier's crown.

units.la: 15. Pio homini non vult licere in persequutione fugiat.Libro de fuga.
units.tr: 15. He does not want a godly man to be allowed to flee in persecution. Book on flight.

units.la: 16.Animas prius pati apud inferos, quam corpora scribit: De resurr. carnis.
units.tr: 16. He writes that souls suffer in the underworld before bodies do. On the resurrection of the flesh.

units.la: 17.Quod Deum corpus esse affirmauit, alii excusarunt, alii reprehenderunt.
units.tr: 17. That he affirmed God to be a body: some excused this, others censured it.

units.la: 18. Habet præterea multas alias peculiares opiniones hic pater: Spiritum sanctum minorem Christo esse scribit: quia à Christo accipiat. De Trinitate. 19.Eos duntaxat baptizandos censet, qui Christum nosse potuerunt: De Baptismo.
units.tr: 18. This father also has many other peculiar opinions. He writes that the Holy Spirit is less than Christ, because he receives from Christ. On the Trinity. 19. He thinks only those should be baptized who were able to know Christ. On Baptism.

units.la: 20. Iohannis Baptisma nihil cœleste vult præstitisse: Ibidem.
units.tr: 20. He holds that John's baptism conferred nothing heavenly. Ibid.

units.la: 21. Claues soli Petro personaliter datas, & super ipsum Ecclesiam extructam asserit: Lib.de pudicit.
units.tr: 21. He asserts that the keys were given personally to Peter alone, and that the Church was built upon him. Book on modesty.

units.la: Cypriani errores notantur hi. 1. Quod baptizatos ab hæreticis denuo tingendos duxerit.
units.tr: The following errors of Cyprian are noted. 1. That he thought those baptized by heretics must be baptized again.

units.la: 2. Quod nimis anxie & superstitiose vrget in cœna aquam vino miscendam ideo, quod sanguis & aqua ex latere Christi fluxerit.
units.tr: 2. That he urges too anxiously and superstitiously, in the Lord's Supper, that water be mixed with the wine, because blood and water flowed from the side of Christ.

units.la: 3. Quod sensit Baptismum ministri mali & impii non esse legitimum.
units.tr: 3. That he held that the baptism of a wicked and impious minister is not valid.

units.la: 4. Quod Spiritum S. Christo minorem dixerit, Ep.ad Pompei.
units.tr: 4. That he called the Holy Spirit less than Christ. Letter to Pompeius.

units.la: 5. Quod Baptismum absolute & simpliciter ad salutem necessarium putat: unde alius error ei nascitur, nimirum passionem latronis vicem Baptismi supppleuisse.
units.tr: 5. That he thinks baptism absolutely and simply necessary to salvation; from this another error arises in him, namely that the thief's suffering took the place of baptism.

units.la: 6. Quod satisfactionibus remissionem peccatorum tribuit, Serm.de lapsis.
units.tr: 6. That he attributes the remission of sins to satisfactions. Sermon on the lapsed.

units.la: 7. Quod lapsos non desperare quidem de Domini misericordia iubet, nec tamen veniam pœnitenti condicere. ibid.
