units.tr: 7. That he bids the lapsed indeed not despair of the Lord's mercy, yet does not promise pardon to the penitent. Ibid.

units.la: 8. Quod ceremonias Montanisticas, ut consecrationem & unctionem post Baptismum, à Tertulliano acceptas retinet, defendit, vrget, libro 1. Ep.vlt.
units.tr: 8. That he retains, defends and urges the Montanist ceremonies taken over from Tertullian, such as consecration and anointing after baptism. Book 1, last letter.

units.la: 9. Quod doctrinam de Iustificatione fidei cum iustitia operum confuderit.
units.tr: 9. That he confused the doctrine of justification by faith with righteousness by works.

units.la: 10. Quod nimis hyperbolice commendat virginita-tem.
units.tr: 10. That he commends virginity too extravagantly.

units.la: 11. Quod cœnam Domini quasi ad salutem simpli-citer necessariam etiam infantibus dari permiserit: sermone de lapsis.
units.tr: 11. That he allowed the Lord's Supper to be given even to infants, as if it were simply necessary to salvation. Sermon on the lapsed.

units.la: 12. Quod bella gerere Christianis illicitum esse putarit, lib.2.Ep.2.
units.tr: 12. That he thought it unlawful for Christians to wage war. Book 2, letter 2.

units.la: 13. Quod noua deuotione viuentes admonuit, vt post mortem suam apud Deum memores essent, lib.1.Ep.1.
units.tr: 13. That he exhorted the living, with a new devotion, to remember him before God after his death. Book 1, letter 1.

units.la: 14. Quod opinionem istam tuetur, baptisma ipsum esse sine spiritu S.qui tunc primum daretur & accipe- retur, quando Episcopus ad invocationem spiritus S. manus baptizatis imponeret.
units.tr: 14. That he defends this opinion: that baptism itself is without the Holy Spirit, who was then first given and received when the bishop laid hands on the baptized at the invocation of the Holy Spirit.

units.la: Lactantii hi notantur nævi.1. Quod periculo-sa loquendi formula Deum patrem ex se ipso dicit esse procreatum, lib.1.cap.7.
units.tr: The following blemishes of Lactantius are noted. 1. That in a perilous form of speech he says God the Father was begotten of himself. Book 1, chapter 7.

units.la: 2. Quod filii Dei æternitatem non agnouit. lib.4.c.6.
units.tr: 2. That he did not acknowledge the eternity of the Son of God. Book 4, chapter 6.

units.la: 3. Quod contra fidem historiæ sacræ scribit, Christum nunquam se ipsum Deum dixisse: quia non ser-uasset fidem: si missus, vt Deos tolleret & vnum asse-reret, induceret alium præter vnum, lib.4. cap.14.
units.tr: 3. That, contrary to the faith of sacred history, he writes that Christ never called himself God, because he would not have kept faith: if he was sent to destroy the gods and assert the one God, he would have introduced another beside the one. Book 4, chapter 14.

units.la: 4. Quod negat Pilatum sententiam in morte Christi protulisse, lib.4.cap.18.
units.tr: 4. That he denies that Pilate pronounced the sentence in the death of Christ. Book 4, chapter 18.

units.la: 5. Quod Christum in Galilæam ait profectum, no-luisse Iudæis se ostendere, ne eos ad pœnitentiam ad-duceret: lib.4.cap.20.
units.tr: 5. That he says Christ went away into Galilee and was unwilling to show himself to the Jews, lest he lead them to repentance. Book 4, chapter 20.

units.la: 6. Quod spiritum S. ne quidem nominet, imo quod in Epistolis ad Demetrianum, authore Hieron. Spiri-tus S. substantiam negauit, & errore Iudaico dixit, eum vel ad patrem referri, vel ad filium, & sanctificaftificationem vtriusque personam sub eius nomine de-monstrari.
units.tr: 6. That he does not even name the Holy Spirit; indeed, that in his Epistle to Demetrianus, (Jerome being the authority), he denied the substance of the Holy Spirit and, in Jewish error, said that he is referred either to the Father or to the Son, and that the sanctification of each person is shown under his name.

units.la: 7. Quod de praecipuo Christi incarnati officio, sa-cerdotali nimirum tacuit & ideo tantum Christum humanam naturam assumpsisse contedit, vt quem-admodum pater, ita & ipse filius esset ἀπάτωρ atque ἀμήτωρ, lib. 4. cap. 13. Vtque religionem sanctam Dei transferret ad gentes, lib. 4. cap. 11. Vt vniuersis gentibus, quae sub coelo sunt, singularis & veri Dei mysterium sanctum reuelaret, & vnum illis Deum nunciaret, libro 4. cap. 12. Denique vt exempla virtutis homini praebere posset, lib. 4. cap. 25.
units.tr: 7. That he was silent about the chief office of the incarnate Christ, namely the priestly one, and therefore contends that Christ assumed human nature only so that, just as the Father, so the Son himself would be without father [ἀπάτωρ] and without mother [ἀμήτωρ]. Book 4, chapter 13. And that he might transfer the holy religion of God to the nations. Book 4, chapter 11. That he might reveal the holy mystery of the singular and true God to all nations under heaven, and announce to them one God. Book 4, chapter 12. Finally, that he might offer men examples of virtue. Book 4, chapter 25.

units.la: 8. Quod superstitiose de efficacia signi crucis disseruit, lib. 4. cap. 24.
units.tr: 8. That he discoursed superstitiously about the efficacy of the sign of the cross. Book 4, chapter 24.

units.la: 9. Quod Angelos tum demum homini custodes adhibitos fuisse ait: cum humanum genus augmentari coepit, lib. 2. cap. 15.
units.tr: 9. That he says angels were assigned as guardians to man only when the human race began to increase. Book 2, chapter 15.

units.la: 10. Quod terrae potestatem ab initio Diabolo tributam a Deo, duoque daemonum genera facta esse asserit: alterum terrenum, alterum coeleste, ibid.
units.tr: 10. That he asserts that power over the earth was given by God to the Devil from the beginning, and that two kinds of demons were made: one earthly, the other heavenly. Ibid.

units.la: 11. Quod bonos Angelos hominum tutelae adiun-ctos, dominatorem coeli fallacissimum ad vitia pel-lexisse, & mulierum congressibus inquinasse, suosque fecisse satellites & ministros existimat, lib. 2. cap. 15.
units.tr: 11. That he thinks the good angels, joined to the protection of men, were seduced by the most deceitful lord of heaven into vices and polluted by intercourse with women, and that he made them his own followers and ministers. Book 2, chapter 15.

units.la: 12. Quod noue dixit, diem, quem primus oriens subministrat, Dei esse: noctem autem, quam occidens extremus inducit, eius, qui Deum aemulatur, scilicet Diaboli, lib. 2. cap. 9.
units.tr: 12. That he newly said that the day, which the rising sun supplies, is God's, but the night, which the setting sun brings on, belongs to him who emulates God, namely the Devil. Book 2, chapter 9.

units.la: 13. Quod hominem ex diuersis & repugnantibus rebus rebus à Deo factum putat, libro 2. capit. 12.
units.tr: 13. That he thinks man was made by God from diverse and conflicting things. Book 2, chapter 12.

units.la: 14. Quod hominem mortalem atque imperfectum è terra fictum affirmat, lib. 2. cap. 5. & 14.
units.tr: 14. That he affirms man, mortal and imperfect, was fashioned from earth. Book 2, chapters 5 and 14.

units.la: 15. Quod eundem, immortalitatem propriis viribus adipisci, statuit, ibid.
units.tr: 15. That he holds that the same man attains immortality by his own powers. Ibid.

units.la: 16. Quod fingit Deum infinitam multitudinem animarum creasse, quas primo fragilibus & imbecillibus corporibus illigatas constitueret inter bonum malumque medias, ut constantibus ex utrisque naturis virtutem proponeret, ne immortalitatem delicate asequerentur, &c. lib. 7. c. 5.
units.tr: 16. That he invents that God created an infinite multitude of souls, which he at first placed, bound to fragile and feeble bodies, midway between good and evil, so that by the virtue set before them from both natures they might not attain immortality too easily, etc. Book 7, chapter 5.

units.la: 17. Quod cum libro 5. & 6. de iustitia Christianorum orationem ex professo instituerit: tamen de Philosophica tantum seu legis iustitia disputat, & iustitia fidei, quae Euangelii propria est, ne verbulo quidem meminit.
units.tr: 17. Although in books 5 and 6 he set out expressly to treat of the righteousness of Christians, he disputes only of philosophical or legal righteousness, and does not so much as mention the righteousness of faith, which is proper to the gospel.

units.la: 18. Quod spiritum sive animam hominis iustitia operibus emereri, ut fiat aeternus spiritus, lib. 4. c. 25.
units.tr: 18. That he holds that the spirit or soul of man earns by works of righteousness that it becomes an eternal spirit. Book 4, chapter 25.

units.la: 19. Quod iis tantum ignosci scribit, qui ad peccatum imprudenter incauteque labuntur, veniam non habere, qui sciens peccat. Ibid.
units.tr: 19. That he writes that only those are pardoned who fall into sin imprudently and carelessly, and that one who sins knowingly has no forgiveness. Ibid.

units.la: 20. Quod de perfectione hominis renati contradictorias sententias tuetur, & quidem in uno eodemque libro, nimirum 6. fatetur, quod nemo esse sine delicto possit, quam diu carnis indumento oneratus est, cap. 13. & tamen cap. ult. verum Dei cultorem nihil vult aliud precari, nisi peccatis suis veniam.
units.tr: 20. That he defends contradictory opinions about the perfection of the reborn man, and indeed in one and the same book, namely book 6: he admits that no one can be without sin as long as he is burdened with the garment of flesh (chapter 13), and yet in the last chapter he wants a true worshipper of God to ask for nothing but forgiveness of his sins.

units.la: 21. Quod militia homini iusto illicita esse putat, nec accusare quenquam crimine capitali, lib. 6. c. 20.
units.tr: 21. That he thinks warfare unlawful for a righteous man, and that one should not accuse anyone of a capital crime. Book 6, chapter 20.

units.la: 22. Quod de fine saeculi, novissimo iudicio & imperio perio mille annorum periculosas opiniones contra Scripturam libro 7.cap.14. & cateris, inseruit. Sed satis est naevorum: plures videris in Centuriarum scriptoribus.
units.tr: 22. That concerning the end of the age, the last judgment and the thousand years' reign, he introduced dangerous opinions contrary to Scripture, in book 7, chapter 14 and elsewhere. But enough of the blemishes; you will see more in the writers of the Centuries.

units.la: Hinc autem neminem meminimus eo impudentiae progressum esse, ut argutando patrum nostrorum naevos in ipsam Christianam religionem aut Theologiam transferre fuerit ausus.
units.tr: Here, however, we do not recall anyone who has gone so far in impudence as to dare, by quibbling, to transfer the blemishes of our fathers to Christian religion itself or to theology.

units.la: Nostri saeculi, (quod est errorum & haeresium feracissimum, & in quod tanquam in sententiam veterum errores iam diu consopiti, quasi ex orci cineribus eruti confluunt) Theologos, Theologorumque quorundam scripta praesertim vero Eristica, quorum maxima pars affectuum, pessimorum consultorum, est soboles, si ad normam Scripturae Canonicae & sanctae veritatis examinaueris, forte plures, & foediores inueneris errores.
units.tr: In our age, which is most fertile of errors and heresies, and into which the old errors, long since lulled to sleep, flock together as if dug up from the ashes of the underworld, if you examine the theologians, and the writings of certain theologians (especially the eristic ones, most of which are the offspring of the passions, the worst counsellors) by the standard of canonical Scripture and sacred truth, you will perhaps find many more and fouler errors.

units.la: Positis iam & agnitis dissidentium nostrorum Theologorum variis erroribus, qua, quaesto te, consequentia illorum sententiam in sanctam Theologiam, cuius vnusquisque vult videri Doctor, effundes? Hoc si non valet in Theologorum auditorio, quid quaesto Philosophia peccauit, vt ei idem non dicatur ius, cum par vtrobique sit ratio?
units.tr: Granting and acknowledging the various errors of our dissenting theologians, by what logic, I ask you, will you pour their opinion into holy Theology, in which each one wants to be seen as a teacher? If this does not hold in the theologians' lecture hall, what, I ask, has philosophy done wrong that the same right should not be given to it, since the reasoning is equal on both sides?

units.la: Ramo vero nostro eiusque beneficio multum reformatae Philosophiae quod obiicitur 1. Antiquitas, ad id iamdudum solide a multis est responsum. Sed heus! Si Theologi dicunt ex Augustino: Non audiam9: Hac dico hac dicis: Sed audiamus: Hac dicit Dominus: Eodem iure Ramus in Philosophicis dicit: Non audiamus: Hac dicit antiquitas: Hac Aristoteles: Sed audiamus: hac dicit Rerum veritas & sana Ratio. Si Theologus ex Tertulliano dicit: Veritati nemo praescribere potest, non spacium temporum, non patrocinia personarum, non priuilegia regionum: Idem & Philosophus sanus de veritate suae doctrinae dicere poterit. Si Cypriano consuetudo sine veritate vetustas erroris: Et Ramo fuit consuetudo in scholis philosophandi sine veritate & ratione, non immerito fuit erroris vetustas. Si idem recte pronunciauit: Si solus Christus audiendus est, non debemus attendere, quid aliquis ante nos faciendum putauerit, sed quid qui ante omnes est Christus prior fecerit: neque enim hominis consuetudinem sequi oportet, sed Dei veritatem: recte quoque fecit Ramus non attendens, quid pagani Philosophi sentiendum vel faciendum putauerint, sed quid omnium antiquissima veritas & Sana Ratio suaserit.
units.tr: As for the objection raised against our Ramus, and against the philosophy greatly reformed through his help, namely (1) antiquity, this has long since been solidly answered by many. But look! If the theologians say, following Augustine, I will not listen; this is what you say, this is what I say, but let us listen: Thus says the Lord; by the same right Ramus says in philosophical matters: Let us not listen: thus says antiquity, thus says Aristotle; but let us listen: thus says the truth of things and sound reason. If the theologian, following Tertullian, says: No one can prescribe against truth: not the length of time, not the patronage of persons, not the privileges of regions, a sound philosopher may likewise say this about the truth of his teaching. If, with Cyprian, custom without truth is the antiquity of error, then for Ramus the custom of philosophizing in the schools without truth and reason was rightly called the antiquity of error. If Cyprian rightly pronounced: "If Christ alone is to be heard, we should not consider what someone before us thought ought to be done, but what Christ, who is before all, did first; for we ought to follow not the custom of man but the truth of God," then Ramus also did rightly in not considering what the pagan philosophers thought ought to be felt or done, but what the most ancient truth and sound reason has suggested.

units.la: Legit Ramus hoc Lactantii: Neque illi, qui nos temporibus antecesserunt, sapientia quoque antecesserunt. Quae si omnibus aequaliter datur, ab antecedentibus occupari non potest. Et Iureconsultus ait: Quod ab initio vitiosum est, tractu temporis non convalescit. Legit Ramus illud Quintiliani: Neque enim id statim legenti persuasum sit, omnia quae magni autores dixerunt, utique esse perfecta. Nam & labuntur aliquando & oneri cedunt, & indulgent ingeniorum suorum voluptati, nec semper per intendunt animos, & nonnunquam fatigan-tur: cum Ciceroni dormitare interdum Demosthe-nes,Horatio vero & Homerus ipse videatur. Summi enim sint, homines tamen, &c. 2. Nouitas, quæ datur Ramea Philosophiæ vitio, non est vi-ciosa Veritas prima non est noua:noua tractā-di ratio, non est danda vitio. Nouum enim nō omne ideo repudiandum, quia nouum: nec antiquum ideo retinendum, quia antiquum. Sed ita demum, si illud fiat temere, sine ratio-ne, ex leuitate, cum detrimento alterius. Istud vero cum sincero iudicio, quod melius sit no-uis sine ratione inductis. Ramo vitiosum, pro dolor est, in aliis quod laudatur. Innouare licu-it Agricolæ, domino Philippo etiā in philoso-phicis: Luthero in negotio religionis, Ramo nihil. Qualis fuit nouitas visa religionis repur-gatio: talis & iam artium Ramea instauratio. Lapsus fuerit in nonnullis? quid tum, & quis ab omni parte beatus, quis à lapsu immunis? Sed omnia sunt ingrata, nihil, fecisse benigne, est. Magna Dei beneficia, sensu reprobo æsti-mamus maleficia. 3. An recte Ramus notas il-las scientificas fecerit artium conformandarū leges iudicarunt alii, clamat ipsa rerum euidē-tia. Sed Aristotelis non fuit hæc mens. Con-certant Logici. Sed posito & dato, quod Ari-stoteles iis aliter sit visus. Hoccine est cœlum terræ miscere. Et si Aristotelis mens id nun-quam cogitarit, constituerit veritas ipsa, & re-quisiuerit ipsa natura & bonitas artium. 4. Breuitas, quæ exprobratur, non est obscura, sed perspicua & facilis, teste ipsa Ramea institutionis experientia; cuius institutionis successum feliciorem non modo multi inuident nobis, sed quidam insuper, nescio quo affectu, Diabolis assignant, eamque superstitiosae hominum in Papatu ad idolorum & statuarum adorationem, sanationi comparant. Iudicet haec, qui & omnia regit, & nouit, Dominus tanti beneficii autor. 5. Quod Ramus paulo immitius Aristotelis scripta & interpretes exceperit & tractarit, id aequus iudex pensitatis rerum circumstantiis mitius & aequius interpretabitur. Consideret quibus cum hostibus ipsi negocium fuerit, quomodo ipse Ramus exceptus & tractatus, consideret Dn. Lutheri etiam in suis agitandis aduersariis vehementiam heroicam, consideret & hominis humanitatem. 6. Notam perniciei religioni Christianae a Philosophia Rami allatae, qui illi inurere satagunt, primum legitime istam demonstrent: Interim Ramei pii bona conscientia, & innocentia doctrinę nituntur. Quod sit Sacramentariorum errorum genitrix & nutrix, expresse negant & diluunt Libavius, Buscherus, Rennemannus & alii: ideoque eo nos Lectorem remittimus; malis multorum affectibus condonantes malum iudicium.
units.tr: Ramus read this from Lactantius: Those who came before us in time have not also come before us in wisdom; and if wisdom is given equally to all, it cannot be seized by those who went before. And the jurist says: What is faulty from the beginning does not grow stronger with the passage of time. Ramus read that passage of Quintilian: For let no reader be persuaded at once that everything great authors have said is certainly perfect. For they sometimes slip and give way under the burden, and indulge the pleasure of their own talents, and do not always keep their minds stretched, and sometimes grow weary: Demosthenes sometimes seems to nod off in the presence of Cicero, and Homer himself seems to do so in the presence of Horace. For they are great, yet they are men, etc. (2) Novelty, which is attributed to Ramist philosophy as a fault, is not a vicious thing: the first truth is not new, and a new method of treatment should not be counted a fault. For not everything new is to be rejected merely because it is new, nor is what is old to be kept merely because it is old; but this holds only if the innovation is made rashly, without reason, out of levity, and to another's loss; whereas the innovation made with sound judgement, because it is better, is not to be condemned simply because it is new and unsupported by reason. Among Ramus's followers, alas, what is praised in others is held against him. Innovation was permitted to Agricola, to Master Philip even in philosophical matters, and to Luther in the business of religion, but not to Ramus. As the novelty seen in the purging of religion was, so is the Ramist restoration of the arts now. Has he slipped in some points? So what? Who is happy in every respect, who is free from slips? But all things are ungrateful, and to have acted kindly counts for nothing; we reckon the great benefits of God as evils, with a reprobate sense. (3) Whether Ramus rightly set up those scientific marks and whether others have judged the laws of arranging the arts, the very evidence of things cries out. But this was not the mind of Aristotle. The logicians dispute. But granted and given that Aristotle had seen it differently, is this not to mix heaven with earth? And even if Aristotle's mind never thought of this, truth itself has established it, and the very nature and goodness of the arts have required it. (4) The brevity that is reproached is not obscure but clear and easy, as the very experience of the Ramist teaching attests; and not only do many envy us this more fortunate success, but some, with I know not what feeling, assign it to the devils, and compare it to the superstitious worship of idols and statues among men in Popery. Let him who rules all things and knows all things, the Lord, the author of so great a benefit, judge these matters. (5) That Ramus treated and handled the writings and interpreters of Aristotle somewhat more harshly, a fair judge, weighing the circumstances of the matters, will interpret more mildly and more fairly. Let him consider with what enemies Ramus himself had to deal, and how he himself was received and treated; let him consider the heroic vehemence of Dr. Luther also in attacking his adversaries, and consider the man's humanity too. (6) As for the stigma of ruin to the Christian religion brought against the philosophy of Ramus, those who labour to brand him with it should first prove it lawfully. Meanwhile the Ramist pious man rests on a good conscience and the innocence of his doctrine. That it is the mother and nurse of the errors of the Sacramentarians, Libavius, Buscherus, Rennemann and others expressly deny and refute; and therefore we refer the reader to them, pardoning the evil judgement of many on account of their evil feelings.

units.la: 12. Sophismatis Elenchus.
units.tr: 12. Refutation of a Sophism.

units.la: SI Christi Apostoli nulla artium philosophicarum doctrina & scientia fuerunt tincti, & tamen dexterrime ac felicissime EvanEuangelium Christi tradiderunt hominibus, suoque docendi ministerio fuerunt defuncti: certe nunc quoque ministris Euangelii & ecclesiæ non est necessaria vllius Philosophiæ cognitio.
units.tr: If the Apostles of Christ were imbued with no knowledge or learning of the philosophical arts, and yet most skilfully and most happily delivered the Gospel of Christ to men and discharged their ministry of teaching, then certainly now too the ministers of the Gospel and of the Church have no need of any knowledge of philosophy.

units.la: At quod antecedit est verum: fuerunt enim testibus Euangeliographis, idiotæ & piscatores. Ergo & quod inde consequitur, est verum.
units.tr: But the antecedent is true: the Evangelists bear witness that the Apostles were unlearned men and fishermen. Therefore the consequent that follows from it is also true.

units.la: Responsio.
units.tr: Answer.

units.la: Sophisma hoc est ex non paribus tanquam paribus. Nam Apostoli habuerunt spiritum sanctum, qui & Philosophiæ veræ autor fuit. Potuit is in ipso momento dare quæ ad persuadendum valerent. Sed nos forte hunc spiritum doctorem non habemus eo gradu, ideo temerarium est, illorum exemplo nostram palliare negligentiam. Deus eo medio agebat per illos, per nos alio vult agere medio, scilicet, multis laboribus & sudoribus paremius nobis docendi aliquam tolerabilem facultatem, quam ipse mox ornat sua benedictione, & coronat in nobis dona sua. Ideo grande peccatum est, oblata diuinitus media proficiendi negligere. Damnat dominus seruum illum, qui vnicum talentum in terram defodit. Sic mihi peccare videntur in Deum, qui ingenium qualecunque acceperunt a domino, artibus liberalibus & linguis ac Philosophiæ cognitione non expoliunt.
units.tr: This sophism passes off unequal things as equal. For the Apostles had the Holy Spirit, who is also the author of true philosophy. He could at that very moment give them what was fit for persuading. But we perhaps do not have this Spirit as a teacher to the same degree, so it is rash to cover our negligence with their example. God worked through them by that means; through us he wishes to work by another means, namely that we, by much toil and sweat, first acquire for ourselves some tolerable ability to teach, which he then soon adorns with his blessing and, in us, crowns with his gifts. Therefore it is a great sin to neglect the means of making progress that have been offered by God. The Lord condemns the servant who buried his single talent in the ground. So those seem to me to sin against God who have received from the Lord whatever talent they have, and do not refine it with the liberal arts, with languages, and with knowledge of philosophy.

units.la: Sic etiam respondet ipse Flacius Illyricus in Clave Scripturae: Vtilis, inquit, & plane necessaria est Dialectica & Rhetorica, & reliqua Philosophia cognitio. Nec valet obiectio, Quod ista Apostoli non didicerint: acceperunt enim illi cognitionem linguarum, & aliarum utilium rerum ex cognitione Spiritus sancti. Videmus & hodie multos, alioqui rudes, ita coelesti quodam intelligentiae lumine donatos, illustratosque esse, ut vel obscurissimas controversias summa dexteritate diiudicare possint.
units.tr: So too Flacius Illyricus himself answers in his Key to Scripture: Dialectic, he says, and Rhetoric, and the rest of the knowledge of philosophy, are useful and plainly necessary. Nor does the objection hold, that the Apostles did not learn these things: for they received knowledge of languages and of other useful things from the knowledge of the Holy Spirit. We see today too many men, otherwise unlearned, so endowed and illuminated with a certain heavenly light of understanding that they can judge even the most obscure controversies with the greatest skill.

units.la: Harum ergo humanarum & externarum rerum scientiam, & Apostolus in Christianis, praesertim Doctoribus requirit, inquiens, Tit. tertio, Discant autem etiam nostri bonis operibus praeesse in necessarios usus, ut non sint inutiles, ubi omnino eis praecipit artes liberales & mechanicas discere. Sic 2. Tim. 2. iubet Theologiam hominibus tradi ad docendum & discendum idoneis, quo illi etiam porro aliis exponere possint: ut manifeste logicas scientias aut organa requiras in studiosó ad Theologiam adhibendo. Eodem modo Hemmingius in Ep. Dedic. Syntag. inquit: At, si quis Enthusiasta obiecerit, Apostolos fuisse rudes harum rerum: igitur neque iam requiri in Doctoribus Ecclesiae, sed sufficere Spiritum sanctum. Et si Spiritus Christi Doctor veritatis semper est implorandus, ut nos doceat, & in veritate dirigat: tamen discernendum est inter miraculosam instructionem: qualis fuit Prophetarum: deinde Apostolorum qui die Pentec.per Spiritum sanctum plene sunt edo-čti de mysterio Euangelii: deinde paucorum a-liorum & ordinariam, qualis est eorum, qui successerunt Apostolis. Hanc commendat A-postolus suo discipulo, cum ait: Attende lectio-ni, neque potest hæc ordinaria instructio, quam requiro in interprete Scripturarum, vtiliter fieri, sine rerum multarum notitia, quæ ex Philosophia petenda est. Proinde vt & recte sapiamus, & bene agamus, opus est nobis & Philosophia & Theologia; illa quidem, vt ministra: hac vero, vt imperatrice. Quando ergo humana sapientia, quæ Philosophia dicitur, submittit se diuinæ scientiæ, id est, Theologiæ, eique seruit, vtilissimum est ipsius ministerium. Verum si, vt Agar ancilla dominari voluit Saræ heræ suæ, ita Philosophia incipiat dominari Theologiæ: vt meretrix de familia Dei eiicienda est.
units.tr: Therefore the Apostle also requires knowledge of these human and external things, especially in Christians who are teachers, saying in Titus 3: Let our people also learn to excel in good works for necessary uses, so that they may not be unfruitful; where he plainly commands them to learn the liberal and mechanical arts. Likewise in 2 Timothy 2 he bids theology be handed on to men fit to teach and to learn, so that they in turn may be able to expound it to others; so that you clearly require the logical sciences, or instruments, to be applied by a student to theology. In the same way Hemmingius, in the dedicatory epistle of his Syntagma, says: But if some Enthusiast objects that the Apostles were unlearned in these things, and therefore that teachers of the Church are no longer required, and that the Holy Spirit suffices: then, although the Spirit of Christ, the Teacher of truth, is always to be implored to teach us and to guide us in the truth, still a distinction must be made between miraculous instruction, such as that of the Prophets; then that of the Apostles, who on the day of Pentecost were fully taught by the Holy Spirit about the mystery of the Gospel; and finally the ordinary instruction of a few others, such as that of those who succeeded the Apostles. The Apostle commends this to his disciple when he says: Attend to reading. And this ordinary instruction, which I require in an interpreter of Scripture, cannot be carried out usefully without a knowledge of many things, which must be sought from philosophy. Therefore, that we may both think rightly and act well, we need both philosophy and theology: the former as a servant, the latter as mistress. When human wisdom, which is called philosophy, submits itself to divine knowledge, that is to theology, and serves it, its service is most useful. But if, as Hagar the maidservant wished to rule over Sarah her mistress, philosophy begins to rule over theology, it must be cast out of God's household like a harlot.

units.la: 13. Sophismatis Elenchus qui est specialis de Logica damnum religioni afferente, & ab vsu Theologico plane excludenda.
units.tr: 13. Refutation of a Sophism, specifically concerning the harm that Logic does to religion, and that it must be wholly excluded from theological use.

units.la: HActenus conteetum est bellum vniuersale, quo tota Philosophia, omnesque eius partes impugnantur: Superest bellum particulare, quo præcipue quidam tum imperiti, tum periti inuadunt ex instrumentariis & generalibus artibus Logicam, eamque insimulant multorum damnorum Reip, ChriChristianę allatorū, ex specialib. rerum doctrinam subministrantibus Physicam, eamq; omnis prorsus incertitudinis accusant.
units.tr: Hitherto the universal war has been fought, in which all of philosophy and all its parts are attacked. There remains a particular war, in which some men, both unskilled and skilled, principally assail Logic among the instrumental and general arts, and accuse it of many harms done to the Christian commonwealth and religion, and charge the Physics, which supplies the doctrine of particular things, with a complete lack of certainty.

units.la: Aduersus Logicā, qui arma sua mouent, tum pestem fidei eam esse clamant, tum ab omni rerum sacrarum tractatione amouendam variis contendunt conclusiunculis.
units.tr: Those who take up arms against Logic cry out that it is a plague to the faith, and they contend with various little arguments that it must be kept away from every handling of sacred things.

units.la: Pestiferam esse Ecclesiæ Logicam ita quidam argutantur:
units.tr: Some argue as follows that Logic is a pestilence to the Church:

units.la: Quod venenatam fidei, religionis, & Ecclesiæ Christianorum affert pestem; id vtique in negotio fidei, in tractatione religionis, in domo domini, tanquam præsentissimum venenum vitari debet.
units.tr: Whatever brings a poisonous plague to the faith, to religion, and to the Church of Christians, that certainly must be avoided in the matter of faith, in the handling of religion, in the house of the Lord, as the most present poison.

units.la: Logica autem fidei, religioni, & Ecclesiæ Christianorū venenatam affert pestē. Probant hoc testimoniis, tū publicis, tum priuatis, quæ etiam experientia omniū temporum comprobata esse opinantur: adeo, inquiunt, nocuit religioni Dialectica, vt ei tū apud Ethnicos, tum apud Christianos omniū hęresium semina, fundamenta, incrementa & munimenta sint ferenda accepta: quo quis ab arte Dialectica ex hæreticorū assectis fuit instructior, eo insurrexit armatior aduersus veritatē religionis Christianæ. Hinc conquesti sunt venerandæ antiquitatis patres: Dialecticæ armis à prauorum dogmatum autorib. veritatem labefactatam esse. Hinc Ambrosius: Facessant Dialectici, vbi credendum est pi- scatoribus Apostolis.
units.tr: But Logic brings a poisonous plague to the faith, to religion, and to the Church of Christians. They prove this by testimonies, both public and private, which they think are also confirmed by the experience of all times: so greatly, they say, has dialectic harmed religion, that the seeds, foundations, growth and defences of all heresies, both among the heathen and among Christians, are to be credited to it; the more skilled anyone was in the art of dialectic from among the adherents of heretics, the more armed he rose up against the truth of the Christian religion. Hence the venerable Fathers of antiquity complained that the truth had been undermined by the weapons of dialectic, in the hands of the authors of perverse doctrines. Hence Ambrose: Let the dialecticians depart, where we ought to believe the fishermen, the Apostles.

units.la: Ergo Logica, vt praesentissimum venenum in ne-gotio jdei, in tractatione religionis, in domo domini vitari debet.
units.tr: Therefore Logic, as the most present poison in the matter of faith, in the handling of religion, in the house of the Lord, must be avoided.

units.la: Responsio.
units.tr: Answer.

units.la: Assumptionem negamus ob fallaciam non causae, tanquam causae. Causa enim est, cuius vi res est. Dialecticae vi pestis & pernicies fidei ac veritatis non est. Dialectica enim homini non perniciem, sed perfectionem affert. Rationem eius defectu virtutis & excessu malitiae laborantem deducit in gyrum suum, ut suo munere veritati Dei & Rei conuenienter, sobrie, religiose, sapienter possit uti. Hac, lo-quente Cicerone, hanc habet rationem & virtutem, ne cui falso assentiamur, neve unquam captiosa fallamur, eaque quae de bonis & malis dicere-mus, ut tenere tuerique possimus. Nam sine hac arte quemuis arbitramur a vero abduci fallique posse. Hac facit, ut de rebus omnibus conuenienter cogitare, prudenterque iudicare possimus. Hac facit, ut interpretandis praestantium autorum consiliis & inuentis, variaq; prudentia & politissimi iudicii laudibus explicandis, iuuentutem erudiamus. Hac facit, ut res angustas amplificare, obscuras interpretando explanare, rem universam in partes tribuere, latentem definiendo explicare ambigua videre & distinguere possimus. Hac facit, ut quo homines bestiis maxime praestant, id est, ratione, consilio, iudicio hominibus ipsis praestemus & antecellamus. Hac denique non tantum iis prodest, qui Rempublicam consilio gubernant, sed & iis plurimum prodest, qui populum docere iustitiam, religionem, pietatem in proin professo habent. Hæc autem omnia facit bene male nihil: quatenus ipsa logica qua logica operatur.
units.tr: We deny the assumption, because it commits the fallacy of taking something that is not a cause for a cause. A cause is that by whose power a thing exists. Dialectic by its power is not a plague or ruin of faith and truth, for dialectic brings a man not ruin but perfection. It takes the reason that labours under lack of virtue and excess of malice and brings it back into its own orbit, so that it may use its function properly, soberly, religiously and wisely in relation to the truth of God and of the thing itself. As Cicero says, this art has the power and the virtue that keeps us from assenting to what is false and from being deceived by captious arguments, and enables us to hold and defend what we say about good and evil. For without this art we think anyone can be drawn away from the truth and deceived. It makes us able to think about all things in a fitting way and to judge them prudently. It makes us able, by interpreting the counsels and discoveries of distinguished authors and by explaining their various wisdom and the praises of a most refined judgment, to educate the young. It makes us able to amplify narrow matters, to explain obscure ones by interpretation, to divide the whole matter into its parts, to explain what is hidden by definition, and to see and distinguish ambiguities. It makes us excel and surpass other men in what distinguishes men most from beasts, namely reason, counsel and judgment. Finally, it is of great benefit not only to those who govern the state by their counsel, but also to those who have made it their profession to teach the people justice, religion and piety. Yet logic does all these things well and does nothing badly, insofar as logic itself operates as logic.

units.la: Logica itaque pestis causam non habet. Quid igitur? causa inquam est, cuius vi res est, & cuius vi res est, causa est. Sophisticæ vi pestis & pernicies fidei, religioni & Ecclesiæ infertur. Hæc enim à Diabolo progenita optima arte pessime abutitur, dum pro decretis Logicæ veritatis, affert somnia & deliramenta fallacis ἀλογίας. Hæc hominis auget imperfectionem, peruersitatem, ignorantiam. Hæc veritati Dei & Rei inconuenienter & dissentanee non tam disserit, quam sophisticatur, male inuenit, male disponit, male diiudicat. Peruertit itaq; hominis intelligentiam & iudicium, eoq; venenum alii pestiferum propinat.
units.tr: Logic therefore has no cause of plague. What then? I say that a cause is that by whose power a thing exists, and that by whose power a thing exists is a cause. By the power of sophistry the plague and ruin of faith, of religion and of the Church is brought about. For sophistry, begotten by the Devil, makes the worst possible use of the best art, while in place of the rules of logical truth it offers the dreams and nonsense of fallacious illogicality [ἀλογίας]. It increases man's imperfection, perversity and ignorance. It does not so much reason about the truth of God and of the thing itself in a fitting and consistent way as it twists it into sophistry; it finds badly, arranges badly, and judges badly. Thus it perverts the understanding and judgment of man, and so hands the poisonous draught on to others.

units.la: Prosyllogismus Assumpti est paralogismus ex impertinentibus & male accommodatis testimoniis, quippe quæ testantur, non de logica sed de sophistica: non de vero dialecticæ vsu, sed de peruerso sophistarum abusu. Quare non meis, sed Philippi Melanchthonis P. M. verbis ad hoc truncandum sophisma uti liceat Ne, inquit, deterreamur à Dialectica studio, propterea quod scripserunt aliqui, dialectica armis à prauorum dogmatum authoribus labefactatam esse veritatem. Hæc enim non est artis, sed malorum ingeniorum & prauæ institutionis reprehensio. Sit ut in aliis studiis natura recta & veritatis amans & artem sobrie discat, eamque modeste graviterque ad inquisitionem veritatis adhibeat, non exerceatur Sophistica, non amentur captiones & præstigiæ, vt multæ prauæ naturæ similes Autolyci, Sysiphi, Euribati, & aliorum impostorum delectantur ludis captionum & calumniis. Et horum similes fuisse & esse multos malorum dogmatum mangones, vt ita dicam, satis apparet, qui nequaquam Dialectici sunt aut fuerunt, sed potius sophistę seu impostores, & non solum aliarum doctrinarum, sed etiam Dialecticæ deprauatores.
units.tr: The prosyllogism of the assumption is a paralogism drawn from irrelevant testimonies, badly applied, which bear witness not to logic but to sophistry, not to the true use of dialectic but to the perverse abuse of the sophists. Therefore, to cut short this sophism, let me use not my own words but those of Philip Melanchthon, of blessed memory: Let us not, he says, be deterred from the study of dialectic because some have written that dialectic has been used as a weapon by the authors of wicked doctrines to undermine the truth. For this is not a criticism of the art, but of wicked minds and of a bad education. In other studies, let a person of upright nature who loves truth learn the art soberly and apply it modestly and seriously to the search for truth; let him not practise sophistry, nor love trickery and deceptions, as many of a perverse nature, like Autolycus, Sisyphus, Euribatus and other impostors, delight in the games of captious argument and in slander. That there have been and still are many such dealers in wicked doctrines, so to speak, is plain enough. They are in no way dialecticians, nor have they ever been, but rather sophists or impostors, and corrupters not only of other teachings but also of dialectic itself.

units.la: Patres Dialecticæ & Dialecticorum nomine vsi sunt per ἀντιλογίαν pro sophisticis & sophistis: quod inde liquet, quod loquantur de Dialecticis, qui tales videri volebant & superbe eius gloriabantur nomine; de iis qui rerum & religionis veritatem logicis legibus non propugnabant, sed strophis sophisticis expugnare satagebant; de iis, qui eo tempore suis impostu-ris doctrinam Euangelii peruertebant. Alioquin magnifice de vsu Logico in sacris sentiunt Patres. Augustinus enim de Christ.doctrina lib. 2. cap. 31. ait, Disputationis disciplina ad omnia genera quæstionum, quæ sunt in sacris literis penetranda & dissoluenda plurimum valet. Et cap. 37. Scientia conclusionum & definitionum & distributionum plurimum lectorem Scripturarum adiuuat. Et rursum alibi de cog. vera vitæ: Dialectica, inquit, differendi potens potenter dubia quaque definiens, cunctas Scripturas euibrans atque euiscerans, cunctam humanam annihilans. Hieronymus in Ezech. Vere quicquid in sæculo peruersorum dogmatum est, quicquid ad terrenam renam scientiam pertinet & putatur esse robustum, hoc Dialectica arte subuertitur, & instar incendii in cineres fauillasque dissoluitur, ut probetur esse nihili, quod putabatur fortissimum.
units.tr: The Fathers used the name of dialectic and dialecticians by antiphrasis for sophistry and sophists. This is clear from the fact that they speak of dialecticians who wished to be seen as such and proudly boasted of that name; of those who did not defend the truth of things and of religion by logical laws, but laboured to overthrow it with sophistical twists; of those who at that time were perverting the doctrine of the Gospel by their impostures. Otherwise the Fathers think highly of the logical use in sacred matters. Augustine, for example, in On Christian Doctrine, book 2, chapter 31, says: The discipline of disputation is of great value for penetrating and resolving all kinds of questions that are found in the sacred letters. And in chapter 37: Knowledge of conclusions, definitions and distinctions greatly helps the reader of the Scriptures. And again elsewhere, in On the True Religion: Dialectic, which is powerful in disputing, powerfully defining every doubtful point, shaking and disembowelling all the Scriptures, and reducing all human [error] to nothing, he says. Jerome, on Ezekiel: Truly, whatever there is of perverse doctrine in the world, whatever pertains to earthly knowledge and is thought to be strong, is overthrown by the art of dialectic and, like a fire, is dissolved into ashes and cinders, so that what was thought most strong is shown to be nothing.

units.la: Obiectio II.
units.tr: Objection II.

units.la: Ratio captiuanda in sacris non est soluenda ad vsum sacrorum.
units.tr: A reason that is to be taken captive in sacred matters should not be loosed for use in sacred matters.

units.la: Dialectica est ars rationis captiuanda in sacris.
units.tr: Dialectic is the art of reason that is to be taken captive in sacred matters.

units.la: Dialectica itaque ad vsum sacrorum dilatanda non est.
units.tr: Dialectic therefore should not be extended to the use of sacred matters.

units.la: Propos. valet ex vi parium contrariorum: Assumptio vero tum ex testimonio Pauli, qui dicit, Captiuandam esse rationem nostram in obsequium Christi: tum ex testimonio Logicorum, quibus Logica est ars rationis.
units.tr: The major premise holds by the force of parallel contraries. The minor premise is supported both by the testimony of Paul, who says, "Our reason is to be taken captive in obedience to Christ", and by the testimony of the logicians, for whom logic is the art of reason.

units.la: Responsio.
units.tr: Answer.

units.la: Propositionem veram concedimus, tum ex mente Pauli intellectam, tum identitate oppositionis non mutata.
units.tr: We grant the major premise, both as it is understood in Paul's meaning and because the opposition of terms has not changed.

units.la: Assumptio proprie assumptio non est: non enim ex propositione assumitur, ex qua terminum medium assumere iure debebat, scilicet, non artem rationis sed ipsam rationem. Negamus igitur consequentiam, cum syllogismus habeat quatuor terminos, Logicam, extensionem ad vsum sacrorum, artem rationis, & ipsam rationem.
units.tr: The minor premise is not, strictly speaking, a minor premise. It is not taken from the proposition from which it rightly ought to have taken the middle term, namely not the art of reason but reason itself. So we deny the inference, since the syllogism has four terms: logic, its extension to the use of sacred matters, the art of reason, and reason itself.

units.la: Deinde Logica non immerito quadantenus est ars captiuandæ rationis in fidei obsequium, siquidem docet captiuare rationem suo modo, quatenus docet differere rebus ipsis tum sacris tum prophanis conuenienter rerum veritati de rebus conuenientem & consentientem docet instituere dissertatio- nem. Rebus igitur diuinis & mysticis Ortho- doxus Logicus disserit conformiter, inuenit argumenta ex affectione vera & natura re- rum sacrarum, rerum affectioni & naturæ conuenienter disponit ac dextre iudicat, ca- ptiuat rationem hominis, ne rerum sacrarum & Dei veritati inconuenienter disceptet, sed vt de iis non ex affectione & natura rerum ter- renarum & hominis æstimet. Captiuat ita- que rationem vinculis logicis, quæ eam ob- stringunt, vt de rebus sacris, rerum sacrarum naturæ conuenienter, sobrie & religiose, de rebus vero humanis earum affectioni con- sentanee disserat. Captiuat rationem, dum eam vult distinguere doctrinarum genera & principia, ne confundantur: dum vetat, ne notiones ac regulas logicas detorqueat eo quo non congruunt, ne non recte aut minus expli- cate accommodet ad propositum, ne ex iis ali- quid sophistice deducat, quod à norma do- ctrinæ sacræ deflectit, &c. Captiuata itaque ratio sanæque logicæ vinculis ligata non est arcenda à studio Theologico, sed pie adhi- benda. Sic itaque inuertimus argumentum:
units.tr: Moreover, logic is not undeservedly, in some measure, the art of taking reason captive to the obedience of faith, since it teaches reason to be captive in its own way, insofar as it teaches us to reason about things, both sacred and profane, in a manner fitting to the truth of the things, and to construct a discourse that agrees and accords with the things. Therefore the orthodox logician reasons about divine and mystical things in conformity with them. He finds arguments from the true character and nature of sacred things, arranges and judges them fittingly in accordance with that character and nature, and so takes the reason of man captive, so that it does not dispute improperly about sacred things and the truth of God, but judges of them not from the character and nature of earthly things and of man. Thus he takes reason captive with the logical bonds that restrain it, so that it may discourse about sacred things soberly and religiously in keeping with their nature, and about human things in keeping with their character. He takes reason captive when he wants to distinguish the kinds and principles of the doctrines, so that they are not confused; when he forbids it to twist the notions and logical rules to where they do not fit, or to apply them wrongly or insufficiently explained to the matter at hand, or to deduce from them anything sophistically that departs from the standard of sacred doctrine, and so on. Reason so taken captive and bound with the sound bonds of logic is therefore not to be kept away from theological study, but is to be applied to it devoutly. So we turn the argument around thus:

units.la: Quo captiuatur ratio nostra in obsequium fi- dei, id à doctrina fidei tractanda excludendum non est.
units.tr: What takes our reason captive in obedience to the faith must not be excluded from the treatment of the doctrine of the faith.

units.la: At logica Christiana carnalis & cæca ratio ca- ptiuatur, mediante spiritus Dei actione. Logica itaque à doctrina fidei tractanda non est excludenda.
units.tr: But Christian logic takes captive carnal and blind reason, through the action of the Spirit of God. Therefore logic is not to be excluded from the treatment of the doctrine of the faith.

units.la: Obiectio III.
units.tr: Objection III.

units.la: Quod in Ecclesia debet silere, eius vsus Ecclesia non est obtrudendus.
units.tr: What ought to be silent in the Church must not be forced upon the Church in its use.

units.la: Mulier seu Iesabella humanae rationis sileat in Ecclesia, teste Apost.
units.tr: A woman, or Jezebel, of human reason, let her be silent in the Church, as the Apostle witnesses.

units.la: Ergo humanae rationis vsus Ecclesia non est obtrudendus.
units.tr: Therefore the use of human reason must not be forced upon the Church.

units.la: Responsio.
units.tr: Answer.

units.la: Propositio laborat elencho disparatorum. Negata enim vna specie vsus, non est negandus totus disparatorum numerus. Nam negato disparatorum vno, affirmatur aut certum ex disparatis reliquis, aut quædam, aut reliqua omnia. Huc etiam coincidit sophisticus processus à negatione vnius speciei ad negandum totum genus.
units.tr: The proposition suffers from the fallacy of disparates. For when one species of a use is denied, the whole number of disparates is not thereby to be denied. For when one of the disparates is denied, either a certain one of the remaining disparates is affirmed, or some, or all the rest. To this also amounts the sophistical process of moving from the denial of one species to the denial of the whole genus.

units.la: Propositio suis terminis constricta sic vera est: Quod in Ecclesia debet silere, idipsum perorare non debet, ita vt vnum vni contrarie opponatur, vnoque affirmato negetur alterum. Hinc iam assumo : Logica silere debet in Ecclesia, id est, de suis documentis & decretis non perorare: interim Logicus Theologus non tacet in Ecclesia: interim verbi diuini tractationem logico organo fieri non debere non sequitur.
units.tr: Restricted to its own terms, the proposition is true in this form: What ought to be silent in the Church ought not to hold forth on the same matter, so that one thing is opposed contrarily to another, and when one is affirmed the other is denied. From this I now assume: Logic ought to be silent in the Church, that is, not to hold forth on its own teachings and decrees; meanwhile the logical theologian is not silent in the Church; meanwhile it does not follow that the treatment of the divine Word must not be done with the logical organon.

units.la: Assumptio non est testimonium Apostolicum, loquitur enim de propria muliere. Neque est argumentum firmum à simili præter Dei verbum, & tamen ex Dei verbo adhibito.
units.tr: The minor premise is not an apostolic testimony, for it speaks of one's own wife. Nor is it a firm argument from likeness, apart from the Word of God, and yet it is drawn from the Word of God when applied.

units.la: Falsitas denique conclusionis ex contraria veritate apparet ei, qui considerat fidei tum theorian, tum praxin. Theorian fidei appello cognitionem & contemplationem rerum credendarum ad salutem. Haec non fit nisi mentis & rationis humanae munere. Nulla cognitio, nisi ea quae mente, intelligentia & ratione fit. Intelligere est mentis & intelligentiae proprium opus, sicut velle voluntatis. Bene & spiritualiter intelligere est renatae mentis & spiritus opus: intelligere tamen manet mentis actio. Depravate & male intelligere est opus mentis depravatae & corruptae. Sic igitur argumentor:
units.tr: Finally, the falsity of the conclusion appears from the contrary truth to anyone who considers both the theory and the practice of the faith. By the theory of the faith I mean the knowledge and contemplation of the things to be believed for salvation. This is achieved only by the function of the mind and human reason. There is no knowledge except that which is produced by the mind, understanding and reason. To understand is the proper work of the mind and understanding, just as to will is the work of the will. To understand well and spiritually is the work of the reborn mind and spirit; yet understanding remains an action of the mind. To understand in a depraved and wrong way is the work of a depraved and corrupted mind. So I argue thus:

units.la: Quo res credendas percipimus & contemplamur, id cessare in fidei nostra theoria nequit.
units.tr: What enables us to perceive and contemplate the things to be believed cannot cease in the theory of our faith.

units.la: Atqui mentis, rationis, seu intelligentiae facultatibus, face spiritus praeeunte, homo fidelis res credendas percipit & contemplatur. Qua de re legat aliquis Frederici Petri libellum de fide in hominis mente, voluntate & corde.
units.tr: But by the faculties of the mind, reason, or understanding, with the Spirit going before, the believing man perceives and contemplates the things to be believed. On this matter let someone read the little book of Frederick Peter on faith in the mind, will and heart of man.

units.la: Ergo facultas mentis & rationis nostra in theoria fidei neutiquam cessare potest.
units.tr: Therefore the faculty of our mind and reason can by no means cease in the theory of the faith.

units.la: Hic autem velim te distinguere ipsam mentem ipsiusque facultatem ab eius corruptione & caecitate naturali.
units.tr: Here, however, I would have you distinguish the mind itself and its faculty from its corruption and natural blindness.

units.la: Praxin intelligo salutarem rerum credendarum applicationem ad se, quae est syllogismi practici tanqua assumptio practica, qua credenda ad salutem fideiq; articulos fideles singuli ad se suamq; personam peculiariter applicant. Hinc adeo est, quod quidam ex numero doctorum non infiinfimus asseuerare non erubuit, neminem nisi Dialecticum, qui syllogismū possit legitime conficere, seruari: propositā propositionem ex promissionibus generalibus gratiæ, deducta assumptione ex sensu conscientiæ & testimonio spiritus, &c. vt, Qui veram agit pœnitentiam & credit in filium Dei, non peribit, sed vitam æternam habebit. Ego scio me agere pœnitentiam, & credere in filium Dei. Ego igitur scio me non periturum, sed vitam nacturum æternam. Quid? quod nemo in lucta cōscientiæ cum Deo, in pugna aduersus hostes suos possit quis feliciter agere, nisi ex verbo Dei depromptis argumentis, iisque logice dispositis & conclusis: Si non naturaliter, saltem cryptice. Huc deniq; accedit, quod sancti in hac terra in mortis suæ præmeditatione soleant à Deo integrum morbisq; non læsum rationis & iudicii vsum, vt in mortis agone non muti, non surdi, nō sensibus distorti & turbati ad vltimum vsq; vitæ halitum cum Deo patre per filiū in spiritu sancto tum propter se, tum propter proximum agere possint, piis votis plerunque expetant.
units.tr: By practice I mean the saving application of the things to be believed to oneself, which is the practical minor premise of the practical syllogism, by which individual believers apply to themselves and to their own persons the articles of faith and what must be believed for salvation. Hence it is that one of the not least among the teachers has not blushed to assert that no one is saved except a dialectician who can legitimately construct a syllogism: the major premise drawn from the general promises of grace, the minor premise drawn from the sense of conscience and the testimony of the Spirit, and so on, as: Whoever truly repents and believes in the Son of God will not perish, but will have eternal life. I know that I repent and believe in the Son of God. I therefore know that I shall not perish, but shall obtain eternal life. What then? No one can act successfully in the struggle of conscience with God, in the fight against his enemies, unless the arguments are taken from the Word of God and are logically arranged and concluded, if not naturally, at least in a hidden way. Finally, to this is added that the saints in this earth, in the premeditation of their death, commonly pray to God that they may have the whole and unimpaired use of reason and judgment, so that in the agony of death they are not mute, not deaf, not distorted or disturbed in their senses, and may act with God the Father through the Son in the Holy Spirit, both for themselves and for their neighbour, up to the last breath of life.

units.la: Obiectio IV.
units.tr: Objection IV.

units.la: Quod sensibus humanis nititur in religionis articulis vsum non habet.
units.tr: That which rests on human senses has no use in the articles of religion.

units.la: Ratio humana nititur sensibus externis.
units.tr: Human reason rests on the external senses.

units.la: Ratio igitur humana in religionis articulis vsum non habet.
units.tr: Therefore human reason has no use in the articles of religion.

units.la: Propositio probatur: Articuli enim religionis Christianæ sola fide & non sensibus sunt percipiendi.
units.tr: The proposition is proved: the articles of the Christian religion are to be perceived by faith alone and not by the senses.

units.la: Assumptio probatur vulgato axiomate Physicorum: Nihil est in intellectu, quin prius fuerit in sensu.
units.tr: The assumption is proved by the common axiom of the natural philosophers: There is nothing in the intellect that was not first in the senses.

units.la: Responsio.
units.tr: Answer.

units.la: Propof. est limitanda: Visus enim rei non est vniformis. Ratio quidem & sensus non habent hunc vsum in articulis fidei, vt extra Dei verbum sola & proprie constituant eorum fundamenta. Verbum Dei vnicum est credendorum fundamentum, canon vnicus. Huic vero si vspiam inseruit & succenturiatur ratio & sensus, contrarium ei mendacium apertius arguitur. 1. Deus enim ipse indidit nobis sensus externos, vt sint testes veritatis, non autem deceptionis organa. 2. Experientia, omnium iudicio vnum est ex πειρᾶς seu primis fundamentis veritatis in re qualibet. Experientia autem fit per sensus exteriores: Ergo si sensus externi fallunt, nihil fere certi relinquitur. 3. In ipsis quoque miraculis omnibus nusquam Deum legimus deceptos voluisse hominum sensus: aqua in vinum versa, id quod gustui visum est, reuera illud erat. Excitati à morruis homines fuerunt vere viui homines, quales cerneban- tur, nec diuersum exemplum miraculorum dari potest. 4. Ecclesiae antiquae orthodoxae argumento ex sensibus petito Marcionitas & alios eiusmodi impostores negantes veram Christi humanitate, refutarunt. Eodem etiam argumeto hodie pontificiorū Transsubst. impuimpugnatur. 5. Ipse Christus discipulis fidem suæ resurrectionis facturus, illos ad sensus remittit Ioan. 20. videte manus meas & pedes, quia ego ipse sum, contrectate me & videte.
units.tr: The proposition must be qualified, for the use of sense is not uniform. Reason and the senses do not have this use in the articles of faith, that they alone and properly establish their foundations apart from the Word of God. The Word of God is the sole foundation of what is to be believed, the one canon. But if reason and the senses serve this Word anywhere and act as its supporters, the contrary falsehood is more plainly refuted. 1. For God himself has given us external senses so that they may be witnesses of the truth, not instruments of deception. 2. Experience, by the judgment of all, is the first principle, that is, the primary foundation of truth in any matter whatever. But experience comes through the external senses. Therefore, if the external senses deceive, almost nothing certain remains. 3. Moreover, in all the miracles we never read that God wished to deceive men's senses: water turned into wine, and what the taste perceived was really that. Men raised from the dead were truly living men, such as they were seen to be, and no different example of miracles can be given. 4. The ancient orthodox Church, by an argument drawn from the senses, refuted Marcionites and other impostors of this kind who denied the true humanity of Christ. By the same argument the Papists' transubstantiation is today assailed. 5. Christ himself, about to make his disciples believe in his resurrection, refers them to the senses, John 20: See my hands and my feet, that it is I myself; handle me and see.

units.la: Sic Thomæ inquit: Mitte digitum tuum huc, & vide manus meas, &c. 6. Sensum nullum habere vsum in fidei articulis, vel saltem quoad instrumentum perceptionis vel hinc liquet falsum: quod per auditum acquiratur fides, dicente Paulo: Fides ex auditu, auditus autem per verbum Dei. Sed applicentur ista ad thesin, seu Logicam, de qua disputatur: Ratio nititur externis sensibus: Logica est ars rationis. En hic tertium argumentum duplicatur. Si dixeris: Logica est ratio, falsum dixeris: Adiunctum enim non est ipsum subiectum. Neque sequitur: Si ratio nititur externis sensibus, Logica quoque nititur externis sensibus. Est enim ratio dispar in vsu: Ratio vtitur ministerio externorum sensuum, vt res per eos percipiat oblatas & intelligat. Ratio item vtitur arte logica, eiusque cosiliis & præceptis, vt iis instructa & confirmata de rebus intelligibilibus possit recte ratiocinari, siue res illæ sint ab externis sensibus petitæ, siue nobiscum natæ, siue etiam per gratiam infusæ.
units.tr: So he says to Thomas: Put your finger here and see my hands, etc. 6. That the senses have no use in the articles of faith, or at least as the instrument of perception, is shown false by this: faith comes by hearing, as Paul says: Faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of God. But let these things be applied to the thesis, or Logic, which is under dispute: Reason rests on the external senses; Logic is the art of reason. Here the third argument is doubled. If you say: Logic is reason, you say what is false: the predicate is not the subject itself. Nor does it follow: If reason rests on the external senses, Logic also rests on the external senses. For reason differs in its use: reason uses the service of the external senses so that it may perceive and understand the things offered through them. Reason likewise uses the logical art, with its counsels and precepts, so that, instructed and strengthened by them, it may reason rightly about intelligible things, whether those things are drawn from the external senses, or are born with us, or are even infused by grace.

units.la: 1. Instant: Quicquid creditur, non videtur.
units.tr: 1. They object: Whatever is believed is not seen.

units.la: Omnes articuli fidei creduntur.
units.tr: All articles of faith are believed.

units.la: Ergo nulli articuli fidei videntur: Et per consequens, sensuum vsus hic nullus est.
units.tr: Therefore no articles of faith are seen. And consequently the use of the senses here is nil.

units.la: Propos. probant ad Hebr. 11. Vbi fides esse dicitur rerum sperandarum substantiam, & argumentum non apparentium.
units.tr: They prove the premises from Hebrews 11: Where faith is said to be the substance of things hoped for, and the evidence of things not seen.

units.la: Responsio.
units.tr: Answer.

units.la: Consequens vltimum ex primo non po-teft exprimi. Negato enim vno sensu non sta-tim omnes negantur. Etsi igitur non videa-tur id, quod creditur, audiri tamen potest & debet.
units.tr: The last consequence cannot be drawn from the first. For when one sense is denied, not all are denied at once. Although, then, what is believed is not seen, it can and should nevertheless be heard.

units.la: Deinde proposito non est vniuersaliter ve-ra. Multa sunt in articulis fidei, quæ de Chri-sto credimus, quæ & tempore Christi à fide-libus sunt visa & credita. Propositionis profyl-logismus non est plena fidei definitio, sed de-scriptio eam explicàs ab vna aliqua parte, quæ statim nō excludit quicquid extra hanc descri-ptionem fidei tribuitur.
units.tr: Next, the proposition is not universally true. Many of the articles of faith that we believe concerning Christ were also seen and believed by the faithful in Christ's time. The syllogistic proposition is not a full definition of faith but a description which explains it from one particular side, and which does not at once exclude whatever is ascribed to faith outside this description.

units.la: 2.Instant. In sacris non agitur logicis argumen-tis & rationibus sed tantum testimoniis spiritus san-ƈti, quæ sunt argumenta inartificialia.
units.tr: 2. They object: In sacred matters we deal not with logical arguments and reasons but only with the testimonies of the Holy Spirit, which are inartificial arguments.

units.la: Ergo in sacris nullus potest esse visus rationum & notionum Logicarum.
units.tr: Therefore in sacred matters there can be no use of logical reasons and notions.

units.la: Responsio.
units.tr: Answer.

units.la: Antecedens est falsum tum quoad sacram scripturam, tum quoad fidei confirmationem ex sacra scriptura. Quoad sacram scripturam: ipse Deus in verbo suo non ἀλόγως sed ponderosis rationibus de se suaque voluntate erga nos disserit : Christus in concionibus suis, in redargutionibus Iudæorum insigni logica, egregiisque rationibus & argumentis artificialibus est visus : Apostoli etiam, præcipue vero Paulus quam solidis argumētis artificialibus suam demonstrat doctrinam! Hæc qui negat, is aut nunquam recte legit ac per-penpendit sacras scripturas, aut logicis literis nusquam fuit tinctus. Quoad fidei cõfirmationẽ, articulos fidei nostræ principaliter quidẽ confirmamus testimoniis spiritus sancti: at alicubi ipsissima non habemus verba articuli, opus est igitur deductione syllogistica, quæ ex testimonio diuino nectit syllogismum, cuius argumentum ratione quæstionis potest esse artificiale. Deinde plerique doctores in suis disputationibus de veritate articulorum fidei primo loco afferunt oracula Dei, secundo rationes artificiales, tertio cõsensu orthodoxorũ patrum. Quid? quod ad stabiliendam scripturæ fidem solent afferri humanæ rationes: de quibus videatur in libellis de certitudine religionis Christianæ.
units.tr: The antecedent is false, both as regards Holy Scripture and as regards the confirmation of faith from Holy Scripture. As regards Holy Scripture: God himself in his Word does not speak unreasonably [ἀλόγως] but with weighty reasons about himself and his will towards us. Christ in his sermons, in refuting the Jews, is seen to use notable logic and excellent reasons and artificial arguments. The apostles too, and especially Paul, how solidly he demonstrates his doctrine by artificial arguments! Whoever denies this has either never read and weighed the sacred Scriptures rightly, or was never steeped in logical letters. As regards the confirmation of faith: we indeed confirm the articles of our faith chiefly by the testimonies of the Holy Spirit; but in some places we do not have the very words of the article, and so there is need of a syllogistic deduction, which from the divine testimony forms a syllogism whose argument, given the nature of the question, can be artificial. Next, most teachers in their disputations about the truth of the articles of faith adduce first the oracles of God, second artificial reasons, third the consensus of the orthodox Fathers. What more? To establish the faith of Scripture, human reasons are customarily brought forward; on these see the little books on the certainty of the Christian religion.

units.la: Obiectio V.
units.tr: Objection V.

units.la: Sapientia humana Deo est stultitia.Logica est sapientia humana.Logica igitur Deo est stultitia.
units.tr: Human wisdom is foolishness to God. Logic is human wisdom. Therefore logic is foolishness to God.

units.la: Responsio.
units.tr: Answer.

units.la: Propositio est particularis contra legem syllogisticam. Non omnis enim humana sapientia est stultitia Deo, sed ea qua de Paulus loquitur, qui eam vocat mundi sapientiam sophisticis argutiis insurgentem aduersus Euangelium crucis Christi: alioqui humana quædam sapientia est Dei donum in homine à Deo effecta: & dicitur humana sapientia, quæ est de rebus humanis: vtraque Deo non est stultitia. Assumptio itidem est falsa: aliud enim est esse sapientia: aliud est esse organum num sapientiæ. Logica non est sapientia, seu habitus mentis, sed eius quoddam organum, quo sapienter de quibusuis rebus possumus differere. Deinde Logica non est humana seu mundi sapientia, quæ dicitur carnalis, etsi carnales & ψυχικοί, quibus sapientia diuina fuit & est stultitia, eam primo formarint; & quidam adhuc excolant: nostra autem logica corrigit carnalem & sophisticam sapientiam, & veram docet.
units.tr: The proposition is particular, which breaks the rules of syllogism. For not all human wisdom is foolishness to God, but only that of which Paul speaks, who calls it the wisdom of the world, rising up with sophistical subtleties against the Gospel of the cross of Christ. Otherwise, some human wisdom is a gift of God, produced in man by God, and is called human wisdom because it concerns human affairs; neither kind is foolishness to God. The minor premise is likewise false: being wisdom is one thing, and being an instrument of wisdom is another. Logic is not wisdom, or a habit of mind, but a certain instrument by which we can reason wisely about any subject whatever. Next, logic is not human or worldly wisdom, which is called carnal, although carnal and psychic men, to whom divine wisdom was and is foolishness, first shaped it, and some still cultivate it. Our logic, however, corrects carnal and sophistical wisdom and teaches the true kind.

units.la: Quod Theologica non possint logicè tractari sequentibus rationibus ostenditur.
units.tr: That theological matters cannot be treated logically is shown by the following arguments.

units.la: Obiectio I.
units.tr: Objection I.

units.la: Si res Theologica possent tractari instrumento logico, Theologia subiiceretur Logicæ.
units.tr: If theological matters could be treated by the logical instrument, theology would be subject to logic.

units.la: At non hoc: Ergo nec illud.
units.tr: But this is not so. Therefore neither is that.

units.la: Propositionem probant: Tractari enim ab aliquo est eidem subiici ad tractandum.
units.tr: They prove the major premise: for to be treated by someone is to be subjected to that person for the purpose of treatment.

units.la: Assumptum probant: Domina non debet subiici famulæ: Theologia est domina, Logica est famula. Ergo Theologia non debet subiici Logicæ.
units.tr: They prove the minor premise: A mistress ought not to be subject to a maidservant. Theology is the mistress; logic is the maidservant. Therefore theology ought not to be subject to logic.

units.la: Responsio.
units.tr: Answer.

units.la: Fallacia est homonymias in voce Subiici, quæ aliquando politice, aliquando logicè accipitur. Domina non subiicitur famulæ πολιτικῶς: domina enim imperat, non seruit ei: At interim domina subiicitur famulæ λογικῶς, id est, domina est obiectum famulæ, quæ operam suam circa eam exerceat. Sic Theologia non subiicitur logicæ, vt veritatem ipsam à logica accipiat. Subiicitur vero, quoad veritatis percipiendæ modum. Imo etiam Logica quodam dammodo imperat (instar ἀρχιτεκτονικὴς) Theologo, quatenus praecipit ei, seu praecepta & normas praescribit de rebus diuinis differendi, & licentius eum vagantem in amplissimis campis in gyrum rationis cogit. Est enim quasi aureum frenum Palladis, quod iniiciendum est Theologo etiam, ne extra metas feratur. Oportet Theologum contineri, & velut coerceri artium septis, nec fas est ei repagulis huius artis effractis, improprie, sine ordine, sine definitionibus, sine distinctionibus docere, ne lux doctrinae obscuretur aut amittatur, & discordiae augeantur, aut aliis erroribus occasio detur.
units.tr: The fallacy lies in the equivocation of the word "subject," which is sometimes taken politically and sometimes logically. A mistress is not subject to her maidservant politically [πολιτικῶς]: the mistress commands; she does not serve. Yet a mistress is subject to her maidservant logically [λογικῶς], that is, the mistress is the object toward which the maidservant directs her work. In the same way, theology is not subject to logic so as to receive its truth from logic; it is subject to logic only in respect of the manner of perceiving truth. Indeed logic also, in a certain sense, governs the theologian, as an architectonic art [ἀρχιτεκτονικὴς] does: it instructs him, prescribes for him the rules and norms of discoursing about divine things, and restrains him when he wanders too freely over the wide fields of reason. It is, as it were, the golden bridle of Pallas, which must be put on the theologian so that he is not carried beyond his limits. The theologian must be contained, and as it were confined within the enclosures of the arts, and it is not right for him, once the barriers of this art are broken, to teach improperly, without order, without definitions and distinctions, lest the light of doctrine be obscured or lost, dissensions multiplied, or occasion given to other errors.

units.la: Obiectio II.
units.tr: Objection II.

units.la: Si Philosophi genuerunt Logicam, tantum propter Philosophiam, vt huic esset praesidio, si & ipsa Logica definitur instrumentum a Philosophis genitum, quo verum a falso in Philosophia discernatur: Logica nō Theologiæ sed Philosophiæ tantum erit instrumentum, nec Theologia subiecta erit Logicæ.
units.tr: If the philosophers produced logic only for the sake of philosophy, so that it might serve as its protection, and if logic itself is defined as an instrument produced by the philosophers by which the true is distinguished from the false in philosophy, then logic will be an instrument of philosophy only, not of theology, and theology will not be subject to logic.

units.la: At vera sunt quæ antecedunt: vt testantur ii, qui Zabarellæ sunt sectatores.
units.tr: But the antecedents are true, as those who are followers of Zabarella attest.

units.la: Ergo & hoc quod ex iis consequitur.
units.tr: Therefore the consequent is true as well.

units.la: Responsio.
units.tr: Answer.

units.la: Connexum propositionis negamus. 1. Non sequitur, Philosophi primum genuerunt Logicam: Ergo vsus Logicæ non extendit se ad Theologiam. Nam quod non Theologi sed Philosophi hac artem primo descripserunt, id mere contingens est & aliter se habere potuit, cū & Theologi iisdem artium inueniendarum & iudicandarum darum instrumentis formare Logicam potu-issent.1. Non sequitur; Philosophi genuerunt Logicam propter solam Philosophiam: Ergo eius vsus ad Theologiam non pertinet. Quia non est videndum nobis tantum, quid Philosophi procreatores Logicæ spectarint, sed quid Deus Logicæ primus parens, nempe, vt sicut reliquarum disciplinarum sic quoq; Logicæ finis sit prin-ceps, vt præsidio sit religioni aduersus sophistas & Pseudidascalos. Ergo etsi quod Logica confert ad Theologiam est præter intentionem & consilium Philosophorum: tamé non est præter consilium Dei. Deinde etsi sit præter intentionem & institutum Philosophorum Logicam inseruire Theologiæ, non tamen est contra institutum & intentionem illorum: vt artifex quidam potest fabrefacere instrumentum ad hunc vel illum vsum tantum, quod fabrefactum vbi animaduertitur aliis etiam vsibus aptum esse, illis etiam adhibet: Nec valet consequutio: Instrumentum hoc factum est ab artifice ad hunc vsum. Ergo illi vsui non inseruit. Sic etiam Logica postquam fuit fabrefacta, Theologiæ etiam vtilis esse compertum est. Et sic præter quidem, non autem contra institutum Philosophorum vsui est Theologiæ.Ideoque non valet consequentia: Logica facta est, vt esset instrumentum tractandâ Philosophiæ. Ergo non est instrumentum tractanda Theologia. Assumptio ex authoritate Zabarellistarum parum authoritatis & fidei meretur, præcipue cum destituatur solidis rationibus. nibus. Definitio item allata Logicæ vitiosa est; nimis enim angusta cum definito reciprocari nequit.
units.tr: We deny the connection of the proposition. (1) It does not follow that the philosophers first produced logic; therefore the use of logic does not extend to theology. For that it was not theologians but philosophers who first described this art is a purely contingent matter, and it could have been otherwise, since theologians too could have formed logic from the same instruments for discovering and judging arts. (2) It does not follow that the philosophers produced logic for philosophy alone; therefore its use does not pertain to theology. For we must consider not only what the philosophers who produced logic intended, but what God, the first parent of logic, intended: namely, that, as with the other disciplines, the chief aim of logic should be a defense of religion against sophists and false teachers. Therefore, even if what logic contributes to theology lies beyond the intention and purpose of the philosophers, it is not beyond the purpose of God. Next, even if it is beyond the intention and design of the philosophers that logic should serve theology, it is not against their design and intention. A craftsman may make a tool for this or that particular use; but when, once it is made, it is seen to be suitable for other uses too, he applies it to those as well. Nor does the inference hold: This instrument was made by the craftsman for this use; therefore it does not serve that use. So also logic, once it was made, was found to be useful for theology too. Thus its use for theology is beyond the intention of the philosophers, but not against it. Therefore the inference does not hold: Logic was made so that it might be the instrument for handling philosophy; therefore it is not the instrument for handling theology. The minor premise, resting on the authority of the Zabarellists, deserves little authority or credence, especially since it lacks solid reasons. The definition of logic given is also faulty, for it is too narrow to be convertible with what it defines.

units.la: Instant. Ergo contingens est, quod Dialectica Theologiæ vtilis eidem inseruiat: Dialectica à Philosophis Philosophiæ nomine est genita. Ergo non Theologiæ, sed Philosophiæ proprium instrumentum est.
units.tr: They object: Therefore it is contingent that dialectic, which is useful to theology, serves it. Dialectic was born by the philosophers in the name of philosophy. Therefore it is not the proper instrument of theology, but of philosophy.

units.la: Responsio.
units.tr: Answer.

units.la: 1. Quod Logica à Philosophis propter Philosophiam inuenta vtilis est Theologiæ quoque, contingens hoc quidem est, respectu Philosophorum inuentorum: sed interim non contingens ratione Theologiæ, nec contingens respectu Dei, cuius consilium amplius, altius, superius. 2. Instrumentum dicitur & definitur ab vsu, qui à forma proficiscitur. Si igitur vsus Logicæ in Theologia magnus est, si Logica, quod Theologi doctiores fatentur, plurimum confert ad Theologiam; certe etiam instrumentum & administra vocabitur. 3. Ipse etiam Zabarella distinguens, ait, Logicam esse organum Philosophiæ, & conferre ad Philosophiam primario: ad Theologiam vero secundario.
units.tr: 1. That logic was invented by the philosophers for the sake of philosophy and is also useful to theology is indeed contingent with respect to the philosophers who discovered it. But it is not contingent with respect to theology, nor contingent with respect to God, whose counsel is broader, higher, and loftier. 2. An instrument is named and defined by its use, and its use proceeds from its form.
