So if logic has great use in theology, and if, as the more learned theologians admit, logic contributes greatly to theology, then surely it will also be called an instrument and a handmaid. 3. Zabarella himself, drawing the distinction, says: Logic is the organ of philosophy, and contributes to philosophy primarily, but to theology only secondarily.

units.la: Obiectio III.
units.tr: Objection III.

units.la: Si ex sola Philosophia Logica est procreata, solius etiam Philosophiæ erit instrumentum.
units.tr: If logic was produced from philosophy alone, it will also be an instrument of philosophy alone.

units.la: At verum est prius: testante Philosophorum experientia. Ergo & posterius.
units.tr: But the former is true, as the experience of the philosophers attests. Therefore the latter also.

units.la: Responsio.
units.tr: Answer.

units.la: Propositionis conexio est infirma. Nō enim, si ex sola Philosophia Dialectica procreata est à Græcis Philosophis, eo quod Theologicam doctrinam non haberent: continuo erit tantum Philosophiæ instrumentum, & non etiam Theologiæ. Nam potuit etiam extrui ex sanctis Scripturis, & diuinis Ecclesiæ Doctorum disputationibus: & quod obseruata extructa est à Philosophis, & quidè Ethnicis, hoc omnino est contingens & accidentarium. Potuissent enim homines Theologi ante Græcos Philosophos Logicam fabricare & constituere. Et si contingens est, ac per accidens fit, si Theologus vtatur Logica, necesse est vt Theologo insit per se tractare res Theologicas absque Logica & absque rationis vsu.
units.tr: The connection of the proposition is weak. For it does not follow that, if dialectic was produced by the Greek philosophers alone, because they had no theological doctrine, it will therefore be only an instrument of philosophy and not also of theology. For it could also have been constructed out of the holy Scriptures and the divine disputations of the teachers of the Church. That it was in fact formulated by the philosophers, and indeed by pagans, is entirely contingent and accidental. For men who were theologians could have devised and established logic before the Greek philosophers. And if it is contingent, and comes about only by accident, when a theologian uses logic, then it must be that a theologian can treat theological matters in themselves without logic and without the use of reason.

units.la: Obiectio IV.
units.tr: Objection IV.

units.la: Distincta non sunt commiscenda.
units.tr: Distinct things must not be mixed together.

units.la: Logica hominum & Logica Dei ita sunt distincta, vt huic cum illa nihil commune sit.
units.tr: The logic of men and the logic of God are so distinct that the one has nothing in common with the other.

units.la: Hoc ita probatur: In verbo enim Dei multa sunt, quæ lumen naturæ & rationis humanæ acumen excedunt, vt pleraque principia Theologica.
units.tr: This is proved thus: For in the Word of God there are many things which exceed the light of nature and the keenness of human reason, such as most theological principles.

units.la: Responsio.
units.tr: Answer.

units.la: Propositio vera est de veræ distinctionis terminis veraque commistione: alias poterit quippiam esse distinctum ab aliquo in propriis, quod tamen cum eo communicare poterit in quodam communi vsu. Assumptio, quæ Logica Dei à Logica nostra plane diuellit, nec quicquam commune hanc cum illa habere opinatur, fallit & fallitur. Nam Logica nostra est pars imaginis divinae in homine, cum sit radius sapientiae Dei quasi sparsus in mentes nostras. Etsi autem longe sit perfectior ipsius Dei Logica, quam nostra: tamen non omnis inde neganda est communitas. Imo si Deum patefactum & loquentem cum hominibus, ad quos se accommodat, spectes, Logica nec alia nec illustrior in Philosophorum libris appareret, quam est Spiritus sancti in scriptis Propheticis & Apostolicis, & Ecclesiasticorum Scriptorum monumentis. Logica Dei est αὐτοτυπος: nostra est ἐκτυπος ad illam scilicet expressa.
units.tr: The proposition is true concerning the terms of a real distinction and a real mixing; otherwise something could be distinct from another in its own nature and yet share something with it in some common use. The assumption, which entirely tears God's logic away from our logic and supposes that the two have nothing in common, is mistaken and misleads. For our logic is a part of the image of God in man, since it is a ray of the wisdom of God, as it were scattered into our minds. And although God's own logic is far more perfect than ours, nevertheless no community between them should be denied. Indeed, if you look at God revealed and speaking with men, to whom he accommodates himself, logic does not appear in the books of the philosophers either different or more illustrious than the logic of the Holy Spirit in the prophetic and apostolic writings and in the records of the ecclesiastical writers. God's logic is autotypal [αὐτότυπος]; ours is ectypal [ἔκτυπος], that is, expressed from it.

units.la: Ad Prosyllogismum assumpti respondetur: distinguendum est inter ipsas res & modum tractandi, inter res & notiones quae imponuntur rebus. Res, media, principia petuntur ex Theologia: modus vero seu forma tractandi, methodus ratiocinandi & notiones sunt logicae. Exempli causa: Axioma Theologicum est: Christus est Deus, quod ignorat per se Logica & Philosophia. Probandum hoc est medio aliquo. Hoc medium etiam Theologicum est, non Philosophicum, non Logicum.
units.tr: As for the prosyllogism of the assumption, the answer is this: one must distinguish between the things themselves and the manner of treating them, between the things and the notions that are imposed on the things. The things, the means and the principles, are sought from theology. The mode or form of treating them, the method of reasoning and the notions, are logical. For example, the theological axiom is: Christ is God, which logic and philosophy do not know of themselves. This must be proved by some middle term. This middle term is also theological, not philosophical, not logical.

units.la: Media enim & principia Theologicae quaestionis probandae & concludendae ex Theologia, non ex Logica aut Philosophia depromuntur: quia quaestio illa ad Logicam & Philosophiam κτήσει (proprietate) non pertinet: pertinet interim ad Logicam χρήσει (usu:) Quia Logicus illam tractat, praecepta sua & regulas con-
units.tr: For the means and principles of a theological question to be proved and concluded are drawn from theology, not from logic or philosophy, because that question does not belong to logic and philosophy by possession [κτήσει]. It does, however, belong to logic by use [χρήσει], because the logician treats it, adapting to it his precepts and rules for

units.la: κτήσει (proprietate): the Greek and italic words in the text are as printed. concludendi ad eam accommodatas: seu Theo-logus Logicus hic eandem in ratiocinando rationem & normam sequitur, quam observat Philosophus Logicus, conclusionem Philosophicam ex Philosophicis principiis inferens.
units.tr: (Greek κτήσει, rendered proprietate: the Greek and italic words in the text are as printed.) concluding. Thus the theologian who uses logic follows in his reasoning the same rule and norm that the logical philosopher observes, when he infers a philosophical conclusion from philosophical principles.

units.la: Vna enim tantum est via componendi, resoluendi, demonstrandi, omninoque ratiocinandi & differendi de quauis quæstione, siue ea sit Philosophica, siue Theologica. Antitrinitarius dicit, Vnum esse Deum, non Trinum, quod hæc inuoluant contradictionem. In hoc refellendo utor terminis Logicis, dicens, Vnum & tres esse quidem oppositá: nec simul consistere: Vnum vero & Trinum non esse opposita: quod vnus de essentia, trinus vero de personis in unitate essentiæ dicatur: Qui respectus diuersorum est, quæ consentire possunt.
units.tr: For there is only one way of composing, resolving, demonstrating, and in short of reasoning and disputing about any question, whether it is philosophical or theological. The Antitrinitarian says: God is one, not three, because these propositions involve a contradiction. In refuting this I use logical terms, saying: "One" and "three" are indeed opposites, and cannot stand together; but "one" and "three" are not opposites, because one is said of the essence and three of the persons in the unity of the essence. This is a relation of different things, which can agree.

units.la: Neque vero Logice differere de rebus sacris est Logicam cum Theologia permiscere. Cum enim Theologus Logicus lumen Logicum infert in sacra, non magis sacra prophanis aut prophana sacris miscet, quam cum demonstrationem Theologicam Grammaticorum canonibus congruentem facit, & ad rectum laudabilemque vsum conformat, vt sit pura emendataque & solœcismis vacet (quod congrue loqui vulgo dicunt) ne audiat forte istud: Est bonus Theologus, sed malus Grammaticus.
units.tr: Nor, indeed, does reasoning logically about sacred things mean mixing logic with theology. For when the logical theologian brings logical light into sacred matters, he mixes sacred things with profane no more than when he makes a theological demonstration agree with the rules of the grammarians and shapes it to correct and laudable usage, so that it is pure and emended and free of solecisms (which people commonly call speaking properly), lest he hear that saying: He is a good theologian, but a bad grammarian.

units.la: Obiectio V.
units.tr: Objection V.

units.la: Si pleraque Theologica sunt diuina mysteria, plerapleraque Theologica Logicis notionibus ac legibus & rationis iudicio subiici non possunt.
units.tr: If most theological matters are divine mysteries, then most theological matters cannot be subjected to logical notions and laws and to the judgment of reason.

units.la: Abscondita enim à ratione humana ex ratione explicari nequeunt.
units.tr: For things hidden from human reason cannot be explained from reason.

units.la: Mysteria diuina sunt abscondita à ratione humana.
units.tr: Divine mysteries are hidden from human reason.

units.la: Ergo mysteria diuina ex ratione humana explicari nequeunt.
units.tr: Therefore divine mysteries cannot be explained from human reason.

units.la: At verum est antecedens. Ergo & consequens.
units.tr: But the antecedent is true. Therefore the consequent too.

units.la: Responsio.
units.tr: Answer.

units.la: Ad propositionem eiusque Prosyllogismu respondet Rudolphus Goclenius triplici ratione. Primo, inquit, Logicus non ex ratione vt promptuario, sed secundam rectam rationem ex diuinis Scripturis mysteria explicat. Et Logicus tractans diuina mysteria non subiicit ea rationis iudicio, perinde ac si demum id in rebus diuinis verum ac rectum statuat, quod iudicio suo naturali probat. Nam Theologica tractare logice, est κηρύγματα, decreta & praecepta artis logicae ad res diuinas applicare, & rerum spiritualium doctrinam, de cuius veritate & certitudine Logico vt Christiano constat, erudite, artificiose, scienter explicare: videre deniq;, Maiestas materiae Theologicae, de qua explicandum est, quae argumenta admittat, quae respuat. Exempli causa: Deus non potest considerari per omnia argumentorum genera, tum propter summam naturae diuinae perfectionem ac à creaturis differentiam: tũ propter nostriingenii & captus imbecillitatem tatem & angustiam. Exempli causa: In Trinitate pater proprie principiu filii dicitur: ἀπὸ vero non nisi analogice & improprie. Deus non est genus patris, Filii & Spiritus S. Pater, Filius & Spiritus sanctus non sunt species Dei, propter diuinae naturae singularitatem & eminentiam ἀκαταλυπτον.
units.tr: Rudolphus Goclenius answers the proposition and its prosyllogism with three reasons. First, he says, the logician does not explain mysteries from reason as from a storehouse, but from divine Scripture, according to right reason. A logician who treats divine mysteries does not subject them to the judgment of reason, as if he held only what he proves by his natural judgment to be true and right in divine things. For to treat theological matters logically is to apply the decrees and precepts of the art of logic to divine things, and to explain the doctrine of spiritual things (whose truth and certainty are known to the logician as a Christian) learnedly, skilfully and knowingly. Finally, it is to see the majesty of the theological subject matter: which arguments it admits and which it rejects. For example: God cannot be considered through every kind of argument, both on account of the supreme perfection of the divine nature and its difference from creatures, and on account of the weakness and narrowness of our intellect and capacity. For example: in the Trinity the Father is properly called the principle of the Son, but from [ἀπὸ] only analogically and improperly. God is not the genus of the Father, Son and Holy Spirit; the Father, Son and Holy Spirit are not species of God, on account of the singularity and eminence of the divine nature [ἀκαταλυπτον].

units.la: Secundo; Non etiam eo inficias, Theologiam afferre συμπληρωμα, id est, perfectionem & supplementum Logicae, & habere quaedam maxime propria, quae ad regulas logicas non congruunt, aut non per omnia eis conueniunt. Itaque in diuinis explicandis interdum necesse est nos esse ἀγροικοτεροι, id est, agrestiores & νηπιάζοντες seu puerorum in cunis balbutientium persimiles.
units.tr: Second, I do not deny that theology brings a complement [συμπληρωμα], that is, the perfection and supplement of logic, and that it has certain features most proper to itself, which do not fit the logical rules, or do not fit them in every respect. Therefore in explaining divine things it is sometimes necessary for us to be more rustic [ἀγροικοτεροι], that is, more rough, and to babble [νηπιάζοντες], very like children stammering in their cradles.

units.la: Tertio: Sicut apud artifices sunt normae quaedam materiales ac regulae, quibus non semper vtuntur exquisite rectis, sed interdum a rectitudine aliquantulum recedentibus: propter materiam enim, ex qua materialia opera construenda sunt, saepe coguntur regula uti aliquantum obliquata, cuiusmodi erat regula illa Lesbia, de qua Arist. meminit 5. Eth. cap. 10. quae plumbea erat, vt ad lapidum figuram flecteretur. Ac ita non semper materiam ipsi regulae, sed quandoque regulam materiae accommodare oportet, vt inquit Zabar. Eodem modo propter singularitatem vel praeeminentiam & maiestatem materiae in Theologia aliquando vtitur Logicus notionibus Logicis, non exquisitissima & visitata prorsus, sed par-rum rum obliquata vel peculiari ratione, non tamen penitus peruersa: vt quando Christo partes tribuit, quippe quæ à peruulgatis partibus aliquid discrepans habeant: aut quando Deum Totum vocat, ideoque interdum, vt verbum absit à calumnia, castigatione vtitur per particulam quasi, aut similem, Scholasticorum exemplo. Sic canones logicorum etiam ad sacra aliquādo (intellige cum materia quasi quodammodo contumax est & refractaria) applicantur, vt durioribus applicabatur lapidibus Lesbia regula. Creans ex nihilo applicatur ad causam efficientem analogice, cum efficiens proprie producenti ex subiecto tributur. Sic proportionis vox applicatur ad λόγον vnientem & carnem vnitam. Infiniti (λόγῳ) ad finitam carnem proportio est, non quidem quantitatis ratione, qualis est proportio dupli ad dimidium, quanti ad aliud quantum: sed qualis est agentis ad patiens, actus ad potentiam, independentis ad dependens, perfecti ad imperfectum, sustentantis ad sustentatum, perse subsistentis ad subsistens in alio.
units.tr: Third, just as among craftsmen there are certain material norms and rules which they do not always use in their exact straightness, but sometimes depart somewhat from straightness: for on account of the material from which material works must be built, they are often compelled to use a rule somewhat bent. Such was that Lesbian rule, which Aristotle mentions in Ethics 5, ch. 10, which was of lead so that it could be bent to the shape of the stone. Thus one must adapt not always the material to the rule, but sometimes the rule to the material, as Zabarella says. In the same way, on account of the singularity, or the pre-eminence and majesty, of the material in theology, the logician sometimes uses logical notions that are not the most exact or altogether customary, but somewhat bent or used in a peculiar way, yet not wholly perverted: as when he assigns parts to Christ, since these have something differing from the commonly known parts; or when he calls God a Whole, and therefore sometimes, to speak without offence, qualifies the expression with the particle as if, or something similar, after the example of the Scholastics. So the canons of the logicians are sometimes applied to sacred things too (understand: when the matter is somewhat stubborn and unyielding), just as the Lesbian rule was applied to harder stones. Creating out of nothing is applied to efficient cause analogically, whereas efficient cause is properly attributed to the producer as distinct from the subject. So the word proportion is applied to the Word uniting and the flesh united. The proportion of the infinite (Word) to the finite flesh is indeed not one of quantity, such as the proportion of double to half, or of one quantity to another; it is rather that of agent to patient, act to potency, independent to dependent, perfect to imperfect, sustainer to sustained, what subsists in itself to what subsists in another.

units.la: Sic datur Deo & creaturæ in ente analogia non ratione συμμετρίας, id est, commensurationis certæ, seu ὡρισμένης determinatæ, qualis est inter vnum & duo, sed imitationis ac participationis, qualis analogia est ἀρχέτυπα & ἔκτυπα, exemplaris & imaginis. Atque ita Logica nonnunquam ad veritatis cœlestis normam reducitur.
units.tr: Thus there is analogy between God and creature in being, not by reason of symmetry, that is, of a fixed and determinate commensuration such as there is between one and two, but of imitation and participation, such as the analogy of archetype and ectype, exemplar and image. And thus logic is sometimes brought back to the norm of heavenly truth.

units.la: I. Instant. Quod rationem nostram excedit, ad id ars rationis suos terminos applicare & rationis munere explicari nequit.
units.tr: I. Objection. What exceeds our reason, the art of reason cannot apply its terms to, and it cannot be explained by the office of reason.

units.la: Mysteria rationem nostram excedunt.
units.tr: Mysteries exceed our reason.

units.la: Ad mysteria igitur ars rationis suos terminos applicare, eaque rationis munere explicari nequeant.
units.tr: Therefore the art of reason cannot apply its terms to mysteries, and they cannot be explained by the office of reason.

units.la: Responsio.
units.tr: Answer.

units.la: Distinguenda sunt mysteria non revelata à revelatis: distinguenda item ratio hominis psychici, quae spiritualia carnaliter diiudicat, à ratione hominis spiritualis spiritualiter diiudicante: distinguendus item modus explicandi, qui aliis tribuitur instrumento logico, aliis vero ipsi Dei verbo. Mysteria quatenus sunt revelata logice tractari & enunciari possunt, ut qua sunt patefacta nostro intellectui per logicos intelligendi modos: quatenus autem non revelata, eatenus nobis sunt inperscrutabilia, nec logice tractabilia. Deinde animalis homo, etiamsi sit logicae peritus, tamen quia res mysteriorum non intelligit: non enim intelligit ea quae sunt spiritus Dei: ideo carnalis rationis munere de mysteriorum rebus convenienter differere non potest. Tertio, rationis quidem munere logicoque tractandi modo explicamus mysteria, sed religiose fundamento explicationis observato ex verbo Dei. Aliquid igitur rationem nostram potest excedere, quod tamen verbo Dei revelatum ab eadem recipitur. Aliquid item quoad formam inteinteriorem arcanum nobis esse potest, quoad alias vero circumstantias nobis diuinitus explicatum.
units.tr: Unrevealed mysteries must be distinguished from revealed ones; likewise the reason of the natural man, who judges spiritual things in a carnal way, must be distinguished from the reason of the spiritual man, who judges spiritually; and likewise the mode of explaining, which belongs to one thing, the logical instrument, and to another, the Word of God itself. Mysteries, insofar as they are revealed, can be treated and stated logically, since they have been made plain to our intellect through logical modes of understanding; insofar as they are not revealed, they are to that extent unsearchable for us and not open to logical treatment. Next, the natural man, even if he is skilled in logic, nevertheless does not understand the things of mysteries, for he does not understand the things of the Spirit of God; therefore by the office of carnal reason he cannot fittingly discourse about the matters of mysteries. Third, we do indeed explain mysteries by the office of reason and the logical manner of treatment, but with the foundation of the explanation religiously observed from the Word of God. Something, then, can exceed our reason and yet, revealed in the Word of God, be received by reason. Likewise something may be hidden from us as to its inner form, while as to other circumstances it has been explained to us by God.

units.la: Assumptio itaque plane & plene si reuelatum Dei verbum spectamus, sique hominem illuminatum habemus, vera non est. Sicut & propositio: vt enim maximæ, sublimes & cœlestes res eodem modo loquendi Grammatico explicantur, eadem modificatione Rhetorica explicantur: ita quoque fieri potest, vt eodem modo differendi tractentur & disponantur. Etsi enim superent rationem nostram, quod ad ὃν attinet, tamen τὸ ὂν intelligimus: cognitio nostra licet non sit perfecta, tamen aliquid in speculo videmus, & imperfectio rei plenam negationem non infert.
units.tr: Therefore the assumption is plainly not true, if we look fully at the revealed Word of God and have an enlightened man; nor is the proposition. For just as the greatest, sublime and heavenly things are explained by the same manner of grammatical speech, so they can be explained by the same rhetorical modification; so too they can be treated and arranged in the same manner of discourse. For although they exceed our reason as far as that which is [ὃν] is concerned, nevertheless we understand being itself [τὸ ὂν]. Our knowledge, though not perfect, nevertheless sees something as in a mirror, and the imperfection of a thing does not imply a complete negation.

units.la: Mysterium est stupendum, quod Christus est persona, quæ est Deus & homo, mediatrix inter nos & patrem: Et tamen hæc prædicatio logica est, prædicatur definitio de definito. Magnum est mysterium, teste Apost. coniunctio spiritualis Christi cum Ecclesia. At hoc mysterium exponitur & declaratur modo loquendi, docendi & differendi in rebus humanis visitato, vbi comparatur Christus capiti, Ecclesia corpori, Christus marito seu sponso, Ecclesia vxori seu sponsæ. Profundum est electionis nostræ mysterium, & tamen id nobis si loca eius resoluatur logicis argumetis & enunciationibus explicatur.
units.tr: It is a stupendous mystery that Christ is a person who is God and man, the mediator between us and the Father. And yet this predication is logical: a definition is predicated of the thing defined. The mystery of the spiritual union of Christ with the Church is great, as the Apostle witnesses. But this mystery is expounded and declared in the mode of speaking, teaching and reasoning customary in human affairs, where Christ is compared to the head, the Church to the body, Christ to the husband or bridegroom, and the Church to the wife or bride. The mystery of our election is profound, and yet, if its parts are resolved by logical arguments and statements, it is explained to us.

units.la: Quid? quod commentatores, explanatores & interpretes verbi diuini & catechese⁂n mysteria & Sacramenta non tantum definiunt & partiantur (quæ sunt insignia Logicæ munera) sed ad causarum & aliorum argumentorum descendunt explicationem.
units.tr: What of it? Do not commentators, expositors and interpreters of the divine word, and writers of catechisms, not only define and divide mysteries and sacraments (which are the proper offices of logic), but also descend to the explanation of causes and other arguments?

units.la: 2. Instant. Res singularis, cuius singularis & plane inusitatus est modus, requirit quoque modum prædicandi & disponendi singularem & inusitatum, adeoque singularem Logicam.
units.tr: 2. Objection. A singular thing, whose mode is singular and altogether unusual, also requires a singular and unusual mode of predicating and arranging, and so a singular logic.

units.la: Atqui arcanum est res singularis modum habens arcanum.
units.tr: But a mystery is a singular thing having a hidden mode.

units.la: Ergo & modum requirit prædicandi & disponendi singularem.
units.tr: Therefore it also requires a singular mode of predicating and arranging.

units.la: Responsio.
units.tr: Response.

units.la: Propositió est dubiæ fidei: Discrimen enim modi non necesse est tollere similitudinem & identitatem ipsius rei, & inducere diuersum enunciandi modum, vt: Singulare est, quod Adamus fit ex terra, enunciandi tamen modus est vsitatus, Adamus supernaturali modo extitit, nos naturali: ille per creationem, nos per generationem. Naturæ tamen Adami & nostræ identitas est, nec inducitur diuersus modus prædicandi, cum dicitur, Adamus est homo, ab hoc, Abelus est homo. Christus singulari & inusitato modo est homo ex virgine, & tamen quia nobis ὁμοούσιός est, idem tantum non est prædicandi modus vbique, nempe essen-tialis. Christus est homo & Petrus est homo, etsi hoc differt, quod Christus non tantum homo sed & Deus est, Petrus vero est homo tantum.
units.tr: The proposition is of doubtful truth. A difference in mode does not necessarily remove the likeness and identity of the thing itself, nor does it require a different way of stating it. For example, it is a singular thing that Adam was made from earth, yet the manner of speaking is ordinary: Adam came into being in a supernatural way, and we in a natural way, he by creation and we by generation. Yet Adam's nature and ours are identical, and a different mode of predication is not introduced when one says "Adam is a man" and "Abel is a man." Christ is man in a singular and unusual way, born of a virgin; yet because he is of one substance [ὁμοούσιος] with us, the mode of predication is not the same everywhere. It is essential predication. Christ is man and Peter is man, though this differs in that Christ is not only man but also God, whereas Peter is only man.

units.la: Obiectio VI.
units.tr: Objection VI.

units.la: Quod ad modos rerum creatarum & mundanarum est commensuratum, id rerum diuinarum modis applicari non potest.
units.tr: What is commensurate with the modes of created and worldly things cannot be applied to the modes of divine things.

units.la: Omnia praecepta Logica ad modos rerum mundanarum & creatarum sunt commensurata.
units.tr: All the precepts of logic are commensurate with the modes of worldly and created things.

units.la: Praecepta igitur Logica ad modos rerum diuinarum applicari nequeunt.
units.tr: Therefore the precepts of logic cannot be applied to the modes of divine things.

units.la: Prop. probatur: Quia isti modi rerum creatarum & increatarum, mundanarum & diuinarum longissimo distant interuallo, nec conuenire possunt.
units.tr: The major premise is proved: because these modes of created and uncreated, worldly and divine things are separated by an immense interval and cannot agree.

units.la: Assumpt. probatur: Praecepta enim Logica sunt inductione obseruatorum exemplorum efformata: At haec exempla a primis authoribus sunt ex communi vsu mundano obseruata.
units.tr: The minor premise is proved: for the precepts of logic were formed by induction from observed examples; but these examples were observed by the first authors from ordinary worldly usage.

units.la: Responsio.
units.tr: Response.

units.la: Propositio vniuersalem veritatem non habet: eadem enim ratione voces Grammaticae & ornamenta Rhetorica ad res diuinas applicari nô possent, seu res diuinae vocibus Grammaticis & ornamentis Rhetoricis exponi & efferri non possent: siquidem primi Grammatices & Rhetorices authores inductione exemplorum ex rebus mundanis & terrenis obseruatorum vsi pepererunt earum praecepta. Iam vero spiritus S. demittês se ad captum nostrum in mysteriis etiam in sublimibus nostris vtitur vocibus, nostrisq; tropis & figuris.
units.tr: The proposition has no universal truth. By the same reasoning, the parts of grammar and the ornaments of rhetoric could not be applied to divine things, or divine things could not be expressed and set forth by grammatical words and rhetorical ornaments. For the first authors of grammar and rhetoric derived their precepts by induction from examples observed in worldly and earthly things and their use. Yet the Holy Spirit, condescending to our capacity, uses in the mysteries, even in our most sublime matters, our own words, tropes and figures.

units.la: Assumptio sua item laborat falsitate. Etsi enim primi authores Logicæ obuia quæque in bene differentium vsu exempla, & quidem pleraque de rebus humanis obseruarint, non tamen præcepta Logica ad certos certarum rerum modos alligarunt, cum generalem attem seu organum vniuersale rerum omnium tractandarum essent nobis fabricaturi, & quia in S. literis vsus differendi apparet, & maximus & sanctissimus, hodieque Christiani de religionis articulis mirifice disceptent, cur non etiam Christianis Logicis exempla optimi logici ϛ λόγος Christi & spiritus sapientiæ ac veritatis religiose obseruare liceat? cur non præcepta artis differendi Christianus Logicus sobrie applicet ad res diuinas, & rerum spiritualium doctrinam, de cuius veritate minime omnium ambigit? cur non Logice, scienter & artificiose explicare liceat sacra, quæ tamen iubemur ὀρθῶς τέμνειν καὶ ἀναλύειν? cur non fontes errorū, quibus aduersarii cœlestis veritatis implicati sunt, indicare eosque obstruere Logice fas sit? Argumenta Logica omnia sunt generalia & rebus quibusuis applicabilia, non sunt ad certi generis res certarum vel rerum modos adstricta, sed earum definitiones modos includunt omnes, vt: causa est, cuius vi res est, cuius vi diuina vel humana, modo causandi supernaturali vel naturali. Sic subiectum est, cui quomodolibet aliquid adiungitur: nullus hic modus certus subsubiiciendi rationem determinat &c. Idem iudica de propos.
units.tr: The minor premise is likewise false. Although the first authors of logic noted the examples that came to hand in the practice of those who argue well, and mostly from human affairs, they did not bind the precepts of logic to fixed modes of fixed things. They meant to fashion a general instrument, an organon, for handling all things. And since in the Holy Scriptures the practice of disputing appears both very great and most holy, and since Christians today dispute wonderfully about the articles of religion, why should it not be lawful for Christian logicians to observe religiously the examples of the best logician, the Word [λόγος] of Christ, and of the spirit of wisdom and truth? Why should not the Christian logician soundly apply the precepts of the art of disputing to divine things, and to the teaching of spiritual things, whose truth he doubts in no way at all? Why should it not be lawful to explain the sacred matters logically, knowingly and skilfully, though we are commanded to cut and analyse them rightly [ὀρθῶς τέμνειν καὶ ἀναλύειν]? Why should it not be lawful to point out, by logic, the sources of error in which the adversaries of heavenly truth are entangled, and to block them? The logical arguments are all general and applicable to any things whatever. They are not bound to a certain kind of thing or to the modes of certain things, but their definitions include all modes. For example: a cause is that by whose power a thing is, whether by divine or human power, by a supernatural or natural mode of causing. Likewise the subject is that to which something is attached in some way; no fixed mode determines the manner of underlying. Judge the propositions by the same standard.

units.la: Obiectio VII.
units.tr: Objection VII.

units.la: Si Logica tam generale esset instrumentum, vt enunciationes & praedicationes de Deo & mysteriis eius ad terminos & notiones Logicas reduci possint, tum & sequentes etiam sic reducerentur.
units.tr: If logic were so general an instrument that statements and predications about God and his mysteries could be reduced to logical terms and notions, then the following could also be so reduced.

units.la: At non hoc. Ergo nec illud.
units.tr: But they cannot. Therefore neither can those.

units.la: Assumptio probatur inductione multorum exemplorum.
units.tr: The minor premise is proved by induction from many examples.

units.la: Exemplum I.
units.tr: Example I.

units.la: Filius Dei est genitus à patre: Item, Spiritus sanctus à patre & filio procedit: Hic propositio non est logica, nec argumenta sunt logica: Quia essent causa & effectum: At pater non est causa Filii: Omnis enim causa natura & duratione est prior. Pater non est prior filio. Deinde Filius & spiritus S. non possunt dici effecta: Hoc enim vetat religio, quia non sunt creati vel facti, vt voluit Arrius.
units.tr: The Son of God is begotten of the Father. Likewise, the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son. Here the proposition is not logical, nor are the arguments logical, because they would be cause and effect. But the Father is not the cause of the Son, for every cause is prior in nature and duration, and the Father is not prior to the Son. Further, the Son and the Holy Spirit cannot be called effects, for religion forbids this, since they are not created or made, as Arius maintained.

units.la: Responsio.
units.tr: Response.

units.la: Filius est à patre genitus: est axioma simplex proprium. Spiritus S. procedit à patre & filio: est axioma compositum, copulatum, affirmatum, verum. Sed quae argumenta dicis? respondeo, Haec & alia resolui possunt in argumenta, si non simpliciter, saltem castigatione aliqua adhibita, vel reductitie, vel analogice. Si dico: Filius Dei est secunda persona trinitatis ab aterno à patre genita, audio definitum & definitionem in axiomate simplici. Iam si dico, Filius Dei est à patre genitus.
units.tr: The Son is begotten of the Father is a simple, proper axiom. The Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son is a compound, conjoined, affirmative and true axiom. But what arguments do you mean? I answer that these and others can be resolved into arguments, if not simply, at least with some correction applied, either by reduction or by analogy. If I say, "The Son of God is the second person of the Trinity, begotten from the Father from eternity," I hear the defined and the definition in a simple axiom. Now if I say, "The Son of God is begotten of the Father,"

units.la: patres. genitus: hic relatam causam & effectum audio: Causa est cuius vi res est, vi Dei patris per aeternam generationem est filius : pater itaque est causa filii: & quidé efficiens.Id enim, à quo res est, est effici-ens: A patre est filius: pater itaque efficiens est filii: & quidem per æternam emanationem. Quod Arrius obiicit, causam priorem effecto est erroneum:Causa enim, qua causa effectum suum ne cogitatione antecedit quidé.Rerum & quidem non omnium, non notionum logicarum ista est antecessio. Deinde effectum non est idem quod creatum , sed latissime patens logice notat id, quod vi quacunque cuiuscunque causæ existit. Sic filius à patre per vim æternæ generationis est, sic spiritus S. à patre & filio est per vim æternæ promanationis seu processionis. Hæc vis & hic modus qui nos latet, e sacris literis affertur, eique Logicæ sobrie suæ artis notiones applicat citra ἀπιβείας periculum.Horres voces causam & effectum : spe-cta sensum in vocibus recte intellectis, respice & alios Orthodoxos patres ita loquutos.
units.tr: Fathers. "Begotten": here I hear a related cause and effect. "A cause is that by whose power a thing is": by the power of God the Father, through eternal generation, the Son is; the Father therefore is the cause of the Son, and indeed an efficient cause. For that from which a thing is, is an efficient cause. The Son is from the Father; the Father, therefore, is the efficient cause of the Son, and indeed through eternal emanation. As for Arius's objection that a cause must be prior to its effect, it is erroneous. A cause does not precede its effect even in thought, and this precedence belongs to things, not all things, and not to logical notions. Further, "effect" does not mean the same as "created." Logically it signifies very broadly whatever exists by any power of any cause. Thus the Son is from the Father by the power of eternal generation, and the Holy Spirit is from the Father and the Son by the power of eternal procession or proceeding. This power and this mode, which is hidden from us, is brought forward from the sacred writings, and logic applies its notions soundly, in its own art, without danger of impiety [ἀπιστίας]. You shudder at the words "cause" and "effect"; look at the sense of the words rightly understood, and consider that other orthodox Fathers also spoke this way.

units.la: Exemplum II.
units.tr: Example II.

units.la: Pater est Deus: Item Filius est Deus. Hic nulla sunt argumenta logica.
units.tr: God is the Father: likewise the Son is God. There are no logical arguments here.

units.la: Responsio.
units.tr: Answer.

units.la: Axiomata sunt simplicia, propria, affirmata. In quibus communius, superius, latius de subiecto patre & filio dicitur. Et licet Deus sit totum perfectionis quod ἀμέιςον est, habet tamen se instar totius logici ad personas quasi partes, vt Deus sit quasi Totum essentiale, personæ vero quasi partes essentiales, non quidem componentes, sed distinguentes.
units.tr: These are simple, proper, affirmative axioms, in which the subject, Father and Son, is predicated of something more common, higher and wider. And although God is the whole of perfection, which is indivisible [ἀμέριστον], he stands to the persons as a logical whole stands to its parts, so that God is like an essential whole, and the persons are like essential parts, not composing him but distinguishing him.

units.la: Exemplum III.
units.tr: Example III.

units.la: Deus est essentia seu spiritus: Quæ hic argumenta?
units.tr: God is essence or spirit: what arguments are there here?

units.la: Responsio.
units.tr: Answer.

units.la: Cum describitur Deus à Theologis: Deus est essentia spiritualis, &c. nulli non fatentur esse Dei descriptionem, quæ constat genere seu differentia. Ergo hic descriptum & descriptio est. Et quo modo ei conuenit descriptio & differentia, eodem modo conuenit ei etiam genus. At illa conueniunt Deo nostræ notionis respectu: illa vt Deum nō componunt, (compositio enim συνθεσις faciens logicas descriptionis partes, vt accidit rebus intellectis nullam etiam compositionem habentibus; sic etiam non est realis compositio) ita genus Deum non ad inferiora detrudit. Genus est totum suis partibus essentiale: Atqui spiritus & essentia sunt eiusmodi, quæ omnem suam essentiam communicant sibi subiectis speciebus, nempe essentiam spiritualem, incorpoream, intelligentem & volentem: Item reuera proprium esse habere, nec esse in alio vt habens esse in subiecto. Obiectiones videris resolutas in Problem. & Apologetica Gocl.
units.tr: When the theologians describe God, God is a spiritual essence, etc., nobody denies that this is a description of God, which consists of genus and difference. Therefore what is described here is also a description. And whatever description and difference apply to him, the genus applies to him in the same way. These terms apply to God as we conceive him: they do not compose God (for composition [σύνθεσις], which makes the logical parts of a description, is not a real composition, just as things understood which have no composition either). Likewise the genus does not drag God down to lower things. A genus is a whole that is essential in all its parts. But spirit and essence are of such a kind that they share their whole essence with the subject species: namely, spiritual, incorporeal, intelligent and willing essence. Likewise, in truth, to have being of itself, and not to be in another as a thing having being in a subject. You will see the objections resolved in the Problemata and the Apologetica of Goclenius.

units.la: Exemplum IV.
units.tr: Example IV.

units.la: Ex nihilo factus est mundus.
units.tr: The world was made out of nothing.

units.la: Responsio.
units.tr: Answer.

units.la: Quidam faciunt hic materiam & materia-tum: rum: non placet nihil dici materiam accuratius rimantibus huius dicti sensum, qui hic est: Cum prorsus nihil esset, fecit Deus mundum: Propositio haec est composita ex relatione temporis enuncians argumenta subiectum & adiunctum.
units.tr: Some here make a matter and a thing made from matter. It does not please those who examine the sense of this saying more carefully, that "nothing" should be called matter. Its sense here is: When there was absolutely nothing, God made the world. This proposition is compound, made up of a relation of time, and it states an argument with subject and attribute.

units.la: Exemplum V.
units.tr: Example V.

units.la: Filius Dei est homo: seu, Deus est homo.
units.tr: The Son of God is man, or, God is man.

units.la: Respondeo.
units.tr: Answer.

units.la: Melanchton sentit esse praedicationem Logicam inusitatam: Beurhusius non Logicam. Libauius ita distinguit: Cum dicitur in doctrina incarnationis filii Dei, Deus est homo, non sunt haec accensenda dissentaneis, cum in Christo consentiant essentialiter. Una enim persona constituitur ex τῷ λόγῳ, & humana natura; tanquam ex membris unius integri. Quod si extra Christum ea dicantur, manifestum est quod dissentiant, scilicet disparate. Alius putat partem παρὰ φύσιν praedicari de toto nempe de persona hoc sensu: Christus qui homo est, habet in se tanquam partem essentialem sua persona, aeternam verbi substantiam. Christus, qui Deus est, habet in se ut partem essentialem sua persona humanitatem assumptam.
units.tr: Melanchthon thinks this is an unusual logical predication; Beurhusius thinks it is not a logical one. Libavius distinguishes thus: when it is said in the doctrine of the incarnation of the Son of God that God is man, these are not to be counted as disagreeing terms, since in Christ they agree essentially. For one person is constituted out of the Word [τῷ λόγῳ] and human nature, as out of the members of one whole. But if these things are said outside Christ, it is plain that they disagree, namely as separate things. Another thinks that a part is predicated against nature [παρὰ φύσιν] of the whole, namely the person, in this sense: Christ, who is man, has within himself, as an essential part of his person, the eternal substance of the Word. Christ, who is God, has within himself, as an essential part of his person, the humanity he assumed.

units.la: Sic autem negat Christum Deum & hominem in hac enunciatione esse disparata: quae arctissime consentiunt non sunt disparata: Deus & homo arctissime in Christo consentiunt: qua una sunt hypostasis: etsi naturae ipsae in se consideratae disparata sint. Ergo Deus & homo in ChriChristo non sunt disparata. Quid igitur tu inquis? Da sensum & dabo argumenta. Si dederis hunc: Diuinitati τῷ λόγῳ personaliter est vnita humanitas assumpta, dabo subiectum cum suo adiuncto. Subiectum est λόγος, diuinitas assumens, sustinens & gestans. Adiunctum inseparabile ἐκ λόγου, & quidem substantiale assumptum sustentatum & gestatum est humanitas. Si dederis hunc: Christus est Deus & homo, dabo totum integrum & partes: Christus est totum compositum: partes huius personæ sunt diuinitas & humanitas: Sed hac de propositione postea. Potest & hic sensus esse: Christus est Deus respectu Deitatis, est homo respectu humanitatis. Item, Etsi sit homo, tamen est simul Deus: In his erunt diuersa, quia in Christo sola ratione dissentiunt.
units.tr: But he thus denies that Christ as God and man is disagreeing in this statement; terms that agree most closely are not disagreeing. God and man agree most closely in Christ, since they are one hypostasis, even though the natures themselves, considered in themselves, are disagreeing. Therefore God and man in Christ are not disagreeing. What then do you say? Give the sense and I will give the arguments. If you give this: the assumed humanity is personally united to the divinity of the Word, I will give the subject with its attribute. The subject is the Word, the divinity assuming, sustaining and bearing. The inseparable attribute, which proceeds from the Word, and indeed the substantial assumed humanity, is sustained and borne. If you give this: Christ is God and man, I will give the whole and its parts: Christ is a compound whole; the parts of this person are divinity and humanity. But of this proposition more later. This sense can also be: Christ is God with respect to the deity, he is man with respect to the humanity. Likewise, Although he is man, nevertheless he is at the same time God. In these there will be different things, because in Christ they differ only in concept.

units.la: At, inquis, cum Deitas & humanitas sint disparata, absurdum est τὸ Deus & homo fieri non disparata?
units.tr: But, you say, since deity and humanity are disagreeing, is it absurd that "God" and "man" should not be disagreeing?

units.la: Respondeo. Minime hoc absurdum est. Distinguendum enim est inter abstractum seu denominans & concretum seu denominatum, inter ipsam formam & id, quod habet formam, inter rei essentiam, & inde deductam denominationem. Flauedo & dulcedo etiam in melle inter se consideratæ disparatæ qualitates sunt: at inde exsistunt diuersa dulce & flauum esse, quæ cum melle consentiunt, vt duo adiuncta cum vno subiecto. Sic etiam in vnione sunt & manent disparata Deitas humanitas, sed homine & Deum esse in Christo sunt diversa; transeuntia in consentanea, cum personam Christi constituant, ut partes totum.
units.tr: I answer: by no means is this absurd. For one must distinguish between the abstract or denominating term and the concrete or denominated term, between the form itself and that which has the form, between the essence of a thing and the denomination derived from it. Yellowness and sweetness, considered in themselves in honey, are disagreeing qualities; yet from them there arise the different things, to be sweet and to be yellow, which agree with the honey, as two attributes with one subject. So also in the union the deity and the humanity are and remain disagreeing; but to be God and to be man in Christ are different things, which pass over into agreeing things when they constitute the person of Christ, as parts constitute a whole.

units.la: Neque vero absurdum est & infrequens contraria sublata oppositionis identitate transire ad castra diversorum. Omnis enim diversitas tollit oppositionem, qua sublata migrant ad diversa & consentanea.
units.tr: Nor is it absurd or unusual that, once the identity of opposition is removed, contraries pass over into the camp of the different. For every difference removes opposition, and when that is removed they migrate to different and agreeing things.

units.la: Obiicis: Praeternaturalis est modus unionis personalis naturarum duarum in Christo. Ergo hoc axioma, filius Dei est homo, non est logicum, sed inusitatum.
units.tr: You object: The mode of the personal union of the two natures in Christ is beyond nature. Therefore this axiom, the Son of God is man, is not logical but unusual.

units.la: Respondeo. Negamus consequentiam: Quia a rerum inusitato modo non sequitur inusitata & irregularis ratio disponendi. Mysticus & arcanus est modus unionis nostri seu Ecclesiae cum Christo. Ergo modus praedicandi inusitatus est. Nos membra sumus corporis eius, ex carne eius, & ex ossibus eius: Praeternaturaliter ferrum natavit: Christus praeternaturaliter ieiunavit quadraginta dies: ambulavit in superficie maris. Ergo modus praedicandi hic est φύσιν & irregularis. Hyperphysico modo edo carnem Domini: Ergo enunciatio inusitata est ad nullum modum logicarum praedicationum congruens, Ego edo carnem Domini. Christi persona inexplicabiliter, singulariter & hyperphysice constat ex λόγῳ & natura humana: Ergo haec, Christi persona constat ex λόγῳ & humana natura, non habet rationem vitatae huius essentialis, quae est partium de toto, distributionis de distribu-to, Homo constat ex anima & corpore.
units.tr: I answer: we deny the consequence, because an unusual and irregular manner of arranging a statement does not follow from an unusual manner of the thing itself. The mode of the union of us, that is, of the Church, with Christ is mystical and secret. Therefore the mode of predicating is unusual. We are members of his body, of his flesh and of his bones. Supernaturally iron floated; Christ fasted supernaturally forty days; he walked on the surface of the sea. Therefore the mode of predicating here is against nature [παρὰ φύσιν] and irregular. In a supernatural way I eat the flesh of the Lord. Therefore the statement I eat the flesh of the Lord is unusual and fits no mode of logical predication. The person of Christ consists inexplicably, singularly and hyperphysically of the Word and human nature. Therefore this, that the person of Christ consists of the Word and human nature, does not have the character of the familiar essential distribution of parts of a whole, of the distributive of the distributed: Man consists of soul and body.

units.la: Regeris: Res ipsa est physice inusitata. Ergo & propositio rei est logice inusitata.
units.tr: You reply: the thing itself is physically unusual. Therefore the proposition about the thing is also logically unusual.

units.la: Respondeo. Negatur consequentia: Sicut enim non sequitur, Res monstrosa est & prodigiosa. Ergo Propositio est monstrosa: sic non sequitur: Res est inusitata: Ergo Propositio est inusitata. Huius foetus saltus in utero materno est inusitatus: Conuersio Pauli Apostoli est inusitata & extraordinaria. Ergo propositiones ipsae sunt extraordinariae, peregrinae & inusitatae ac irregulares.
units.tr: I answer: the consequence is denied. For just as it does not follow that a monstrous and prodigious thing is monstrous, therefore the proposition is monstrous, so it does not follow that the thing is unusual, therefore the proposition is unusual. The leap of this foetus in its mother's womb is unusual. The conversion of the Apostle Paul is unusual and extraordinary. Therefore the propositions themselves are extraordinary, foreign, unusual and irregular.

units.la: Quaestio: An Christo Σταυρώσιμω logice recte tribuantur partes?
units.tr: Question: Whether logical parts are rightly attributed to Christ Crucified [Σταυρώσιμω]?

units.la: Negantis partis sententia nititur his rationibus. 1. Repugnat perfectioni diuinae, ut Deus fiat alicuius rei pars, ut veniat in compositionem alicuius entis per se. 2. Simplicissima diuinitas cum alio componi nequit. 3. Augustinus contra Maximum ait: Una est persona substantia gemina Christus, quia Deus & homo est, neque tamen Deus vel homo pars huius personae dici valet. 4. Gabriel Biel inquit: Humana natura non est pars Christi, quia non est pars verbi: Nec Deitas est pars Christi, quia est eadem realiter verbo. Et: Nulla partium de toto separatim praedicatur, ut non dicitur, homo est anima. At filius Dei praedicatur de Christo. Ergo filius Dei pars Christi dicendus non est. 5. Si Christus esset ex Deo & homine mine compositus, neque Deus esset, neque homo, sed tantum Christus, sicut homo cum componitur ex carne & anima, neque anima est neque caro, sed homo: Non igitur dicendum, Christum componi ex Deo & homine.
units.tr: The opinion of those who deny that there are parts rests on these reasons. (1) It is repugnant to the divine perfection that God should become a part of something, entering into composition with an entity that is complete in itself. (2) The most simple deity cannot be composed with anything else. (3) Augustine, against Maximus, says: Christ is one person of twofold substance, because he is God and man, yet neither God nor man can be called a part of this person. (4) Gabriel Biel says: The human nature is not a part of Christ, because it is not a part of the Word; nor is the Deity a part of Christ, because it is really the same as the Word. And: No part is predicated separately of the whole, for one does not say "man is soul." But the Son of God is predicated of Christ. Therefore the Son of God is not to be called a part of Christ. (5) If Christ were composed of God and man, he would be neither God nor man, but only Christ, just as when man is composed of soul and flesh, he is neither soul nor flesh, but man. Therefore it should not be said that Christ is composed of God and man.

units.la: Pars Affirmans affert patres Græcos & Latinos, itemque Concilia, in quibus cum de vnione humanæ naturæ in Christo agitur, nihil aliud pene auditur, quam Christum Dominum cum ante incarnationem persona esset simplicissima, cœpisse per eam esse personam compositam ex verbo diuino & natura humana, idque propria & vera non metaphorica compositione, quod ipsum è Scholæ Doctoribus defendit Thomas Aquinas.
units.tr: Those who affirm the parts appeal to the Greek and Latin Fathers, and likewise to the Councils. In these, when the union of the human nature in Christ is discussed, one hears almost nothing else than that the Lord Christ, whose person was most simple before the incarnation, began through it to be a composite person, made up of the divine Word and human nature, and that this is a real and true composition, not a metaphorical one. Thomas Aquinas defends this among the teachers of the School.

units.la: Hanc litem Rudolphus Goclenius tollit distinctione inter partes Physicas & Logicas. Venit quidem Filius Dei in compositionem non vnius per se naturæ, sed vnius per se subsistentis. Verum Filius Dei & assumpta natura humana rationem partium Physicarum non habent, quæ important imperfectionem, ita vt compositum sit eis perfectius.
units.tr: Rudolph Goclenius settles this dispute by distinguishing physical parts from logical parts. The Son of God indeed enters into a composition, not of one nature existing by itself, but of one subsistent existing by itself. But the Son of God and the assumed human nature do not have the character of physical parts, which imply imperfection, such that the composite would be more perfect for them.

units.la: Logicæ igitur partes sunt verbum & humanitas, ex quibus totum Christus constituitur, qui proprie neque tantum est verbum neque humana natura tantum, sed ἀνθρωπος persona, in qua humanitas cum λόγῳ hypostatice est coniuncta.
units.tr: The logical parts, then, are the Word and the humanity, from which the whole Christ is constituted. Christ properly is neither only the Word nor only the human nature, but the person [ἄνθρωπος], in whom the humanity is hypostatically joined with the Word [λόγῳ].

units.la: Logicas hic partes dico, quia persona Christi & sti & persona verbi ratione tantum non re differunt (cum Christus sit persona verbi habens humanam carnem.) Quo respexerunt Græci cum λόγον σύνδετον dicunt, itaque hoc commode dextreque accipiendum.
units.tr: I call these parts logical here, because the person of Christ and the person of the Word differ only in reason, not in reality, since Christ is the person of the Word having human flesh. The Greeks had this in view when they speak of the "composite Word" [λόγον σύνδετον], and so this should be understood in a fitting and proper sense.

units.la: Neque vero etiam repugnabo tibi admodum, si χεῖρας partes vocare velis, & dicere humanitatem quasi partem esse personæ Christi, & vnionem duarum naturarum per totius ex duabus diuersæ naturæ partibus constitutionem, tanquam proportionale quiddam declarari, cum Catholica pie confiteatur Ecclesia, quod sicut anima rationalis & caro vnus est homo: Ita Deus & homo vnus sit Christus, & ita verbum & caro aliquo modo respondeant, seu analoga sint Physicis vel logicis partibus componentibus.
units.tr: Nor indeed will I strongly oppose you if you wish to call them parts [χεῖρας], and to say that the humanity is, as it were, a part of the person of Christ, and that the union of the two natures is explained by a certain proportional analogy, the whole being constituted from parts of two different natures. For the Catholic Church piously confesses that just as the rational soul and flesh are one man, so God and man are one Christ. Thus the Word and the flesh correspond in some way, or are analogous to the physical or logical component parts.

units.la: Atque hoc dicere non est Logicam peruertere, sed eam ad veritatis normam reducere, vt Gabrielis vtar verbis, & quoquo modo ad sacra accommodare, vt intellectio adiuuetur.
units.tr: To say this is not to pervert logic, but to bring it back to the standard of truth, to use Gabriel's words, and in some way to adapt it to sacred things, so that understanding may be helped.

units.la: ʼΑναβασις ad axioma, Λόγος est Deus.
units.tr: Ascent [ἀνάβασις] to the axiom: The Word [Λόγος] is God.

units.la: In axiomate, λόγος est Deus, compositio est summe inter se consentaneorum & essentialium: Deus est notio essentiæ communis, latius patens. Λόγος est notio personæ, propria, angustior. Hinc talis fit apodixis: Quod habet analogiam cum aliqua prædicatione, idrecte adeam reducitur. Axioma hoc, λόγος yo͏ᵋille est Deus, habet analogiam cum propria & regulari praedicatione: estque simile huic: Cato est homo: Sicut enim hic species de indiuiduo: sic illic communicabile de incommunicabili, commune essentiale de proprio seu indiuidua substantia praedicatur. Deinde in praedicatione regulari consentaneum de consentaneo affirmatur, vel dissentaneum de dissentaneo negatur. Hic, λόγος ille est Deus, simpliciter consentaneum de consentaneo, vt essentiale de substantiali seu hypostatico affirmatur. Tò Deus enim habet conditionem termini communis, qui pluribus vt tribus hypostasibus conuenit, & Deus est quidditas (sic enim loqui consueuerunt, qui rerum quam verborum studiosiores sunt) & λόγος, seu filii Dei. Ergo hic, λόγος ille est Deus, habet ἀναλογίαν, συγγένειαν & conuenientiam cum regulari attributione.
units.tr: In the axiom "The Word is God," the composition is of things that are highly consonant with one another and essential. God is the notion of the common essence, and has a wider reach. The Word [λόγος] is the notion of the proper person, and is narrower. Hence such a demonstration arises: What has analogy with some predication is rightly reduced to it. This axiom, "that Word is God," has analogy with a proper and regular predication, and is like this: "Cato is a man": For as here the species is predicated of the individual, so there the communicable is predicated of the incommunicable, the common essential of the proper or individual substance. Then, in a regular predication, the consonant is affirmed of the consonant, or the dissonant is denied of the dissonant. Here, "that Word is God," the consonant is simply affirmed of the consonant, as the essential is affirmed of the substantial or hypostatic. For "God" has the condition of a common term, which belongs to several, as to three hypostases, and God is the quiddity (for so they are accustomed to speak, who are more zealous about things than about words), and so is the Word, or the Son of God. Therefore "here, that Word [λόγος] is God, has analogy [ἀναλογίαν], kinship [συγγένειαν] and agreement with regular attribution."

units.la: Quaeritur, Axioma hoc: Haec virgo est mater, quae argumenta disponat?
units.tr: Question: What arguments does this axiom set out: "This virgin is a mother"?

units.la: Respon. Diuersa. Quia quae sola ratione & respectu dissentiunt sunt diuersa. Virgo & mater in Maria dissentiunt solo respectu incidente: Virgo est naturaliter, sed mater supernaturaliter & speciali miraculo: Virgo est, qua virum non cognouit & incorrupta mansit: mater, qua peperit, quod ex sua ipsius substantia concepit.
units.tr: Answer: different ones. For things that differ only by reason and by respect are different. Virgin and mother in Mary differ only by an incidental respect: she is a virgin naturally, but a mother supernaturally and by a special miracle. She is a virgin in that she did not know a man and remained uncorrupted; a mother in that she bore what she had conceived from her own substance.

units.la: Quæst. Aqua vinum factum est: axioma mi-raculi quanam habet argumenta?
units.tr: Question: Water was made wine: what arguments does this axiom of a miracle have?

units.la: Respon. Materiam & materiatum. Aqua est materia supernaturalis & miraculosæ transmutationis: vinum ipsum materiatum miraculosum.
units.tr: Answer: matter and the thing made from matter. Water is the matter of the supernatural and miraculous transmutation; the wine itself is the miraculous thing made from it.

units.la: Quæst. Qua in hoc: Mortui viuent?
units.tr: Question: What arguments in this: "The dead live"?

units.la: Respon. Aliis sunt subiectum & adiuncta: nobis vero diuersa ex diuerso temporis respectu: sunt quidem contraria priuantia mortuum esse & viuere: sed perit hic identitas oppositionis, & diuersitas temporis præteriti & futuri incidit. Assumunt itaque diuersorum naturam. Idem iudicabis de hoc: Idem numero penitus corruptum reparabitur, &c.
units.tr: Answer: for other things they are subject and adjuncts, but for us they are different because of a different respect of time. "Being dead" and "living" are indeed contrary privatives, but the identity of the opposition is lost here, and the difference between past and future time intervenes. They therefore take on the nature of different things. You will judge the same of this: "The same in number, wholly corrupted, will be repaired," etc.

units.la: Quæst. Qua in hoc axiomate argumenta: Euangelium est potentia Dei ad salutem omni credenti?
units.tr: Question: What arguments lie in this axiom: The Gospel is the power of God unto salvation to everyone who believes?

units.la: Respon. definitum & definitio, cuius genus est metonymicum pro organo & medio potentiæ diuinæ. Sicut & in hoc Pauli, Baptismus est lauacrum regenerationis: est breuis quædam descriptio. Sicut & in isto: Panis cœna frac-tus est communio corporis Christi, vbi panis fractus est definitum, communio corporis Christi, id est, sacramentum seu organum communionis corporis Christi est definitio.
units.tr: Answer: The definiendum and the definition, whose genus is used metonymically for the instrument and means of the divine power. So also in this saying of Paul: "Baptism is the washing of regeneration"; it is a brief description. So also in this: "The bread which we break in the Lord's Supper is the communion of the body of Christ," where "the bread which we break" is the definiendum, and "the communion of the body of Christ," that is, the sacrament or instrument of communion with the body of Christ, is the definition.

units.la: Quæst. Sed hic: Hoc est corpus meum, quæ putas argumenta Logica?
units.tr: Question: But here, "This is my body": what logical arguments do you think there are?

units.la: Respon. dissident interpretes. Da sensum & dabo argumenta. Alius hanc mentem affert : Hic panis est sacramentum seu signum repræsentans, offerens & exhibens corpus Christi pro nobis traditum. Seu, est communio, hoc est, sacramentum & sanctum organum communionis corporis Christi pro nobis fracti. Hæc interpretatio disponit definitum cum definitione, quæ explicat: quid sit in visu sacro panis. Simplicius si prima argumenta quæris, panis ut signum est adiunctum, corpus Christi ut signatum est subiectum. Alius ita exponit: In & cum pane est corpus Christi: hic sunt itidem subiectum, & adiunctū, quicunq; etiam modus afferatur: adiunctum enim suo subiecto logice quomodo libet adiungitur. Alius per hoc intelligit transmutatum Christi corpus, ut sit identica loquutio, qua idem de seipso dicitur, eruntque argumenta aut paria, aut nomina, aut nulla. Quidam ita interpretatur, ut hoc duplicem habeat respectum, principaliter quidem notet corpus, ut idem sit, corpus hoc est corpus meum: hoc respectu identica est prædicatio: minus vero principaliter designet panem, hoc sensu: panis est corpus Christi: Argumenta hic sunt subiectum & adiunctum.
units.tr: Answer: The interpreters disagree. Give me the sense and I will give you the arguments. One interpreter brings out this meaning: "Here the bread is a sacrament, or a sign representing, offering and exhibiting the body of Christ delivered up for us." Or: "It is the communion, that is, the sacrament and holy instrument of communion with the body of Christ broken for us." This interpretation sets the definiendum alongside the definition, which explains what the bread is in the sacred action. More simply, if you ask for the primary arguments: the bread, as sign, is the adjunct, and the body of Christ, as the thing signified, is the subject. Another explains it thus: "In and with the bread is the body of Christ"; here too there are subject and adjunct, whatever mode is alleged, for the adjunct is logically joined to its subject in whatever way. Another understands by this "the body of Christ transmuted," so that the statement is an identical one, in which the same thing is said of itself, and the arguments will be either equal, or nouns, or none. Someone else interprets it so that it has a twofold reference: it principally denotes the body, so that the sense is "this body is my body," and in this respect the predication is identical; but it less principally designates the bread, in this sense: "the bread is the body of Christ." Here the arguments are subject and adjunct.

units.la: Tales sunt vulgi Phrases : hoc est vinum Rhenanum, id est, in hoc dolio est vinum Rhenanum. Hic sunt mille aurei: id est, in hoc marsupio sunt mille aurei. Hoc est triticum, id est, in hoc sacco est triticum, &c. Alii hic synecdochen faciunt, qua de toto complexo plexo dicitur principalis eius pars: hi faciunt igitur totum & parte. Sed tandem manum de hac tabella, ne quem malum offendat.
units.tr: Such are the common phrases: "This is Rhenish wine," that is, in this cask there is Rhenish wine; "Here are a thousand gold coins," that is, in this purse there are a thousand gold coins; "This is wheat," that is, in this sack there is wheat, and so on. Others here make it a synecdoche, in which the principal part is predicated of the whole that includes it; these therefore make the whole and the part. But I will at last take my hand from this table, lest I offend anyone.

units.la: VENTILATIO QVÆstionis,
units.tr: THE DISCUSSION OF THE QUESTION,

units.la: An Logica Theologo sit utilis ac necessaria, in rerum Theologicarum tractatione.
units.tr: Whether logic is useful and necessary for the theologian in the treatment of theological matters.

units.la: QVidam peruersa, de Logica, opinione imbuti sunt, ex eo, quod propter sophisticum abusum, vel à pia antiquitate alicubi eam improbari audiant, vel hodie etiam conuitium ei fieri ab iis, quos Logica minus propitios habet, quique eam Theologis indignam, & Religioni Christianæ perniciosam proclamant.
units.tr: Some people are steeped in a perverse opinion about logic, because they hear that it is condemned in some places on account of its sophistical abuse, or from pious antiquity, or because today those who are not well disposed towards logic revile it, proclaiming it unworthy of theologians and harmful to the Christian religion.

units.la: 2. Fert igitur animus, propitio Logici lumi-nis autore, & veritatis Sole τῷ λόγῳ, veræ Logicæ scientiam ac sobriam pie differendi facultatem Theologo in sua professione non esse indignam, sed utilem ei & pernecessariam, ostendere.
units.tr: 2. Therefore, with the favour of the author of the logical light, and of the Sun of truth, ho logos [τῷ λόγῳ], my intention is to show that the knowledge of true logic and the sober ability to argue piously is not unworthy of the theologian in his profession, but useful and very necessary to him.

units.la: 3. Cuicunque enim ratione & differendi facultate, sibi à Deo concessa, est bene vtendum, eidem certe quædam prodest & necessaria est Logices cognitio: quemadmodum, cui bene loquendum & dicendum est, eum præceptis Grammaticæs & Rhetorices purum & ornatum tum sermonem informantibus instrui convenit.
units.tr: 3. For whoever must make good use of the reason and the faculty of disputation granted him by God certainly benefits from and needs some knowledge of logic, just as one who must speak and express himself well ought to be instructed in the precepts of grammar and rhetoric, which shape speech to be pure and ornate.

units.la: 4. Logica enim suis consiliis & praeceptis informat & instituit rationem humanam, naturalemque differendi facultatem, ut ea bene in omnibus uti possimus.
units.tr: 4. For logic shapes and trains human reason and our natural faculty of arguing by its counsels and precepts, so that we may use it well in all things.

units.la: 5. Quaedam, dico, cognitio: sive ea sit a naturae felicioris aptitudine, sive ab artis institutione, sive etiam ab illustrantis Spiritus gratia.
units.tr: 5. I say some knowledge, whether it comes from the more fortunate aptitude of nature, from the instruction of an art, or also from the grace of the illuminating Spirit.

units.la: 6. Ars autem certior dicitur dux quam Natura: utramque si corrigit & perficit Ϛ λόγος coelestis Spiritus, perfectior & sanior est Logica Logici animalis scientia.
units.tr: 6. Moreover, art is said to be a surer guide than nature. If the heavenly Word and Spirit corrects and perfects both, then logic, the science of the rational creature [logos, ὁ λόγος], is more perfect and sounder than the mere science of the natural animal.

units.la: 7. Iam vero Theologo esse ratione & differendi facultate sibi diuinitus donata, bene etiam in rerum diuinarum tractatione utendum qui negat, eum vult aut ἄλογον, & omni ratione carentem, aut esse Sophistam, ratione sua male abutentem.
units.tr: 7. Now, whoever denies that the theologian must also make good use, in the treatment of divine things, of the reason and faculty of argument divinely given to him, wants him to be either irrational [ἄλογον], lacking all reason, or a sophist, who misuses his reason.

units.la: 8. Ratione, inquam, debet uti, quae est animae insita facultas, qua res intelligibiles intelligimus, cognoscimus & diiudicamus: quamque ideo etiam Deus homini dedit, ut doctrina diuina possit ab eo percipi, intelligi & cognosci.
units.tr: 8. I say he must use reason, the faculty implanted in the soul by which we understand, know and judge intelligible things, and which God therefore gave to man so that divine doctrine could be perceived, understood and known by him.

units.la: 9. Rationem insuper & intellectum requirit ipsa fides, cum notitiam & intelligentiam rerum credendarum in mente postulat: neque profecto mens nostra intelligit res vlla alia facultate, quam rationis & intellectus.
units.tr: 9. Moreover, faith itself requires reason and understanding, since it demands knowledge and comprehension of the things to be believed in the mind; and our mind certainly understands nothing by any faculty other than that of reason and understanding.

units.la: 10. Intellectum autem & rationem, quae per peccatum deprauata & obscurata est, spi-ritus & lucis diuinæ radiis collustratam ex-optamus.
units.tr: 10. We therefore desire that the understanding and reason, which have been corrupted and darkened by sin, be illuminated by the rays of the divine Spirit and light.

units.la: 11. Ideo bene vti decet ratione, hoc est, Ve-ritati Dei & Rei, Logicisque regulis congru-enter, pie, inquam, & religiose, sapienter & prudenter de rebus diuinis differendum est.
units.tr: 11. Hence it is fitting to use reason well, that is, in agreement with the truth of God and of the matter, and with the rules of logic: divine things must be argued about piously and religiously, wisely and prudently.

units.la: 12. Maiestasque Theologiæ, est Logicæ, v-bi alicubi deficit, & præcepta habet rebus creatis tantum competentia complementum & ἐπανόρθωμα quoddam.
units.tr: 12. The dignity of theology is that where logic fails at some point, theology supplies a completion and a certain correction, since logic has precepts suited only to created things.

units.la: 13. Lumen etiam cœlestis gratiæ & Spiritus, Logicum naturæ lumen perficit non perimit, adolet non abolet, purius & illustrius reddit non extinguit.
units.tr: 13. The light of heavenly grace and Spirit also perfects the natural light of logic and does not destroy it; it nourishes it and does not abolish it; it makes it purer and clearer and does not extinguish it.

units.la: 14. Ratio vero carnalis, non illustrata, spiri-tualia carnaliter iudicans, contra Dei & Rei veritatem sophistice disserens, à verbi diuini tractatione est excludenda.
units.tr: 14. But carnal reason, unilluminated, which judges spiritual things carnally and argues sophistically against the truth of God and of the matter, must be excluded from the treatment of the divine Word.

units.la: 15. Deinde qui debet esse διδακτικὸς & ἱκανὸς διδάξαι τὰς ἑτέρας, docendique obire munus, eum par est docendi præceptis, naturæ δυνάμεις formantibus & firmantibus, esse instructum.
units.tr: 15. Furthermore, whoever ought to be didaktikos and hikanos didaxai tas heterous [διδακτικὸς & ἱκανὸς διδάξαι τὰς ἑτέρας], able to teach others and to discharge the office of teaching, must rightly be instructed in the precepts of teaching, which shape and strengthen the powers [δυνάμεις] of nature.

units.la: 16. Etiamsi enim Ratio docendi à natura (vt ait Philippus pag. 3. Dial.) sumat initium: tamen ars monstrat metas, ne aberret natura sine arte in ratiocinando.
units.tr: 16. For although the method of teaching takes its beginning from nature (as Philip says, p. 3 of the Dialogue), art nevertheless shows the limits, lest nature without art go astray in reasoning.

units.la: 17. Atqui Episcopum & Theologum Paulus in 1. Epist. ad Timotheum cap. 3. vult esse διδακτικὸν & ad docendum aptum, & Christus iubet ministros suos docere. Marc. vlt.
units.tr: 17. But Paul, in 1 Timothy 3, wants the bishop and the theologian to be didaktikon [διδακτικὸν] and apt to teach, and Christ commands his ministers to teach (Mark, last chapter).

units.la: 18. Ergo Episcopum & Doctorem verbi di-uini, uini, docendi praeceptis imbutum, ad docen-di munus accedere par est.
units.tr: 18. Therefore the bishop and the teacher of the divine Word, steeped in the precepts of teaching, ought rightly to approach the office of teaching.

units.la: 19. Iam vero Dialectica Melanchtoni pag. 1. est ars seu via recte ordine & perspicue docendi. Eidem pag. 3. non nascuntur res in Dialectica, sed in ea traditur modus & forma docendi: & Ramus in Scholis Metaph. Logica est ars differendi, ideoque docendi.
units.tr: 19. Now, Melanchthon's Dialectic, p. 1, is the art or way of teaching rightly, in order and clearly. On the same page 3 he says that things are not born in dialectic, but in it is handed down the method and form of teaching; and Ramus, in the Scholae Metaphysicae, says that logic is the art of arguing, and therefore of teaching.

units.la: 20. Et quidem Melanchtoni eidem versatur Dialectica circa omnes materias seu quaestiones, de quibus docendi sunt homines pag. 2. & 1. de quocunque ait negotio fuerit instituta explicatio, sumitur a Dialectica modus docendi, definiendi, diuidendi, coagmentandi vera argumenta, & refutandi falsa, pagina 3.
units.tr: 20. Indeed, according to the same Melanchthon, dialectic is concerned with all the subjects or questions about which men are to be taught (p. 2), and (p. 1) whatever explanation is set out concerning any business, the method of teaching, of defining, dividing, joining true arguments together and refuting false ones is taken from dialectic (p. 3).

units.la: 21. Docendi autem sunt homines de verbo Dei, & Theologus instituit explicationem de negocio religionis. Vnde & idem ait Mel. pag. 4. Si concionatori dicendum erit de poenitentia, exponet & ipse definitiones, partes, causas, effectus, &c.
units.tr: 21. But men must be taught about the Word of God, and the theologian sets out the explanation of the business of religion. Hence the same Melanchthon says (p. 4): If the preacher must speak about repentance, he will himself set out the definitions, parts, causes, effects, and so on.

units.la: 22. Recte igitur Poëta, quisquis fuerit: Vt bene doctrinam tradas, Dialectica disce, Ignari Logices, nunc, quae indiuulsa cohaerent, Diuellunt: nunc, quae male diuulsere minute Concidunt: alibi, quae fas distinguere, in vnum Conglomerat chaos, & passim coelo infera miscet: Aut res confundunt, malus vt popa iura culina.
units.tr: 22. Rightly, therefore, the poet, whoever he was, said: To teach doctrine well, learn dialectic. Ignorant of logic, now they tear apart what hangs together inseparably; now they cut into tiny pieces what they have badly torn apart; elsewhere they heap into one chaos what it is right to distinguish, and everywhere they mix heaven with the underworld; or they confuse matters, as a bad cook spoils the broth.

units.la: 23. Praeterea cuicunque vsus Logicae analyticus est vtilis & necessarius, eum Logicarum praecepræceptionum scientia tinctum esse necesse est.
units.tr: 23. Moreover, whoever needs the analytic use of logic, which is useful and necessary, must necessarily be imbued with the science of the precepts of logic.

units.la: 24. In explicando autem, retexendo recteque secando Dei verbo & sermone veritatis, opus est Theologo vsu Logices analytico.
units.tr: 24. Now, in explaining, unfolding and rightly dividing the Word of God and the discourse of truth, the theologian needs the analytic use of logic.

units.la: 25. Logica enim Analysis, docête P. Ramo, præcipit hæc tria omni Analytico: cerne quæstionem: aperi inuentionem: demonstra iudicium: hoc est, ostendendum est thema, de quo disseritur: aperienda sunt argumenta, quibus de themate disseritur, monstranda est dispositio, per quam ex argumentis de proposito themate disseritur.
units.tr: 25. For logical analysis, as Master Ramus teaches, prescribes these three things to every analyst: look at the question; open up the invention; demonstrate the judgement. That is, the theme under discussion must be shown; the arguments by which the theme is discussed must be laid open; and the arrangement by which, from the arguments, the theme is discussed must be shown.

units.la: 26. Disserit enim Logicus de themate, ex argumentis, per dispositionem.
units.tr: 26. For the logician argues about the theme, from the arguments, by means of the arrangement.

units.la: 27. Præcipit igitur & Theologo analytico seu verbum Dei explicanti, secanti & retexenti, ut thema, quod explicatur, ostendat, ut sciat auditor, quid in contextu disseratur & proponatur.
units.tr: 27. Therefore the same art also prescribes to the theologian who analyses, unfolds and expounds the Word of God that he show the theme being explained, so that the hearer knows what is being argued and set forth in the context.

units.la: 28. Deinde, ut argumenta, quibus propositum in verbo Dei thema, vel declaratur vel probatur, ordine enucleet, & propositæ quæstioni dextre applicet, ut sciat auditor, quibus rebus propositum in verbo Dei thema explicetur.
