units.tr: 28. Next, that he unfold in order the arguments by which the theme proposed in the Word of God is either explained or proved, and apply them skilfully to the question put, so that the hearer knows by what means the theme proposed in the Word of God is explained.

units.la: 29. Denique ut ex partibus propositæ in verbo Dei tractationis demonstret dispositionem & ordinem, ut sciat auditor quo modo & ordine explicetur propositum per enucleatas rationes.
units.tr: 29. Finally, that he demonstrate from the parts of the treatment proposed in the Word of God its arrangement and order, so that the hearer knows in what manner and order the proposed theme is explained through the unfolded reasons.

units.la: 30. Logicæ igitur Analyseos adeoq; Logicarum rum præceptionum scientia Theologo est vti-lis & necessaria.
units.tr: 30. Therefore the analysis of logic, and thus the science of the precepts of logic, is useful and necessary to the theologian.

units.la: 31. Verum hic disputatur: An Theologica possint tractari logice. Negat non nemo.
units.tr: 31. But here it is disputed whether theological matters can be treated logically. Some people deny it.

units.la: 32. Nos in Theologicis tractationib.vsum Logicæ agnoscimus & amplectimur, sed casl-tum, sobrium & religiosum.
units.tr: 32. In theological treatments we acknowledge and embrace the use of logic, but one that is chaste, sober and religious.

units.la: 33. Diuina ita tractanda logice censemus; non vt diuina ad Logicæ & rationis regulam, seu ad logisimos hominum cogantur, sed vt rationis & Logicæ regula ad diuina dirigatur & adæquetur.
units.tr: 33. We judge that divine things should be treated logically in such a way that divine things are not forced under the rule of logic and reason, or under the judgements of men, but that the rule of reason and logic is directed and adapted to divine things.

units.la: 34. Atque sic termini logici possunt sobrie accommodari diuinis, & theologica enunciata in argumenta resolui logica, si non simpliciter, saltem cum castigatione aliqua adhibita: si non directe, saltem reductitie, si non exquisite saltem analogice,
units.tr: 34. And so logical terms can soberly be applied to divine things, and theological statements can be resolved into logical arguments: if not simply, at least with some qualification applied; if not directly, at least by reduction; if not exactly, at least by analogy.

units.la: 35. Neque enim præcepta Logica, cum generalia esse debeant, terminis certorum modorum certis rebus propriorum constringuntur; neque necesse est, vt modus & ratio communis creaturarum, ab argumenti loco excludat notiones rerum diuinarum.
units.tr: 35. For logical precepts, since they must be general, are not confined to the terms of certain modes proper to certain things; nor is it necessary that the common mode and reasoning of creatures exclude from the place of argument the notions of divine things.

units.la: 36. De diuinis loquimur & dicimus, secundum eosdem eiusdem Grammaticæs & Rhetorices regulas, & fieri potest, vt res sublimes & cœlestes eodem modo loquendi & dicendi exponantur, quo res humiles & terrenæ. Proinde etiam fieri potest, vt eodem modo differendi arguantur & disponantur.
units.tr: 36. We speak and say of divine things according to the same rules of grammar and rhetoric, and it can happen that sublime and heavenly things are set forth in the same manner of speaking and saying as lowly and earthly things. Accordingly, it can also happen that they are argued and arranged in the same manner of arguing.

units.la: 37. Et multa Physice inusitata possunt Grammatice matice vsitatis verbis & Syntaxi vsitata pro-nunciari: possunt item logice vsitato genere enunciationis disponi.
units.tr: 37. Many things that are unusual in natural philosophy can also be expressed in ordinary grammar, with common words and ordinary syntax. Likewise they can be arranged logically in the usual manner of statement.

units.la: 38. Neque discrimen modi necesse est tollere similitudinem & identitatem rei ipsius, & inducere diuersum modum disponendi & enunciandi.
units.tr: 38. A difference of manner need not remove the likeness and identity of the thing itself, nor require a different way of arranging and stating it.

units.la: 39. In Mysteriis interim diuinis Dialectica fasces submittat, & sese discipulam ad summi Magistri, qui est sapientia Patris, pedes abiiciat.
units.tr: 39. In the divine mysteries, however, let dialectic lower its rods of office and cast itself down as a pupil at the feet of the supreme Teacher, who is the wisdom of the Father.

units.la: 40. Dato etiam in diuinis vero & perspicuo enunciationis sensu, dari possunt affecta Logica argumenta, si non exquisite, saltem per analogiam.
units.tr: 40. Even granting that the sense of a divine statement is true and clear, logical arguments may still be applied to it, if not precisely, at least by analogy.

units.la: 41. Logica siquidem argumentorum inuentio rerum ipsarum affectioni & veritati respondere debet.
units.tr: 41. For the invention of logical arguments ought to correspond to the nature and truth of the things themselves.

units.la: 42. Nam ex earum habitudine & vera inter se affectione, non opinione nostra, argumenta sunt metienda.
units.tr: 42. For arguments must be measured by the relation of things and their true mutual nature, not by our opinion.

units.la: 43. Quo igitur quis penitius & accuratius res siue humanas siue diuinas earumque affectiones perspexerit, eo acutius is & accuratius argumenta inuenerit.
units.tr: 43. Therefore the more deeply and accurately someone has perceived things, whether human or divine, and their natures, the more sharply and accurately he will devise arguments.

units.la: 44. Hinc adeo est, quod diuersi, de rebus non diuersis, argumenta diuersa constituant: & res eadem respectu diuerso, ad varia argumentorum genera referantur.
units.tr: 44. Hence it is that different people set up different arguments about the same things, and one and the same thing, viewed in different respects, is referred to various kinds of argument.

units.la: 45. Mutata rerum affectione, nomina etiam argumentorum sunt mutanda.
units.tr: 45. When the nature of things changes, the names of the arguments must change too.

units.la: 46. Porro autem cuiuscunque partes sunt discerdiscernere verum à falso, & iudicare consequentias syllogismorum ac inconsequentias paralogismorum, eius interest ratiocinandi & disputandi praecepta cognoscere.
units.tr: 46. Moreover, whoever has the task of distinguishing true from false, and of judging the validity of syllogisms and the invalidity of paralogisms, has an interest in knowing the rules of reasoning and disputation.

units.la: 47. At minister Dei in Euangelio Iesu Christi debet discernere verum à falso, & confirmato iudicio legitimae consequentiae robur, & sophisticum inconsequetiae fucum dignoscere.
units.tr: 47. But a minister of God in the Gospel of Jesus Christ must distinguish true from false, and by a settled judgment recognise the strength of a valid consequence and detect the sophistical deceit of an invalid one.

units.la: 48. Probare quippe, ex Apostolico praecepto, debet omnia, & quod bonum est tenere: probare debet Spiritus, convincere debet contradicentes: exemplo etiam debet Apostolorum, errores pseudoapostolorum, pseudoprophetarum, & antichristi confutare.
units.tr: 48. For by the apostolic precept he ought to prove all things and hold fast what is good; he ought to test the spirits and convince those who contradict; and, following the example of the Apostles, he ought to refute the errors of false apostles, false prophets and antichrist.

units.la: 49. Et cum omne dogma Ecclesiae aut expressis verbis in scriptura contineatur: aut per consequentiam ex ea deducatur: & nullum dogma tam absurdum sit, quod non scripturae testimoniis probari velit, & multi multa afferant: videndum est praecipue Theologo, an bona & necessaria consequentia, an vero paralogismis sophisticisque conclusiunculis inde extruatur.
units.tr: 49. Since every doctrine of the Church is either contained in express words of Scripture or deduced from it by consequence, and since no doctrine is so absurd that someone will not wish to prove it by testimonies of Scripture, and many people bring forward many things, the theologian above all must see whether a doctrine is built on a good and necessary consequence or rather on paralogisms and sophistical little conclusions.

units.la: 50. Hoc autem ut facilius animaduertatur, opus est syllogisticarum legum adeoque Logices cognitione. Recte enim antea citatus Poeta: Soluere vis dextre Thebanæ ænigmata Sphingis AEmulus Oedipodis? vis solvere Gordia lora? Discutere errorum nubem? Dialectica disce.Scilicet vt sancto est Hieronymus ore locutus:Quicqd in hoc seculo peruersi dogmatis vsquaest;Quicquid in humana Sophia bene forte putatur:Hoc totum logico subuertitur ariete, & instarIncendi in cineres dissoluitur atque fauillas.
units.tr: 50. For, as the poet quoted above rightly says: Do you wish, a rival of Oedipus, to solve the riddles of the Theban Sphinx with a skilful hand? Do you wish to loosen the Gordian knots? To scatter the cloud of errors? Learn dialectic. Indeed, as Jerome spoke with holy mouth: Whatever perverse doctrine exists anywhere in this age, whatever is perhaps thought good in human wisdom, all of it is overthrown by the logical ram, and like a fire it is dissolved into ashes and embers.

units.la: 51. Denique in bene & perspicue docendo cum Theologi sit ὀρθοτομεῖν, sectari ordinem bonum, auersari autem ἀταξίαν omnem, adeoque intelligentiae & memoriae auditorum inseruire: idque fiat obseruatione Methodi, quae, vt Ramus ait, est omnium logicarum virtutum praestantissima: Logicae eum doctrinae, quae est de Methodo, peritum esse conuenit.
units.tr: 51. Finally, since it is the theologian's task to cut straight the word of truth [ὀρθοτομεῖν], to follow good order and to avoid all disorder [ἀταξία], and so to serve the understanding and memory of his hearers, and since this is done by observing method, which, as Ramus says, is the most excellent of all the logical virtues, it is fitting that the theologian be skilled in the logical doctrine of method.

units.la: 52. Recte enim ait Zabarella lib.1. de Meth. Nullam facultatem bene docere aliquis potest, nisi, & illius partibus disponendis, & in singulis theorematibus declarandis, tradendaque rerum absconditarum cognitione Methodum seruet.
units.tr: 52. For Zabarella rightly says in the first book of On Method: no one can teach any discipline well unless he keeps method both in arranging its parts, and in explaining each theorem, and in delivering knowledge of hidden things.

units.la: 53. Et recte idem Poeta: Ordine fac doceas, & dexter habebere doctor! Ordine fac discas: & bene doctus eris.
units.tr: 53. And the same poet rightly says: Teach by putting things in order, and you will be counted a skilled teacher! Learn in order, and you will be well taught.

units.la: 54. Ita autem Dialectica Christianorum sit praeceptrix, ne sit deceptrix; ita sit dux & doctrix, ne sit seductrix.
units.tr: 54. Thus let dialectic be the instructor of Christians, not their deceiver; let it be their guide and teacher, not their seducer.

units.la: 55. Res ipsas Theologicas Theologus petit ex fontibus sacris non Philosophicis & profanis (quo sensu accipimus quod dixit Ambrosius: Facessant Dialectici. vbi credendum est piscatoribus Apostolis.
units.tr: 55. The theological matters themselves the theologian seeks from sacred sources, not from philosophical and profane ones (in which sense we take what Ambrose said: let the dialecticians depart, since we must believe the fishermen Apostles).

units.la: 56. Modus tamen & norma tractationis illarum rerum peti potest ex Logica vera.
units.tr: 56. Yet the method and rule of treating those matters can be drawn from true logic.

units.la: 57. Non igitur facimus ab iis, qui indignum Theologo Logicæ studium existimant, qui Logicam tantum rerum Philosophicarum tractandarum organum ex Zarabella docent, quique ei dicam scribunt, dum causam falsorum in Ecclesia dogmatum in eius vsum reiiciunt.
units.tr: 57. So we do not agree with those who think the study of logic unworthy of a theologian, who teach logic from Zabarella only as an instrument for treating philosophical matters, and who write against it, while they blame its use for the false doctrines in the Church.

units.la: Vsus seruetur Logicæ, tollatur abusus.
units.tr: Let the use of logic be preserved; let the abuse be removed.

units.la: Testimonia Doctorum quorundam, de Logicæ in sacris vtilitate & necessitate.
units.tr: Testimonies of certain teachers concerning the usefulness and necessity of logic in sacred matters.

units.la: Augustinus de Christ.doctrina libro 2.cap.31.
units.tr: Augustine, On Christian Doctrine, book 2, chapter 31.

units.la: Disputationis disciplina ad omnia genera quæstionum, quæsunt in sacris literis penetranda & dissoluenda, plurimum valet.
units.tr: The discipline of disputation is of great value for penetrating and resolving all kinds of questions that are found in the sacred letters.

units.la: Et cap. 37. Scientia conclusionum & definitionum & distributionum plurimum lectorem scriptturarum adiuuat.
units.tr: And in chapter 37: The knowledge of conclusions, definitions and divisions greatly helps the reader of the Scriptures.

units.la: Et rursum alibi de cog. vera vitæ: Dialectica, inquit, differendi potens, potenter dubia quæque definiens, cunctas scripturas euibrans atque euiscerans, cunctam humanam annihilans.
units.tr: And again elsewhere, in On the True Life: Dialectic, he says, being able to argue, powerfully defining every doubtful matter, shakes and disembowels all the Scriptures, and annihilates all things human.

units.la: Et lib.de ord.
units.tr: And in the book On Order.

units.la: Quando ergo ratio ad alia fabricanda transsiret, nisi sua ipsius machinamenta distingueret, notaret, digereret proderetque ipsam disciplinam disciplinarum. narum, quam Dialecticam vocant? hac docet docere, hac docet discere.
units.tr: When reason would pass on to fashion other things, unless it distinguished, marked and arranged its own contrivances, would it set forth the discipline of disciplines, which they call Dialectic? This teaches teaching; this teaches learning.

units.la: Hieron. in Ezechiel.
units.tr: Jerome, on Ezekiel.

units.la: Vere quicquid in seculo peruersorum dogmatum est, quicquid ad terrenam scientiam pertinet & putatur esse robustum, hoc Dialectica arte subuertitur, & instar incendii, in cineres fauillasque dissoluitur, vt probetur esse nihili, quod putabatur fortissimum.
units.tr: Truly, whatever there is of perverse doctrine in the age, whatever pertains to earthly knowledge and is thought to be strong, this is overthrown by the art of dialectic, and like a fire it is dissolved into ashes and embers, so that what was thought the strongest is proved to be nothing.

units.la: Lutherus Tom. Germ. Ien. I. Pag. 310.
units.tr: Luther, German edition, vol. 1, p. 310.

units.la: <bl>Das möchte ich gerne leiden/ daß Aristotelis Bücher von der Logica, Rhetorica, Poetica, behalten/ oder sie in ein ander kurtz Form bracht/ nützlich gelesen würden/ junge Leute zu üben/ wol zu reden und predigen/ aber die Comment und Secten müssen abgethan/ und gleich wie Ciceronis Rhetorica, ohne Comment und Secten/ so auch Aristotelis Logica einfor-mich/ ohne solch groß Comment gelesen werden.</bl> Aber itzt lehret man weder reden noch predigen daraus/ und ist gantz ein disputation und mu-deren daraus worden. Daneben hette man nun die Sprachen Lateinisch/ Griechisch/ und Ebreisch/ die Mathematicas disciplinas, Historien/ welches ich befehl verstendigern/ und sich selbst wol geben würde/ so man mit ernst nach einer Reformation trachtet/ und fürwar viel daran gelegen ist/ denn hie sol die Christliche Jugendt und vnser edlest Volck/ darinnen die Christenheit bleibet/ geleret und bereitet werden. Darumb ich acht/ daß kein Bäpstlicher noch Keyserlicher werck möchte geschehen/ den gute Reformation der Vniuersiteten/ wiederumb kein Teuffelischer erger wesen / denn vnreformierte Vniuersiteten.
units.tr: <bl>I would gladly allow that Aristotle's books on logic, rhetoric and poetics be kept, or be brought into some other short form and read usefully, to train young people to speak and preach well. But the commentaries and sects must be abolished, and just as Cicero's Rhetoric is read without commentaries and sects, so Aristotle's Logic too should be read plainly, without such great commentary. But now one teaches neither speaking nor preaching from it; it has become entirely a disputation and a mess of such things. Besides, one would also have the languages, Latin, Greek and Hebrew, the mathematical disciplines and histories, which I commend to be understood, and which would of their own accord yield good results if one seriously sought a reformation; and indeed much depends on this, for here the Christian youth and our noblest people, in whom Christendom remains, are to be taught and prepared. Therefore I think that no Papal or Imperial work could be greater than a good reformation of the universities, and conversely no devilish thing could be worse than unreformed universities.</bl>

units.la: Philippus Melanc.in Epist.dedic.Dial.
units.tr: Philipp Melanchthon, in the dedicatory epistle to his Dialectic.

units.la: Hos & adhortor, & propter gloriam Dei, & propter Ecclesiæ salutem obtestor, ne Dialecticen negligant, nec applaudant insulsis sermonibus eorum, qui vituperant eam, & Ecclesiæ inutilem esse clamitant.
units.tr: I also exhort them, and for the glory of God and the salvation of the Church I beseech them, not to neglect dialectic, nor to applaud the silly talk of those who disparage it and cry out that it is useless to the Church.

units.la: Et postea; veram incorruptam natiuam Dialecticen, &c. affirmo non modo in foro, & in iudiciis, aut in Philosophia, sed etiam in Ecclesia valde vtilem esse. At vt de Ecclesia nunc dicam, &c. Et infra; Nec deterreamur a Dialectica studio propterea, quod scripserunt aliqui, Dialectica armis veritatem a prauorum dogmatum autoribus labefactatam esse. Hæc enim non est artis, sed malorum ingeniorum & prauæ institutionis reprehensio. Sit, vt in aliis studiis, natura recta, & veritatis amans, & artem sobrie discat, eamque modeste & graviter ad inquisitionem, & illustrationem veritatis adhibeat, non exerceatur sophistica, non amentur captiones & præstigiæ, vt multæ prauæ naturæ similes Autolyci, Sisyphi, Eurybati, & aliorum impostorum, delectantur ludis captionum & calumniis. Et horum similes fuisse, & esse multos malorum dogmatum mangones, vt ita dicam, satis apparet, qui nequaquam Dialectici sunt aut fuerunt, sed potius sophistæ aut impostores, & non solum aliarum doctrinarum, sed etiam Dialecticæ deprauatores.
units.tr: And afterwards: I affirm that true, uncorrupted, natural dialectic is very useful not only in the forum and in courts, or in philosophy, but also in the Church. But that I may now speak of the Church, etc. And below: Nor should we be deterred from the study of dialectic because some have written that dialectic, as a weapon of truth, has been weakened by the authors of perverse doctrines. For this is a fault not of the art but of wicked minds and bad training. Let the student, as in other studies, be of upright nature and a lover of truth, learn the art soberly, and apply it modestly and gravely to the inquiry into and illustration of truth; let him not be practised in sophistry, nor love captious tricks and deceptions, as many of bad nature, like Autolycus, Sisyphus, Eurybatus and other impostors, delight in games of captiousness and calumny. That there have been, and are, many such dealers in bad doctrines, so to speak, is clear enough; they are by no means, nor were they ever, dialecticians, but rather sophists or impostors, and corrupters not only of other doctrines but also of dialectic itself.

units.la: Flacius Illyr.de ratione cognoscendi S. literas pag. 15.
units.tr: Flacius Illyricus, de ratione cognoscendi S. literas, p. 15.

units.la: Postquam dehortatus est à Pseudophilosophia & abusu impostura q; Philosophie, de qua
units.tr: After he has warned against pseudo-philosophy and the abuse of philosophy, of which he writes thus to the Colossians:

units.la: Ap.ad Col.sic scribit.Neq₃ enim interea fanaticos homines sequi debemus, quib.humana scientia prorsus sunt inutiles, aut etiam noxia ad cognitionem S. literarū & doctrina coelestis.Oportet enim discere linguas & eruditas Grammaticas.Vtilis ac plane etiam necessaria est Dialectica ac Rhetorica, & reliqua Philosophia cognitio. Nec valet obiectio, quod ista Apostoli non didicerint: acceperunt enim illi cognitionem linguarum, & aliarum vtiliū rerum ex cognitione Spiritus S.Videmus & hodie multos, alioqui rudes, ita coelesti quoda intelligentia lumine donatos illustratosque esse, vt vel obscurissimas controuersias summa dexteritate diiudicare possint. Harum ergo humanarum & externarū rerum scientiī & Apostolus in Christianis, praesertim Doctoribus requirit, inquiens Tit.3. Discant autē etiam nostri bonis operibus aut sumptionibus praeesse in necessarios vsus, vt non sint inutiles, vbi omnino eis praecipit artes liberales & mechanicas discere.Sic 2.Tim.2.iubet Theologia hominib.tradi ad docēdum & discendum idoneis, quo illi etiā porro aliis exponere possint: vt manifeste Logicas scientias aut organa requirat in studioso ad Theologiam adhibēdo.Sit ergo in domo iuxta Theologiam, veluti iuxta matremfamilias Saram etiam Agar, Philosophia gentilis, sed seruiat ac ancilletur,non dominetur: non sit architectonica sed famula:nec intret in cubiculum conscientia, aut ad tribunal iudicii rerum causarumq₃ ac deliberationū sacrarum, nisi quatenus sua Theologia permiserit: qua super omnes scientias, artes, cogitationes, consilia, conatus & actiones hominum & angelorum suprema architectonica est. Idem pag. so. Vult etiam Apostolus Tit. 1. Doctore sacrarum literarum esse idoneum ad argumentandum, & refutanda sophismata seductorum, quo pertinent non tantum forma verorum argumentorum, ac fallacia falsorum, & materia aut loca inuentionis: sed etiam tota tum sermonis doctrina, tum singularum propositionum, ac denique etiam ipsarum rerum solidior cognitio.
units.tr: Nor indeed must we follow fanatical men, to whom human learning is wholly useless, or even harmful, for the knowledge of the Holy Scriptures and of heavenly doctrine. For it is necessary to learn languages and the learned grammars. Dialectic and rhetoric, and the knowledge of the rest of philosophy, are useful and indeed quite necessary. Nor does the objection hold, that the apostles did not learn these things: for they received the knowledge of languages and of other useful things from the knowledge of the Holy Spirit. We see today that many, otherwise unlearned, are so endowed and illumined with a certain heavenly light of understanding that they can decide the most obscure controversies with the greatest skill. Therefore the Apostle also requires knowledge of these human and external things in Christians, especially in teachers, saying in Titus 3: Let our people also learn to excel in good works for necessary uses, that they may not be unfruitful. Where he plainly commands them to learn the liberal and mechanical arts. So in 2 Tim. 2 he bids theology be handed on to men fit to teach and to learn, so that they in turn may be able to expound it to others; whence it manifestly requires the logical sciences, or instruments, to be applied by the student of theology. Let philosophy then be in the house alongside theology, as Hagar beside Sarah, the mistress of the household: a gentile philosophy, but let her serve and be a handmaid, not rule. Let her not be architectonic but a servant; let her not enter the chamber of conscience, nor sit at the tribunal of judgment over sacred matters, causes and deliberations, except insofar as her mistress theology permits; theology, which above all sciences, arts, thoughts, counsels, endeavours and actions of men and angels is the supreme architectonic. The same, p. 50: The Apostle also wills in Titus 1 that a teacher of the Holy Scriptures be fit to argue and to refute the sophisms of seducers; to which pertain not only the form of true arguments and the fallacy of false ones, and the matter or places of invention, but also the whole doctrine of speech, of single propositions, and finally a more solid knowledge of the things themselves.

units.la: Tit. 3. vult exponentem sacras literas esse idoneum ad docendum, sicut & 2. Tim. 2. Quo tota doctrina Logices, aut Grammatica, Dialectica & Rhetorica pertinet vna cum quadam naturali dexteritate: quæ tamen multo est præstantior, si sit supernaturalis superneq; per S. sanctum allata: cuiusmodi decus ac salutare iudicandi, differendique organum multis cœlitus donatum videmus.
units.tr: Titus 3 wills the expounder of the Holy Scriptures to be fit for teaching, as also 2 Tim. 2. To this pertains the whole doctrine of logic, or grammar, dialectic and rhetoric, together with a certain natural dexterity; which nevertheless is far more excellent if it is supernatural and brought by the Holy Spirit from above: such is the grace and salutary organ of judging and disputing that we see given from heaven to many.

units.la: Iohan. Wigandus & Matt. Iudex in præfat. Syntagmatis vet. Testam. pag. 5.
units.tr: Johann Wigand and Matthias Judex, in the preface to the Syntagma of the Old Testament, p. 5.

units.la: Hasce ergo metas (loquitur de artib. logicis) & ad res theologice grauissimas ac saluberrimas inda-gandas, euoluendas, docendas atq; discendas, censemus esse conuenientissimas & vtilissimas. Cum enim sint dona Dei, Theologia nequaquam aspernatur ea: sed recte, dextre, & prudenter donis iis vtitur. Sed nobis videmur audire quosdam tragicè exclamitantes & vociferätes: quid tandem Theologia cum Philosophia habet commercii? Quid vero ad eiusmodi importunos homines sedandos proferemus? Nam inscitia & ruditatis extrema videntur patrocinium ex proposito suscepisse. Sed furore nonnihil represso, sedatis animis parumper auscultent. Plane & diluci-de affirmamus id quod omnibus notissimum est, Res Theo-
units.tr: These limits (he speaks of the logical arts) we judge to be most convenient and most useful for investigating, unfolding, teaching and learning the most weighty and salutary theological matters. For since they are gifts of God, theology by no means spurns them, but uses these gifts rightly, skilfully and prudently. But we seem to hear some who cry out tragically and shout: what in the end has theology to do with philosophy? And what shall we bring forward to calm such troublesome men? For they seem to have deliberately undertaken the defence of extreme ignorance and rudeness. But with their fury somewhat restrained, and their minds calmed a little, let them listen. We affirm plainly and clearly what is best known to all: theological matters

units.la: Theologicas non gignit Philosophia, neque ex ea peti debent, sicuti etiam nec possunt. Tatum vero ex fontibus Israel, hoc est, ex authenticis Bibliorum monumentis res sacras & articulos fidei hauriri conuenit: qui secus facit, principiaque Philosophica cum articulis fidei commiscet, grande nefas committit, & fulmen anathematis merito suo incurrit. Ipsa autem noticia rerum metas tibi suggerit, quibus in rebus sacris euoluendis, tradendis ac percipiendis magno cum fructu uti possis. Non enim fastidiunt S. litera illa humana adiumenta, saluis tamen atque incorruptis suis rebus, id quod ante omnia excipi observarique debet. Non repudiat Theologia artes dicendi & linguas. Cum enim ea in hominum coetu docenda sit, nequaquam verba hominum, industriam, prudentiam & dexteritatem in docendo refugit. Deus certe ipse non est Deus ἀταξίας. Spiritus sanctus & sacrarum literarum & bonarum artium auctor non delectatur confusione in exponendis rebus diuinis, quin & in coetibus atque ceremoniis piorum, Deus vult ordinem & εὐχημοσύνων coli.
units.tr: Philosophy does not produce theological matters, nor ought they to be drawn from it, nor indeed can they be. Sacred things and the articles of faith ought to be drawn wholly from the fountains of Israel, that is, from the authentic monuments of the Bible. Whoever does otherwise, and mingles philosophical principles with the articles of faith, commits a great wickedness and rightly incurs the thunderbolt of anathema. Yet the very knowledge of things suggests to you the limits within which you may use them with great profit in unfolding, teaching and grasping sacred matters. For those Holy Scriptures do not disdain those human aids, provided their own matters remain safe and uncorrupted; which above all must be excepted and observed. Theology does not reject the arts of speaking and languages. For since it is to be taught in an assembly of men, it by no means shuns human words, diligence, prudence and skill in teaching. God certainly is not a God of disorder. The Holy Spirit, the author both of the sacred letters and of the good arts, does not delight in confusion in setting forth divine things; indeed, in the assemblies and ceremonies of the pious God wills order and decorum to be observed.

units.la: Idem in praefat. Syntag. Noui Testamenti.
units.tr: The same, in the preface to the Syntagma of the New Testament.

units.la: Neque vero solum in rebus Philosophicis metae illae locum habent: sed etiam, ac vel inprimis, in diuinis. Nam haec multo accuratiori explicatione, atque altiori consideratione, quam vllae aliae, indigent. Nec est in libris sacris veteris & noui Testamenti, vt quidam nimis crasse & insulse iudicant, mera confusio: verum in iis quoque optimus ordo, atque adeo ipsissima methodus elucet, modo eruditum acpium habeant lectorem.
units.tr: Nor do those limits have a place only in philosophical matters, but also, and above all, in divine ones. For these require a far more accurate explanation and a higher consideration than any others. Nor is there, as some judge too crudely and foolishly, mere confusion in the sacred books of the Old and New Testament; rather in them too the best order and indeed the very method shines forth, provided the reader is learned and attentive.

units.la: Iacobus Scegkius 1. Topi. pag. 64.
units.tr: Jacob Schegk, Topics, 1, p. 64.

units.la: Vecordia & inertia illorum reprehendenda est, qui nullis rationibus, nullaque Dialectica & Philosophia, id est, ἀνεἰβεία tractandas explicandasque Theologicas quastiones arbitrantur, obliti scilicet Paulina orthotomia, qua probanda sunt omnia, & qua bona ac vera sunt, retinenda. Aperitur illo Philosophia contemtu fenestra omnibus hæreticis: qui spiritualia spiritualib. comparare nequeunt, & nec diuidere, nec componere vera analysi seu ὀρθοτομία quaquam possunt.
units.tr: The folly and sloth of those is to be reproved who think that theological questions are to be handled and explained by no reasons, no dialectic and no philosophy, that is, without art; forgetting, of course, the Pauline orthotomia, by which all things are to be proved, and what is good and true is to be retained. By that contempt for philosophy a window is opened to all heretics, who cannot compare spiritual things with spiritual, and by no true analysis or orthotomia can they either divide or combine.

units.la: Et pag. 76. Logodædalus persuasissimum est, Philosophia ἀνεἰβεία contaminari Theologiam: cum nulla re magis depravetur veritas, quam inscitia vera & solida Philosophia, cuius ipsi nullum habent gustum.
units.tr: And on p. 76: Logodaedalus is quite convinced that theology is contaminated by unskilled philosophy, since truth is corrupted by nothing more than by ignorance of true and solid philosophy, of which they themselves have no taste.

units.la: Guil. Hilden. Top. 8. pag. 2.
units.tr: Guil. Hilden. Top. 8. pag. 2.

units.la: Dialectica licet nullius rei perfectam essentiam & naturā declarandam suscipiat: tamen nihil est, siue sit Ethicum, siue Physicum, siue Theologicum, quod non ambitu artis huius concludatur, quod non veritatis inquirendæ rationem hinc petat.
units.tr: Although dialectic does not undertake to declare the perfect essence and nature of any single thing, there is nothing, whether it be ethical, physical or theological, that is not concluded within the compass of this art, and that does not seek from it the method of inquiring after truth.

units.la: Moses Pflacherus in præfat. Analysis Typicæ edit. 3. Tubingensi.
units.tr: Moses Pflacherus, in the preface to his Analysis Typica, third Tübingen edition.

units.la: His sane hominibus, quos artificiosa scriptura tractatio tam male propitios habet, respondendum esse video. Et primo quidem hoc ipsis libenter damus, vim illam Spiritus sancti inexplicabilem, in Rhetorum pigmentis & Dialecticorum vinculis non esse positam. Absit enim à nobis ista cogitatio: & tā exilis de sacris literis æstimatio. Nā angustior est & sublimior Theologiæ materia, quam vt humanæ Philosophiæ funfundamento, & corrupta rationis iudicio nitatur. Verum enim vero non de re ipsa, & sacra scriptura substantia, quae omnem humanum sensum logé excedit, quaestio est: sed de modo & methodo, quà sancti Dei homines, in doctrina caelesti nobis tradenda, vsi sint. Neque enim Prophetas, Euangelistas, & Apostolos ἀμεταδότως dixisse & scripsisse existimandum est. Equidem non elaborarunt illi ad ostentationem, à qua per omnem vitam fuerunt alienissimi. Interim tamen certum est, eos non confuso & perturbato dicendi genere, instar foliorum Sibyllae, vsos esse. Quomodo enim Legati Dei, qui Deus est ordinis, non confusionis, nullum in oratione sua ad genus humanum πρεσβευτικῶς, ordinem tenerent? videmus profecto, sanctissimos illos Dei legatos, in suis concionibus, alia ex aliis colligere, argumentari, accusare, minari, solari, docere, mouere: quae omnia praeceptis Dialecticis & Rhetoricis explicantur. Et quod Christus ipse argumentationibus vsus sit, cum in suis tuendis, tum in aduersariis convincendis, author est Augustinus contra Cresconium. cap. 14. Quis vero in vi argumentationum & probationum Paulo neruosior? cap. 20. Quis in medio argumenti sumendo, & eo apto, diligentior? Quis in refellendo acutior? Quae omnia sine aliqua artis Dialecticae & Rhetoricae ope, meo quidem iudicio, non euenerunt. Etsi enim Spiritus Domini per illos loquebatur: is tamen inusitato genere dicendi vsus non est, sed eo, quod hominum natura, ad explicationem rerum necessariarum, ipse indiderat, & quod per artes dicendi ille, qui omnium scientiarum & artium est author, hominibus largitus est. Neq; enim bene dicedi faculfacultas Dialecticis & Rhetoribus accepta ferenda est: sed Deo, qui, vt hominem omnibus creaturis anteposuit, ita singulari & eximio dono sapientiæ & eloquentiæ exornauit. Hinc D. Ambrosius lib. 4. epist. 63. non dubitauit asseuerare, eos, qui primi de arte dicendi scripserint, præcepta omnia ex diuinis libris collegisse. Et quamuis concederetur, sacros scriptores illa Rhetorum & Dialecticorum præcepta in scribendo non obseruasse, nec ea secutos esse: quis tamen ab illorum scriptis scriptorumque interpretatione remoueat ea, quæ in omni oratione diserta cernuntur, cum illi Spiritum Domini secum haberent: cuius beneficio homines diserti sunt: cuius etiam instinctu artes illæ inuentæ & traditæ sunt. Demus eos (inquit Ambrosius) non scripsisse secundum artem: at certe secundum gratiam scripsisse fatendum est, quæ omnem artem longe superat. Quæ cum ita sint, nulla fit verbo diuino iniuria: cum artificium dicendi, quod in eo est, sancta cum veneratione obseruamus: neque sacros illos scriptores, S. sancti amanuenses, in ordinem cogimus, cum ordinem, in scribendo ab ipsis obseruatum, in docendo interpretandoque accurate & religiose sequimur: idque exemplo præstantissimorum Theologorum, cum Græcorum, tum Latinorum, facimus. Videatur Augustinus in lib. de doctrina Christiana, vbi copiose & luculenter ostendit, artium & Philosophiæ adminicula à Sacrorum commentatione non remouenda esse, sed potius dextre & vtiliter vsurpanda. Legantur conciones, lucubrationes & commentarii Basilii, Chrysostomi, Hieronymi, quorum summa est in explicando & declarando industria, ex ipsis artium & Phi& Philosophiæ penetralibus petita. Et quid opus est verbis? Euincit ipsa experientia, multo maiore dexteritate in sacris literis earumque interpretatione versari, negotiorum seriem, rerum causas, initia, progressus, fines, circumstantias, argumentationes, & quæcunque alicuius momenti sunt, perspicacius rimari atque obseruare eos, qui aliquam Philosophiæ cognitionem habent, & bonis artibus imbuti sunt, quam qui eas nunquam degustarunt.
units.tr: I see that I must answer these men, whom an artful handling of Scripture has made so ill-disposed towards it. First, we gladly grant them this: that the inexplicable power of the Holy Spirit does not lie in the embellishments of the rhetoricians or the bonds of the dialecticians. Far be that thought from us, and such a meagre estimate of the sacred letters. For the matter of Theology is too narrow and too lofty to rest on the foundation of human philosophy and the corrupt judgment of reason. The question, then, is not about the thing itself, the substance of Scripture, which altogether exceeds human understanding, but about the manner and method in which the holy men of God used in delivering heavenly doctrine to us. For we must not suppose that the Prophets, Evangelists and Apostles spoke and wrote [ἀμεταδότως] without any sharing of what was divine. Certainly they did not labour for display, from which they were most remote their whole lives. Yet it is certain that they did not speak in a confused and disordered kind of style, like the leaves of the Sibyl. For how would the envoys of God, who is a God of order and not of confusion, keep no order in their address to the human race [πρεσβευτικῶς]? We see, surely, that those most holy envoys of God, in their sermons, gather one thing from another, argue, accuse, threaten, console, teach and move; and all these things are explained by the precepts of the dialecticians and rhetoricians. And that Christ himself used arguments, both in defending his own position and in refuting his adversaries, Augustine vouches in his book against Cresconius, chapter 14. Who was more sinewy than Paul in the force of his arguments and proofs? (chapter 20). Who was more careful in choosing a middle term for an argument, and one fitted to it? Who was sharper in refutation? All of which, in my judgment, did not come about without some aid of the art of dialectic and rhetoric. For although the Spirit of the Lord spoke through them, he did not use an unusual manner of speaking, but that which human nature itself had implanted for the explanation of necessary things, and which he who is the author of all sciences and arts has bestowed on men through the arts of speaking. For the skill of speaking well is not to be credited to the dialecticians and rhetoricians, but to God, who, as he set man above all creatures, so adorned him with a singular and outstanding gift of wisdom and eloquence. Hence Ambrose, book 4, letter 63, did not hesitate to assert that those who first wrote about the art of speaking gathered all their precepts from the divine books. And even if it were granted that the sacred writers did not observe the precepts of the rhetoricians and dialecticians in writing, nor followed them, yet who would remove from their writings, and from the interpretation of them, those things which are seen in every eloquent speech, since they had the Spirit of the Lord with them, by whose benefit men are eloquent, and by whose impulse those arts were invented and handed down? Let us grant, says Ambrose, that they did not write according to art; yet surely we must acknowledge that they wrote according to grace, which far surpasses all art. Since these things are so, no wrong is done to the Word of God when we reverently observe the art of speaking that is in it; nor do we force those holy writers, the amanuenses of the Holy Spirit, into an order, when we carefully and devoutly follow the order which they observed in writing, in teaching and in interpreting. And we do this after the example of the most outstanding theologians, both Greek and Latin. Let Augustine be consulted in his book On Christian Doctrine, where he shows at length and clearly that the aids of the arts and of philosophy are not to be removed from the study of the sacred writings, but rather to be used skilfully and profitably. Let the sermons, writings and commentaries of Basil, Chrysostom and Jerome be read, whose chief diligence in expounding and explaining is drawn from the very inner shrines of the arts and philosophy. And why need there be words? Experience itself proves that those who have some knowledge of philosophy and are steeped in the liberal arts, far more skilfully engage with the sacred letters and their interpretation; they observe and trace out more keenly the sequence of affairs, the causes of things, beginnings, progress, ends, circumstances, arguments, and whatever is of any weight, than those who have never tasted them.

units.la: Elenchus vltimi Sophismatis aduersus Physicam.
units.tr: Refutation of the last sophism against natural philosophy.

units.la: Quicquid nulla nititur certitudine, id ipsum ad Rempub. nullam afferre potest vtilitatem: Certis enim necesse est consiliis innitatur, certaque experientia & ratione firmatum sit, ex quo ad Rempub. aliquod debet exundare emolumentum.
units.tr: Whatever rests on no certainty can bring no advantage to the commonwealth. For it must rest on sure counsels and be confirmed by certain experience and reason, if it is to yield any benefit to the commonwealth.

units.la: Atqui doctrina Physica rerum naturalium in abscondito latentium magna laborat incertitudine: certitudo admodum rara est in physicis. Id ipsum probatur argumentis partim Theologorum, partim vero ipsorum Philosophorum. Theologicum primum hoc est:
units.tr: But the physical doctrine of natural things, which lie hidden, suffers great uncertainty: certainty is very rare in physics. This is proved by arguments partly from the theologians and partly from the philosophers themselves. The first theological argument is this:

units.la: 1. Ecclesiastæ cap. 3. verf. 11. Cuncta fecit bona in tempore suo, & mundum tradidit disputationi eorum, vt non inueniat homo opus, quod operatus est Deus ab initio vsque ad finem. Ergo omnia Dei opera adeoque res naturales sunt homini imperuestigabiles.
units.tr: 1. Ecclesiastes 3:11. He has made everything beautiful in its time, and has given the world over to their debate, so that man cannot find the work that God has done from beginning to end. Therefore all the works of God, and so natural things, are beyond human investigation.

units.la: Respon. Consequentiam negamus propter prauam Hebraei fontis versionem. Tramellius enim & Iunius ita legunt: Deus scilicet: vnum quodquodque facit pulchrum suo tempore etiam cum seculo, (seu quadiu seculum est) exponit animo illorum (excepto eo quod non assequitur homo) opus quod facit ipse Deus a principio ad finem usque. Hinc contrarium potius sequitur, nempe Deum opera a principio ad finem usq; a se facta hominum animis exponere, ut in iis sese occupent, excepto tantum illo genere operum, quae hominis captu superant, & q Deus sibi asseruat in arcano consilio suo. De quib. etiam Physica nō est solicita.
units.tr: I deny the consequence, on account of a faulty rendering of the Hebrew source. Tremellius and Junius read it thus: "God indeed makes each thing beautiful in its time, even with the age (or as long as the age lasts). He sets out before their minds (except what man does not grasp) the work that God himself does from beginning to end." Hence the opposite follows: God sets before men's minds the works he has made, from beginning to end, so that they may occupy themselves with them, except only that class of works which exceed human capacity and which God reserves to himself in his secret counsel. Physics is not concerned with these either.

units.la: 2. Eccles. 8. verf. 16. vel Iunii 9. ver. 1. Et intellexi, quod omnium operum Dei nullam possit homo invenire rationem, eorum quae fiunt sub sole, & quanto plus laboraverit quaerendo, tanto minus inveniat, etiamsi dixerit sapiens se nosse non poterit reperire.
units.tr: 2. Ecclesiastes 8:16, or in Junius 9:1: And I perceived that man cannot find the reason for all the works of God that are done under the sun; and however much he labours in seeking, he will find less; even if the wise man says he knows, he will not be able to find it.

units.la: Resp. Neq; sic simpliciter Tremel. & Iunius ex Hebraeo legunt, scilicet homine omnino non posse vllā rerū, q sub sole sūt invenire ratione, sed sic, animaduerti totū op⁹ Dei nō posse homine assequi illud opus, q̃ fit sub sole. 2. Salomo nō loquitur absolute de reb. Physicis & creatis, quatenus sunt & cognoscuntur, sed de rebus mundanis disserit, ratione administrationis, quatenus scilicet regitur & administratur. Statuit n. istius administrationis duo genera, unū ab hominib. cap. 8. vsq; ad verf. 15. alterū a Deo cap. 9. q̃ utrūq; ita varium esse ostendit, ut nihil certi de eo humanitus ab vllo homine definiri possit. Hic itaq; docet in genere obseruatione administrationis Dei humanas mentes superare, idq; postea trium partium inductione. 1. est de euentu personarum omniū. 2. de euētu factofactorum atq; conatuum. 3. de euentu consiliorum. Non autem sequitur, homo non potest assequi rationé administrationis diuinæ, qua hic mundus regitur. Ergo scire non potest rerum creatarum naturas.
units.tr: Reply: Tremellius and Junius do not read it simply from the Hebrew to mean that man can by no reasoning find anything that is under the sun, but rather: I perceived that man cannot attain that work of God which is done under the sun. Second, Solomon does not speak absolutely about physical and created things, insofar as they exist and are known, but discusses worldly affairs with respect to their governance, insofar as they are ruled and administered. For he sets up two kinds of this administration: one by men, in chapter 8 down to verse 15, and the other by God, in chapter 9. He shows that both are so varied that nothing certain about them can be defined by any man. Here, then, he teaches in general that the observation of God's administration surpasses human minds, and he proves this afterwards by an induction of three parts: first, concerning the outcome for all persons; second, concerning the outcome of deeds and efforts; third, concerning the outcome of counsels. It does not follow, however, that man cannot attain the principle of divine providence by which this world is governed. Therefore he cannot know the natures of created things.

units.la: 3. Eccles. 1. ν. 12. Et dedi (scilicet ego Salomon) cor meum ad disquirendum & inuestigandum cum sapientia omne, quod fit sub caelo. Hanc occupationem malam Deus dedit filiis hominum, ut occupet se in ea.
units.tr: 3. Ecclesiastes 1:12. And I (namely I, Solomon) gave my heart to seek out and search with wisdom all that is done under heaven. This wretched business God has given to the sons of men, that they may occupy themselves with it.

units.la: Respondet Danæus, hoc non ἁπλῶς & absolute, sed κατὰ τι tantum & comparate ad verum Dei cultum salutisq; doctrinâ dictum esse (ut innuit ν. 15. quo docet, perquisitatione illam rerum ne minima quidem rem contortam corrigere, aut perditâ repræsentare posse, nedum caeleste vitâ subministrare.) Neq; enim damnat Salomo, aut improbat veram cognitionem de rerum natura, quâ illi summâ Deus pro summo beneficio dederat, & propter quâ tum à regina Saba, & aliis vicinis regib. colebatur. Sed si hæc Physica cognitio cum vera pietate, si cum fide, si cum vero Dei metu, si cum interna animi regeneratione, si cum cognitione æternæ salutis & vitæ conferatur, est certe molesta quædam animi occupatio infructuosa & fatigans nos potius, q; conscientiam nostram sustentans & consolans. Mala enim occupatio hic designat laboriosam & molestam, ut postea interpretatur versf. 14.
units.tr: Danaeus replies that this was not said simply and absolutely [haplōs], but only in some respect [kata ti] and in comparison with the true worship of God and the doctrine of salvation. He hints at this in verse 15, where he teaches that such inquiry into things cannot straighten even the least crooked thing or restore what is lost, much less supply heavenly life. For Solomon does not condemn or disapprove of true knowledge of the nature of things, which God had granted him in the highest measure as a great benefit, and on account of which he was honoured by the queen of Sheba and other neighbouring kings. But if this physical knowledge is compared with true piety, with faith, with true fear of God, with inner regeneration of the soul, with knowledge of eternal salvation and life, it is certainly a kind of troublesome and unfruitful occupation of the mind, wearying us rather than sustaining and comforting our conscience. For the "wretched occupation" here means laborious and burdensome, as he later explains in verse 14.

units.la: 4. Iob 36. ν. 24. Memento quod ignores opus Dei, de quo cecinerunt viri. Omnes homines vident eum, unusquisque intuetur procul. Ecce Deus magnus vincens nostram scientiam.
units.tr: 4. Job 36:24. Remember that you do not know the work of God, of which men have sung. All men see him; each one looks at him from afar. Behold, God is great, surpassing our knowledge.

units.la: Resp. Vitium est ex male intellecto verbo Hebraeo. Tremellius enim & Iunius ita verterunt, Recordare vt amplifices opus eius, quod contemplati sunt mortales. Deinde non loquitur de naturis à se creatis, seu reb. Physicis, sed de opere Dei extra ordinem naturæ facto temporibus Noachi, scilicet diluuio. Hinc itaque nulla Physicæ scientiæ incertitudo infertur.
units.tr: The fault lies in a misunderstood Hebrew word. Tremellius and Junius rendered it: "Remember to magnify his work, which mortals have contemplated." Further, the passage does not speak of natures created by him, or of physical things, but of a work of God done outside the order of nature, namely the deluge in the time of Noah. Hence no uncertainty of physical science follows from it.

units.la: Hæc cum quibusdam Theologis obiicit Fran. Vallesius. Philosophi incertitudinem scientiæ Physicæ partim generaliter partim specialiter probat.
units.tr: Francis Vallesius brings these arguments forward together with some theologians. The philosophers prove the uncertainty of physical science partly in general and partly in particular.

units.la: Generaliter quarumuis rerum incertam notitiam asserunt cum Academici, tum Sceptici.
units.tr: In general, both the Academics and the Sceptics assert that we have uncertain knowledge of any things whatever.

units.la: Academici nil certo sciri posse, sed ad verisimilitudinem quādam & probabilitatem posse procedere disputationes docent.
units.tr: The Academics teach that nothing can be known for certain, but that disputations can proceed to a certain likelihood and probability.

units.la: Sceptici vero nihil de vlla re affirmantes neque negantes, de omnibus æque dubitant.
units.tr: The Sceptics, however, affirming nothing about any thing and neither denying anything, doubt all things equally.

units.la: Incertitudinis & dubitationis argumenta petunt, partim à cognoscentis conditione, partim à cogniti seu obiecti scibilis, partim à medii cognitionis ratione.
units.tr: They seek the arguments for uncertainty and doubt partly from the condition of the knower, partly from the knowable nature of the thing known or object, and partly from the means of knowing.

units.la: I.
units.tr: I.

units.la: I. A cognoscentis conditione ita argumentabantur:
units.tr: I. They argued from the condition of the knower as follows:

units.la: Si organa cognoscentis quib. scientia acquiritur, vti sensus non sunt vniformia & constantia, sed varia varia & subinde mutabilia, per ea certa acquiri scientia nequit.
units.tr: If the organs of the knower by which knowledge is acquired, such as the senses, are not uniform and constant but varied and at times changeable, certain knowledge cannot be acquired through them.

units.la: At antecedens verum. Primum enim constat, compositione & temperie organorum homines singulos ab aliis nō nihil differre, singulos etiā bene valentes ab ægrotantib. & ipsosmet bene valentes à seipsis nondum ægrotantibus, sed naturaliter mutatis, per ætates, per animi motus, per casum, mordētes cogitationes, per corporales motus. Propter hanc differentiā & miram varietatem organorum sensuum, mel mihi potest videri album & dulce: Ictérico vero flauum & amarum: experimur etiam eidē homini eundē cibum nunc esse suauem, nunc ingratum, eandē rem illi rotundam, huic oblōgam videri. Visus etiam, cum sint oculorum multiplices colores, mire variat. Deinde hæc varietas organorum sensuum exteriorum, parit eorundem sensibilium diuersas phantasias. Hinc non minor est iudiciorum quam sensuum varietas, cum vix duobus hominibus eadē res placeat, sed quod alius probat, alius detestatur, & eadē de re alius lætetur, alius mœreat, alius irascatur. Quin & idem homo iisdem verbis nunc irascitur, quibus nuper placabatur. Sæpe etiam eadem de re mutamus sententiam.
units.tr: But the antecedent is true. For first, it is evident that individual people differ somewhat from one another in the make-up and temperament of their organs: healthy people differ from the sick, and the healthy differ from themselves when not yet sick but naturally altered by age, by emotions, by chance, by gnawing thoughts, and by bodily motions. Because of this difference and the remarkable variety of the sense organs, honey may seem to me white and sweet, while to a jaundiced person it seems yellow and bitter. We also experience that the same food is sometimes pleasant and sometimes unpleasant to the same person, and that the same thing looks round to one and oblong to another. Sight too varies greatly, since the colours of the eyes are manifold. Moreover, this variety of the external sense organs gives rise to diverse impressions of the same sensible things. Hence the variety of judgments is no less than the variety of senses, since scarcely two people like the same thing, but one approves what another detests, and at the same matter one rejoices, another grieves, another is angry. Indeed the same person is sometimes angry at the very words by which he was lately soothed. Often too we change our opinion on the same matter.

units.la: Ergo & consequens verum est.
units.tr: Therefore the consequent is true as well.

units.la: Resp. Negamus huius Syllogismi omnem scientiam tollentis connexionē, propter captionem ex accidente. Axioma n. est logicum. Ea quæ fiūt per accidēs, nō debent, neq; possunt,
units.tr: Answer: We deny the connection of this syllogism, which destroys all knowledge, on account of the fallacy of accident. For the axiom is a logical one: things that happen per accidens ought not, and cannot, overturn or subvert things that happen per se.

units.la: Y vel peruertere vel euertere ea quę fiunt per se. Iam vero cognoscentib.sensionis & sensoriorum varietas seu varia affectio ex accidenti accidit, non per se & sua natura. Ipsa quidem patibilitas mutationis, & aptitudo ad recipiedas varias affectiones, quib. affecta varie operantur & patiuntur, naturaliter inest organis sensuum, sed ipsa passio affectio praeternaturalis, actu varians mutatio, & a statu bene habentis naturę deturbans non per se, sed ex accidenti competit illis. Sensus igitur, quod secus rem percipit, atq; in se est res per accidens ita sentit. Hoc a accidens vera & germanam sensus actione deprauas est impedimentum, vel alia morbosa affectio & vitiosa intemperies organi. Hos ipsos male affectos sensus no statuimus singulares observatores, e quorum inductione mesetia decepta a sensib. efficiat vniuersalia & artium perceptiones. Etenim de sensib. per se & sua natura naturaliter, & bene agentib. nos loquimur, sensus metis bene affectae satellites & nuncios veros recte sentientes requirimus, no extrema aliqua intemperie peccantes.
units.tr: Now the variety and changeableness of the senses and of sensible things, or their varied affection, happens to the knowers accidentally, not per se and by their nature. The very passibility to change, and the aptitude to receive various affections by which affected things act and are acted upon in various ways, is naturally present in the organs of sense; but the passion itself, a preternatural affection, a variable change actually occurring, and a departure from the good state of nature, belongs to them not per se but per accidens. The sense, therefore, which perceives a thing otherwise than it is in itself, perceives it thus per accidens. This accidental thing is an impediment that spoils the true and genuine action of sense, or else a morbid affection and vicious intemperature of the organ. We do not set up these diseased senses as singular observers from whose induction the mind, deceived by the senses, forms universals and the perceptions of the arts. For we speak of senses per se and by nature, acting naturally and well; we require the senses of a well-affected mind as true satellites and messengers, correctly perceiving, not those sinning through some extreme intemperature.

units.la: Neque verum est oculorum varios colores varie ipsa visibilia colorare, vt non suo colore videantur. Deinde etia varietas & multitudo diuerse opinatiu & iudicatium hominu vel ex prauitate iudicii, vel ex affectu, vel ex praeconcepta opinione, vel ex sensus deceptione orta, nequaquam tollit & euertit omne rerum certam scientia: sed ita varie de iisdem rebus sententium sententiae, aliae sunt opiniones falsae, aliæ vero scientiæ veræ: Illæ q corrupta ratione, hæ quæ recta ratione sunt discussæ ac æstimatæ. Quapropter ista per accidens sensuum & iudicii adueniens ad eandem res peruersitas non debet radicitus euellere è disciplinis sensuum rectè sentientium, & rationis bene iudicantis perceptam de iisdem rebus veram scientiam.
units.tr: Nor is it true that the varied colours of the eyes colour the visible things variously, so that they are not seen in their own colour. Further, the variety and multitude of differing opinions and judgments of men, arising either from perversity of judgment, or from emotion, or from a preconceived opinion, or from deception of the senses, by no means removes or overturns all certain knowledge of things. Rather, the opinions of those who judge the same things in various ways are such that some are false opinions and others true sciences: the former are discussed and valued by corrupt reason, the latter by right reason. Therefore that perversity which accidentally attaches to the senses and judgment regarding the same things ought not to uproot from the disciplines of rightly perceiving senses and of well-judging reason the true knowledge of those things.

units.la: 2. Ab obiecti cogniti mutabilitate ita ratiocinantur.
units.tr: 2. They reason from the mutability of the object known as follows.

units.la: Rerum semper mutabilium & varias in se ipsis vicissitudines subeuntium, non potest esse scientia, sed tantum apparens opinio.
units.tr: There cannot be knowledge of things that are always changeable and undergo various alterations in themselves, but only apparent opinion.

units.la: Atqui rerum creatarum omnium perpetua est mutabilitas & mira varietas. Eadem enim res secundum substantiam prorsus non mutatur, sed quod alio modo obiiciatur eidem homini, eodem tempore videtur diuersa. Nam res quam plurimæ alio colore videntur integræ, alio commutatæ. Vt argenti fructum candidum videtur, eius vero ramenta nigra. Aqua quæ nunc nigra, nunc decolor esse videtur, in glaciem concreta fit candidissima.
units.tr: But the perpetual mutability and wonderful variety of all created things is a fact. For the same thing is not changed at all according to its substance, but since it is presented to the same man in different ways, at the same time it appears diverse. For very many things look one colour when whole and another when altered. Thus the fruit of silver appears white, but its filings black. Water, which sometimes appears black and sometimes colourless, becomes very white when turned to ice.

units.la: Resp. Negamus propositionem. Rerum enim singularium mutabilitas non infert negationem scientiæ earundem. Rerum enim sempiternarum & constantium, sicut est vniformis, & vniusmodi scientia secundum esse sempiternum: ita & rerum caducarum & variantium scientia est diuersa & multiplex: atque tum non tantum sciuntur rerum mutamutabilium essentiæ, sed & accidentes mutationes, quæ cadunt in res illas. Unde Physica est scientia & ipsarum rerum naturalium, & accidentium, qualitatum & mutationum naturalium. Quare etiam ipsarum mutationum in naturarum essentiis est scientia.
units.tr: Answer: We deny the proposition. For the mutability of singular things does not imply the denial of knowledge of them. Just as there is one uniform and identical knowledge of eternal and constant things according to their eternal being, so the knowledge of perishable and varying things is different and manifold. Then not only the essences of changeable things are known, but also the accidental changes that fall upon those things. Hence Physics is the science both of natural things and of their accidents, qualities and natural changes. Therefore there is also knowledge of the changes themselves within the essences of natures.

units.la: Deinde licet singularia sint mutationib.obnoxia, generales tamen notiones ab ipsis indiuiduis, eorumque mutationib.quas experientia obseruauit, abstractæ sunt perpetuæ & semper veræ. Deniq; eadem res potest varios suscipere colores vel diuerso tempore in eadem sui parte, & hi tũ mutati colores per sensum percepti sciuntur, vel eodem tempore in diuersis partibus, & illi ipsi sciri possunt, alius nempe color in externa superficie esse potest, alius in partibus internis. Illa certe qualitatum diuersitas non negat scientiam, sed variantem eiusdem rei secundũ accidetia scientiam affirmat.
units.tr: Further, although singulars are subject to change, general notions abstracted from the individuals themselves and from the changes in them that experience has observed are perpetual and always true. Finally, the same thing can take on various colours either at different times in the same part of it, and these changed colours perceived by sense are known; or at the same time in different parts, and these too can be known, for one colour may be on the outer surface and another in the inner parts. That diversity of qualities certainly does not deny knowledge, but affirms a knowledge of the same thing as it varies according to its accidents.

units.la: Ex parte medii, per quod sensus apprehendunt obiecta, sic argumentantur: Si sensile medio commisceatur & per illud mutatur, nullum purum sensile sensus percipit, adeoque pura rei cuiusquam notitia haberi non potest.
units.tr: On the part of the medium through which the senses apprehend objects, they argue thus: If the sensible is mixed with the medium and is changed through it, the sense perceives no pure sensible, and so a pure knowledge of any thing cannot be had.

units.la: At verum primum. Nam gustabile nihil est, quod è diuersis constans partibus in ipsa lingua, cum saliua non miscetur, vnde, vt ex aliis omnibus condituris, saporem variare necesse est. Colores quoque cum coloribus miscentur in medio. Colores etiam oculorum cum extrinsecus subeuntibus speciebus varie miscentur.
units.tr: But the first is true. For there is nothing tasteable, made up of various parts, that is not mixed with saliva on the tongue, so that, like all other seasonings, its flavour must vary. Colours too are mixed with colours in the medium. The colours of the eyes also mix variously with the species coming in from outside.

units.la: Respon. Medium sensionis non impedit, sed adiuuat sensionem, non per se deprauat & adulterat, sed perficit sentiendi actionem. Medium itaque vt non est sensionis impedimentum & corruptio, ita neque scientiae per sensum comparandae euersio.
units.tr: Answer: The medium of sensation does not hinder but aids sensation; it does not per se corrupt and adulterate but perfects the act of sensing. Therefore, just as the medium is not an impediment to and corruption of sensation, so it is not an overthrow of the knowledge to be acquired through the senses.

units.la: Medium autem est vel Temperatum seu purum, vel Distemperatum seu impurum. Per pura & temperata media deferuntur sensiles res pure & perfecte, vt sunt, ad sensorium. Atque huiusmodi pura, ac impermista media ad veram sensionem requirunt scientiarum artifices, vt inde scientia mentis actione concipiatur. Per impura vero & distemperata species rerum sensilium inficiuntur & labefactantur, adeo non vt purae in se sunt, sed mediorum contagio sorditatae ad sensum perueniunt, adeoque vera rei per sensus perceptio fieri non potest. Sic gustabile per saliuam temperatam percipitur, vt est eius sapor, per saliuam vero bile distemperatam, vt febricitantis, inficitur, & non suum, sed bilis amarum saporem repraesentat. Sic medium pellucidum purum mittit visibilia obiecta, vt sunt in suis coloribus ad oculos: aer vero & vitrum coloratum ac impurum, suum quoque colorem cum sensilis colore permiscet. Propositio itaque particulariter accepta tantum de impuris & non bene temperatis mediis loquitur, de quibus non est quaestio, quaeque non per se talia sunt, sed per accidens.
units.tr: A medium, however, is either tempered, that is pure, or distempered, that is impure. Through pure and tempered media sensible things are conveyed purely and perfectly, as they are, to the sense organ, and the practitioners of the sciences require such pure and unmixed media for true sensation, so that knowledge may be conceived by the action of the mind. But through impure and distempered media the species of sensible things are infected and weakened, so that they do not reach the sense as they are in themselves, but defiled by the contagion of the media, and so a true perception of a thing through the senses cannot happen. Thus the tasteable is perceived through temperate saliva as it is in its flavour, but through saliva distempered by bile, as in a feverish person, it is infected and represents not its own flavour but the bitter flavour of bile. Likewise a clear, pure medium transmits visible objects to the eyes as they are in their colours, whereas air and coloured, impure glass mix their own colour with the colour of the sensible. The proposition, therefore, taken particularly, speaks only of impure and ill-tempered media, which are not the subject of the question and which are not such per se but per accidens.

units.la: Hactenus ii Philosophi qui omnem scienscientiam ab hominibus tollunt: ii vero, qui peculiariter Physicam scientiam esse negât, naturalesque res omnino non sciri contendunt, sequentibus pugnant rationibus.
units.tr: So far those philosophers who take all knowledge away from men. Those who especially deny that there is a physical science, and contend that natural things cannot be known at all, fight with the following arguments.

units.la: I. 1. Singularia non sunt ἐπίστητά, seu singularium non est scientia. Res naturales sunt omnes singulares. Ergo rerum naturalium nullum est ἐπιστήμα.
units.tr: I. 1. Singulars are not knowable (ἐπίστητά), that is, there is no science of singulars. Natural things are all singular. Therefore there is no science (ἐπιστήμα) of natural things.

units.la: Propositionem probant. Ea quorum est scientia apprehenduntur mente. At singularia sensu tantum, non mente apprehenduntur. Singularium itaque scientia non est.
units.tr: They prove the proposition thus: That of which there is science is grasped by the mind. But singulars are grasped by the senses only, not by the mind. Therefore there is no science of singulars.

units.la: Assumptionem probant. Quicquid est in rerum natura ratione ea, qua est, singulare est. At res naturales sunt & exsistunt in rerum natura. Deinde sunt sensiles. Sensus autem nō nisi sunt singularium.
units.tr: They prove the assumption thus: Whatever exists in the nature of things, by the very mode in which it exists, is singular. But natural things are and exist in the nature of things. Further, they are perceptible to the senses. But the senses deal only with singulars.

units.la: II. 2. Scientia est rerum aeternarum, perpetuarum, & eodem modo se perpetuo habentium. Res naturales autem sunt interitui obnoxiae, neque eodem modo se semper habent. Sunt enim mobiles. Moveri autem est se aliter habere nunc quam antea, constantque materia corporea corruptibili.
units.tr: II. 2. Science is of eternal, perpetual things that always stand in the same way. But natural things are subject to decay and do not always stand in the same way, for they are mobile. To be moved, however, is to stand otherwise now than before, and they consist of corruptible corporeal matter.

units.la: Hinc Vallesius pag. 495. Non solum autem, inquit, non est hactenus comparata scientia physicarum assertionum, sed ne comparari quidem potest. Quia Physicus non abstrahit a materia. Materialium vero notitia cum pertineat ad sensus, non potest ultra opinionem procedere. Scientia enim est vniuersalium & intelligibili-um.
units.tr: Hence Vallesius, p. 495: "Not only has a science of physical assertions not been acquired so far, but it cannot even be acquired. For the natural philosopher does not abstract from matter. Yet since knowledge of material things belongs to the senses, it cannot go beyond opinion. For science is of universals and intelligibles."

units.la: Respon. Per distinctionem. Distinguen-dum est inter notiones primas, & secundas: sic etiam inter res ipsas, quæ scientiæ ac artis præceptis, vt exempla singularia subiiciuntur, & inter ipsas pceptiones artificiosas & notiones vniuersales à singularibus per mentis actione abstractas.
units.tr: Reply: by distinction. One must distinguish between first and second notions, and likewise between the things themselves, which are subjected as singular examples to the precepts of a science or art, and the artificial conceptions themselves and the universal notions abstracted from singulars by an act of the mind.

units.la: Dicimus igitur ad vtriusque argumenti assumptionem. Etsi res Physicæ, qua exi&unt in rerum natura, sunt singulares, caducæ & mutabiles: earum tamen genera, generales notiones diuturna experientia cognitæ sunt vniuersales æternæ & scientificæ. Physicus quoque artifex non considerat res vt singulares, is enim mente abstrahit vniuersalia. Mēs enim nostra vtitur, sensibus, vt satellitibus. Quod à sensibus accipit hoc singulare est, quod vero ipsa effingit ex collectione singulariū istorum ad se transmissorum, vniuersale est: verum itaque non est, quod ait Vallesius, physicum non abstrahere à materia, si præsertim de physico artifice artem efformante sermo illi est.
units.tr: We say, therefore, in answer to the assumption of each argument: Although physical things, which exist in the nature of things, are singular, perishable and changeable, nevertheless their genera, known through long experience as general notions, are universal, eternal and scientific. The natural craftsman too does not consider things as singulars; for he abstracts universals by the mind. For our mind uses the senses as its attendants. What it receives from the senses is singular, but what it itself forms from the collection of these singulars conveyed to it is universal. Therefore it is not true, as Vallesius says, that the natural philosopher does not abstract from matter, especially if his discourse concerns the natural craftsman who shapes his art.

units.la: Quod vero dicitur in assumptione profyllogismi probantis propositionem primi syllogismi de mente, quod non apprehendat & cognoscat singularia, verum non videtur. Nam cum logica sit entium & non entium, sitque tota rationis & intelligentiæ ars, non modo intelintelliget vniuersalia, sed & singularia, quo-modo enim posset Logici ratio in singulari-bus disserendis versari? Secundo sequetur ea-rum rerum, quarum est sensio, non esse intellectio-nem. At sensus rationi, vt nuncii, & satellites sunt subordinati, easdemque species rerum cognoscendas & iudicandas menti offerunt. Tertio etiam postulat subordinatarum facultatum ratio, vt quicquid cognoscit facultas inferior, cognoscat etiam superior, & vbi facultas inferior definit, ibi superior incipiat.
units.tr: But what is said in the assumption of the prosyllogism, proving the proposition of the first syllogism, namely that the mind does not apprehend and know singulars, does not seem true. For since logic is of beings and non-beings, and is the whole art of reason and understanding, it understands not only universals but also singulars; for how could the reasoning of the logician be concerned with discussing singulars? Secondly, it would follow that there is no understanding of those things of which there is sensation. Yet the senses are subordinate to reason, as messengers and attendants, and offer to the mind the kinds of things to be known and judged. Thirdly, the order of subordinate faculties also requires that whatever the inferior faculty knows, the superior faculty knows too, and where the inferior faculty ends, the superior begins.

units.la: Quare suprema mentis facultas ratione comprehendit & cognoscit, quæ inferior, sed non sola, verum alia præterea, hoc est, non tantum singularia, verum etiam vniuersalia. Quarto differentiam inter indiuiduum & vniuersale, hominem & hunc hominem mens intelligit. Necessario itaque vtrumque cognoscit, & singulare & vniuersale. Est enim discriminans facultas non nisi vna, cum discernere vnum ab alio vnus sit actus, vna cognitio, vnum iudicium.
units.tr: Hence the highest faculty of the mind comprehends and knows by reason what the inferior faculty knows, but not only that; it also knows other things, that is, not only singulars but also universals. Fourthly, the mind understands the difference between the individual and the universal, between man and this man. It therefore necessarily knows both, the singular and the universal. For the faculty of discrimination is one only, since to distinguish one thing from another is one act, one cognition, one judgment.

units.la: Ab eadem igitur facultate illa est discriminatio, quæ fieri non potest, nisi vtrumque intelligatur.
units.tr: Therefore the discrimination belongs to the same faculty, and it cannot take place unless both are understood.

units.la: Denique & ex singularibus per inductionem concludere accidens, est mentis actio, & mens suam ipsius actionem cognoscit, quæ singularis est. Singularia igitur a mente etiam apprehenduntur, non per conceptum & speciem vniuersalis. Quia vniuersale est le est indifferens ad omnia singularia. Et quéadmodum generaliter & indistincte seu confuse repræsentat vniuersale omnia : ita distincte multum. Ergo per conceptum vniuersalis non potest distincte & determinate cognosci hoc vel illud singulare. Sed huic præmissæ disfertationi de certitudine, licet difficili, finem faciam, si primum admonuero gradus certitudinis & firmitatis esse in artibus, quomodo supremum gradum habet Theologia, propter immutabilem veritatem ipsius auctoris, & subiectarum rerum constantiam : Proximum gradum habent artes mathematicę, certissimis nitentes demonstrationibus. Physica certitudine his subordinatur, neq; tam certa est propter rerum variam mutabilitatem & propter imperfectionem intellectus nostri. Sed de his hactenus.
units.tr: Finally, to conclude from singulars by induction something accidental is an act of the mind, and the mind knows its own act, which is singular. Singulars, therefore, are also apprehended by the mind, not through the concept and species of the universal, since the universal is indifferent to all singulars. And just as it represents all things generally and indistinctly or confusedly, so it represents them distinctly only in a very limited way. Therefore this or that singular cannot be known distinctly and determinately through the concept of the universal. But I shall bring this disputation on certainty, however difficult, to an end, if I first remind you that there are degrees of certainty and firmness among the arts: as Theology holds the highest degree, on account of the unchangeable truth of its Author and the constancy of its subject matter; the mathematical arts hold the next degree, resting on most certain demonstrations. Physics is subordinate to these in certainty, and is not so certain, on account of the varying mutability of things and the imperfection of our understanding. But so much for these matters.

units.la: Assertiones de Logicæ Maiestate & seruitute: & Philosophiæ vsu etiam insacris.
units.tr: On the Majesty and Servitude of Logic, and the Use of Philosophy even in Sacred Matters.

units.la: INsapientiæ & humanæ & cœlestis studiis Dialecticæ, cum ministerium tum magisterium, iudicium & imperium aliquod agnosco: hoc est, Dialecticam docendi & intelligendi res tam sacras quam profanas, & ministram, & magistram, & iudicem & reginam seu temperatricem quodammodo statuo.
units.tr: I acknowledge that Dialectic has in the studies of both human and heavenly wisdom a ministry as well as a magisterium, a judgement and a kind of rule. That is, I hold that Dialectic, in teaching and understanding sacred and profane things alike, is a servant, a teacher, a judge, and in a way a queen or governess.

units.la: 1. Ministerium seu famulitium Dialecticæ certum est, quia vtitur ea cum Philosophus tum Theologus in docendo. Nam spiritus Dei non seruat aliam rationem &formam res explicandi, ratiocinandi, probandi, refutandi, nisi quam Logica monstrat. Ac intelligenti rationisque compoti creatura intellectum &rationem ideo dedit, vt vox diuina accipi, intelligi & percipi possit.
units.tr: 1. Dialectic's ministry or service is certain, because both the philosopher and the theologian use it in teaching. For the Spirit of God does not follow any other method or form of explaining, reasoning, proving and refuting than the one Logic shows. And God gave the intelligent, rational creature intellect and reason for this very purpose, so that the divine voice could be received, understood and grasped.

units.la: 3. Magisterium & imperium Logicae hinc claret, quod praecipit & imperat Philosopho & Theologo, vt recte definiat, distinguat, concludat, disponat, deerrantem à metis suis tanquam in viam & intra septa reuocat ; repagula sua effringentem reprehendit & castigat dicens. Non licet tibi esse soluto legibus logicis.
units.tr: 3. The magisterium and authority of Logic is clear from this: it instructs and commands the philosopher and the theologian to define, distinguish, conclude and arrange correctly. It recalls the one who strays from his bounds, as if back onto the road and within the fold, and it rebukes and chastises the one who breaks down its barriers, saying: It is not permitted for you to be released from the laws of logic.

units.la: 4. Iudicium eius hinc patet, quia iudicat de omnibus tractationibus, definitionibus, Syllogismis Theologicis, an sint legitimi, &c.
units.tr: 4. Its judgement is evident from this, because it judges all treatments, definitions and theological syllogisms, whether they are legitimate, etc.

units.la: 5. Iudicio etiam Logico & Philosophico Contradictionis vt ipsam Dialecticam totam & Philosophiam omnem, sic quoque Theologiam subiicio.
