Hanc enim legem non in aes, sed in animos nostros quasi incisam, Quodlibet est aut non est, & impossibile est, duas contradictorias simul veras aut simul falsas esse, sanxit Deus qui est absolute verax, & quae sunt affirmat esse, nec miscet ea, quae sunt, & ea quae non sunt. Ac est regula diuini & humani iudicii aeterna & immota, & pugnare cum hac diuina lege & pariter amplecti contradictoria, est ordine mentis diuinae turbare, delere omnes certas notitias, & totam rerum vniuersitatem confundere euertere: vt si quis pariter affirmaret, Deum esse, & Deum non esse, ignem calidum esse & ignem non calidum esse, furiosius arma cœlo inferret (θεομαχίαν hoc est Græcis) quam Titanes, de quibus poemata loquuntur: vt grauissime iuxta ac sapientissime & valde pie scripsit Melanchthon.
units.tr: 5. I subject to the logical and philosophical judgement of contradiction not only Dialectic as a whole and all philosophy, but theology too. For God, who is absolutely truthful, has enacted this law, graven not in bronze but in our minds: Everything either is or is not, and it is impossible for two contradictories to be both true or both false at once. He affirms that things which are, are, and does not mix together what is and what is not. This is the eternal and unchanging rule of divine and human judgement. To fight against this divine law, and to embrace contradictories alike, is to disturb the order of the divine mind, to destroy all certain knowledge, and to confound and overturn the whole universe of things. So if someone affirmed alike God is, and God is not; fire is hot, and fire is not hot, he would bear arms against heaven more madly (in Greek this is theomachy) than the Titans of whom the poets sing, as Melanchthon wrote most weightily, most wisely and most piously.

units.la: 6. Dialectica Theologiæ ita magistra est & imperatrix, vt in mysteriis diuinis fasces submittat, & discipulam se esse testetur atque ad pedes summi & verissimi Magistri sese abiciat qui patris sapientia est, illiusque sermonem & decreta absque omni etiam illorum perspecta ratione reuerenter, religiose, sanctèque amplectatur.
units.tr: 6. Dialectic is so much the teacher and mistress of theology that in the divine mysteries it lowers its rods, declares itself a disciple, and casts itself at the feet of the highest and truest Teacher, who is the wisdom of the Father. It reverently, religiously and holily embraces his word and decrees, even without any thorough rational grasp of them.

units.la: 7. Ita igitur est præceptrix, ne sit deceptrix, ita dux & doctrix, ne sit seductrix.
units.tr: 7. So then it is a teacher so as not to be a deceiver; a guide and instructor so as not to be a seducer.

units.la: 8. Idem de tota Philosophia iudica. Docent nostrates relationum fundamentum esse accidens. Id in imperscrutabili adorandæ Trinitatis mysterio non est dicendum de paternitate: quia diuinæ relationis illius fundamentum est substantia.
units.tr: 8. Judge the same of all philosophy. Our people teach that the foundation of a relation is an accident. This must not be said of paternity in the unsearchable mystery of the adorable Trinity, because the foundation of that divine relation is substance.

units.la: 9. Res ipsæ Theologicæ petendæ sunt ex fontibus sacris, non Philosophicis ac profanis: (quo sensu accipiendum est quod dixit Ambrosius, Facessant Dialectici, vbi credendum est piscatoribus Apostolis.)
units.tr: 9. Theological matters themselves must be sought from sacred sources, not from philosophical and profane ones. (This is the sense in which what Ambrose said should be understood: Let the dialecticians depart, where we must believe the fishermen, the Apostles.)

units.la: 10. Etsi modus & norma tractationis earum petatur ex Logica.
units.tr: 10. Even though the mode and norm of treating them is sought from Logic.

units.la: 11. Non tamen negandum est, quin Philosophia & iudicium recte rationis voci Propheticæ & Apostolicæ interdum suo testimonio suf-fragetur.
units.tr: 11. Yet it must not be denied that philosophy and the judgement of sound reason sometimes lend their testimony in support of the prophetic and apostolic voice.

units.la: 12. Itaque Theologo non sunt infirmanda principia rationis & naturæ, nisi eo adigatur certis scripturæ sanctæ testimoniis.
units.tr: 12. Therefore the principles of reason and nature are not to be weakened by the theologian, unless he is compelled to it by certain testimonies of holy Scripture.

units.la: 13. Et si quid in scriptura Deus tradit, quod etiam naturali luce hominibus notum fecit, id non propterea sic dicendum est Logicum aut Philosophicum, quin simul sit Theologicum.
units.tr: 13. And if God hands down in Scripture anything which he has also made known to humans by the natural light, it must not for that reason be called merely logical or philosophical rather than theological.

units.la: 14. Tale est hoc, Marci 16. Iesum Nazarenum quæritis, qui crucifixus est, surrexit, non est hic, ecce locus vbi positus erat. Et Luc. 24. istud: Videte manus meas & pedes meos, nam ego sum, contrectate & videte, nam Spiritus carnem & ossa non habet, prout cospicitis me habere. Hic vtitur Christus argumentis Physicis, quæ Theologicæ veritati ὁλως ξύμφωνα sunt.
units.tr: 14. Such is this, Mark 16: You seek Jesus of Nazareth, who was crucified; he is risen, he is not here; behold the place where they laid him. And Luke 24: See my hands and my feet, for it is I; handle me and see, for a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see me have. Here Christ uses physical arguments, which are wholly consistent [ὅλως ξύμφωνα] with theological truth.

units.la: 15. Transsubstantiatio in Domini mensa refutatur etiam Philosophicis rationibus, quæ non sunt contra Theologiam, quæ vrget, à Paulo Apostolo panem, non speciem panis nominari, a Seruatore nostro vinum, non speciem vini. Inter illas autem hæc vna est. Sicut subiectum non potest exui omnibus accidentibus, sic accidentia non possunt actu subsistere sine subiecto: Remanent autem panis & vini accidentia in sensus incurrentia, vt sapor, odor, & visibilis quantitas: Necesse igitur est vt maneat etiam substantia panis & vini.
units.tr: 15. Transubstantiation at the Lord's table is also refuted by philosophical arguments, which are not against theology. Theology insists that Paul the Apostle calls it bread, not the appearance of bread, and our Saviour calls it wine, not the appearance of wine. Among those arguments this is one: just as a subject cannot be stripped of all its accidents, so accidents cannot actually subsist without a subject. But the accidents of bread and wine remain, falling under the senses, such as taste, smell and visible quantity. It is necessary, therefore, that the substance of bread and wine remain too.

units.la: Idem apparet hinc, quod vinum asservatum diutius accessit & panis computrescit, ac in vermivermiculos conuertitur : Quæ nec solis acci- dentibus, nec corpori & sanguini domini in- corruptibili adscribi possunt. Hoc non est φανλως φιλοσοφιν.
units.tr: This is also evident from this: wine kept too long turns sour, and bread rots and turns into worms. These cannot be ascribed either to the accidents alone or to the incorruptible body and blood of the Lord. This is not idle philosophising [φαύλως φιλοσοφεῖν].

units.la: 16. Iustitiam & peccatum originis esse de hominis essentia quidam scripserunt.
units.tr: 16. Some have written that righteousness and original sin belong to the essence of man.

units.la: Hi ex nostris literis sic refutantur. Quod de essentia rei est, aut est materia, aut ratio formalis rei, constituens rem. Sed iustitia, & peccatum originis neutrum sunt in homine, neque materia, neque forma hominis sunt. Ergo non sunt de hominis vt loquuntur essentia.
units.tr: These are refuted from our writings thus: What belongs to the essence of a thing is either its matter or its formal reason, constituting the thing. But righteousness and original sin are neither in man, nor are they the matter or form of man. Therefore they are not of the essence of man, as they put it.

units.la: 17. Quid ? quod diuus Paulus Rom. 1. 2. Actorum 14. & 17. aduersus gentiles ac Philosophos disputans erroris ac impietatis eos conuincit, rationibus ex Philosophia petitis.
units.tr: 17. What? Does not the divine Paul, in Romans 1, 2, Acts 14 and 17, when disputing against the Gentiles and philosophers, convict them of error and impiety by arguments drawn from philosophy?

units.la: 18. Licet igitur etiam argumentis rationis vti in Theologia, sed consentientibus cū præeunte voce diuina, & talibus, quibus suffragatur vocis diuinæ testimonium.
units.tr: 18. It is therefore permitted to use arguments of reason in theology too, but ones that agree with the preceding divine voice, and such as the testimony of the divine voice supports.

units.la: 19. Nihilominus verum manet, quod scriptura sit mensura nostræ fidei, ideoque μέτρον etiam nostræ vel affirmationis vel negationis.
units.tr: 19. Nevertheless it remains true that Scripture is the measure of our faith, and therefore the rule [μέτρον] of our affirmation or negation as well.

units.la: 20. I nunc & deinceps labora vt persuadeas hominibus non esse, quæ sentiuntur, hoc est, vt hominibus oculos effodias.
units.tr: 20. Go now, and from now on labour to persuade men that the things they perceive are not so; that is, gouge out men's eyes.

units.la: I nunc & Dialecticæ atque Philosophiæ dicam scribe, dum caussam falsorum in Ecclesia dogmatum in eam reiicis, cum tamen nihil sit expeditius quam Theologum Philosophum & Logicum contra omnium hæreticorum errores disputare, quippe qui videat non modo quid contra falsum dici possit, vt candidissime dicit Schegkius, nobilis ille φιλόσοφος & doctrinæ sacræ minime omnium rudis.
units.tr: Go now, and say that I write against Dialectic and Philosophy, since you lay the cause of false doctrines in the Church upon them, when nothing is more easily done than for a theologian who is also a philosopher [φιλόσοφος] and logician to dispute against the errors of all heretics. For such a man sees not only what can be said against the false, as the most candid Schegk says, that noble philosopher and by no means the least untrained in sacred doctrine.

units.la: I nunc & sine discrimine clama perpetuo de excludenda Ratione Humana à Tractatione rerum Sacrarum, qua quidem vociferatione id videris postulare (quod λίαν μέγα αἴτημα est) vt homines sint animalia bruta, quibus ipse tanquam vulpes anseribus impune quiduis concionari possis.
units.tr: Go now, and cry out without distinction, forever, about excluding Human Reason from the treatment of sacred things. By that outcry you clearly demand (which is a very great petition [λίαν μέγα αἴτημα]) that men be brute animals, to whom you yourself, like a fox among geese, could preach whatever you liked with impunity.

units.la: FINIS.
units.tr: THE END.
